en: Śrīḥ.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.
"From whom indeed [these beings arise]," [He who is] possessed of all powers, the adversary of everything that is to be abandoned,
and the "Omniscient One."

It has been stated that Brahman—characterized by an uninterrupted continuity of auspicious qualities—is the object of inquiry, as established by the scriptural passages concerning the cause of the world, such as those beginning with [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1]. Now, the unsuitability of the scriptural passages concerning the cause of the world to propound an inferential *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth is being explained through the sūtra beginning with "Because of seeing, [the cause] is not the one not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*).
This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is that which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) the cause of the world, namely the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) inferred from reasoning as propounded by others; or is it Brahman, characterized as previously described?

Regarding the phrase "from which indeed these [beings arise]," the inclusion of the definition-statement is for the purpose of indicating that, by restating His causality, His definition is being established; furthermore, because the determination of the cause's distinction from both consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*) depends upon an investigation of the scriptural passages that establish that causality, this section investigates those causal passages. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the passages establishing causality are included.

For this very reason, it was stated that [the subject] "speaks of the cause of the world" by way of being common to both restatement (*anuvāda*) and prior statement (*purovāda*). "To be investigated" (*jijñāsya*) means to be examined as being authoritative. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Pradhāna and so forth," the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) alone, specific instances of consciousness (*cid-viśeṣa*), and specific instances of the non-conscious (*acid-viśeṣa*) are included. The phrase "by such [passages]" means either by the remainder of the quarter (*pāda*) or by the remainder of the chapter (*adhyāya*). The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the causal statement containing general terms which expresses [Brahman's] volition (*saṅkalpa*) and is endowed with both a proposition (*pratijñā*) and an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

In this context, the statement concerning the knowledge of Being (sadvidyā) alone is the direct subject matter of this section. Other statements regarding such a cause are made the subject matter only by way of the knowledge of Being, and not directly, because at the time of selecting the specific scriptural passage for the subject, those other passages were not selected.

The word "this" (*idam*) cites the object of inquiry. Regarding that, it says "there is doubt. For it is when there is doubt that the application of reasoning (*nyāya*) occurs. Here, the doubt arises from two possibilities: whether the effect, denoted by the word "this," necessarily possesses a similarity of characteristics with its cause, or whether it is denoted by the word "that" (*sa*). This is because the term expressing the subject (*dharmin*) is common to both [possibilities]. [The opponent might argue: "It is omniscient and of true resolve," or "It is exactly as previously defined"—[thus ends the fragment].
What is established? That it is the Pradhāna.
Why?

Because the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," speaks of the causal state of that entity denoted by the word "this"—which consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is the object of experience for sentient beings, and exists in various forms as modifications such as ether and so forth. For indeed, being an effect is simply the attainment of a different state by a substance that serves as the cause. Therefore, whatever substance possesses a certain nature in its state as an effect, that very same substance possesses that same nature in its state as a cause.

And regarding the statement, "The effect consists of truth and so forth," [the opponent argues that] the *pradhāna* alone—existing in a state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*—is indeed the cause; for that very same [cause], when all its specificities have been withdrawn, is the mere Being (*sanmātra*), as in the passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"—this "Being" is the *pradhāna*.
Thus, between the two horns encompassed by the doubt, the meaning is that the horn "the *pradhāna*" is the one supported by reasoning. (Śrutaprakāśikā)

The qualifiers beginning with "of that which is denoted by the word *idam*" (this) are intended to establish the primacy (*pradhānatva*) of the cause; they do not contradict its being a distinct Puruṣa (Spirit) characterized differently from that [cause]. For the natural application of the word *idam* is toward external objects (*parāgartha*), and not toward a conscious principle whose nature is immediate awareness (*pratyag-rūpa*). This is the sense. The phrase "of that which has become the object of enjoyment for a conscious being" is used to exclude the possibility that the world—being composed of both consciousness and unconsciousness—is included within the denotation of the word *idam* even in its conscious aspect.

Because the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) cannot possess the status of being either an effect or a cause, it is not included within the category of effects; rather, its state is simply that of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). The sense is that only the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) possesses the nature of being an effect. Regarding the phrase "and *sat*": since we observe that the world is connected with pleasure, pain, and delusion—which are the effects of *sattva* and the other qualities—how can the cause be devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)? Therefore, it must consist of *sattva* and the rest. Regarding the phrase "the ether and so forth": the intention is to ask whether the cause exists in a state of unity, or if it is a cause composed of the qualities (*guṇamaya*).

The meaning is that "diversity" refers to the effect existing in a state of multiplicity. The sense is that it is logically untenable for a single-natured *puruṣa* to possess effects of manifold forms. Regarding the phrase "the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*": since everything in a state of disequilibrium is observed to be an effect, if the *pradhāna* were likewise [in a state of disequilibrium], there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress due to its dependence on further causes; therefore, the sense is that the *pradhāna* is established as being in a state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*.

"Only one" (*ekameva*) excludes the distinction between name and form (*nāma-rūpa*); "without a second" (*advitīyam*) excludes any inequality of qualities; and with the intention of [showing] "only Being" (*sadeva*), it is said that all particularities have been withdrawn. It is designated as "pure Being" (*sanmātra*). And for this very reason, there is the non-difference (*ananyatva*) of cause and effect.

That which is "without sound" (aśabda) is not inferential; that is to say, it is not the Pradhāna. It is not what is propounded by the statements of those who maintain that the Pradhāna is the cause of the world, such as [the passages]: "He created these worlds," and "He reflected."
Thus [it is said].

This very point will be established in the section beginning with "Not so, because of the difference in character" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*). Here, it is stated that "the sṛṣṭi-passages are not capable of establishing the Pradhāna"; however, the contradiction regarding the nature of things (*vastuvirodha*) will be refuted in that very same place.

As for what was said—that this statement, because it possesses a proposition (*pratijñā*) and an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is indeed of the nature of inference—that is incorrect; for there is no employment of a reason (*hetu*). [It is as stated in the Upaniṣad: "By which the unheard becomes heard..."

Thus, when it is intended to demonstrate that through the knowledge of one [thing] there is the knowledge of all, the citation of an illustrative example is indeed for the purpose of showing the possibility of that [knowledge], for one who considers it impossible in its entirety. For, precisely from the hearing of the scriptural texts such as "He saw" (*īkṣati*), the absence of even a scent of inference is understood. || 5 ||

It has been stated that [the world] cannot be the effect [of Brahman] in the absence of a similarity [in form], because causality would be impossible. Regarding the passage beginning with "here" (*atretyādi*), this refers to the sūtras beginning with *na vilakṣaṇatvāt*. This is the resolution of the suspicion of redundancy regarding these sūtras. The contradiction of the object (*vastuvirodha*) means a contradiction with the capacity of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*). Here, the determination of the meaning is achieved through reasoning applied to the statement (*vākya-tarka*); whereas there [in the earlier section], the determination of the meaning is achieved by way of investigating and refuting external reasoning based on fallacious arguments arising from mere conceit (*ābhimānika-vyāyabhāsa*). Thus, they are distinct in meaning.

Thus, the causality of that which consists of qualities such as *sattva* and is denoted by the word "this" (*idam*), as well as the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one, are both resolved.

"Because of the non-apprehension of the reason (*hetu*). If the speaker intends to employ inference, then the reason—the primary constituent [of an inference]—must necessarily be stated. The point is that in its absence, there is no such intention to infer. As for the statement, "By which the unheard... the example is not apprehended": it is also improper to imply the reason through the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), for that which implies must be established by no other means (*ananyathāsiddha*). Since the proposition is established otherwise (by other means), it is not [the means of implication]. It is common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having established the proof, it is stated that the example cannot logically imply the reason (*hetu*). The presentation of an example is not solely for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*); rather, since it also serves to demonstrate the exclusion of impossibility, it is not an impeller [of the reason] because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*). This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "absence of even a trace of inference": the status of being an inference was suspected based on the commonality between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example; however, the intention is that this suspicion is also dispelled by the existence of uncommon reasons such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*). || 5 ||
Now, it might be argued: "The primary act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) mentioned here does not belong to the conscious [Self], but rather a secondary (figurative) seeing belonging to the Pradhāna;
for [the text says] 'that fire saw' and 'those waters saw'."

Thus, [the term is used] through association with the primary sense of "seeing. Furthermore, there occurs a metaphorical attribution of the attributes of a conscious being even to insentient things; for example:
"The rice plants wait for the rain," and "By the rain, the seed rejoiced."
Having restated this objection—that "therefore, the act of seeing is figurative"—he refutes it: "If it be argued that it is figurative, we say no, because of the word 'Self' (ātman). (1.1.6)

The word "atha" (now) introduces the subsequent sūtra; it raises the doubt that the term "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) may be used in a figurative sense. "Pertaining to a conscious being" means consistent with consciousness. By the word "here," the intention is that the context must be considered. "Pertaining to the Pradhāna" means consistent with insentience. The word "placing" (*dhāna*) [is used] because it is impossible for the first act of seeing to result in non-conscious material elements such as fire and so forth. Two sentences have been cited to show the general tendency [of the usage]. The intention is that the principle of "the majority" (*agryaprāya*) remains operative in the absence of a subverting factor.

The word "deity" (*devatā*) in the phrase "this is the deity" (*seyam devatā*) also, by this same logic—as in the case of "these three deities"—does not contradict its figurative sense, because it is appropriate for it to refer to non-sentient objects; this is the intended meaning.

Thus, the statement occurs in a context where primary ritual acts (*pradhānakarma*) predominate, and it serves to suggest that [the act] is a primary ritual act. Just as, upon seeing something written in a section primarily concerning the first-born (*agrya*), one concludes, "This must be the first-born."

As for what was said— that because of its association with figurative seeing, the designation "seeing" is applied even to the Existent (Sat) in a figurative sense, intended to refer to the state prior to creation— [we reply]: indeed,

it is precisely through the entry of the Supreme Self, as expressed in the passage, "Let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate names and forms," that fire and the other elements possess substantiality and receive their respective names.

Furthermore, in the passages "That heat [tejas] thought" and "Those waters thought," the designation of "thinking" (īkṣaṇa) is indeed primary; therefore, by virtue of this association as well, [the term must be understood in its primary sense].
The intention of the Sūtra is that, in the passage "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), any suspicion of a figurative sense has been cast far away. || 6 ||
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna is not what is denoted by the word "Sat.
Now, [the author] states that it does not even exist: thus, having provisionally accepted the association with figurative seeing (*gauṇekṣaṇa*), the refutation was stated.
Regarding the phrase "of fire, water, and food" and so forth,
the word "also" (api) is used. Therefore, with respect to the primordial [matter] consisting of consciousness and the unconscious, He is the Self-possessor (ātmanvān),
because the initial act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) has Him as its locus.

The intended meaning is that "there is indeed nothing whatsoever that does not have that as its essence. The purpose of the particle *eva* (indeed) is to indicate that for the word [‘Being’], that alone is the primary [meaning]. The purpose of the particle *api* (also) in the phrase "light and so forth" is to convey the sense that they are like the word ‘Being’. Regarding the phrase "of the Supreme Self alone": the Supreme Self alone is to be presented as the primary object of predication by virtue of being the substantive; the sense is that light and so forth are merely the means [to that presentation]. "The state of being a reality" (*vastutvam*) means the state of being a reality in the form of that [Supreme Self]. The "state of being a reality" of light is simply "light-ness" (*tejastvam*).

The "substantiality of water" (*apāṃ vastutvam*) means its being water; the "substantiality of earth" (*pṛthivyāḥ vastutvam*) means its being earth; and the "substantiality of gods, humans, and so forth" (*devamanuṣyādīnāṃ vastutvam*) means their possessing the respective states of divinity, humanity, and so on. "Partaking of a name" (*nāmabhāktvam*) means being denotable by a name. The word *iti* indicates a reason. The word *api* (also) is intended to include other grounds for the suspicion of figurative usage, such as association (*sāhacaryāt*). Regarding the phrase "completely set aside": the intention is that even though there is an association with a figurative act of seeing, the first act of seeing is non-figurative because of the word *ātman*; furthermore, the association with a figurative act of seeing is itself unestablished solely on account of the word *ātman*.

In this section, that which is to be established is clearly stated in two sūtras: first, that the thesis (pratijñā) and the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) do not imply the reason (hetu); and second, that among those things which favor both the primary and secondary meanings, it is the one favoring the primary meaning that must be followed. ||6||

The phrase "from this" (*itaśca*) dispels the suspicion that [the passage] has as its object a subordinate thesis. By defining the attribute of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), which is conducive to causality, the status of the Existent (*sat*) as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established. Now, through the statement "But the Cause is to be meditated upon," the status of the Supreme Self is proven by means of the attribute of being the bestower of liberation, which is unique to the causal reality; such is the connection. [This is so] because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to That. (Sūtra 1.1.7)
Having instructed Śvetaketu, who desires liberation, in the contemplation of his identity with the Existent through the words "That thou art," [the teacher speaks] to him who is established therein.

The passage, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [Brahman]," teaches that liberation, characterized by the attainment of Brahman, has only the falling away of the body as its intervening obstacle. Furthermore, if the non-intelligent *pradhāna* were taught as the cause, then the teaching that meditation on its essential nature is the means to liberation would be untenable. The phrase "of one who is devoted to That" (*tanniṣṭhasya*) in the Sūtra is an explanation of the word "his" (*tasya*) in the Śruti text "for him" (*tasya tāvat*).

By the word "desirous of liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ*), the doubt that this is an injunction to view the conscious [Self] as the *pradhāna*—which is superior because it is the material cause of the entire universe—is refuted, since such an injunction would otherwise be possible for the sake of perceiving inferior fruits. Regarding the phrase "consisting of Being" (*sadātmakatva*): the intention is that the word "that" (*tat*) in the Sūtra is intended to indicate that the word "that" in the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) refers to the "Being" under discussion, and thus is devoted to teaching that [the Self] consists of Being. By the word "contemplation" (*anusandhāna*), the meaning of the word "devotion" (*niṣṭhā*) is expressed.

By the word "obstacle" (antarāya), delay is indicated; the meaning is that the delay lasts until the fall of the body. Regarding the phrase "characterized by the attainment of Brahman": the sense is that Brahman itself—established by other scriptural passages such as "Then I shall attain [Brahman]" (*atha sampatsye*) and "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (*satā somya tadā sampanno bhavati*)—is the object of the action. Regarding "liberation" (mokṣa): the intention is that the term "liberation" used in the Sūtra refers specifically to the attainment of Brahman preceded by the fall of the body, and not merely the fall of the body itself.

"According to one's resolve," and so forth. Just as in the case of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) or holy fields (*kṣetra*), the utility of the meditation on the non-intelligent (*acid-upāsanā*) for liberation, as well as the attainment of a fruit corresponding to that meditation, is established by the authority of the scriptures; this is the meaning of the Śruti text "according to one's resolve.
To the doubt, "Why should this not be so? [the author] says this:
"And therefore, from such meditation, the abandonment of what is to be discarded (*heyaprahāṇa*) is untenable."

Thus, for one intent upon that [Prakṛti], there would only be identification with the insentient. Furthermore, no scripture is more affectionate than even a thousand parents; it would not teach such an identification with the insentient, which is the cause of being struck by the three kinds of suffering.
For even those who maintain the doctrine of Primordial Matter (Pradhāna) as the cause do not accept liberation for one who is intent upon Pradhāna. || 7 ||
For this reason also, the Pradhāna is not [the cause]; and because there is no statement that it is to be abandoned. (1.1.8)
If the Pradhāna alone were the cause denoted by the word "Sat," then for Śvetaketu, who desires liberation—

The attainment of the non-conscious (*acetana-sampatti*) means the acquisition of the non-conscious (*acit-prāpti*), which is the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). For transmigratory existence is indeed the connection with the non-conscious brought about by karma. That the word *sampatti* has the sense of "acquisition" is made clear by the immediately following commentary: "the attainment of the non-conscious, which is the cause of the affliction by the threefold suffering. Regarding the phrase "mother and father": the meaning is that while a mother and father are intent merely upon nourishing one in a single birth, the scripture, however, is intent upon providing every kind of protection throughout many births, both in this world and the next.

The Puranic statement, "Indeed, the scripture is more affectionate than a thousand mothers and fathers," has been recalled. Nor does it [the scripture] merely "teach"; the sense is that there would be no culmination in the purpose of the scripture. Thus, its utility for liberation is refuted by both its contradiction of the logic established by the Śruti and the absence of a culminating purpose.

The intention of the Sāṅkhya, even when saying "through the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower," is merely to advocate for the thorough understanding of Pradhāna, as one would understand a disease, and not its worship. For this reason as well, [the passage] is not so; the statement "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is not an instruction for the contemplation of being the Self of Reality (sad-ātmakatva). Rather, they do not accept that "I am gross.
If it were that very nature [of the Self], it would have to be taught only as something to be abandoned, because it is opposed to liberation.
And that is not done; on the contrary, [it is understood] precisely as something to be accepted, as in "That thou art."
"It is taught that for him there is delay only so long. (8)
And for this reason also, the Pradhāna is not [the cause]:
because it would contradict the initial proposition (pratijñā). 1.1.9.

If the Pradhāna were the cause, there would also be a contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñā*). For at the beginning of the discourse, the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one was proposed; and that [knowledge] occurs because of the non-difference between cause and effect, [specifically] from the knowledge of the *Sat* which is the cause.

This [preceding section] is thus a restatement of the delusion regarding the body as the Self. Therefore, the intention is that the connection with the subsequent Sūtra arises from the doubt: "Is the conscious Being denoted by the word *Sat* to be known by the seeker of liberation for the sake of its abandonment?"

The word "pratyuta" (on the contrary) means that the contemplation of the Self as Being (*sad-ātmaka*)—just like the contemplation of "I am fat" and so forth—is not taught to be something to be abandoned; rather, its very worthiness of being accepted (*upādeyatva*) is stated. And this [worthiness of acceptance] would be untenable if the primary intent were the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), because in the contexts concerning the *pradhāna*, it is presented as something to be abandoned in the statement, "it casts this off. This is the meaning. The intention is that there is not merely an absence of favorability toward it, but rather actual hostility, because it contradicts the initial proposition (*pratijñā*). Since there is a contradiction with the opening statement, the reasons found in the subsequent sentences are weak.
He dispels the doubt that the Pradhāna alone is what is to be established [by the scripture] with the word "But" (paraṃ). || 8 ||

Regarding the word "pradhāna" (the primary cause): the sense is that the intention of the author of the Sūtras is that whatever was stated in accordance with your own view is, in fact, contrary to your own view. Regarding the phrase "it has been promised": although the word "all" (*sarva*) does not appear in the initial statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), it is nonetheless implied by such passages as, "O Venerable One, when what is known, does all this become known? and, "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known."

The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, which is the effect of that [Brahman], must be established as being known precisely through its cause. However, if Pradhāna were the cause, this would be contradicted because the class of conscious beings could not be the primary effect of Pradhāna; thus, the knowledge of the class of conscious beings cannot be established through the knowledge of Pradhāna. || 9 ||
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna is not [the cause]:
because of the merging [of the soul] into itself (svāpyaya). 1.1.10.
Referring to that very thing denoted by the word "Sat" (Being), [the text] says:

"Understand from me, my dear, the state of deep sleep (*svapnānta*)," because this is consistent with the meaning of the passage in the same context which begins, "When a person here is said to be sleeping. [This refers to] "all creatures."

And because of the natural force (*svārasya*) of what is about to be stated, it is said, "By knowing [That], everything is known. The phrase "knowledge of everything" does not mean merely the knowledge of all insentient effects—as in the expression "all that is made of clay"—because sentient beings (*cetana*), who are understood through the natural force of the word *prajā* (progeny) being in grammatical apposition with the word *sarva* (all) in the passage, "O Somya, all these creatures have Being as their root," are also included among the various effects to be known by virtue of having Being as their root. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "of cause and effect": the sense is that this does not apply to the conscious and the unconscious (*cid-acit*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatkārya" (its effect), etc.: the point is that because of the analogies of the lump of clay and its effects, and because of the natural force of the word "prajāḥ" (progeny) in the statement "sanmūlāḥ" (having Being as their root), the consciousness of even a sentient being must be understood as being solely of the nature of an effect. Just as one knows a village through the knowledge of Devadatta, the "knowing of all" here is not figurative.

The sense is this: if the knowledge of all were merely figurative, then the question "How so, O Blessed One? would be inappropriate, as it would already be evident to the world; furthermore, it is observed that the knowledge of all is established in its primary sense precisely through examples such as clay and its effects, which are not different from it. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "from this": the proposition that the knowledge of one thing entails the knowledge of all things is based on the relationship of cause and effect; likewise, the dissolution of the conscious being into the Supreme Self during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is based on that same relationship. Therefore, the intention is that [the author] states the dissolution in deep sleep as the reason, because of the commonality of being based on the relationship of cause and effect.

"‘That very same’ means that here too the word ‘Being’ (sat) has as its object the reality that is the cause of the world; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, the suspicion of a different meaning based on the word ‘Being’ having the same referent as the word ‘Self’ (sva-śabda), which designates the individual soul (jīva), is dispelled. ‘Wherein’ refers to the cause of dissolution, as indicated by the scriptural statement regarding dissolution into the Cause."
But the Pradhāna is not denoted by the word "Sat" (Being), for it is Brahman alone that is so described.
"O dear one, then he becomes united with Being (*sat*). He has gone to his own self (*svam apīto bhavati*).

Therefore they say of him, 'he sleeps' (*svapiti*), for he has gone to his own self. Thus, it designates the soul in deep sleep as "united with Being," explaining that it has "gone to its own self"—that is, it has dissolved (*pralīna*) into itself. And dissolution means merging into one's own cause. Furthermore, the non-conscious *pradhāna* cannot be the cause of the conscious soul. [The phrase "he has gone to his own self" means that the soul has merged into the Self alone.]

It is stated in the scripture concerning the evolution of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*) that Brahman itself—whose body is the reality of consciousness (*cidvastuśarīraka*) and which has become its very self—is designated by the term "jīva. That Brahman, denoted by the word "jīva," even during the time of deep sleep—as in the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*)—is denoted solely by the word "Being" (*sat*), because of the absence of contact with name and form; thus it is said: "My dear, then he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own Self. Likewise, in the same context, due to the absence of contact with name and form, there is union with the Intelligent One (*prājña*) alone.

It is stated: "Embraced by the intelligent Self (prājña), he knows nothing external, nor anything internal. Indeed, until liberation, the arising of knowledge regarding objects distinct from itself occurs precisely because of the individual soul’s (jīva) embrace by name-and-form (nāma-rūpa). For at the time of deep sleep, having abandoned name-and-form, it is embraced by Being (sat); then again, in the waking state, having embraced name-and-form, it becomes possessed of those respective names and forms. This is clearly declared in another Śruti passage:
"When, sleeping, he sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very Prāṇa alone. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21)
"From this Self, the vital breaths depart according to their respective locations.
Likewise, "whether they become a tiger here, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a gadfly, or a mosquito, whatever they are, they become that."

Thus it is said; likewise, regarding the soul in deep sleep, the scripture states: "He is embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman). Therefore, that which is denoted by the word *sat* is the Supreme Brahman—the omniscient Supreme Lord, the Puruṣottama himself. Thus says the author of the Vṛtti:

"O gentle one, at that time he becomes united with Being (sat); by means of this union and non-union, this is determined. And it says: 'He is completely embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman)'.
— Thus [ends the section]. ||10||

Likewise, regarding the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptam*): because its object is the supreme cause, which possesses attributes such as seeing and does not depend on the body and senses that are to be created, and because it is in harmony with other concordant scriptural passages, the intention here is that the word "Being" (*sat*) does not refer merely to the individual soul (*jīva*) in its subtle state of extremely contracted knowledge. The term "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) is used for the purpose of excluding the individual soul; for the scriptural text "by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā*) is concordant with the statement "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*).

The term *parameśvara* (Supreme Lord) is used both to indicate His role as the controller of individual souls (*jīva*) even during their dissolution [into Him], and to exclude any other principle superior to the Lord. The term *puruṣottama* (Supreme Person) refers to His distinction from the person in deep sleep, as well as to His status as a specific deity. Regarding the phrase "by means of union and non-union": this means by the two processes of union and departure mentioned in the passages, "Having become united with the Existent, they do not know, 'We are being united with the Existent,'" and "Having come from the Existent, they do not know, 'We are coming from the Existent.'"

Its "attainment" (*sampatti*) means abiding in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) devoid of the outward-flowing expansion of knowledge; "emergence" (*nirgama*) means the outward-flowing expansion of knowledge. The intention of the commentator is that by the word "dissolution" (*svāpyaya*), non-attainment is also intended. The word "own" (*sva*) refers to the Supreme Self as qualified by the individual soul.

Therefore, according to the scriptural text, "He becomes merged in his own Self" (*svam apīto bhavati*), the meaning is this: the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) in its waking state—characterized by an outward-turned expansion of cognition corresponding to attachment, greed, and so forth, as well as the conceit of names and forms such as "human" and so on—now, being embodied by the *jīva* that is free from the turbidity of conceit regarding external and internal forms caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of gods, humans, and the like, including passion, hatred, greed, and delusion, has become absorbed within Himself.

Therefore, it is logically established that deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) is the abiding within one’s own self, which is the causal state consisting of the specific condition of the individual soul (*jīva*) devoid of identification with the forms produced by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-ākāra*). Furthermore, this state is a temporary attribute. This constitutes the fact that Brahman is the cause. || 10 ||
4. The Omniscient One—tha; and for this reason also, the Pradhāna does not exist.
Because of the commonality of destiny. (1.1.11)
"In the beginning, this universe was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever that blinked. He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1:
"He created these worlds.")
"From the Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth.
"This Rigveda is the breath of this great Being."

The same interpretation that applies to these and other passages concerning creation—that is, their mode of operation—is applicable here as well, because this passage shares the same meaning as them. In all of those passages, the Lord of All is understood to be the cause; therefore, it is concluded that here too, the Lord of All alone is the cause. ||11||
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna is not [the cause]:
"And because [Brahman] is mentioned in scripture" (1.1.12).

For indeed, it is heard in this very Upaniṣad that this Being denoted by the word "Sat" possesses, by virtue of being the Self, the agency of differentiating name and form, omniscience, omnipotence, the state of being the support of all, freedom from sin and other such qualities, as well as the possession of true desires and true resolves; [as stated in the passages]:

"Entering with this living self, let me manifest names and forms"; "All these creatures, my dear, have their root in the Sat, their abode in the Sat, and their rest in the Sat"; and "All this has that as its essence; that is the True, that is the Self."
"Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have, all that is contained within this"; "In him, desires are contained";
"This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true.
And likewise, other scriptural passages [state]:

"He has no master in the world, nor a ruler, nor indeed any mark; He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is neither His progenitor nor His ruler. "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and assigned names, remains calling them forth"; "He has entered within as the Teacher of men, the Self of all";
"the Self of the universe, the ultimate refuge."
"The Lord of all, the Self, the Sovereign.
And: "Whatever is seen or even heard in this world, both within and without—all that is pervaded by Nārāyaṇa."
"This one, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the sole god, is Nārāyaṇa," and so forth.

For this very reason, it should be understood that the doctrine of Brahman as mere consciousness devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*) has also been refuted by the author of the Sūtras through these scriptural citations; for he establishes that Brahman, which is to be inquired into, is "endowed with attributes such as seeing and so forth, which are ultimate and primary."

For in the doctrine of non-differentiation (*nirviśeṣavāda*), even the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is ultimately unreal. "Brahman," which is to be known through the Vedānta, is proposed as the object of inquiry; and that [Brahman] is conscious, as established by such sūtras as "Because of seeing, [Brahman] is not the insentient" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*). Consciousness consists in the possession of the quality of sentience (*caitanya*). Therefore, one who lacks the quality of seeing is indeed equivalent to *pradhāna* (primordial matter).

Furthermore, in the doctrine that Brahman is mere light devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣaprakāśamātra*), even its nature as "light" is difficult to establish. For "light" is indeed a specific entity that renders both itself and others fit for practical usage (*vyavahārayogyatā*). Since a featureless reality lacks both these characteristics, it would be insentient (*acit*), like a jar or other such objects. If it is argued that "even in the absence of those two forms, it possesses the capacity for them," we reply: "That is not so. For that capacity is nothing other than its power (*sāmarthya*). Indeed, if it were endowed with the quality of power, the doctrine of being devoid of attributes would be abandoned.
If it is argued: "Then this one distinction is accepted on the basis of the authority of scripture (śruti)."

Well then! For that very reason, omniscience, omnipotence, the state of being the Lord of all lords, the state of being the Lord of all lords, the state of being a mine of all auspicious qualities, the state of being the adversary of everything that is evil, and so forth—all these must be accepted. Furthermore, possessing power (*śaktimatva*) consists in being conducive to specific effects; and that [conduciveness] can only be defined by the specific effect itself. If the specific effect lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the state of "possessing power," which is defined solely by that [effect], would likewise lack any means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, for one who maintains that the reality is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣavastuvādin*), even the status of being a "reality" lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). It has already been stated previously that perception, inference, scripture, and one's own experience all have as their object that which possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣagocara*). Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) alone—who is capable of the creative vision, "May I become many in the form of this world consisting of diverse sentient and insentient beings"—is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). ||12||
Thus ends the section concerning the "Beholding" (Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa). || 5 ||

In the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is an absence of the capacity to establish the linguistic usage of self and other; the meaning is that in the absence of a defining agent (*nirūpaka*), there is an absence of the object to be defined (*nirūpya*).
This concludes the section on the "Consisting of Bliss" (*Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*) [1.1.6].

Thus, the distinction of Brahman—the object of inquiry—from Pradhāna, which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* and is composed of insentient matter that serves as the object of enjoyment for sentient beings, has been stated.

Now, it is established that Brahman is distinct from the pure inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is impure due to its immersion in the ocean of manifold and infinite suffering caused by contact with *prakṛti*—which is of the nature of the three *guṇas* and subject to *karman*—and that Brahman is the opposite of everything to be abandoned (*heya*) and is unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*).
"Consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because of repetition" (1.1.13).
The Taittirīyas study as follows:
"This very person consists of the essence of food," having introduced the subject in this way.
"Therefore, from this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss."

"Thus," and so forth. Since it has been established by the four sūtras that the cause of the world is to be investigated, the intellect—which, because of its well-known status as being established through perception and other means, first descends upon the non-intelligent—having been turned away from that by means of [the mention of] "seeing" and so forth, is now directed toward the intelligent entity. The meaning is that the intellect, which was previously descending upon the inner self (pratyagātman) established by the notion of "I"—which, although less well-known than the non-intelligent, is more well-known than the Supreme Self—is now turned away from that.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) the Supreme Self, distinct from the individual self (jīva)—which is denoted by the term *jīva* and is the recipient of bondage and liberation—or is it that very same [individual self]?
What is correct? That it is the inner self (pratyagātman).
Why? Because [the scripture says]: "Of that, this very one is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā)."
Thus, because the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is heard to have a body; for the embodied self (śārīra) is the individual soul (jīvātman), which is connected with a body.

But is it not the case that, for the sake of easy comprehension of Brahman— which has been established as the cause of the world— the text, after enumerating the [sheaths] beginning with *annamaya*, teaches that very cause of the world as "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*)? And since that cause of the world is said to be omniscient and the Lord of all, on account of the scriptural mention of "seeing" in the passage, "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*).
It has been rightly said: "But he is not distinct from the individual soul (jīva)," as in the passages,
"Having entered by means of this living self" and "That thou art, O Śvetaketu."

This is because there is an indication of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*), which was previously designated as the cause. For grammatical coreferentiality is intended to establish identity, as in the case of "This is that Devadatta. Furthermore, a creation preceded by deliberation (*īkṣā*) is indeed possible for the conscious individual soul.
Therefore,

in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the true nature of the individual soul (jīva), divested from its association with the non-intelligent (acit), is taught as that which is to be attained. This is stated as the defining characteristic of the nature of the soul when free from the non-intelligent:
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
For liberation is indeed the attainment of that very nature.
"Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain."
"Or rather, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless."
Thus, the true nature of the individual soul (jīva), which is dissociated from ignorance, is taught as the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) as that which is to be attained.

For instance, the particle *eva* (indeed) indicates a lack of natural appropriateness [in the opponent's view], because the statement "the person consists of food" (*annamayaḥ puruṣaḥ*) is perfectly justified for the purpose of revealing the true nature of the Self by means of the maxim of the moon and its branch. This is because a *eva* connected with a verb has the function of excluding absolute non-connection. The intended meaning is that being a witness (*sākṣitva*) itself constitutes being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*).

By the author of the Sūtras stating "and because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśācca*)—thereby citing the designation of difference as the reason for the final conclusion—it is understood that the intention was to show that the designation of identity serves as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Thus, the sense is that since the distinction from the individual soul (*jīva*) was not established by the preceding section, another section must be commenced. Therefore—because of the scriptural mention of being embodied (*śārīratva*), and because identity is apprehended through the force of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—"it is taught" (*upadiśyate*); the meaning is that it should be understood in this manner.

"Free from the non-sentient" (*acidviyuktā*) is the statement of its definition; the mention of its specific qualities is for the purpose of understanding that [definition]. He says that [the state] exists in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is free from the non-sentient. "Of that form" (*tadrūpā*)—he says this to show that the essential nature free from the non-sentient is explicitly stated to be the goal to be attained (*prāpyatva*). The word "hi" indicates well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). "Thus" (*iti*)—the word "from hearing" (*śravaṇāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder. With the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he concludes by demonstrating that [the state] possesses the quality of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*) consistent with being an object of attainment.

The phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*) means that the body is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇamātra*) and not a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*); therefore, by means of its dissociation, qualities such as being unlimited bliss (*aparicchinna-ānandatva*) and so forth are taught.

Having first pointed out the body, [the text proceeds] to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of five functions which is within it and sustains it, then to the mind (*manas*) which is within that, and finally to the intellect (*buddhi*) which is within that.

Having pointed out, in various places, the sequence of entry into understanding as "consisting of breath," "consisting of mind," and "consisting of consciousness," [the text] teaches the individual self (jīvātman), which is the innermost of all, as "another inner self consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), thereby concluding the series of inner selves. Therefore, it is determined that the very nature of the individual self is the Brahman introduced in the passage, "He who knows Brahman attains [Brahman]," and that this same [Brahman] is what is taught as "consisting of bliss."
But is it not the case that from the statement, "Brahman is the tail, the support," it is understood that Brahman is something other than the one consisting of bliss?

It is not so; Brahman itself, by way of its own specific nature, is designated as having the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*), being described in terms of head, wings, and tail—just as the "food-made" (*annamaya*) body, as a whole, is [designated] by means of its own parts which are not distinct from itself.

Regarding the term *buddhi*: by the etymology "that by which one discerns" (*vijñāyate anena*), *vijñāna* is *buddhi*. In the expression *vijñānamaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*); this is because the suffixes in *prāṇamaya* and *manomaya* are likewise used in their own sense, because [the text] will later state—without such a suffix—that "consciousness performs the sacrifice" (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*), and because the words *buddhi* and *vijñāna* are employed as having the same meaning in the passages "he whose charioteer is consciousness" (*vijñānasārathi*) and "but let the intellect be the charioteer" (*buddhiṃ tu sārathim*). This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase *buddhyavataraṇa*:

It is established by implication that the state of being unlimited bliss is also possible for the nature of the perfectly pure Self, because of the scriptural mention of its "embodiedness" (śārīratva), its grammatical coordination with the individual soul (jīva-sāmānādhikaraṇya), and the term "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya).

The summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the word [“Brahman”] refers to the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); because [qualities] such as being attained (*prāpyatva*) are possible even in the case of the pure essential nature; because the body is merely an incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), so that being attained and so forth are possible in the form of the nature disjoined from it; and because the suffix *mayaṭ* has its own primary meaning (*svārthika*), lacking the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). In this regard, two reasons are proving factors (*sādhaka*), while the others are of the nature of objections raised against the opponent’s arguments or alternative explanations (*anyathāsiddhi*).

"Something else" (anyat): because the genitive case in "its tail" (*tasya pucchaṃ*) conveys a relationship with the whole, and since a relationship resides in two terms, there is an understanding of distinction (*vyatireka*) through the fact that the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) possesses that [tail] as its attribute; this is the meaning of "something else.
Alternatively, [it may mean] being included within that, or being included within another, or first, the body.
Or [it is] included within that—vā;
there—tha; [it is] included within all—vā; indeed—dha; it is designated—da.

By the passage beginning with "This indeed is its head," [the text] indicates [Brahman] by way of having a head, wings, and a tail; likewise, Brahman as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indicated by means of pleasure (*priya*) and the rest, which are not distinct from itself. In that context, Brahman—which is the support for pleasure, joy, delight, and bliss conceptualized as its limbs—is the "indivisible form" (*akhaṇḍarūpa*), described as "the tail, the foundation."
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, if Brahman were something other than that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya), it would have been pointed out as follows: "Different from this one consisting of bliss, there is another inner Self, which is Brahman. But it is not pointed out in this way.
This is what is meant:
The Brahman introduced at the beginning with the words, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," is [described as] "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

Thus, having established through its defining characteristics a form that is distinct from everything else, and having designated that very same thing with the word "Self" (ātman) in the passage, "From this very Self," the text—manifesting its nature as the Self by way of being the innermost of all—transcends the layers beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) and proceeding through those consisting of breath (prāṇamaya) and so forth, which were each designated as the Self within their respective layers. It concludes with the designation of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) as the Self in the statement, "There is another inner Self, the one consisting of bliss. Therefore, it is determined that Brahman, which was introduced by the word "Self," is indeed the one consisting of bliss.
But is it not the case that,
after stating "Brahman is the tail, the support," [the text continues]?
"If one knows that Brahman exists, he becomes [real]; if he knows that Brahman does not exist, he becomes non-existent. Therefore, they know him as existing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1).

This passage shows the existence or non-existence of the Self based on the knowledge or ignorance of Brahman, not based on the knowledge or ignorance of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Furthermore, it is not reasonable to entertain a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the *ānandamaya*, since its nature—consisting of joy, delight, and so forth—is known to all people. Therefore, this verse was not cited with reference to the *ānandamaya*. Consequently, Brahman is other than the *ānandamaya*.
It is not so;
for [the texts state]: "This tail is the support," "The earth is the tail, the support," and "The Atharva-Āngirasas are the tail, the support."
"By the word 'ātman'" means that the very same [subject] which was introduced by the word "Brahman" is now designated by the word "ātman."

"Now, as for the word 'nanu' (but surely): if the completion of the explanation of the term 'Self' (ātman) were intended to apply to the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), then it should have been designated by the word 'Self. However, this was not done; rather, it was designated by the word 'Brahman. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss does not hold primacy. Consequently, the meaning is that Brahman, which is the tail, alone is the primary subject to be established. And [the objection] 'na ca... is not tenable'—by the word 'āśaṅkā' (objection), the meaning contained within the two scriptural passages cited has been explained."

The meaning is that since [the existence of Brahman] is well-known to the whole world, it is impossible to deny; therefore, a speculative argument (āśaṅkāvāda) regarding its non-existence is as improper as one regarding its existence.

Regarding the passage "this is the tail," etc.: once it is determined that the terms *brahman*, *ātman*, and *ānandamaya* have a single referent, and having clearly understood that the mention of *brahman* is equivalent to the mention of the *ānandamaya*, he states the reasoning for the primacy of the *ānandamaya*.
1. By being the innermost self of all—(variants: *sarvāntarātmakatvena* in Dha; *rātmatayā ātmatvena* in Vā; *tadantarātmakatvena* in Na). 3. It is determined—(variant: *niścīyate* in Ṭa).
Having stated, "The Great is the tail, the support," [the texts] have cited in various places:
"From food indeed, beings are born."

Just as these verses [beginning with] "ityādi" do not have the tail alone as their subject matter, but rather aim to establish the Person consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, so too here this verse, "He is indeed bliss," aims to establish the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and not a tail distinct from the one consisting of bliss.

Even though the one consisting of bliss is Brahman itself, it is entirely reasonable to raise a doubt regarding the existence of that unlimited bliss which is manifested in the form of pleasure, joy, and so on. For even the designation of a "tail" is due precisely to its being unknown as unlimited bliss.

If it is argued that Brahman is not the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) because it lacks the nature of being a limb (*avayavitva*) starting from the head, then Brahman would also not be the tail, for it lacks the nature of being the tail and the support (*pratiṣṭhātva*).

Now, if it is said that this is merely a figurative representation (*rūpaṇa*)— namely, that Brahman is the "tail and support" because it is the substratum of that entity which is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) and of ignorance itself— [then we reply as follows].
The meaning is that since the preceding verses in this section do not have the purpose of establishing the tail alone, this verse as well does not have the purpose of establishing the tail alone.

Regarding the phrase "of the one consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), he removes the objection that doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the well-known bliss is untenable. Regarding the phrase "even of the Brahma-tail," he intends to employ a *pratibandi* (a counter-argument by analogy). This is based on such scriptural passages as "Brahma is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*) and "Bliss is Brahma" (*ānando brahma*).

When it is objected that—since Brahman has been described as bliss and since bliss is well-known—it is not reasonable to doubt its existence or non-existence; [we reply: you must establish that this Brahman, whose nature is bliss, is unknown precisely because its bliss is unlimited. This point is the same here as well. Well then, there will be a figurative description of that Brahman consisting of bliss—which is excluded from non-happiness and so forth—as having "pleasure for its head" and so on.

And thus, by the text "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," that which is distinct from other entities—namely, those that are subject to modification, insentient, and limited—is set forth; and its distinction from what is not bliss is taught by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). Consequently, in Brahman, whose nature is an indivisible, single-flavored bliss, the suffix *mayaṭ* in the word "consisting of bliss" should be understood as being used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*), just as it is in the case of "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*).

Therefore, the innate nature of the individual self (jīvātman)—which is divided into various diverse categories such as gods and so forth through the conceptual construction of ignorance—is said to be "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), being an undivided, single-flavored state of uniform happiness; thus, the "consisting of bliss" is the innermost self (*pratyagātman*).
This being the case, we reply: "The one consisting of bliss [is the Self], because of repetition.
The one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self. Why?
"From practice.
"From non-happiness" means that specific modifications of mental activity (vṛtti), such as those characterized by the head and so forth, are [referred to] as non-happiness.

"And thus" (tataśca): the meaning is that the previously stated objections have been refuted and other supporting arguments exist. Here, since Brahman—designated by the word "Satya"—cannot be a modification of anything, its being denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is also untenable.

Therefore: dispelling the doubt as to how there could be degrees of suffering and happiness for the inner self (pratyagātman), which is of the nature of immeasurable bliss, he concludes the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
Beginning with "This is the inquiry into bliss," it continues until,
"from which words turn back."

By this statement ending thus, bliss—which is being practiced in a sequence of hundredfold increase culminating in a state of unsurpassed intensity—is impossible within the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which partakes only in infinitesimal fragments of pleasure amidst infinite suffering; rather, it makes known the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone as its own substratum—Him who is the opposite of everything to be abandoned, who is solely composed of auspiciousness, and who is distinct from all else. As it is said: "Different from this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Ānandavallī 5.2).

The individual soul (*jīva*) consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), for it is perceived as distinct from mere intellect (*buddhi*) by means of the suffix *maya*. In the case of *prāṇamaya*, however, the suffix is accepted in its primary sense [of "consisting of"]; but here, since it is possible for the soul—which possesses that [intellect]—to exist, it is not logical to assume it is meaningless. We have already established that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is both bound and liberated, and is indeed known. Furthermore, regarding the suffix *maya* and so forth, the possibility of its meaning will be explained immediately hereafter. [End of section on] *prāṇa*.

Fulfilling the expectation of "whose is the practice?", he explains the word "cause" (*hetu*) with the passage beginning "This very [bliss] of bliss," and so forth. By the phrase "crowned by the state of being unsurpassed," he intends the meaning of the text, "from which words turn back. By the phrase "being practiced," he intends the meaning of the sentence, "That is one hundredfold the bliss of Brahman. The meaning is that it is multiplied in a sequence of increasing hundredfold increments. The intention is that the word *abhyāsa* (practice) is derived from the verbal root *as* in the sense of action, ending in the suffix *ghañ*.

The phrase "endless suffering" (anantaduḥkha) expresses the connection with attributes contrary to unsurpassed bliss. The term "limited" (parimita) expresses the absence of unsurpassed bliss. The meaning is that [liberation] is impossible because of the perception of contrary attributes and the perception of their absence. Here, "opposition" (pratyanīkatva) is intended to mean the power of removal; for even for one who is liberated, the attainment of unsurpassed bliss preceded by the cessation of what is to be discarded occurs solely through the grace of the Supreme Self.
Thus, it is stated that the word *ānandamaya*—supported by the reasoning that unsurpassed bliss is incompatible with the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—has the Supreme Self as its referent.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), the particle *hi* indicates that this is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through the natural force of the word itself. For the state of being a knower—as in "I know"—is indeed perceived of the Self (*ātman*), and not of mere intellect (*buddhi*). The intention is that the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), which denotes the act of knowing, would be unnatural (*asvarasa*) to refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) based on its etymology as "that by which one knows. This is because there is no other alternative, such as denoting a modification (*vikāra*) or abundance (*prācurya*), since those meanings are impossible here. Thus, [the suffix -maya] means "possessing that" (*tadvat*).

The meaning is that the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*) is possible. Regarding the term "bound" (*baddha*): here the suffix *mayaṭ* does not have its usual sense; for the Self is by nature pure consciousness (*jñapti*). Knower-ship (*jñātṛtva*) is indeed merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). Since even that [knower-ship] does not exist in the state of liberation, this is the answer to that [objection]. [The commentary continues: "Because it is the opposite of all other things," "for thus," "as he said," "having its own meaning," "the state of having its own meaning," "the knower, for this very reason. (Note: The text provided contains various manuscript variants indicated by letters such as *da*, *cha*, *tha*, *dha*, etc., which I have integrated into the translation where relevant.)

[The term] *anarthaka-svam*—or rather, [it means] the impossibility of the meaning of the suffix *-maya*. How then, in the verse concerning the "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), does it say:
"Consciousness performs the sacrifice"?
Thus, the employment of the term "consciousness alone" (vijñāna-mātra) is justified;

there is no fault in saying that even the very nature of the self, as the knower, is called "consciousness" because of its self-luminosity, since the nature of the knower is defined solely by consciousness.

For words such as "dharma," which denote the nature [of a thing], convey the very essence of the substratum (dharmisvarūpa) by way of its attributes (dharma), just like the word "cow" and others; this is according to the rule:
*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

Or rather, the suffix *lyuṭ* is resorted to in the sense of the agent; or, having recourse to its inclusion in the *nandy-ādi* group, the suffix *lyu* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule "nandi-grahi," etc. And for this very reason, [the following applies].

"It is consciousness that performs the sacrifice, and it also performs ritual acts"—thus the scripture declares that consciousness is the agent of the sacrifice and other such acts. For agency is not possible for that which consists of mere intellect (*buddhi*).

For among the non-conscious elements—such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, which precede that consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) and serve as instruments for the conscious—the agency that is the attribute of the conscious is not heard of in scripture. Therefore, the scriptural passage, distinguishing between the conscious and the non-conscious by means of their respective specific attributes such as having a locus (*nilayanatva*) and lacking a locus (*anilayanatva*), declares:
"Consciousness and unconsciousness."
Thus, by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna), he speaks of that quality, namely sentience.
Likewise, in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa, in place of the section found in the Kāṇva recension which reads, "He who dwells in consciousness," [the Mādhyandina recension has a different reading].

The Mādhyandinas, studying the section beginning with "He who dwells within consciousness" (*ya āni tiṣṭhan*), clarify that the "living self" (*jīvātman*)—as designated by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) found in the *Kāṇva* recension—is indeed the conscious self; furthermore, they maintain that the neuter gender of the term "consciousness" (*vijñānam*) is intended to signify its nature as a reality (*vastutva*). Thus, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), is distinct from and internal to the living self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
This is so even though [it is said] that "consciousness performs the sacrifice."

Thus, in common worldly usage, only knowledge itself is apprehended, not the knower; nevertheless, in the passage, "There is another inner self consisting of consciousness," it is the possessor of that [knowledge], the knower himself, who is taught. For example:

In the passage, "From food indeed creatures are born," even though the word "food" is used, it does not refer to mere food in this world; rather, in the statement, "This person, verily, consists of the essence of food," what is indicated is one who is made of that— that is, a modification thereof.

"They make it clear": because the word *vijñāna* is heard in the place of the word *ātman*, its reference to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is untenable. For even the word *ātman* is inherently unsatisfactory when applied to things other than the conscious self. If [the passage] were to refer to the internal organ, both words—*vijñāna* and *ātman*—would be unsatisfactory. However, if they refer to the conscious self, the only unsatisfactoriness would be that of the word *vijñāna* alone; this is the distinction, in that it is not [unsatisfactory] for both. As for the neuter gender: [it is explained as follows].

Since the word *vijñāna* ends in the suffix *-lyuṭ*, it must take the gender appropriate to its substantive; therefore, how can that which has the Self as its object be neuter? To this, [the author says]: "In this way" (*tadevam*). "That" (*tat*) means by the arguments already stated. "In this way" (*evam*) means because it has been established that the word *vijñāna* refers to consciousness (*cetana*).

By establishing that the word *vijñāna* in the verse refers to the knower (*jñātṛ*), it has been stated that the word *vijñānamaya* also refers to the knower. Now, even though the verse itself lacks reference to the knower, he asserts that the word *vijñānamaya* does refer to the knower with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). The meaning is this: although the sense of the suffix *-maya* (meaning "consisting of") is abandoned in the [preceding] explanatory passage (*hitavākya*), it should not be abandoned in the passage containing that term (*tadvati vākye*). As for the phrase "just as": because the verse deals with a portion of the subject matter already stated in the preceding Brāhmaṇa passage, there is identity of purport (*aikārthya*) between the verse and the Brāhmaṇa.

The meaning is: "as in the case of the verse concerning that which consists of food" (*annamaya*). The phrase "consisting of that" (*tanmayaḥ*) is a restatement of the sense of the suffix *-maya-* found in the Vedic passage. The phrase "its modification" (*tadvikāraḥ*) is its explanation.
Having kept all of this—[the variants] *nirdiṣṭaḥ* (vā), *ślokena* (i, kha, gha, cha)—in mind, the author of the Sūtras himself...
He states immediately thereafter: "Because of the designation of difference."
As it has been said: regarding that which is designated as the cause of the world,
[the texts state] "having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman)" and "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).

And because of the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*), it follows that even the cause of the world does not differ from the essential nature of the individual soul;
thus, [it is] of the individual soul alone...
The true nature [of the Self],
which was introduced in the passage "He who knows Brahman attains the Supreme," is taught here as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), by way of its exclusion from what is not bliss.

That is incorrect; for even though the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses consciousness, it is impossible for it to possess the capacity for an infinite and diverse creation preceded by its own volition—as expressed in such passages as, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and it emitted heat. Indeed, even in its pure state, such cosmic activity as creation and so forth is impossible for it.

The meaning is that by stating, "He says this...," the author of the Sūtras—by declaring that the sentence, "From this very one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya)," establishes the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para)—speaks while keeping in mind that the word *vijñāna* refers to the knower (*jñātṛ*) and the supporting arguments for that.

"Of the individual soul," and so forth. To state the refutation that the opponent's reason—like a reason whose time has passed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*)—is not capable of proving the probandum, because difference is established through the comprehension of the superimposition of contradictory attributes by means of the contextual sentences and the nominal stems of the words in grammatical apposition; [the author] demonstrates the establishment of difference, which contradicts the unity favored by the opponent, by means of the contextual sentences that provide the specific qualities denoted by those terms. "Because the connection with creation is untenable," etc.

The meaning is that the status of a creator is untenable for one who is bound, because during the state of dissolution, when the body and the instruments [of perception] have been withdrawn, it is impossible for one subject to karma to bring about the creation of the manifold world by mere volition alone.
This will be established under the aphorisms: "Excluding the activity of the world" and "Because of the indicative mark of equality only in respect to experience."
If it were not accepted that Brahman, which is the cause, possesses the nature of the individual soul (jīva),
[then the scriptural passages] "by this living self" and "That thou art" would be contradicted.

If it is asked, "How is this grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) possible?"—or rather, how could the nature of a *jīva*—who is subject to various activities such as thinking and blinking, which are dependent on karma that produces manifold and infinite suffering—be identical with Brahman? [Brahman] is that which is free from even a scent of all defects, possesses true resolve, is omniscient, omnipotent, the cause of everything, and the locus of an infinite multitude of countable auspicious qualities of unsurpassed excellence.
If you argue that this is possible because one of the two [terms] is false, then:

O sir, of what [relation] is this? Is it of some [ordinary] relation, or rather of Brahman, whose nature is exclusively auspicious and opposed to all that is to be abandoned (*heya*)? If you say: "It is a false appearance of a connection with the abandonable, occurring because Brahman—whose nature is exclusively auspicious and opposed to the abandonable—is the locus of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*)," [we reply: it is of a false form.

This which is being stated is contradictory: namely, that Brahman possesses an exclusive orientation toward auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all that is to be abandoned (*heya*), and yet simultaneously serves as the locus for beginningless ignorance and the locus for false appearances consisting of infinite objects of suffering. For the connection with that which is to be abandoned consists precisely in being the locus of ignorance and its effects—the appearance of suffering. To possess such a connection and to be the opposite of it are indeed mutually exclusive.

Nevertheless, do not say that there is no contradiction because it is false (*mithyā*). Even that which is false is indeed not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), for you maintain that "all Vedāntas" are commenced for the purpose of its refutation. And the connection with a refutable non-goal is contradicted by the fact that [Brahman] is solely composed of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of what is to be abandoned.
What can we do?
[For it is said: "By which the unheard becomes heard."

Thus, having asserted that "by the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all," [the text] establishes the state of being the sole cause of the entire universe through such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "It thought: 'May I be many. "Then it willed: 'May I be many.'"
If it is argued that, having thus established the Brahman’s nature as one whose will is true,

the identity of that very Brahman with the individual soul (jīva)— the locus of infinite suffering— is taught through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), and that on the basis of the impossibility of this otherwise, one must postulate that Brahman itself is the locus of ignorance (avidyā) and so forth; [we reply:]...
Even if it were based on scripture, one should not conceive of something that is logically untenable or contradictory.
Now, [if you argue:

"The connection with what is to be abandoned (*heya*) alone is ultimately real, whereas the nature of being solely auspicious (*kalyāṇaika-svabhāvatā*) is illusory!"—alas, in that case, would the scripture, which was composed with the desire to revive the consciousness of those afflicted by the threefold suffering, truly revive them correctly by teaching: "Affliction by the threefold suffering alone is its ultimate reality, while its nature as solely auspicious is a mere construction of delusion"?

Now, if it is argued that— out of a desire to avoid this fault— one must conceive that for Brahman, the state of being a jīva, suffering, and so forth, as well as its nature as the cause of the world, its possession of true resolve, and its being a mine of auspicious qualities, are all illusory (mithyā), apart from its essence as non-dual pure consciousness (nirviśeṣacinmātra)— then, oh, how skillful you are at failing to examine your own words!

The proposition that "by the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all" will not be established if everything is false, because of the non-existence of anything to be known. Just as the knowledge of one thing has the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as its object, so too, if the knowledge of all things likewise has the ultimate reality as its object and is included therein, then it can be said that by the knowledge of that [one], there is the knowledge of all. For, by the knowledge of the ultimate reality of a mother-of-pearl shell, the "unreal silver" resting upon it is not thereby known.
If it is asserted that there exists only a causeless, undifferentiated reality alone,

then even the illustrative example— "O dear one, as by a single lump of clay everything made of clay is known"— is not tenable; for by the knowledge of the lump of clay, the knowledge of its modification is what is demonstrated.

If it is argued that even there, the unreality of the modification (*vikāra*) is intended, [we reply: for one who desires to hear [the teaching], the unreality of the modification of clay—like that of a rope-snake and so forth—is not yet established; therefore, the introduction of the example "Just as, my dear" (*yathā somya*) as something already well-known in order to demonstrate the possibility of the proposed thesis would be inappropriate. Furthermore, prior to the arising of the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art," we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether supported by reasoning (*tarka*) or not, which brings about the unreality of the entire class of modifications. This is the meaning of the sūtra: "The non-difference from That [Brahman] [is established] on account of the words concerning the origin and so forth. (*tadananyatvam ārambhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ*).
This will be explained hereafter. Likewise:
"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support;
all this has that as its self."

By such passages [the text establishes] that this world has the nature of Being (*sat*); that prior to creation there was the abandonment of the differentiation of name and form; that at the time of the world's origin, Brahman—denoted by the word "Being"—does not depend on any other external cause distinct from itself; that there is a unique and extraordinary resolve, namely, "May I alone become manifold in the form of infinite moving and stationary beings"; and that in accordance with that resolve, there occurs a creation characterized by an extraordinary and specific sequence of infinite and diverse entities among all insentient things.

The manifestation of infinite names and forms occurs precisely through the entry of the individual soul (jīva), which is His own self, into all things; that everything other than Himself has its root in Him, its abode in Him, is impelled by Him, is sustained by Him alone, and is established in Him—these and other infinite distinctions have been expounded as being cognizable solely through the scriptures.

By virtue of its connection with that [Brahman], even in other contexts, such qualities as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), the state of having all defects removed, omniscience, universal lordship, having all desires fulfilled, having true resolve, and the possession of unsurpassed bliss which is the source of all joy, are established by the thousands—qualities that lie beyond the scope of all other means of knowledge. Thus, if the word *tat* (That), which refers back to the subject matter at hand—the Brahman characterized by infinite attributes inaccessible to anything else—were intended merely to teach a featureless reality alone, it would be as incoherent as the ravings of a madman.
