Regarding the phrase "the state of being self-directed": this refers to the state of being self-directed as realized through the fruit of being the sixfold abode (*sadāyatana*), as well as self-sustenance. For sustenance occurs through governance, and its life-force through that very sustenance. This is intended to dispel the doubt that the mention of qualities is merely a restatement for the sake of prohibition—as expressed in the phrase "based solely on scripture"—for the sense is that a restatement cannot function as an injunction.

The phrase "by way of being related to that" indicates a failure to consider other scriptural passages (*śruti*). The meaning is that "freedom from all defects" consists in the state of having qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*). The statement "beyond the scope of all other means of valid cognition" is said in order to show that "novelty" (*apūrvatā*) is an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*) regarding the qualities (Śrutiprakāśikā).

By the word "prakṛta" (the subject at hand), a contradiction with the contextual passage is intended. By this, the contradiction with the etymological derivation of the word *tat* (that) is stated, insofar as it would refer to something characterized by a form already under discussion anywhere.

Furthermore, the word "that" (tyam) denotes the individual soul (jīva) as qualified by transmigratory existence. If this word were also intended to establish the undifferentiated essential nature [of Brahman], its own primary meaning would have to be abandoned. Moreover, it has already been stated previously that for an entity whose very nature is the light of the undifferentiated, concealment by ignorance is impossible, as it would entail the destruction of its essential nature and other such consequences.
This being the case, one must resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), abandoning the primary meanings of both co-referential terms, "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam).

Now, it might be argued: since words functioning in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) cannot have their primary intention (tātparya) directed toward the qualifying portions, the qualifiers are excluded; and because they establish the oneness of the thing-in-itself (vastumātra), there is no occasion for the charge of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā). For example, in the case of the two words "blue lotus" (nīlam utpalam), because they aim at establishing the oneness of the qualified object (viśeṣya), the two qualifiers—namely, "blueness" and "lotusness"—are not intended to be expressed.

For if that were intended, it would follow that the form qualified by blueness and the form qualified by lotus-ness would be established as identical; however, that is not possible. Indeed, that object is not qualified by the word "lotus" through its form qualified by blueness, because that would entail the mutual inherence (*samavāya*) of a genus and a quality. Therefore, by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), only the oneness of the object as characterized by both blueness and lotus-ness is expressed.

Likewise, in the case of the [cognition] "This is that Devadatta," there is the word *tat* (that), which refers to Devadatta as qualified by a past time and a distant location, and the word *tvam* (you), which refers to him as being in a proximate location. The referent of the word *tvam* is a conscious being facing oneself. Facing oneself (*ābhimukhya*) consists in being made known by one's own speech. And such knowability is naturally established for the ignorant transmigrator. Therefore, the meaning of *tvam* is qualified by those characteristics suitable for being fit for instruction. Thus, the [unreal] aspects are abandoned; this is the intended sense. And this being so...

The meaning is that if it is accepted that [the word] aims at presenting the nature of the object as devoid of distinctions by conveying the mere thing through its connection with the primary sense, then the acceptance of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) follows.
The meaning is that [the compound] is intended to convey a single object;

otherwise, because there would be a plurality of qualifiers, the status of having a single object would not be established. This has indeed been stated many times in the first sūtra. Regarding the phrase "not a definition" (*na lakṣaṇa*), he shows that it is undesirable for it to be what is expressed (*vācya*). This is indicated by the words "for not," and so forth.

The underlying intention held in mind is this: if there were simultaneous denotation, it would entail the loss of the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*); furthermore, when a qualified unity presented by the bases of two words is conveyed by a common case-ending, it would follow that the universal (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) components—which serve as qualifiers—would become one with the substantive component, just as the substantive itself does. Therefore, the position of sequential denotation must be accepted. [This refers to] "the universal and the quality."

The meaning is as follows: if *utpalatva* (lotus-ness) were present in that which is qualified by the quality of blue (*nīlaguṇaviśiṣṭa*), then *utpalatva* would exist in the qualifier just as it does in the qualificand; such is the sense of "the reverse. Regarding the phrase "characterized by blueness" (*nīlatvopalakṣitā*): the intention is that the cognition of blueness and so forth is abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "precisely because of the impossibility of the intended meaning" (*tātparyāsambhavādeva*): the word "precisely" (*eva*) implies "because it has already been stated [above]" (*pūrvamapyuktāt*). The intention is "because it is presented as something external."

In both feet [of the verse], there is the characteristic *tha* and *dha*, not *na*. Following that, *tha* and *dha* [occur]. 7. The nature of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*)—*i*, *vā*. Of the two activities—*i*, *vā*.
Identity of the qualificand (*viśeṣyaikya*)—*vā*. It is established—*i*, *vā*.

For things that have come into existence—such as the nature of a blue lotus—it is impossible to establish a qualification by the present time; therefore, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), only the identity of the essential nature as characterized by both place and time is established.

Although the qualifier perceived upon hearing a single word such as "blue" is not conveyed at the time of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to contradiction, nevertheless, because the primary portion of the denoted meaning is conveyed, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); rather, there is merely a lack of intention to express the qualifying portion. Since this is the very nature of coreferentiality everywhere, there is no fault whatsoever—thus [it is said].

This is without substance; for in all sentences, what is conveyed by words is merely a specific relation (*saṃsarga*) among meanings already established through linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). In that regard, even for words such as "blue" occurring in a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the meaning established by convention is precisely that which is qualified by blueness and so forth; it is expressed as conjoined with the meaning of other words. Just as when it is said, "Bring the blue lotus," that which is qualified by blueness and so forth is indeed brought;
and just as in the statement, "A herd of elephants, intoxicated with rut, stands in the Vindhya forest."

Thus, in the case of two words, it is only the object qualified by their respective qualifiers that is cognized; likewise, in the Vedānta sentences involving "co-referential" (samānādhikaraṇa) designations, Brahman must be understood as being qualified by each of those respective qualifiers.

Furthermore, when there is an intention to express a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), an object qualified by one [attribute] should not be further qualified by another; rather, the very nature of the object itself (*svarūpa*) is what is to be qualified by all the qualifiers. For it is said: "Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the application of words with distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single referent. Through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or through exclusion (*nivṛtti*), the fact that the very same object is presented by other words—by way of being endowed with a different aspect from the aspect presented by another word—is the function of co-referentiality. As in: "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, and red-eyed."

"Not dejected, not miserable, and irreproachable"—thus [it is said]. However, where two qualifiers incompatible with co-occurrence (samanvaya) are indicated by words in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) regarding a single object, even there one of the two words must be understood in a non-primary sense (amukhyavṛtti), but not both. For example, "The Vāhīka is an ox. But in cases such as "blue lotus," because there is no contradiction in the application of both qualifiers, a single entity qualified by both is conveyed.

This might be so; if it were merely the state of being the counter-correlate of two qualifiers that would exclude oneness. But this is not the case; for it is precisely the state of being qualified by two attributes incapable of being subsumed in a single substratum (*dharmin*) that excludes oneness. And this incapacity is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of "pot-ness" and "cloth-ness."

In cases such as "blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), however, no contradiction is perceived—unlike [the case of] "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) or "ring-wearer" (*kuṇḍalin*), or like "possessing color" (*rūpavat*), "possessing taste" (*rasavat*), or "possessing fragrance" (*gandhavat*). Not only is there no contradiction, but through the difference in the grounds for the application of the terms (*pravṛttinimitta*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in "residing in a single object" actually establishes the state of being qualified by two distinct attributes. Otherwise, if there were identity merely at the level of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), there would be no ground for the application of multiple words, and thus grammatical coreferentiality itself would not exist.

If qualifiers, disregarding their own specific relations, were intended merely to point toward the essential nature of the thing (*vastusvarūpa*), then since the thing would have been pointed out by a single one, any further qualifier would be entirely redundant. If, however, one were to admit a difference in the form of the object being pointed out by each subsequent qualifier, it would follow that the thing possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*) by virtue of those forms.

"By another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntara*)—the sense is that there is no incompatibility (*ayogyatva*) merely because of being a qualifier. "Blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*): the contradiction is not merely a matter of having different substrata, but rather a necessary restriction (*tanniyama*). And there is no such contradiction between blueness and lotus-ness, because they are sometimes perceived together; this is the sense. "Stick-ness" (*daṇḍitva*) etc.: a stick and so forth are "separately established" (*yutasiddha*), whereas color and so forth are "inseparably established" (*ayutasiddha*).

The sense is that, just as there is a distinction between being established separately (*yutasiddhatva*) and not being established separately (*ayutasiddhatva*), the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is also not a cause for contradiction. [Regarding the phrase] "not merely": since two non-synonymous words require a basis when they refer to a single object, and because their application to that object would be impossible without it, the qualifier is intended because of its absolute utility. "Otherwise" means in the event of abandoning the qualifier.

"Disregard" (*anādara*) means the absence of primary intent (*tātparya*). Just as there is no primary intent regarding a branch that serves merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), but rather the primary intent is directed toward the moon itself—such is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "by another indicator": our position is that we accept specific distinctions in the forms of knowledge, power, and so forth, which are indicated by indicators such as "birth" and the rest; thus, there is no pointlessness. Regarding the phrase "in that form": even ultimately, a state of possessing attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) is unavoidable.

And this being the case, since one accepts that it is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) by admitting other forms to be characterized, the logical conclusion is that it is more appropriate to accept that those very things intended as secondary characteristics are actually primary qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*); such is the meaning.

In the case of the cognition "This is that Devadatta" as well, there is not even a trace of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because there is no contradiction. For there is no contradiction between something that has passed away by virtue of its connection with another place and its existing in the present by virtue of its connection with a proximate place. Precisely for this reason, those who maintain the stability of things establish the identity of an object connected to two points of time through the recognition "This is that. Otherwise, if there were a contradiction with experience, everything would necessarily be momentary.
As for the contradiction regarding the connection with two places, it is resolved by the difference in time.

Since words in grammatical apposition denote a single object qualified by multiple qualifiers, for this very reason, in the injunction "one purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed [cow]," the purchase is prescribed as being accomplished by means of a single one-year-old cow qualified by qualities such as ruddiness. As it has been said:
"When there is a single purpose, there is a restriction because the substance and the quality function together in a single action."

"Because there is no contradiction"—that is, because there is no contradiction in the connection with the two qualifiers that constitute the primary meaning. Regarding the phrase "in another place": although they are specified as qualifiers of the object, the connection with another place and the connection with the proximate place are intended [here] as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of past and present time. This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other limiting adjuncts of time. The words "past" (*atīta*) and "present" (*vartamāna*) refer to what is connected with past and present time.

"By virtue of being connected with another place" means [being connected] with a past time delimited by such limiting conditions (*upādhi*) as connection with another place. "Because there is no contradiction with the proximate... means because there is no contradiction with its connection to the present time, which possesses limiting conditions such as connection with a proximate place. Furthermore, "pastness" is intended here in relation to something else; it is not intended in relation to an entity that persists through both times. Precisely for this reason—namely, because there is no contradiction in its connection with two times—it is "established."

The phrase "toward the Buddhists" (*saugatān prati*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is that for one who seeks to refute the Buddhist position, the acceptance of the contradiction regarding the connection with two times is itself contradictory. "Otherwise"—that is, by way of the contradiction regarding the connection with two times. "In the face of the contradiction of cognition" (*pratītivirodhe*) means in the face of the contradiction with the cognition whose object is the stability of the thing. "Of all" (*sarveṣām*).

The intention is that, given the contradiction of a single entity being associated with two different places and two different times, the injunction for performing a means to achieve a result in another place and time, as well as the teaching on the eternity of the self (*ātman*), would be invalid. Regarding the phrase "two places": the meaning is that for a delimited object, its connection with a location not previously occupied by itself is contradictory only in the case of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*), but not when occurring sequentially (*kramabhāvitva*).

The phrase "precisely because of this" (*yataḥ... ata eva*) reveals the intention behind the discussion in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*: namely, that the previously stated proofs for one's own position and refutations of the opposing positions are to be understood as being established by way of worldly usage (*laukikaprayoga*). This is the underlying meaning.

The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) considers it thus: although the word "aruṇayā" (with the red one), like the word for "form" (ākṛti), denotes the quality of redness as extending to the substance itself—since a quality also has the nature of being a qualifier of a substance—nevertheless, a restrictive connection with the "one-year-old cow" (ekahāyanī) is not possible for the quality of redness; for it is impossible to enjoin two separate meanings simultaneously, such as "he buys [the cow] with a one-year-old cow" and "and that [cow] must be red."

Consequently, by splitting the sentence "with a red one" (*aruṇayā*), the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) is expressed without distinction as extending to all substances prescribed by the context. The use of the feminine gender in the word "with a red one" is for the purpose of indicating all substances of every gender prescribed by the context. Therefore, there would be no restriction to the connection with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), and in that case, the redness would not apply [to it alone].
To this it is replied:

"When there is a single purpose, there is a restriction because of the single function of the substance and the quality. In the case of the phrase "with a red, one-year-old [cow]," once it is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that there is a single purpose for the two words denoting the substance qualified by redness—the one-year-old cow and the quality of redness—then, regarding the substance (the one-year-old cow) and the quality (redness), [the rule applies] by means of the word "with a red [one]."

In that context, "thus" (*evam*) means the intention is that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) are indeed those stated by us, as intended by the author of the Sūtras (Jaimini). Regarding "even though" (*yadyapi*): although a word denoting a quality, like a word denoting a generic form (*ākṛti*), has as its essential nature the property of being a qualifier of a substance (*dravya*), and thus—even if it extends only as far as the substance itself—it nevertheless does not establish extension as far as the specific substance that serves as the locus for the "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*). This is the meaning. Regarding "two meanings" (*arthadvaya*): [the two meanings are the substance and the quality].

By the sentence "He purchases with a one-year-old cow," the relationship between the one-year-old cow and the purchase is established. By the sentence "And that purchase is to be performed with a reddish-brown [cow]," it is understood that the purchase—characterized by having the one-year-old cow as its means—is to be accomplished by means of the substance that is reddish-brown. Thus, it is stated: "The purchase is to be accomplished by means of the one-year-old cow, and furthermore, it must be performed with a reddish-brown one."

And thus, because it is impossible to enjoin two matters—the connection of the one-year-old cow with the sacrifice and the connection of its redness—within a single sentence; this is the meaning. "Context" (prakaraṇam) refers either to the intermediate context or the major context. "All substances" refers to the cloth, the sacrificer, and so forth. "Without distinction" means without distinction in their connection to the context.

Regarding the phrase "here it is said": the meaning is that once this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached, the author of the Sūtras states his own established conclusion (*siddhānta*). With the words beginning with "by the red one" (*aruṇayā*), he explains the literal meaning of the Sūtra. In response to the inquiry, "Between which two [words] is there a single purpose?"—since a word is necessarily related to its referent, and because the specific words are situated within a proximate sentence—the terms "of the two words *āruṇya*... have been supplied (*adhyāhṛta*). The term "established" (*siddhe*) refers to the substance qualified by redness and qualified by the state of being a one-year-old cow. [The commentary continues: "in one way as a qualifier," "in all genders," etc.

Since the two [qualities] are expressed by the same word as being related through the relationship of qualifier and qualified, there would be no contradiction in their connection with the single action called "purchase"; thus, there would be a rule that redness (aruṇimā) must be connected with the single tawny cow (ekahāyanī), which serves as the means for the purchase.

If, like the connection of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) with the purchase, the connection with redness (*aruṇima*) were also to be understood through syntactical construction (*vākya*), then there would be the injunction of two separate meanings by a single sentence. But this is not the case; for by the word "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*) alone, a substance qualified by redness is already denoted. Through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "one-year-old," only its being a one-year-old is understood, not its connection with the quality. Indeed, the meaning of coreferentiality is simply the identity of the qualified substance.

"Cohabitation" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed defined as "the occurrence of words whose grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are distinct in reference to a single object. This means that when the oneness of meaning is established—because the two words expressing those [objects] function with respect to a single substantive through their respective qualifiers by virtue of being in a state of cohabitation—the result follows. The phrase "due to the absence of contradiction" means because there is no contradiction in the form of the contingency of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*). Regarding the passage beginning with "of redness" (*aruṇimnaḥ*): since it does not depend upon a context (*prakaraṇa*) common to all substances, the restriction is established solely by virtue of its position within the sentence.

In this context, the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the quality (*guṇa*) and the substance (*dravya*) is to be understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); the identity of the qualified object is to be understood from grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); and the connection with the act of purchase (*kraya*) is to be understood from the sentence (*vākya*). Thus, the sole function of the sentence is to convey the connection with the act of purchase. Since there is no possibility of enjoining two distinct meanings within a single sentence, and thus no resulting split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) does not connect with all substances mentioned in the context; rather, it connects only with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*). This is the meaning of the Sūtra.

"Of that substance qualified by redness (*aruṇima-viśiṣṭa-dravyasya*). "The state of being a one-year-old cow alone" (*ekahāyanītvamātram*) means that the substratum of the state of being a one-year-old cow is the identity of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyaikyam*). By this, the difference in the subject matter of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (the section on generic form) and the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section on redness) is stated. The meaning of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* is that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has the property-bearer (*dharmin*) as its primary referent. The *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, however, establishes that multiple nominal stems sharing the same case-ending have the identity of the qualificandum as their intended meaning.

"Unity of the qualified substance" (*viśiṣṭadravyaikya*). It is stated thus so that when "unity of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭaikya*) is said, it may not be understood as the unity of the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*); by the word "substance" (*dravya*), the qualified portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) is intended. [The author] states the passage defining grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "distinct" (*bhinnati*). The meaning is that it has been stated that grammatical coreferentiality is not the occurrence of two words denoting the qualifier and the qualified in a relationship of qualifier and qualified. Therefore...

For this very reason, in expressions such as "the cloth becomes red," there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) due to their having a single purpose (*aikārthya*). For the function of the sentence lies in connecting the cloth with the action of becoming; however, the connection with color is already expressed by the word "red" itself. This coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is to be understood merely as "the cloth is a substance connected with color."

Thus—having presented [an object] as qualified by one quality, by two, or by many, by each individual term, whether collectively or distributively, and having made it known through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that "the single object is qualified by all its qualifiers," the expression of its connection with an action is not contradictory. For example: "Devadatta, who is dark-complexioned, young, red-eyed, carrying a staff, and wearing earrings, stands"; "One should prepare a curtain with a white cloth"; "Bring a blue lotus"; "Bring a blue lotus"; or "Bring a cow that is white and has beautiful eyes."
"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt. Likewise:
"One purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow."
Thus [it is said].

For this very reason—namely, that the connection with a quality occurs through the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the mutual connection occurs through identical case-endings (*samānavibhakti*), and the connection with the action (*kraya*) occurs through the sentence (*vākya*)—all three functions follow the manner already described. Regarding the word "red" (*rakta*): for even though the sentence "the cloth becomes" (*paṭo bhavati*) is complete in itself, the employed word "red" is connected as part of a single syntactical unit because it gives rise to an expectancy, such as "What kind of cloth is it? The phrase "or separately" (*vyastena vā*) means: [The cloth] is red. In this case, although the sentence "the cloth becomes" is complete in itself, the word "red" is employed; because it gives rise to an expectancy such as "What kind of cloth is it?", it is connected through being part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). This is the sense. Or [it may be] separately.

In this context, it is intended that [the word] be either ending in a case suffix denoting a kāraka (case-role) or ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*). An example of its connection with multiple nominative qualifiers is "Devadatta."

The point is this: just as the disparity between the two words "raktaḥ paṭaḥ" (the red cloth), which denote non-conscious things, and the word "aruṇayā" (with the red [cow]), which denotes a conscious being, does not serve as a determining factor [for grammatical connection], so too the disparity between being in the nominative case and being in a case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (grammatical relation) is not a determining factor. This was stated with the intention that the same applies even to internal and external qualifiers, such as "daṇḍī" (staff-bearer) and "kuṇḍalī" (earring-wearer). The phrase "śuklena vāsasā" (with a white garment) is an example of the syntactic connection of a single word ending in a *kāraka* case-ending.

"Blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*) is an example of the object (*karman*) as a *kāraka*. "Blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*) is an example of a compound (*samāsa*). "The cow" (*gām*) is an example of the connection of multiple words ending in case-inflections (*kāraka-vibhakti*). "To Agni" (*agnaye*) is a Vedic example concerning the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) *kāraka*. "The sacrificial cake on eight potsherds" (*puroḍāśam aṣṭākapālam*) likewise establishes the object (*karman*) *kāraka*. Similarly, [the word] "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*). For instance, there is the connection of number such as singularity and so forth with the singular number (*ekavacana*) and other suffixes.

This is what is meant: just as in the expression, "One should cook rice in a pot with wooden sticks," a single action qualified by multiple factors is perceived simultaneously, so too each individual factor denoted by a collection of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is perceived simultaneously—qualified by its respective various qualifiers—at the very moment that factor is apprehended. Thus, it conforms to the action without any contradiction, as in such cases as: "A capable cook should cook milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and boiled rice (*śālyodana*) in a vessel of equal measure with dry *khadira* wood. And so forth.

That is not tenable; for nowhere is there observed in either common usage (*loka*) or the Veda an instance where a word denoting a quality stands in grammatical apposition with a word denoting a substance, such that it expresses the quality alone. Furthermore, the claim that "a word for a quality occurring in a sentence where a substance has already been introduced denotes the quality alone" is also inconsistent; for even in cases such as "white," although a substance is introduced, what is expressed is precisely the substance as qualified by the quality. In the case of "the white of the cloth," the cognition is of the cloth as qualified by whiteness; this is brought about by the employment of a non-identical case-ending (*asamānavibhakti*), and not by the fact that a substance has been previously introduced.

In that very context, regarding expressions such as "the white part of the cloth," where there is a reference using a common case ending, a substance qualified by whiteness (*śauklya*) is perceived. "The cloth...

Furthermore, as for the claim that because the purchase (*kraya*) is already encompassed by the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), the connection of the redness (*aruṇimā*) with the purchase is impossible—that too is inconsistent;

for there is no contradiction in the connection of a word denoting a quality with a word denoting the substance that lacks a conflicting quality, since such a quality-word denotes the quality residing in that [substance], and thus its connection with the verb is not obstructed.

That is not tenable. For in cases such as "one should sacrifice a white [animal]," the Mīmāṃsakas accept that words expressing qualities extend to the substance possessing those qualities (guṇin), based on the principle established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*. The reason for these words extending to the quality alone is their occurrence within a sentence where a substance has already been mentioned. However, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which sets aside that [reason], it is accepted that they denote the substance possessing the quality.

In that regard, the reason stated for the [word] being limited to the quality alone is accepted. In the present case, there is limitation to the quality alone, as in the worldly and Vedic usages. The meaning is that it is improper to claim that [the word] denotes the quality alone, because the state of being a word denoting a quality situated within a sentence containing a substance—which serves as an exception to the rule of being limited to the qualified entity—is established by the existence of such co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in sentences like "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*), which functions as an exception to that rule.
Thus.

"Indication by means of a non-identical case-ending" (asamānavibhaktinirdeśaḥ) means an indication by means of a case-ending that is not identical [to the word denoting the substratum]. It does not mean the mere absence of indication by an identical case-ending; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even in expressions such as "the white one goes" (śveto yāti), the term would refer only to the quality (guṇa).

The intention is that it is improper to assume a deviant factor (vyabhicārin) as the determinant (prayojaka) and to assume its exclusion (apavāda) in cases of deviation, because there exists a non-deviant determinant.

"By being restricted to the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow)—because [the word] has no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*) with respect to the *ekahāyanī*. For syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) exists only when there is an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) in the case of a division [of meaning]. Since that [expectancy] is absent here, there is no connection with the purchase; this is the meaning.

The mention of "words devoid of contradictory qualities" is for the purpose of excluding cases such as "blue, white," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "as a verbal action": since the word denoting a quality extends itself to the substrate of that quality (*guṇin*), the quality-qualified entity constitutes a single instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, because the redness (*aruṇimā*) connects with the purchase by means of the substance, the impossibility of its connection with the purchase is untenable; this is the meaning.
3. Even though it consists of three substances, why is there no perception of a cloth?—tha; 4. [the objection] "it is contradictory to the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow)"—tha, dha;
5. by that—tha, dha; 6. connection with the action—8. tha, dha.
Regarding the phrase "of the word"—

in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) [of the *Śrībhāṣya* 1.1.13], it is also untenable to claim that once the syntactic connection (*śābda anvaya*) of redness with the substance is established by the aforementioned reasoning, their mutual connection is then established by implication (*arthat*) because the substance and the quality cannot both serve as means for the purchase. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated.

Therefore, in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the teaching of identity must be described as occurring precisely without discarding the attributes denoted by the two words. However, this is not possible for one who does not accept a Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—who is distinct from the conscious being that exists in both pure and impure states and partakes in limitless suffering due to beginningless ignorance—and who instead accepts [only] a continuous stream of infinite auspicious qualities that are the opposite of everything to be abandoned.

If it is argued that even for one who accepts [the identity], if one resorts to the view that words in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) have as their purport the demonstration of the oneness of a single entity qualified by its attributes as they actually exist, then it would follow that the Supreme Being would partake in all the defects perceived in the word "thou" (tvam)—to this we reply: this is not so; for even by the word "thou," it is the Supreme Being Himself who is denoted as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of the individual soul.

This is what is meant: The Supreme Brahman—the cause of all—which is denoted by the word *sat*, from which every trace of defect has been removed, and which possesses a multitude of countless, unsurpassed, and non-surpassable auspicious qualities along with the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), having willed, "May I become many," created the entire universe beginning with fire, water, and earth; and into that universe, established with its various arrangements such as the gods and so forth, He [entered] as the conscious principle within the class of individual souls (*jīva*) in bodies corresponding to their respective karma.

Having entered [them], and having himself "entered" by his own will as the inner self (antarātman) within the living beings, he differentiated name and form within such aggregates—beginning with the gods and ending with himself—which had assumed the forms of deities and so forth. The meaning is that he made such an aggregate alone the reality and the denotation of words.

Regarding the phrase "this has been said": this undertaking is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that, if the word *tvam* (thou) denotes the Supreme Self by way of the individual soul (*jīva*), why could the word *tat* (that) not likewise denote the individual soul by way of the Supreme Self? The phrase "denoted by the word *sat*" means that the word *sat*, which signifies the causal reality, refers to an entity endowed with attributes consistent with its causality; such is the intended meaning.

It should be understood that through the grasping of the subject in the thought "May I be many," all names and forms—beginning with fire and so forth—are first perceived in their generality as belonging to the Supreme Self; subsequently, by means of scriptural passages concerning the differentiation of names and forms preceded by the entry [of the Self] into them, it is determined that [the Self] possesses names and forms indirectly (through the medium of those elements).

In the *Upabṛṃhaṇas*, regarding the qualities of the Blessed One which are stated without distinction—such as having a glossy complexion (*snigdhavarṇatva*) and so forth, as well as qualities such as truthfulness (*satyasandhatva*) and so forth—it is observed that some are mediated by the divine form (*divyavigraha*) while others are non-mediated (*advāraka*). Similarly, here too, the connection with qualities must be accepted according to the scripture (*yathāśruti*), both as being mediated by the sentient and insentient entities that constitute the body of the Lord, and as being non-mediated. This is the intended meaning. "May I become many" (*bahu syām*): the meaning is, "May I possess many names and forms."

By the word *pramukha* (foremost), the creation of other principles (*tattva*) is intended. The phrase "beginning with the gods" (*devādīti*) is a description of the world's form for the purpose of explaining the subsequent division of the conscious and unconscious portions (*cida-cidaṃśa*) that will be discussed; it is not a description of the state prior to the entry of the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding the term *cetana* (conscious): the meaning is that being conscious (*cetanatva*) is the determining factor (*prayojaka*) for having a body. By the word *jīvavarga* (the class of souls), the singular number used in the expressions "knowledge" (*vijñāna*) and "by the soul" (*jīvena*) is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*); this is explained by the fact that these terms have the same referent as [the plural] "of the conscious ones" (*cetanānām*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with their own karma," the intention behind the reference "by this [jīva]" in the passage "by this living self" is explained as follows: the word "this," which qualifies the Supreme Self as characterized by the *jīva*, has as its referent the diversity manifested through the medium of the *jīva*; and since the diversity of *jīvas* is dependent upon the diversity of karma. Regarding the phrase "by his own will": the meaning is that dependence and independence constitute the difference in the causes for the entry [of the Self].

When these things, consisting of consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*), are thus established in the relationship of the door and the one who possesses the door, [the text says] "he differentiated name and form" (*nāmarūpe vyākarot*). This means that he brought about the various states of the respective deities and so forth, as well as the respective words for them. "Of such a composite" (*evam-rūpa-saṅghātasya*) means: of the composite consisting of consciousness, unconsciousness, and the Lord (*īśvara*).

"Gandhasatyasaṅkalpatva" means having the power of true resolve regarding fragrance; "gandhaṃ satyasaṅkalpa" means [the same]. "Dha kalyāṇaguṇam" means possessing auspicious qualities; "niratiśaya kalyāṇaguṇagaṇam" means possessing a multitude of unsurpassed auspicious qualities; "navadhikātiśayakalyāṇaguṇa" means possessing an immeasurable and infinite multitude of unsurpassed and unsurpassable auspicious qualities.

The expression "anena jīvenā'tmanā"—meaning "by me, who am the living soul"—indicates that the individual soul (jīva) has Brahman as its self. Furthermore, this fact that the soul has Brahman as its self is understood from the entry of Brahman into the world as the inner self of all individual souls.

"In this [passage], 'It created all this—whatever there is here. Having created that, It entered into that very thing. Having entered it, It became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)'—the two categories of sentient and insentient entities indicated by the phrase 'all this' are distinguished and designated by the terms *sat* and *tyat*, as well as by the terms *vijñāna* and *avijñāna*. Furthermore, because the entry of Brahman even into the conscious entity is declared therein, it is understood from this very differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) that all expressive words denote the Supreme Self as qualified by the insentient and the individual soul."
Moreover:
"All this has that as its self."

Thus, having pointed out the phenomenal world mixed with consciousness as "all this," it was established that "this is its Self. And in this way, because Brahman is the "Self" of everything conscious and unconscious, the entire world, including the conscious, becomes its "body.
Accordingly, other scriptural passages state:

"By me" (*mayā*) is an explanation of the word "self" (*ātman*). For when the word "self" signifies "I," the state of having Brahman as one's essence (*brahmātmakatva*) is demonstrated. Regarding the phrase "this... two things": here, the intention is that the term "all" (*sarva*) is used without restriction. In the passage, "Having entered, let me evolve names and forms," it is understood that the evolution of names and forms is preceded by entry. In the passage, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," it is understood that entry is preceded by creation.

Therefore, there is no intended meaning of temporal sequence here; rather, it is only the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) that is intended, because in the sentence "Tvaṣṭṛ, fashioning its form, enters it," one understands that the acts of creation and entering are simultaneous. Consequently, the use of the gerund (*lyap*) ending in the word "having entered" (*anupraviśya*) in the Commentary is for the purpose of making known the distinction between the two acts of entering. Thus—from the scriptural passage cited—because it thus teaches the differentiation of names and forms up to the Supreme Self as the agent...

"This is its self-nature" (aitadātmyam) is the statement that implies [the world] being the body [of Brahman]. It demonstrates— having divided the two categories of sentient and insentient beings— that they possess the nature of the Self.

"Having entered within, the Teacher is the Self of all beings," beginning with: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal."

"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal," and so forth;
"He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth"; "He who moves within the waters, whose body is the waters."
Beginning with these words and continuing with,
"He who moves within the Imperishable, whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know—

he is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa," and so forth, [the texts] designate the conscious universe as His body and teach the Supreme Self as His very Self.
In passages such as "The four [and] fifteen nights... they go to godhood" (*devatvam gacchanti*), the meaning is that "they become gods.

Since the body is a mode (*prakāra*) of the embodied being (*śarīrin*), and because words expressing a mode ultimately terminate in the possessor of the mode, it is logical that words denoting the body terminate in the embodied being. For a "mode" is indeed that aspect of an object perceived as "this is thus," which is perceived as "thus" within that object.

Since the cognition of that [object] depends upon that very thing, and because it is dependent on it, it is logical that its final determination (paryavasāna) occurs in that very thing; thus, even the word that expresses it culminates in that very thing.

For this very reason, words denoting forms (ākṛti) such as "cow," "horse," or "human"—which function as qualifiers—ultimately terminate in the individual body (piṇḍa) that is the qualified object; for the body is a qualifier of the conscious being because it is the body of that consciousness, and the conscious being, whose body is the individual form, is itself a qualifier of the Supreme Self. Thus, they ultimately terminate in the Supreme Self alone. Therefore, since the Supreme Self alone is the denoted meaning (vācya) of all words, their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with a word denoting the Supreme Self is indeed primary.

Now, an objection is raised: "In expressions such as *'khaṇḍo gauḥ'* (the spotted cow) and *'khaṇḍaḥ śuklaḥ'* (the white spotted one), we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between words denoting universals (*jāti*) and qualities (*guṇa*) and words denoting substances (*dravya*). However, when substances themselves function as qualifiers of another substance, the use of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) is observed—as in *'daṇḍī'* (staff-bearer) or *'kuṇḍalī'* (wearing earrings). This indicates that a word [denoting a universal or quality] does not extend its denotation up to the embodied substance (*śarīrin*). This is correct; for just as in the case of words denoting universals and qualities, this is established by the logic of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*."

When a certain category of entity exists solely as a mode (*prakāra*) [of another], its inseparable establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*), subsistence (*sthiti*), and cognition (*pratīti*)—since words denoting that [mode] denote a substance qualified by their own designatum—it is entirely appropriate for them to stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting that same substance as qualified by another attribute.

However, where a substance established independently (*pṛthaksiddha*) and residing in itself is only occasionally and in some cases conceived as a mode of another substance, there the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) is applied; thus [the distinction] is faultless.

Thus, because the individual soul (jīva), as qualified by the non-sentient (acid), is a mode of the Supreme Self (paramātman) by virtue of being His body, words such as "I" and "you"—which are specific designations for the individual soul—denote the Supreme Self alone; this is concluded through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "That thou art" (tat tvam asi). This being the case, the individual soul stands in the relation of a body toward the Supreme Self.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇye*): the intended meaning is "without depending on a possessive suffix. Regarding the phrase "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*): the meaning is that the probandum—namely, coreferentiality—occurs by transcending both those words denoting only a genus and those denoting only a quality. The point is that, in the case of coreferentiality independent of a possessive suffix, one must state a determinant that follows all instances of usage; however, the property of being either a genus or a quality is underinclusive (*avyāpta*).

"Non-separate" (*apṛthak*), and so forth. "Establishment" (*siddhi*) means existence (*sattā*), characterized by the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Abiding" (*sthiti*) refers to the word "non-separate," which is common to establishment and the rest. By the word "cognition" (*pratīti*), what is intended is that non-separate cognition is self-evident. The meaning is that the state of being a word denoting a thing whose sole nature is its mode (*prakāra*) is the cause for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*). The qualification "provided it is other than an abstracting term" (*niṣkarṣaka-śabda-anyatve sati*) is to be understood as the subject.

The meaning is as follows: "Thus it is faultless" means that it has been established as a valid probans (*prayojaka*)—one that excludes [the fallacies of] the staff, the earring, and so forth (which require a possessive suffix), and which conforms to all instances of usage without depending on a possessive suffix; therefore, there is no defect such as under-extension (*avyāpti*). By this, the intended refutation of the suspicion regarding the probative force of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) and other such arguments, as stated in the first sūtra, is presented.
That—because the objection has been refuted. "In this way" means by the previously explained method. "Withdrawn" refers to the continuation of that. 4 By means of the realizations (pratipatti)—dha.

Of some substance—either of a living being (jīva) or of the Supreme Self (paramātman)—which is the efficient cause (karaṇyaprayojaka): [this applies] to those words denoting it—sometimes [so]. (Notes: tha 12; bhā, vā 14; paramātmānaṃ 1; karaṇyaprayojakam – dha;
tadvācakānāṃ – ā, i, vā; kadācit-tha, dha.)

The suffix *matvarthīya* (denoting possession) is understood [in the sense of] "that which is fit for separate existence" (*pṛthaksiddhyarha*). Because they are specifications of the individual soul (*jīva*), the attributes residing in the individual soul do not touch the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is due to the logical connection (*anvaya*); just as attributes such as childhood, youth, and old age residing in one's own body do not touch the individual soul itself.

Therefore—in the case of the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi)—the word "That" denotes the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is the cause of the universe, whose will is true, who is the source of all auspicious qualities, and from whom every trace of what is to be discarded has been eliminated; and the word "thou" denotes that very same [Self] as having the embodied individual soul (jīva) as its body. Thus, this grammatical coordination is taken in its primary sense (mukhyavṛtta), it is not in conflict with the context, it is not in conflict with any of the Śrutis, and there is an absence of even a scent of defects such as ignorance (avidyā) in Brahman, who is faultless and consists solely of auspiciousness.

Therefore, even the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*), by way of [the soul] being a qualifier, brings about its very otherness; thus, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed other than the individual soul consisting of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*), namely the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
As it has been said:
"From this very Self..."
In this very context, it is understood that for the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), the Supreme Self alone is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*).
With reference to the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), the text says:
"Of that, this indeed is the embodied self; he who belongs to the former."

Thus: the meaning is that the embodied self of the preceding *annamaya* (consisting of food), which is established in another scriptural passage as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who is the ultimate cause, is indeed the embodied self of this *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath) as well.
This should be understood in the same way for the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) and the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness).
However, in the case of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the reference "this very same" is intended to show that its nature is non-different [from the Self]. How so?

According to the principle already stated, even for the one consisting of cognition (*vijñānamaya*), it has been understood that the embodied self is indeed the Supreme Self. This being the case, when it is said, "He who is the embodied self of the one consisting of cognition is the very same embodied self of the one consisting of bliss," it is understood that the one consisting of bliss—the Supreme Self whose status as the Supreme Self is known through repetition—is the Self of the Supreme Self itself.

Furthermore, because it is established by the sense of the passage that the bodies consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth are indeed bodies, the subsequent reference "of the former" (*yaḥ pūrvasya*) serves to fulfill its prior statement (*purovāda*). The two terms "established by another Śruti" and "being the supreme cause" (*paramakāraṇabhūta*), along with the demonstrative "He who" (*yaḥ*) used as a reference to something well-known, are intended to indicate both that this is established by another Śruti and that it is established by this very [present] treatise.
"To show" means that this reference is like [the passages] "the Lord of the self of the whole world," "no one rules over him," and "there is no other seer than he.
"How so? is a question seeking the logical justification for this. The meaning is: how does it serve to demonstrate that [the Self] has no other self?

Regarding the passage "of the former" heard in reference to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the term "of the one consisting of knowledge" (*vijñānamayasya*) is stated for the purpose of explaining the word "former. "By what was previously stated" refers to what was said concerning the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) and the others. "Is understood" [means as follows].

Because of the previous instruction that the bliss which has been practiced is related to Brahman in the passage, "Knowing the bliss of Brahman," and because Brahman is denoted by the word "bliss" in the statement, "Bliss is Brahman," and because the word "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is used in place of the word "bliss" in the passage, "Having entered this Self consisting of bliss," it follows that the words "bliss" (*ānanda*) and "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) are synonyms.

And thus, the entire collection of sentient and insentient entities distinct from oneself is one's own body; therefore, that alone is the *śārīra* (embodied) Self, free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). For this very reason, the learned declare: "The scripture which proceeds with reference to this Supreme Brahman is the *Śārīraka*. Consequently, the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), the Supreme Self, is indeed other than the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness), the individual soul (*jīva*). ||13||
He says: "This one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is not other than the individual soul (jīva), because of the hearing of the suffix *mayaṭ*, which denotes a modification;
for [the rule] states, 'The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in these two senses'."

Having stated this, it is recorded in the grammatical tradition that the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) after words beginning with "vṛddha" and "śara. This word "Ānanda" is indeed a "vṛddha" word.
But surely, the suffix *mayaṭ* is also used in the sense of abundance; for it is stated: "The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs when expressing that which constitutes the principal subject matter."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti; just as it is said,
"The sacrifice consists of food," so this very thing will come to pass.

"It is not so; for in the opening statement, 'consisting of food' (*annamaya*), the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) is observed. Therefore, by virtue of what is appropriate, it is proper that this [term *ānandamaya*] also has the sense of a modification alone. Furthermore, even if it were to mean 'abundance,' the distinctness from the individual soul (*jīva*) would not be established. To explain: when it is said 'abounding in bliss' (*ānandapracura*), the presence of suffering is unavoidable. For the abundance of bliss implies the scarcity of suffering. And the very nature of being an individual soul consists precisely in being mixed with suffering. Therefore, it is proper that the sense of modification, which follows from what is appropriate, is indeed correct."
Furthermore— in common usage, as in "made of clay," "made of gold," or "made of wood," and in the Veda,
such as "the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood" and "the *sruk* ladles are made of *śamī* wood."

In expressions such as "a girdle made of darbha grass" (*darbhamayī raśanā*), because the suffix *mayaṭ* is frequently used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), that very meaning first presents itself to the mind. And the state of being a modification of bliss certainly exists for the individual soul (*jīva*), since it is of the nature of bliss by its own essence; its state of transmigratory existence is precisely this [modification]. The point is that even if the sense of "modification" were accepted, it is untenable in your view as well, because a modification is impossible in the case of the individual self.

"It is not so," he replies by means of the principle of "predominance" (*agryaprāyanyāya*). This is because of the observation at the beginning [of the chapter]. Because of propriety—that is, because it is appropriate to accept what was established at the outset. Regarding the phrase "of bliss": since its nature consists in abundance, when a correlative is required, the smallness inherent in suffering—which is well-known as being associated with pleasure—is taken as that correlative; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, even though there is abundance, the difference from the individual soul (*jīva*) is established.

In the Veda, there is a sequential order: "The sacrificial material is made of *śamī* wood," and "The offering-ladles (*srucaḥ*) are made of *śamī* wood"; thus, that [usage] must be sought as the basis for this. The use of the suffix *-tara* in the word *prathamataram* is intended to exclude the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), since it occurs frequently even in the sense of a constituent part (*avayava*).

"It is merely a modification (*vikāra*)"—because of the hearing of the suffix *mayaṭ*, which denotes a modification, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is not distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*).
Having restated this, he refutes it: "If it be said that [Brahman is not the cause] because of the word 'modification,' no; because of abundance (prācurya). (1.1.14)
This is not correct; why?

Because of abundance—the abundance of bliss (*ānanda*) in the supreme Brahman. Furthermore, because the suffix *mayaṭ* can be used in the sense of abundance. What is meant is this: since it is impossible for bliss, when practiced in a sequence of hundredfold increments, to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus, it is determined that "this bliss has Brahman as its locus. Since no modification (*vikāra*) is possible in that Brahman, and since the application of the suffix *mayaṭ* is possible even in the sense of abundance, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is the supreme Brahman.

"It is indeed a modification of that" means that for that [Self], which is by nature of the form of bliss (*ānanda*), its state as a living being (*jīvatva*) consists in its connection with conditions such as suffering; therefore, the living being is a modification of bliss. The statement regarding its eternity and so forth is made with reference to its essential nature as bliss.
The expression "having restated" is used because the doubt is easily resolved.
"This is not tenable" is said with the intention that the second *nañ* (negation) negates the validity of the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣimatasyopapannatvam*).

"Regarding the sense of abundance (*prācuryārtha*): the meaning is that there is not merely the existence of the sense of abundance, but also a required etymological power (*śabdaśakti*) [of the word]. Regarding "of that which is being repeated" (*abhyasyamānasya*): the connection with the bliss being repeated is intended to indicate other reasons as well, which appear in the subsequent sūtras. Regarding "due to the impossibility of modification" (*vikārāsambhavāt*): the meaning is that the unsuitability [of the Self] for having the sense of modification is the reason."

Due to propriety and the established usage of the suffix *mayaṭ*, its meaning as "modification" (*vikāra*) is not possible here because it would contradict the sense of the passage. Furthermore, propriety is already abandoned in the case of *prāṇamaya* itself, since the meaning of "modification" is impossible there. Therefore, in that context, the state of being "composed of breath" (*prāṇamayatva*) belongs to the fivefold wind merely by virtue of possessing the function of breath; or else, it is due to the predominance of the breath-function among the five functions, namely prāṇa, apāna, and so forth. Nor is there a lack of established usage for the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), as seen in examples such as "the sacrifice is composed of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*) and "the journey is composed of carts" (*śakaṭamayī yātrā*).
Because this is seen in such passages as these:
as for what was stated— that the abundance of bliss implies the existence of only a small amount of suffering— [that is not so].

That is incorrect; for "abundance of that" means its predominance. And that [predominance] does not imply the existence of the other, but rather excludes its scarcity. The existence or non-existence of the other, however, must be determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In this case, its absence is understood through another means of knowledge, namely by the passage beginning with "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*). In that context, it is only in this sense that [the term] "scarcity" is required.

It must be stated: "The abundance of the bliss of Brahman is what is being expressed by the other [texts], such as 'That is one human bliss' and so forth; compared to the bliss of the individual soul (*jīva*), the bliss of Brahman is in a state of unsurpassed excellence—it is abundant."

As for what was said—that the individual soul (*jīva*) can be a modification (*vikāra*) of bliss—that too is untenable; for the individual soul, whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is knowledge and bliss (*jñānānanda*), to undergo a transformation (*pariṇāma*) into some form—like clay into the form of a jar or the like—is contradicted by all Śruti, Smṛti, and reason. However, it will be established later that during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), "knowledge and bliss are contracted" due to "karma. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is other than the individual soul; it is the Supreme Brahman. || 14 ||
[Śrī Bhāṣya 1.1.15] For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other than the individual soul (jīva); it is the supreme Brahman.
And because of the designation of its cause. (1.1.15)
"For who indeed could breathe, who could inhale, if this bliss were not present in the ether? For he alone causes bliss.

Thus, it is designated as the cause of bliss for living beings, in that he alone brings bliss to the living beings. Therefore, it is understood that this *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), the one who causes bliss, is distinct from the living being who is to be caused bliss; that is, the Supreme Self. Furthermore, it will be stated immediately thereafter that "the *ānandamaya* itself is what is denoted here by the word 'bliss'. ||15||

Regarding the phrase "taddhetu" (the cause of that): by this, the previously mentioned abundance of bliss (*ānanda-prācurya*) is also established. For the capacity to bestow liberation, which is otherwise difficult to achieve, is indeed the ultimate cause of bliss. Furthermore, just as a man who possesses abundant wealth gives to another the wealth desired by him—this is the immediate sequence of the Sūtra. By the words "from another" (*anyāt*) and "for living beings" (*prāṇyāt*), it is stated that [Brahman] is the cause of the happiness of enjoyment and liberation; or rather, its causality with respect to existence and its causality with respect to happiness have been stated. The correct meaning is precisely what was stated previously.

"And for this reason" means that the conclusion is that the identity of the object and the agent is not possible. "The one consisting of bliss alone" means that it is the one denoted by the word *ānanda* (bliss) whose nature as a giver of bliss has been stated, but not the one *consisting of* bliss (*ānandamaya*). ||15||

[The blissful one is the Supreme Self: For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss is other than the individual soul; and he is celebrated as being exactly the one described in the words of the mantra. 1.1.16.

It is proclaimed that Brahman itself, as described in the Vedic mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). That, however, is the supreme Brahman, distinct from the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). For it is said: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

Thus, Brahman is indicated as the goal to be attained by the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding the phrase "this [verse] was recited concerning that": "that" refers to Brahman; having brought it before one's mind—that is, having taken it up as the subject to be explained—the *ṛc* itself is meant to provide clarity regarding that meaning through this "mantra" for those who study it.
It has been stated that the Brahman to be attained by the living soul, the worshipper, is indeed distinct from it. And immediately thereafter:
"From this very Self, indeed, ether was produced."

Beginning with this, that very point is further clarified by subsequent Brahmana passages and mantras. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is distinct from the individual soul (jīva). || 16 ||
To this, he recites the following: "Not the other, because of impossibility" (1.1.17).
The one denoted by the term *jīva*, being other than the Supreme Self, does not even in its state of liberation become the one described in the mantra-text. Why? Because it is untenable.
For such a self, unconditioned omniscience (*vipaścitva*) is not possible. Indeed, this very [omniscience] is the unconditioned omniscience, as expressed in:
"He desired, 'May I be many; may I procreate.'"

Thus, it will be explained by demonstrating his nature as one whose volition is true. For "vipaścit" means "one who sees in various ways. The word "vipaścit" is derived by eliding the syllable "ya" from the root "paśyat," according to the rule for words such as "pṛṣodara.
Furthermore, regarding this "vipaścit" who is known through the wording of the mantra:

Beginning with the words "He desired," that which will be described—such as the creation, maintenance, and the state of being the inner self of the world brought about by His own volition—is clearly distinct from the essential nature of the liberated self. || 17 ||
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other than the inner self (pratyagātman) in both states;
and because of the designation of difference. 1.1.18.

Beginning with the words, "From this very Self, indeed, ether [arose]," the passage that reveals the Brahman described in the mantra-text designates its distinction even from the individual soul (jīva), just as it did from food, breath, and mind: "Different from this [self] consisting of cognition, indeed, is the inner Self consisting of bliss. Therefore, because of this designation of difference from the individual soul, it is known that this "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) described in the mantra-text is indeed something other [than the jīva]. ||18||

Regarding the phrase "kiñca" (furthermore), by this another point—the impossibility of [the Lord's] omniscience—is stated. This sūtra is supplementary to the previous one (māntravarṇika-sūtra) because it aims to refute the charge of the reason stated therein being otherwise established; since it does not intend to present an independent reason, the word "ca" (and) is not employed. || 17 ||

"From this [it follows]" (*itaśca*). Thus, by these two sūtras, the reason situated at the beginning has been connected. Now, he connects the clearer reason located in the middle with the immediately following sūtra. That the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) was established in the first sūtra through its connection with unsurpassed bliss, which is denoted by the word ending in the suffix *mayaḥ* within a portion of its own statement. Therefore, the reason residing in its own statement is also stated here: "Because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśāt*).
If the nature of the individual self were Brahman in its pure state, then [the distinction] would be like that of the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth.

The one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other [than the individual soul]—this is understood from the commentary (bhā.). For this reason also, the one consisting of bliss is other than the individual soul; "for this reason also" means that the one consisting of bliss is other than the individual soul.
And [the scripture] teaches his union with Him in this [state]. (1.1.20)
In this one consisting of bliss, the scripture teaches the "union with that" of this living being—that is, union with bliss—stating:
"He is indeed essence; for having obtained that very essence, he becomes blissful."

Thus, when it is stated that "this one who is designated by the word *jīva* becomes blissful through the attainment of that which is denoted by the word *rasa*," what sane person would say: "That by whose attainment one becomes blissful is that very thing [itself]"? This is the meaning.

Thus, when it has been determined that "the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the supreme Brahman," then in such passages as "that which is this space is bliss" and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," the word "bliss" (ānanda) refers precisely to the one consisting of bliss; just as [it refers to the self] by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna).
It consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). For this very reason, there is the designation of distinction in the passage: "Knowing bliss as Brahman. And for this very reason, "...".
"Ānanda, 'it approaches the self consisting of bliss'— this is the declaration of the fruit.
And in the subsequent section, [there is a reference] to those previously mentioned in the preceding section, beginning with that consisting of food."
"He understood: 'Food is Brahman. He understood: 'Breath is Brahman. He understood: 'Mind is Brahman.
He understood: 'Consciousness is Brahman.'"

Because it is established thus, even the statement "Bliss is Brahman" is understood to be a teaching regarding the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) alone; and for that very reason, in that context as well, [the text says] "having approached the Self consisting of bliss."
Thus it has been concluded.

Therefore, it is established that the "Supreme Brahman" is a distinct entity from that which is denoted by the term "Pradhāna," and is likewise a distinct entity from the reality denoted by the term "Jīva. || 20 || ||20||
The section on the internal [organ] (antar-adhikaraṇa). ||1-1-7||
[The meaning of the section: Even the status of being an object of meditation by virtue of residing within the eye belongs not to a particular individual soul (*jīva*), but to the Supreme Self alone.

Although such things as "the creation of the world through desire," "the possession of extraordinary bliss," and "being the cause of fear and fearlessness" are not possible for individual souls of meager merit, they are certainly possible for those of distinguished merit, such as Āditya, Indra, Prajāpati, and so forth. To refute this doubt, [the Sūtra states]:
"On account of the teaching of attributes belonging to Him who is within. (1.1.21)
This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"That golden person who is seen within the sun, with a golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to his very nails."

The meaning intended in the introductory passage beginning with "even though" (*yadyapi*) is as follows: although the doubt that [the one in the cave] is the individual soul (*jīva*) was previously dispelled in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) because only a mere connection with the body was heard, a new doubt regarding its being the *jīva* might arise again through the perception of a specific relationship characterized by the relation of instrument and agent (*upakaraṇopakaraṇitva*) with a specific body possessing a particular configuration such as hands and feet; therefore, this section is commenced as a supplement to the section on the "Consisting of Bliss" (*ānandamaya*) for the purpose of dispelling that doubt. This is the sense intended in the introductory text beginning with "even though."

Regarding the phrase "He who is this": because it is designated as something already well-known, one should not suspect that it is merely a restatement (anuvāda), for this matter has not been established by any other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). It is like the statement, "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni. The word *āditya* [is used] because the Supreme Self, who is golden and resides within the sun and the eye, is inferred from such attributes as being risen above all evil.
3. These and other such [passages]—Ā. 4. [They] occur—Bhā:
"As the lotus flower is like the afterglow of a monkey (*kapyāsa*), so are his two eyes; his name is 'Ut'. He has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils."
"Of him, the *ṛc* and the *sāman* are the two joints... thus with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the self:

that person who is seen within the eye—he is indeed the *ṛc*, he is the *sāman*, he is the *uktha*, he is the *yajus*, he is the *brahman*. Of this very one, the form is the same as the form of that [celestial being]; whatever the joints of that are, those are his joints; whatever the name of that is, that is his name."
Thus [it is said].

In this regard, a doubt arises: is this person dwelling within the orb of the eye and the sun, possessing sovereignty caused by the accumulation of merit and denoted by such terms as "Āditya" and so forth, merely the individual soul (jīva); or rather, is it the Supreme Self (paramātman) distinct from that?
What is logical?
That it is the very soul (*jīva*) that has accumulated merit.
Why?
Because of the scriptural statement regarding "possessing a body. For the connection with a body is possible only for individual souls (jīvas).
Indeed, the connection with a body is for the sake of union with merit, demerit, pleasure, and pain. The state of liberation is described as being attained through bodilessness.
For this very reason, it is said of one who is free from connection with karma:
"Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain;
but for one who is truly bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, through an excellence of merit (*puṇya*), an excellence of knowledge and an excellence of power (*śakti*) are possible. For this very reason, his status as the Lord of the World, the Lord of Desire, and so forth, is appropriate for him alone. From that same source follows his being the object of worship (*upāsyatva*), his being the bestower of fruits (*phaladāyitva*), and his utility for liberation (*mokṣopayogitva*) by virtue of his capacity to destroy sins (*pāpakṣapaṇa*). Even among humans, some who have accumulated merit are seen to be superior in terms of knowledge, power, and other qualities; from them come the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and others; from them the gods; and from them Indra and the rest. Therefore, [the Lord] is one among those beginning with Brahmā.

There is a fourfold doubt as to whether [the body] makes known its distinction from both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the evolutes (prākṛta), or not; these are the other established conclusions (siddhāntas).

In this context, the preceding sections are the prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣas*); within these prima facie views, the relationship between cause and effect is as follows: the word "evil" (*pāpman*) refers merely to sin; "removal" (*apahati*) means destruction; the prohibition of birth does not concern birth rooted in karma; and the body (*vigraha*) is not distinct from that of ordinary beings.

At that time, since it is impossible for the connection with a body to be based on mere will, and since it is impossible for such a connection to exist in another [the Supreme Self] due to its being dependent on karma, the Person residing within the sun and so forth must be the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because of the consistency with the *antarāditya* passage, and because even in the *Ānandavallī* passage, the *Ānandavallī* teaches the individual soul; thus, all passages concerning the cause refer to the individual soul who has accumulated a preeminent store of merit.

In the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), the relationship between the cause and the effect is as follows: when the word *pāpman* refers solely to karma; when the word *apahṛta* refers to absolute non-existence; when the negation of birth refers to birth rooted in karma; and when the body (*vigraha*) is distinct from that of ordinary beings; then, because such a body exists by His will and because it is possible for it to belong to the Supreme rather than the individual soul (*jīva*), the Person dwelling within the eye and the sun is the Supreme. Since this is consistent with the [Upanishadic] unity of meaning, the status of the Supreme Self for that which is propounded in the Ānandavallī is unshakable; and due to this unanimity, all statements concerning the Cause refer to the Supreme Self.

"From this very reason" means: since the connection with a body has as its purpose the experience of pleasure and pain rooted in karma, liberation—which is devoid of the connection with karma—is said to be attained through the state of being bodiless (*aśarīratā*).

"Even among humans" refers here to such passages as, "That is one human bliss.
