"By accumulated merit" means that scriptural texts such as "having shaken off evil" (*apahatapāpman*) do not speak of a state of being independent of karma; rather, they refer to one who possesses a body caused solely by merit.

Thus, in each successive kalpa, by means of a particular excellence of merit (*puṇyaviśeṣa*), he attains such sovereignty and even performs the creation of the world and so forth; therefore, the scriptural passages concerning his being the cause of the world and the inner self of the world apply to this very one who has accumulated a particular excellence of merit, who is omniscient and omnipotent. Consequently, there is no such thing as a Supreme Self (*paramātman*) distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). This being the case, [the scripture says]:
"Neither gross, nor subtle, nor short..."

Statements such as these have the *jīvātman*’s own nature as their intended meaning; likewise, the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*) are devoted to teaching that very nature and the means for its attainment—as in:
"This one has risen above all evils."

This is taught by the passage beginning with "ityādi. Indeed, "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) means being "struck away" from karma—that is, being devoid even of the slightest trace of subjection to karma. For individual souls (*jīvas*) are subject to karma by virtue of their participation in pleasure and pain dependent upon karma. Therefore, freedom from evil is an attribute belonging exclusively to the Supreme Self, who is other than the individual soul. Preceding that [freedom from evil] are such attributes as "lordship over the worlds and desires," which is based on His own essential nature (*svarūpa*), as well as "truthfulness of resolve" and so forth, and "being the inner self of all beings"—all of which are attributes belonging to Him alone. As it is said:
"This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true.
Likewise:
"This is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa."
Thus:

"He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and so forth. Such qualities as the capacity for the creation of all sentient and non-sentient beings preceded by His will of truth (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), being the cause of fear and fearlessness without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), being beyond the limitations imposed by speech and mind, and the possession of unsurpassed and unsurpassable bliss—these natural attributes, which cannot be accomplished through action, are not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*).

In the sections concerning the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it indicates the well-known usage of the word "sin" (*pāpa*) as referring to both merit and demerit. Furthermore, since the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) consists in being a means to undesirable results while being non-worldly (*alaukika*), it is logical that even "merit" (*puṇya*) can be designated by the term "sin. The expression "one whose sins have been destroyed" (*apahatapāpman*), because it is used without restriction, declares that [the Self] inherently possesses the power to destroy sins both within itself and in others; thus, its nature as being opposed to all that is to be abandoned (*heyapratyanīkatva*) is established. "Preceded by that," and so forth.

The meaning is that it is "intrinsic" because it is preceded by the state of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*). Thus, when two meanings—one well-known and one not—are possible as having a single underlying cause, the fact that they are denoted by a single word expressing the well-known meaning has been demonstrated here.

Because the one residing within the sun is recognized here through its association with the quality of being "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*), which is taught in the *Ānandavallī*, the *Daharavidyā*, and the *Subālopaniṣad*, the qualities mentioned in those various places are intended to be the attributes of this very Golden Person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*). With this intention, His nature as having "true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and so forth, as well as His state as the inner self of all beings (*sarvabhūtāntarātmatva*), are stated. The scriptural passage "This is the Self" refers to His possession of true resolve and other qualities preceded by freedom from evil; the passage "This is all... refers to His state as the inner self of all beings preceded by those same qualities.

Regarding the phrase "He desired": being the cause of the universe is indeed the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, which is known through the Vedāntas. As for the objection that if it is a cause, then—due to its connection with a body—it cannot be distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), we reply:

that is not so; for possessing a body does not necessarily entail subjection to karma, since even one whose resolve is true (*satyasaṅkalpa*) may have a connection with a body by the mere force of his will.

Now, it might be argued: what is called the "body" is an aggregate of elements that are transformations of *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*. Connection with such a body is not possible by the mere "will" of the Person (*puruṣa*), who is free from evil and whose resolve is true; for [such a connection] would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārthatvāt*). However, for one who is subject to karma and ignorant of his own true nature, connection with the body is unavoidable—even against his will—for the sake of experiencing the fruits corresponding to his karma. Thus [it is said].

"This might be so," [one might object], "if his body were composed of the three *guṇas* and thus material (*prākṛta*). But since it is 'conformable to His own will' and 'conformable to Himself,' it is indeed non-material (*aprākṛta*); therefore, everything is consistent. This is what is meant: in the Supreme Brahman alone—who is distinct from all else by virtue of being the sole essence of infinite knowledge and bliss, opposed to every form of evil—there exist natural, unimpeded, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitudes of auspicious qualities.

If "having true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpa*) is [the attribute], it is preceded by being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*). And that serves as a means of recognition for the identity with Nārāyaṇa, because of its agreement with the *Subālopaniṣad*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "for not," the intention is that, in a matter where scripture alone is the authority, an inference based on worldly correlations cannot establish subjection to karma. He states that the "one of true resolve" is established otherwise.

The word "consisting of the three guṇas" indicates that [the self] is to be abandoned, because it is said: "Sattva is light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. The phrase "of one who is ignorant of its own true nature" refers to the cause for the performance of karma.

The passage beginning with "This has been said" is commenced for the purpose of removing the following doubt: Since He who is inherently omniscient and omnipotent does not depend on instruments for the sake of knowledge or activity, He would have no need for a body. Furthermore, if He possessed form and other qualities, He would be subject to material nature (*prākṛta*). If He were eternal, multiple and occasional incarnations would be impossible. And if He assumed the forms of animals and so forth, there would be a connection with karma rooted in those births, according to the principle that "by non-verbal acts one attains the state of birds or beasts. To resolve this doubt, it is said: "Of the Supreme alone. Just as the essential nature of the Supreme Brahman is His own inherent [qualities]...

In the very same way, her divine form—which is conceived as having a single nature corresponding to one's own desires—is also natural, being a treasury of an infinite multitude of qualities such as divine, wonderful, eternal, irreproachable, unsurpassed brilliance, beauty, fragrance, delicacy, charm, youth, and so forth.

By favoring His devotees, He assumes various forms according to their respective paths of practice—He who is an ocean of boundless compassion, gentleness, affection, magnanimity, and sovereignty; from whom every trace of that which is to be abandoned has been removed; who is free from all evil; the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama, Nārāyaṇa.

In such passages as "From which indeed these beings are born," "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and "In the beginning, there was indeed only Nārāyaṇa—neither Brahmā nor Īśāna"—the Supreme Brahman is understood to be the sole cause of the entire universe. Furthermore, in such passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" and "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss," its nature is understood to be of such a character. [It is] "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa).
"Stainless"—"free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst; whose desires are true and whose resolves are true";

"for him there exists neither effect nor instrument, and no one is seen equal or superior to him; his supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are inherent"; "Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords, Him, the supreme Deity of deities."

"He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him. "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth.

"All moments of time were born from the luminous Puruṣa," and so forth—in these passages, having denied that the Supreme Brahman possesses natural, rejectable qualities or a connection with a natural, rejectable body, as well as subjection to karma rooted therein, they declare His auspicious qualities and auspicious form.

This very form is indeed his own essential nature (*svābhāvika*); yet, out of compassion for his devotees, the Blessed One, who is supremely merciful, assumes by his own will forms corresponding to their perception, such as the bodies of gods, humans, and so forth. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "Though unborn, he is born in many ways.
And the Smṛti says:
"Though he is unborn and of imperishable self, though he is the Lord of all beings..."

"Abiding in my own nature, I manifest through my own *māyā*. For the protection of the virtuous and for the destruction of the wicked. [From the word] *vidyutaḥ*—meaning "from the color of lightning. This is because it is appropriate to accept a meaning consistent with such statements as "having the color of the sun" (*ādityavarṇam*) or "having the color of gold" (*rukmavarṇam*). Furthermore, the body that has the color of the sun is not material (*prākṛta*), according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that it is "beyond darkness" (*tamasaḥ parastāt*). For *tamas* (darkness) is indeed the extremely subtle primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Thus, the distinction from its effects is established.

Otherwise, it would be stating that the nature of *tamas* is different from itself; in that case, the suffix *-tāt* in the word "parastāt" (beyond) and the description of its being "of the color of the sun" would be redundant. Therefore, since the absence of contact with *tamas* is stated specifically of that which is qualified by a form (*vigraha*), the distinctiveness of that form is established. [The phrase] "prākṛta-heya" and so forth implies: "For a negation occurs only of something that exists in some place."

Therefore, the presence of qualities to be prohibited and abandoned within *prakṛti* and the individual souls (*jīvas*) conjoined with it is indicated by the word "prākṛta" and so forth. Since a specific injunction regarding a body is observed, the general prohibition of a body must refer to something other than that [specific one], just as in the case of "one should not kill" (which excludes the sacrificial animal) or "without qualities" (which refers to the Supreme). Because a specific prohibition is observed, a general prohibition of the body results in a specific application, just like the word "animal" in the phrase "one should sacrifice with an animal," and like the word "without qualities. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the term "supremely compassionate": the fact that [the Lord] shares the same class of being (*sājātya*) with gods and others is not caused by *karma*; the meaning is that it is for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees (*upāsaka*).

By the phrase "not being born" (*ajāyamāna*), there is a negation of birth in the form of association with a material body for the sake of pleasure and so forth, which is caused by *karma*. And by the phrase "He is born in many ways," there is an injunction regarding birth in the form of association with a non-material body for the purpose of protecting the world, caused by His own will. One must accept that this scripture has as its subject matter the incarnations (*avatāra*); only if this is the case will the consistency with the corroborative passages (*apabṛṃhaṇa*) such as "though He is unborn" be established.

Thus [it is said]. For the devotees (upāsakas) are indeed the virtuous; their protection alone is the primary objective. However, the destruction of the wicked is merely incidental, since that is accomplished even by a mere resolve. "To his own nature" (prakṛtim svām): "nature" (prakṛti) means inherent disposition (svabhāva). The meaning is: "abiding in His own inherent disposition, and not in the disposition of those subject to transmigratory existence.
"By His own power of illusion" (ātmamāyayā). 3.
The meaning is: "by means of knowledge in the form of His own volition.

Lexicographers record that the word *māyā* is a synonym for *jñāna* (knowledge), as in the statement: "*māyā*, *vayuna*, and *jñāna* [are synonyms]. And the venerable Parāśara said: "O King, in whom all these powers are established..."
"That form of Viśvarūpa is different from its lack of uniformity; it is another, great form of Hari. "O Lord of Men, He creates forms consisting of all powers."

"Those known as divine, sacred, and human [forms] possess movement through their own sport; for the benefit of the worlds, they are not born from the cause of karma. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Mahābhārata*, the non-material nature (*aprākṛtatva*) even of the form of the incarnation is stated: "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an aggregate of elements. Therefore, since the Supreme Brahman alone possesses such a form, this [form] is also His very attribute. [The one] residing in the solar orb and the eyes is none other than the Supreme Self, distinct from the individual souls (*jīva*) such as those of the sun and others. ||21||
Therefore, [the following is stated]: "And because of the designation of difference from the beginning, [He] is other. (1.1.22)
The distinction of this Supreme Self from the individual souls, such as those in the sun and others, is declared:

"He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within"; and "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, who controls the self from within."
Thus:
"He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), of whom the Imperishable is the body, whom the Imperishable does not know;
he who moves within Death (mṛtyu), of whom Death is the body, whom Death does not know."

And [the text] says: "This is Nārāyaṇa, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God. Thus, having designated all individual souls (*jīvas*) as the body of this supreme self who is free from evil, it designates him as their inner self. Therefore, it is established that the supreme self is indeed other than all individual souls, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha. ||22||
Thus ends the section concerning disappearance (Antaradhikaraṇa). ||7||
The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa) ||1-1-8||
From the statement, “from which indeed these beings are born,” it is understood that Brahman is the cause of the world.
When the inquiry arises as to what that cause of the world is:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"; "It created fire"; "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."

When the cause of the world is indicated by common terms such as, "He created these worlds," and "From this very Self, indeed, space was produced," it has been stated that it is Brahman— distinct from Pradhāna, the individual soul (kṣetrajña), and so forth— because of its specific nature consisting of the qualities of seeing, bliss, and form.

Now, even in those doctrines that designate [the cause] by specific terms such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) while asserting its causality of the world and its sovereignty over the world, it is established that Brahman—defined by the aforementioned characteristics—is indeed the very same entity denoted by the terms "ether" and so forth, which is well-known as consisting of both the sentient and the insentient; this is demonstrated in the remainder of the chapter beginning with the sūtra, "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśas talliṅgāt*).
[The word "ether" (ākāśa) denotes Brahman] because of its characteristic mark [as found in scripture]. 1.1.23.
This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"What is the goal of this world? "Space," he replied.
"Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone; they dissolve back into space. Space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort."
Thus [it is said].
What is obtained? The well-known ether.
Why?

In a matter that is to be understood solely through scripture (*śabda*), whatever meaning is established by linguistic convention and perceived by the word must be accepted as such. Therefore, it is the well-known ether (*ākāśa*) alone that is the cause of the entire collection of moving and unmoving beings. Consequently, Brahman is not something distinct from that [ether].

[Objection: But was it not stated that Brahman is distinct from the insentient and from the individual soul (jīva) on account of [the texts describing] creation preceded by reflection and so forth? [Reply: It is true that this was stated; however, it is incorrect.
For instance, when it is said, "That from which these beings are born... that is Brahman," there arises an expectation for specific details such as, "From what are these beings born?

Since a specific [cause] is understood from passages such as, "All these beings indeed arise from Ākāśa alone," and once it is determined that "Ākāśa alone is the cause of the world's birth and so forth," [one might object that the term *sat* in] "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" [refers to Ākāśa].
In these and other such passages, words such as "existent" (*sat*) and so forth possess a common form, yet they denote that very same particularity, namely, space (*ākāśa*).

Likewise, in passages such as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," the word "Self" (*ātman*) also applies to that very thing. For even its exclusive nature as consciousness is not possible [in that context], just as one says "a jar is made of clay. Furthermore, by the etymological derivation "it pervades, therefore it is the Self," the word "Self" applies all the more to space as well.

Therefore, when it has been thus determined that "Brahman, the cause, is indeed space (*ākāśa*)," [the objection] "But [how can there be] seeing and so forth? arises. Because of the contradiction in meaning, the meaning established by conventional usage (*vyutpatti*) is abandoned. By the word "and so forth" (*ityādi*), the expectation—"What do they go toward? By what do they live?"—is intended to be expressed. Regarding the phrase "because of the perception of a specific [meaning]," the perception of a specific reality through this specific sentence is stated as the reason. Regarding the phrase "when it has been determined": the meaning is that when it has been determined that "Brahman, described in the sentences characterized as restatements of the cause understood from the *Sadvidyā* and other passages, is indeed space."

"Common forms" means having a common nature. The maxim "Or the goat [is meant] because of the wording of the mantra" is intended here. In that very context—"in space alone"—the meaning is that the word *ātman* is also common with respect to the word *ākāśa*. Regarding the term "attains" (*āpnoti*): even by the etymological power of the components of the word *ātman*, it refers to *ākāśa*. The sense is that while the word *ākāśa* has a fixed conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*), its conventional force would have to be set aside; however, it is more appropriate to set aside the conventional force of the word *ātman*, which possesses a conventional power applicable to multiple meanings.

"Beholding and so forth. The meaning is that because of the superior authority of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) must be interpreted in conformity with it. For if, in the event of a requirement for a specific detail, [it is] not determined—[this is from] the *Śrībhāṣya* 1.1.8.

Those [qualities] consistent with that [nature of Brahman] are to be described as secondary (gauṇa). For if the cause had been expressed by common terms such as "Being" (sat) and so forth, then, in accordance with the meaning of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and other such qualities, it would have been determined that a specific conscious being alone is the cause. But since the word "ether" (ākāśa) determines a specific entity, there is no need for a conclusion to be reached based on the inherent nature of the meaning.
But is it not the case that from the statement, "From the Self, space was produced," the fact that space is also an effect is understood?

True; for all things, such as ether, air, and so forth, there are two states: the subtle state and the gross state. Among these, the subtle state of ether is the cause, while its gross state is the effect. The statement, "From the Self, ether was produced," means that from its own subtle form, it itself became manifest in a gross form.

"Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone," because of the scriptural hearing that the origin and dissolution of the entire world proceed from space alone; thus, by such statements, [the author] establishes the superior strength of the mention of the word "space" over words such as "Being" (sat) and so forth, on the grounds that it determines that "that very thing is the cause, Brahman. The sense is that this applies even through common terms, provided there is no other specific term [to the contrary]. [The phrase] "But by the word 'space'" [is used].

According to the maxim that "conventional meaning (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological meaning (yoga)," since the conventional sense is the object of immediate cognition, it must be accepted over even an etymologically derived sense that is apprehended with delay. Because words such as *sat* (Being) depend upon the consideration of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), their application is delayed; whereas the word *ākāśa* (Ether), being more powerful due to its swift application, establishes the required specific [meaning] through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Since there is no other specific [meaning] to be determined by the nature of the thing itself, "seeing" and the other qualities must conform to that [meaning of Ether].
They are to be described; therefore, the meaning is that the status of being a cause characterized by consciousness is not established.
Regarding the word "nanu": the underlying doubt is that it is logically inconsistent for that which is understood as an effect to be the ultimate cause.

Regarding "satyam": there is acceptance of its being an effect, but there is no admission that this status would preclude its being a cause. The mention of air (*vāyu*) and so forth serves as an illustration. By the term "subtle state" (*sūkṣmāvasthā*), the state of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is meant. In the statement "from the Self, space [arose]," the word "Self" (*ātman*) refers to itself [the Supreme Self].

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "origin and dissolution, etc.," its role as the cause of persistence through the provision of space is expressed; for it is stated here that it is the "final resort" (*parāyaṇam*).

Since Brahman is thus not distinct from the well-known ether (ākāśa), for this very reason such scriptural indications as "If this ether were not bliss" and "The ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form" are even more appropriately established. Therefore, Brahman is not distinct from the well-known ether.

This being the case, we reply: "Ākāśa [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark. That which is denoted by the word "Ākāśa" is an entity distinct from the well-known, insentient ether; it is none other than the Supreme Self, characterized as previously described.
Why?

On account of its characteristic marks. For characteristic marks of the Supreme Self are found here, such as being the sole cause of the entire universe, being greater than all, and being the ultimate refuge. Indeed, the status of being the cause of the entire universe is not possible for insentient matter, which is what is commonly denoted by the word "ether" (ākāśa); nor is it possible for sentient beings, because they themselves are effects [of that cause]. Furthermore, the status of being the ultimate refuge means being the supreme goal to be attained by sentient beings; and that is not possible for insentient matter, which is opposed to all human purposes.

Furthermore, "being superior to all" means being "unconditioned"—that is, possessing unsurpassed excellence over all others by virtue of all auspicious qualities. That too is not possible for the non-conscious [insentient].

By the word "and so forth" (*evamādi*), the following scriptural passages are intended: "Brahman is Ka, Brahman is Kha," "They told him of breath and of that space," and "Established in the highest heaven."

"Thus" means as in the preceding section; however, here it is not stated as "because of the teaching of its attributes," but rather as "because of its characteristic mark" (*talliṅgāt*), because what is intended as the reason is an object already established in another scriptural passage and now being restated. For a "characteristic mark" (*liṅga*) is indeed that which is perceived through another means of knowledge as being connected to a particular subject. Regarding the word "all," the term "entire" (*nikhila*) is used with the intention that the meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) is not restricted.

The word "jagat" (world) is used to exclude the possibility that the word "bhūta" refers merely to the four elements beginning with air. The intention is that by stating [the Lord] is the cause of all beings (*sarvabhūta*), it is implied that He is the cause of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of both the sentient and the insentient. In this context, because no other efficient cause is heard and because of consistency with other scriptural passages, His status as the "sole cause" is stated with the intention of encompassing every kind of causality, including being both the efficient and the material cause. By the word "nikhila" (entire), the impossibility of space (*ākāśa*) being the sole cause is also intended.

For space cannot be an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). The phrase "because it is insentient" means that, due to its insentience, it is not included within [the nature of] the Self's own essence, and thus it is something to be abandoned. The word "entire" (*sakala*) means that liberation is the direct goal of all persons; the meaning is that [space] is opposed to that [liberation] by being a cause of bondage.

As for what was stated—that when there is a desire for a specific cause of the world, because the word "ether" (ākāśa) provides that specific [cause], everything else must be described as conforming to it—that is incorrect; for [the scripture says]:
"All these beings, indeed, arise from ether alone."

This is because of the reference as if [the term] were already well-known (*prasiddhavannirdeśāt*). A reference as if well-known indeed presupposes the attainment [of the object] through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And the other means of knowledge are precisely such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*). Since those [passages] establish Brahman in the manner just described, that Brahman established by them is referred to by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) as if it were already well-known. Furthermore, it is possible for the supreme Brahman to be denoted by the word "ether," because it illuminates; for [Brahman] "shines forth" (*ākāśate*) and "causes to shine forth" (*ākāśayati*).

Furthermore, by this word "ether" (ākāśa), which—though capable of conveying a specific distinction—is denoting a non-conscious particularity that cannot possibly possess the status of being a cause with respect to the conscious element, [the text] states:
"It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

Thus, the subversion of the meaning of the sentence—which is capable of establishing a previously unestablished subject matter characterized by omniscience, the realization of true intentions (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), and so forth, as determined by the supplementary passages such as "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—does not ascend to the rank of valid authority (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, the general consistency of a single sentence, which is capable of establishing a previously unestablished subject matter qualified by numerous unprecedented attributes, cannot be set aside by a single statement that merely appears to be a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Those specific scriptural passages such as, "He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? and "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" establish this with certainty.

Thus, by means of these supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*), Brahman alone—established by such texts as "Being only, my dear," which is the sole cause of the entire universe and characterized by numerous unprecedented attributes (*apūrva-artha*) not common to anything else—is [referred to] by the word "Ākāśa" as if it were something well-known.
This is indicated by the passage beginning with "All these beings indeed," and so forth. || 23 ||
The Section on the Vital Breath (Prāṇa) ||1.1.9||
"They enter into breath alone, and from breath they emerge. This deity is connected with the Prastāva. Had you chanted the Prastāva without knowing her, your head would have fallen off."

Here, the word *prāṇa* also, like the word *ākāśa*, refers to the Supreme Brahman alone, distinct from the well-known vital breath; for there are characteristic marks such as the entry and exit of the entire universe—which are unique to that [Brahman]—indicated as if it were the well-known [breath].

But there may be a further doubt: "Since it is observed that the entire range of beings born exists and functions in dependence upon the vital breath (prāṇa), it is well known that prāṇa alone deserves to be designated as the cause of the world.
The refutation, however, is: "Because [the capacity to enter and emerge] is absent in stones, wood, and so forth, as well as in those whose nature is purely conscious"; for the text says:
"All these beings indeed enter into prāṇa alone, and from prāṇa they emerge."
Thus, [the objection] is not tenable. Therefore, because it "causes all beings to breathe," the Supreme Brahman alone is designated by the word "Prāṇa."

Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Brahman alone—which is distinct from the well-known ether, vital breath, and so forth; which is the sole cause of the entire universe; and which possesses an infinite multitude of auspicious qualities such as freedom from sin, omniscience, and the power of true resolve—is denoted by the words "ether," "vital breath," and the like. ||24||
Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa). 9.
"Your head would have fallen off" means that your own existence would not be maintained.
Regarding the phrase "like the word 'ākāśa'," all that was previously stated concerning the predominance of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and its refutation should be kept in mind.

Regarding the phrase "of the whole": here, one should consider both the objection raised by way of a suspicion of non-contradiction and the clarification of that contradiction. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "stability, activity, etc.," cessation is meant, as well as the knowledge and the desire-to-act which serve as the causes of activity. The sense is that since stability is established as a cause for arising by virtue of being a cause for activity, its inclusion is logically implied. Regarding the phrase "by way of being the cause of the world": the sense is that causality toward the composite [world] is possible. || 24 ||
(70) Thus ends the section concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the section concerning light (*jyotis*). 1.1.10.

The *Atuḥpara* states: "That which is endowed with some unsurpassed, preeminent quality pervaded by the state of being the cause of the world, and which is designated by words such as 'Light' (*jyotis*) and 'Indra' despite their well-known application to other objects, is indeed called the 'Supreme Brahman'—as established by the sūtras beginning with 'Because of the mention of Light and the feet' (*jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt*)."
It is light, because of the mention of its feet. (1.1.25)

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything— in the highest worlds, the unsurpassed— this indeed is that light which is within a person here."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: Is this object denoted by the word "light" (jyotis)—which possesses unsurpassed radiance—the well-known light such as the sun and so forth, which serves as the causal Brahman? Or is it the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), who is of a different nature from the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient beings, the ultimate cause, of immeasurable luster, omniscient, and whose will is infallible?

"On the heights" (pṛṣṭheṣu) means on the upper [regions], according to such scriptural passages as "With three feet he stands above" and "Above the darkness. The term "on all sides" (viśvataḥ sarvataḥ) is stated with the intention of referring to both the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi). "Unsurpassed" (anuttamaḥ) means that there is no one superior to him; thus he is unsurpassed. "From all sides" (viśvataḥ) means from the entire region of the earth. "From every side" (sarvataḥ) means from the entire region of the intermediate space (antarikṣa). The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) arises because of the possibility of construing it as "on the heights" [meaning] on the external [regions]. For the sun indeed shines even in the upper worlds by means of its rays.
What is appropriate? That it is the well-known light itself.
Why?

Even though it is mentioned as something well-known, since no specific mark pervaded by the Supreme Self—such as those found in the cases of "ether" or "breath"—is seen within its own sentence, and since there is no possibility of recognizing the Supreme Person, and because of the instruction on its identity with the "light within the belly," the light in question is indeed the well-known [physical] light; yet, due to its connection with unsurpassed radiance pervaded by causality, it is the Brahman that is the cause of the world.

This being the case, we reply: because of the mention of the feet of light. The light described as connected with heaven, which possesses unsurpassed radiance, is indeed the Supreme Person. Why? Because all beings are designated as the feet of this very [light] in the passage: "A foot of Him are all beings; three feet of His are the immortal in heaven. Thus, all beings are spoken of as the feet belonging to this [Supreme Being].
This is what is meant:

although in this sentence, "Now, that light which is beyond heaven," no characteristic mark (liṅga) exclusive to the Supreme Person is perceived; nevertheless, because the Supreme Person was designated as being connected with heaven in the preceding passage, this light is recognized (pratyabhijñāyate) as being that very same one by virtue of that connection. Furthermore, the instruction regarding its identity with the gastric fire is an injunction for meditating upon it as having that nature for the sake of a specific result; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Furthermore, that the gastric fire has that [Brahman] as its essence was stated by the Blessed One himself: "Having become the Vaiśvānara fire, I abide within the bodies of living beings.

"All beings" refers to sentient beings conjoined with non-sentient matter (acit) who are included within the effected world (kāryajagat). The word "in heaven" (divi), however, refers to a specific non-material (aprākṛta) abode situated outside all the individual and collective threads [of the universe]; this is because of the scriptural hearing: "on the backs of all," meaning "on the backs of everything. The word "all" (sarva) is an explanation of the word "universe" (viśva); this is an indicative mark (liṅga) for the absence of motion.

Because the word "viśva" (the universe) is applied to the individual manifestations existing within the world—as in the statement, "Thus from the Imperishable the universe arises here"—the word "viśva" refers to the individual (vyaṣṭi). By process of elimination, the word "sarva" (all) refers to the collective totality (samaṣṭi). For this very reason, the Commentator also stated in his prose commentary: "existing beyond the entire collection of effects and causes. And its three-footed nature is possible through non-material (aprākṛta) distinctions of objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment.

And thus, the distinct designation "in his world" (*asya divi*) and the attainment of immortality (*amṛtatva*) become primary. This is what was stated. [Objection: Since the preceding sentence mentions the "foot" (*caraṇa*) as being connected with heaven (*dyu*), how can this sentence have the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as its subject? If it is argued that they share a single subject matter, then how is there a single subject matter?

Regarding the term *kaukṣeya* (belonging to the belly), he refutes the reason for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the phrase *phalāya*, the meaning is: "for the sake of the fruit already mentioned," namely, "he becomes pleasing to the sight and renowned. Regarding the phrase *tadātmakatva* (having that as its essence), the sense is: in the passage, "One should meditate upon this as both seen and heard," the words *tat* (that) and *etat* (this) refer to the light whose essence is that [breath]; for it has been introduced as having that as its essence. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

The intention is as follows: on the basis of such scriptural and traditional (smṛti) passages as "He who eats food, the giver of wealth," "Four kinds of people worship Me," and "Viṣṇu indeed bestows all fruits," it is logical that the Supreme Self—the bestower of all fruits—is here the cause of the results corresponding to the meditations on the light within the eye and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the light within the belly": since it is possible for knowledge to have its object as it truly is, the reliance on the view of superimposing [the idea of] that onto what is not that (as asserted by the opponent) is improper; this is the sense. || 25 ||

[Objection: It is not so, because of the mention of a specific meter (chandas). [Reply: No; for there is a scriptural injunction regarding the fixing of the mind in that way, and such is seen [in other passages]. 1.1.26.
In the preceding passage,
having designated the metre named Gāyatrī by stating, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," [the text continues].
"This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse," thus [referring to] the cited passage:
"Such is his greatness."

If it is argued that because this *ṛc* also concerns the meter (*chandas*), there is no mention of the Supreme Person here—[the answer is] "Or rather, the Gāyatrī [is meant]. That is not so; for there is a scriptural injunction regarding the fixing of the mind upon It. By the word "Gāyatrī," mere meter is not denoted here, because it is impossible for mere meter to be the Self of all. Rather, the fixing of the mind on the Gāyatrī is enjoined here specifically with respect to Brahman. The meaning is that the contemplation of the similarity between the Gāyatrī and Brahman is taught for the sake of a specific result. And this is possible:
"Of this [Brahman], one foot are all beings; its three-footed immortal part is in heaven. Thus, there is a similarity between Brahman, which has four feet, and the four-footed *gāyatrī*.
And a four-footed *gāyatrī* is seen in certain places, as for example: "Indra, the lord of Śacī, oppressed by Vala, the unshakable bull, victorious in battles."
"Those five and these other five become ten," beginning thus, [it continues] up to:
"This is that Virāj, the food-eater."
Thus it is said. ||26||
For this reason as well, Brahman alone is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*: "And because the designation of the quarters beginning with 'beings' is thus appropriate" (1.1.27).

Having pointed out the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart, [the question arises: how is there a four-footed nature? To this, he says "so indeed. In response to the doubt—"How can the primary meaning of the word *gāyatrī* not be intended here?"—he explains the portion of the Sūtra. Wind, fire, sun, moon, and water, as well as breath, speech, eye, ear, and mind, constitute the *virāj* because they number ten. The meaning is that the application of a word denoting one similar thing to another similar thing is the scriptural justification (*śruti-samādhi*). [The term] *annāt* means both "from food" and "that which eats food"; thus, *annāt*. ||26||

Regarding the phrase "bhūtādi": in the preceding sūtra, the impossibility of the Gāyatrī being the Self of all as stated in the mantra "a foot of this" was explained; here, however, the impossibility of the four-footed nature mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "Gāyatrī indeed" is explained. "Bhūta" refers to the category of living beings. "Pṛthivī" refers to this world—the locus for the performance of actions and the enjoyment of their fruits. "The body" refers to the statement: "This is that four-footed [Gāyatrī]."
—Thus, this designation is appropriate only for Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī. ||27||

It is thus faultless that the very same Supreme Person—described in the passage, "Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this; all beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven"—and further characterized as four-footed in the verse, "I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness," possesses a splendor that is non-material (aprākṛta), even though His material form has been mentioned; therefore, He alone is rightly denoted by the word "Light" (jyotis). ||28||
Thus ends the section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa). 10.
The Section Concerning Indra and Prāṇa (Indraprāṇādhikaraṇa) || 1.1.11 ||

It has been stated that the light denoted by the word *jyotis*, which is endowed with unsurpassed brilliance, is designated as the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) just like [the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice] commonly known. Now, he says that even Indra—who is heard of as the object of meditation by virtue of being the means for attaining immortality pervaded by causality, and who is denoted by the words *prāṇa* and so forth—is indeed the Supreme Person:
"The *prāṇa* [is Brahman], because of the [contextual] correspondence" (1.1.29).

In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, regarding the Pratardana-vidyā, [the author] states "niratiśaya" and so forth, thereby stating the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*). Regarding "jyotiḥ": the sense is that the section "jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt" is appropriately connected immediately after "ata eva prāṇaḥ," because the sequence of ether (*ākāśa*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), and fire (*tejas*) is logically established. By the phrase "prasiddhavad" (as if well-known), the fixed order of succession between the two sections is stated.

Regarding the phrase "sarvāṇi ha vā," we observe that in the two preceding sections there is a reference to their subject matter as if they were well-known, using the word "yat" (that which) here as well in the expression "atha yadataḥ. Therefore, the section on Light (*jyotir-adhikaraṇa*) is connected with the two preceding sections. The sense is that this being the case, it follows that the subsequent section must occur immediately after the section on Light. By the phrase "pervaded by causality," he states the meaning that runs through the intermediate sub-sections (*peṭikā*).

The meaning of the connection [between this section and the previous one] is as follows: it was stated in the preceding section that the Supreme Person is denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*); however, that is incorrect, because something other than the Supreme Person—namely, Indra and others who are denoted by such words—is what is taught in the Vedāntas. This is the doubt with which the connection is made. In this regard, the abundance of indicatory marks (*liṅga*) that challenge the status of [the Supreme Person] as the cause should be considered (Śrutaprakāśikā).
That which is designated by the terms "Indra" and "Prāṇa," and which is the self of Indra, is intended to be Brahman;
for it is seen that [Brahman] is referred to in the concluding section by such terms as "Bliss," "Immortality," and so forth.
"Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through both battle and manliness," beginning thus, [Indra said],
"Choose a boon."

When Pratardana said this to Indra, who was speaking thus: "Choose for yourself a boon, whatever you consider most beneficial for humanity," it is heard [in the scripture]: "He said, 'I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātman); worship me as life and immortality.'"

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this one who is designated by the words Indra and Prāṇa as the object of meditation that is most beneficial merely the individual soul (jīva), or is it the Supreme Self (paramātman) distinct from that?

"Choose a boon," [Indra said]. In this regard, in the printed editions, the following sequence is observed: "Pratardana, indeed... and by human effort. Indra said to him: 'I shall grant you a boon. Pratardana replied: 'You yourself choose a boon for me—whatever you consider most beneficial for a human being. In this context, if the sentence "Choose a boon" had not occurred previously, and only the sentence "I shall grant you a boon" were present, Pratardana would have simply said, "Give me a boon."

But it is not "You yourself choose a boon for me. Therefore, it appears that the reading "varaṃ vṛṇīṣva" (choose a boon), which is found in manuscripts from that period and supported by the Bhāṣya, is indeed the appropriate one.

Regarding the phrase "designated by the words Indra and Prāṇa": it is stated thus because [the subject] is designated by the word "Indra" in the opening passage as "of Indra," and by the word "Prāṇa" in the statement "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self. Since the word "Prāṇa" occurs within a sentence that establishes a mark (*liṅga*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it serves to indicate the reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*); therefore, in the Sūtra, the subject (*dharmin*) is designated by the word "Prāṇa" and not by the word "Indra. Is it correct to say that the intention of the author of the Sūtras is that the status of being the object of inquiry belongs to what is designated by the word "Indra" only in a secondary sense? [The opponent argues: It is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone.
Why?

Because the word "Indra" is well-known to refer specifically to a particular individual soul (jīva), and the word "prāṇa," being in grammatical apposition with it, must also function in reference to that same entity. This soul, designated as Indra, was addressed by Pratardana as follows: "Choose for me yourself that boon which you consider most beneficial for a human being."

"‘Meditate upon Me...’—thus He taught that meditation on one’s own Self is the most beneficial. And the most beneficial is precisely the means for attaining immortality. For it is only through meditation on the Cause of the Universe that there is the attainment of immortality, as stated:
‘For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute].’"
Thus it is understood. Therefore, when the doubt arises that Indra—who is well-known to possess the nature of a living soul (jīva)—is indeed the causal Brahman, [the question is raised:

is the description of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ and so forth intended to be consistent with those [worldly] signs? To resolve this, there is an inquiry: does the statement "Worship me" refer to the worship of himself [as Indra], or to the worship of the Supreme Self abiding within him?

The relationship between the means and the end in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: when there is the statement "Worship me," it refers to the worship of Indra himself; since qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth must be described as being concordant with [his] deeds like the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s sons, and because these qualities are not primary [in the case of Brahman], Indra—who is the object of worship as that which is most beneficial—is the cause of the world, existing in the well-known state of a living soul (*jīva*).

The relationship between the king and the fruit is as follows: when there is the instruction to meditate on the Supreme Self in its own state with the words "Meditate on Me," then—because the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ and other such deeds must be described in accordance with qualities such as bliss, and because qualities like bliss are primary—the Supreme Self is indicated by the terms Indra and Prāṇa, which function as the object of meditation that is most beneficial; thus, it is Brahman, the cause of the world, known through all the Vedāntas.

"Because of common usage" (*prasiddheḥ*): by this, it is indicated that the position [of the opponent] regarding the mere individual soul (*jīva*) as the subject (*pakṣa*) does not arise. "Of that which is co-referential with it" (*tatsamānādhikaraṇasya*): how can the word *prāṇa* have the individual soul as its referent? By this, it is also implicitly indicated that there is no possibility of raising a doubt that the word *prāṇa* refers primarily to the vital breath. "The cause of the world" (*jagatkāraṇa*): this demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of being the object of meditation for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) by the state of being the cause. "Therefore" (*ataḥ*): this is the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is stated: "The vital breath [is Brahman], because it is so followed through. This being designated by the terms "Indra" and "prāṇa" is indeed the Supreme Brahman, which is a distinct entity from the individual soul (jīva).
"This very prāṇa is the conscious self (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal."

Thus, it is only when this is the case that the subsequent occurrence of the terms "bliss," "undecaying," and "immortal" in grammatical apposition with the subject introduced by the words "Indra" and "prāṇa" is logically justified. ||29||
It is not merely the individual soul;
if it be argued that it is not so because of the instruction regarding the Self of the speaker, [we reply] that there is indeed an abundance of references to the inner self in this [section]. 1.1.30.

*Anugama* (corroboration) is the connection of what was introduced in a preceding statement with a subsequent statement. It is said that this occurs because a reason for a conclusion (*siddhānta-hetu*), which was not explicitly manifested in its own sentence, is manifested by a subsequent statement. However, in the *Ākāśādhikaraṇa* and the *Jyotiradhikaraṇa*, the term "because of corroboration" (*anugamāt*) is not used, since the reason for the conclusion is indeed already manifested in the preceding sentence of its own context. Regarding the phrase "Bliss, undecaying," he explains the word *tathā* in the Sūtra as referring to the form of the probans (*sādhaka-ākāra*). *Prāṇa* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

"Because of such a concordance"—that is, because of the concordance with the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is the construction of the sūtra. "Only when that [Supreme Self] exists"—the meaning is: only when the Supreme Brahman is indicated by the words *indra* and *prāṇa*. *Prāṇa* refers to the Supreme Self. "Because of such a concordance"—the construction is: because of the concordance as the Supreme Self. The word *tathā* (such) is an adverbial modifier of the action of concordance. The intention is that what is intended is a concordance characterized by the possession of the qualities of both the probandum and the probans residing in the intellect. ||29||
As it has been stated: because that which is designated by the term "Indra-prāṇa" is identical in meaning with [the description] "blissful, undecaying, and immortal," this is the supreme Brahman.
That is not tenable;
for [the text says], "Know me alone," and "I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self; meditate upon me as life, as immortality."
For Indra is indeed the speaker [of such things] by statements such as "I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ," and so forth;

thus, he teaches to Pratardana that his very self—whose status as a living being is well known through the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son and other deeds—is to be meditated upon. Therefore, since it is understood from the beginning that it is a "particular living being,"...

If it is argued that the conclusion—“Ānanda is undecaying and immortal,” and so forth—should be described in a manner consistent with that [conclusion], the author refutes this by stating: “For there is an abundance of internal connection in this [text]. The connection pertaining to the Self is “internal connection” (*adhyātmasambandha*). Its “abundance” (*bhūmā*) means its greater extent or multiplicity; that is, the multiplicity of connections due to the multiplicity of things related to the Self as their substratum. And that [abundance] is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self, who is the speaker here.
"Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes, and the spokes are fixed upon the nave, even so are these elements (bhūta-mātrā)."

"Resting solely in wisdom, the elements of wisdom are rested in breath. Having designated the collection of insentient things by the term "elements of being," and having designated the class of sentient beings as their support by the term "elements of wisdom," [the text] points to Indra—the subject under discussion—who is denoted by the word "breath" as the support even for that, and identifies him alone as "bliss, undecaying, and immortal."

Thus he teaches. The meaning is that this quality of being the substratum of all things, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient, is possible only in this Supreme Self, who is distinct from the individual soul (jīva).
Alternatively: "For in this [section], there is an abundance of internal connection.

Internal connection refers to the connection with attributes common to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Indeed, an abundance—that is, a multiplicity—of such [connections] exists in this context. To illustrate: first, [it is said]:

The phrase "tadyathā" (just as) expresses the connection by way of being that which is contained; it indicates that this is not merely a concluding statement, but that [the same relationship] exists previously as well. With the intention of expressing plurality, the passage beginning with "sa eṣa prāṇa eva" is cited. Regarding the phrase "prajñāmātrābhis-tayā": the sense is that it is not logical for the senses to have the elements such as earth as their substratum. Regarding the term "cetana-vargam" (the group of conscious beings): the sense is that the singular number used for the word "prajñātman" (the conscious self), which is topical here, is intended to denote the genus.

"Having pointed out its support as well..."—the sense is that since the mutual expectancy expressed in the preceding sentence, "These indeed [are...]," is not satisfied by stating another support for the mere *prajñāmātrās*, their status as an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntatva*) is untenable. Regarding the word "upadiśati" (he teaches): thus has the meaning of the Vedic statement been set forth, supported by the absence of contradiction in meaning, the failure of the relationship between the illustration and the illustrated (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika-bhāva-vaighaṭya*), primacy, topical context, and commonality of usage.

The citation of this sentence, "This very one is the vital breath (prāṇa)," is for the purpose of demonstrating that there are other sentences as well that have Brahman as their subject matter. By this, it is established that the natural sense of the whole is stronger than the natural sense of the opening statement (*upakrama*). Thus, since the strength of the natural sense of the whole is already established by implication, it is appropriate to state it explicitly; hence the phrase "in another way" or "alternatively. In the previous interpretation, the word *adhyātma* means "in the self" (*ātmani*).

In this context, however, the word *adhyātma* refers to that which exists within the Self (*ātman*). Regarding the objection raised by the opponent—that "a concluding statement is set aside by the introductory statement"—the following response is given: the introduction and the conclusion are constituent parts of a sentence. When there is a mutual contradiction between these two constituent parts, it is the introduction that possesses greater force; this does not apply when there is a contradiction with the whole (the sentence itself).
As it is said: "Choose for yourself the boon that you consider most beneficial for humanity."

And from the words, "Cry out to me...," it is understood that Indra, who is designated by the word *prāṇa*, is the object of worship—the means for attaining liberation which is unique to the Supreme Self. Likewise:
"He alone causes him to perform good deeds whom He leads upward from these worlds; he alone causes him to perform evil deeds whom He leads downward."

Thus, the quality of being the instigator of all action is an attribute of the Supreme Self. Likewise, as it is said: "Just as the rim of a wheel is fixed upon the spokes, and the spokes are fixed upon the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed upon the faculties of cognition (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the faculties of cognition are fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa)," the quality of being the support of all is likewise an attribute of that very [Self]. Similarly, [it is said]:
"‘He is indeed that very Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātmā), blissful, undecaying, and immortal’—these too are attributes of the Supreme Self alone.
‘He is the lord of the worlds; He is the ruler of all.’"

And this [description] is possible only with respect to the Supreme Self (paramātman). Thus, because there is an abundance of internal (adhyātma) connections present here, it is the Supreme Self alone that is designated by the terms "Indra" and "Prāṇa" in this context. || 30 ||
How, then, is the instruction regarding Indra—who is known to have the nature of a living being—that his own self is the object of worship consistent?
To that, he says:
"This is what is meant."
"Entering by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"; "All this has that as its self (aitadātmyam)";
"He who has entered within is the ruler of people, the self of all";
"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who rules the self from within."

"By such scriptural passages as, 'This is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa,' having understood the Supreme Self whose body is the individual soul (jīvātman), and having realized that even words denoting the individual soul—such as 'I' and 'you'—ultimately terminate in the Supreme Self alone, [the Lord] taught that the Supreme Self, whose body is his own self, is indeed to be worshipped, saying: 'Know Me alone,' and 'Worship Me.'"

As in the case of Vāmadeva: Just as Vāmadeva, perceiving that the Supreme Brahman is the inner self of all, that everything has that [Brahman] as its body, and that words denoting bodies ultimately refer to the embodied one, pointed to Brahman as having his own self as its body by using the word "I," and then designated Manu, Sūrya, and others through grammatical coordination with it: "Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I became Manu and Sūrya'; 'I am the seer Kakṣīvān, a sage, a wise man'"; and as it is said:
"Because the Infinite is omnipresent, He alone exists as I."
"From me everything comes; I am everything; everything is in me, the eternal," and so forth he says. ||31||

In this section, he states—following an objection—the reason why words denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) and words denoting specific insentient objects are used to refer to the "Supreme Brahman" which is the object of worship: "If it be argued that [the Supreme Brahman] is not [meant here] because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*), we say no; because of the threefold nature of meditation, because [these marks] are based [on the Supreme], and because of the connection with that [Supreme] in this context. (1.1.31)

"Let one not desire to know speech, but let one know the speaker"; "I struck you who had three heads"; "I delivered the Arunmukha Yatis to the hyenas"—from such marks of the individual soul (jīva), as well as from the statement:
"As long as the vital breath (prāṇa) dwells in this body, so long is there life."

Furthermore, because of the characteristic mark of the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) in the passage, "Now, verily, the vital breath alone, being the self of wisdom, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise," [the word *bhūman* does not refer to Brahman]—if this is argued, [we reply]:

no, because of the threefold nature of meditation (*upāsā-traividhyāt*). The designation by various terms is for the purpose of teaching the threefold nature of meditation. That is to say, the meaning is that there are three kinds of contemplation to be taught: the contemplation of Brahman, who is the cause of all, in its own essential nature; the contemplation of it as having the class of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-varga*) as its body; and the contemplation of it as having the objects of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment as its body.
This threefold contemplation of Brahman is also adopted in other sections [of the Upanishads]: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and "Bliss is Brahman."
In such passages as these, there is a reflection upon the essential nature [of Brahman]:

"Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat); the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and non-consciousness, the true and the untrue—He became the True. The "chief vital breath" (mukhyaprāṇa) has five functions. The word "chief" (mukhya) is intended to exclude the [other] senses and so forth. When there is an expectancy for what is to be negated by the negative particle (nañ), the word "adhyātma" from the Sūtra is supplied as being not too remote.

By the word "upāsanā" (meditation), he explains its nature as a cause. By the phrase "to instruct," the causality is made clear by way of its purpose. By the word "nikhila" (entirety), he explains its threefold nature: meditation on the essential nature (*svarūpa*), and meditation characterized by qualities (*guṇa-viśiṣṭa*) without an intermediary.

In such cases, there is meditation [on the Self] as the body of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-śarīra*), and as the body that is the object of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment (*bhogya-bhoga-upakaraṇa-śarīra*). The meaning here in this context is that this threefold meditation is indeed appropriate.

This is what is meant: wherever there is an association of the Supreme Self with the common attributes of specific individual souls (jīvas), such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, and specific non-intelligent principles (acetanas), such as Prakṛti and others; or wherever there is observed grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between words denoting those [individuals] and words expressive of the Supreme Self—in those cases, it is intended to establish the realization that the Supreme Self is the inner self (antarātman) of each of those respective intelligent and non-intelligent particulars.
Therefore, it is established here that the one designated by the terms "Indra" and "Prāṇa" is indeed the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the individual soul. || 31 ||
Thus ends the section concerning Indra as the vital breath (the *prāṇādhikaraṇa*). 19.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the Śrī Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya.

The passage from the Ānandavallī has been cited here because it serves as the reason for clarifying the meaning of other scriptural texts devoted to the threefold meditation—that the Lord is the "embodied one" (tatprakārin) due to His entry into both the conscious and the unconscious. However, something else is intended [by this citation].

"In this case as well" refers to the explanation of the phrase "here, because of connection with that. "Bliss, undecaying, immortal" refers to identification in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). "I am the vital breath" refers to identification characterized by the non-conscious (*acid-viśiṣṭa*). Thus, the meaning is that threefold identification is appropriate here.

Regarding the phrase "wherein": the point is that this principle does not apply solely to the Pratardana-vidyā, but rather to all such contexts. Regarding the mention of Hiraṇyagarbha and others: the scripture is recalled which states, "The Supreme Self is established; He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra. Since it has been determined by the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka—which is devoted to no other—that Nārāyaṇa alone is the object of worship in all vidyās, the sense is that even in the worship of Indra and others, it is Nārāyaṇa as their inner controller (antaryāmī) who is to be worshipped.

Because the section concerning the Pāśupatas will be discussed later; and because [the term] "peculiar to the Supreme Self" means that its status as being devoted to a qualified meditation is understood from its connection with attributes peculiar to the Supreme Self and from its grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with words denoting Him. || 31 ||
"Meditate upon me"—
this indicates the subject matter of the section.
In the Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya, in the first chapter on Concordance (Samanvayādhyāya), the second quarter (pāda), [Adhikaraṇas 1–6]:

In the first chapter: a person who has studied the Vedas and has acquired a thorough understanding of the true nature of ritual action through hearing the *Mīmāṃsā* of Action; having realized that mere rituals yield results that are limited and unstable; and having developed an inclination toward the nature of Brahman and its worship—which are understood from the Vedānta texts as yielding infinite and stable results—becomes desirous of liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal; and [recognizing] that the power of words consists in making known an already established, perfected reality, [he turns to] the Vedānta texts regarding the Supreme Brahman.

It has been stated that one who has ascertained the status of [the Vedas] as a valid means of knowledge should begin the study of the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, which constitutes its specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*), for the sake of establishing the commencement of the treatise.

"Regarding the phrase 'In the first quarter' (*prathame pāde*) and so forth: for what purpose is there here a summary of the subject matter of the first quarter? It is for the sake of making clear that the subject matter which follows throughout the quarters recurs in each individual section (*adhikaraṇa*). The statement of this recurrence is for the purpose of establishing the connection (*saṅgati*) with the [remaining] three quarters. And this connection with the three quarters exists because it is intended by the author of the Sūtras. Indeed, the division of the quarters is due to a difference in subject matter; and their sequence is due to specific connections. In this regard, the authority is the order of the traditional transmission."

Here, by means of this summary of the topics of the [first] section (*adhikaraṇa*), the doubt as to whether the three subsequent sections (*tripādī*) should not be commenced is also implicitly resolved; for the purpose of this summary is to indicate that the scriptural passages (*śruti*) which will be cited in the three sections are subjects governed by the principles established in the section of the first *pāda*. Therefore, even though it has been shown in the first *pāda* that the Vedānta texts have the Supreme Self as their purport, the necessity of commencing the three subsequent sections is established.

Even though in the first pāda, in the *Īkṣati* and *Ānandamaya* sections, the distinction of the Cause from the sentient and the insentient has already been established, the commencement of subsequent sections is indeed for the purpose of determining the meaning of the scriptural passages concerning their specific subjects by means of the principles of the preceding sections; it is the same here as well.

Since the four aphorisms constitute the introduction to the treatise, they are included within the first quarter by virtue of their meaning; however, this is not because the first quarter or the first chapter possesses a unique exclusivity.

"One who has studied the Vedas" means one who has completed the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) and the Upanishads (*saśiraska*). The reason why ritual action does not culminate therein—and why it does not culminate even further—is given by the words "merely," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the doubt that there might be no etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word [for Brahman] with respect to an established reality, it was demonstrated that the Vedic statement, "From which indeed these [beings arise]," teaches the Supreme Brahman—the sole cause of the great bliss consisting in the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, characterized by its infinite, diverse, stable, and multiform nature as the enjoyer, the enjoyed, the instruments of enjoyment, and the locus of enjoyment.

We have declared that the Supreme Brahman, the sole cause of the universe, is not the object of any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whatsoever, but is known solely through the authority of the Śāstra.

We have stated that the status of Brahman as being established by the authority of scripture (*śāstrapramāṇakatva*) is maintained because the Vedānta sentences are coherently integrated (*samanvaya*) with the Supreme Brahman—which, though devoid of connection with activity or cessation, is itself the supreme human goal by its very nature.

We have established that "Brahman," which is to be known through the Vedāntas as the sole cause of the entire universe, is indeed a specific conscious being distinct from the *pradhāna* inferred [by the Sāṃkhyas] due to its connection with such qualities as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*). Furthermore, He possesses natural, unsurpassed, and infinite bliss, omniscience, and is the cause of fear and fearlessness for all sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "the first sūtra has determined the scope," etc.: [an objection is raised] that the Upaniṣadic statements alone are sufficient; what is the purpose of the inquiry into Brahman? To this, the response is given by the words "its procedure" (*tad-itikartavyatā*), etc. The phrase "for the sake of establishing the commencement of the treatise" (*śāstrārambha-siddhaye*) is to be supplied (*anuṣajyate*) to each of the subsequent three sections (*adhikaraṇas*); thus, it is stated that the four sūtras as a whole serve the purpose of establishing the commencement of the treatise.

By means of the qualifiers beginning with "ananta" (infinite), he states the intended meaning of the word "asya" (of this) from the Sūtra. The terms "ananta" and "vicitra" (wonderful) refer generally to both the enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment. The state of being the sole cause of great bliss is what is intended by the statement "tadvijijñāsasva" (seek to know That); for indeed, the definition of that which is to be sought after by one afflicted by the threefold suffering has been stated. The use of the word "eka" (sole/one) in the phrase "ekakāraṇam" (the sole cause) is intended either with the view that "the distinction of non-contradictory qualifiers does not bring about a distinction in the qualified object," or with the intention of expressing the oneness of the efficient and material cause.
Because of "concomitance"—that is, because the scripture is concomitant with Brahman alone, who is the supreme human goal, as it is that which establishes Him;

and because He is distinct from the individual soul (jīva)—who is designated by the term "jīva" in both its bound and liberated states—on account of attributes such as having true volition, being the inner self of all sentient and insentient beings, and so forth; thus we have concluded in the Samāmnāya.
And we have declared that he possesses a divine form, uncommon and caused by extraordinary deeds.

We have already explained that he who is designated as the cause of the world—though appearing as such through terms denoting specific non-conscious entities like ether and vital breath—is indeed that very one who is distinct from all other conscious and non-conscious beings.

Furthermore, that which is denoted by the word *jyotis* (light) is possessed of an uncommon and unsurpassed brilliance; since it is recognized as such through its connection with the celestial realm (*dyu*), we shall maintain that it is indeed that very same [light].

We have concluded that it is the Supreme Person alone— who is the unique and ultimate cause and the means for attaining immortality— who is designated by words such as "Indra" and others from the perspective of the scriptures.

Thus, it has been stated: the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa alone, who transcends the scope of all other means of valid cognition, who is distinct from all other things due to being an ocean of boundless and sublime qualities such as omniscience and the truthfulness of His resolve, is the object to be known through the Vedānta.
The two words "intrinsic" (*svābhāvika*) and "unobstructed excellence" (*anavādhikātiśaya*) are connected with each respective qualifier.

Regarding the term "ākāśa": the reason for not mentioning "space" (ākāśa) and "the locus of the vital breaths" (prāṇādhikaraṇa) separately is that the underlying logic (*nyāya*) is not significantly different. Regarding "supreme" (*parama*): this refers to immortality (*amṛtatva*), which is common to the supreme cause. Its attainment is the reaching of supreme similarity (*paramasāmyāpatti*). Regarding "transcended" (*atipatita*): this is for the purpose of refuting fallacious arguments (*kutarka*) such as "because he is a person (*puruṣa*), like us and others"; the sense is that those [arguments] are sublated by the means of knowledge that apprehend the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). The word "Puruṣottama" intends the meaning of the section concerning light (*jyotiradhikaraṇa*). The word "Nārāyaṇa" intends the *Pratardana-vidyā*.

The meaning is that because the statement "Worship Me" (*mām upāsva*)—in accordance with the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*—is devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa as the object of all meditations, the subject matter pervading this chapter is the existence of a Cause that is distinct from both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).

Henceforth, in the second, third, and fourth quarters (pādas), although Brahman alone is that which is to be known through the Vedānta, there arises the doubt that certain Vedāntic passages are intended solely to establish the nature of specific entities not included within the categories of *pradhāna* or *kṣetrajña*. Anticipating this, the text establishes, by way of refuting such doubts, that Brahman is the source of all auspicious qualities as proclaimed by those respective passages.
21. The Section Concerning Being Established Everywhere (Sarvatraprasiddhyadhikaraṇa) || 1.2.1 ||
33. Because the teaching is established everywhere. (1.2.1)

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, indeed, man consists of resolve (*ṛtumaya*); according to his resolve in this world, so does a person become after departing from here; let him form a resolve: 'He who consists of mind, whose body is breath, whose form is light,' and so forth."

Regarding the word "atha": since the phrase beginning with "sarvaṃ khalu" will be cited in the second interpretation, the phrase beginning with "atha khalu" is employed here as required by the first interpretation. Since the subsequent sentence containing the second sūtra term "bhārūpaḥ" will be taken up later, the portion ending with "bhārūpaḥ" is included here. By the word "ādi," other [terms] are understood. Here, according to the "night-logic" (*rātri-nyāya*), "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) is connected as the object of meditation;
for even that which is merely explanatory (*ārthavādika*) must be accepted if it is required by an injunction (*vidhi*).

If only the passage beginning with "He should perform the seasonal rite" (*sa ṛtuṃ kurvīta*) were taken up, then—because no fruit is heard of there—the previously enjoined meditation might, by the maxim "that which has no fruit is a subordinate part of that which stands in proximity to what has a fruit," become a mere subsidiary to that prior meditation. Therefore, the phrase "Now then" (*atha khalu*) is employed in order to demonstrate the connection with a distinct fruit.

The phrase "Now then" (*atha khalu*) is included as a constituent part of the text in order to dispel the doubt that it would be improper to enjoin another form of meditation for one who is already qualified for the meditation enjoined by the rule "One should meditate on [the Self] as tranquil. The underlying sense is that since the individual soul (*jīva*) is subject to a great abundance of various types of meditation, the injunction of multiple meditations is entirely appropriate.
