By taking as reasons its being produced from that, its dissolving into that, and its dependence on that for life, the Supreme Self alone— the Universal Self— is declared to be "consisting of mind" (manomaya) through the teaching found in the passage, "All this, indeed, is [Brahman]."
In this regard, it is understood that [the text] points out: "He should form a resolve; he has the vital breath as his body. (Śrībhāṣya 1.2.1)

Regarding this meditation thus set forth, there arises a doubt concerning the object of worship (*upāsya*): is it the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) characterized by qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), or is it the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)?
What is appropriate? That it is the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). Why?

Because the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are instruments of the *kṣetrajña*, whereas for the Supreme Self, there is a negation of those very things in the passage, "For He is without breath, without mind" (*aprāṇo hyamanāḥ*). Nor is it the case that—
The "Brahman" previously specified in the statement, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," can here be connected as the object of worship; [therefore, it is said:
"Sit down, being tranquil."

Thus, because [the passage] has been employed for the purpose of teaching that Brahman constitutes the self, which serves as the means for the attainment of peace and liberation through the practice of meditation.

Nor is it reasonable to say that because the meditation expressed in "He should perform the ritual" has an expectancy for an object of meditation, Brahman— though situated in another sentence— is connected [to it]; for that [meditation] has no such expectancy, as it is satisfied by the qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) mentioned within its own sentence.

Because the requirement for both [the subject and the predicate] is satisfied merely by changing the case-ending of that which is indicated as having no other purpose in the phrase "consisting of mind, having vital breath as its body."

Regarding the phrase "of the mind and the vital breath": since the mere connection with the mind is not clearly a characteristic of the individual soul (jīva), and because the specific relationship characterized by the status of instrument and agent—which *is* a characteristic of the individual soul—is not explicitly stated, this section is intended to deal with passages containing obscure characteristics of the individual soul; with this intention, it is said, "because of being an instrument of the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). And it is not possible... [to connect them], meaning that they are already complete in themselves through having another purpose.

Regarding the phrase "by that which is included in its own sentence": because there is no interrupting factor, the unity of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is intended. Consequently, since the expectancy for a qualificand is satisfied by the word *ātman*—which resides within its own sentence, serves no other purpose, and possesses the same grammatical gender—the extraction of the word *brahman*, which resides in another sentence, has a different purpose and a different gender, is not appropriate; this is the sense. [The term] "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*).

Since the words *manomaya* and so forth, which end in the nominative case, cannot be construed with the word expressing the act of meditation (*upāsīta*), the word *brahma* must be supplied here—this is the answer to that objection. Furthermore, because the word *ṛtu* does not construe with the accusative case ending either, when a change of case-ending is required to establish the state of being the object of perception (*paśyanta*), it is logical that the change of case-ending applies only to a proximate word that stands in need of completion; it does not apply to a word situated in another sentence that is already complete in itself. This is the meaning.

*Ubhayākāṅkṣā* (mutual expectancy) refers to the mutual requirement between the term "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, and the phrase "one should perform" (*kartuṃ kurvīta*). The word *siddheḥ* is in the ablative case; it is construed with the phrase "it is not proper to state.
[The reading] *pūrvavākyanirdiṣṭam* [is correct], or else *ā*, *vā*, *pariṇāma*, or *ī*.
[The reading] *upāsyākāṅkṣatvāt* [is correct], or else *dha*, *abhyārthatayā*, or *i*.

When the living nature [of the self] has been thus determined, it is concluded that even the word "Brahman" in the concluding statement "This is Brahman" is employed with reference to the living self alone for the sake of honor.
"He who is fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind—those who know him become immortal. "He is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech;
but by the purified mind," and so forth.

In such passages as: "The breath of breath," "Now, verily, the breath alone is the conscious self; having taken hold of this body, it causes it to rise up," and "All these beings, indeed, enter into breath alone, and from breath they emerge."

"Consisting of mind" (*manomayatva*) means being graspable by a purified mind. "Having vital breath as its body" (*prāṇaśarīratva*) means being the substratum of the vital breath and its controller. This being the case, even the word "Brahman" in the passage, "This is my Self within the heart; this is Brahman," is used in its primary sense.
By the words "for it is without breath and without mind," [the text] negates that knowledge depends on the mind and that the stability of Brahman depends on the vital breath.

The phrase "with the heart and with insight" (*hṛdā manīṣā*) is a statement concerning a specific relationship through the commonality of the mind (*manas*). Here, "heart" (*hṛt*) refers to devotion (*bhakti*), and "insight" (*manīṣā*) refers to fortitude (*dhṛti*). This is because the first half-verse is read as a single unit, and it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "With devotion and with fortitude, one whose self is composed perceives here the very nature of knowledge. The word "abhiklṛptaḥ" means "to be grasped. The phrase "not with the eye" is a statement expressing a specific relationship through a particular aspect of the mind.

"The life-breath of the life-breath" means its support. In the passage beginning with "All these indeed," it was previously stated that the word "prāṇa" refers to the Supreme Self through its etymological (yaugika) sense. Now, this same passage is cited as referring to the Supreme Self even by way of its ultimate (aparyavasāna) sense. The intention is that, according to the principle of the Vaiśvānara section, it is logical for it to refer to the Supreme Self in both ways.

"Grāhyatvam" (the state of being the object). The meaning is that it was stated "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) with the intention of referring to a specific relationship characterized by the object (*grāhya*) and the subject (*grāhaka*). And by the words "Thus, indeed... (*evaṃ ca*), he expresses the natural force of the concluding summary. By the passage beginning with "dependent on the mind" (*mana āyattam*), he states the meaning of the prohibitive statements regarding the mind and so forth, which is not inconsistent with what has been said. The specific relationship consisting of the controller-controller-ship, the controlled-controlled-ship, and so forth, between the object and the subject is what is enjoined; the specific relationship characterized by the instrument-instrumentality is what is prohibited—this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, in the passage "All this is indeed Brahman; it originates from that, dissolves into that, and breathes in that—meditate on it as peaceful," meditation itself is enjoined here: "Being peaceful, one should meditate upon Brahman, which is the self of all. [This is followed by:
"He should form a resolve."

Thus, this is a restatement for the purpose of taking up its very qualities; and the qualities to be taken up are those such as "consisting of mind" (manomayatva) and so forth. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should meditate upon Brahman, which is the self of all, as possessing qualities such as consisting of mind."

Indeed, the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is indicated by the word "all. Furthermore, the state of being Brahmā and so forth exists for the inner self (pratyagātman) precisely because it is conditioned by specific karmas rooted in beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyā). However, for the Supreme Brahman—who is omniscient, omnipotent, free from sin, whose scent of all defects such as ignorance has been dispelled, and who is the source of everything that is to be abandoned—the state of being "all" is not tenable.
Thus, when the entire world has been indicated, that which is enjoined as being of the nature of that [world] by means of the word "Brahman" is the Supreme Brahman alone,
not the inner self (pratyagātman). Why?

Because of the teaching of what is well-known—by way of the reason "tajjalān" (from that, into that, in that), and because of the teaching as something well-known in the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman. On account of the reasons that [the world] is born from Brahman, merged into Brahman, and exists dependent on Brahman for its life, when it is said, "All this world has Brahman as its self," it is understood that "that very [Brahman], whose origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world are well-known in the Vedāntas, is the Brahman referred to here."

And that is indeed the Supreme Brahman. For it is said, beginning with: "That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at their passing—desire to know that; that is Brahman"; and continuing:
"He understood that bliss is Brahman; for indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born."

By such passages as these, the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe are shown to proceed from the Supreme Brahman itself—that "Vipaścit" (the All-seeing) who possesses unsurpassed and limitless bliss, as established in the preceding section. Likewise, [it continues:]

"He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs; he has no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him"—thus, the Supreme Brahman alone is designated as the cause of the "lord of the organs," that is, the individual soul (*jīva*). In this way, the causality of the Supreme Brahman alone is established everywhere. Therefore, because [the world] is born from the Supreme Brahman, because it is dissolved into Him, because it breathes by means of Him, and because it consists of Him, their identity is logically established.

"Even for one who is liberated, even for one whose essential nature is undivided, the identity with the world— which is the cause of the world's birth, maintenance, and dissolution— is not possible"; this will be explained in the section beginning with "except for the activity regarding the world."

The claim that He alone is the cause because the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of the world have karma as their instrumental cause is also not tenable; for even though they are caused by karma, the Lord alone is the cause of the world.
Therefore, the Supreme Self alone is denoted here by the word ‘Brahman’. Scholars highly esteem this very meaning of the Sūtra, as the author of the Vṛtti has stated:
“‘Sarvaṃ khalu’ [refers to] Brahman, the Self of all” (Bo. Vṛ).
Thus [ends the first section]. || 1 ||
34. And because the intended qualities are applicable [to Brahman]. (1.2.2)

The term *jagajjanmasthitipralayakāraṇatvanimitta* is a bahuvrīhi compound; the meaning is "that which is the cause [of the world] by virtue of its being the cause of its birth, maintenance, and dissolution. Regarding the phrase "even though karma is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*)": karma is certainly not the instrumental cause in the form of the creator (*kartṛ*) nor the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. Both [causal roles] belong to the Lord alone; karma, however, is merely the cause of inequality (*vaiṣamya*). This is just as, although the construction of jars and other objects is caused by the karma of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the karma of the enjoyer possesses neither the status of a creator nor that of a material cause.

Indeed, both of those [the potter and the lump of clay] are present only in the case of the potter and the lump of clay. Furthermore, in the phrase "tajjalān," the word *tat* does not denote the object of an action (*karman*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that there is no identity for the individual soul (*jīva*) based on its being the cause of the world. By the words "imameva" and so forth, the author asserts that the meaning explained through the second interpretation is indeed the traditional one. Regarding the word "sarvam": the meaning is that Brahman—the Lord (*īśa*), i.e., the Supreme Self—is described as the self of all by the sentence beginning with "sarvaṃ khalu."

Furthermore, the qualities about to be described— namely, "consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, whose form is light," "whose resolve is true," "whose self is space," and "possessing all works and all desires"— are possible only in the Supreme Self.

"He who contains all odors, all tastes, who has pervaded all this, who is without speech and without concern"—he is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), meaning he is to be grasped by the mind alone when it is purified. For he is indeed "grasped by the mind" when that mind has been cleansed by the worship of the Supreme Self, which is aided by the seven means such as discrimination and detachment. By this, his nature as being exclusively composed of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of everything to be abandoned is expressed; for he is grasped only by those with pure minds, being distinct in essence from everything else.

"Prāṇaśarīraḥ": He who sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of all beings in the world; he whose body is the vital breath—meaning that which is supported by, subject to, and subordinate to him—is *prāṇaśarīraḥ*. It will be demonstrated later that being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate are the grounds for applying the term "body" (*śarīra*). "Bhārūpaḥ": having a luminous form. This means he is endowed with unsurpassed splendor due to his non-material, unique, and unsurpassed auspicious divine form. "Hata-saṅkalpaḥ. "Ākāśātmā": having a nature as subtle and transparent as space.

"Satyasaṅkalpaḥ" (one whose resolve is true): [this refers to] the state of being intended to be spoken (*vivakṣitatvam*)—that is, the state of being the object of the desire to speak—of those very qualities that are about to be stated, as opposed to all other causes which are not intended. "Vakṣyamāṇatvāt" (because they are about to be stated): the meaning is that by the word "intended," the state of being about to be stated is indicated. [Objection: With respect to the first sentence, "All this indeed... (*sarvaṃ khalu*), it is the collection of qualities found in the subsequent sentences that is "about to be stated. Since qualities propounded by a non-human (authorless) statement cannot possibly be preceded by human desire, how can there be "the state of being intended"? [Response: [This is answered by the term] "manomayaḥ" (consisting of mind).

In order to avoid contradiction with the prohibitive statements, he explains the general term *manomaya* (consisting of mind) in accordance with the specific statements: "by the mind alone" (*manasaikena*). The sense of the word "alone" (*eka*) is that it contains an emphasis of exclusion, similar to expressions such as "one who drinks only water" (*abbhakṣaḥ*) or "one who subsists on air only" (*vāyubhakṣaḥ*). This is because it accords with the scriptural passage: "It is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech; but by the purified mind" (*na cakṣuṣā gṛhyate, nāpi vācā, manasā tu viśuddhena*). Regarding the term "impure": being graspable by an impure mind is pervaded by the quality of being fit for rejection (*heyatva*).

Therefore, the sense is that by the cessation of the pervader (vyāpaka), there is the cessation of the pervaded (vyāpya); thus, the status of being characterized by both marks (ubhayaliṅgakatva) is established. Even for the liberated one (mukta), the state of being perceivable by a pure mind (viśuddhamanogrāhyatva) is not possible. If the mind perceives the liberated one through its own independence, then the mind is impure. If [it perceives him] as being coextensive with Brahman (brahmaparyantatvena), then only Brahman, as qualified [by that], is perceivable by a pure mind. Regarding the term "consisting of light" (bhārūpa): the meaning "having knowledge as its nature" (jñānasvarūpa) is extremely strained; for the word "form" (rūpa) denotes a quality (dharma).

The word "bhā" refers to radiance (*dīpti*). Its quality of being radiant is established through its etymological derivation (*vigraha*). With the intention of showing consistency with such scriptural passages as "of solar hue, beyond darkness" (*ādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt*) and "golden-hued" (*rukmavarṇam*), [the Lord] is described as having a luminous form (*bhāsvararūpaḥ*). "Subtlety" (*sūkṣmatvam*) means pervasiveness (*vyāpyatvam*). "Transparency" (*svacchatvam*) means purity (*nirmalatvam*). By the phrase beginning with "possessing all" (*sakaleta*), [it is shown that] in space alone...

"Of space as well": either he is the self-nature of space, thus "space-self" (*ākāśātmā*); or, because he shines by himself and illuminates others as well, he is "space-self. "Possessing all actions"—action is that which is performed; he whose action is the entire world is "possessing all actions" (*sarvakarmā*). Or, he whose activity is everything is "possessing all actions. "Possessing all desires"—desires are those things desired, namely objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and so forth; the meaning is that all such purified varieties belong to him. "Possessing all odors, possessing all tastes"—[as stated in the scripture] "without sound, without touch... [and so on].

By such statements as these, there is a negation of ordinary smell, taste, and so forth. The meaning is that he possesses all kinds of non-ordinary, unique, faultless, unsurpassed, auspicious smells and tastes which constitute his own objects of enjoyment. "He has taken all this into himself" (*abhyāttaḥ*): from the beginning up to the aforementioned [qualities] ending with taste, he has appropriated this entire collection of auspicious qualities. The suffix *kta* in the word *abhyāttaḥ* should be understood in the sense of the agent (active voice), as in the expression "the Brahmins have eaten. He is "speechless" (*avākī*); "speech" (*vāk*) means utterance; that [speech] does not belong to him.

"He is without speech" (*avākī*). Why? He says: "Because he is indifferent" (*anādaraḥ*). Since all desires have been attained, there is nothing left to be desired; thus, he is devoid of longing. For this very reason, he is "without speech," meaning he speaks little. Because his sovereignty is complete, he sits in silent tranquility, having treated the entire world—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—as if it were mere straw. These intended qualities are appropriate only in the Supreme Self. || 2 ||
But because of the impossibility [of such a birth], the embodied soul [is not the one who transmigrates]. 1.2.3.

The meaning is that for those who contemplate this ocean of qualities, there arises no suspicion regarding the assumption of a body in this context; for even the slightest scent of connection with the qualities under discussion cannot possibly apply to the "jīva"—who is like a firefly, bound by the causes of the body and subject to immeasurable suffering, and existing in states both bound and liberated. || 3 ||

"He is 'avākī' (without speech)" means that he does not possess such [speech]; this is a statement of the resultant meaning (*phalitārtha*). To the question "Why?", he says: "For what reason?"—this is the sense. Regarding the word "avāpta" (attained): the concern that "avākī" might mean a mere lack of capacity for speech is set aside by the term "anādara" (disregard); this is the intention. By the term "ajalpākaḥ" (one who does not chatter), he shows that the prohibited "vāk" (speech) is of a nature to be abandoned (*heyarūpa*).
With the words "these two," he concludes the meaning of the Sūtra.

The word "yogya" (fit) in the phrase "of the fit one" serves to include even the state of liberation by means of the term "embodied" (*śārīra*). Although it would have been sufficient to say, "But not the other, because of impossibility" (*anupapattestu netaraḥ*), the specific mention of the term "embodied" is intended to clarify that it is impossible for the liberated soul (*jīva*) to be the subject of the teaching. The inclusion of the "bound" [soul] is for the sake of providing an illustrative example.

The intention is that just as it is impossible for the subduer to be identical in nature with that which is to be subdued, so too is it impossible for the benefactor to be identical in nature with that which is to be benefited. This impossibility regarding the qualities under discussion should be applied to each respective quality. The syntactical connection is: "For those who reflect [upon this], no doubt arises."
36. And because of the designation of [the self] as both the agent and the object of action. (1.2.4)

"Having departed from here, I shall attain this"—thus the Supreme Brahman is designated as that which is to be attained, and the individual soul (jīva) as the attainer. Therefore, the attaining individual soul is the worshiper, and the Supreme Brahman to be attained is the object of worship; thus it is understood that "this [Brahman] is indeed other than the attainer. ||4||
37. Because of the distinction in sound. (1.2.5)

"I shall fully attain" means "I have attained. "From this" [means]: for the object of worship (upāsya) and the worshiper (upāsaka) are indeed the attained and the attainer respectively. Therefore, the meaning is that the Brahman which is the object of worship is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), who is the worshiper. If it is argued that the very nature [of the soul] itself is what is to be attained, [we reply: that would result in a violation of the natural sense of the scripture. Here, the designation "this" refers to the reality denoted by the word "Brahman."

Regarding the phrase "due to a difference in designation": in order to resolve the doubt that the status of being the object attained (*prāpyatva*) and the status of being the attainer (*prāptṛtva*) are possible through a difference in states, [the author] demonstrates the application of distinct designations within one and the same state by means of the two subsequent sūtras. In this sūtra, a reference using non-identical case endings is intended.
In the passage, "This is my Self within the heart," the embodied self (*śārīra*) is designated by the genitive case; however, the object of meditation (*upāsya*) is designated by the nominative case.

Thus, in this same context, a distinction between words is heard in the Vājasaneyaka Śruti regarding the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). For example: "As rice, or barley, or millet, or the grain of millet—so is this person within the inner self (antarātman), golden; like a smokeless light.

Here, by the word "within the inner self" (*antarātman*), ending in the locative case, the embodied soul (śārīra) is indicated. By the word "the golden person" (*puruṣo hiraṇmayaḥ*), ending in the nominative case, the object of meditation is indicated. Therefore, the Supreme alone is the object of meditation. ||5||

"And I am seated within the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. "He who, undeluded, thus knows Me as the Supreme Person. "The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine."
The Smṛti shows that by the words "go to Him alone for refuge," the embodied one who is the worshiper and the Supreme Self who is the object of worship are indicated. || 6 ||

31. "If it be argued that [Brahman] is not [the cause] because of its being designated as 'small' and because of such designations, we say no; for it is so designated only because it is to be perceived [in a subtle way], and like the ether. (1.2.7)

The word "of all" (*sarvasya*) is for the purpose of identifying the term "heart" (*hṛdaya*) through the recognition [in the phrase] "This is my Self within the heart. The subsequent sentence, "He who knows me," is for the purpose of making known that [Self] is the object of worship. The explicit statement of "the Lord" (*īśvara*) is a direct declaration of the lordship of that which resides in the heart. Furthermore, the inclusion of the words "Go to Him alone for refuge" is for the purpose of demonstrating the worship of that which dwells in the heart. In the phrase "of all," the word "all" refers to living beings (*jīva*), because it refers to those entities that serve as the substrata for memory and other functions dependent upon another.

The distinction of the one denoted by the term *puruṣottama* from the individual soul (*jīva*) is stated in that very same place. The word "all beings" (*sarvabhūta*) also refers to the individual soul, because it is the locus of delusion and because it is mounted upon the machine known as the body. Here, the word "and" (*ca*) serves either to conjoin two reasons for dispelling an intermediate doubt or to indicate an additional point. || 6 ||
‘Alpāyatanatva’ means having a small abode; its designation is the designation of smallness.

This is because [the Self] resides in the very minute abode of the heart, as in the statement, “This is my Self within the heart,” and [as it is said to be] “smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley.”

If it is argued that this is not the Supreme Self, but rather the individual soul (jīva) alone—because of its designation by its own nature as being "subtler than the subtle" (aṇīyastva) through such passages, and because the Supreme Self is understood from texts like "That which the wise perceive as all-pervading, extremely subtle, and imperishable, the source of beings," to be unlimited, whereas the individual soul is designated as being only the size of the point of an awl—then [the reply follows].

This is not so; for it is the Supreme Self alone that is designated as "minuter" (*aṇīyān*) by way of being an object of contemplation. That is to say, it is to be contemplated in this manner, to be seen in this manner, and to be meditated upon in this manner. However, its essential nature is not merely minuteness itself. Moreover, it is designated as being like space (*vyoma*). And its natural greatness is also designated in this very context:
"Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate region, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds.
Therefore, the designation of smallness is solely for the purpose of meditation. For instance:

Because of the designation of being subtler than the subtle (*aṇīyastva*); because of the designation of being the cause that projects subtlety; and because of the designation of subtlety itself. Having enjoined meditation with the words, "All this, indeed, is Brahman, for it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within it (tajjalān); therefore, one should approach it with tranquility," and [further] having enjoined the meditation: "One should meditate upon Brahman as the Self of all, by virtue of being the cause of the origin and dissolution of all, by virtue of entering into all as their Self, and by virtue of being the sustainer of all."
"Now, indeed, man consists of will; as is his will in this world,
so does he become after departing from here"—
thus, having stated that the attainment of the goal corresponds to one's mode of meditation, [the text continues].
"He should form a resolve," thus,
having referred back to meditation for the purpose of enjoining its attributes,

[it continues]: "Consisting of mind, having breath as its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, possessing all works, all desires, all odors, all tastes, encompassing all this, without speech, without concern."
Thus, having established that the essential nature and qualities of the Supreme Person—distinguished by sovereignty over the universe—are to be accepted, [the text] states:
"This is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet.

Having thus described the abiding of the Supreme Person, who is to be meditated upon as one's own Self, within the heart of the meditator in His subtle form for the purpose of meditation, [the text continues:]

"This is my Self within the heart, greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the heavens, greater than these worlds—the Self of all. Having understood from the scripture that everything has Brahman as its essence, and being free from passion, hatred, and the like, [one should meditate].

The meaning is that one should meditate upon Brahman, which possesses the qualities to be described hereafter. By the phrase "Brahman is the self of all," it is shown that the opening statement is not in conflict with its subtlety (*aṇīyastva*). Now, the words "atha khalu" and so forth serve to indicate the continuity of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*). Regarding the term "anūdya" (having referred back): the sense is that just as the oblation enjoined by the rule "one offers the Agnihotra" is referred back by the word "juhoti" in the rule "one offers with curd" for the purpose of prescribing curd as the instrument of the oblation, so it is here.

The phrase "jagadaiśvarye" is a restatement of the expression "tajjalān. Regarding the "intrinsic qualities"—that is, qualities that are not mediated [by anything else]—these indeed do not depend upon *prakṛti* or *puruṣa*. Having pointed out the form to be attained by the one who is "abiding within the heart" and being meditated upon, [the text says]: "He whose actions are all, whose desires are all, whose scents are all, whose tastes are all; he has pervaded all this; he is without speech and without need."

"This is my Self within my heart; this is Brahman"—having thus established this contemplation, namely, "Such is the Supreme Brahman; out of supreme compassion, for the sake of our awakening, He is present within our hearts," [one reflects]:
"After departing from here, I shall attain Him."

Thus, having prescribed the meditation as well as the contemplation on the certainty of attainment with the words, "He who has this [knowledge] truly, for whom there is no doubt," it is concluded that for such a meditator endowed with the certainty of attaining what is to be attained, there is no uncertainty regarding that attainment. Therefore, the smallness of the abode and the minuteness [of the Self] are for the purpose of meditation. ||7||

40. "If it be argued that [the Supreme Brahman] would attain experience [of pleasure and pain], we say no, because of the difference. (1.2.8) If it is admitted that the Supreme Brahman, like the individual soul (*jīva*), resides within the body, then—just as in the case of the soul—it would follow that He too would undergo the experience of pleasure and pain resulting from connection with the body. To this, the Sūtra replies: "Because He is such [as described]. This states the meaning of the phrase "because He is to be perceived" (*nicāyyatvāt*). The repetition [of the term *hṛdi*] is for the sake of indicating both His being the object of meditation and His being the goal to be attained. Because He resides in the heart...

The repetition of qualities such as "being the performer of all actions" is for the purpose of making known its abiding in the heart and for the purpose of contemplating its accessibility. Thus, because omnipresence is declared here, previously, and subsequently, and because the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the nature of being small is mentioned, the meaning is established that the smallness found in the middle [of the passage] is merely adventitious (aupādhika).
"Existing within the body" means existing within the heart.

"That is not [the reason]," because of the specific nature of the cause. For it is not merely existing within the body that is the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain; rather, it is being subject to karma in the form of merit and demerit. And that is not possible for the Supreme Self, who is free from all evil. Thus says the Śruti:
"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating."
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the section [concerning] the universal establishment. 1.
13. The Section on the Eater (attradhikaraṇa) || 1.2.2 ||
In this context, the self (ātman) indicated by the rice and its condiments is subject to doubt: is it the individual soul (jīva) or the supreme self (paramātman)?
What is the correct position? That it is the *jīva*. Why? Because the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is caused by karma, and that is possible only for the *jīva*.

The form of the doubt is this: Is the "eater" (*attā*) the *jīva* or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? For the sake of resolving this, one must consider whether this state of being an eater consists in the enjoyment of the fruits of karma, or whether it consists in the withdrawal of the universe. Furthermore, is the previously introduced context of Brahman interrupted here, or not? Regarding the phrase "drinking the *ṛta*," are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the *jīva* being indicated, or the *jīva* and the Supreme Self? This is because of the expression "the two drinking."

Is it to be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) like the word "umbrella," or by the primary power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) as referring to the instigator and the instigated? Or rather, is it not so? Does the vision of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) expressed in the passages "that which is difficult to see" and "which [is attained] by means of the vital breath" imply secondary indication, or not? And regarding the question at the beginning, "Who is this that remains after death," does it concern the individual soul or the Supreme?

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if the question at the beginning, "That which one hears when [the body] has died," refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), then—following the lead of that opening—the reference to the drinking of *ṛta* in the passage beginning with "Him, difficult to see," cannot logically be made to refer to the relationship between the instigator and the instigated. Consequently, the sentence "The two who drink the *ṛta*" must be taken as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, the context of Brahman is interrupted here, and the state of being an "eater" established in this passage consists in being an enjoyer of the fruits of action; therefore, the conclusion is that "the eater is the individual soul."

In the Siddhānta: when the question "Who is this? refers to the Supreme Being, then—in accordance with the opening statement—it is logical that the reference to the drinking of *ṛta* in the passage beginning with "Him, difficult to see," establishes the relationship between the one who acts (*prayojya*) and the one who causes to act (*prayojaka*). Since the sentence beginning with "The *ṛta*" pertains to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is no interruption of the context of Brahman; therefore, the nature of being an "eater" established here consists precisely in being the sustainer of the universe. Thus, the conclusion is: "The Eater is the Supreme Self."

Regarding the phrase "of the state of being an enjoyer" (*bhoktṛtvasya*): the meaning is that this refers to [the enjoyership] understood through the capacity for rice and condiments. Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul alone" (*jīvasyaiva*): the meaning is that the Supreme Self's status as an enjoyer is precluded by such texts as "the inner self of all beings, free from evil," "He does not increase nor decrease by action," and "The other, not eating. "Because that is possible" means because the possibility of being an enjoyer of the fruits of action exists [for the individual soul].

Since embodied beings denoted by the terms *brahman* and *kṣatra* consist of both female and male, a relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed is possible among the individual souls (*jīva*) corresponding to those respective forms. Because the souls are eternal and thus not subject to death, the statement regarding "death as a condiment" (*mṛtyūpasecana*) is also tenable, with the underlying intention that death is subordinate to the soul. This is the sense.
To this it is replied: "The Self [is meant], because of the mention of both the moving and the non-moving.
The Self is indeed the Supreme Self. Why? Because...

Because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving—"the state of being the consumer" (*attṛtva*) is possible for Him alone, as He is the consumer of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings. Nor is this state of being a consumer caused by karma; rather, it is the power of destruction belonging to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
This is seen in this very passage: "He reaches the end of the path—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. And so it is said:
"Because of the statement, 'Death is its condiment,' [it follows that] both Brahminhood and Kshatriyahood [are included]."

Thus, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is understood here as the food to be eaten (*audana*). For that which is called a "sauce" (*upasecana*) is itself being eaten while also serving as the cause for the eating of something else. Therefore, since even Death is being eaten as a sauce, it is understood that what is intended here is the eating of the entire world—beginning with the Brahmins and Kshatriyas, comprising all that is moving and non-moving—which is being moistened by that [Death]. And such eating occurs only at the time of dissolution (*upasaṃhāra*). Consequently, this state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), characterized by the power of dissolving the world in this manner, belongs to the Supreme Self alone. || 9 ||

"Not so" (na ca). The sense is that it is untenable for the individual soul (*jīva*) to possess the quality of being the devourer (*attṛtva*) with respect to the entire realm of moving and non-moving beings. In this context, the first reason is the hearing of words denoting the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) regarding the fact that the state of being the devourer—the agency of Viṣṇu in the destruction of the moving and non-moving—is [the subject]; likewise, by the words "and thus" (*tathā ca*), etc., the second reason is stated.

Regarding the phrase "for [it is] a condiment": death is the condiment. If it were simply stated that it is "not an obstacle" (*abādhaka*), no specific form would be established; for the state of being non-obstructive is common to clods of earth, grass, and so forth. However, the specific form consists in being the cause of another's consumption while itself being consumed; it is by virtue of this alone that a figurative usage is appropriate—this is the intended meaning. The principle established here is: setting aside the common form, a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense should be described by means of a subordinate form. Therefore... [the word *ataḥ*].

Even though there is no expectation of death during the dissolution of the entire universe, it is intended here that death is being consumed and that the dissolution of individual beings (*vyaṣṭi-saṃhāra*) occurs by means of that [universal dissolution]. Thus, by the force of the fact that death serves as the "condiment" (*upasecana*), the meaning is that the words *brahma* and *kṣatra* are intended to indicate the entirety of the moving and non-moving world. This is because the state of being the eater (*attṛtva*)—that is, the state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)—is seen to belong to the Cause of all, and nothing else is the cause for the eating; therefore, it is the [Brahman] being sprinkled with [death as a condiment].
Also, on account of the context (Sūtra 1.2.10).
Moreover, this context concerns the Supreme Brahman alone; for it has been introduced as follows:
"The wise man, having realized the great, all-pervading Self, does not grieve"; and "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
Only whomsoever this [Self] chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. Thus indeed is the subject under discussion.
For even the statement, "Who indeed knows where he is? recognizes that very same [Self] as being difficult to comprehend without His grace, as was previously introduced. || 10 ||
To this it is replied:
"For the two selves have entered the cave, because that is seen [in scripture]. (1.2.11)

The phrase "drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*) demonstrates a break in the context (*prakaraṇa*). For a context is weaker than an indicative mark (*liṅga*); here, a break in the context is established by the force of the indicative mark of drinking the *ṛta*. [The opponent argues: "It refers only to the enjoyer of the fruits of action. This break is appropriate because the sentences beginning with "the all-pervading" (*vibhu*) are separated [from the present topic]; however, the sense is that there is no such break for the sentence "drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), which is not separated from the sentence beginning with "of whom Brahman and... (*yasya brahma ca*).

The phrase "of one accompanied by another" is intended to dispel the doubt that there might be equal primacy between the two. The expression "only the enjoyment of the fruit of karma" is used because, just as in the statement "all-encompassing power of destruction," no other explanation for the drinking of *ṛta* is easily conceivable; this is the underlying sense. The thought is that the term "drinking" (*pibantau*) is applied figuratively to the instrument (the intellect) in some way—as an accessory—and thus it is said, "the two who drink the *ṛta*."

"In the Sūtra [it is said], 'the two have entered the cave' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7), because of the abundance of well-known instances of the Supreme Self entering the cave—as in the verse, 'He who knows Him hidden in the cave'—and because there is no such renown for either the intellect (*buddhi*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The word 'for' (*hi*) in the Sūtra indicates that the meaning of the Sūtra serves as a supporting reason for the ultimate conclusion; this is the intended sense.

Neither the vital breath nor the individual soul (*jīva*), nor both the intellect and the individual soul, are described as 'having entered the cave and drinking the Truth' (*ṛta*); rather, it is the individual soul and the Supreme Self who are so designated."
Why?

Because that is seen: in this context, it is observed that the entry into the cave is predicated of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self alone. Regarding the Supreme Self, for instance: "Him, difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret place, situated in the cavity of the heart, ancient... [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12].
"Having known the God through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow. And regarding the individual soul as well:
"Aditi, the goddess consisting of the divine powers, who comes into being with the vital breath, having entered the cave [of the heart], she abides there; she was born through all beings."

Thus: she "eats" (*atti*) the fruits of actions, and so is called *Aditi*, meaning the individual soul (*jīva*). She "comes into being with breath" (*prāṇena saṃbhavati*), that is, she exists together with the vital breath. She is "consisting of the deities," meaning her enjoyment is dependent upon the sense organs. "Entering the cave and abiding there" means she dwells within the interior of the lotus of the heart. "She was born from the elements" means that, accompanied by the elements such as earth and the rest, she is born in various forms such as gods and others.

This being the case, the designation "the two who drink the ṛta" is to be understood as being like "the umbrella-bearers are going. Alternatively, the status of being the agent of drinking is possible for both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), in the sense of the instigated and the instigator. || 11 ||

The phrase "thus" (iti) is connected with the statement "the designation of entering the cave is seen. Regarding the term "fruits of action" (karmaphalāni): since the word "aditi" is well-known in the Vedas as referring both to the mother of the gods and to the earth, this [specification] is intended to exclude those meanings. Since the conventional meaning [of "aditi"] cannot logically enter a cave, the sense is that the etymological (yoga) sense must be accepted. By the term "fruits of action," the meaning of the word "ṛta" is also shown.

Alternatively, if one were to resolve this by the maxim "the umbrella-bearers are going" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*), there would be the fault of resorting to figurative indication (*lākṣaṇikatva*); therefore, the primary interpretation is maintained. According to the stated method—that "the prompter is also the cause"—since the causative agency (*prayojaka-kartṛtā*) of the Supreme Self is a specific form of agency, the designation "the two who drink the truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*) is natural when [the word *pibantau*] denotes that [agency]. This is the intended meaning.

Moreover, this natural sense of the explanation is consistent only if both possess consciousness; for the statement "both have entered the house" does not refer to a man accompanied by a staff, but rather refers to two men.

Two principles have been taught here: 1) when there is no actual movement, between two possible meanings, that which is consistent with the context is to be accepted; 2) the dual number is to be employed only for things of the same class. ||11||
44. And because of the qualification. (1.2.12)

In this context, it is the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone that are presented everywhere as characterized by the roles of the worshiper and the object of worship, and the attainer and the goal to be attained. For instance: "Having known and realized the adorable God who is born of Brahman, one attains this ultimate peace. Here, "born of Brahman" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), because it is born from Brahman and is a knower. "Having known that adorable God"—that is, having understood the individual soul, the worshiper, as being of the nature of Brahman—this is the meaning. Likewise:
"That which is the bridge for those performing sacrifices, the imperishable Brahman which is supreme..."
"May we be able to reach the fearless further shore, the Nāciketa.

Here, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is said to be the object of worship. "Nāciketa" means that which is to be attained through the Nāciketa rite. By such passages as, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot," the individual soul (jīva) who is the worshiper is described. Likewise, [the text continues:]
"The man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the mind with the reins reaches the end of the journey—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus, the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) are designated as the "attainer" and the "attained," respectively. Here too, by the terms "shadow and light," those very two are specifically distinguished by way of ignorance and omniscience.

"Upāsyatva" (the state of being an object of worship), and so forth. The intention is that the other attributes mentioned in those respective passages are included within [the categories of] being the goal to be attained (*prāpyatva*), the attainer (*prāptṛtva*), the means (*upāyatva*), and the worshipper (*upāsakatva*). By "brahmaja" (born of Brahman), he refers to the worshipper. Regarding "śakemahi" (may we be able): the ellipsis is "to worship and to attain.

By "upāsaka" (worshipper), the meaning is that the individual soul (*jīva*) is denoted as being accompanied by the equipment for worship, such as the body and so on. "Ihāpi" (here also) refers even to the passage "the two who drink the *ṛta*. By the phrase "by way of ignorance and omniscience," [he refers to] the statement "the two, the knower and the ignorant. Now, it might be argued: [text continues...]

"Regarding this doubt concerning the deceased person—some say 'it exists,' and others say 'it does not exist'"—since this begins with a question regarding the true nature of the individual soul (jīva), it is understood that this entire section concerns the individual soul.

This is not so; for this question does not arise from a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) as distinct from the body. Were that the case, it would be impossible for him to have requested two previous boons. To explain: at the conclusion of his father’s sacrifice, which was to be completed with the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*), the youth Naciketas—the foremost of theists—fearing that the sacrifice would be defective due to the deficiency of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being given, desired to ensure the perfection of his father’s rite even by the gift of his own self, and thus asked, "To whom will you give me?"

Thus, having asked his father repeatedly, and having entered the abode of Death because his father was angered by his persistence, while Yama had departed from his own abode, he fasted there for three nights due to not seeing him. When Death, fearing his fast and intent on providing a remedy, offered him three boons, he—due to his excess of faith—chose with the first boon the favor of his father toward himself. All this would be impossible for one who does not know the self to be distinct from the body.

The statement has been recalled. Because it shares the same meaning as the cited statement, this very same meaning applies to the words "shadow" (chāyā) and "sunlight" (ātapa) as well. The sense is that in the sūtra "viśeṣaṇācca," the specific qualifiers in the form of "shadow-ness" and "sunlight-ness" are also intended.

Now, it might be argued: in this context, it is improper for the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) to be the subjects [of the inquiry], because the introductory portion (*upakrama*) has the individual soul as its purport.

By the second boon, the knowledge of fire (*agnividyā*), which is the means to the fruit to be experienced by one whose experience of the body as the self has transcended, was chosen. That too is not possible for one who does not recognize the self as distinct from the body.
Therefore, that which is sought by the third boon—

"Regarding this doubt concerning a person after death—some say 'it exists,' others say 'it does not exist'—may I be instructed by you in this; this is the third of the boons. Here, this question is posed with the desire to know the true nature of liberation, characterized by the attainment of Brahman which is the supreme goal of human life, and with the inquiry into the reality of the higher and lower selves and the meditation upon the Supreme Self, which serves as the means thereto. Thus, the phrase "regarding this doubt concerning a person after death" does not intend merely the separation from the body, but rather the complete liberation from all bonds. As it is said: "After departing, there is no consciousness."

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: when a human being qualified for liberation has departed—being entirely freed from all bonds—there arises this inquiry consisting of "is" or "is not" regarding his true nature, caused by the conflicting views of disputants; in order to dispel that, may I, having been instructed by you, know—that is, understand—the reality of his true nature.
For indeed, they disagree in many ways:

(1) some declare that liberation consists in the total destruction of the very nature of the self, which is mere consciousness. In order to indicate that the favor of the father and the acquisition of the knowledge of fire are each an independent cause, the phrase "all this" and "that too" are stated twice.

Regarding the word *atra*: the meaning is "in this [act] which is being performed," namely, that which is chosen (*varaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "mokṣa... is performed": the meaning is that this question is asked with the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) concerning liberation—that is, for the sake of the knowledge of liberation and its related inquiries. In the interrogative sentence beginning with "yeyam" (which is this), the question regarding the essential nature of liberation (*mokṣa-svarūpa*) is explicitly stated; however, it is understood that by way of the manner of the answer, questions concerning meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth are established by implication. Thus, the separate mention of "for the sake of discernment" (*vijñānāya*) and "with the desire to know" (*jijñāsayā*) is intended to make known this distinction.

The sense is shown that once the question regarding the attainment of liberation has been addressed, the questions concerning the means of attainment (*prāpaka*) and the goal attained (*prāpta*) are also implicitly included. The phrase "I may know" (*vidyām*) serves to dispel the suspicion that the word *vidyām* is an accusative case form functioning as an object. The term "consisting of existence and non-existence" (*astināstyātmikā*) refers to forms such as "it exists" or "it does not exist."

1. Some—the Buddhist Mādhyamikas—[hold that liberation is] the cessation of ignorance regarding that which exists as mere consciousness. 2. Others [hold it to be] the state of isolation (*kaivalya*) characterized by the total destruction of all specific qualities such as knowledge in a self that is like a stone. 3. Still others [hold it to be] the same.

4. Others, however—accepting the Supreme Self as one whose evil has been destroyed—maintain that liberation consists in the cessation of the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), which arises from association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), through the removal of those very adjuncts.

5. But those proficient in the three Vedas [maintain]: that the individual soul (*jīva*)—who is the sole cause of the entire universe; whose essential nature consists solely of infinite knowledge and bliss that is the adversary of all things to be abandoned; who is a mine of natural, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities; who is distinct from everything else; who is the Self of all; who is the Supreme Brahman; who exists as the body and the mode (*prakāra*) of that Supreme; whose nature is favorable and unlimited consciousness; whose sole essence is the experience of the Supreme Self; and who possesses beginningless karma...

They declare that liberation (*mokṣa*) is precisely the experience of the innate Supreme Self (*paramātman*), preceded by the eradication of ignorance (*avidyā*), for one whose true nature is obscured by ignorance. In this regard, Mṛtyu, having been questioned by Naciketas—"May I know through your grace the nature of liberation and its means"—examined him by demonstrating the difficulty of understanding that subject and by tempting him with the granting of various enjoyments. Having recognized his fitness, [he taught] the knowledge of the principles of the higher and lower selves (*parāvara-ātmatattva*), the meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātmopāsana*), and liberation characterized by the attainment of that state.
(The others—i.e., the followers of Śaṅkara).

3. Others—the dialecticians (*tārkika*s). [Regarding the phrase "like a stone": the sense is that because the self lacks the nature of consciousness by its very essence, it is "like a stone. The specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇāḥ*)—that is, the particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇāḥ*)—are cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental states (*bhāvanā*).
Starting from the passage, "Him, who is difficult to see, hidden, and entered into... [the text continues].

Having taught up to the point, "Thus he reaches the end of the path, that highest step of Viṣṇu," [the text] further taught the specific details required for that; thus everything is consistent. Therefore, it is established that "the Eater is indeed the Supreme Self. 12.
14. The Section on the Intermediate [Subject] || 1.2.3 ||
45. On account of the intermediate state. 1.2.13.
The Chandogas recite this:
"That person who is seen in the eye—He said, 'This is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.'"
4) Now, what is the supreme self?—thus [it is asked].
What is correct?
1) That it has the nature of a reflection.
Why?
Because it is designated as something well-known, and because of the use of the word "is seen," which denotes immediate perception.

2) Or rather, it is the individual soul (jīvātman), for its presence in the eye is particularly evident; thus, its being well-known is appropriate. Indeed, when the eyes are opened and one looks upward, people ascertain the staying and moving of the individual soul within the body. 3) "By means of rays, this [soul] is established in this [body]."

Or not?—this is the inquiry: Is the context of Brahman interrupted by the knowledge of the fires situated in the middle? Or not? Is the knowledge of the fires an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman? Or not? Is the fruit of the knowledge of the fires conducive to being an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman? Or not? Such is the investigation.

The conclusion of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here is as follows: when the fruit of the knowledge of the fires (*agnividyā*) is not conducive to being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), then—due to the absence of the knowledge of the fires being an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman, due to the interruption of the context of Brahman, and due to the absence of a reference here to the previously introduced Brahman—the [attainment of] immortality and so forth must be taken in a primary sense as one of the reflections and the like.

The conclusion in the Siddhānta is as follows: when the fruit of the knowledge of the fires (*agnividya*) is consistent with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidya*), then, because the knowledge of the fires does not interrupt the context of the knowledge of Brahman by virtue of being a subordinate member (*anga*), it is possible to refer here to the Brahman under discussion; and since immortality and other such qualities inherently possess their primary status, the conclusion is that [the object of the teaching] is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The well-known instances of the reflected image, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the sun are to be understood respectively as the direct perception (*aparokṣaprasiddhi*), the logical proof (*yauktikaprasiddhi*), and the scriptural authority (*śrutiprasiddhi*). This is indicated by the use of the words "this" (*ya*) and "who" (*eṣa*), which refer to them as if they were already established.

"From proximity"—that is, from the understanding of proximity. The meaning is: because the soul's proximity to the body is understood [to exist] in the eye. "They determine that which has been opened," etc. Just as when it is said, "In this action, his capacity is seen," it is thereby said, "That action indicates his capacity," so too when it is said, "It is seen in the eye," it is thereby said, "The soul's abiding in the body is determined by means of the eye. This is the meaning.

The other [interpretations] should be understood as being consistent with the introductory context. Therefore, the mention of immortality, being the center of all blessings (*saṃyadvāmatva*), and so forth, is of the nature of praise. Furthermore, the use of the particle *iti* in the phrase "this is the Self" (*eṣa ātmā*) indicates the intended meaning.

Thus, it is well-known from the Śruti that [the Self] is established in the eye, or else it refers to a particular deity, since it is appropriate to refer to these [well-known entities] as if they were familiar. When it is thus argued that one of these [is meant], we reply: [It is] the Inner [Self], because of the appropriateness [of the attributes].

The Supreme Self is within the eye. Why? Because [the text] says: "He said, 'This is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. They call him 'the one to whom all blessings go' (saṃyadvāma), for all blessings (vāmāni) flow toward him. He is indeed 'the leader of blessings' (vāmanī), for he leads all blessings. He is indeed 'the leader of light' (bhāmanī), for he shines in all worlds. Since these qualities are appropriate only for the Supreme Self, [it is He]. || 13 ||

46. And because of the designation of abode and so forth [Brahman is the inner ruler]. "Abiding in the eye"—such things as the governing [of the senses] belong to the Supreme Self alone, as designated in such passages as, "He who dwells in the eye. Therefore, and for this reason, [the inner ruler is the Supreme Self].
A particular deity—namely, Āditya. "In these alone" means, however, not in the Supreme Self.

"In the final conclusion (rāddhānta), these qualities... means that immortality and other such attributes, being without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), are not possible in the case of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth. A single indicative mark (liṅga) situated at the beginning [of a passage] is weak when in conflict with many subsequent qualities. Therefore, the intention is that the mention of immortality and so on is not merely a figurative praise (stuti). Furthermore, it should be noted that in passages such as "Thus he said," the use of the particle "iti" is seen to refer to the actual meaning [of what was said]. The syntactical connection is: "On account of the logical possibility (upapatti), the one within the eye is the Supreme Self. ||13||
And by the scriptural text "He who [is] in the eye," as well as from the designation of his abode and so forth,
and from qualities such as being the controller and immortality, [it is established that] the Supreme Person [is the one within].

"He who is this person in the eye"—it is he alone who is understood [thereby]. Therefore, the reference as something well-known is appropriate for the Supreme Self. For that very reason, the designation of direct perception in the phrase "he is seen" is also appropriate, because he is seen by yogis. || 14 ||
47. "And because of the mention of [Brahman] as distinguished by bliss. For this reason as well, the eye is the locus of the Supreme Person (puruṣottama).

This is for the purpose of prescribing the place of meditation upon the Brahman under discussion—which is characterized by bliss in the passage "Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is Brahman"—and for the purpose of prescribing qualities such as being the center of all blessings (saṃyadvāmatva).
This is because of the statement, "This person who is in the eye. The word *eva* (only/just) indicates that the reason is independent [of any other].

Regarding the word "sthitau" (in the state of abiding): since the opposite case, "anavasthiteḥ" (because of non-abiding), will be stated later, and in accordance with the scriptural text "dwelling in the eye," the word "sthāna" (place) is explained as meaning "abiding" (*sthitiparatayā*), and not as meaning "location" (*pradeśaparatayā*). The explanation of the word "ādi" (etcetera) in the Sūtra is "niyamanam" (restraining). Here, by the word "ādi," qualities such as being the supporter (*dhārakatva*) and so forth are intended; this is precisely because of its well-known status in the Śruti. For that Reality, as established by the scriptures, is both to be meditated upon by yogins and is perceptible.
Having stated, "That which is invisible," it is further said, "The wise perceive it. || 14 ||

"Sukhaviśiṣṭam" means qualified by the nature of bliss (*sukhatva*); it is like the expression "individuals" (*vyaktayaḥ*). Alternatively, according to the principle that "its essence consists of those qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*), it means qualified by bliss as its attribute (*dharmabhūta-sukha*).

"Because of the mention of worship (*upāsana*). This means that because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) by the word "Brahman" in the passage, "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman," referring to the Brahman mentioned in the question, "What is Brahman? Regarding "independence": the two reasons stated in the preceding sūtra depend upon the statement of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), for it will be said later, "because of non-abiding and impossibility. The point is that this reason, however, is independent of the statement of negative concomitance.
The phrase "Kaṃ brahma" refers here to the eye for the purpose of meditation on that which is full of bliss (*sukha*).
For, because of its designation and its stability here, the Supreme Person resides within the senses.
Now, an objection may be raised: because it is intervened by the knowledge of the fires (*agnividyā*), the Brahman under discussion in the passage "What is Brahman? does not remain proximate here.
For instance, the fires are described as:
"Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman."
Having thus taught the knowledge of Brahman,
[the text] begins with "Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him," and so forth, and taught the meditation upon the fires.
Nor can it be said that the knowledge of the fires is a subordinate limb of the knowledge of Brahman.

Because the knowledge of Brahman is heard to have results not included within [the cycle of rebirth], such as the attainment of full lifespan and the non-interruption of one's lineage, which are contrary to that [cycle].

To Upakosala, who was tormented by the fear of worldly existence—consisting of birth in a womb, old age, death, and so forth, preceded by various afflictions other than the attainment of Brahman—the teacher said: "I am filled with diseases;
O dear one, this is your knowledge of Me and the knowledge of the Self."

Thus, because of the instruction given in combination, it is understood that the knowledge of the fires (agnividyā) is an auxiliary to the knowledge of the Self, which has liberation as its sole fruit. And when its status as an auxiliary is thus understood, it follows that "the mention of the fruit is an explanatory praise (arthavāda)."

Nor is any fruit opposed to liberation heard of here; for these fruits—"He destroys evil-doing," "He becomes one with the world," "He attains a full lifespan," "He lives long," "His descendants do not perish," and "We enjoy him both in this world and in the next"—are consistent with that which is under discussion, namely liberation. "He destroys evil-doing" means he destroys the sinful karma that is an obstacle to the attainment of Brahman.

When sin, which is opposed to that [knowledge], is cast off, he becomes a dweller in the world; he attains the world of Brahman. He reaches the full span of life: until the completion of the meditation on Brahman, he reaches all the life required for it. He lives long—he lives unafflicted by diseases and the like, living until the attainment of Brahman. His lower persons do not perish—his disciples, grand-disciples, and so forth, as well as his sons, grandsons, and others, become knowers of Brahman.
"In his lineage, no one ignorant of Brahman shall be born."

And thus it is heard in another Vedic text as the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman: "We indeed enjoy him, both in this world and in that world; we—the fires—enjoy him, meaning we protect him from all obstacles to the attainment of Brahman."

Therefore, since the knowledge of Agni is an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman, there is no contradiction in its proximity; thus, it is stated for the purpose of prescribing a location for the meditation under discussion—which is characterized by bliss—and for the purpose of prescribing its attributes.
Is it not indeed Brahman?
For it was said: "But the teacher will tell you of the way."

Thus, since only the goal (*gati*) remains as the subject to be established by the Teacher, it is understood that the goal alone is what must be taught. How then can it be said that [the statement] has the purpose of teaching the place (*sthāna*) and its qualities (*guṇa*)?
To this, it is replied:
"But the Teacher will tell you the goal."

The intention of this [passage] is as follows: in order to revive Upakośala—who was despondent because he had not obtained that knowledge when his teacher departed after failing to instruct him in the science of Brahman—the fires of the teacher, namely the Gārhapatya and others, being pleased by his service, instructed him in the essential nature of Brahman alone and in the science of fire which is its subordinate limb.

The phrase "not of him" (*nāsyeti*) shows that because one is born into a family where the knowers of Brahman arise, the result is conducive to the knowledge of Brahman. Regarding the word *bhujāmahe*: from the root *bhuja* meaning "to protect" and "to eat," the form *bhuj* takes the *ātmanepada* ending by the rule "*bhujo'navane*" (Pāṇini 1.3.66). Therefore, since this root is *parasmaipada*, its meaning here is "to protect. Thus, the sense is "we protect. In the Śruti, the meaning of the prefix *upa* is indicated by the prefix *pari*.

The intention is that the assistance extending as far as the removal of obstacles constitutes the fulfillment of the status of the knowledge of fire (*agnividya*) as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman.

Regarding the word *nanu*: if both the location (*sthāna*) and the quality (*guṇa*) were indeed intended as injunctions (*vidheya*), then Brahman would have to be mentioned again for their sake. But that is not the case, because the Teacher has not previously stated them—he will state them later. Therefore, the subsequent passage concerning the location and so forth does not have the Supreme Self as its subject; the meaning is that this sentence has another purpose. [As it is said: "Knowledge truly received from the Teacher reaches its highest perfection."

Having reflected on the meaning of this Vedic text, and thinking, "In order that he may attain the state of being most excellent, let the Teacher himself instruct him regarding Brahman— possessing qualities such as being the center of blessings (saṃyadvāma)— the locus for its meditation, and the path beginning with light (arcirādi)," [it is said]:
"But the Teacher will tell you the way."

Thus they said. The mention of the "path" (*gati*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the remainder of the knowledge to be taught. For this very reason, the Teacher (*ācārya*), having begun with the words, "But I shall tell you that whereby, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus," taught Brahman—characterized by auspicious qualities such as being the center of blessings—as the object of meditation located in the eye, and also taught the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Therefore, [the path must be mentioned].

Because of the mention here of the very same Brahman previously introduced as qualified by bliss in the passage "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," this one who has the eye as his locus is the Supreme Self. || 15 ||

But how is it understood that the supreme Brahman is denoted by the words "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," when you claim that what is mentioned here is [the Brahman] which has the eye as its locus? For—

The word *sādhiṣṭha* is explained by the word *sādhutamatva*. The meaning is that the expression "the most excellent" (*sādhiṣṭham*) is a designation emphasizing the abstract quality (*bhāvapradhāna*). Regarding the mention of "the goal" (*gati*): this refers to the intention of those who say, "The teacher is the speaker of the remainder of the knowledge to be taught," and "But the teacher shall tell him the goal. Regarding "the quality of being the center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāmatva*), etc.: "blessings" (*vāmāni*) means desirable or praiseworthy things; that in which they all converge or meet together is "the center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāmaḥ*).

The term *saṃyadvāma* means being the locus of all auspicious qualities (*sarvakalyāṇaguṇāśrayatva*) or having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). *Bāmanītva* is the quality of bringing about what is beautiful for those who have taken refuge in Him. *Bhāmanītva* is the possession of a radiant form that pervades all worlds. Therefore—the meaning is that because the removal of Upakosala’s dejection was required, because [the teaching] is most excellent when heard from the mouth of a teacher, and because the instruction was incomplete [otherwise], the mention of "going" (*gati*) is intended as a mere illustration. || 15 ||

2. Having stated "prāpayati" (he causes to reach) or "vā" (or), [it is said] "yathā-vā" (as or like), and likewise "tathā—tha" (so—tha); thus, by the rule "yathā-da," Brahman is denoted—i.e., "eva ca-tha" (and indeed—tha), because of the application of the suffix "tha" here.
In the passage, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," it appears that the meditation on the well-known physical ether and worldly pleasure as Brahman is being enjoined;
[as is the case in] "Name is Brahman."
Because of the similarity with such statements as "The mind is Brahman"; regarding this, he says:
48. And for this very reason, that [mind] is Brahman. (1.2.16)

Because in that context, "That which is Ka is indeed Kha" is a designation of the ether (ākāśa) as qualified by bliss; therefore, that ether denoted by the word "Kha" is the Supreme Brahman. This is what is meant: when the fires said, "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," Upakośala replied:
"I understand that this breath is Brahman, but I do not understand *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*."

[Śrī Mādhyama 1.2.2] Regarding their mutual exclusion: [if it were so], Brahman would have the nature of being either "bliss alone" or "consciousness alone"—thus, with the desire to point out one of these two modes, [the text says]:
"I do not perceive either bliss or space."
Having spoken thus, the fires, knowing Upakosala’s intention, said:
"That which is indeed *kaṃ* (bliss) is the same as *kha* (the ether); that which is the divine *kaṃ* is the same as *kha*."

Thus they said. The meaning is that the very nature of Brahman as bliss is indeed unlimited. Therefore, it is concluded: "Having the vital breath (prāṇa) as its body" means that Brahman, characterized by the vital breath, is itself of the nature of unlimited bliss; for [the scripture says]:
"And he [taught] to him the vital breath, and that space, and the eye. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1)
Thus, in the passage "What is Brahman?

Brahman is bliss," unconditioned bliss is presented as Brahman; therefore, the Supreme Brahman alone is the subject under discussion there. And that very same [Brahman] is designated here as having the eye as its locus. Thus, the eye-locus is the Supreme Self. || 16 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "of Upakosala," etc.: in the statement, "That which is indeed *kaṃ* (bliss) is the same as *khaṃ* (space), and that which is *khaṃ* is the same as *kaṃ*," one should not suspect that it is an injunction for a meditative visualization (*dṛṣṭividhi*). For if that were the case, it would be inappropriate for [the subsequent text] "But I do not know *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*" to serve as its answer. The intention is that an injunction for a different visualization cannot be an answer to the inquiry regarding the knowledge of another object of visualization.

Thus, because of the statement of ignorance—"I know [it] thus, O Ketu"—and because this was taught to one seeking liberation (mumukṣu) who is ignorant of any other object, and because it is impossible for it to be an injunction regarding a perceived thing (*dṛṣṭi*), the sentence beginning with "Whatever indeed is pleasure" cannot reasonably be an injunction for a meditative perception (*dṛṣṭividhi*). Furthermore, by the mutual exclusion found in the statement of the fires, "Our science and your science," and by the arrival of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) which was previously under discussion, any suspicion that Brahman is merely a qualification for a meditative perception is dispelled. And [the text says], "And the breath... [etc.].

Because it is logical that the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) should be consistent with the introduction (*upakrama*), the concluding statement "and [he taught] *prāṇa*" has the aforementioned meaning as its purport. The phrase "and *prāṇa*" is a summary of what was stated in "Brahman is *prāṇa*. The phrase "and that in space" is a summary of the meaning of the passage beginning with "What indeed is pleasure. In the expression "that space," the word "that" (*tat*), which refers back to the subject under discussion, intends to convey the nature of bliss. And "that alone" [is the meaning]; otherwise, a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result.

The meaning is that if there were multiple sentences, a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would be untenable; such is the intention. Regarding the word "iti": because it is established that the very subject under discussion, namely "Brahman is Ka," has the eye as its locus, the person in the eye is the Supreme Self—this is the sense. || 16 || And because the path of one who possesses the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is described [in scripture]. 1.2.17. [Note: *vidhīyate* is noted as a variant reading for *dha*. 49. Śrutopaniṣatkagatyabhidhānācca || 1-2-17 ||

For one who has heard the Upaniṣads—that is, for one who has realized the true nature of the Supreme Person—the path beginning with light (arcirādi) is presented in other Vedic texts as that which is to be meditated upon; this path leads to the attainment of the Supreme Person, characterized by non-return. To Upakosala, who had heard about the Person in the Eye, [the teacher said], starting from: "They pass into the light itself; from the light, into the day; from the day, into the waxing half of the month...
and so forth.
"From the moon to lightning, there a person who is non-human;

he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman. Those who proceed by this do not return to this human condition. Because he teaches thus at the end, this Person in the eye is the Supreme Self. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "of one who has heard the Upaniṣads," it is explained that although the entire [text] is to be explained, it is specified here by being set apart for the sake of exposition. The passage beginning with "having attained" and so forth is intended to exclude those meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsanā*), which—though existing—are devoid of the path consisting of light and the rest (*arcirādigati*). By the term "Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣa*), the scriptural text "That person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (*taṃ tvaupaniṣadaṃ puruṣam*) is recalled. This refers to what is being propounded in another scriptural passage.
