In another section of the Chāndogya itself, there is the passage beginning with "Those who know thus," and so forth; in the Vājasaneyaka, the passage beginning with "Those who know this thus," and so forth; and in the Paryaṅka-vidyā of the Kauṣītakins, the passage beginning with "He [goes] to the world of Agni," and so forth. The meaning is that [the soul's journey] is established by these. The intention is that the designation "one who has heard the Upaniṣads" (śrutopaniṣatkṛt) is intended to indicate other scriptural passages that make known that the contemplation of the path is an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman. Regarding the phrase "non-return": [this would not be possible] if the Person in the Eye were not Brahman.

This does not contradict the principle of "the nature of one's resolve" (*tatkratu-naya*). The statement, "Now, whether they perform [rites] here... or not," occurs prior to the passage beginning with "to the light itself" (*arciṣam eva*). In this context, the singular number in "in this" (*asmin*) refers to the class [of beings], in accordance with the plural number in "they [go] to the light" (*te 'rciṣam*). The journey of the five [fires] is restated here for the purpose of prescribing non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*).
[The Teacher has stated in the *Upadeśasāhasrī* that the person within the eye is the Supreme Brahman alone, not the individual soul (*jīva*).

Furthermore, because the very same path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) which is declared for those who have heard the Upaniṣads is here said to be the destination of the worshipper, therefore he too must be the Supreme Person.
50. "And because of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other. (1.2.18)

Because reflections and the like do not necessarily abide in the eye, and because immortality and other such qualities cannot possibly exist in them when they are devoid of attributes, none other than the Supreme Self can be the "Person in the Eye" (akṣipuruṣa), such as a reflection. First, regarding a reflection: since it depends on the proximity of another person, its constant presence is impossible. Regarding the individual soul (jīva) as well: since its function resides in a specific location that serves as the root of all the senses in order to facilitate the operations of all the sense organs, it does not abide in the eye. And as for the deity—
Because it is stated that "He is established in this [eye] by means of rays," it is logical that He—though residing in another location—presides over the sense organs;

therefore, His residence is not within the eye itself. Furthermore, attributes such as unconditioned immortality and so forth are simply impossible for all these [individual souls]. Therefore, the Person in the eye is the Supreme Self. || 18 ||
The Glorious Commentary 1.2.4: Section 1.2.4, On the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin).
And in the passage beginning with "And because of the designation of abodes and so forth," [it says]:
"He who dwells in the eye."

Having established as a proven fact that the abiding, controlling, and so forth in the eye, which are being set forth by such passages as "He who dwells in the eye," belong to the Supreme Self alone, the identity of the Person in the Eye with the Supreme Self has been demonstrated. Now, that very point is further supported:
51. [The Person in the Eye is the Supreme Self] because its attributes are designated in the context of the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), the elements, the deities, the worlds, and so forth. (1.2.19)

Thus, having pointed out someone who abides within and penetrates—acting as the inner controller (antaryāmin)—of the elements such as earth, water, fire, air, ether, moon, stars, and light; of the divine beings; and of all living beings; and of breath, speech, eye, ear, mind, skin, understanding, and semen; and of all that belongs to the self, [the text] teaches: "This is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal."
In the Mādhyandina recension, however, there are the following parallel passages: "He who dwells in all worlds," "He who dwells in all Vedas," and "He who dwells in all sacrifices."
In place of the expression "he who dwells in consciousness," [one should read] "he who dwells in the self."
The word "iti" indicates a synonym; the phrase "the Self of Being, the inner ruler, the immortal" provides the specific distinction.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is this inner controller (antaryāmī) the individual self (pratyagātman), or rather the supreme self (paramātman)?
Why? Because in the supplementary passage [it says], "the seer... the hearer."

Thus, because scripture teaches that knowledge is dependent on instruments, and because the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) is taught to be the Seer himself, and because other seers are denied by the statement, "There is no other seer than He"—this being the position reached, it is replied: The Inner Ruler among those [entities] designated as "with respect to the gods" (adhidaiva), "with respect to the worlds" (adhiloka), and so forth, is the Supreme Self, because His attributes are declared therein. In those passages marked by the terms "with respect to the gods," "with respect to the worlds," and so on, the one heard as the Inner Ruler is the Supreme Self, who is free from evil.
Nārāyaṇa.

Both [sets of] passages are cited in order to make known that, in addition to those passages consisting of the "deity above" (adhidaiva) and so forth established in the Kāṇva recension, there are further passages concerning the "worlds above" (adhiloka) and so forth present in the Mādhyandina recension. Thus, the meaning is that in both sets of passages, the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the Supreme Self.
Why?
Because its attributes are designated as such—this is indeed an attribute of the Supreme Self, namely, that being one alone, it governs all worlds, all beings, and all gods.
For instance, there is the question of Uddālaka:
"He who governs from within this world and the next world, and all beings..."
Having begun thus, [the text says],
"Speak of that inner controller (antaryāmin)," and the answer to that is—

"He who dwells in the earth"—this [phrase] refers to the fact that none other than the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is omniscient and whose will is infallible, can possess the governance of all kinds, the state of being the Self of all by virtue of being the body of all, and the act of entering within all worlds, all beings, all gods, all Vedas, and all sacrifices. For it is said:
"He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all."

"Having created that, He entered into that very thing; having entered into it, He became both the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)"— such Vedic passages from the Upaniṣads declare that the Supreme Self alone is the ruler of all and the Self of all.
Likewise, in the Subālopaniṣad: "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here—not even a root or a support.
These creatures are born from Him; the divine, singular God is Nārāyaṇa. Both the eye and that which is to be seen are Nārāyaṇa."
Beginning with "The ear and that which is to be heard are Nārāyaṇa," it continues:
"The unborn, one, eternal, who is deposited within the secret cave of the body; whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth, whom the earth does not know."
"Of whom water is the body," and so forth;

"Of whom death is the body, who moves within death, whom death does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, the one divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, free from evil. Thus, the supreme Brahman alone is established as the Self of all, the "embodiment of all," and the "ruler of all. Furthermore, immortality is an inherent attribute belonging to the Supreme Self alone.

It has been stated that because [the Lord] is omniscient and possesses true resolve, if He were unaware of those to be governed or if His resolves were futile, the governance of all would be impossible. Regarding the phrase "from the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)," this is because the Subālopaniṣad, in a similar context, states: "The Person alone is all this. With the words "For thus," etc., he shows other scriptural passages (śruti) demonstrating that the governance of all and so forth is possible for the Supreme Person alone.

As for the phrase "of the Supreme Self alone": the sense is that since He alone is the governor of all, while others fall within the category of the governed, the restrictive emphasis "of this very one" is implied.
1. Likewise—not [is there] ownership of all bodies, nor is there the status of being the controller of all;

nor is the capacity for seeing and so forth of the "Supreme Self" dependent upon instruments; rather, it is by its very nature, due to its omniscience and the fact that its will is true, [exercised] by itself alone. And thus says the Śruti:
"He sees without eyes, he hears without ears."
"Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper.

Furthermore, words such as "seeing" and "hearing" do not denote knowledge produced by instruments such as the eyes; rather, they denote the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of form and so forth. And that direct perception of form and so forth arises from the instruments such as the eyes for the individual soul (*jīva*), whose innate knowledge is obscured by karma; but for the Supreme [Self], it exists by its very nature.
The statement "There is no other seer but He" also declares, based on the preceding context, that there is no seer other than the Controller who is the Seer. [And it continues:
"Him whom the earth does not know."

By such statements as "The Self which does not know," and so forth, it is shown that [the Self] governs even while remaining unperceived by those things to be governed, such as the earth and the self; this is precisely what was stated previously: "The unseen seer, the unheard hearer."
Having thus concluded with the passage beginning "There is no other seer than He," the existence of another controller for that Controller is denied.

Because the inner ruler is taught as the Self of the individual soul— which is indicated by the genitive case in the words "this is your Self" and "that is your Self"— the inner ruler cannot be the individual self (pratyagātman). || 19 ||
52. And [the Self] is not the one remembered [in the state of deep sleep], because its attributes are not mentioned there; and [it is] the embodied [Self]. (1.2.20)

The "Smārta" is the Pradhāna (the primordial material cause). The "Śārīra" is the Jīva (the individual soul). Neither the Smārta nor the Śārīra is the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī); this is because of the mention of attributes not belonging to them—that is, because of the mention of attributes impossible for those two. By their very nature, the capacity to see all, the capacity to rule all, being the Self of all, and inherent immortality do not admit even a scent of possibility in those two.

This is what is meant: just as the insentient principle of the Smṛti is not capable of omniscience, controllership, being the self of all, and so forth, so too is the individual soul (jīva); for these are not its attributes. ||20||

I.53. For both [recensions] study this one by distinguishing it [from the others]. (1-2-21) "Both"—namely the Mādhyandinas and the Kāṇvas—study even this embodied self (*śārīra*) by distinguishing it, along with speech and the other [organs], as that which is to be controlled by the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), just like those [organs] which are insentient.
"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self,
who controls the self from within— he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal," so say the Mādhyandinas.

And the Kāṇvas [read]: "He who dwells in consciousness," and so forth; the meaning is that they study him as distinct from that [consciousness] by virtue of being governed by the Supreme Self. Therefore, it is established that the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who is distinct from the individual self (pratyagātman) and is free from all evil. || 21 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin). 4.

Regarding the passage beginning with "He who [dwells] in the self," etc.: here, the repetition of the word *yat* (who) is for the purpose of indicating that He exists as the sovereign controller through His perfection within each individual object. The expression "that is yours" (*sa te*) is an indication of distinction (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, it is unsatisfactory to take words such as "gods" (*deva*) and so forth as referring merely to the physical body; moreover, that [interpretation] would be untenable in the absence of any exception (*apavāda*). If the word "self" (*ātman*) were taken in its own primary sense [as the individual soul], then expressions such as "dwelling" (*tiṣṭhan*) and so forth would also be unsatisfactory.

Because of the requirement for the reading of the *kāvya* (the poetic verse), it is improper for the word "Self" (*ātman*) to have its own specific denotation [as the individual soul] in the phrase "He who dwells in consciousness. Furthermore, there is a lack of natural consistency in the interrogative statement; such is the distinction. The intention to be understood is that the repetition of the word "who" (*yaḥ*) is possible even when [the referent] is one. "The Supreme Self" (*paramātman*): the meaning is that because of the hearing of attributes that differentiate [it from the individual soul], the designation by way of distinction is established. The sense is not merely that there is no exception to the negative indications and so forth, but rather that there is also an exception to the lack of natural consistency in those [indications]. ||21||
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa). 4.
For both [are indeed so].
16. The Section Concerning Him Whose Qualities are Invisibility and the Like (Adṛśyatvādiguṇakādhikaraṇa) || 1.2.5 ||
54. [The Brahman is] that which has the qualities of being invisible and so forth, because of the statement of its attributes. (1.2.22)

The followers of the Atharvaveda study: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained—'that which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet; eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and imperishable, that which the wise perceive as the source of all beings' (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6). Likewise, later on:
"Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme."
Thus [it is said].

In this regard, a doubt arises: Is the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) characterized by qualities such as invisibility here, and the one "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ*) both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; or is it the Supreme Self alone in both cases? With the words "Now," etc., [the author] has taken both sentences as the subject matter with the intention that the term "characterized by qualities such as invisibility" refers to the Imperishable, while by the masculine designation "higher than the high Imperishable," both [entities] are intended. "Invisible" (*adṛśya*) means not an object of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*). "Ungraspable" (*agrāhya*) means not an object of actions such as taking or rejecting performed by the hands and so forth (Śrutaprakāśikā).

"What is the doubt here? [The answer is: It is suspected that the Imperishable (akṣara), characterized by qualities such as invisibility, is Primordial Matter (prakṛti), and that the one who is "higher than the high Imperishable" is the individual soul (jīva); however, it is not suspected that both possess the nature of both. This applies to both cases in the two respective passages. "What, then, is the prima facie view? It is that these two are Primordial Matter and the Person (puruṣa).
Why?
Because of this Imperishable, [it is said]:
"The unseen seer."
As in such passages, the specific conscious attribute of being a "seer" (draṣṭṛtva) and so forth is not heard here; rather,

by the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable," the "Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña), the collective Puruṣa who is higher than this Imperishable which itself is beyond all modifications, is established.

The form of the doubt is as follows: Is that which is described as being beyond the Imperishable (akṣara) and higher than it the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa—possessing qualities such as invisibility and so forth—or is it the Supreme Self? For the sake of resolving this, there arises an inquiry: Does the denial of visibility and other attributes—which are observed to belong to earth and the rest—present a basis that is of the same nature as earth and the rest, namely, something insentient? And does the employment of the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) as an illustrative example strengthen the implication of an insentient basis? Or is it not so?

Does the word ‘viśva’ (the universe) in the passage, "From the Imperishable, the universe originates here," denote the phenomenal world consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious? Or does it denote only the unconscious?

If it denotes the unconscious, then—since the analogy of the spider supports the presentation of that which has the unconscious as its substratum, and since the attributes such as visibility being negated serve to present the unconscious—the one characterized by invisibility and other qualities would be the Pradhāna; and the one beyond that would be the individual soul (jīva).

When the word "Viśva" denotes the world consisting of both the sentient and the insentient, then—since the analogy of the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) does not support the presentation of the insentient—the visibility and other attributes being negated do not themselves present the insentient either. Thus, the Supreme Self is characterized by qualities such as invisibility; and because no other entity exists beyond the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self is that which is "higher than the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "of this imperishable" (*asya akṣarasya*): even in the Antaryāmin-vidyā, the state of being unseen (*adṛṣṭatva*) alone does not establish the identity with the Supreme Self; rather, it must be accompanied by the quality of being the seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) and so forth. Here, however, because that accompaniment is absent, the quality of being unseen does not serve to distinguish [the subject] from the intellect (*buddhi*). This is the meaning. Furthermore, by the words "unseen, yet the seer" (*adṛṣṭo draṣṭā*), the intended connection is established. The sense is that there is grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed as "from the imperishable which is beyond all modifications," based on the natural force of the indication through the same case-ending (*samānavibhakti-nirdeśa*) (Śrutaprakāśikā).

This is what is meant: the denial of visibility and other qualities—which would otherwise reside in gross, insentient elements such as earth that possess form and so forth—necessarily brings to mind something of the same genus as earth, but subtle and insentient; and that is precisely the *pradhāna*. Furthermore, its status as the "Supreme" (*para*) is well-established as belonging only to the collective person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*). And it is this *pradhāna*, presided over by Him, that produces the entire range of transformations beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the specific elements. It is in this context that the "illustrative examples" (*dṛṣṭāntāḥ*) are presented.
"As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], as herbs arise upon the earth,
and as hair and body-hair grow from a living man, so does this entire universe arise from the Imperishable."
Thus, it follows that in this section, only primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa) are being expounded.

This being the case, we reply: "The one possessing the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is the Supreme Person], because of the mention of His attributes. That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth—the Imperishable (akṣara) and that which is higher than the high—is indeed the Supreme Person.
Why?
Because of the mention of His attributes.

"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" [refers to one] who brings about [the perception of] form and so forth. Words such as "brāhmaṇa" and the like apply to those of the same genus, such as kṣatriyas and so on, who are proximate [to the referent], but not to outcastes (śvapacas) or animals. Words such as "not young" and "not thin" apply to that very same substratum (dharmin) which is the locus of a proximate different state, but not to another substratum; for it is logical that they convey what is proximate.

Thus, when there is an expectation for a specific substratum (*dharmin*) for qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*), since that which is being negated—visibility—is understood to reside in non-conscious matter (*acetana*), it is possible for those very qualities like invisibility to belong to that same entity in its subtle state. The sense is that it is improper to resort to a different, extraneous substratum, as that would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Regarding the phrase "and that": the sense is that non-consciousness (*acetanatva*) is not pervaded by visibility and so forth, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) found in the case of the mind (*manas*) and other such things.

The phrase "as on the earth" is an illustration [of how things proceed] even in the absence of the superintendence of a conscious being. The phrase "as of that which exists" is an illustration [of how things proceed] depending merely on the proximity of a conscious being. The word "therefore" concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Indeed, words such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), which are joined with the negative particle (*nañ*) having another referent, recall the statement "the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣa*) from the passage "the Person higher than the high" (*parātparaṃ puruṣam*).

By such means, His very attributes, such as omniscience and so forth, are declared. For instance, after denoting the Imperishable (*akṣara*) characterized by invisibility and other qualities through the passage beginning "by which that Imperishable is attained," and after declaring the origin of the universe from that—namely, "from the Imperishable the universe here comes into being"—[the text proceeds].

"He who is all-knowing, the knower of all, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from him this Brahman, as well as name, form, and food, are born. Thus, omniscience and other attributes are established for the Imperishable (akṣara), which is the source of beings. Subsequently, it is said: "Higher than the high Imperishable."

Thus, the subject under discussion—the Imperishable (akṣara) which is the source of beings and possesses qualities such as invisibility—is indeed omniscient, and it is designated as "the Supreme. Therefore, in the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ*), the word "Imperishable" ending in the ablative case does not denote the aforementioned Imperishable that possesses qualities such as invisibility; for since that omniscient source of the universe is higher than everything, it is impossible for anything else to be higher than it. Consequently, in this context, the word "Imperishable" refers to the insentient subtle element of matter (*bhūtasūkṣma*).

Regarding the phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*): An objection might be raised—surely the *akṣara* (the Imperishable) is *prakṛti* (primordial matter); whereas the Omniscient One is the individual soul (*jīva*) of preeminent merit who, by his mere presence, assists *prakṛti*, or it may be the liberated soul characterized by that state. It is in response to this doubt that [the Sūtra] says: "Therefore... The intention is that the word "*akṣara*" refers to the *akṣara* under discussion [in the preceding context]. "For this reason also, neither the Pradhāna nor the Puruṣa [are meant], because of the designation of difference and distinction" (1.2.23).

For the context distinguishes the Imperishable—the source of beings—from both Pradhāna and the individual soul; that is to say, it sets it apart by means of such factors as the fulfillment of the promise that through the knowledge of one, all is known. Likewise, the difference of the Imperishable from those two is designated:
"Higher than the high Imperishable."
By such statements as these;

for instance, "He taught the knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son"—thus the knowledge of Brahman, which is the foundation of all knowledge, has been introduced. And it is the higher knowledge alone that is the foundation of all knowledge.
Desiring to know this very science, which is the foundation of all sciences and was obtained by Aṅgiras through the lineage of teachers beginning with the four-faced Brahmā,
Śaunaka— who was indeed a great householder— approached Aṅgiras according to the prescribed rule and asked: "Venerable sir, when what is known does all this become known?"

Thus, because the knowledge of Brahman is the foundation of all knowledge, and considering that "by the realization of Brahman, everything becomes realized," he asked about the true nature of Brahman.
To him, he said: "There are two kinds of knowledge to be known, as those who know Brahman have declared—the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā)."
Thus, the meaning is that two kinds of knowledge are to be acquired by one who desires Brahman.

It should be understood that there are two types of "non-cognition" (*avijñāna*) regarding the object of Brahman—namely, those of the nature of being indirect and direct—according to the Vedic revelation. And the Blessed Lord Parāśara said:
"O Great Sage, both knowledge and action have been declared to be the cause for attaining That."
"Knowledge is likewise said to be twofold: arising from scripture and from discernment.
Regarding that, the lower [knowledge] consists of the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.

By this passage, ending with the words "the treatises on dharma," indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) arising from scripture— which serves as the cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman— is described; for the Veda, together with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the treatises on dharma, and Mīmāṃsā, is the cause for the production of the knowledge of Brahman.

"Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained"—this refers to knowledge in the form of devotion, characterized by the direct realization of Brahman, which is termed "meditation. By the passage beginning with "That which is invisible, ungraspable," the essential nature of the Supreme Brahman—the object of two types of knowledge, namely the indirect and the direct—is described.

By the passage beginning with "As the spider emits and withdraws [its web]," the origin of the entire universe—consisting of both sentient and insentient entities—from the supreme Brahman, the imperishable (akṣara) whose nature has been described, is stated. By the use of the word "the whole" (viśvam), it is not merely the insentient that is meant;

rather, both are intended, meaning that both serve as the cause for knowledge consisting of meditation. And by saying "and so it is said," it is shown that the claim that these two types of knowledge have different objects is contrary to the corroborative texts (upabṛṃhaṇa). "And from discrimination" means that it has arisen.

Regarding the phrase "of that which possesses its limbs" (*sāṅgasya*): the meaning is that because the scripture, together with its ancillaries (*saparikara*), is the cause for the knowledge of that [Reality], it is called "lower knowledge" (*aparā vidyā*). By the previously cited corroborative statement, "Knowledge is twofold," the fact that the sentence beginning with "Therein, the lower... has as its object the knowledge arising from scripture is made clear. Then, by the word "now" (*atha*) in the sentence beginning with "Now, the higher" (*atha parā*), he states that the object of that [knowledge] is the knowledge produced by discrimination (*viveka*). The connection [of the text] is with the word "stated" (*uktam*).
"Like a spider," etc., means the explanation of its being the source of all beings (*bhūtayoni*).
By the passage, "By austerity (*tapas*) Brahman grows; from it food is born;

from food, vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), truth (*satya*), the worlds, and immortality in ritual acts," the manner of the universe's origination from Brahman is stated. Here, "by austerity" means by knowledge (*jñāna*).
Because it will be stated later that "his austerity consists of knowledge," [the self] is accumulated— that is, it is built up— as in the thought,
"May I become many."

The meaning is that by means of this knowledge in the form of volition (*saṅkalpa*), Brahman becomes intent upon creation. From that, "food" (*anna*) is produced; it is called "food" because it is eaten. The subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which constitute the objects of enjoyment for the entire class of enjoyers and were previously undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), are born from the Supreme Brahman—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the entire range of modifications (*vikārajāta*), beginning with vital breath (*prāṇa*) and mind (*manas*) and extending up to the ritual actions (*karman*) that serve as the means for attaining the fruits of heaven and liberation, is born from that very same source.
[As stated: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

By such passages, "omniscience," "the power of true resolve," and so forth—which constitute the instruments for creation—are described. From the Supreme Brahman, who is omniscient and possesses true resolve, from the Imperishable (akṣara), this Brahman in its effected form arises—differentiated by name and form, and consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
By the words "That is the Truth" (tad etat satyam), the unconditioned reality of the Supreme Brahman is declared.
The worlds are the mountains of heaven. And "immortality in ritual acts" means immortality dependent upon ritual acts; the sense is that ritual action is the means to immortality.

By the phrase "of the class of enjoyers residing in the universe," the word "truth" (*satya*) found in this sentence is explained. The meaning is: "of the class of enjoyers who are denoted by the word 'truth'."

"Who is omniscient" means as follows: just as in the sentence "He offers with curd," the word "offers" (*juhoti*) refers back to the oblation enjoined in "He performs the *agnihotra*," and thereby prescribes curd as its instrument; likewise, by referring back to the Cause, there is the prescription of attributes such as omniscience. Furthermore, by the phrase "and it is born in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed," the word "food" (*anna*) is explained. For the etymology of the word "food" is: "it is eaten (*adyate*) and it eats (*atti*) the beings."—"The rituals which the seers beheld in the mantras..."
"These were transmitted in many ways during the Tretā age;
perform them, being constant and desiring Truth"—thus [the text means]:

those who desire the Imperishable Person, the mine of auspicious qualities such as omniscience and the power of true resolve, who are themselves eternally real, and who, being detached from other fruits for the sake of attaining Him, perform the rites seen by the sages in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, which are appropriate for the various castes and stages of life, and which have been transmitted in many ways through the three sacred fires.
Beginning with "This is your path," and so forth.

By the passage ending with, "This is your holy, well-prepared world of Brahman," [the text] describes the manner of performing ritual actions; it declares that among the rites enjoined by Śruti and Smṛti, even if there is a deficiency in one particular action, those others which have been performed become fruitless, and what is improperly performed is equal to what was not performed at all. It further states: "For these eighteen forms of sacrifice are but rafts, among which the highest and the lowest are rituals.
Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good fall again into old age and death."

By such statements as these, having first described the "inferior karma" performed by those who act with an attachment to results and a lack of knowledge— thereby mentioning their return to worldly existence— and then,

by the passage beginning with "But those who practice austerity and faith," having again praised the karma performed by the wise when free from attachment to results as leading to the attainment of Brahman, [the Lord says:]...

By the passage beginning with "Having examined the worlds," having prescribed the approach to a teacher for one who is detached from the fruits of mere ritual action and who desires to know the knowledge that—supported by the aforementioned actions—is the means for attaining Brahman, [the text continues] with:
"This is the truth: as from a well-kindled fire..."

By means of this passage, beginning with "Thus... and ending with "...O dear one, he shatters the knot of ignorance here," [the text] clearly describes the universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) of the aforementioned Supreme Person— the Imperishable, the Source of Beings, the Supreme Brahman— by way of His being the inner Self of all beings and having the universe as His body, along with His unmentioned essential nature and attributes, and also His creation of the universe.

By the passage beginning with "Manifest and near" (*āviḥ saṃnihitam*), the method of meditation upon that very same Imperishable (*akṣara*)—which is beyond even the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) and superior to the Puruṣa, being the Supreme Brahman established in the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*), whose nature is unsurpassed and infinite bliss—is taught. Having taught that the mode of meditation consists of supreme devotion (*parabhakti*), and having shown that for the one who meditates, the fruit is the experience of Brahman equal to Brahman itself following the liberation from ignorance (*avidyāvimoka*), the section is concluded.
Therefore, because of these specific qualifications and because of the designation of difference, neither the Pradhāna nor the Puruṣa are being propounded in this section.
56. And because of the presentation of form. (1.2.24)
"Agni is his head; the sun and moon are his eyes; the quarters of space are his ears; the Vedas are his opened mouth;
the wind is his breath; the universe is his heart; and the earth is indeed his feet—for he is the inner self within all beings."
Such a form as this belongs only to the Supreme Self, who is the inner self of all beings; therefore, he is the Supreme Self. ||24||
17. The Section on Vaiśvānara (1.2.6)
57. Vaiśvānara [is the Supreme Self], because of the distinction of common terms. (1.2.25)
The Chāndogas recite this:
"Learn this very Self, Vaiśvānara, as it truly is; tell us that indeed," and having thus begun, they continue:
"But he who worships this very Self, Vaiśvānara, as the measure of a span and as the all-pervading one..."
Thus, there arises a doubt in this regard: can it be determined whether this Vaiśvānara Self is the Supreme Self or not? Or is it not determinable?
The Section on Vaiśvānara (1). First, regarding the digestive fire:

"This is Agni Vaiśvānara... by whom this food is cooked, which is eaten here; its sound indeed exists, as long as one hears it by covering the ears. When he is about to depart [from the body], he does not hear that sound."
Thus [it is said].
And in the third [chapter] of the Mahābhūta:
"The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the great banner for the sake of the entire world."
Thus [it is said].
3. And regarding the deity:
"May we abide in the good favor of Vaiśvānara; for he is the king, the sovereign glory of all beings."
Thus:
4. And with respect to the Supreme Self—it was cast into that very Self, the Vaiśvānara fire within the heart.
Thus, it is said:
"This very Vaiśvānara, the universal-formed Prāṇa, rises as Agni.
Furthermore, even the indicative marks (liṅgas) perceived in the opening and other parts of the passage can be interpreted so as to be consistent with all [the texts].

This being the case, it is replied: Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self because of the distinction of the common term. Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the distinction of the common term. "Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means that which is distinguished. The meaning is that the common term "Vaiśvānara" is distinguished by attributes that are unique to the Supreme Self.
For instance, the great sages beginning with Aupamanyava, having assembled and deliberated, "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?", [concluded]:
"Venerable sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi indeed [knows] this Self at present."
"He studies the Vaiśvānara; let us go to him.

Having learned of Uddālaka’s knowledge regarding the self as Vaiśvānara, they approached him. And Uddālaka, perceiving that these men were seekers of the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara-self and considering himself to be incomplete in his own understanding of it, said to them:
"Sirs, this Aśvapati, the King of Kekaya, currently knows this self—"

"He studies the Vaiśvānara [section]; let us go to him," and so forth. This is not an explanation of the meaning of the suffix in the word *viśeṣya* (qualified); rather, it is an explanation of the genitive case contained within the compound *sādhāraṇaśabdaviśeṣāt*. The meaning is that the genitive is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and not in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The term *viśeṣa* is introduced with the intention that this derivative word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix serves as the cause for the genitive in the sense of the object. Alternatively, by stating "it is qualified (*viśeṣyate*), therefore it is a qualification (*viśeṣa*)," he indicates that the suffix *ghañ* has the sense of the object.

The compound *sādhāraṇaśabda eva viśeṣaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya*. Regarding the word *dharmaiḥ*, the term *dharma* refers to gender (*liṅga*). The statement "because it is being qualified" expresses the resultant meaning (*phalitārtha*), not the literal denotative meaning (*ābhidhānika*). The two occurrences of the word *kim*—in the questions "What is the Self? (intending to ask what is to be known) and "What is Brahman?"—the word *kim* is used either with the desire to know whether the two properties of selfhood and Brahman-hood are one or many in that single entity denoted by the words "Self" and "Brahman."

The application of the two [statements] is as follows: regarding the phrase "and of oneself," he states the purpose of the scriptural passage in the context of the subject matter, beginning with "In my kingdom there is no thief.
Then those [sages], with Uddālaka as the sixth, approached Aśvapati. Having honored those great seers individually according to their merit, he said, "In my kingdom there is no thief..."

By means of this passage, beginning with these words and ending with "O venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice," he makes known his fitness for receiving gifts by virtue of being established in his vows; and at the same time, he demonstrates that even those who know Brahman must avoid what is forbidden and perform the duties prescribed by injunction.
He said, “I shall give as much wealth to each of you priests as I shall give to the venerable ones;
please stay.
And those seekers of liberation, desiring to know the Vaiśvānara Self, said, “Tell us that very Self of ours. Thus it was.
By those desiring to know Brahman— which is the Self of the individual souls (jīvātman)—

in response to the inquiry, "Who is the Self? What is Brahman?", and by those seeking one who knows it, having approached the knower of the Vaiśvānara-Self, the Vaiśvānara-Self, when questioned, is understood to be the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Since the discourse begins with the two terms "Self" (*ātman*) and "Brahman," and subsequently employs the terms "Self" and "Vaiśvānara" everywhere, it is understood that the word "Vaiśvānara," which is used in place of the word "Brahman," denotes "Brahman. Furthermore:
"He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all Selves"; and, "Just as a tuft of cotton placed in a fire would be consumed, even so are all his evils consumed."
And this result of the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self, which will be stated hereafter, makes it known that the Vaiśvānara Self is the "Supreme Brahman. ||25||

For this reason as well, Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self—the word "iti" here denotes a manner or mode. The recognition of such a form would serve as an inference for the status of Vaiśvānara as the Supreme Self; for in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the form of the Supreme Person is well-known to be thus. As it is said in the Atharvaṇa:
"Fire is His head, the sun and moon His eyes, the quarters His ears, and the revealed Vedas His speech."
"Vāyu is his breath, the universe is his heart; from his two feet the earth arose, for he is the inner self of all beings.
Here, "Agni" refers to the heavenly world;
"that world, indeed, is Agni."
Thus says the Śruti. And the sages remember it thus:

"Know him whose head the wise call the sky, whose navel is space, whose eyes are the moon and sun, whose ears are the quarters, and whose feet are the earth—he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings."
"May fire be his mouth, heaven his head, space his navel, the earth his feet;
may the sun be his eye and the quarters his ears—salutation to him, the soul of the worlds.
Thus it is said.
And here, beginning with Heaven, [the elements] are described as the head and other limbs of Vaiśvānara by the great seers such as Aupamanyava and others; for it is thus stated by them:

Regarding the phrase "the word *iti*": this is the response to the objection that the word *iti* is redundant because the status of being a logical reason (*hetutva*) is already established by the word "inference" (*anumāna*). The statement "He is the subduer of the quarters" (*abhibhūr dhāma*) is cited because it is intended to refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). "Speech manifested" (*vāgvivṛtāḥ*) refers to the functions of the organ of speech. "Vāyu is the vital breath" (*prāṇa*)—the great wind itself is the vital breath that sustains the body. "The entire universe is his heart"—the whole world is his specific fleshy portion called the heart located within the body.
The earth is his two feet—the two feet themselves are the earth. He is the inner self of all beings—because he has all beings as his body, he is the inner self of all.
Regarding "Agni here": the sky is heard of as being his head, as in the text, "Agni is the head."

In the passage, "Whose mouth is fire," the word "fire" (agni) refers to the well-known physical fire, because it is mentioned separately in the phrase, "The sky is his head. Having been questioned by the Kekayas, "You indeed know this Vaiśvānara Self; tell us about that very one," and desiring to instruct them regarding the Vaiśvānara Self, Aśvapati—having understood through the impossibility of explaining otherwise that "some portion of the Vaiśvānara Self has been known by these [pupils] and some portion remains unknown"—questioned them one by one out of a desire to ascertain both the known and the unknown portions. In that regard:
When asked, "Aupamanyava, which Self do you meditate upon? he replied,
"The sky itself, O Venerable King."

When he had spoken thus, [the teacher], while subverting his notion that the heaven was the self of the complete Vaiśvānara and teaching that "the head of Vaiśvānara is the heaven," proclaimed for that heaven—which is but a portion of Vaiśvānara—the name of its quality, "Sutejas" (the Well-Luminous).

Thus, since the Sun, Wind, Ether, Water, and Earth have each been described as being meditated upon individually through the Satya-sacrifice and other rites, their respective names—“Viśvarūpa,” “Pṛthagvartman,” “Bahula,” “Rayi,” and “Pratiṣṭhā”—which denote individual qualities, as well as their status as the eyes, breath, trunk (sandeha), bladder (vasti), and feet of the Vaiśvānara Self, have been taught. Here, *sandeha* refers to the middle part of the body.
Therefore, because this form is characterized by having heaven as its head and so forth, just like that of the Supreme Person, “Vaiśvānara” is indeed the Supreme Person alone. || 26 ||
Furthermore, having raised the doubt that there is indeed no definitive conclusion, [the author] refutes it:

59. "Not so, because of the mention of sound and other qualities, and because of its abiding within; if it be argued that this is not the case, we say no, because of the teaching of what is seen [in scripture], because of impossibility, and because they also study him as being a person. (1.2.27)

The meaning is that this should be understood as applying to [the categories] beginning with "dyu" (heaven). Furthermore, the word "smṛta" (remembered) brings to mind that which is being recognized; for in the *Tarkapāda*, in the sūtra "And because of remembrance" (*anusmṛteśca*), the authors of the sūtras used the word "remembrance" (*anusmṛti*) in the sense of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

As for what was stated—that Vaiśvānara is determined to be the Supreme Self—that is not so; because, on account of the word and other factors, as well as because of his abiding within, the gastric fire (*jāṭharāgni*) is also perceived here. In the section concerning the Vaiśvānara-vidyā of the Vājasaneyins—
First, regarding the word:

the term "Agni" is heard in the scripture as being in grammatical apposition with Vaiśvānara, in the passage, "This is that Agni Vaiśvānara. Furthermore, in this context, a threefold conceptualization of fire is made for Vaiśvānara, who resides in the heart and other organs, as it is stated: "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire."

Furthermore, by the passage beginning, "Whatever food may come first, that is to be offered in sacrifice; whatever first oblation he may offer, let him offer it with 'Svāhā to Prāṇa'," it is understood that Vaiśvānara is the substratum for the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Likewise, the Vājasaneyins record the internal abiding of Vaiśvānara within this person: "He who knows this very Agni Vaiśvānara, who is of the form of man and is established within the person..."

Thus, if it is argued that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "fire," because of the conceptualization of the three fires (*agnitretā*), because of being the locus for the offering of breath (*prāṇāhuti*), and because of being established within, Vaiśvānara is understood to be the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) as well, and therefore his status as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not absolute—then [the Sūtra] says "no" (*na*) to explain what was stated. This is because the two reasons from the other Śruti passage are remote; thus, those two are explicitly mentioned here.

The conceptualization of the three fires and their status as the substratum for the oblation of breath (prāṇāhuti) found in this specific context is included by the word "and so forth" (ādi), because of its proximity. With this intention, it was stated: "In the section concerning the Vājins, they recite the Vāja [hymn]."

In this context, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and in this section," it is indicated that [the quality of being the abode] exists for the *vājins* as well. By the phrase "the three fires," only the status of being the substratum for oblations is established. By the phrase "that which is the food," the specific nature of being the substratum for oblations is intended. What is intended to be expressed is "abiding within" accompanied by the designation of the word "fire. For the mere state of abiding within is possible even for the Supreme Self; indeed, it is heard in scripture: "He who knows this Vaiśvānara fire, which is of the form of man and abides within man, as such... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1).

The portion of the sūtra beginning with "From sound, etc. (ŚB 1.1.23) refers merely to the suspicion regarding the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), and not to the deity or the elemental [fire]; this is because of the mention of its being "established within" (*antaḥ-pratiṣṭhāna*), and because other reasons are associated with that.
Indeed, him alone—da...

That is not so; for it is taught as being seen thus: because there is an instruction for the meditation upon the previously mentioned Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Brahman whose body is the three worlds, as being characterized by the gastric fire—that is, by having the gastric fire as His body. For by words such as "fire" (agni), it is not merely the gastric fire that is set forth, but rather the Supreme Self as qualified by the gastric fire. If it be asked, "How is this understood? [the answer follows].

Because of impossibility—that is, because it is impossible for the mere digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) alone to have the three worlds as its body. The meaning is this: the word "fire" (*agni*), which is perceived as referring to the digestive fire, stands in grammatical apposition with Vaiśvānara who is understood to have the three worlds as his body; thus, it denotes the Supreme Self alone as qualified by that [digestive] body. As stated by the Blessed One: "Becoming Vaiśvānara, I abide within the bodies of living beings;
joined with the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, I digest the four kinds of food."

Thus; the meaning is: having become one whose body is the digestive fire (jāṭharānala). Therefore, the meditation on that which is qualified by this [fire] is taught here. Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins also study him as a person (puruṣa).

The word *tannati* removes the doubt that [the Vaiśvānara] has the stomach as its object. The phrase "by being the body of the digestive fire" is according to the intention of the Śruti text: "He whose body is fire. The word "meditation" (*upāsana*) is an explanation of the word "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) used in the Sūtra; for there are Vedic usages such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" and "When He, the high and the low, is seen," and here it is heard: "One meditates upon Vaiśvānara."

Since it is possible for [the passage] to have the ultimate reality as its object, it is improper to resort to the view that it has a non-ultimate reality as its object; thus, there is no suspicion of its being equivalent to meditative views such as "The mind is Brahman. For in the case of the gastric fire, attributes such as having the sky as its head are utterly contradicted [by experience]. By the phrase "as having the gastric fire as its body," the possibility of the ultimate reality being the subject matter is demonstrated. Furthermore, because it is impossible to perceive the inferior fire within the superior Supreme Self, the perception of fire does not apply to the Supreme.

Because both the marks of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the marks of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) are observed, one must admit that the intent is a specific form of meditative worship (*viśiṣṭopāsana*). This is the meaning of the passage being established and made known in the *Pratardana-vidyā*. "How so? and so forth: the sense is, "How can that which is well-known as referring to the mere physical fire have as its object that which is qualified by [the Supreme Self]? By the phrase "as has been stated," he confirms—by means of traditional scripture (*smṛti*)—that words well-known to refer to the digestive fire are applied to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who is qualified by that [fire].

Regarding the phrase "and also in the person" (*puruṣamapi ca*): here, the particle *ca*, being separated [from the preceding word], has the sense of a conjunction of reasons (*hetu-samuccaya*). It means that not only is there the nature of fire (*agnitva*) and abiding within the person (*puruṣe'ntaḥ-pratiṣṭhitatva*), but it is also studied as being denotable by the word "person" (*puruṣa-śabdavācyatayā*). [Objection: Is it not the case that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is also perceived here, because of the instruction regarding meditation on that which is qualified by the aforementioned triad of worlds? [Reply: No, for it is not exclusively the Supreme Self, because of the teaching of meditation characterized by those [qualities]. Thus, its status as the Supreme Self is not absolute.
"This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed this Puruṣa; for it is not the mere digestive fire that possesses the nature of Puruṣa,
but rather the Supreme Self alone, when free from limiting adjuncts."
Thus [is] the state of being the Puruṣa! As for example:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," and "The Puruṣa alone is all this."
In such passages as these, [the rule applies]. || 27 ||
60. For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being. (1.2.28)
For the very reasons already stated, and because of the mention of "the deity," there is no possibility that the third great element (mahābhūta) could be Vaiśvānara either. || 28 ||

This is the intended meaning. "Puruṣatva" means being denotable by the word "puruṣa. Regarding the term "unconditioned" (nirupādhika): the status of the individual soul (jīva) as being denotable by the word "puruṣa"—as seen in such passages as "These two puruṣas exist in the world" and "These two are the primary puruṣas"—is based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the presence of other words like "pradhāna" (primordial matter) or qualities like "saltiness"; it does not apply to the soul inherently. Therefore, the status of being denotable by the word "puruṣa" belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self (paramātman) in its unconditioned state.

Therefore, the idea that the gastric fire possesses the nature of the Puruṣa is refuted from afar; this is the sense. By the words "Just as" and so forth, [the author] demonstrates the well-known status of the Supreme Self through authoritative means when it is intended to speak of its unconditioned Puruṣa-nature, because of the reference made as if it were already established in the passage, "This very Agni Vaiśvānara is the Puruṣa," and because such a designation depends upon a supporting means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). || 27 ||

"For this very reason": the doubt regarding the gastric fire (*jāṭhara*) was already resolved in the preceding sūtra; here, the doubt concerning two other meanings is resolved. Regarding the deity and the third [meaning], the elemental (*bhūta*), their status as having the three worlds as a body is established because, unlike the gastric fire, they lack limitation. As for the deity, its possession of the three worlds as a body is due to its being the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*).

Furthermore, because the third [element] among the great elements (*mahābhūta*) has been made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*) and has evolved into the form of the three worlds, heaven, earth, and so forth would constitute the head and other limbs of that aggregate. Therefore, the objection regarding impossibility—that the assumption of the three worlds being the body [of Brahman] is untenable—constitutes a further doubt.
"From those mentioned" refers to the designations by the terms *ātman*, *brahman*, and *puruṣa*. (28)
61. Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception. 1.2.29.

The word "Agni" also, by virtue of its connection with a specific quality such as "leading in front" (*agranayana*), applies to fire; however, since that very same quality, when free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) and reached its ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāgata*), is possible in the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self—characterized by this specific common attribute—is what is denoted in this context. Thus [it refers] to the Supreme Self alone. —29—
Thus it is determined.

Likewise, as for the statement, "But he who knows this very one, the span-long, the all-measuring," how can the limitation by measure—relating to the space from the supreme Brahman, which is unlimited, down to the earth—be logically established? To this, he says:
62. "On account of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. (1.2.30)

The teacher Āśmarathya maintains that the Supreme Self is of the size of a span (prādeśamātra) for the purpose of manifesting itself as a lay devotee (upāsaka); [in this sense], heaven is its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath, space its middle body, and the waters its bladder.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "intended by leading to the foremost," it is intended that [the goal] is to be attained as the foremost. Regarding the expression "of that which has reached the limit": since the meaning of the constituent parts of the word "fire" (*agni*) is fully present in Brahman, the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word "Brahman" must not be abandoned. However, because the fullness of the meaning of the constituent parts of the word "Brahman" is impossible in fire, the conventional usage of the word "fire" alone must be abandoned; this is the sense. As for the statement "the Supreme Self is qualified": the word "Brahman" is more powerful due to its conformity with the introductory section (*upakrama*) and other criteria.
The meaning of the word "agni," however, should be interpreted in accordance with that [context]; such is the intended sense. ||29||

Regarding the phrase "on account of manifestation": this sūtra is intended to dispel the doubt that the quality of being limited (paricchinnatva) could possibly belong only to the third great element (fire) and its corresponding deity. It is for the sake of manifestation—that is, for the ease of understanding—since limitation indeed facilitates comprehension.
Here, however, limitation is understood through the measures (mātrā) such as the head and so forth;
this is the opinion of the sage Āśmarathya, namely, that it is for the sake of the manifestation of the meditator.

Even though [the Self] is qualified—according to the logic of "Heaven is indeed His head" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.2), where the constituent parts ending with the earth are designated as "feet"—there is a limitation by a measure associated with the "regions" beginning with heaven; for this occurs solely on account of manifestation, since [the Self], having pervaded everything, is devoid of measurement. || 30 ||
If it is asked, "For what purpose is the supreme Brahman described as having the form of a person through specific parts beginning with the head?"—to that, [the Sūtra] says:
63. *Anusmṛterbādariḥ* (1.2.31). The teacher Bādari considers that it is for the sake of meditation (*upāsana*) in that manner.

"But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self as such—as the 'Abhivimāna'—eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Indeed, meditation is taught here for the sake of attaining Brahman! "This one, thus"—the meaning is: in the manner described, in the form of the Cosmic Person (*puruṣa*). He eats that food which is the object of enjoyment existing in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves; that is, he experiences everywhere the Brahman that exists by its own nature as unsurpassed and infinite bliss.

As for that food which is eaten individually by all selves subject to karma—each being unique and not shared with others—that is not included here, because it is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation. || 31 ||

By the phrase "the region beginning with light" (*dhūprabhṛtipradeśa*), the word "mere region" (*pradeśamātra*) has been explained. Regarding the term *abhivimānam*, he explains the prefix *abhi* as "of one who has pervaded everything. He explains the word *vimāna* as "of one whose pride (*māna*) has departed. || 30 ||

The word *mūrchati* [is explained as follows]: It is not possible for the Supreme Self, whose nature is non-material (*aprākṛta*), to possess the state of being composed of material parts such as a head and so forth; rather, the intention is that this applies only to the deity.
*Anusmṛti* means meditation (*upāsana*). The meaning is that the anthropomorphic form exists for the sake of meditation. ||31||

Bādarāyaṇa has declared that the conceptualization of the worlds and so forth as having their heads and other parts, as well as the meditation upon them in that very manner, is intended for the purpose of instruction.

If the Supreme Self is indeed Vaiśvānara, how then can there be the teaching that the chest and other parts are his "altar" and so forth? For this [teaching] is appropriate only if the gastric fire is accepted;
to this, he says: 64. "On account of the meditation [on the Self as the universe], Jaimini [thinks so]; for thus [the scripture] shows. (1.2.32)

The teacher Jaimini maintains that this instruction regarding the chest and other parts as being the altar and so forth is intended to establish the nature of the *agnihotra* for the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) performed daily by the practitioners—which is itself an act of worship directed toward this very Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self whose body extends from heaven down to the earth.

For this scriptural passage demonstrates both the fruit appropriate to the meditation on the Supreme Self and the attainment of the status of an *agnihotra* through the oblation of breath. Thus says the scripture: [text follows].

"If one, not knowing this, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, it would be as if he were to cast away the live coals and offer the oblation in ashes"—this is the meaning of "if. By means of the purpose [of the description], the exclusion of the elements, the third [the individual soul], and the deities has been established through the fact that [the Self] is limited by a measure connected to a specific location starting from the Supreme Self, and that it is "human-shaped" (*puruṣavidha*). Now, the phrase "as far as" (*yāvatā*) serves to exclude the suspicion that [the Self] refers to the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*); the sense is "on the contrary.
"Accomplishment" (*sampatti*) means "bringing about"; it is the superimposition of something upon what it is not.

"...reveals the Supreme Self. The sense is that the fact that the perfection of the *agnihotra* is for the purpose of propitiating the Supreme Self is made known precisely by the specific fruit mentioned in the passage beginning with "In all worlds... and so forth. "One who does not know this"—meaning one who does not understand that the chest and other parts serve as the implements for the *agnihotra*. "*Agnihotra*" refers to the offering to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "He offers"—the meaning is that he performs [this rite]. Jaimini [holds] that because of the perfection of the *agnihotra*-nature through the offering to the vital breath, [the sage] spoke of the arrangement of the chest and so forth as being known as the Veda;
for so says the Śruti.
"Now, for one who, knowing it thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.
Just as a tuft of cotton, when thrown into a fire, is utterly consumed, even so are all his evils utterly consumed. ||32||

Having taught the attainment of Brahman as the fruit by means of the passage beginning with "In all worlds," [the text] teaches the Prāṇāgnihotra, which is an "auxiliary" (*aṅga*) to this very meditation, starting with the words "Of that indeed, of this... It brings about the identification within the body of the worshipper— of the fire, sun, and so forth, which constitute the limbs of Vaitānara who was previously taught as the object of meditation— with those named "Sutejas," "Viśvarūpa," and so on, from the head down to the feet.

“The head itself is the brilliant splendor”: for the worshiper, the head itself is the sky, which has become the head of the Supreme Self—this is the meaning. “The eye is the universal form”: this means the sun. “The breath is the various scents”: this means the wind. “The trunk is the vast expanse”: for the worshiper, the middle part of the body itself is the space that has become the middle part of the body of the Supreme Self—this is the meaning. “The bladder itself is wealth”: his bladder itself is the waters that constitute its constituent parts—this is the meaning.
“The earth itself is the feet”: his feet themselves are the earth that constitutes its feet—this is the meaning.

In this manner, the lay follower (upāsaka), having contemplated the Supreme Self as Vaiśvānara—the embodiment of the three worlds—residing within his own body, and having conceptualized his own chest, hair, heart, mind, and mouth as the altar, the sacrificial grass, the household fire, the southern fire, and the offering fire respectively; and having further conceived the oblation of breath (prāṇāhuti) as the Agnihotra sacrifice itself—he should worship the Supreme Self, Vaiśvānara, by means of such a Prāṇāgnihotra. Thus it is said.
It is taught by such passages as, "The chest itself is the altar, the hair is the sacrificial grass, and the heart is the Gārhapatya fire.
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self, the Puruṣottama alone, is Vaiśvānara. || 33 ||
The third chapter of the first book, which indicates the subject matter of the treatise, is titled "The Chapter on the Exclusion of Connection with Others. Its name is *adhikaraṇa*.
The meanings of the locative case; *Krama-saṃgraha-sūtra* numbers.
The substratum of earth and the other elements is the Supreme Self alone—not the individual soul (jīva).

The referent denoted by the word "Bhūman" is the Supreme Brahman indicated by the word "Satya"—not the individual soul or anything else. The referent denoted by the word "Akṣara," which is pointed out as the support even of primordial matter (pradhāna), is the Supreme Self alone.

Since it is stated, "He sees the Person," the object that serves as the goal of the act of seeing denoted by the word "Person" (puruṣa) is indeed the Supreme Self; it is not the cosmic aggregate person (samaṣṭipuruṣa).
This is the section concerning the heaven, earth, and so forth (dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa), Sūtra 1.3.1.
Section on the Abundant (Bhūmā), 7–8;
Section on the Imperishable (Akṣara)
Section on the Object of the Act of Seeing (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa)
The Section on the Subtle (Daharādhikaraṇa):
The referent denoted by the term "subtle ether" (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Self alone; it is neither the elemental ether nor the individual self.
The section concerning "the measured" (*pramitādhikaraṇa*):
The subject matter declared by the Śruti as being limited to the measure of a thumb is the Supreme Self alone; it is not the individual soul (*jīva*) subject to karma.
23–24 [vā] The Section Concerning the Deities (Devatādhikaraṇa)
25–29: The section concerning the eligibility for the meditation on Brahman as taught in the Śruti; this indeed exists even for the gods.
30–32: The section concerning the honey (madhu).
Even for those who have attained the status of gods and so forth, there is indeed eligibility for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations [or the Jyotiṣāṃ-jyotiḥ-vidyā].
Section on those other than Śūdras (Sūtras 33–39): Those other than the three higher castes have no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
This is a supplementary portion of the Section on Established Knowledge.
Section 42–44: The Topic of Designation as Something Else (*arthāntaratva-vyapadeśa*). The ether (*ākāśa*) that brings forth names and forms is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

[This concludes] the *Śrī Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, in the first chapter on Concordance (*samanvaya*), specifically the section within the "Three Feet" (*tripādī*) that excludes other [meanings], consisting of an investigation into Vedic passages containing clear indicia of the individual soul (*jīva*) and others.
Third Pāda [Adhikaraṇas 1–10]:
18. The Section on Heaven, Earth, and so forth (Dyubhvādy-adhikaraṇa) [1.3.1]
66. That which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. 1.3.1.
The followers of the Atharvaveda study [this passage]:

"In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, as well as the mind together with all the vital breaths—know Him alone as the one Self; cast off other words; this is the bridge to immortality.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this...?
Is the one who is perceived as the locus of the earth and so forth the individual soul (jīva),
or the supreme self (paramātman)?
What is logical? That it is the individual soul (jīva). Why?
In the subsequent verse, "Where the channels converge like the spokes in the nave of a chariot wheel,

there this one moves within, being born in many ways," the text refers back— by means of the locative case in the word "where" (*yatra*)— to that abode of heaven, earth, and so forth which was introduced in the preceding passage; having stated that it is the substratum of the channels, it further [continues].

Regarding the statement, "This one moves within, being born in many ways," its being born in many ways is described; both its connection with the channels (nāḍīs) and its being born in many ways in the form of gods and so forth are attributes of the individual soul (jīva) alone. This is true even in this world.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): the inquiry is whether the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For that purpose, the question is whether the collection of passages beginning with "In whom heaven [rests]" constitutes a section distinct from the one characterized by qualities such as invisibility, or whether it is non-distinct. For that purpose, the question is whether the connection between the mind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth is characterized by the relationship of instrument and agent, or whether it is characterized by the relationship of locus and thing located.

For that purpose, the question is whether attributes such as being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, and being the immortal bridge (*amṛta-setu*), are possible for the individual soul who enjoys the fruits of action, or for the one who does not eat.

When [the attributes] such as being the fruit of karma arise, then, because the connection with the mind and so forth takes the form of the instrument and its possessor (*karaṇatadvattā*), and because that [connection] interrupts the context, the abode of heaven and so forth would be the individual soul (*jīva*).

When, however, [attributes] such as being the bridge to immortality—which are properties of one who does not eat—arise, then, because the connection with the mind and so forth takes the form of the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), there is no interruption of the higher context; thus, it follows that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Regarding the phrase "connection with the channels" (*nāḍīsambandha*): because the channels, by virtue of their connection to the sense organs, serve as the cause for the expansion of the individual soul's (*jīva*) cognition; and because the connection of the soul with the channels is well-established through such scriptural passages as, "Having moved back along them, he rests in the pericardium," and "Going upwards by that [channel], one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions at the time of departure"; the meaning is that this connection is a mark (*liṅga*) of the soul. The phrase "in the form of gods, etc. is an explanation of the word "manifoldly" (*bahudhā*). In the *Antarāditya-vidyā*, there is the possession of a divine body assumed by its own will, not produced by karma.

The statement, "It is woven with the mind and along with the vital breaths (prāṇas)," which describes the state of being the substratum for the five vital breaths and the mind, refers exclusively to the attributes of the individual soul (jīva). Thus, since its status as the individual soul is certain, such qualities as being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth must be somehow reconciled [with that status].
This being the case, we reply: the abode of heaven and so forth is the Supreme Brahman, because of its own word. The abode of heaven, earth, and the rest is the Supreme Brahman. Why?
Because of its own word—that is, because of a term that is unique to the Supreme Brahman.
The phrase "This is the bridge to immortality" is a term unique to the supreme Brahman. Furthermore, the statement, "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here;

there is no other path for the journey," and the word "Self" (ātman) when used without limiting adjuncts, is primarily applied to the supreme Brahman. For the Self is so called because it pervades (āpnoti); such all-pervading sovereignty over everything other than itself is possible only for that [supreme Brahman].
Therefore,
that [word] too belongs to him alone:
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."
And these and other subsequent terms are indeed words for the Supreme Brahman;
for even that [Brahman] can have the channels as its substratum, as it is said:
"It hangs down, continuous with the veins, resembling a hanging membrane."
Starting from this point,
because of the scriptural statement: "In the middle of that crest-lock (śikhā), the Supreme Self is established."
The phrase "being born in many ways" is also consistent with the supreme Brahman; for it is said:
"Though unborn, he is born in many ways; the wise perceive his source."

—thus, for the sake of being a refuge for the gods and others, the Supreme Person (*paraḥ puruṣaḥ*)—as stated in the scriptural designation—manifests Himself in many ways by His own will, endowed with the specific forms, configurations, qualities, and actions of each respective class, while never abandoning His own essential nature. The *Smṛti* also says:

Regarding the phrase "and the word *ātman*": according to the Śruti passage, "The Teacher who has entered within is the Self of all beings," the word "*ātman*" does not denote mere pervasiveness; rather, it denotes a specific pervader, because it possesses both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) significance. For the word "*ātman*" is never employed in reference to space and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that it denotes a specific pervader in the form of a controller. The phrases "He is the bridge of immortality," "the *ātman*," and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," etc., are what are meant by "words denoting its own nature."

Regarding the phrase "being the substratum of the channels" (nāḍyādhāratvam): the meaning is that being the substratum of the channels is possible for the Supreme Self by way of the heart. He states the resolution of the reason put forward by the opponent:

Regarding the term "unborn" (*ajāyamāna*): the sense is that there is no specific cause for birth, nor any specific result thereof. Regarding the phrase "Smṛti also": he speaks thus to clarify that point. Regarding "of the gods and others": this refers to the purpose of the Lord’s incarnations (*avatāra*). Regarding "according to each respective class": this establishes the ease with which one may take refuge in Him. Regarding "His own": this refers to the attainment of desired goals by those who possess such refuge. By His own will—though He is unborn and of imperishable nature, though He is the Lord of all beings...
"Abiding in my own nature, I manifest through my own *māyā*.
Thus, the state of being the substratum for the instruments of the individual soul, such as the mind and so forth, is logically possible only for the Supreme Being, who is the support of all. || 1 ||
For this reason as well, [the object of the knowledge of Brahman] is the Supreme Person: 67.
And because of the designation of being approached by the released (mukta). 1.3.2.
This Puruṣa, who is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, is designated as that which is to be attained even by those liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra:

"When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman, then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality. "Just as rivers, flowing along, go to their rest in the ocean, casting off name and form..."

"Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person, higher than the high. For it is only those who are liberated from the bondage of *saṃsāra*—having shaken off merit and sin (*puṇya-pāpa*), being stainless (*nirañjana*), and "completely released from name and form"—who [attain this]. Indeed, *saṃsāra* consists precisely in the participation in name and form, which is occasioned by the contact of consciousness with the intellect (*cit*) as bound by merit and sin. By his own volition (*svasaṅkalpena*), through this, he becomes subject no longer to karma; he is "born"—that is, he manifests.

"Abiding in my own nature"—that is, relying upon my own essential being; that is to say, having assumed a divine body which serves as the material basis for my descent. "By my own *māyā*"—meaning by my own knowledge, or by my own resolve. "I manifest"—that is, I descend.

The citation of the two scriptural passages is for the purpose of showing that the mere abandonment of name and form exists even in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*); furthermore, it is intended to demonstrate that this is preceded by the shaking off of merit and demerit on the part of the one whose name, form, and vital breaths have been cast off. Since the word "liberated" (*mukta*) is not explicitly heard in the cited scriptural passage, he shows the teaching of liberation by stating "from the bondage of *saṃsāra*. He states the qualifiers mentioned in the two passages with the words "shaken off," etc.

Therefore, by those whose merit and sin have been shaken off, who are stainless—meaning free from contact with material nature—and who have attained supreme equality with the highest Brahman, that Person who is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, is designated as the goal to be attained; He is the Supreme Brahman. ||2||

Having established that [the object of the passage] is indeed the Supreme Brahman by means of words such as "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) and so forth, [the Sūtra-author] states—on the grounds that the term "inner self" (*pratyagātman*) lacks such uncommon attributes—that this [object] is indeed the Supreme [Brahman]:
68. It is not the individual soul, because of the absence of words denoting it; and because of the mention of the vital breath. (1.3.3)

But it is not the supreme Brahman in every respect. The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been stated previously; now, the meaning is that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is being stated for the sake of strengthening that [conclusion].

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): since it has already been stated that [Brahman] is to be approached by the liberated, no suspicion regarding the "Pradhāna" arises; therefore, as there is nothing left to be refuted, the intention is that its mention serves as an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntatayā*). He explains the word "anumīyate" (is inferred), which presents the Pradhāna, as follows: because of the inclusion of the term "bahulam" (in various ways) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the sense is that the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karmani*). The form "ānumānam" is derived from the base "anumāna" with the addition of the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *śeṣe*, followed by the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the initial vowel.
