The phrase "tadvāci" (denoting that) is used to exclude the apprehension that it might mean "atacchabdāt" (from a word not denoting that), which would imply a word denoting something other than that;
[the compound] "arthābhāve" is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule "yadavyayam" (whatever is an indeclinable). || 3 ||
For this reason as well, this [Self] is not the inner self (pratyagātman): 69. "Because of the designation of non-difference" (1.3.4).

By such passages as, "On the same tree, the person is immersed and grieves, deluded by his lack of sovereignty (anīśayā); but when he perceives the other, the Lord, who is adored, and His majesty, he is freed from grief," He is designated as distinct from the individual soul (jīva). The term *anīśayā* refers to *prakṛti*, which has become the object of experience;
the word *artha* is not included in the Sūtra, but rather the word *artha* is supplied [from the commentary], because the Sūtra itself is very concise.

"From this [it follows]" means that because it immediately follows the sūtra which refutes the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*), the objective of the subsequent sūtra is likewise the refutation of the individual soul. The word "this" refers to the Self who is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. By the term "designation of difference," the meaning of the word "other" in the mantra "on the same tree" is intended.

Regarding the phrase "anīśayā" (by the non-ruler): by the force of the feminine gender, it is stated that *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is the substantive. Regarding "svasmāt" (from itself): this points to the correlative obtained through the force of the word "anya" (other). Regarding "sarvasya" (of all): in accordance with other means of knowledge, he states the "ruler-to-be" (*īśitavya*) obtained through the force of the word "īśa" (ruler). Regarding "prīyamāṇam" (being pleased): this explains the word "juṣṭa" (enjoyed/pleased); the sense is that the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*). Regarding "mahimānam" (the greatness): the sense is that the word "ca" (and) is employed because its force necessitates a conjunction.

"Of the nature of governance" (*niyamanarūpam*): the word "thus" (*iti*) refers to a mode present in the mind. The sense is that because of hearing the word "Lord" (*īśa*), the mode of being the governor is present in the mind. "Then" (*tadā*): this is due to the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*. "The living soul (*jīva*) grieves while being deluded"; when he sees another than himself who is the Lord of all, who is full of bliss, and the majesty of this Lord—which consists in the governance of the entire universe—then he becomes free from sorrow. ||4||
70. Because of the context (prakaraṇa). 1.3.5.

Furthermore, this context pertains to the supreme Brahman—this has already been demonstrated in the sūtra "On account of the mention of attributes such as invisibility" (1.2.21). Here, any suspicion of a break in the context is removed by the connection with the channels (nāḍīs), the state of being born in many ways, and the fact of being the support of the mind and the vital breath (prāṇa). ||5||
71. And because of abiding and eating. (1.3.6)

"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. By this, it is established that one [bird] eats the fruit of action, while the other, not eating the fruit of action, remains merely within the body, shining by its very nature. In that context, the one who does not eat the fruit of action, being radiant and omniscient, must be the Immortal Bridge (*amṛtasetu*), the Self of all, and the abode of what is to be tasted; it cannot, however, be the inner self (*pratyagātman*) which eats the fruit of action and grieves.
Therefore, it is established that the abode of "that which consists of being" (bhūman) and so forth is the Supreme Self. Thus ends the section on "That which consists of Being" (Bhvādy-adhikaraṇa).

Regarding the phrase "and by abiding and eating," [the author] states a reason that was not previously mentioned and which constitutes the primary cause. The word "sthiti" (abiding) is placed first either because of the rule "that which has fewer syllables comes first" (*alpāctaram*), or because of the rule "that which is more worthy (*abhyarhita*) should be used first. Abiding is more worthy because it serves as the cause for the non-interruption of the context by means of identifying [the individual soul] with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). In the *Bhāṣya*, this is explained according to the order of the scriptural text (*śruti*), and not according to the order of the Sūtras.

Regarding the term "omniscient" (*sarvajña*): qualifiers such as "omniscient" and "the bridge to immortality" (*amṛta-setu*) have been stated because they are relevant to the context. Although both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self] are under discussion, the quality of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth belongs to the Supreme Self because omniscience and other such qualities reside in a common substratum, because [the Supreme Self] is inherently capable [of this], and because the connection with the mind and vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not secondary in the case of the Supreme Self. The phrases "not eating" (*anaśnan*) and "eating" (*adan*) are a restatement of the reasons given in the Sūtra.

Regarding the word "grieving," another sense is intended here for the scriptural reason "because of the designation of difference. For the corresponding scriptural passage is: "He grieves, being deluded. That passage also serves to establish that [the Self] has the Supreme Self as its referent, by means of rejecting that it refers to the inner self (pratyagātman); the point is that negative concomitance (vyatireka) is supplementary to positive concomitance (anvaya). ||6||
4. Because of the mention of differentiation; 5. because of the context; 6. because of the state of abiding.
Thus ends the section on the root *bhū* and others. 1.
19. The Section on Abundance (Bhūmādhikaraṇa) || 1.3.2 ||
72. [The Self] is the Infinite (bhūman), because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith (samprasāda). (1.3.7)
The Chandogas recite this:

"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and knows something else—that is the finite (alpa)."
In this context, this word *bhūma* is derived as ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). For instance, the word *bahu* is listed among the *pṛthv-ādi* group; from that [it is formed].

Regarding the term "bhūmā" (the Infinite): since it was established that the passage refers to the Supreme Self because the context of the Supreme Self is not interrupted, the connection [of this section] arises from the doubt: "In that case, might it not refer to the individual soul (jīva) because the context of the individual soul is not interrupted? This is a connection by way of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Previously, in the passage, "The mind is woven with all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)," it was stated that the one connected with the *prāṇas* is the Supreme Self. Here, however, because that very same one connected with the *prāṇas* is heard to be subject to injury, the state of being an individual soul is perceived; thus, there is also a connection by way of the subject matter (*artha*).

Regarding the phrase "this is the Bhūman," the author demonstrates the establishment of the doubt concerning the subject of inquiry by following the method of etymological derivation of the word "Bhūman" in order to show the possibility of a doubt regarding its specific referent. With the words "tathā hi" (for instance), he establishes that the suffix denotes an abstract state (bhāvapratyaya). He states: "It is recited [in scripture]:
because it is taught as being superior to the individual soul (jīva), the Bhūman here is the Supreme Person, specifically for Nārada by his teacher Sanatkumāra."
When the suffix *iman* is applied according to the rule "pṛthv-ādibhya imanij vā," [the form] "bahor lopo bhū ca bahoh" [applies].

Thus, when there is a modification of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the form "bhūmā" arises. "Bhūmā" means "abundance" (*bahutva*). Furthermore, in this context, the word "bahu" denotes extensiveness (*vaipulya*), not numerical plurality;

for it is heard [in scripture] as being the counter-correlative of "the small" (*alpa*): "Where one sees another, that is the small. Precisely because it is intended to establish the counter-correlative with respect to the subject (*dharmin*) indicated by the word "small," it is determined to refer to the subject itself, and not merely to a quality (*dharma*). Therefore, "bhūmā" means "vast" (*vipula*). And here, the Self (*ātman*) is understood to be the substantive qualified by that vastness.

For, having begun with "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and having taught the knowledge of the Bhūman, it concludes with that very same [Bhūman] in the words, "All this is indeed the Self."

Here a doubt arises: is this the inner self (*pratyagātman*) characterized by the quality of abundance (*bhūma*), or is it the supreme self (*paramātman*)? [This is stated] for the purpose of excluding [the possibility that *bhūman*] belongs to a class of words based on form (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Regarding the term "in a modification" (*vikāre*): there is the elision of the first vowel of the suffix following the word "much" (*bahu*), according to the rule *ādeḥ parasya*; furthermore, the word "much" (*bahu*) is replaced by the word "become" (*bhū*). Thus, there is a modification of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

And here, regarding the word *ayām* (immeasurable): the word *bahu* is seen used in the sense of number, as in "many persons" (*bahavaḥ puruṣāḥ*), and in the sense of vastness, as in "whether little or much" (*alpaṃ vā bahu vā*). Therefore, [the term *ayām*] is for the purpose of excluding number. Thus, because the word *bahu* is observed to be used in both the senses of number and vastness, while the word *alpa* is not observed to be used in the sense of number, the word *bahu* has a meaning that conforms to the word *alpa* and cannot be established otherwise. Having commenced...
"Because of the conclusion" means that the word "Self" (ātman) is seen at both the beginning and the end [of the passage].

Regarding this, a doubt arises: 1. Is the "plenum" (*bhūman*) the inner self (*pratyagātman*), or the supreme self (*paramātman*)? 2. Does the word "plenum" terminate its meaning within the inner self—which is indicated by the term "breath" (*prāṇa*)—through the resolution of the question and answer, or does it refer to something beyond that? 3. As for the statement, "But he indeed speaks with excess who speaks with the Truth," what is appropriate?
[Is it] the inner self? Why?

To Nārada, who had approached with the desire to know the Self—having heard from the venerable Yājñavalkya that "the knower of the Self overcomes sorrow"—and after [Yājñavalkya] had taught the objects of meditation beginning with Name and ending with Prāṇa, [Nārada] asked such questions as, "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than Name?
and "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than Speech? and so forth.

Furthermore, counter-answers such as "Speech, indeed, is greater than name" and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech" are seen in the sections preceding the Prāṇa; however, we do not see such [a statement] regarding the Prāṇa itself. Therefore, it is understood that this instruction concerning the Self extends only up to the Prāṇa. Consequently, the word "Prāṇa" used here refers to the inner Self (pratyagātman) associated with the vital breath, and not merely to a specific type of air.

Does this [passage] enjoin truthful speech (*satyavacana*) as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to one who speaks beyond the vital breath (*prāṇātivādin*)? Or does it state that the one who meditates upon the Supreme, denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*), is a speaker beyond the vital breath? 4. Is there recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the speaker beyond the vital breath in this sentence? No? 5. Does the word "but" (*tu*) contradict the proposition? No?—thus [the questions].

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: since the word "but" (*tu*) does not contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), recognition is possible for the one who speaks of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, the sentence "But this [one] indeed" (*eṣa tu vai*) is intended to enjoin truthful speech as an ancillary part of that [practice]. Because there is no entity other than the vital breath, the word "plurality" (*bhūman*) culminates in the vital breath; thus, the "Plurality" (*bhūmā*) is the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: When the word "but" (*tu*) contradicts the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), then, due to the absence of such recognition regarding the one who speaks beyond the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and because the statement "He speaks beyond by means of Truth" refers to speaking beyond through the meditation on Truth (*satya-upāsaka*)—thereby establishing the existence of a reality distinct from the vital breath—and because even at the conclusion of the question and answer, the word "plenitude" (*bhūman*) does not terminate in the vital breath, [it follows that] the plenitude is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Furthermore, passages such as "The vital breath is indeed the father, the vital breath is indeed the mother" demonstrate the sentience of the vital breath. [Otherwise, one would be called] a "slayer of the father... a slayer of the mother."

By such statements as these—since there is mention of censurable speech on account of being a "harm-doer" (*hiṃsaka*) toward those endowed with breath, such as ancestors and others, when one causes their destruction; and since there is mention of the absence of such censurable speech even when those same beings have departed from breath, despite being subjected to extreme destruction—it is determined that the conscious entity alone is designated by the word "breath" (*prāṇa*) as being fit for harm. For, even among non-mobile beings, which are devoid of breath, we observe the presence or absence of harm depending on whether they possess consciousness or not. Thus, this "breath" indicated as being fit for harm is conclusively identified as the "inner self" (*pratyagātman*) alone.

For this very reason, one should not conclude from the presentation of the analogy of the hub and spokes that "the Supreme is indicated by the word *prāṇa*"; for there is no possibility of injury (*hiṃsā*) to the Supreme, and because all insentient matter other than the individual soul—including both the objects of its enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment—exists dependent upon the individual soul, the analogy of the hub and spokes is appropriate precisely for the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

And this very "plurality" (bhūman) is what is designated by the word "vital breath" (prāṇa); for there is no question such as "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than the vital breath? nor is there a reply such as "That indeed is greater than the vital breath," prior to the mention of "plurality," because the context of the "vital breath" remains uninterrupted.

Furthermore, having stated that one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) is an "exceeding speaker" (ativādin), [the text] identifies that very person again with the words, "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker."

Regarding the phrase "by whose truth he speaks beyond [others]," having taught "speaking the truth" as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the knowledge of the true nature of the previously mentioned vital breath is presented as the "principal" (*śeṣin*) of that speech which is to be adopted:
"When one truly knows, then one speaks the truth."

Having thus taught this, and having instructed [the disciple] in reflection (*manana*), faith (*śraddhā*), steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), and effort (*prayatna*) for the sake of its accomplishment; and for the purpose of commencing that [practice], having taught the knowledge of the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—designated by the word "Life" (*prāṇa*) as that which is to be attained—as being of the nature of bliss; and having taught the vastness of that bliss through the instruction, "But the Infinite (*bhūman*) alone is to be sought to be known," it is thus taught that the very form of the inner self, when separated from ignorance (*avidyā*), is abundant bliss.
And there is no contradiction with the opening statement, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. Therefore, the inner Self is qualified by the quality of plenitude (bhūman).
Since it is thus qualified by the quality of plenitude...
The inner self (*pratyagātman*); for this very reason, [it is said] regarding the inner self which is the referent of "I":
"Therefore, I alone am below; I am above."

The one distinguished by the quality of plenitude (*bhūma*) is not the inner self (*pratyagātman*), but rather the supreme self (*paramātman*). Why? Because of the teaching that [the latter] is superior to the state of serene confidence (*saṃprasāda*). "Serene confidence" refers to the inner self, as is well known from the Upanishads: "This serene confidence, having risen up from this body, having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form. The meaning is: because there is a teaching of that which is designated by the word "Truth" (*satya*)—distinguished as "plenitude"—as being superior to the serene confidence, i.e., the inner self. And that which is designated by the word "Truth" is the supreme Brahman.

This is what is meant: just as among the categories beginning with Name and ending with Breath, each subsequent one is designated as being distinct from the preceding ones because it is superior to them, so too that which is designated by the word "Satya" is superior to the inner self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word "Prāṇa," and is therefore indeed a different entity; thus, that very thing indicated by the word "Satya" is the Bhūman, and it is taught that "the Bhūman is the supreme Brahman called Satya.
Thus says the author of the Vṛtti:
"But the Infinite alone [is Brahman]," for the Infinite is "Brahman," since it is taught as being superior to the Self through the succession beginning with Name.
If it is asked, "How is it understood that the teaching of the Real is given as something superior to that which is indicated by the word 'Prāṇa'?"— [the answer follows].
The teaching on "complete clarity" (*samprasāda*) in the Sūtra was made with the intention of referring to its pure essential nature.

Regarding the word "satya": the sense is that, because there is no break in the context following the word "satya," it is precisely that which is denoted by the word "satya" which is qualified as *bhūman*.

Regarding the phrase "this has been stated": for after what has been previously indicated, a subsequent mention serves as the reason for a difference in meaning (*arthāntaratva*) due to the superiority of each succeeding term in relation to its preceding counterpart. As for the example: this refers to the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). By the word "evam," the reason is intended.

"But the *bhūman* (the Infinite) indeed... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23.1]. Because this subsequent instruction is given as being superior to what was previously specified, the meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the author is that the *bhūman*—designated by the word "Truth" (*satya*) and taught as the object of meditation—is superior to the individual soul (*jīva*) denoted by the word "Prāṇa," and that the Supreme Brahman is even greater than that. By the phrase "above the Self," the status of the one designated by the word "Prāṇa" as the individual self (*jīvātman*) is established;
as stated in the *Śrī Bhāṣya* (1.3.2):
"He who sees thus, thinks thus, and knows thus, becomes a speaker of the transcendent."

Thus, having stated that the knower of the vital breath (prāṇa) is an "excessive speaker" (ativādin), [the text] says, "But he indeed speaks excessively who speaks excessively by means of Truth"; here, by the word "but" (tu), it distinguishes the speaker of Truth from the previous speaker of the vital breath.

"For this very reason— in the passage 'But he indeed speaks with surpassing speech'— there is no recognition of the one who speaks with surpassing speech regarding the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, it is understood that the truth which is the cause of his being a speaker with surpassing speech is superior to the vital breath, which was the cause of the previous state of speaking with surpassing speech."

But surely—it was argued that speaking the truth is taught as an ancillary duty (aṅga) specifically for one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, there is no break in the context of the vital breath.

This is not correct; for by the word "but" (tu), a different person altogether is understood as the "one who speaks beyond" (ativādī), and not merely that same speaker of the vital breath being characterized by the ancillary duty of speaking the truth.

It is understood that [the author] intends the view of the *Vṛttikāra*, and not that the subject is the fivefold vital breath (*pañcavṛtti-prāṇa*). Therefore, the purpose of citing the *Vṛttikāra*'s text is to make it known that the presentation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is intended by the *Vṛttikāra* precisely by relying on the fact that the one denoted by the word "prāṇa" is the individual soul (*jīva*). The phrase "he distinguishes" (*vyāvartayati*) means that he distinguishes [it] by way of superiority. However, because of the excellence of the worshipper, the excellence of the object of worship caused by that [excellence] is to be stated; thus, the distinction from the worshipper is mentioned through the natural force of the particle *tu*.
For the word "tu" (but/however) has an unrestricted application; it distinguishes between the property and the substratum without distinction.

"From this very reason" (*ata eva*): the word *etad* (this) is common to both what has been discussed and what is about to be discussed; it does not refer exclusively to what has been discussed. Furthermore, because it functions as a reference back to what occurred later, it does not have the previously discussed matter as its primary referent. Moreover, the natural force of the particle *tu* (but) serves to mark a break in the context. Therefore, the meaning is that for another proponent of the theory of "excessive speech" (*ativādin*), there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the former [proponent].

"Because no other Agnihotra-sacrificer is perceived. The Agnihotra-sacrificer stands in the place of the *ativādin* (one who speaks beyond); the Agnihotra sacrifice stands in the place of the meditative worship (*upāsana*). That which is to be worshipped stands in the place of the material substance and the deity. Here, there is no perception of another Agnihotra-sacrificer because no other Agnihotra sacrifice is perceived; and that [absence] is because no specific material substance or deity is perceived. And that is because of the word "speaking the truth," which does not indicate a specific material substance or deity such as curds and so forth.
As it is said: "But he indeed is an Agnihotra-sacrificer who speaks the truth."

In such cases as these, since no other Agnihotrin is perceived, one must resort to the strained interpretation that the injunction regarding speaking the truth is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) prescribed for the very Agnihotrin who is already perceived [in the context]. Here, however, the Supreme Brahman—which is denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*)—is perceived as the cause for being an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādī*). For the word "Truth," [it is said]:
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."
In such passages as these, [the term] is applied to the supreme Brahman.

Therefore, it is possible that one who is devoted to that [Prāṇa] and speaks with surpassing words (ativādin) may be superior to the former; thus, the distinctness established by the natural sense of the sentence must not be sublated. For "speaking with surpassing words" means speaking of one's own object of meditation as surpassing other entities in terms of being a human goal. Because the knower of Prāṇa speaks of the inner Self—designated by the word "Prāṇa"—which surpasses all objects of meditation from Name up to Hope, he possesses the status of an ativādin.

Since even that [the former] is a human goal possessing excellence, it is only for one who maintains that the Supreme Brahman is the object of worship—by virtue of its being a human goal without superior—that there is direct status as an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond);
thus it is said: "But he indeed is an ativādin who speaks beyond by means of Truth."

Because of the capacity for establishing [a distinction]. Thus, the meaning is that here, due to the absence of a word designating another Agnihotra performer, the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "but" (*tu*) is broken. Regarding the phrase "But here" (*atra tu*): here, however, another speaker of the transcendental (*ativādī*) and another object of meditation (*upāsya*) which serves as its cause are perceived, because the word "Truth" (*satya*), which is capable of designating that [other Agnihotra], is present; therefore, the natural force of the word "but" must not be set aside. Consequently, the meaning is that another speaker of the transcendental is established.

Regarding the phrase "for [the word] *ativādin*": the term *ativādin* is certainly not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring only to one who speaks excessively regarding living beings (*prāṇātivādin*). This is because the author of the Sūtras has shown—following the principle of the *prokṣaṇī*-sūtra, "In the case of *prokṣaṇī*s, [the meaning is derived] from connection with the purpose"—that when the understanding of its own primary meaning is attained through the very power of the etymological parts (*avayava-śakti*), the author of the Sūtras rejects the existence of a conventional name (*nāmatva*) for that which has lost its etymological components. For when the comprehension of the primary meaning is possible through the power of the etymological parts, it is improper to postulate a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "ativādin" does not reside solely in one who speaks excessively regarding the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "tasyāpi": since this ground for the application of the term (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*) is fully present only in the worshiper of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the intention of the Teacher—who says, "he who speaks beyond by means of Truth"—is that the word "ativādin" is used in its primary sense only with respect to him. The sense is that the natural force of both the particle *tu* and the word "ativādin" lies precisely in our own position.

In the phrase "by truth" (*satyena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*). The meaning is: he who speaks beyond [all things] as characterized by the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of meditation. For this very reason, the disciple makes this request:
"May I, O Venerable Sir, speak beyond by means of truth.
And the teacher—
"But truth indeed must be sought to be known," he said.

Furthermore, in the passage "From the Self, the vital breath [is born]," the origin of that which is designated by the word "Self" is stated. Therefore, it is understood that the Self introduced in the opening statement, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," is distinct from that which is designated by the word "vital breath."

As for what was stated—that because neither a question such as, "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than breath? nor an answer such as, "Yes, that which is greater than breath is speech," are observed, it is understood that the instruction concerning the Self (ātman) commenced here culminates in an instruction concerning breath—that is incorrect. For a shift to a different subject matter is not understood through questions and answers alone; since that is possible even by means of other authorities (pramāṇas), and another authority has indeed been mentioned.

Regarding the word "third": the sense is that the mention of a "third" is untenable only in the case of speaking the truth (*satyavāda*), as well as the futility of the prefix (*ati*). For this very reason—namely, because the word "truth" (*satya*) refers to another object of meditation—the disciple prays, "O Venerable One, may I excel through truth," and not, "may I excel through vital breath" (*prāṇa*); such is the meaning. And as for the teacher, he says, "Truth indeed must be sought to be known," and not, "vital breath alone [must be sought]" (Śrutiprakāśikā).

By means of another reason intended by the Sūtra—namely, "as the Self" (ātmatas)—he explains the teaching that [the Self] is superior to the serene being (samprasāda), thereby establishing that there is a distinct object of meditation.

The phrase "And it has been said" (uktaṃ ca) means that further evidence has been stated: for while the question and answer constitute one mark, even in their absence, the hearing of the word "but" (tu) and the fact that the vital breaths (prāṇas) originate from the Self are additional marks. This is the meaning.

To him who asked, "Is there, O Blessed One, anything greater than breath? this was the intention: although among the insentient things beginning with Name and ending with Hope—each preceding one being surpassed by the next in terms of the abundance of human purpose—the teacher did not declare anyone to be an "exceeding speaker" (ativādin) merely for knowing those respective objects. However, [the teacher did so] regarding one who knows the true nature of the inner Self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word "breath," considering that such a person possesses a superior excellence in the abundance of human purpose.

"He who sees thus, thinks thus, and knows thus, becomes an 'ativādī' (one who speaks beyond)," it is said; this refers to the state of speaking about that which transcends all objects. Thinking that the instruction regarding the Self was concluded right here, the disciple did not ask any further questions.
But the teacher, considering even this to be surpassed, [taught] the Supreme Brahman, denoted by the word "Satya" (Truth), which is the unsurpassed human goal.

"But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly by means of Truth"—thus [the teacher] himself introduced the subject. When the Supreme Brahman, which is the supreme human goal, had been thus introduced, the disciple, desiring to know the true nature of that Brahman and the method of its meditation, said: "Venerable Sir, may I speak surpassingly by means of Truth?"
Thus he prayed.

Then, for the sake of establishing the status of being an "exceeding speaker" (ativādin) caused by the direct realization of Brahman, there is the meditation upon Brahman, which serves as the means for the direct realization of Brahman.

"Thinking that [the teaching] has human purpose as its goal" means thinking that the instruction regarding the Self culminates in that [Supreme Self]. Regarding "he briefly introduced": even in the *Bhagavadgītā*, after concluding the yoga of the individual self (jīvātman) with the words, "Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi," the Blessed One himself introduced the meditation on the Supreme Self (paramātman) with the verse: "Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with faith, his inner self absorbed in Me, he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined. The sense is that it is just like that.

By the phrase "having the direct realization of Brahman as its cause," the meaning of the statement, "When one truly knows, then one speaks the truth," is explained. The word *vijānāti* (he knows) refers to direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) and not to knowledge produced by the scriptures; for from the passage, "When one reflects, then one knows," it is understood that the meaning of "knowing" is accomplished through reflection (*manana*). "He speaks the truth"—having taught that "Truth indeed must be sought to be known," [the text] teaches that reflection on Brahman is the means to that, saying, "Understanding indeed must be sought to be known."

Having thus instructed [on hearing], and considering that reflection is for the purpose of establishing what has been heard— thereby regarding hearing as already established by the instruction on reflection— he taught faith in Brahman, which is the means to hearing, saying,
"Faith indeed is to be sought after," and he also taught devotion to That (Brahman), which is the means to that (faith).

Having taught that "the culmination (niṣṭhā) indeed must be sought to be known," and having further taught that the activity (kṛti)— which consists of effort and exertion and serves as the means to that— must also be sought to be known, [it is stated] that for the sake of accomplishing the activity consisting of the commencement of hearing and so forth, the nature of bliss of Brahman, denoted by the word "Truth" (satya) and constituting the goal to be attained, must be known.

"He speaks beyond" (*ativadati*); this is the meaning, because "speaking beyond" (*ativāda*) is the subject under discussion. When one realizes Brahman directly, then one speaks beyond. Therefore, the meaning is that for the sake of that direct realization—which is the cause of being a "speaker beyond"—one should perform the meditation on Truth (*satyopāsana*), which serves as its means. Regarding the phrase "hearing... faith": Brahman is indeed the object of hearing, reflection, meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), and attainment. And faith directed toward that [Brahman] arises for the purpose of hearing it, reflecting upon it, seeing it, and attaining it.

In this context, by the phrase "faith which is the means for hearing," it is faith regarding the act of hearing that is intended. *Śraddhā* means zeal. *Tanniṣṭhā* means steadfastness in that Brahman; it is the resolve—"Brahman alone is to be heard, nothing else"—which constitutes steadfastness. For indeed, when there is certainty regarding the necessity of hearing, zeal for hearing arises. Regarding the term *tadudyoga*: the meaning is an action (*kṛti*) characterized by effort, which is what the word *udyoga* denotes.

And that [practice] consists in the restraint of the mind by means of reflecting upon the worthlessness of other things to be heard. For one whose mind is inclined toward another object due to the notion that it is desirable, the firm conviction—"Brahman alone is to be heard, nothing else"—does not arise. Regarding the phrase "hearing and so forth": the intention is that once it is known that the object of inquiry is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and that it is unsurpassed, it becomes possible for the mind to turn away from other human goals that possess degrees of excellence. Regarding the phrase "the nature of bliss": [it refers to the fact that Brahman is of the nature of bliss].

The understanding that the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is unsurpassed arises from the scripture itself at the stage of initial comprehension, and is further established through spontaneous encounters with virtuous people and the like. Since the sequence beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) is heard in the passage, "When indeed one has faith... and so forth, the Commentary states that these [faith, reflection, etc. stand in the relationship of means and end. Regarding the word "attainment" (*lābha*) in the scriptural text, "When indeed one attains happiness," the intention is that the root *labh* signifies "to understand" (*prāpti*), as it refers to the acquisition of knowledge.

For it is not possible that the attainment of unsurpassed happiness occurs prior to hearing and so forth. Regarding the phrase "it is to be desired to be known" (*vijijñāsitavyam*), the words "to be desired to be known" denote objects other than the Truth (*satya*) and signify that which is to be accomplished.

Having taught that "bliss indeed is what one must desire to understand," [the text continues] that bliss which is unsurpassed and vast is the supreme goal of human life; therefore, the unsurpassed vastness of that very Brahman, whose nature is bliss, is what must be known— thus, "it is precisely that which one must desire to understand."
Having thus instructed, this definition of Brahman, which consists of unsurpassed and vast bliss, is stated:
"The Infinite (bhūman) is that wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else; that is the Infinite."
Thus it is said.

The meaning is this: when Brahman, whose nature is infinite and unsurpassed bliss, is being experienced, the "experiencer" perceives nothing else whatsoever other than that; for the entire aggregate of things is included within the very nature of Brahman and its manifestations (*vibhūti*). Therefore, while experiencing Brahman—which is characterized by the qualities of manifestation (synonymous with sovereignty) and consists of unsurpassed bliss—he perceives no other thing at all, precisely because of the non-existence of any entity apart from it.
Because everything that is experienced is of the nature of happiness alone, one does not perceive suffering; for that alone is happiness which, when being experienced, is favorable to the person.

The meaning is as follows: because the sentence "where there is no other" prohibits the seeing, hearing, and so forth of anything else, there might arise a doubt that the object of sight (*dṛśya*) is false; therefore, this is stated in order to dispel that [doubt]. The phrase "in what is being experienced" is supplied by implication (*adhyāhāra*) due to the nature of the matter; for it is not from the existence of Brahman that one fails to see another entity in the form of suffering. "Other than that" means other than Brahman, which is of the nature of bliss. "He does not see" means he does not see anything else, such as that which is of the nature of suffering, nor anything distinct from it.

In this context, the reason for the absence of the perception of suffering is its nature as infinite and unsurpassed bliss. Regarding the word "of the whole" (*kṛtsnasya*): the intended meaning is that all qualities such as knowledge are included within His essential nature (*svarūpa*), and the entire universe is included within His manifestation (*vibhūti*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the intended reasons. Therefore—because the bliss-nature of Brahman and the inclusion of His entire manifestation within it are established by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). A quality whose object is the manifestation is called a "manifestation-quality" (*vibhūtiguṇa*).

That very [Brahman] is *niyamana* (the act of governing), which is synonymous with *aiśvarya* (sovereignty); Brahman is that which is qualified by this. For the experience of being qualified by sovereignty is not possible without knowledge of that which is to be governed, since there can be no cognition of the object to be defined (*nirūpya*) without the defining attribute (*nirūpaka*). Regarding the phrase "of that which is distinct from it": the vision of anything other than the qualified Brahman is prohibited; the meaning is not that the vision of anything else [in general] is prohibited. Regarding the word "of all": the meaning is "of [Brahman] together with its manifestations" (*savibhūtika*).

"Simply because of the previously mentioned reason"—this is the emphasis of the word *eva*. Regarding "conducive" (*anukūla*): being conducive means being desired in itself. And that [desirability] exists even without being a means to what is desired, by virtue of being the cessation of the undesired.

Now, an objection may be raised: this very world, being experienced as something other than Brahman, consists of suffering and limited pleasure; how then can it become purely of the nature of bliss when experienced as having Brahman as its essence, by virtue of being His manifestation (*vibhūti*)? It is replied: for the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) who are subject to karma, the entire world is experienced as "other than Brahman," and thus it becomes suffering and limited pleasure in accordance with their respective karmas.

Therefore, because the experience of the world as something other than Brahman—as limited, as pleasure, and as pain—is caused by karma, it is the ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of karma. For one who is liberated from that, that very same world becomes nothing but bliss, being subsumed within the experience of Brahman as characterized by His powers and qualities. This is just as milk being drunk by one afflicted with bile results in little pleasure or even the opposite according to the degree of the bile, yet that same milk serves only for pleasure to one who is not afflicted by bile.

Just as the play-apparatus of a prince, when not contemplated as being of that nature [i.e., as belonging to the prince], does not attain the state of being dear; yet, when contemplated as being of that nature, it becomes most beloved—so too, the world, which is the play-apparatus of Brahman—the very essence of unsurpassed bliss and a mine of infinite, unsurpassable, and innumerable auspicious qualities—is indeed conducive to unsurpassed love when it is contemplated as being of that same nature.

Therefore, experiencing Brahman—which is characterized by sovereignty over the world and consists of unsurpassed, infinite bliss—one perceives nothing else whatsoever other than that, nor does one perceive suffering. The remainder of the passage establishes this very point:

"Now, [it may be objected]: 'Indeed, it is not logical that a single entity should at one and the same time be embraced by contradictory natures consisting of both pleasure and pain. Furthermore, it is impossible to deny that the world has the nature of suffering; therefore, its nature as pleasure must be abandoned. This is the intended objection. To this it is replied: There is no contradiction, because even though Brahman is by its own nature of the form of unlimited bliss, it is possible for it to appear otherwise due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Karma, as well as the cognition of non-Brahman-nature caused by the concealment [of Brahman's true nature], constitute these limiting adjuncts."

(This is the intended meaning. The two examples beginning with "yathā" [illustrate] respectively: first, how that which is naturally sweet may become unfavorable due to its connection with a defect; and second, how that which is not an object of favorable cognition may become favorable through the knowledge of its connection with something else.

This refers to the state of being characterized by suffering due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-duḥkha-rūpatā*); upon the disappearance of those adjuncts, there is no further persistence [of that suffering]. If words such as *rati* and so forth are taken to mean "delight" (*prīti*), then a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound is employed [as in the passage]:

"He who sees thus, thinks thus, and understands thus, becomes one whose delight is in the Self (*ātmarati*), whose play is in the Self (*ātmakrīḍa*), whose union is in the Self (*ātmamithuna*), and whose bliss is in the Self (*ātmānanda*); he becomes self-sovereign (*svarāṭ*). For him, there is freedom of movement in all worlds. But those who know otherwise than this are ruled by others (*anyarājānaḥ*) and their worlds are perishable."
"Worlds exist; in all those worlds, there is no freedom of movement for them. *Svarāṭ* means one who is not subject to karma; *anyarājānaḥ* means those subject to karma. Likewise:
"The seer does not see death, nor disease, nor even suffering.
The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way."
And thus it is said.

Furthermore, that Brahman consists of unsurpassed bliss has been elaborated upon in the section beginning with "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.12). Therefore, since the term *bhūman* is taught as denoting Brahman—which is designated by the word "Truth" (*satya*) and is a distinct entity from the inner self (pratyagātman) referred to by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*)—the *bhūman* is the Supreme Brahman. ||7||
73. And because of the logical consistency of the nature of things (dharmopapatti). || 1.3.8 ||
Those attributes that are traditionally taught of this "Fullness" (bhūman) are also applicable only to the Supreme.
The phrase "this is the immortal" refers to its inherent immortality.
By the phrase "in his own glory," he is shown to have no other support; [as stated in the scripture:
"He alone is below."
and so forth;
"this entire universe is that very [Self]"—
this is "being the self of all."
The attributes such as being the originator of everything beginning with the vital breath— as in "from the Self [comes] the vital breath" and so forth— belong to the Supreme Self alone.

As for that which is taught as "being the self of all" through the passage beginning with "I alone am below," that is taught as the meditation upon Brahman, distinguished as the "Fullness" (bhūman), by means of the "I-grasping" (ahaṅgraha).

Because the instruction begins with the teaching on the grasping of the "I" in the words, "Now, therefore, the instruction on the 'I'," and because it is stated in such texts as the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa that the inner self (*pratyagātman*)— which is the referent of "I"— is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), this instruction on the grasping of the "I" is intended for the contemplation of the Supreme Self by way of its having the inner self as its body; for since the inner self culminates in the Supreme Self, the word "I" also culminates in the Supreme Self.

Since the Supreme Self is the self of all because He constitutes the body of everything, the Supreme Self is also the Self of the inner self (pratyagātman). This is shown by such passages as: "That indeed," and "Now follows the instruction regarding the Self."
It is stated by the passage ending with "All this is indeed the Self."

To establish this very point—that everything originates from the Supreme Self, who is the very Self of the inner self (pratyagātman)—it is said: "From Him, indeed, who sees thus, who thinks thus, who knows thus, [comes] breath from the Self... space from the Self."

By these and other such statements, the meaning is that the origin of everything proceeds from the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is present as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of the worshipper. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the knowledge that the Supreme Self has the individual self (pratyagātman) as its body, "meditation through identification" (ahaṅgrahopāsana) must be performed. Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Self is characterized by plenitude (bhūman). ||8||
Thus ends the section concerning delusion (Bhramādhikaraṇa) ||2||
20. The Section Concerning the Syllable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) ||1-3-3||
74. The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it exists even at the end of space. (1.3.9)
The Vājasaneyins record in the Gārgī-praśna:

"He said: 'O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare that this indeed is that Imperishable (akṣara); it is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long; it is without blood, without fat, without shadow,' and so forth."
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this imperishable (akṣara) the primary matter (pradhāna), or the individual soul (jīva), or rather the supreme self (paramātman)?
What is appropriate? "The Pradhāna. [The opponent says:

"The Imperishable (akṣara). The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that, although "being established in one's own glory" was stated in the preceding section, that is heard in scripture as belonging to something distinct from the Supreme Self.
And there arises the doubt: "Is it the Supreme Self?"—this is the doubt. [The question is: Is the Imperishable (akṣara) the Primal Matter (pradhāna), or is it the individual soul (jīva)?
For that purpose—it is to determine whether there is a rapidity of verbal cognition regarding that which is not the object of worldly means of knowledge.

In the passage, "In what, indeed, is space woven to and fro," the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is mentioned: does it refer to elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) or to unevolved space (*avyākṛtākāśa*)? And as for its support, is it by mere existence or by command?

1. When there is the understanding that the word "ether" (ākāśa) denotes the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), and its supporting [the elements] occurs through its existence; then, since such supporting is impossible for the Pradhāna, the Imperishable (akṣara) which supports it must be the Pradhāna. But the Imperishable is the Supreme Brahman, because of the manifestation of the manifest here, and because of the Śruti stating that everything is woven across and woven along within the Imperishable.
1. It is the Pradhāna alone—why? Because [the scripture says]:
"Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme."

Because the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) is seen to be used for the Pradhāna in such passages as these, and because qualities such as "not gross" and so forth are consistently associated with it there.

If it is argued that the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) is seen even in reference to the Supreme [Brahman] in passages such as "by which that Imperishable is attained," we say no; for when both a term well-known from other means of knowledge and one well-known from scripture are available, there is no contradiction in adopting the more commonly recognized meaning. Furthermore:

Since that which is established by other means of knowledge is what is first understood, after it has been established—beginning with the words, "That, O Gārgī, which is above the sky and below the earth"—that the entire universe existing in the three periods of time rests upon the ether (*ākāśa*) as its causal substrate, the question is asked: "Upon what, then, is this ether woven like warp and woof? When it is thus asked what the cause of the ether is—that which serves as its substrate—the *akṣara* (the Imperishable) being replied to is understood to be the *pradhāna* (the Primal Matter), which is established by other means of knowledge as the cause of all modifications and the substrate thereof. Therefore, the *akṣara* is the *pradhāna*.
This being the position, it is said: "The Imperishable [is Brahman], because of its supporting everything up to the ether. The "Imperishable" is the Supreme Brahman.

Alternatively, when the word "ether" (ākāśa) denotes the unevolved ether (avyākṛtākāśa), and "supporting" means existing by its mere presence, then since that is possible even for the individual soul (jīva), the Imperishable that supports it would be the individual soul.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): when the fact that the object of the word's cognition falls within the scope of worldly means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*) is irrelevant, and since the "unmanifested space" (*avyākṛtākāśa*) is what is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), and its supporting is through governance (*praśāsana*), then—because that [supporting] is impossible for individual souls (*jīva*)—the Imperishable (*akṣara*) which serves as its support is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (Śrutaprakāśikā)

"Not by another means of knowledge" (na pramāṇāntareti): inference depends solely upon perception; however, scripture requires both [perception and inference] at the initial stage of linguistic acquisition. Therefore, there is a delay for that which is established by scripture compared to that which is inferential. This is because, between the worldly and the non-worldly, the worldly possesses greater force due to its priority in common usage. The point is that even among the means of proof such as direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga), the former possesses greater force because it is the cause of quicker comprehension. "Due to the absence of contradiction" (virodhābhāvāditi): this means that the word "akṣara" refers to the Pradhāna.

Regarding the term *ambarānte*: the word *anta* signifies a limit (*avadhi*). Since there is no contradiction in the effect, namely space (*ambara*), being located in that very same place with respect to both space and time, why [is it not so]? Why [is it not possible]?

"Because of the support of the end of space": "space" (ambara) means the ether (ākāśa); its "end" (anta) refers to the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which is the limit; thus, "the end of space. "Because of the support of that" means because this Imperishable is taught as being the substratum of that.
The meaning is this:

in the passage, "In what, indeed, is space woven like warp and woof?", that which is designated by the word "space" (ākāśa) is not the sky containing air and water, but rather the unevolved (avyākṛta) state that lies beyond it. Therefore, the Imperishable (akṣara), which is spoken of as the substratum even for that unevolved state, cannot itself be the unevolved.
But how is it known that the word "ākāśa" refers [to space] and not merely to air? It is said:

"O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—all that is woven, warp and woof, upon ākāśa alone."
As for the claim that what is established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is understood prior to what is well-known from scripture—this is not so;

for when the word *akṣara* conveys its own meaning through its etymological power (*avayavaśakti*), it does not depend on another means of knowledge. Whatever means of knowledge apprehends the nature of an object at the stage of grasping the relationship between word and meaning, that same means need not be relied upon at the stage of actual communication. ||9||
That is not so;

for in that case, let the individual soul (jīva) be the one indicated by the word "akṣara," since it is possible for it to be the substratum of the entire non-sentient reality (acid-vastu), including everything down to the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma), and because the attributes being stated, such as "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth, are applicable to it. [As it is said:
"The unmanifest dissolves into the akṣara."

"Of whom the unmanifest is the body... of whom the imperishable (akṣara) is the body," and "The perishable consists of all beings; the immutable (kūṭastha) is called the imperishable (akṣara)," and so forth—in these passages, the term *akṣara* is seen to be applied even to the inner self (*pratyagātman*). To this, the reply is given: 75. And [it is Brahman] because of its command. (1.3.10)

And that support of the ends of space occurs solely by the command of this Imperishable; thus it is taught: "By the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. By the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart. By the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, moments, hours, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years stand held apart."

Regarding the word "akṣara": the power residing in the individual components (*avayava-śakti*) alone is the cause for the comprehension of the meaning; no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is required. For the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) does not depend upon perception that grasps both the staff and Devadatta in order to convey its own meaning.

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*): because the unmanifest is mentioned separately in the phrase "the unmanifest in the Imperishable" (*avyaktamakṣare*), it is understood that the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Thus, the unmanifest is mentioned here in order to make this known, as it is praised [in scripture] as being sustained by the command of the Imperishable. (Bhagavad Gītā 15.16)
That sustenance is due to the command [of God]; thus, the ignorant soul is not the cause.

[This is known] from the passage beginning with "Because of the possibility of being the support" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9). "Praśāsana" means supreme governance. Furthermore, such a sustaining of all things dependent upon its own command is not possible for the individual self (pratyagātman), whether in the state of bondage or liberation. Therefore, the Supreme Person alone is the governor; He is the Imperishable (akṣara). ||10||
76. And because of the exclusion of other states. (1.3.11)

"Being something else" (*anyabhāvaḥ*) means otherness, such as being the *pradhāna* or other [principles]. This otherness of this Imperishable (*akṣara*) from the Supreme Person is negated in the subsequent portion of the passage: "That, indeed, O Gārgī, is this Imperishable: unseen yet seeing, unheard yet hearing, unthought yet thinking, unknown yet knowing. There is no other seer than this, no other hearer than this, no other thinker than this, no other knower than this. In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof."

Or rather, it is the exclusion of the existence of another; that is, the exclusion of the positive existence of another—this is "the exclusion of the existence of another. Just as this Imperishable (akṣara), while being unseen by others and yet being the seer of others, is the substratum of everything distinct from itself, so too, one who says, "It is unseen by another and, while being its seer, there is no other that is its substratum," says:
"There is no other seer than this."

This is the remainder of the passage; by excluding the existence of anything else, it denies that this Imperishable (akṣara) possesses the nature of primordial matter (pradhāna) or the nature of the individual self (pratyagātman).
Furthermore:
"Under the governance of this Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, humans praise one who gives,
the gods [praise] the sacrificer, and the ancestors depend upon the giver."

Thus, it is understood that the Imperishable (akṣara), which is the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) who has become the Supreme Brahman, is He by whose command all ritual action—whether Vedic or Smṛti-based, such as sacrifice, charity, and oblation—is set in motion.
Moreover:

"O Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities without knowing this Imperishable (akṣara), even for many thousands of years, that act of theirs is finite. O Gārgī, whoever departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable. But he, O Gārgī, who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, he is a Brāhmaṇa.

It is thus established that that which is the Imperishable—the ignorance of which leads to the attainment of saṃsāra and the knowledge of which leads to the attainment of immortality—is indeed the Supreme Brahman. ||11||
Thus ends the section concerning the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) ||3||

Furthermore, he explains the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) with the phrase *iti ca*. The word "and" does not refer to a conjunction of what has already been stated (*pūrvavat*), as in the previous case; rather, the intention is that it refers to a conjunction of what has not yet been stated. The term *anvāyattāḥ* means "subordinate" or "dependent. This word applies generally to gods, humans, and ancestors.
The words ending in the accusative case are to be construed with the verb *praśaṃsanti* ("they praise"). [As it is said:
"That which is wretchedness arises from lack of awakening, and that which is true Brahminhood arises from awakening."
"That syllable is to be awakened through the path of the sounds as previously described. [11]
Moreover, 11. The Section Concerning the Object of Vision (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa) || 1.3.4 ||

[The one who meditates is] the Supreme Self alone, not the collective person (samaṣṭipuruṣa). 77. Because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing (īkṣati-karma), He [is the Supreme Self]. 1.3.12.

The followers of the Atharva Veda study this in the *Satyakāma-praśna*: "But he who meditates upon that supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable *Om* consisting of three measures—he, having attained union with the heat [of the sun], is freed from evil just as a snake is freed from its skin; indeed, led up by the Sāmans, he goes to the world of Brahman, and from this mass of living beings, he beholds the Puruṣa dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high."

The expression "He" (*saḥ*) here serves to maintain the continuity of the proposition regarding the subject to be established throughout all the sections (*adhikaraṇas*) in this chapter. For example, in the first chapter, there is the mention of the word "other" (*anya*) in the phrase "And because of the designation of difference, [He] is other"; likewise, in the second chapter, there is the mention of the word "Brahman" (*brahma*) in the phrase "And for this very reason, He is Brahman"; and similarly, in the fourth chapter, there is the mention of the word "the Wise One" (*prājña*) in the phrase "If it be said that He speaks, no, He is not the Wise One. It is just like those cases. Previously, the status of the Supreme Self as the Seer was stated in the passage, "The unseen Seer."
In that case, there arises the doubt that the Supreme Self is not what is described as the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarma*); thus, this constitutes the connection [of the topic].
By "with the Sāmans"—as in the expression "he sits singing this Sāman"—it means accompanied by the chanting of the Sāmans.

In this context, the words "meditates" (*adhyāyati*) and "beholds" (*īkṣati*) have the same object, because beholding is the fruit of meditation. According to the principle, "As is one's resolve in this world, so is a person [in the next]," that which is the object of meditation alone is what is attained; therefore, [it refers to] "the Supreme Person."
Thus, [the word is eternal] also because the object, which serves as the grammatical object (*karman*) in both instances, is recognized as being the same.

In this regard, a doubt arises: Is the one designated here as the "Supreme Person" the four-faced Brahmā, the lord of the cosmic egg who is the aggregate of individual souls (jīvasamaṣṭi), or is it the Lord of All, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)?
What is logical? That the *kṣetrajña* is the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*).
Why? [Because of the scriptural passage:
"O Venerable One! He who, among men, meditates upon the syllable Om until the end of his life..."

Having begun with the question, "What world does he conquer by means of that?", the text first describes the attainment of the world of men for one who meditates on the *praṇava* as having one measure (*ekamātra*). Then, it describes the attainment of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) for one who meditates on it as having two measures (*dvimātra*). Finally, for one who meditates on it as having three measures (*trimātra*), what is designated as the goal to be attained is the "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*). This is understood to be the world beyond the intermediate space, belonging to the four-faced Brahmā, who is the collective totality of individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*). Furthermore, the Lord of that world who is beheld by the meditator is indeed the four-faced Brahmā himself, as indicated by the phrase:
"Higher than this mass of living beings (*jīvaghana*)."

And thus, it is logically established that the Supreme Person is superior to the individual person (*jīva*)—the collective being residing in the world of Brahmā (*caturmukha*)—who is a dense aggregation of the body, senses, and so forth, along with those very bodies, senses, and so forth. Therefore, the "Supreme Person" mentioned here must be the collective being, the four-faced one himself. Once his identity as the four-faced one is certain, qualities such as "being undecaying" and so on must be interpreted in some way or another [as applying to him].

This being the position, we reply: "He is [the Supreme Self], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. "The object of the act of seeing" means He—the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the designation; for He is designated as the object of the act of seeing by virtue of His being the Supreme Self. This is evident from the verse cited as the subject matter of the act: for instance, "He sees"—[and so forth].

"Of the four-faced one's world": the meaning is that the world of the four-faced one is reached through the sequence of the earth and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). "From this": the reference "beyond the supreme mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*) is established through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words "mass of living beings" and "supreme. "As a collective whole" (*samaṣṭi*): Brahmā’s status as the collective person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*) is in relation to the states of gods, animals, and so forth. "Are to be led": [this refers to the souls].

The intention is that the explanation is established either by the sense of enduring for a long time, or by taking it as referring to the nature of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) himself in his state of complete purity. For this very reason, the reference at the beginning as "the higher and the lower" has also been successfully explained.
"By this very syllable *om*, the wise man attains that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme.

Indeed, these attributes—"supreme," "peaceful," "undecaying," "fearless," and "immortal"—are the very nature of the Supreme Self alone; for it is said, "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman."
This is established by such scriptural passages as these;
furthermore, the designation "higher than the highest from this mass of living beings" refers specifically to the Supreme Self, and not to the four-faced Brahmā.

For he too is included under the term "mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*). Indeed, whoever possesses embodied existence caused by karma is called a "mass of living beings," and that is heard to apply to Caturmukha as well.
In such passages as, "He who created Brahmā in the beginning," and so forth.

As for what was further stated—that the Brahmaloka, which is indicated as being above the Antarikṣaloka, is understood to be the world of the Four-faced One (Caturmukha), and therefore the Four-faced One resides there—that is incorrect; for [the scripture says]:
"That which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, and fearless."

Since it has been determined by such passages that the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarma*) is the Supreme Self, the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), which is designated as the "abode" of the seer, cannot be the perishable world of the four-faced [Brahmā].

"Of this form" (*etadrūpam*) means the essential nature (*svarūpa*) indicated by a word ending in the neuter gender; for if it referred to the Four-faced One (*Caturmukha*), it would have to end in the masculine gender. "This is the nectar" (*etadamṛtam*): by this, the purpose of the word *saḥ* from the Sūtra is shown. Since the thesis to be established is already accomplished through the context alone, its specific purpose must be stated.

In response to the inquiry, "How can the designation 'peaceful' and 'fearless' establish [the object] as the Supreme Self? it must be stated that this is because the Supreme Self is well-known in other Vedic texts (*śruti*) as being of such a nature. Therefore, the purpose of the word "that" (*saḥ*) is to indicate its recognition as such through its renown in other Vedic texts. As for the phrase "even of the four-faced one": the underlying sense is that the status of being four-faced exists precisely because he possesses a body.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "at the beginning," the verse-quarter "to him indeed he imparts the Vedas" is also intended. Consequently, because the four-faced Brahmā is a created being, because his knowledge is limited by its dependence on instruction, and because he is subject to karma, it is established that he is included under the term "the mass of individual souls" (*jīvaghana*).
1. "Amṛta is fearlessness"—da; 2. "This [world] is fear, while that is amṛta"—tha; even for the Four-faced One—da.
Furthermore:
"Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so, indeed, is he freed from evil."—da.

"He is led by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman"—this, being stated as that which is to be attained by one who is liberated from all evils, does not refer to the abode of the four-faced [Brahmā]. For this very reason, with reference to this very world of Brahman, it is heard in the illustrative verse: "That which the seers know."
Thus [it is said]. "Sages" (kavayaḥ) refers to the wise (sūrayaḥ). And that which is perceived by the wise is indeed the supreme station of Viṣṇu, according to such passages as:

"The wise always behold that supreme station of Viṣṇu. Nor is the world of the four-faced Brahmā beyond the intermediate space, because there exist many worlds in between, such as the heavenly worlds (svargaloka) and others. Therefore: "O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the wise person—"

In response to the question, "By that very means, one follows after the One," that other effect which was indicated as Brahman is divided into two types—pertaining to this world and pertaining to the hereafter. Having stated the fruit for those who meditate on the single measure (the *praṇava*) as consisting of attaining the human world in this life, and having stated the fruit for those who meditate on the double measure as being the hereafter-world characterized by the term "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*), [it proceeds to describe] the Supreme Brahman through the triple measure.

*Kavayaḥ* means those who see beyond [the ordinary]. Because they are not subject to karma, their knowledge is uncontracted. *Sūrayaḥ* are well known as those preeminent in knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is that by the force of the sense, there is a recognition of the *sūris*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "from these and so forth," such scriptural passages as "The wise ones (*viprāsaḥ*) who praise," "Where the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*) first-born, who are ancient," and "Where the former Sādhyas, the gods, abide," are intended.

The meaning is that this is not the world of the four-faced Brahmā (Caturmukha), because it is the abode of one whose status as the Supreme Self has been ascertained through qualities such as agelessness; because it is the destination to be attained by one who is liberated from all karma; and because it is recognized by the wise as being visible. Therefore, in accordance with the natural sense of the many cited passages, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "Brahman is the syllable Om" is based on the relationship between the signified and the signifier; for immediately thereafter, both the syllable Om and Brahman are designated by the two words "one" (*etena*) and "the other" (*ekataram*).

"By means of" (ayanena) means by way of a means (upāyabhūtena). "Either one" (ekataram) refers to either of the two: the causal Brahman or the effected Brahman. Regarding the phrase "having distinguished" (vibhajya): the meaning is that "distinction" (vibhāga) is intended because they are later proclaimed as having separate fruits. || 12 ||

For those meditating on the "Supreme Person" by means of the syllable *praṇava*, the text teaches that the Supreme Brahman itself is the object to be attained; thus, everything is consistent. Therefore, the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarma*) is the Supreme Self. || 12 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa). ||4||
22. The Section Concerning the Youth (Daharādhikaraṇa) ||1.3.5||
78. The child [is Brahman], because of the subsequent [passages]. (1.3.13)
The Chandogas recite this:

"Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace—smaller than that is the ether within it; what is inside that is to be sought, that indeed is what one must desire to understand."

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) situated within the lotus of the heart a particular instance of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), or is it the inner self (*pratyagātman*), or is it the supreme self (*paramātman*)? [The word] *daha* [is used here]. In the preceding section, the status of the supreme self was established for that which was described as "the person dwelling in the city, higher than the high. Here, the connection is that the non-supreme nature of the one dwelling in the city—who is denoted by the word "ether"—is being refuted. The doubt arises because, in the case of the supreme self, no other thing to be sought after is possible; and in the case of the other two alternatives, the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared (*upamānopameyabhāva*), and so forth, would be untenable.

The doubt is as follows: Is the "small ether" (daharākāśa) the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), or the individual soul (jīva), or the Supreme Self (paramātman)? To resolve this, one must investigate whether the mention of something else that is to be sought within it contradicts the small ether's being the Supreme Self, or not? Furthermore, regarding the mention "that which is within it," does it refer to a collection of qualities belonging to the small ether, or does it have another meaning? And as for the freedom from sin and other attributes mentioned in the statement "this is the Self," are these the characteristics of the individual soul as described in the Prajāpati discourse?

Is it so, or not?—this is the inquiry: if these are attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*), is there consistency with the scriptural texts concerning its being "free from sin" and so forth, or not?
What, then, is the reasonable position? That it is a particular great element (*mahābhūta*). Why?
Although the word "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known to refer both to the elemental ether and to Brahman, it refers here to the elemental ether because of its greater conventional usage in that sense,
and because it is perceived as the substratum for that which is to be sought within it, according to the statement: "That which is within it is what must be sought."
This being the position reached, it is replied: "The small [space] is [Brahman] because of the subsequent [reasons]. The small ether is the supreme Brahman. Why?
Because of the reasons found in the subsequent parts of the passage.

"This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"—thus, the attributes heard in the context of the small ether (*daharākāśa*)—namely, its nature as the Self devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhikātmatva*), freedom from evil and so forth, and the possession of true desires and true resolves—make it known that the small ether is the Supreme Brahman. This is further established by such passages as: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds."

By the statement, "Whatever desire he desires, that arises for him from his mere resolve; endowed with that, he exults," the attainment of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva) by the knower of the small ether (daharākāśa) is declared, which makes it understood that the "Supreme Brahman" resides within the small ether.

Furthermore, the relationship of comparison and object compared—expressed in the words, "As large as this space is, so large is this space within the heart"—is not possible if the small space (daharākāśa) were the elemental space (bhūtākāśa). If it is argued that this relationship of comparison is based on the limitation [of the space] by the heart, then, in that case, it would be impossible for that which is limited by the heart to be the support of everything, including heaven and earth.

But surely— even if the small ether were the Supreme Self, its being comparable to the external ether would not be possible, because of the scriptural statement in such passages as "greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space," that it is greater than everything.

The term "unconditioned" (*nirupādhika*) is used with the intention that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is capable of distinguishing the [Supreme Self] even from the individual soul (*jīva*). By "unconditionedness," it is intended that even qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) are unconditioned;
that is, they are not delimited by specific bodies such as those of gods and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "freedom from evil and so forth," although it would have been possible to include "having true desires" and other qualities by the word "and so forth" (ādi), they are mentioned separately in order to indicate that these qualities are of two kinds, namely, those consisting of injunctions and those consisting of prohibitions.

Regarding the term "upamāna" (standard of comparison): the meaning is that the relationship of being both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison cannot coherently belong to one and the same thing.

Regarding the phrase "nanu ca" (but surely): the intention of the objection is that it is not logical for even that which possesses a larger magnitude to share a commonality with a medium magnitude, just as [it is not logical] for that which possesses a smaller magnitude.

It is not so; for this passage aims at removing the smallness that results from the fact that the "small ether" (daharākāśa) resides within the center of the heart-lotus. Just as the statement, "The sun moves like an arrow," although the sun possesses great speed, is intended to remove the notion of its slowness of motion.
Now, it might be argued:
"This Self is free from evil."
By such statements as these, the small ether (*daharākāśa*) itself is not being pointed out;

for, in the passage "In this [ether] there is a small ether within; that which is within it is what must be sought," something other than that [small ether], residing within the small ether, is introduced as the object to be sought. Here, [the text says] "This is the Self, free from evil... [and so forth].
Thus, it is appropriate to point out that very thing which is to be sought;
this might be so, provided that the Śruti itself did not distinguish between the small ether and that which dwells within it; for indeed, it did so distinguish them.
Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; within it is a small space (ākāśa). That which is inside that [space] is what one must seek to discover.
