Therefore, since even the gods and others possess the requisite desire and capability, it is established that they have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. ||29||

Śrī Bhaṇyam 1.38] 25. The Middle Section within the Section on Limited Capacity [1.3.8]. Summary of the Section: Even for those who have attained the status of the Vasus and other deities, there is eligibility for the Madhu-vidyā and other meditations.
95. On account of impossibility in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and others, the Jaiminiyas hold that there is no eligibility. [1.3.30]
It has been stated that gods and others also possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
What is the conclusion?
There is no qualification for those [meditations] on the honey and so forth—this is what Jaimini thinks. Why?

Because of impossibility. For it is not possible that the Ādityas, Vasus, and others could be worshipped by other Ādityas, Vasus, and others; nor can the state of being a Vasu and so forth be attained by those who are already Vasus and so forth, since they have already attained it.

In the Madhuvidyā, the worshipability and the status of being the Vasus and so forth of the "parts" of the Sun—which is designated as "honey" by virtue of being the substratum for the essence obtained through the rays and accomplished by means of rituals taught in the Ṛgveda and other scriptures—is heard in scripture as the goal to be attained;
this is set forth beginning with the passage: "That Sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods."

Having stated, "That which is the first nectar, that the Vasus subsist upon," if the fruit were merely the status of being a Vasu, then because only the deities such as the Vasus would be the objects of meditation, and because those deities lack the capacity to conclude that specific knowledge (vidyā), the word "that" (yat) would refer to something distinct from them; thus, they would have no entitlement to it.
"He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Vasus themselves, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar with the eye as his mouth," and so forth. || 30 ||
And because [the word] exists in the sense of "light. (1.3.31)

"The gods meditate upon that light of lights as life and immortality"—thus, the meditation upon the supreme Brahman, which is light, is heard [in scripture] as being practiced by the gods. While the meditation on the supreme Brahman is common to both gods and humans, the specific mention of the gods as practitioners indicates the cessation of other forms of meditation for them. Therefore, the Vasus and others have no qualification for these [other meditations]. || 31 ||
This being the case, it is replied: 97. But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] existence, for there is indeed [scriptural authority]. (1.3.32)

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa considers that even the Ādityas, Vasus, and others possess the qualification for these [meditations]. For it is possible for the Ādityas, Vasus, and others as well to attain Brahman after first attaining the state of Vasu or Āditya through the meditation on Brahman in its own respective forms. Furthermore, there is a requirement for those who are currently Vasus and others to attain the status of Vasu and so forth in another *kalpa*.
For here, the meditation upon Brahman in its three states— as effect, cause, and both— is enjoined;
"Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods."
Beginning from this point and extending until "then,
rising up from there," the Brahman existing in its specific state as the effect of the sun and so forth is taught as the object of meditation.
By the term "meditation on Brahman in its own state," the contradiction between the action and the agent is resolved.

Regarding the phrase "for here": when it is established that meditation culminates in Brahman and its fruit culminates in the attainment of Brahman, there is indeed no contradiction between the object of action and the agent, nor is there an absence of the attainment of the fruit. How so? To this [it is replied]:

"‘This indeed,’ and so forth: Brahman, whose body is the individual soul (jīva) characterized by the names and forms such as ‘Āditya’ and the rest, exists in its state as an effect; the meditation upon that is enjoined. Now, ‘then from that,’ and so forth: now, even though [the soul] possesses the names and forms of Āditya and the rest, prior to creation, Brahman—the inner ruler (antaryāmī)—exists in its causal state as the mere individual soul devoid of the names and forms of Āditya and the rest; the meditation upon that is here enjoined."
For the sake of attaining the status of a Vasu in another birth, one who is independent should perform the worship of another; for Bādarāyaṇa has indeed said this regarding them.

Now, by the passage beginning with "Then, rising upwards from there," Brahman—which exists as the inner self within the sun and is in its causal state alone—is taught as the object of meditation. Thus, one who meditates upon Brahman in both its effected and causal states, having attained the status of Vāsudeva and so forth at the end of a kalpa, reaches the supreme Brahman itself, the cause, at the conclusion of that period.

"Verily, for him it neither rises nor sets; for him there is but one continuous day, who knows this secret doctrine (brahmopaniṣad) of Brahman in this way"—since this entire Madhu-vidyā is heard as a "secret doctrine of Brahman" (*brahmopaniṣad*), and since its fruit is heard to extend up to the attainment of Brahman, it is understood that the meditation being enjoined pertains to Brahman itself in its state as the sun, which is the portion of the sun that serves as the object of enjoyment for the Vasus and others. Therefore, such a form of meditation is possible even for the Vasus, Ādityas, and so forth. And thus, because Brahman alone is the object of meditation, [the fruit belongs to them as well].
The statement, "That which the gods [know as] the light of lights," is also appropriate. Regarding this, the author of the Commentary (Vṛttikāra) says:
"For there is indeed the possibility [of Brahman being designated] in the Madhu-vidyā and others, because Brahman alone is to be perceived everywhere."
Thus [ends the section]. 32.
The middle section within the section concerning the measured [number of verses]. 8.
26. Within the section concerning those who have exerted themselves, the section concerning those other than Śūdras [Śūdrādhikaraṇa]. (1.3.9)
98. For it is indicated by the hearing of [the Lord’s] disregard for Śuka and by his rushing toward him. (1.3.33)
It is now considered whether a Śūdra also possesses the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), or not.
What is logical?
That it exists.
Why?
Because the qualification [for Vedic study] is conditioned by both the desire for the goal and the capacity [to understand it], and because these are possible even for a Śūdra.

Although a Śūdra lacks the qualification for rites to be accomplished through the knowledge of the sacred fires (*agnividyā*) because he does not possess that knowledge, nevertheless, since the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*) consists merely of a mental activity, his qualification for it certainly exists. Even though meditation requires scriptural action, it requires only such action as is appropriate to one's particular caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*); therefore, for a Śūdra, the very service to the higher castes appropriate to his own caste shall constitute the required action.

As for the statement, "Therefore, a Śūdra is excluded from sacrifice," this merely reiterates what is already established by logic: namely, that he lacks qualification for sacrifices and the like which are to be accomplished through the knowledge of the sacred fires.

Now, an objection is raised: how can the meditation on Brahman be possible for one who has not studied the Vedas, who has not heard the Vedānta texts, and who is ignorant of the nature of Brahman and the methods of its worship?

It is replied: even for one who has not studied the Vedas and has not heard the Vedānta passages, knowledge of the nature of Brahman and the method of its worship is possible through the hearing of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Furthermore, there is permission for even a Śūdra to hear the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

Because these two independently serve as the cause for the realization of Brahman, and because a continuous stream of memory regarding Brahman is possible even for one who has not studied the Vedas, Śūdras also possess the qualification [for knowledge] by virtue of this capacity.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: When the word "Śūdra" is understood etymologically, then the address "O Śūdra! found in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* does not indicate [eligibility] because it lacks dependence on the realization of Brahman; rather, since it indicates the realization of Brahman independently, the understanding of Brahman comes from the Veda alone. Consequently, for one who has not studied the Veda, such understanding is impossible, and due to a lack of capacity, there is no eligibility for the meditation upon Brahman. "Vidyā" means Vedic knowledge. "Agni" refers to the consecrated fire.

"It is restated because it is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). For this matter is not to be understood solely through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), such that there would be a restriction to the literal words or an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*). Rather, it is established by logic. And the logic—consisting in the impossibility of one who lacks the knowledge of the fires (*anagnividyā*) being qualified for rites accomplished by the knowledge of the fires—is common to both ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*). This much, however, does not imply a lack of qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), because the logic applies specifically to the domain of ritual actions accomplished by the knowledge of the fires.

The meaning is that since rites such as sacrifices are accomplished through the knowledge of the sacred fires (*agnividyā*), whereas the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is independent of them, this [exclusion] is established by the logic of the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those who are not Śūdras) in the Karma-kāṇḍa.

In such passages as, "One should cause the four castes to hear [the Veda], having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront," and others; and we see in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas that Vidura and others were established in Brahman.

Likewise, even in the Upaniṣads, the eligibility of a Śūdra for the knowledge of Brahman is perceived in the Saṃvarga-vidyā. For the teacher Raikva, addressing Jānaśruti—who was desirous of hearing—as "Śūdra," instructs him in the knowledge of Brahman, saying:
"Bring these [cows], O Śūdra; by this very means you shall cause me to speak."
By such statements as these, it follows that even a Śūdra possesses the qualification [for Vedic study].

This being the case, it is replied: the Śūdra has no eligibility (*adhikāra*) "because it is impossible. This is due to a lack of capacity. For one who does not know the nature of Brahman and the method of its meditation, and who is ineligible for the recitation of the Vedas, sacrifices, and so forth—which constitute the limbs of that [meditation]—the capacity to accomplish the meditation is impossible. And for one who lacks capacity, eligibility is not possible even if there exists a desire for the goal. Furthermore, this incapacity results from the absence of Vedic study.

For just as the injunctions for ritual action do not require other things—such as knowledge and its means—since that knowledge is obtained through the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) established by the injunction to study for those belonging to the three higher castes; so too it is with the injunctions for the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*). Therefore, since the very knowledge acquired through the study of the Veda, as established by the injunction to study, is the means for the meditation on Brahman, the Śūdra lacks the capacity for the meditation on Brahman.

Not independently. The permission for a Śūdra to listen to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is for the purpose of attaining fruits such as the destruction of sins, not for the purpose of meditative worship (*upāsanā*). However, Vidura and others were possessed of knowledge because they did not lose the knowledge acquired in other births; and due to the force of their *prārabdha* karma, they were endowed with such a birth. Thus, they possessed steadfastness in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhatva*).

As for the claim that the address "O Śūdra! used in the *Saṃvarga-vidyā* toward the one desiring to hear indicates the eligibility of a Śūdra, he says: "No; for it is indicated rather by his sorrow upon hearing that disrespectful remark, which caused him to run away."

Because Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, though desirous of learning, heard the words of disregard spoken by the swan due to his deficiency in the knowledge of Brahman, he immediately ran toward Raikva, the knower of Brahman; thus it is indicated that "the white (śuk) arose within him. Therefore, he is addressed as "Śūdra," not by virtue of belonging to the fourth caste.

For he is called a *śūdra* because he grieves (*śocati*). By the rule "from the root *śuc*, [the suffix] *ra* and [the substitution of] *d*," when the suffix *ra* is applied, the long vowel is substituted for the root vowel, and the letter *c* is changed to *d*, the form *śūdra* arises. Therefore, it is precisely his state of being subject to grief that is indicated by the application of the word *śūdra*; there is no connection with birth (*jāti*).

"It is not for the purpose of *upāsana* (meditative worship)," because those who lack the qualification for the knowledge of the Vedas—which are to be supplemented (*upabṛṃhaṇīya*)—cannot achieve the fullness of knowledge required for *upāsana* through mere supplementation alone. For it is not possible for one who lacks the qualification for the subject matter of an exposition to attain complete knowledge through the exposition alone; thus, there is a deficiency in its observed efficacy. "Itihāsa... [and so forth].

Since it is prescribed for the purpose of making the meaning of the Vedas clear by means of "causing [them] to grow," if one were to undertake that which is prescribed as an auxiliary (aṅga) independently, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures—just as in the case of knowledge of the Vedic meaning obtained through reading from books—and furthermore, there would be a deficiency in the unseen potency (adṛṣṭa-sāmarthya). Therefore, because non-contradiction is logical and because the injunction for hearing [the Vedas] must not be rendered futile.

Regarding the word *śūdra*: the meaning of the term *śūdra* is "one who sorrows" (*śocitṛ*). The cause of sorrow is the hearing of disrespectful words; its effect is running toward [the speaker]. Regarding the suffix *ra*: the suffix *rak* is established by the context and is drawn in by the letter *ca*. The sense is that the portion "and long" (*dīrghaśca*) from the rule *amitamyohīṃrghaśca* is understood here. For it is precisely sorrow (*śuc*) that is perceived as the thing to be produced (*upapādyatva*), because of its being indicated in the nominative case.

For the words *śravaṇa* and *dravaṇa* end in the fifth case (ablative). Therefore, sorrow alone is the ground for the application of the word "śūdra"—it is indicated by the word "śūdra" in the sense of "destruction. [Variant readings: *kṣayārtham*—Da; *śūdraśabdena*—Tha;
*sūcyate*—Da.]

It is said that Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a giver of much wealth and a giver of much food. While he was a leader among the righteous, two great souls, who were pleased with his virtue and desired to arouse in him a longing for the knowledge of Brahman, were traveling at night not far from him in the form of swans. One of them said to the other:
"O Bhallākṣa! O Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out equal to the sun; do not touch it, lest it consume you."
Thus, having overheard this statement in the form of a praise of Jānaśruti, the other haṃsa replied: "Alas! Who are you that speak of him as if he were Raikva with the cart?"

Thus [he asks]: "Who is this Jānaśruti that you speak of as if he were Raikva Sayugvān, the knower of Brahman, the most excellent in qualities? That Raikva alone is the most virtuous person in the world. What quality does this Jānaśruti possess, who is not a knower of Brahman, even though he is endowed with great wealth? What is that quality produced by his merit whose splendor might burn me like the splendor of Raikva? This is the meaning.

When he was addressed thus, being asked by the other, "Who is this Raikva?", he replied: "Raikva is he in whom both whatever good action is performed in the world and whatever knowledge resides in all conscious beings are included within his own knowledge and action."

Having learned that they had arrived, Raikva himself approached them, and having presented him with two hundred cows, a necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules, he requested of Raikva: "O Venerable One, instruct me in that deity which you worship. The meaning is: "Instruct me in that supreme deity whom you worship."

And that Raikva, who had personally realized the three worlds through the majesty of his own yoga, having understood Jānaśruti’s state of being overwhelmed by grief upon hearing the words of the swan—which contained a rebuke based on his lack of knowledge of Brahman—and having immediately thereafter perceived his exertion through the desire to know Brahman, recognized his fitness for the science of Brahman. Thinking, "The science of Brahman shall be firmly established in this man, who serves me with devotion even without the offering of wealth, by providing him as much instruction as my power permits," he [bestowed it].
Favoring him, and indicating by the address "O Śūdra" that his state of being overwhelmed with grief was a sign of his fitness for instruction, he said this:
"Ah, O Śūdra! Let this [chariot] be right there along with the cows.

The meaning is: "Let this chariot remain right there along with the cows; it is not by giving this much to me that the knowledge of Brahman becomes established in you who are overwhelmed with grief through the desire to know Brahman."
Therefore, by the word "śūdra," it is merely his state of grief that is indicated for the purpose of demonstrating his fitness for the instruction of knowledge;
it does not signify that he belongs to the fourth caste.

Thus, it has been stated that his status as a Kṣatriya is perceived in the narrative occurring at the beginning. He now states that his status as a Kṣatriya is also perceived in the narrative occurring at the conclusion:
100. And because of the indicative mark [found] later regarding Caitraratha, [the chariot belongs to Indra]. (1.3.35)
From this very *saṃvarga-vidyā* being taught to this Jānaśruti, and from the fact that he is later mentioned by the Kṣatriya named Abhipratārin Caitraratha, his status as a Kṣatriya is understood.
How so? [As it is said:
"Now, Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin..."
When Kākṣaseni was being served [food], a religious student (brahmacārī) begged [of her],
saying, "O religious student, we do not partake of this," and so forth.

By this much [of the text], it is understood that Kāpeya and Abhipratārin, as well as the mendicant religious student (brahmacārin), are connected with the Saṃvarga-vidyā. Among them, Abhipratārin is a Kṣatriya; the other two are Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, in this knowledge (vidyā), the connection of a Brāhmaṇa is seen, and in those others, the connection of a Kṣatriya alone is seen; not that of a Śūdra. Hence, from one who is connected to this knowledge...

How so? If Caitraratha were a Kṣatriya, then Jānaśruti would also be a Kṣatriya; however, there is no such rule—this is the meaning. "Being served"—that is, being fed by a cook. That the mendicancy of the two students, Kāpeya and Abhipratārin, is a mark of their belonging to the three higher castes (traivarṇika) is established by the sense of the text.

When, in one instance, a person is understood to be connected with both the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya castes, and in another instance, they are determined to be connected with the Brāhmaṇa caste, then when a doubt arises regarding other persons connected to them, [the decision follows] by the principle of the majority (agrayaprāyanyāya).
It is more appropriate that Jānaśruti, like Raikva the Brāhmaṇa, was also a Kṣatriya; he was certainly not of the fourth caste.

Now, an objection is raised: "In this context, neither Abhipratārin’s status as a descendant of Citraratha nor his status as a Kṣatriya is heard; so how can this Abhipratārin be a descendant of Citraratha? Or how can he be a Kṣatriya? To this, the author replies: "On account of an indicative mark (liṅga). From the indicative mark of Abhipratārin’s association with the descendant of Kapi found in the passage, "Then [they approached] Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni," it is understood that this Abhipratārin has a connection with the descendant of Kapi. Furthermore, elsewhere...

"By this [sacrifice], the Kāpeyas indeed caused Caitraratha to sacrifice"—thus the status of being Caitraratha is heard in connection with the Kāpeyas. Likewise, the kṣatriya status of Caitraratha is established by the text: "From him was born one named Caitraratha, a lord of the kṣatra. Therefore, it is understood that Abhipratārin was both a descendant of Citraratha and a kṣatriya. || 35 ||

Thus, it has been stated that no indicative mark (*liṅga*) is found for a Śūdra’s eligibility [for Vedic study] which would contradict reason. Now, he says that the Śūdra’s lack of eligibility, established by reason, is further supported by Śruti and Smṛti: "Because of the reference to the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and because of the declaration of their absence [in the case of the Śūdra]. (Sūtra 1.3.36)
The meaning is that the status of this person as either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya is determined, and by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), his Kṣatriyahood is established.

Because of the association with Kāpeya—that is, because of the mention in the same textual passage as Kāpeya—the connection with Kāpeya is proven by the force of that shared recitation. By that, his being the son of Citraratha’s priest is established; by that, his Kṣatriyahood is understood. || 35 ||

"Thus, in this way": the meaning is that both kinds of indicative marks (*liṅga*)—those indicative marks that contradict the conventional meaning of the word "Śūdra" and those indicative marks that are consistent with its etymological meaning—serve as evidence for the Śūdra's lack of qualification.
"Now": the meaning is that he states that this lack of qualification is supported by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

Because of the investigation into the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is no qualification for the Śūdra due to the statement regarding the absence of sacraments.
1. Caitraratha’s—du. 2. Śūdra established by logic—da. 3. By means of scriptural texts—du.
In the sections concerning the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana-saṃskāra*) is referred to.
In passages such as "I shall lead you [to the teacher]" and "He led him [to the teacher]," the absence of sacraments such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for a *śūdra* is declared.

"In the case of a Śūdra there is no sin whatsoever, nor does he deserve the purificatory rites; 'the fourth caste is of single birth and does not deserve the purificatory rites'—in such passages as these. || 36 ||
102. And because activity proceeds toward the determination of the non-existence of that [object]. (1.3.37)

"An un-Brahmin is not entitled to explain this; fetch the fuel, my dear," [said Śvetaketu]. Since the instruction in knowledge proceeded only after it was determined that Jābāla, who desired to hear, was not a Śūdra, the Śūdra has no qualification [for Vedic study]. || 37 ||

"There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra"—the meaning is that there is no sin caused by the absence of performing the *saṃdhyā-vandana* and other such rites. "Of a single birth" (*ekajāti*) means that he is not a twice-born (*dvijāti*). || 36 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of Śūdra-hood": the intention is that since the word *tat* (that) would lack consistency with the subject matter of this sūtra if it were to refer back to the term "consecration" (*saṃskāra*) which was the topic of the preceding sūtra, the word *tat* must therefore refer back to the subject under discussion [in the present context]. || 37 ||
Since Jābāla was intent on service and his status as a Śūdra was certain,
and since the instruction proceeded [only after he attained a higher status], a Śūdra does not possess the qualification [for Vedic study].
103. Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda]. (1.3.38)
For a Śūdra, hearing the Veda, studying it, and performing its prescribed rites are forbidden; for it is said:
"A Śūdra is indeed a cemetery; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra," and "Therefore, a Śūdra is unfit for sacrifice even if he speaks much."

Thus [it is said]. "Possessing many cattle" (bahupaśu) means being like cattle. For one who does not hear [the Veda], study, the knowledge of its meaning, and the performance of its prescribed rites are impossible. Therefore, these too are effectively prohibited. || 38 ||
104. And because of the Smṛti. (Sūtra 1.3.39)

By the word *artha*, its performance is intended. "Padyu" means moving on foot. From the very prohibition of pronouncing [the Veda] in close proximity, the prohibition of hearing and studying is established by implication. Therefore, the phrase "therefore a Śūdra" shows the prohibition of the performance of the meaning; that is to say, he is like an animal. While it would have been sufficient to say "one who is slightly incomplete as an animal," the use of the word "similar" (*sadṛśa*) is for the purpose of making known that the sense of being "slightly incomplete" culminates in similarity.

By the Pāṇinian sūtra "vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāt tu," the suffix *bahuc* is prescribed in the sense of "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*), and its placement before the word is also ordained. Regarding the term *adhyayana*: the statement "A Śūdra shall not study" (*śūdro nādhīyīta*) should also be considered here. By this, because of the specific prohibition regarding sacrifice (*yajña*), any suspicion of the Śūdra's eligibility for other Vedic rites is also dispelled. || 38 ||

It is certain that a Śūdra has no entitlement even to meditative worship, because of the prohibitions against hearing, studying, reciting, and performing sacrifices according to the traditional scriptures.
Because of the indicative evidence [that one of Śūdra caste is not entitled to the knowledge taught in the Veda],
and because of Smṛti texts such as "One should not teach him the Dharma," it is understood that a Śūdra has no entitlement to meditative practice.
Furthermore, the prohibition of hearing [the Veda] and so forth is recorded:
"Now, if he hears the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac; for reciting it, his tongue is to be cut off; and for retaining it, his body is to be split asunder."
And [it is said]: "One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow for him. Therefore, it is established that the Śūdra has no entitlement [to Vedic study]. || 39 ||

However, those who assert that Brahman alone—which is consciousness devoid of all distinctions—is the ultimate reality, while everything else is illusory; that bondage is unreal and is to be removed solely by the knowledge of the true nature of reality arising from the [great] sentences (mahāvākya); and that liberation is simply the cessation of that [bondage]—they speak thus.

By them [the proponents of Advaita], it cannot be asserted that there is no eligibility for Śūdras and others regarding the knowledge of Brahman; for even in one who is uninitiated, has not studied the Vedas, and has not heard the Vedāntic texts, the knowledge of the true nature of reality arises from any [source whatsoever] through such statements as: "Brahman alone, which is non-dual pure consciousness, is the ultimate reality; everything else is superimposed upon it and is illusory. And by that much alone, bondage is brought to an end.

Nor can it be restricted that the production of knowledge must occur through the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) alone and not through any other sentence; for knowledge is not dependent on a person, since knowledge arises even against one's will when the causal conditions are present. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Then, indeed" (*atha ha*) refers to the traditional law (*smṛti*) regarding penance for studying [the Upanishads] and so forth, as well as the traditional law prohibiting such instruction. The sense is that both are intended by the word "Smṛti" because they serve to indicate a lack of qualification [for such study].

Regarding the passage beginning with "ataḥ" and so forth: in cases such as "the chariot-maker (rathakāra) should establish the sacred fires," the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is accepted according to the maxim "conventionality sets aside etymological derivation. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to that rule when there is a contradiction in meaning. Conventionality possesses strength when favorable indicative marks (*liṅga*) are present and contradictory indicative marks are absent. It is stated that the presence of contradictory indicative marks constitutes an exception to that [rule of conventionality]. In the case of "the chariot-maker should establish the sacred fires" as well, an favorable indicative mark is found in the statement, "The Ṛbhus are the Saudhanvanas. ||39||

Regarding the phrase "of one who has not been initiated": the sense is that for the cessation of the delusion [that a snake exists] upon hearing the statement "This is not a snake, this is a rope," there is no requirement for initiatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *upanayana*.
By the phrase "when the causal complex is present," he states the reason for its not being dependent on a person.

Nor can it be asserted that the cessation of bondage occurs only when the knowledge of the true nature of reality arises from the Vedic sentences themselves; for the cessation of delusion occurs whenever there is knowledge of the true nature of reality, regardless of its source. Even from a human-authored statement such as "Brahman is the ultimate reality, pure consciousness without attributes; everything else is illusory," knowledge arises, and by that alone, delusion is removed.

Just as even from the words of a trustworthy person—though they be of human origin—the delusion regarding mother-of-pearl as silver and the like is removed for a Brāhmaṇa and even for a Śūdra; in the very same way, for a Śūdra as well, the cessation of the world-delusion will occur through the knowledge of the true nature of reality derived from statements received through the tradition of those who know the Veda.

It cannot be asserted on the basis of such statements as "one should not teach him the Dharma" or "those who know the Vedas do not speak [of it] to Śūdras and the like," for those who have realized their identity with Brahman through sentences such as "That thou art" abide in the very pinnacle of the Veda; having burnt away all [karmic] entitlements, they are no longer subject to prohibitive injunctions. Alternatively, knowledge certainly arises in a Śūdra or others from a statement uttered by someone who has transgressed prohibitions.

If it is argued that it is only when the latent impression of duality has been dispelled by *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) that sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) produce the liberating knowledge; [we reply: even a human-authored sentence would function in the same way for a *śūdra* and others, so there would be no distinction. Furthermore, regarding the injunction for *nididhyāsana*, its purpose is seen to be this: *nididhyāsana* indeed consists in the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of that sentence which expresses the identity of Brahman and the Self and is capable of conveying that meaning; it is this very cultivation that removes contrary impressions. Thus, the injunction for *nididhyāsana* serves a perceptible purpose.

Even practices such as the recitation of the Vedas serve only for the arising of the desire to know (vividiṣā). Thus, when the desire to know has arisen even in a Śūdra, and when contrary mental impressions have been dispelled through human-authored statements, meditative reflection (nididhyāsana), and so forth, knowledge will arise; by that very knowledge, bondage—which is not ultimately real—will cease.

By this very reasoning, since the knowledge of Brahman would be established for Brāhmaṇas and others as well, the poor Upaniṣad would be rendered one whose funeral libations have been offered—that is, it would be utterly useless.

Nor should it be said: "For one who is wandering in the natural, worldly transaction (*laukika-vyavahāra*), the inquiry into the operation of perception and inference arises only when someone has presented [the view] that 'this worldly transaction is an error; however, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is thus'; and therefore, even the scripture (*śruti*) presenting that [ultimate reality] must be accepted."

For this reason, it is the Sāṃkhyas and others alone who, being terrified by the fear of worldly existence, investigate reality through perception and inference, thereby generating a desire to understand the functioning of perception and inference. Once that desire has arisen, it becomes easy to discern—by means of those very same instruments of perception and inference whose natures have been clarified—that "only eternal, pure, self-luminous, non-dual, and immutable consciousness is real; everything else is superimposed upon it."

In such a self-luminous reality, no other specific attribute is admitted that is to be understood through scripture (*śruti*). For even scripture, in your view, merely serves to remove the superimposed forms [of duality].

Nor is it necessary to rely upon the Upaniṣads for the sake of knowing the blissful nature (*ānandarūpatā*) of the existent Self (*ātman*); for the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), which is distinguished from all other non-conscious things, is itself the blissful nature.

"By this very [means]" means: "The scripture is purposeful. Therefore, because its meaning is already established and because it generates the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*), the Śruti is not to be respected even by Brāhmaṇas and others; such is the meaning. "Tapasvinī" means pitiable. The sense is that she possesses numerous observances such as place, time, and vows.
The word "naisargika" (natural) refers to beginninglessness (*anāditva*). The meaning of the passage expressing the doubt is that the Śruti is required as the cause of [the misconception].
[This is] precisely by the Sāṃkhya, Hiraṇyagarbha, Naiyāyika, Vaiśeṣika, Bauddha, Ārhata, and others.

It refers to the Sāṅkhyas and others. However, for one who holds that the knowledge enjoined by the Vedāntic texts as a means to liberation is of the nature of *upāsanā* (meditative worship); and that this [worship] consists in pleasing the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman; and that this is to be understood solely through the scriptures; and that the scripture of *upāsanā*—beginning with the initiatory rite (*upanayana*) and so forth—accepts as its own means only that knowledge produced from the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) by one refined by the sacraments (*saṃskṛta*), which is further assisted by the means such as discrimination (*viveka*), dispassion (*vimoka*), and so on.

The position is this: the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is thus delighted by worship, "releases" the devotee from bondage by destroying the ignorance born of karma through the granting of knowledge regarding the true nature of His own essential self; according to the principle stated above, it follows that Śūdras and others lack the qualification for this. || 39 ||
Thus ends the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). 9.

2. Kṣatriyatva (the status of being a Kṣatriya), 3. Uttaratra (later on), 4. Saṃskāra (sacramental rites), 5. Tadabhāva (the absence thereof), 6. Śravaṇāt (from hearing), 7. Smṛteśca (and from Smṛti). Thus ends the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). || 9 ||

The remainder of the section concerning that which is measured by the thumb: Thus, having concluded the discussion on eligibility (*adhikāra*)—both the primary and the incidental—the author states another reason to support the status of the thumb-sized being as the Supreme Brahman, as understood from its lordship over the past and the future:
"Out of fear of Him the fire burns, out of fear the sun shines."
"Out of fear of him, Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run.

Thus, it is heard that there is a trembling—a shaking—of the entire world, including Agni, Sūrya, and others who abide within this person the size of a thumb (designated by the word "prāṇa"), as well as all those who have issued forth from him; this trembling is caused by the great fear arising from him. The meaning is that when his command is transgressed, the entire world trembles out of great fear, as if from a raised thunderbolt.
And for this reason as well: "The Supreme Person is measured by the size of a thumb, because of the vision of light. (1.3.41)

Between those two very sentences whose subject matter is measured by the thumb, the light of that which is measured by the thumb is seen as the unique attribute of the Supreme Brahman—the shrouder of all splendors, the cause of all splendors, and their sustainer—[as stated]:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire."

"Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. This very verse is heard in the Atharva Veda concerning the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, the quality of being the supreme light is attributed everywhere to the Supreme Brahman, as in such passages as:

"Having attained the highest light, he appears in his own form"; "The gods worship Him, the light of lights, as the immortal life"; and "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven," and so forth. Therefore, that which is measured by the thumb is the Supreme Brahman. 41.
Thus concludes the supplementary section on the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

*Anubhāna* means appearing subsequently. By this, the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established. The point is that the relationship of cause and effect is indeed a fixed order of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparyaniyama*). Regarding the term "supporting" (*anugrāhaka*): the scriptural passage, "By employing whose light the sun shines," and others, serve as the authority for its status as a supporter. *Jyotis* means radiance; this is because of its usage in such phrases as "possessing light, shining, and full of splendor. Regarding the phrase "in such cases": thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) has been stated as the reason based on the word (*śabda*).

The intention is that, by implication, the recognition of another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*) serves to establish that this mantra refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), passages such as "That bright light of lights" and "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light" are intended. (41)
"Being the cause" means that inference occurs subsequently. This concludes the section concerning the designation of [the probans] as being a different object and so forth (1.3.10).
[The meaning of the section: Ākāśa is the bearer of name and form; it is the Supreme Self. 107.
Ākāśa [is Brahman], because of its designation as being different from other things and so forth. (1.3.42)
It is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Verily, that which is called space is the revealer of name and form; that within which they are, that is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self."
Thus [it is said].
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the one indicated by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) here the liberated self (*muktātman*), or is it the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)?

Thus [the inquiry begins]. Previously, while establishing that the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is the Supreme Brahman, the objection regarding its being described as "small" was refuted by the Sūtra, "On account of the mention of smallness. In connection with that mention of smallness, the supremacy of the one measured by the thumb was established. In connection with that, three topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) were discussed.

Now, the connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the doubt that the section beginning with "Space, verily" (*ākāśo ha vai*), which immediately follows the previously discussed Dahara-vidyā because it remains present in the mind, might have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its subject matter, that doubt is now refuted.

Regarding the doubt: Is that which is designated by the word "ether" (ākāśa) the liberated soul (mukta), or is it the Supreme Self (paramātman)? For that purpose, the question arises: Does the phrase "having shaken off the body," along with the fact that the liberated soul is the subject immediately preceding [the mention of ether], lead us to understand that the word "ether" refers to the liberated soul? Or does it not? Furthermore, is it possible for the liberated soul to be the "conductor" (nirvodṛ) of names and forms? Or is it not? And in this context, does being the conductor of names and forms mean by way of possessing names and forms, or by way of being the agent of the manifestation (vyākarta) of names and forms?
Does the designation "that which is within" establish the status of the space as an agent or a fulfiller? Or not?
For the space that is the fulfiller of name and form is indeed the Supreme Lord.
Because it is proclaimed as being distinct from both the bound and the liberated states.
What is correct? That the self is liberated.
Why?
"Having shaken off evil as a horse shakes off its hair, and having freed himself from the mouth of Rāhu like the moon."

"Having shaken off the body, being self-perfected, may I attain the uncreated world of Brahman"—because this refers to the liberated one who has been immediately introduced [in the preceding passage]. Furthermore, by the phrase "that which is between them," there is the designation of that very one as being "freed from name and form. And by the phrase "the guide of name and form," it is he alone who is intended to be characterized by his previous state; for it was he alone who previously manifested the names and forms such as those of the gods.

Its very state, when liberated from name and form and not pertaining to the present time, is called "that Brahman, that Immortal. And the word "ether" (ākāśa) is also applicable to that [Brahman], because of its association with uncontracted luminosity.

[Objection: "But surely," because this [passage] is a supplement to the *dahara* (small) section, it is understood that this very one is the *daharākāśa*; and its status as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) has been determined. [Reply: "Not so," because of the intervention of the *prajāpati* section. In the *prajāpati* section, the form of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) up to the state of liberation is described. Immediately thereafter, with the words "having shaken off evil," that same self in the state of liberation is introduced. Therefore, the "ether" (*ākāśa*) here is the liberated self.
This being the position, it is said: "But the ether [is Brahman], because of the designation of what is different from it.
The ether is the supreme Brahman. Why?

"Because of the designation of being something other [than that], etc. First, there is the designation of being "something other": the statement, "Ākāśa, indeed, is the bearer of name and form," establishes that Ākāśa is distinct from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in its states as bound, liberated, or both. The one in a bound state, undergoing name and form "by the power of karma," would not be able to bear name and form. Since the one in a liberated state lacks the capacity for the activity of the world, it is said, "certainly not name and form [in relation to him]."

The status of being the one who effects differentiation [of name and form] belongs to the Lord alone. For it is established by the Śruti itself that the Lord—who is the bearer of the burden of creating the entire universe—is the differentiator of names and forms: "Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"; and, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him is born this Brahman, as well as name, form, and food."

"In the passages such as, 'The Wise One, having discerned all forms and having created names, abides calling them forth,' [it is shown that] this Ākāśa is the one who brings about (nirvoḍhā) name and form from the inner self (pratyagātman), which is itself devoid of name and form; thus, a designation [is given]. The word "is demonstrated" (*pradarśyate*) is to be supplied. The term "being a different entity" (*arthāntaratva*) indicates the property that establishes that difference. For it was stated that [the text] "establishes the Ākāśa as being a different entity. The meaning is: "because of the designation of distinguishing properties. The phrase "of name and form," etc., follows; and being the bringer-about of name and form is a clear distinguishing property.

Since the word *nirvoḍhṛ* (conveyor) by its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) refers merely to the act of conveying, it is more appropriate for it to refer to the agent according to the maxim "conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) sets aside etymological meaning (*yoga*").

Thus, it is the Supreme Brahman that is a distinct entity. He establishes this very point with the words, "That which is between them. Since this [Brahman] called "space" is "between name and form"—meaning it is untouched by them and is a distinct entity—therefore, because it is free from evil (*apahata-pāpmatva*) and possesses true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), it is their "conveyor"; the meaning is that it is the one who brings them forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), its being Brahman, its being the Self (*ātmatva*), and its being immortal are included.

For attributes such as being "great" (*bṛhat*) without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) belong to the Supreme Self alone. Therefore, the "ether" (*ākāśa*) mentioned here is the Supreme Brahman itself. As for what was said—that because of the phrase "having shaken off the body," the liberated one who is the immediate subject [of the context] is intended—that is not so; for in the statement "I shall attain the world of Brahman" (*brahmalokam abhisambhavāni*), it is the Supreme Brahman that is the immediate subject. Even though, by virtue of being the goal to be attained by the liberated one who attains it, the "Supreme Brahman" is indicated [as the object]; [it remains the Supreme Brahman].
Nevertheless, since it is impossible for one who has attained liberation to carry on name-and-form, that which is to be reached must be understood there as the Supreme Brahman alone.

Furthermore, because the "ether" (*ākāśa*) mentioned here is recognized as the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) under discussion, and because the speech of Prajāpati is intended to describe the nature of the worshiper, it is logical that the small ether itself—the object of worship—is concluded as that which is to be attained. Moreover, the word "ether" has never been seen used for the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Therefore, the ether here is the Supreme Brahman. (42)

He establishes that very point with the words, "That which is between them... Because they lack the state of being subject to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) produced by karma, the Supreme Self is the one who brings them forth by His own will. The meaning is that neither the bound soul (*baddha*), whose activity is dependent on karma, nor the liberated soul (*mukta*), who lacks the volitions and other faculties necessary for the governance of the world, can possibly be the bringer-forth of name-and-form. The term *nirvahitā* is an imitation of the word found in the Śruti. The word "unconditioned" (*nirupādhika*) refers to that which is unlimited; for a condition (*upādhi*) is indeed a limiting factor.

The greatness of the individual soul (*jīva*) arises from knowledge, and that [greatness] depends upon the grace of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Regarding the phrase "greatness and so forth," the word "attributes" (*dharmāḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "The world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) means that Brahman itself is the world. Although it might be thought that—despite the natural force of the context where the subject to be attained, mentioned in the nominative case, is primary—the disruption of that contextual naturalness is justified by the power of the indicative marks (*liṅga*); such is the intended meaning.

As for the phrase "And what is space?": this was refuted by accepting, on the basis of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), that the preceding passage has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its subject matter. In reality, however, by the force of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) supported by the scriptural mention of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), even the preceding passage does not have the individual soul as its subject; rather, the intention is that it has as its subject the Supreme Brahman, which is the ultimate goal to be attained. Regarding the phrase "of the Prajāpati passage": this is intended to dispel the doubt that the Prajāpati passage acts as an interruption. He states another reason with the words beginning with "space."

[Objection: Even so—though it may be argued that there is no other self (ātmāntara) distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman), because of the teaching of identity and the prohibition of duality; and because it is precisely the pure state of the inner self that is designated as the "Supreme Self," "Supreme Brahman," and "Supreme Lord"; therefore, the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) to be attained by the liberated soul under discussion cannot be a different entity; and thus even the ether (ākāśa), which is the sustainer of name and form, must be that very same [inner self]. The objection continues: Although there is no other self distinct from the inner self, due to the instruction on non-duality and the negation of duality—it being the case that the inner self in its pure state alone is designated as the "Supreme Self," "Supreme Brahman," and "Supreme Lord"—therefore, the world of Brahman to be reached by the liberated soul under discussion cannot be a separate entity.
Consequently, even the ether, which is the sustainer of names and forms, ought to be that very same [inner self].
To this, the following [sūtra] is recited: 108. "On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure. (1.3.43)

The phrase "because of designation" (vyapadeśāt) follows. Because the Supreme Self is designated as distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman) during deep sleep and departure [from the body], there certainly exists a Supreme Self that is a different entity from the inner self. For instance, in the Vājasaneyaka:

"It does not exist" means that it is not established by firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Because of the teaching of identity" means that because of the presentation of identity with the individual soul (*jīva*), as taught in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* through such passages as "It should be viewed as one alone," and "This indeed is the great unborn Self, which consists of consciousness"—referring to that which was described as the goal to be attained by the liberated and recognized by the term "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*). "And because of the negation of duality" [is also a reason].

The meaning is: "And because of the negation of difference in the statement, 'There is no diversity whatsoever here. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction, since both the teaching of unity and the negation of difference are individually opposed to difference. Regarding the phrase "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*): for there, at the conclusion of that section, the designation "world of Brahman" is understood to refer to that Supreme Self, as in the passage, "'This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman,' he said. The phrase "by name... [the veins] called Hitā" is a restatement according to the scriptural text.

For this very reason, it is stated in his own work: "He is the one who brings about name and form. The meaning of the passage expressing doubt is that even though another interpretation may appear at first glance, it should not be accepted as the final conclusion.

The phrase "it continues from [the previous rule]" applies here. Just as in the case of "Now, the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*), when it is asked "Of which words?", the term "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) from the entire preceding compound is connected through distribution; such is the sense here as well. In the sūtra, the locative case is used in "during deep sleep and departure" (*suṣuptyutkrāntyoḥ*). Regarding the phrase "as something having a different meaning": this refers to the designation of this sūtra as having a distinct meaning.

"He who is embraced by the Wise (prājña) is described as distinct during deep sleep; and likewise, during departure [from the body], the Supreme Person is other than the individual soul (jīva). "Indeed, [it is] the inner Self of all beings"—thus [it is said]. "Which is the Self? It is this one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) among the vital breaths (prāṇas)."

Thus, for this very subject under discussion—the inner self (pratyagātman)—which is "knowing nothing" during the state of deep sleep, its embrace by the omniscient Supreme Self (paramātman) is recorded in scripture:

"Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña), it knows nothing external, nor does it know anything internal. Likewise, even at the time of departure, [it is said]: "Mounted by the conscious Self, it goes forth, uttering [the sound] 'ha'."

Thus, it is not possible for one who is sleeping or departing—being at that very time someone who knows nothing—to enter into an embrace with or ascend to union with the Self which is itself omniscient; nor can this be with another *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field), because for that [other knower] as well, omniscience is impossible. || 43 ||
For this reason as well—the Supreme Self is an entity distinct from the inner self—it is said:
109. On account of the words "Lord" and so forth (Sūtra 1.3.44).
This Supreme Self is the embracer; He is designated later by such terms as "Lord" (pati) and so forth—as in the passage: "the Lord of all."

Because it is intended to dispel the doubt regarding the non-establishment of the cause of form (*rūpa*), it shows the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) as established by the sense of the context. There is no explicit mention in the Sūtra because it is a proposition concerning a subordinate matter; for an explicit statement is generally found only for a proposition concerning the primary matter. [The phrase] "of the consciousness... refers to that which is under discussion, namely, for the purpose of removing the doubt that the body is embraced by the *prājña* (the conscious self). [The word] "emitting" (*utsarjan*)—the word "body" (*śarīra*) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 43 ||
Regarding the phrase "from here," it is said that [the soul] ascends by means of the mind in its state of liberation. Furthermore,
because of designations such as "the Lord of all" and so forth,
it is firmly established that this Supreme Self is the Intelligent One (Prājña) and is distinct from the individual soul (jīva).

By its very nature— of that one who knows something (*kiñcijjña*), or of him who knows nothing at all (*akiñcijjña*)— [he is] by his own self, the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*); thus it is stated in the *Śrībhāṣya* (1.3.10).

"He is the controller of all, the lord of all; he does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action. He is the lord of all, he is the sovereign of beings, he is the protector of beings, he is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded. The Brāhmaṇas seek to know him through the study and recitation of the Vedas... Only by knowing him does one become a sage (muni).
Desiring this world, those who have renounced the world go forth as wanderers. "He indeed is the great Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth, ageless, immortal, fearless, Brahman."
Thus [it is said].
That this is established by such statements has already been demonstrated; and since the negation of duality follows from that very same source, there is no fault. || 44 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of being something else (*arthāntaratva*) and so forth. 10.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

For that very reason—from the identity of cause and effect and so forth—the meaning is as follows: because it is supplementary to the teaching of identity, the scriptural texts prohibiting difference are intended to negate the distinction between cause and effect established by fallacious reasoning. Here, the fact that the prohibition of difference is based on the identity of the modes (*prakāra*) and the possessor of modes (*prākārī*) is established by implication; for the relationship of mode and possessor of modes is what makes possible the status of the world as the effect of its cause. In this regard, the establishment of the identity of cause and effect is scripturally supported in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.

Therefore, the primacy of the teaching of identity is established by implication. That grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based on the relationship between the body and the embodied will be stated [in the Sūtra]: "Because of the abiding [of the world in Brahman], [Brahman is the cause], according to Kāśakṛtsna" (BS 1.4.22). In that context, the demonstration of primacy—pertaining both to the conscious subject and the non-conscious object—by way of being within the scope of the principle of generic form (*ākṛti-naya*), was accomplished through two sections: "Because of the designation of manifoldness, [the soul] is a part" (BS 2.3.42) and "Because of the designation of both" (BS 2.3.27). Thus, the manner of establishing primacy as it will be explained later is recalled here. This is faultless, with reference to the meaning stated in the two preceding quarters. || 44 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of being a different object and so forth. 10.

28. Section on the Inferential (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa) 1–7: That which is denoted by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad is not the Pradhāna as described by the Sāṃkhya school based on inference;
rather, it is the body alone.
8–10: That which is described in the Śruti as "the one unborn" (ajāmekām) is not the Prakṛti devoid of Brahman as taught by the Sāṃkhya;
rather, it is precisely the Prakṛti whose essence is Brahman as taught in the Śruti.

11–13: The "five groups of five" (pañca pañcajanāḥ) mentioned in the Śruti passage "in whom the five groups of five [dwell]" are simply the five sense organs resting in Brahman, and not the twenty-five principles (tattvas) taught by the Sāṃkhya.
