28. The Section Concerning Those Who Rely on Inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa) ||1.4.1||
110. "If it be argued that for some [the soul] is also inferential, we say no, because [the text] shows that it is grasped as presented through the metaphor of the body. (1.4.1)

It has been stated that Brahman—the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe—is the object of inquiry because it is the means for attaining liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal; [this was established] by the first quarter [of the first chapter], which excludes the possibility that such causality belongs to anything other than the one distinct from both the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit). Regarding the connection between the quarters (*pādas*), as stated at the beginning of the second quarter: "The second and third quarters have as their subject matter those scriptural passages containing indistinct or distinct marks (*liṅgas*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and others, respectively, while the fourth quarter has as its subject matter those passages that establish the individual soul and others with even greater clarity. This constitutes the structural coherence of the quarters.

The author of the Sūtras, however, explicitly stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter that the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) constitutes the subject matter of the first three chapters; for he said, "Some [hold it] to be inferential as well.

Therefore, at the beginning of the fourth chapter, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), wishing to state the connection by way of clarifying the meaning of the three preceding chapters, first restates the meaning of the first chapter and then shows the contents of the second and third, saying: "It has been stated... and so forth.

It is distinct from acid substances such as primordial matter (pradhāna) and from sentient beings in their bound, liberated, or both states; it is free from the scent of all that is to be discarded, omniscient, omnipotent, possessed of true resolve, composed of all auspicious qualities, the inner self of all, and characterized by unimpeded sovereignty.

Now, having raised the objection that there exist in certain Vedic branches some statements—which, while following the shadow of establishing the Pradhāna as the cause, propound through the medium of the Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and so forth, which are established in the Sāṃkhya system as being non-Brahmanic—that this [Pradhāna] is the cause, [the author] refutes it in order to firmly establish that Brahman alone is the sole cause.
The Kaṭhavallī declares:
"Higher than the senses are the objects;
higher than the objects is the mind (manas); higher than the mind is the intellect (buddhi); and higher than the intellect is the Great Self (mahān ātmā)."
"Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.
Thus [it is said].
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the *pradhāna* established in the Sāṅkhya system—which is non-Brahmanic in nature—designated here by the word "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), or not?

By the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the phrase "pradhānādeḥ," the inclusion of *prāṇa*, *ākāśa*, and others is intended. The meaning of the first quarter [of the verse] is stated up to the word "vilakṣaṇam" (distinct). By the words beginning with "nirasta" (cast aside), he shows the meaning of the second and third quarters as well. Furthermore, the distinction [of Brahman] consists in its possessing both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatayā*). By the word "samasta" (all), what is to be abandoned—both that which resides in consciousness (*cidgata*) and that which resides in the non-conscious (*acidgata*)—is intended. By the word "gandha" (fragrance), the exclusion of the liberated soul (*mukta*) is indicated. The meaning of the second quarter, "omniscient and omnipotent" (*sarvajña sarvaśakti*), is thus suggested. [The phrase continues: "samasta..."

The term "consisting of [the three qualities]" (*ātmakam*) refers to the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*). "Unrestrained sovereignty" indicates the meaning of the third quarter [of the verse].

Regarding "being the primary cause": these [scriptural passages] do not merely establish the inferential marks (*liṅga*); rather, they serve as grounds for the suspicion that the very subjects of those marks—Pradhāna and the others—are the causes of the world. Therefore, the sense is that their application to the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth is even more evident. By the word "one" (*eka*) in "Brahma-eka," it is indicated that the three quarters [of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*] are intended to exclude any other connection [to the subject matter]. By the word "stability" (*sthairye*), the meaning of the fourth quarter is indicated.

The stability of the exclusion of other possibilities (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) established in the first two quarters [of the verse] occurs precisely when, in this quarter, the refutation of Pradhāna and other such causes has been accomplished.

[The author] explains: The subject matter consists of those statements which, according to the established tenets of the Tantra, produce the appearance of a sequence of recognition. Doubt arises from the cognition of both the sequence established in the Tantra and its opposite.
Regarding that doubt: Is there in the Kaṭhavallī the apprehension of the Pradhāna as the cause, which is not of the nature of Brahman? Or is there not? What is reasonable? [That it is] the Pradhāna.
Why?

Because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the "systematic process established in the *Tantra*," namely: "The Unmanifest is beyond the Great One; the Puruṣa is beyond the Unmanifest"; for it is that very [process] which is perceived.
And: "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal."

This is because of the negation of that which is distinct from the twenty-five principles, as stated in the *Puruṣasūkta*. Therefore, it follows that "the Unmanifest is the cause. Regarding this, it has been said: "If it be argued that for some, the cause is inferential"—that is, if it be argued that in the branches of certain reciters (*śākhins*), the Pradhāna, which is established through inference, is also traditionally taught as the cause—[we reply: "To this, the answer is: No. It is not the case that by the word "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) here the Pradhāna, which is non-Brahman in nature, is denoted.

"Why?"—this is intended as the first inquiry. For that purpose, there is an investigation into whether the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) in the phrase "higher than the senses" refers to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) which is not of the nature of Brahman, or not. Is there a recognition of the sequence in the enumeration of the principles (*tattva*)? Or not? Are these two terms indicated in the *Jīvatantre* [as referring to] the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), or do they refer to the individual soul and the Supreme Self (*para*)?

Is there here, by means of words such as "senses" (*indriya*) and so forth, a comprehension of the senses and other faculties as they were metaphorically represented in the preceding sentence? Or is there not? In this context, does "supremacy" (*paratva*) consist in being the cause, or in being that which is to be brought under control? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: when [supremacy] consists in being the cause, then—due to the absence of a comprehension of the metaphorically represented senses and so forth, and because the two words [“senses” and “objects”] convey the principle of the individual soul (*jīva-tattva*) in its primordial state, thereby identifying it with the Tantric methodology—it is stated that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which is non-Brahman in nature, is being described; thus, it is understood that its very status is that of the cause.
For that purpose, what [is intended] in this mantra? Regarding that purpose established by the Tantra— the "Mahat-puruṣa" mentioned previously and subsequently—
[the term] "Mahat-puruṣa"—

By the word "avyakta" (the unmanifest), according to our own established doctrine (siddhānta): when supremacy is intended in the sense of being that which is to be brought under control, then—since there is no recognition of the system established in the Tantras through the understanding of the senses and so forth as having their previous forms—the terms "mahat" and "puruṣa" refer respectively to the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). Consequently, the word "avyakta" does not refer to the Pradhāna (primordial matter) which is non-Brahman in nature; thus, there is no perception of its causality here. This is the relationship between the means and the end (phala-phalibhāva).

"Because of the apprehension of that which was set forth as a metaphor for the body"—that is to say, because the body, which was set forth as a metaphor (*rūpaka*) designated by the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), is apprehended here by the word "Unmanifest. This means that among the self, body, intellect, mind, senses, and objects—which have been metaphorically represented as the charioteer, the chariot, and so forth—the body, which was set forth by way of the metaphor of a chariot, is what is grasped here by the word "Unmanifest.

This is what is intended: previously, indeed, it was stated: "Know the Self as the rider, and the body as the chariot; know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3–4)
"The senses they call the horses, and the objects of the senses their paths," and so forth,
up to: "He reaches the end of the journey, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."

By this much [of the passage], having described the seeker who desires to reach the state of Viṣṇu—the further shore of the path of saṃsāra—as the chariot-driver, and having metaphorically represented "his body and so forth" as the chariot and its parts, it is stated that "he alone whose chariot and so forth remain under his control reaches the further shore, the state of Viṣṇu. Then, among those things metaphorically represented as the chariot and so forth—namely the body and the rest—those which are primary in terms of being objects to be brought under control are declared by the verse beginning with, "Higher than the senses... and so on.

In this context, the objects, which are represented as the "pastures," are subordinate to the senses, which are represented as the "horses," because even for one who has mastered the senses, the senses remain difficult to restrain when they are in proximity to their objects. Even more superior to those is the mind, which is represented as the "reins"; for when the mind is inclined toward sense-objects, the absence of those objects is of no avail.

For this reason also, the intellect (*buddhi*), represented as the charioteer, is superior; for in the absence of determination (*adhyavasāya*), even the mind (*manas*) would be ineffective. Of that [intellect] as well, the Self (*ātman*), represented as the rider, is superior due to its primacy as the agent. And because all of this is dependent upon the will of the Self, the Self alone is distinguished as "the Great" (*mahān*). For this reason also, the body, represented as the chariot, is superior; for the activities of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) toward the accomplishment of all human goals are dependent upon it.

Therefore, even beyond that is the Supreme, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) who has become the inner self of all, the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who constitutes the further shore of the path; for everything mentioned above, culminating in the individual self, proceeds in dependence upon His will. Indeed, He is the one who brings about even the meditation performed as the Inner Controller. For it will be stated [in the Sūtras]: "But from the Supreme [comes the agency], because of the scriptural statement of that" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.40), and "The agency of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is dependent upon the Supreme Person. He alone is the ultimate means for the accomplishment of the meditation on the one to be brought under control, and He is the supreme goal to be attained. This is what is being said:
"There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal.
Likewise, in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa, after stating "He who dwells in the self" and so forth, it says, "Perceiving everything, He governs everything."

By the statement, "There is no other seer but this," any other controller is negated. And in the Bhagavad Gītā: "The locus, as well as the agent, the various kinds of instruments, the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny as the fifth [are the causes]."

Thus [it is said]. Here, "destiny" (*daiva*) is none other than Puruṣottama himself, according to the scriptural statement: "And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal. And the means of bringing Him under control is solely taking refuge in Him, as it is said: "The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna."
Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of Māyā.
"Go to Him alone for refuge!

It is thus determined that [the Supreme Lord] is denoted by the word "Unmanifest. Therefore, there is no possibility whatsoever of the "Pradhāna," which is established in the Tantras, being mentioned here.

Nor is there here a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the established procedure belonging to that [Tantric] system; for it is stated that "the objects are higher than the senses" (*indriyebhyaḥ parā hyarthāḥ*), thereby proclaiming the superiority of the objects—sound and so forth—over the senses. Indeed, sound and the rest are not seen to be the causes of the senses in that [system].

Furthermore, the statement "the mind is superior to the objects" is also not consistent with that [theory], precisely because [the mind] is not its cause. Likewise, the statement "the Great Self is superior to the intellect" is also inconsistent; for it is accepted that the word "intellect" (*buddhi*) denotes the *mahat-tattva*. Indeed, it is not possible for the Great to be superior to the Great. Moreover, the qualification of the Great by the word "Self" is not tenable. Therefore, there must be a reference to those very things presented as metaphors.
And he shows that very point: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."
"But it is seen by subtle seers with a refined and subtle intellect. "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self of knowledge (*jñāna*);

he should restrain the knowledge in the Great Self (*mahat-ātman*); and he should restrain that in the Peaceful Self (*śānta-ātman*). Having thus described the difficulty of perceiving this Supreme Person for those whose external and internal organs are unsubdued, the following method for bringing under control the senses and so forth—which have been compared to horses and other animals—is stated:

"One should restrain speech and mind"—one should restrain speech within the mind; [this implies] that the organs of action, which are preceded by speech, are to be withdrawn from their engagement in ritual worship. But how can that which is superior to everything be brought under control by a non-omniscient transmigrating being? If it were possible, the manner of doing so would be heard of somewhere in scripture, yet it is not so heard; for in passages such as "the wise one should restrain speech and mind," no such method is found. Thus it stands.

"Because of being causeless alone. This means that in the passage "The objects are indeed higher than the senses," the method of the *tantra* (system) is for the purpose of excluding the recognition [of the self in the object]. Regarding "than the Great One" (*mahataḥ*) and so forth: the word "self" (*ātman*) is exclusively restricted to consciousness by its very nature; only as a last resort is it accepted as not having that [consciousness] as its primary referent in certain instances.

Even though the term [mahat] is directed toward its own function through the power of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*), since the excellence of the meaning of the parts resides in *pradhāna* even more than in *mahat-tattva*, it is improper for the word "Self" (*ātman*) to be the qualifier of *mahat*. This is the meaning. The apprehension of only those things established as metaphors (*rūpaka-vinyasta*)—this fear is what is meant by the phrase "this is what is said," which connects with the preceding. The non-use of the word "iti" is due to extreme distance. And "he shows" refers to the citation of a portion of the Sūtra. That very [portion] is the supremacy by virtue of being subject to control (*vaśīkāryatva*).

"Of speech"—or rather, because the principle of *mahat* (the Great One) is accepted; the meaning is that one should restrain the organs of knowledge within the mind. In the word "speech" (*vāk*), the second case ending [is used] according to the rule *supāṃ su-luk*.
Thus [there is] elision (*luk*). In the word "manasi," there is a Vedic lengthening of the vowel in the locative case.

"Tadyacchet jñāna ātmani": one should restrain that—namely, the mind—in the intellect (*buddhi*). By the word "jñāna" here, the previously mentioned intellect is denoted. In the expressions "jñāne" and "ātmani," the two locatives are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: one should restrain [the mind] in the intellect which resides in the Self (*ātman*).

"One should restrain the intellect within the Great Self"—one should restrain the intellect within the Great Self, which is the agent. "One should restrain that within the Peaceful Self"—one should restrain that agent within the Supreme Brahman, the inner controller of all. The neuter gender of the word "tat" (that) is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*). The meaning is that the destination of Viṣṇu is to be reached by such a person who is the rider of the chariot. || 1 ||

How can the word *avyakta* (unmanifest) denote the manifest body? To this he says: "He should restrain" (*yacchet*). [The division of words is: *vāk* and *manasī*. "Preceded by speech" (*vāk-pūrvakāṇi*): the word "speech" (*vāk*) is intended as an indicator for all the sense organs. The designation "in the mind" (*manasī*) is based on the rule for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) stated in the rule: "And *ī* and *ū* [are preserved] when they stand in the locative case."

Regarding the phrase "by the word *jñāna*," the intention is that it is unnatural for the term to refer to the *ahaṅkāra*, whereas its reference to the *buddhi* is natural—this is the general view. The aforementioned *buddhi* is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding what is to be rejected or accepted with respect to the non-self as being the self. The sense is that a word denoting knowledge in general primarily denotes a specific kind of knowledge. [The commentary notes: "The two locative endings are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*)."

The sense is that since the word *ātman* inherently denotes exclusively consciousness, and because it is natural for the word *ātman* in the immediately following sentence and this one to have the same meaning, the naturalness of mere grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone should be disregarded. The present tense verb has been supplied (*adhyāhṛta*) in order to clarify the sense of the locative case.

"Buddhi" (intellect): the restraint of speech within the mind—this means bringing about an aversion to activity that is not conducive to the mind. "Restraint of the mind within the intellect"—this means bringing about activity that is conducive to determination (*adhyavasāya*). "Intellect" is that which consists of the determination of objects as things to be abandoned. "Restraint of that intellect within the Self" means bringing about the state of having the Self as its object, in the sense that "He alone is to be realized as that which is to be accepted. "In the Tranquil One" (*śānte*)—meaning in that which is naturally opposed to the six waves [of mental fluctuations].

In the peaceful Self, the "subjugation" (niyamana) of the Great Self—that is, the individual soul (jīva)—consists in the realization of its being subordinate to Him. That very state also constitutes the mastery over the Supreme. Regarding the term "vyatyayena" (by way of transposition): as stated by the grammarians, "The author of the grammar intends a transposition of case endings, verbal suffixes, prefixes, gender, number, tense, consonants, vowels, agent, and the *yaṅ* affix; and that [transposition] is established by means of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Thus, by this transposition of gender, the word "tat" (that) takes a neuter gender. ||1||

Regarding the phrase "it says there," the intention is as follows: since it is certain that the terms *śarīra* (body) and *avyakta* (unmanifest) must have a single referent by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the term *avyakta* must be interpreted in accordance with the term *śarīra* occurring in the opening statement, according to the rule of the section on the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*). Thus, in response to the inquiry, "In what sense does the word *avyakta* function here? he says [the following].
111. But that [mind] is subtle because of its fitness [for such a state]. (1.4.2)

Indeed, the subtle element (bhūtasūkṣma), which is the unmanifest (avyākṛta), becomes the body when it has attained a particular state. That unmanifest, existing here in the state of the body, is denoted by the word ‘unmanifest’ (avyakta). This is because of its fitness—that very non-sentient entity (acidvastu), having undergone modification, is fit for activity as a means to achieve the goals of the person (puruṣārtha), like a chariot.

If the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is accepted as being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), what is the objection to accepting the material cause established in the Sāṃkhya system? For even there, that which is the cause of the elements is called the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*). To this, he says: 112. *Tadadhīnatvādarthavat* (Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful). [Sūtra 1.4.3]

Because it is dependent upon the Supreme Person, who is the ultimate cause, [the subtle element] possesses a purpose; thus, it is the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*). Regarding the word "bhūta" (element): due to the relationship characterized by the identity of substance, the term for the cause is applied metaphorically to the effect. Regarding the phrase "tadarhatvāt" (because of its fitness for that): the word *tat* from the Sūtra is to be explained as *tasya* (of that), which has been indicated here. "Subtlety" is presented by its own specific term. The body is in a gross state and is present in the intellect (*buddhi*) as the object of the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Therefore, the sense is that there is a reference to such a non-conscious substance (*acid-dravya*). [The text continues with] *aci...*

Regarding the term "of the wise" (*pannasya*): even for the conscious reality (*cidvastu*), there occurs a modification consisting of the contraction and expansion of knowledge. To exclude that [consciousness], this was stated:

"it is indeed the cause of the elements. The sense is: it is precisely that which you yourself have accepted as the cause of the elements. For that very same unmanifest (*avyakta*), while abiding in the body, is indeed the source of activity.
Therefore, the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) does not refer to the Pradhāna here.

The description of [the body] as a chariot and so forth, by virtue of its dependence on the Supreme Self, serves a purpose; however, the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) of the Tantric systems has no such role here.

This is what is meant: "We do not deny the unmanifest (avyakta) and its specific transformations in their own right; rather, we deny them as being the body of the Supreme Person, that is, insofar as they lack identity with Him. For it is precisely through identity with Him that primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest accomplish their own purposes. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between their essential nature, their subsistence, and their activity. Thus, by our very non-acceptance [of their independence], the system established in the Tantras is refuted."

For in the Śruti and Smṛti, within the doctrines concerning the origin and dissolution of the world and the majesty of the Supreme Person, Prakṛti, Vikṛti, and Puruṣa are proclaimed as being of His nature; as for example, beginning with the passage:
"The earth dissolves into water," and so forth.

"The subtle elements (tanmātras) dissolve into the source of the elements (bhūtādi); the source of the elements dissolves into the Great One (mahat); the Great One dissolves into the Unmanifest (avyakta); the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (akṣara); the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness (tamas); and Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. Likewise:
"He whose body is the earth, whose body is the waters..."
"He whose body is fire...

whose body is air... whose body is space... whose body is the ego-sense... whose body is the intellect... whose body is the unmanifest... whose body is the imperishable... whose body is death—He is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa."
Likewise:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect alone..."

"This nature of mine, called egoism (ahaṅkāra), is divided eightfold. "But know that there is another, higher nature of mine, distinct from this, which is the life-force (jīvabhūta), O mighty-armed one, by which this world is sustained. "Understand that all beings have these as their source; I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe. "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya."
"All this is strung upon me, like clusters of gems on a thread," and,
"The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and Time itself— these are Viṣṇu."
Thus:
"The Prakṛti which I have described, whose nature consists of the manifest and the unmanifest,
and the Puruṣa as well— these two dissolve into the Supreme Self."
"And the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, is the support of all. Thus it is said. (3)
113. And because [the Lord] is not mentioned as being an object of knowledge. (1.4.4)
If the unmanifest established in the Tantras were intended here, then its status as an object of knowledge would have been stated;

since it is not taught here as an object of knowledge, the Pradhāna is not what is being spoken of. For their doctrine is that [liberation comes] from the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower.

The Tantrikas, who assert that liberation results from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower, accept all of these as objects of knowledge; however, this [Self] is not said to be an object of knowledge. Therefore, what is established in the Tantras is not included here. ||4||

114. "If it be argued that [the text] speaks [of the Unmanifest], we say no, for the wise one [is meant], according to the context. (1.4.5) If it is argued that the knowability of the Unmanifest is stated immediately thereafter in this scriptural passage: "Having perceived Him—who is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless; who is without beginning or end, beyond the Great, and fixed—one is liberated from the jaws of death," then [we reply as follows].
"That is not so"; for it is the Prājña, the Supreme Person himself,
who is presented here in this verse as the one to be perceived.

"The man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the journey—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. And: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; it is seen by subtle seers through their own subtle intellect. Since it is the *prājña* (the conscious one) alone that is under discussion here, the statement "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa" is not a denial of any principle distinct from the twenty-fifth *puruṣa*. Furthermore, the attributes of that Supreme Puruṣa, such as being "beyond sound" (*aśabda*), and so forth, [are established].

"That which is unseen, ungraspable" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15) is a statement from the Sāṃkhya treatise itself that has been incorporated into its own text [in the Bhagavad Gītā]. This refers to the fact that the unmanifest (avyakta) is an object of knowledge. The sense is that since it is logical for the negations of qualities belonging to the manifest—such as sound and so forth—to culminate in the unmanifest, and because of the statement regarding what is "higher than the Great One" (mahat), the cause indicated by the general terms "that which" and "it" is the unmanifest. || 4 ||

Regarding the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ": by this, the fact that the Prājña, who is the object of knowledge, is the subject under discussion as the Supreme Person is shown through the word "Viṣṇu," which is unique to Him.

By the word "is seen" (dṛśyate), the Śruti speaks of that same object of knowledge—described previously in the scripture as "having perceived" (nicāyya)—as being beyond sound and touch, thus identifying it with the Prājña.
If this is argued, it is not so; for, according to the context, it is indeed the Supreme Self that is being described.

115. "And thus there is the presentation and the question regarding these three alone" (Sūtra 1.4.6). For in this context, there is indeed such a presentation—namely, a presentation as objects of knowledge—of only these three: the means, the goal, and the agent; and a question concerning them is likewise observed, but not of anything else, such as the Unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth.

For instance: Naciketas, being desirous of liberation, having obtained through the first of the three boons granted by Death his father’s goodwill—which brings about the soul's fitness for the goals of human existence—obtained through the second boon the knowledge of the Naciketas fire, which is the means to liberation, [saying]:
"O Death, you yourself have taught me; tell it to me, who am full of faith."

"They partake of the heavenly world and immortality; this I choose as my second boon. Here, by the word "heaven" (svarga), liberation—characterized as the supreme human goal—is denoted; by "they partake of immortality," its relevance to the present context is demonstrated. By the word "great" (maha), there is a reference to the Self (ātman), due to the intention to express a preeminence characterized by being accompanied by the retinue of the senses and so forth. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the three": the first word *ca* (and) is used for the conjunction of reasons; the second word *ca* is for the conjunction of the question and the presentation [of the answer]. That [Prakṛti], which has Brahman as its cause, is indeed unborn and presided over by the Light;
for the followers of the Taittirīya recension study the text: "Subtler than the subtle."

No. [This is] because of the well-known Vedic statement: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven... The phrase "having light as its beginning" (jyotir-upakramā) means having Brahman as its cause. For it is so taught by some. The word "hi" indicates a reason; because this Unborn (ajā) has Brahman as its cause, some followers of the Vedic branches—the Taittirīyas—so teach.

Having declared that Brahman is present within the cave of the heart as the object of meditation— stating, "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the cave of this creature"—

and having described the origin of all the worlds and of Brahmā and the others from that [Brahman] through the passage beginning with, "From Him the seven vital breaths arise," the unborn one who is the cause of all is said to have been produced from that.

"One unborn male, delighting in her, lies by the side of the one unborn female who is red, white, and black, and who gives birth to many offspring of similar form; another unborn male abandons her after he has enjoyed his enjoyment.
Thus [it is said].

Since it is being taught that all other classes of entities, being distinct from that [Brahman], are of its nature by virtue of originating from it—just like the vital breaths, the ocean, the mountains, and so forth—this unborn one (ajā) must be understood as the creator of many similar offspring, being experienced by the self under the influence of karma and abandoned by another self that possesses knowledge; thus she is born from Brahman and has Brahman as her essence.

Therefore, based on this remainder of the sentence, and by recognizing her similarity to the others through a parallel passage in another Vedic branch, [she is to be identified as the primordial matter].
The passage "smaller than the small" demonstrates that the context has as its purport Brahman as the cause.

From the statement whose meaning is "not to be measured," it is determined that the unborn [nature] is regulated as being of the essence of Brahman.
Here too, at the commencement of the treatise, beginning with "What is the cause, Brahman? and so forth, [the inquiry is established].

"Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the power of the Divine Self, established by its own qualities"—thus there is the comprehension of the Unborn (ajā), whose nature is the power of the Supreme Brahman; and further on: "The Illusionist (māyī) creates this universe, and another is bound therein by illusion"; "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the Illusionist";
and "He alone presides over each and every womb."
And thus, because of that very perception; in this mantra, there is not even a trace of the understanding of an independent *prakṛti* established by the Tantras. ||9||

How, then, is there the non-born nature (*ajā-tva*) of this primordial matter (*prakṛti*), which begins with light and consists of the forms red, white, and black? Or how can that which is non-born have the quality of beginning with light? To this, he says: "119. And because of the teaching of a figurative conception (*kalpanā*), there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. (1.4.10)

"Of the nature of power" (śaktirūpāyāḥ) means of the nature of an inseparable attribute (apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇarūpāyāḥ). For power is indeed an inseparable attribute that is useful for an effect. "The womb" (yonim) means primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the source of the world. "Of that very [nature]" (tasyā eva) means of that which has Brahman as its self. The phrase "even a scent of the notion of an independent primordial nature" implies that this is understood not only from the consistency with other Vedic branches but also from its own context, through the realization of its identity with Brahman. || 9 ||
And for the one who remains in dissolution, the state of being the agent of honey (the sun) belongs to the Sun;
likewise, it would be so because of the scriptural statements regarding the creation and so forth even by the Unborn (Ajā).
The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of removing a possible doubt. There is no contradiction between this primordial matter (prakṛti) being unborn and its having light as its beginning.
Why?
Because of the teaching of *kalpanā*. *Kalpanā* means *klṛpti*, which is creation. The meaning is: because of the teaching of the creation of the world.
As it is said:
"The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before."

Thus, "kalpana" means creation (*sṛṣṭi*). Here too, in the passage, "From this, the Illusionist (*māyī*) creates this universe," the creation of the world is taught. The meaning is that from this—which is non-different from Himself—namely, from the cause in its subtle state, the Illusionist, the Lord of All, creates the entire universe. By this teaching on "kalpana," one understands that this primordial nature (*prakṛti*) possesses a connection with two states, in the form of both effect and cause.

For at the time of dissolution, she, having attained the state of Brahman, remains in a subtle form with name and form undifferentiated; but at the time of creation, she—having the qualities of *sattva* and so forth manifested, with name and form differentiated, denoted by such terms as "the Manifest" (*vyakta*) and so on, and transformed into the forms of fire, water, and earth—remains in the appearance of red, white, and black. Therefore, there is no contradiction in her being the "Source" (*ājā*) in her causal state and "Beginningning with Light" (*jyotir-upakramā*) in her effected state. This is like the case of honey and so forth: just as by the Lord, in the causal state, the sun exists as a single entity, [so it is here].

How so? For the state of having red, white, and black forms is possible only in the state of being an effect (*kāryāvasthā*). The meaning is that if one accepts [the cause] as having light (*jyotis*) as its starting point at that time, then its being unborn (*ajatva*) is untenable; if it is unborn, then its having light as its starting point is untenable. Regarding the word "and" (*ca*): the word "and" has the sense of "but" (*tu*).

Regarding the term *kalpanam*: by this, he shows that the verbal root has the sense of "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) in order to exclude the interpretation of the word *kalpanā* as meaning "the superimposition of something upon what it is not. *Kalpanam* means creation; this is well-known from Vedic usage such as "He who fashioned the seven worlds" (*prākalpayad yo bhuvanāni sapta*). Therefore, the words "light" (*jyotiḥ*) and "fashioning" (*kalpana*) follow the terminology of the Vedic texts. Such a designation is also seen in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the Sage [Yājñavalkya], as observed in passages such as "Because of the instruction regarding the serene being" (*samprasādādadhyupadeśāt*) and "Equal with light" (*samāno jyotiṣā*).

"Attained to the state of Brahman"—that is, attained to the state of Brahman as the causal condition (*kāraṇāvastha*). Here, what is intended is not the attainment of the state of Brahman by *prakṛti* alone; rather, it is the attainment of the causal state by Brahman, whose body is *prakṛti*. Therefore, and so forth: the effect is Brahman whose body is *jā* in its state as an effect; the cause is Brahman whose body is *jā* in its state as a cause—this is the meaning.

In the state of being an effect (*kāryāvasthā*), the conception of the sun as honey and the conception of its rising and setting are not contradictory, because it serves as the locus of the essence produced by the rituals expounded in the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva* Vedas, and is thus the object of enjoyment for deities such as those of the directions. This is stated in the Madhuvidyā, beginning with "That sun is the honey of the gods," and concluding:
"Then, having risen from there upwards, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the very center."

By this much [it is established]. "Single" means having a single nature. Therefore, by this mantra, only the unborn one whose essence is Brahman is denoted; it is not [the deity] established in the Tantras—this is proven.

Others, however, maintain that in this mantra, a single unborn one (*ajā*) characterized by fire, water, and food is denoted. They should be asked: Are fire, water, and food themselves the single unborn one consisting of fire, water, and food? Or is it Brahman itself in the form of fire, water, and food? Or is it some other entity that serves as the cause of fire, water, and food? In the first case, because fire, water, and food are many, the phrase "the single unborn one" would be contradicted.

Nor should it be said that although fire, water, and earth are many, they attain oneness through the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*); for even after tripartition, their plurality does not disappear, as evidenced by the texts:
"These are the three deities," and "Of these, let me make each one threefold."

Thus, because there is an instruction regarding the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) for each [element]; as for the phrase "just as" and so forth: just as the notions of rising, setting, and being honey-like, as well as their absence, are possible for the sun through its two states; so too, the states of being unoriginated and having light as its primary form are not contradictory in a single substrate characterized by *prakṛti* due to the distinction between states. "Of one" means of that which is one with the Lord, meaning that whose name and form are undifferentiated.

"Of what sort," and so forth. Does the entity being conceived as a single, unborn (*aja*) thing consist of fire, water, and food (*tejo'bannāni*) themselves? Or is Brahman, existing in the state of fire, water, and food, conceived as a single, unborn thing? Or is some single cause of those [elements], indicated by the words "fire, water, and food," figuratively represented as being unborn? This is the meaning. "These three"—this does not mean that the collection is one, but rather that there are indeed three collections;
for thus each [element] is taught to be made tripartite (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).

The second alternative is to be considered: Is that which has been transformed into the form of fire, water, and food *Brahman itself* as the one unborn (*ajā*)? Or does it remain in its own nature, untransformed?
The first alternative is rejected precisely because of the loss of its unity.

As for the second, it contradicts the description "red, white, and black"; moreover, it is impossible to say that *Brahman*, while remaining in its own nature, is characterized by fire, water, and food.

Even in the third interpretation, after designating fire, water, and food by the word "ajā," one must accept that their causal state is what is "to be established" by them; therefore, it is better to take the word "ajā" as denoting the very causal state of fire, water, and food as established by the Śruti itself.

Furthermore, as for the claim that this *prakṛti* is taught by the word ‘*ajā*’ (the unborn) through the imaginative attribution (*parikalpanā*) of being a she-goat—that too is inconsistent, because it serves no purpose. For example, in passages such as "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot," the body and other components are metaphorically described as a chariot and so forth in order to demonstrate the means for attaining Brahman. And just as, in the case of the passage concerning the sun, the honey-nature is imaginatively attributed to the *vasus* and others in order to demonstrate their status as objects of enjoyment—likewise, what utility is there in attributing the nature of a she-goat to this *prakṛti*?

"The second alternative is that it is to be conceptualized. This means the sense of the passage concerning the alternatives is: Are fire, water, and food—the modifications of Brahman—referred to by the word "unborn" (*ajā*), or is it its own essential nature (*svarūpa*)?

Regarding the phrase "even in the second [alternative]": the meaning is that there is a lack of natural consistency with the scripture (*śruti-asvārasya*), because redness, whiteness, and blackness cannot exist in the essential nature of Brahman.

Regarding the third [position]: this alternative was raised for the purpose of establishing the identity of the red, white, and black as belonging to a single species of goat (*ajāti*). By the word "goat" (*ajā*): the meaning is that even by superimposing the sense of fire, water, and food onto the word "goat"—which is not primarily expressive of them—and thereby bringing about the presentation of their cause through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is more appropriate to rely on the view that the text aims to establish the Cause through its primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*).

"Because it would be purposeless. In all cases, the acceptance of the primary meaning—whether established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or through the power of the word's etymological parts (*avayavaśakti*)—is naturally obtained. However, the acceptance of a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning occurs only when the primary meaning is untenable. In that case, the purposes [of resorting to a secondary meaning] are the attainment of an excellence of appropriateness (*aucityātiśaya*) and the establishment of the primary meaning for multiple words. Here, the absence of any such untenability of the primary meaning has been demonstrated; for it has been stated that there is no contradiction between "being unborn" (*ajātva*) and "having light as its beginning" (*jyotir-upakramatva*) due to their being different states.

Therefore, the flaw consists in the absence of a purpose characterized by the attainment of the propriety of the meaning. [The first alternative: ... from the very admission... it is determined... of the sun and so forth... even the alternative... well-known... Vā. (variant).

SB II-45: Not only is there an absence of utility, but there is also contradiction. For that which is the cause of the entire universe—an insentient principle that serves as the means for all sentient beings, who have been connected to it since beginningless time, to experience all pleasure and pain and to attain liberation—there would be the abandonment of its own nature, which is capable of abandoning those connected to it; this would result in the abandonment of its status as the means for achieving a very limited purpose, such as the creation of a tiny number of subjects, by becoming a specific sentient being (a goat) through a chance conjunction with another. Furthermore, it would entail the nature of a specific sentient being (a goat) capable of abandoning its own related entities. Thus, there is a contradiction.
To assert that [the Supreme Self] possesses such a nature for the sake of manifestation is indeed contradictory.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to postulate a different meaning for the word "ajā" (unborn/goat) in the passages "the one unborn," "for the one is unborn," and "another is unborn.
If you argue that the nature of a goat is postulated everywhere [in these cases], [we reply:]...

Regarding the statement, "Another unborn one abandons her once her enjoyment has been exhausted," it is utterly contradictory to conceive of a connection—either by this [body] or by another—with that which is fit for such a connection, namely the state of being a goat, for one who is wise and effecting the absolute abandonment of *prakṛti*. ||10||
Thus concludes the section concerning the cups (Camasādhikaraṇa). 2.
30. The Section Concerning the Comprehension of Numbers (Saṅkhyopasaṅgrahādhikaraṇa) ||1-4-3||
120. [The Sāṃkhya theory is not established] even by the inclusion of the number [of principles], because of their diversity and because of the excess [of categories]. (Sūtra 1.4.11)
The Vājasaneyins record: "In whom the five groups of five and space are established—
knowing that very Self as the immortal Brahman, one becomes immortal."
Thus [it is said].
Is this mantra intended to establish the principles proven in the Kapila-tantra, or not?—thus there is doubt.

"Not by number. Since there is no distinction in the word *ajā* (the Unborn) as it brings to mind independent primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the fact that this primordial matter has Brahman as its self was established based on other scriptural passages. That [conclusion] is untenable here; for if it referred to the Supreme Self, the number would be exceeded, and since the number could be completed even without the Supreme Self, there is the possibility of determining the specific sense that "primordial matter is not of the nature of Brahman. It is with this doubt that the present section is connected.

Regarding the word "vāja": this sentence generates the cognition of a connection with the number twenty-five and the addition of the *tattvas*. If there are other sentences of this kind, they too are the subject matter.

"It is doubted" means that doubt arises from both the connection with the number twenty-five and the perception of an excess of principles (*tattva*). Regarding the mantra "In whom the five groups of five people [dwell]," is it intended to establish the principles as established in the *Kāpila* system, or not? Which is more appropriate:
that it is intended to establish the principles as established in that system?
Why?
Because from the word "pañcajana," which is qualified by the word "pañca," there is the cognition of the twenty-five principles (tattvas).

This is what is meant: the compound "pañcajanāḥ" has as its object a collective aggregate (samāhāra); "the groups of five persons are 'pañcajanāḥ'," just like the expression "five bundles of herbs" (*pañcapūlyaḥ*). The change of gender in "pañcajanāḥ" is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). When the expectation arises as to how many such aggregates there are, they are understood to be "five aggregates" by means of the first word "pañca," which serves as a qualifier for the term "pañcajana," just as in the expression "five [groups of] five-herb-bundles."

Therefore, when the twenty-five categories are understood through the phrase "five five-janas," and there arises the inquiry "Which are they?", since the context concerns liberation, those very principles such as *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and the rest—which are well-known in the Smṛtis as objects to be known by seekers of liberation—are what are understood.

Is there, or is there not, a cognition of the twenty-five principles through the word "five-janas"? Is the separate mention of space (*ākāśa*) an obstacle to its inclusion in the intermediate number? Or is it not? And can the determination that the word "five-janas" refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth be made on the basis of the supplementary portion of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), or not?

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: when there is no contradiction and a definitive conclusion cannot be reached, then—given the possibility of the application of an intermediate number and because a compound refers to a collective aggregate—the term "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) denotes five groups of five; thus, since twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) are understood, this mantra is intended to set forth the principles established in the Tantras.

The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: When the separate mention of *ākāśa* contradicts the connection with the intermediate number [five], and when it is possible to determine through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) that the reference is to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; then, due to the absence of a cause for connecting the intermediate number, and because the compound functions as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the term "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajana*) denotes five categories of things. Since this does not lead to the cognition of twenty-five principles (*tattva*), this mantra is not intended to propound the principles established in the Sāṃkhya system (*tantra*).

Regarding the term "pañcaśabda": the intention is that since it is possible for this word "pañcajana" to conform to the natural force of its perception of a number (*saṅkhyā*), it is improper to abandon that; therefore, it is logical that it is a prior compound (*pūrvasamāsa*) denoting a number. Regarding the term "chāndasa": the sense is that because feminine gender is traditionally prescribed for words such as *tribhuvana* and others, and there is no exception to this rule, its status as *chāndasa* (Vedic/irregular) must be accepted. It is intended that the intermediate numbers—such as being an element (*bhūtatva*) or being a sense organ (*jñānendriyatva*)—serve as the grounds for the inclusion of those specific counts. This, indeed, will become clear later.
"Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), are both nature and modification;

the group of sixteen is only modification; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification. Such indeed is the well-known doctrine of the followers of Kapila. Therefore, the intention [of the Sūtra] is that even by including the number [of principles], the apprehension of twenty-five principles—as established in that system—is not possible in the case of the phrase "five five-people" (pañca pañcajanāḥ); this is the meaning of the word "even" (api) in the Sūtra: "Not even by the inclusion of the number."
How so?

Because a group of five composed of five [sets] of five is impossible. For among the twenty-five principles established in the *tantra*, there exists no genus (*jāti*) or other category that pervades them all and serves as the basis for assigning that number five. Nor should it be argued that such a basis for assigning intermediate numbers certainly exists—namely, "five organs of action," "five organs of knowledge," "five gross elements," "five subtle elements," and "the remaining five"—because the gross elements are not established as a group of five composed of five [sub-sets], since ether (*ākāśa*) is mentioned separately.

Therefore, this compound "pañcajanāḥ" does not concern a collective aggregate; rather, by the rule "directional term and number [form a compound] when they constitute a name," it concerns a proper name. Otherwise, there would be a change of gender in the expression "pañcajanāḥ. There exist certain beings named "pañcajanāḥ," and they are qualified by the number five, as in "the five pañcajanas," just like the expression "the seven saptarṣis. || 11 ||

The number twenty-seven results from inclusion; that is to say, it is based on the intention to regard time as an independent entity. Regarding the phrase "well-known from the Śruti": one should accept what is well-known from the Śruti even over what is well-known from the Sāṅkhya system, because the former is more intimate (antaraṅga).

By the words "by five," etc., it is implied that no single underlying attribute (upādhi) can pervade all five [elements]. For a collection is indeed defined by being grasped through a single common attribute.

"And not... because of the non-establishment of a collection" means that there is no common underlying attribute (*anugata-upādhi*) in the case of the five beginning with the sense of smell (due to the exclusion of space), nor in the case of the five beginning with air, nor in the case of the five beginning with the mind, nor in the triad of qualities (*guṇatraya*), nor in *mahat* and *ahaṅkāra*. "Otherwise" means that the change in gender [of the pronoun] would be forced. "Seven" refers to the usage found in the venerable Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa; this is the intended meaning here.

Regarding the phrase "the seven stainless Seven Sages" (*sapta saptarṣayo'malāḥ*): since the number [seven] is understood as being in a state of neutrality at the time of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *saṃjñin* (the named entity), it is not the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*). Therefore, in order to make known that it is to be construed with the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), it is appropriate to indicate that the number is a qualifier by means of the word "five. This alone constitutes the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the two words; namely, their power to denote the meaning in the analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*). Consequently, the compound (*samāsa*) is justified. Thus, because the [original] number was not intended to be emphasized, qualifying it again with that number is purposeful. || 11 ||
Who, then, are these "five people"? To this he says: 121. Breath and the others, because of the remainder of the passage [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.17].

From the remainder of the passage, "Those who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind," it is understood that the five *pañcajanas* are indeed the five [senses] beginning with breath, which have Brahman as their support. || 12 ||
Now, it might be argued that for both the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas,
this mantra— "In whom the five five-people [dwell]"— is identical.

Regarding the phrase "the life-breath of the life-breath," [the opponent asks] "what then are those? [The reply is: A number [as a qualifier] is inappropriate in a prior compound (pūrvasamāsa), because no specific thing to be numbered is understood from this sentence.

Regarding the phrase "prāṇādayaḥ" (beginning with breath): by establishing that among the breath and the others there is a single common ground in the nature of being sense organs (*indriyatva*), the composition of the Sūtra serves the purpose of determining the meaning of the remainder of the passage. Here, the principle of "the first and the rest" (*agryaprāyanyāya*) is intended to resolve the doubt. There are two words, *prāṇa* and *anna*; there are three words, *cakṣus*, *śrotra*, and *manas*.

Therefore, in accordance with those, since the words *prāṇa* and *anna* also refer to sense organs, the entities beginning with breath are the sense organs; thus, the meaning is that these alone are the "five people" (*pañcajana*). || 12 ||

In the aforementioned supplementary passage, the reading "food" (anna) does not exist for the Kāṇvas. Therefore, it cannot be said that for them the "five five-people" are the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth. To this, the reply is: 122. *Jyotiṣaikeṣāmasatyanne* || 1.4.13 || [The five people are] by means of light for some, since food is absent [in their version].

According to the reading of some—the Kāṇvas—it is understood that when there is no food, the "five people" are the senses; this is for the purpose of showing their supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
This is what is meant: in the mantra preceding the one containing "the five five-people," it says, "The gods worship him, the light of lights, the immortal life."

Thus, when Brahman is designated as "the light of lights," certain luminaries that depend upon Brahman for their own functions are understood; and these are the sense organs which illuminate objects, as is recognized by the non-specific reference "in whom the five groups of five" (*yasmin pañca pañca-janāḥ*).

It cannot be said [that this is not so], because among the Kāṇvas, due to the omission of the word "food" (*anna*), it would be impossible to assign the number five to breath and the others; therefore, the sense is that being "five-fold" (*pañcajanatva*) would be inappropriate.

"By *jyotiṣā*" means by the word *jyotis* ending in the genitive case; this is the meaning. Even in the Sūtra, the word *jyotis* has the sense of the verbal form itself. The meaning is that the lack of conformity (*asvārasya*) of the word *jyotiḥ* in the Sūtra must be tolerated because it is necessary for establishing the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of the Vedic statement.

By the phrase "Brahmā... [the source of] all activities," the meaning of "the breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇaḥ*) and so forth is stated; the intention is that it is like [the statement] "the purifier of purifiers" (*pavitrāṇāṃ pavitram*). By the word "lights" (*jyotīṃṣi*), the quality of being an illuminator is intended. Consequently, the distinction from the organs of action and the like is established, because they lack the quality of being illuminators. Regarding the phrase "certain": the sense is that, when there is doubt as to whether these are the lights such as the sun and so forth or not, a desire for a specific determination remains.

The term "unspecified" (*anirdhāritā*) indicates that there is an expectancy for another sentence which would specify the particular number; consequently, because they are qualified by the number five heard therein, and because no other group of five luminaries is well-known, their status as sense organs (*indriya*) is understood through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Even though for some reciters of the Veda the phrase "of food" and so forth is absent, the sense organs are indeed indicated by the word "luminaries" (*jyotiṣām*).

By the word "of breath" (*prāṇasya*), the sense of touch is understood, because the sense of touch is related to air (*vāyu*); for it is impossible to indicate the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) by the word "light" (*jyotis*). "Of the eye" refers to the visual faculty; "of the ear" refers to the auditory faculty; and "of food" refers to the olfactory and gustatory faculties [simultaneously].

Regarding "dāna": because it is connected with the earth denoted by the word *anna* (food), it is called *anna* in the sense of "that by which [one eats]"; thus, the gustatory organ (*rasanendriya*) is also included. By the term "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*), the mind itself is meant. Since the olfactory and gustatory organs are mentioned together (*tantraṇopādāna*), their number as five is not contradicted. The illuminating organs, ending with the mind, are those designated by the term "five people" (*pañcajana*). To avoid contradiction with that, the olfactory and gustatory organs are mentioned together. Thus, [the verse reads]: "In whom the five groups of five and the ether are established."

Thus, because it is established that the sense organs indicated by the term ‘pañcajana’ and the great elements (mahābhūtas) shown by the term ‘ākāśa’ are all grounded in Brahman, there is no occasion for the twenty-five principles (tattvas) established in the Sāṅkhya system to follow here; for this demonstrates that all principles have Brahman as their substratum. By the word ‘ghrāṇa’, the olfactory organ is understood. Therefore, whether the number [of principles] is included or not in the Vedānta texts, it is established that there is no cognition of the principles established in the Sāṅkhya system. Thus it is concluded. || 13 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number [of elements]. || 3 ||

**Section 31: On Being the Cause (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇam) | 1.4.4** **(Sūtras 14, 15)** **Sūtra 14:** "And [Brahman is] the cause, because of the teaching concerning ether and the rest exactly as they have been described. The proponent of the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause objects again: "It is not the case that creation from a single source is taught in the Vedāntas; therefore, it is not tenable to assert that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For instance, [the objection was] answered in two ways: by the acceptance of that number and by the non-acceptance of it. When the number is included—that is, when the number is possible—and when it is absent—that is, when the number is impossible. (13) **Sūtra 15:** "And [Brahman is] the cause, because of the teaching concerning ether and the rest exactly as they have been described. Furthermore, the proponent of the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause objects: "In the Vedāntas, creation is not declared to proceed from a single source; thus, it is not logical to state that Brahman is the sole cause of the universe. To explain: [The objection was] refuted in two ways—by the acceptance of that number and by the non-acceptance of it. This refers to the inclusion of the number—that is, when the number is possible—and its absence—that is, when the number is impossible. (13)
Thus ends the section concerning the inclusion of the number [of elements]. (Sūtra 3)

Regarding the phrase "by being one-eyed": through the realization that "in which" [all things abide], it is understood that all principles (*tattvas*) have Brahman as their substratum; thus, the independent causality of *pradhāna* is refuted. Now, the connection [of the objection] arises from the doubt: "Perhaps independent causality is indeed perceived, since there is no perception of Brahman as the substratum."

"Furthermore," and so forth. The subject matter consists of a collection of causal statements characterized by the words *cit*, *bodhya*, *vyākula*, *artha*, and *śabda*, which are unavoidable. Precisely because of this confusion, there arises a doubt: "Is that which is to be understood from the Vedānta statements concerning the cause of the world the unmanifest (*avyakta*), or is it Brahman? For instance, in the passages "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadvā idamagra āsīt*) and "That was undifferentiated" (*tad bhedaṃ tarhyavyākṛtamāsīt*), the terms "non-existent" (*asat*) and "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*) are used;
whereas in the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*), creation is declared as preceded by "Being" (*sat*).
"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat)," and thus it begins with the non-existent. Elsewhere, too, it says:

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; that became existent; that evolved. Therefore, because there is a lack of consistency regarding the Creator in the Vedānta texts, it is not possible to determine that Brahman alone is the cause of the world; on the contrary, it is possible to determine that the Pradhāna alone is the cause.
Having stated that the world undergoes dissolution into the unmanifested Pradhāna in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifested," [the text continues]:
"It was manifested by name and form alone."

Thus, the creation of the world from the unmanifested (avyākṛta) itself is declared. For "unmanifested" (avyākṛta) means "unmanifest" (avyakta); the sense is that it is not differentiated, nor made manifest, by name and form. This "unmanifest" is none other than Pradhāna. And because its essential nature is eternal and it is the substratum of transformation, the terms "being" (sat) and "non-being" (asat) found in the statements of those who maintain it to be the cause of the world will not be contradictory in this case, just as they are not in the case of Brahman.

Do these two [passages] refer to Brahman in its state of unmanifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), or do they refer to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)? To determine this, is the reference as a witness in the words "On this point there is also this verse" intended to make it understood that the word "non-existent" (*asat*) refers to the previously mentioned Brahman; or not? And does the subsequent mention of the Ruler in the words "He has entered here" make it understood that the word "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) refers to Brahman; or not? Such a doubt is established by the context of the meaning.

When there is the reference "this very [one]" (*sa eṣa*), which does not lead one to understand that the term refers to Brahman with an unmanifested body (*avyākṛta-śarīra*); and when there is the indication "that too this [one]" (*tad apy eṣaḥ*), which does not lead one to understand that the word "non-existent" (*asat*) refers to the previously mentioned Brahman; then, since the words "non-existent" (*asat*) and "unmanifested" (*avyākṛta*) lack the sense of referring to Brahman in its state of unmanifested name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it follows that the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) is what is taught by the causal statement.

When there is the designation "this [is] also that" (*yadā 'tadapyeṣaḥ*), it makes known that the word *asat* has Brahman as its referent; and when there is the corroboration "he is this" (*sa eṣaḥ*), it makes known that the word *avyākṛta* has Brahman, whose body is the unevolved, as its referent. At that time, because the words *asat* and *avyākṛta* have as their referent Brahman in the state of having names and forms undifferentiated, it is established that Brahman is what is taught by the sentences concerning the cause of the world.

"From one"—that is, from a single-natured cause. "Of the Creator" (sraṣṭuḥ) means that, according to the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, there is no fixed determination of a cause for creation. "As in the case of Brahman" is a counter-example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, when it is established that the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) is the cause, qualities residing in the cause such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth must be interpreted as being intended to signify the Creator's inclination toward creation. Furthermore, even the words "Brahman" and "Self" (*ātman*) apply to the Pradhāna alone because of its greatness and pervasiveness. Therefore, it is the Pradhāna, well-known through Smṛti and reasoning, that is taught by the Vedānta texts as the cause of the world.

This being the position, we reply: "And because [Brahman] is declared as the cause in the case of ether and the rest, exactly as it was described. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). It can be determined that the world originates from the Supreme Brahman alone—He who is omniscient, the Lord of all, whose will is infallible, and from whom every trace of defect has been dispelled.
Why?
Because He is declared to be the cause in the case of ether and the rest, exactly as He was described—that is, as characterized by omniscience and other such attributes.
Brahman, which was established in such passages as "From which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (BS 1.1.2), is referred to here by the phrase "as described.
Of that very same [Brahman], which is one...
"Because [Brahman] is spoken of as the cause in passages such as 'In space, etc.
In such passages, Brahman alone, which is omniscient, is declared to be the cause. For instance: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."

"He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman"—here, it is the very same "wise Brahman" mentioned in the context that is referred to by the words "from that, indeed, from this. Likewise, the omniscient Brahman indicated by "It thought, 'May I be many'" is the very one referred to by "It emitted heat. This should be understood in the same way throughout all passages concerning creation. Therefore, it is conclusively determined that Brahman alone is the single cause of the universe. || 14 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "In the passage, 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat),' it is the non-existent itself that is designated as the cause; how then can the causality of Brahman alone—who is omniscient and whose resolve is infallible—be established? To this, he says:
124. Because of attraction. (1.4.15)

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* and other such texts are intended. Regarding the phrase "Truth, Knowledge": it has been shown that even prior to the demonstration of causality, the consciousness of the subject characterized by causality is demonstrated from the very outset. As for the phrase "the Wise One alone is the subject under discussion": the term "Self" (*ātman*), which is exclusively conscious by its very nature, is employed even before the demonstration of creation in the word "manifested" (*sambhūta*); thus, it is exceedingly powerful.

The intention is that, because the intelligence (*vipaścit*) of that cause was established even prior to that [statement], "the suspicion regarding the strained interpretation of the word 'Self' (*ātman*) has been cast far away. Regarding the phrase "in the same way": since the causality was established in the passage "It emitted heat" (*tattejo'sṛjata*) even before the passage "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), the causality must be understood as being consistent with the act of thinking; it is not the case that the act of thinking must be understood as being consistent with the causality. This is the meaning. As for the phrase "it should be seen": "In the beginning, there was only one."

The meaning is that in passages such as "He saw," since the account of creation occurs [afterwards], the supreme consciousness and its unique attributes, such as seeing, must be understood as existing even prior to that. Because this contradicts many scriptural passages situated at the beginning [of the Upaniṣads], the weakness of the mere scriptural mention of the unevolved (avyākṛta) is established by implication. || 14 ||
In the passage "Non-being indeed was this," [the text] draws in the omniscient cause of all and declares it; for Brahman alone is the cause here.
In the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is likewise the very same Brahman—consisting of bliss, whose will is true, and who is omniscient—that is being referred to.
How so?
[Because the text continues: "Different from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self, consisting of bliss."

By means of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' He created all this, whatever exists here; having created that, He entered into it; having entered into it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)," [the text] declares that Brahman—which consists of bliss, whose resolve is true, which is the creator of all, and which has become the Self of all through its entry into everything—is [the subject].
Regarding all that has been stated with the words, "On this there is also this verse," this verse is cited as a witness:
"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent."

Thus, later on—in the passage beginning with "From fear of Him the wind blows"—that same Brahman is drawn back and its quality of being the ruler of all, its unsurpassed bliss, and so forth, are declared. Therefore, this mantra refers exclusively to that [Brahman]. At that time, because there is no differentiation of name and form, and because [the world] does not exist in relation to it, Brahman itself is denoted by the word "non-existent" (*asat*).
In the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad eva idam agre āsīt*), the same resolution applies.

It is drawn together; that is, the drawing together is promised by the words "Or rather, this was non-existent" (*asadvā idam*) and so forth. With reference to the sentences "By the wise Brahman," "Another inner self, consisting of bliss," and "He desired," the qualities such as being "wise" (*vipaścit*) and so on are stated. Likewise, "in the subsequent [passage]" refers to "Out of fear of Him... (*bhīṣāsmāt*); here, the word "from Him" (*asmāt*) draws in Brahman because it refers back to the subject under discussion.

Regarding the phrase "only non-existent" (*asadeva*): the intention here is that even in that context, because the word "non-existent" (*asat*) referring to the cause in the sentence "this was indeed non-existent" has the same referent, qualities such as having true volitions (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and so forth are established. In that regard, the demonstration of the subsequent reference (*anukarṣa*) by the words "that was existent" (*tat sadāsīt*) to what was denoted by the word "non-existent" is based on the fact that the word "existent" (*sat*) applies commonly to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). For the word "existent" excludes what is insubstantial (*tuccha*), but it does not exclude the unconscious. Indeed, the exclusion of the "non-existent" even in the causal state is to be understood from the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.
As it has been said: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated."
"Thus," it might be argued that *pradhāna* alone is designated as the cause of the world;
"no," it is said in reply. Even there, by the word "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*), it is Brahman itself in its unmanifest body that is designated.
"This very one has entered here unto the tips of the fingernails."
In the passage, "Seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind—

one should meditate [on him] as the Self alone," the pronoun "that" (saḥ) in the phrase "this very one" (sa eṣa) refers back to that which was designated by the word "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta), because it is drawn forward as the internal ruler who has entered within.

"Having created that, He entered into it"; "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest name and form"—from these [scriptural passages], as well as from the well-known manifestation of name and form, there is the "entry into the effect" of the omniscient Supreme Brahman, the Creator. Furthermore, because entry is for the purpose of governance—as seen in the text, "He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all"—such an entry is not possible for the insentient Pradhāna. Therefore, the "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta) refers to Brahman whose body is the undifferentiated.
Regarding what was stated, "It was differentiated by name and form," he shows that this is also an elliptical reference (anukarṣa) in the Śruti passage beginning with "That indeed this...

By the words "Having created that," he declares the well-known fact that the entry and the differentiation of name and form mentioned in the Śruti "That indeed this... are attributes of the Supreme Self.
Thus, it is said: "That very Brahman, whose name and form were undifferentiated, being omniscient and of true resolve, differentiated its own name and form and manifested itself.

This being so, the acts of seeing and so forth are indeed primary [in Brahman]. Furthermore, the words "Brahman" and "Self" cannot in any way apply to the Pradhāna, as they imply unsurpassed greatness, the quality of being a controller, and all-pervasiveness. Therefore, it is established that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. || 15 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the nature of causality. 4.
32. The Section Concerning the Denotation of the World (Jagadvācitvādhikaraṇa) ||1.4.5||
125. Because [the word *prāṇa*] denotes the world. (1.4.16)

Furthermore, the Sāṅkhya objects: "Even though the Vedānta texts establish a conscious principle as the cause of the world, nevertheless, no entity other than the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* established in that system is perceived from them as the cause of the world to be known. For instance, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, the Kauṣītakins record the experiencing *puruṣa* himself as the cause to be known, beginning with the words, 'I shall tell you about Brahman.'"

The scriptural passage (*viṣayavākya*) ending with "he is to be known" has been shown. The nature of the doubt—whether that which is to be propounded by the causal statement is the *puruṣa* who is the presiding agent over primordial matter (*prakṛti*), or rather the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—is established by the context. For that purpose, the question arises: in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, is the Brahman taught as the object to be known the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Self? And is the "agent" designated by the words "the maker of these persons" the individual soul, or the Supreme One?

Regarding the phrase "of whom this is the work" (*yasya vaitat karma*), does the word "work" (*karma*) denote merit and demerit (*puṇyāpuṇya*), or does it denote the world (*jagat*)? Is it appropriate for the word "work" to denote the world because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "this"? Or is it appropriate for it to denote merit and demerit so as not to render redundant the separate mention in the words "the maker of these persons"? Furthermore, given the presence of marks (*liṅga*) indicating the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) understood from the passage beginning "The two [disciples] went to a sleeping man," do these [marks] strengthen the view that [the word "work"] denotes merit and demerit, or rather...?
