Is this not so? Are these [passages] intended to teach the individual soul (*jīva*) through its characteristic marks (*liṅga*), or are they devoted to teaching the Brahman distinct from the individual soul by means of the question and answer beginning with "Wherein" (*akka vā*) and so forth?
For the "action" mentioned in the scriptural text "He whose action this is" must be the world;
indeed, the individual soul, which is subject to merit and the like, is not what is being described here in the Śruti.
"O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons, or whose work this is— he indeed is to be known."

"Who indeed is the maker of these persons, or whose work is this?"—for such a separate designation would otherwise be purposeless. Furthermore, the word "work" (*karman*) is well-known in both common usage and the Veda as referring specifically to action in the form of merit and demerit.
Since the origination of the world is caused by the karma of various enjoyers,
and because the statement "the maker of these persons" is logically applicable only to an enjoyer.

This is the meaning: that which is the cause of these persons who have the solar orb and so forth as their locus, and who constitute the objects of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)—namely, the karma characterized by merit and demerit which serves as the cause for their state of being caused—that indeed is to be known; its specific nature is to be understood as distinguished from what has been discussed in the present context.
Of whom [it was said],
likewise, later on:
"Those two went to the sleeping man."
"He threw him with a staff"— thus,
the arrival of the sleeping man, the striking with the staff, the awakening, and so forth, are "indicative marks" (liṅga) for the purpose of establishing the "enjoyer" alone.
Likewise, even further on, it is the enjoyer alone who is established.

"Just as a merchant eats with his own [people], or as his own [people] eat with the merchant, even so this self consisting of intelligence eats with these selves; ... even so these selves eat with him.
Likewise:
"Who was that person who lay down in this world? Where did he then abide? Whence did he come?"
To him who did not understand the meaning thus asked, Ajātaśatru himself said:

"There are channels called *hitā* belonging to the heart; therein it comes to be at that time... when, having fallen asleep, one does not see any dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this breath alone (*prāṇa*). Then speech enters into him along with all names... the mind enters into him along with all thoughts."

"When he awakens, just as sparks would fly out in all directions from a whirling firebrand, even so from this Self the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) go forth to their respective stations; from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds.

Thus, that very locus of the dissolution and emergence of the instruments such as speech—which exists throughout the states of dreaming, deep sleep, and waking as the substratum of deep sleep—is the individual self (*jīvātman*), [as it is said]:
"Then in this [Self] the vital breath becomes one."
Thus he spoke:
"In this individual self (jīvātman), this word 'prāṇa' is based on its state as a living being;
when it awakens..."

Thus, because awakening is heard of that which is designated by the word "prāṇa," [it cannot be] the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) or the Lord (īśvara), since both deep sleep and awakening are impossible for them.

The statement beginning with "named Hitā" refers to the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) as the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); this is the intended meaning for which the passage is cited. At that time, the word "then" (*tadā*) would refer to the period of deep sleep. "He goes together with all names"—the meaning is that each respective organ has its own specific function ceased. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers these to be the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). "Devas" refers to the sense organs; "worlds" refers to knowledge. The connection is: he has spoken [of the soul] as having deep sleep by virtue of being the substratum of deep sleep.
"Form" (*rūpaḥ*). "Emergence" (*udgama*) is the engagement in their respective functions.

Alternatively, the subject matter is that the word "prāṇa" refers to the fivefold vital breath (pañcavṛttiprāṇa); [and] "dissolution" (apyaya) or "merging" (laya) means the cessation of one's respective functions, which constitutes being the substratum of deep sleep (suṣupti).

The phrase "In this [passage], etc. is intended to dispel the suspicion that the word "prāṇa" is in the nominative case, as well as the suspicion that it refers to either the vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) or the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Alternatively, the two locative endings in "asmin prāṇe" are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa); that is, while this Self exists, the entire collection of instruments, such as speech and so forth, becomes one in the "prāṇa" alone. Even though the word "prāṇa" refers primarily to the vital breath, it is the individual soul (jīva) itself that is being expounded in this context; for the vital breath is inherently an instrument of the soul.

Therefore, since Brahman, which was introduced as the subject to be explained, is indeed the Puruṣa, there is no establishment of an Īśvara distinct from Him. Furthermore, the qualities of consciousness such as "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and so forth, which reside in the cause, are possible only in this [Puruṣa]; thus, it is Pradhāna presided over by this [Puruṣa] alone that is the cause of the world.

This being the position, we reply: "Because He is the architect of the universe. Here, it is not the lowly *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) who, under the sway of merit and demerit, becomes the cause of the transformations of *prakṛti* through the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti* upon himself, that is denoted. Rather, it is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) who is denoted—He from whom every trace of defects such as ignorance has been dispelled, who is a treasure-house of countless, unsurpassed, and excellent auspicious qualities, and who is the sole cause of the entire universe.
Why?

Because in the phrase "and whose this is the work" (*yasyaitat karma*), the word "work" (*karma*) is conjoined with the word "this" (*etad*); and since [the latter] denotes the universe as the effect of the Supreme Person, the word "this" has an unrestricted application due to its meaning, context, and so forth, and thus refers without distinction to the entire universe—comprising all things sentient and insentient—as presented by means of knowledge such as direct perception.

"By the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti*—that is to say, by the superimposition of agency residing in *prakṛti* upon itself; such is the meaning. By the words ending with "is not designated," the intended sense established by the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the word "not" has been stated. With the words "but rather," he states the part of the proposition (*pratijñā*) established by the force of the reason (*hetu*) in the Sūtra.

Regarding the phrase "by means of context, purpose, and so forth": by the word "purpose" (*artha*), what is intended is the suitability for connection with other words situated within its own sentence. "Context" (*prakaraṇa*) refers to the collection of preceding sentences. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the subsequent sentences are intended; alternatively, "context" refers to the entire body of preceding and succeeding sentences, while by the word "and so forth," the indicators of intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*) are intended. Regarding the term "unrestricted" (*asaṅkucita*): the sense is that there is an absence of any factors that would cause restriction. Regarding "entire" (*nikhila*): this word refers back to what is proximate, namely, its presence in the mind (*buddhisthiti*).

And that [word], whether by context, or by connection with another subject under discussion, or by conventional usage—since a restriction [of its meaning] by context and so forth is untenable there—it follows by elimination that it refers to its well-known meaning; for even in that case, [the word] exists [there]. This is the sense. And it is also present in the arrangement [of the text].

Nor is action, characterized as merit and demerit, the subject denoted by the word "karma" here; for, having begun with "I shall declare Brahman to you," the persons residing in the solar orb and other locations— who were pointed out by Bālāki as being Brahman— are shown not to be Brahman.
"Do not indeed speak falsely," [said Ajātaśatru]. Having set aside Bālāki as one who does not speak of Brahman, in order to make known the Brahman unknown to him, Ajātaśatru uttered this statement:
"O Bālāki, he who..."

And so forth. The word ‘karma’ here refers to those presiding deities (adhiṣṭhātṛ) such as Āditya and others who are connected with actions characterized as merit and demerit, as well as the persons belonging to their respective classes, [all of whom] are known by that very [Self]. This word ‘karma’ is intended to make known a specific person not previously understood; it does not denote merely merit and demerit, nor does it denote action in general, but rather denotes the entire world as an effect. In this way alone is the “unknown object” truly taught.

Furthermore, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the instruction that the person— whose natural form is characterized by its connection with action and who is [otherwise] unknown— is "to be known," because the mere connection with action alone serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for the nature of that which is to be known; for this is established simply by saying, "He whose action it is,
he is to be known," without the need for the phrase, "He whose action this is."
And thus, this word is redundant.

The sense is that because the sun and so forth—which constitute a single part of the universe—are the subject under discussion as being "consciousness, unconscious matter, and their mixture," and because the universe as a whole is present in the intellect by way of those parts, it is therefore appropriate to refer to the universe [by the pronoun].

The phrase "or merely denoting action" is stated as an illustration. Just as in the case of that which is under discussion as being "to be known," the word "action" (*karman*) does not denote merely the activity constituting the function of the principal vital air (*mukhya-prāṇa*); for the same reason, it does not denote merely merit and demerit. This is because the vital airs are clearly distinguished from the subject by means of the address using their names and the hearing [of sounds] and so forth; because the context is intent upon making known a specific person unknown to Bālāki; and because the principal vital air is already well-known in the world. Such is the meaning.

The phrase "denoting the state of being an effect of the world" means that it denotes the world as something that has become an effect. This was stated in order to make known that the etymological meaning [of the word *jagat*]—namely, "that which moves" (*gacchati*)—is the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Regarding the term "of the person" (*puruṣasya*): the capacity of a word denoting a connection with action to present [the object] as devoid of action is secondary (*amukhya*). Furthermore, [the word] does not denote a connection with merit, suffering, or action. [The reading] "Brahman" is found in manuscripts *da*, *ca*, *ña*, and *ṭha*; [the reading] "for the sake of knowledge" in *ca*, *ña*, and *ṭha*; [the reading] "connectedness" in *da*; [the reading] "pertaining to the sun" in *tha*; and [the reading] "connection with action" in *i*. [The reading] "to be understood" is found in *tha*.
Regarding the phrase "one who has not understood the meaning" (aviditārtha) [Tha.

13], and as for the separate designation, "He who is the maker of these, or whose work this is," the intention is as follows: As for those persons whom you have designated as Brahman, he who is their maker—that is, they are his effects—what need is there to specify further? He whose effect is the entire universe—all things, whether superior or inferior, conscious or unconscious—are equal in being his effects; that Supreme Person, who is the ultimate cause, is to be known.

Even though the origin of the world is dependent upon the karma of individual souls (*jīva*), the soul is not itself the producer of its own objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and so forth; rather, it experiences everything created by the Lord (*Īśvara*) in accordance with its own karma. Therefore, agency toward [created] persons is not logically possible for it. Consequently, it is the Supreme Brahman alone, well-known in all the Vedāntas as the ultimate cause, that is taught here as the object to be known. || 16 ||

126. If it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained. (Sūtra 1.4.17)

The word "Self" (ātman), though common to both states, is also employed here; for the instruction is: "He by whom action is performed is to be known. Therefore, the meaning is that there is figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

The designation "the maker of these persons" is intended to make it known that the beings mentioned by Bālāki are not Brahman because they are effects. It was stated [in the previous passage]—"He whose work this is"—merely to establish that he is their maker; however, that alone does not establish his status as the cause of the entire universe, endowed with Hiraṇyagarbha and other specific deities who are superior even to the Sun and others mentioned by him. Therefore, [this further statement is made].

"One experiences one's own karma. The sense is that the agency for making a pot and such things does not belong to a person who possesses the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from ritual application (*viniyoga*), but rather to the potter. Therefore... "is well-known. Since the use of the relative pronoun *yaḥ* (who) in the phrases "He who is the agent of these" or "whose this is the work" indicates a form of restatement (*anuvāda*), just as in passages such as "From whom indeed these [beings arise]," the sense is that the Supreme Person, well-known throughout all the Vedāntas, is here restated as the cause. || 16 ||
Now,

as for what was said— that because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and because of the mention of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), it is the enjoyer alone who is taught in this section, and not the Supreme Self— [that is now addressed].
That has been explained—the carrying out of that [process] was stated in the Pratardana-vidyā.

This is what is meant: it has been established there that wherever a passage is determined to be devoted to Brahman through a consideration of its beginning and conclusion, any other indicative marks found therein must be interpreted in conformity with that [primary subject]. Here too, in the opening—"I shall speak of Brahman to you"—Brahman is introduced; and in the middle, as well...
It has been stated that "this work belongs to him" refers not merely to any person, but to Brahman alone, the sole cause of the entire universe. And in the conclusion:
"Having struck down all evils, he attains supremacy over all beings, sovereignty, and lordship."

"Whoever knows thus"—in this way, the scripture declares that the fruit of the exclusive meditation on Brahman is self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), preceded by the destruction of all evil. Therefore, since it is certain that this passage has Brahman as its primary subject, even the indicative marks (*liṅga*) pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) must be interpreted as being subordinate to that [Brahman]. || 17 ||

For in the *Prātardana* section, it was stated that the marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital air (*mukhya-prāṇa*) have Brahman as their ultimate referent due to the threefold nature of the meditation. Since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible in the passage, "Now, in this [state] the breath (*prāṇa*) alone becomes one," it is improper to resort to a non-coreferential construction; and because the application of the word "breath" (*prāṇa*) to Brahman itself is certain, the mention of the breath is appropriate as a mark for the purpose of meditating on Brahman as having the breath as its body (*prāṇa-śarīraka*). But how can the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) have Brahman as their ultimate referent? To this, he says:
In this regard also:
"But Jaimini [holds that the meditations] are for another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and thus some [teachers] also [maintain]. (1.4.18)

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the possibility that the sentence, by mentioning the individual soul (*jīva*), might be understood as being concerned with that [soul]. Master Jaimini considers that the mention of the soul is for another purpose—that is, for the sake of awakening one to the nature of Brahman, which is distinct from the soul.

Its sovereignty consists in its excellence. The "Lord" (*adhipati*) is the Supreme Self, according to the scriptural text: "The Lord of all. Sovereignty is that which belongs to Him. Indeed, the eightfold qualities are called "Brahmic" because they belong to Brahman, as stated in the sūtra: "Jaimini [says it is] Brahmic" (BS 3.4.17).

The instrumental case in "by way of threefoldness" (*traividhyena*) denotes cause; its causality consists in being the purpose. The meaning is: for the sake of establishing the threefold nature of meditation. Regarding the phrase "here too": the meaning is that, by the same logic applied to the introduction of the Prātardana section, the mark of *prāṇa* is shown to have Brahman as its ultimate referent.

Regarding the word "but" (*tu*): the word "but" does not serve to exclude the previously stated resolution; rather, it serves to exclude the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Jaimini, moreover, declares through both question and answer that this reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) is for the purpose of establishing its distinctness from the [Supreme] Soul, even though there are others [who hold otherwise].
1. *Viniścayena*—tha. 2. *Saṃśrayaṇā*—i, vā. 3. *Śarīra*—vā. 4. "How, then, is there the state of having Brahman as the supreme goal?"—vā.
Why?
"Because of the question and the explanation. First, the question:

By the passage beginning with, "The two went to a sleeping man," and so forth, having first awakened the individual soul (jīva)—who is distinct from the vital breaths (prāṇas)—by means of addressing him with the names of the vital breaths while he was asleep and then rousing him with a blow of a staff, the text is seen to be further intent upon awakening [him] to the Brahman who is distinct from the individual soul: "O Bālāki! where did this person lie? Where did he go to? Whence did he come?"
Thus [it is said]. The explanation is also as follows:
"When one has fallen asleep and does not see any dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very breath (prāṇa);
from this self, the vital breaths (prāṇas) emerge according to their respective stations; from the vital breaths, the gods."
"The worlds [belong] to the gods"— thus, the Supreme Self, which is a distinct entity from the individual soul (jīva), is indeed the highest reality.

For when the individual soul (*jīva*) is asleep—that is, when it has rested—there occurs a state of "serenity" (*samprasanna*), an attainment of its own natural stability (*svasthatā*) due to the absence of the turbidity caused by the experience of various pleasures and pains associated with the states of waking and dreaming; and because it emerges from that state again for the sake of enjoyment, this is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For thus it is said: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being (*sat*)."

"Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña), he knows nothing external, nor anything internal"—thus the *prājña* is well known as the substratum of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). This *prājña* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, it is determined that the mention of the individual soul through both the question and the answer is for the purpose of establishing the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the individual soul.

As for what was stated—that in the explanation of the question regarding the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), the place of deep sleep is the channels (nāḍīs) alone, and the aggregate of the organs becomes one within the individual soul itself as designated by the word "prāṇa"—that is incorrect; because the channels are the locus of dreaming, and according to the reasoning already stated, Brahman alone is the locus of deep sleep. Furthermore, it is because of the scriptural declarations concerning the attainment of unity and the dissolution of distinctions within Brahman itself—designated by the word "prāṇa"—of both the individual soul and the aggregate of its instruments, such as speech and the rest, which serve as its adjuncts.

The phrase "by the wise one" refers to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), as found in another scriptural passage (*śruti*), for the purpose of clarifying that the *sadvidyā* text has the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as its subject. Regarding the word "therefore": by this demonstration of the difference in the manner of interpretation, the removal of the doubt concerning the *atideśa-sūtra* (the sūtra on extension) is shown. In the *pratardana-vidyā*, the characteristic marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) are perceived at the beginning; however, the natural force of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) points toward the Supreme Self.

But here, because the marks of the individual soul (jīva) are perceived in the beginning, middle, and end [of the passage], and for that very reason, because there is no indication of the Supreme Self as qualified by consciousness (cid-viśiṣṭatā), and because the threefold nature of meditation is not established, there is the further doubt that the *Prātardana-nyāya* finds no application. The further resolution is that even in the absence of a threefold meditation, there is scope [for this Sūtra] because another purpose exists, namely the communication of Brahman as distinct from the individual soul; thus it is understood.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the channels" (*nāḍīnām*), etc.: in the phrase "then it becomes [one] in them," the word "then" (*tadā*) refers to the state of dreaming. This is because in the immediately following sentence—"when he has fallen asleep... he becomes one"—the word "then" (*atha*) indicates that the state designated by the word "then" is distinct from the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*); furthermore, since the subsequent sentence negates dreaming, it is understood that the preceding sentence introduces the possibility of dreaming and thus has that as its subject. The phrase "in the manner stated" means by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the body, as in the other cited scriptural passage.

"Moreover, some [hold this view]. The Vājasaneyins, in this very dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, teach that the Supreme Self is distinct from the conscious self (vijñānamaya) in deep sleep, stating: "Where was this person consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-puruṣa) then? Whence did he come? When this person consisting of consciousness was asleep there—having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths (prāṇas) by means of his own consciousness—he lies in that space (ākāśa) which is within the heart. And the word "space" (ākāśa) is well-known to denote the Supreme Self.
"Therein is a small inner space.
Therefore, it is understood that the mention of the individual soul (jīva) here is for the purpose of awakening the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, the Prājña, who is a distinct entity from it.

Therefore, since in this passage it is the Supreme Brahman alone—the cause of the entire universe and distinct from the Puruṣa—who is designated as that which is to be known, it is established that the causality of either the Puruṣa as established in the Sāṅkhya system or of the Pradhāna presided over by him is not perceived anywhere in the Vedānta. || 18 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of the world. || 5 ||

"Was he then [in that state]?"—the meaning is: "Was he asleep? "Having taken away the vital breaths"—the meaning is: having taken away with the mind the knowledge produced by the senses, which is denoted by the word "prāṇa. "The mind has its activity ceased. By this, the cessation of the activity of the senses is also implied as a consequence, because they depend upon the mind. "Therefore"—this refers to the determination that, when there is the hearing of a connection with the attributes of the Supreme Self or a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Supreme Self," it is for the purpose of meditation qualified by those respective attributes.

Therefore, because there is no hearing here of an inherence of the attributes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and because the indication is in grammatical apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—which establishes it otherwise—the mark of the individual soul (*jīva-liṅga*) does not serve the purpose of meditation; rather, its purpose is to make known the distinction [between the two]. Regarding the phrase "of the primary" (*pradhānasya*): the mention of the primary here is intended to show that the individual soul cannot logically be the cause without it. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of making known that the two objections raised against the *Īkṣati* and *Ānandamaya* sections have been refuted by these two sections.
Thus ends the section [regarding] the world being an illusion. 5.
2. *tantrasiddhasya* — tha. 3. *sthitam* — ā, i, ṅa, ña, u.
33. Section on the Connection of Sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa) ||1-4-6||
Beginning with this, [the text continues]:

"Verily, O Maitreyī, it is not for the sake of all that everything becomes dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear. Verily, O Maitreyī, the Self must be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. For when the Self, O Maitreyī, has been seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, all this is known."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: Is it the person established in that system (the Sāṃkhya) who is taught here as the object to be seen? Or is it the omniscient one, whose resolve is true, the Lord of all?
What is appropriate? That it is the *puruṣa*. Why?

Because the *puruṣa* alone is perceived in the beginning, middle, and end. First, at the outset, because of the impossibility of [the Self] being fond of wife, children, wealth, cattle, and so forth, it is understood to be the individual soul (*jīvātman*) alone. Furthermore, in the middle as well—

"A mass of consciousness alone, arising from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death"—this [objection] is countered by the qualifying attributes consistent with our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*). The sense is that [the Lord] is the knower of the specific actions of individual souls (*jīva*) and is capable of bestowing their fruits. Thus, the inquiry arises: Is the cause of the world known through the Vedāntas a *pradhāna* presided over by a Puruṣa, or is it Brahman? For that purpose, the inquiry concerns whether the Self (*ātman*) mentioned in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad as the object to be seen is the twenty-fifth principle (*pañcaviṃśaka*), or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Does the connection with beloved relations such as husband, wife, and son at the beginning of the passage lead one to understand that the word ‘ātman’ refers to the twenty-fifth principle (the individual soul)? Or not? Is there an inconsistency in the coordination of all the constituent parts of the sentence with the Supreme Self? Or is there an inconsistency with the twenty-fifth principle?

When there is an inconsistency in the coordination with the Supreme Self, then—since the word ‘ātman’ is understood to refer to the individual soul due to its connection with beloved relations such as husband and wife—it would follow that the twenty-fifth principle is what is stated to be "that which is to be seen," and that the Pradhāna presided over by it is what is to be known according to the Vedānta.

Thus, because of its connection with origination and destruction, it is understood to be that very [self]; likewise at the end, in the passage "By what, my dear, should one know the knower?", it is the knower, the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) alone, who is perceived—not the Lord (*īśvara*). Therefore, it is certain that this statement has as its primary purpose the exposition of the *puruṣa* established in the Sāṅkhya system.
Now, an objection:

since the passage begins with "But there is no hope for immortality through wealth," it is understood that this statement is intended to teach the means for attaining immortality. How, then, can this statement have the purpose of propounding the nature of the Person (Puruṣa)?

This is said: "For this very reason, the presentation of the Puruṣa occurs here! For in this system (tantra), it is precisely the knowledge of the true nature of the Puruṣa's own form—disjoined from the superimposition of insentient attributes—that is declared to be the cause of immortality. Therefore, the true form of the individual self (jīvātman) as disjoined from primordial matter (prakṛti) is taught here for the sake of immortality in the words: 'Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen.'"

Since the essential nature of all selves, when separated from primordial matter (prakṛti), is of a single uniform character, it follows that through the knowledge of the true nature of one's own self as separated from primordial matter, all selves indeed become known; thus, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of the Self is logically established.

When there is an inconsistency in the coordination of the constituent parts of the statement regarding the twenty-fifth principle, then—since the word "Self" (ātman) is not understood to refer to the twenty-fifth due to its connection with the beloved such as husband, wife, and so forth—it follows that what is described as the object to be seen in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is something distinct from the twenty-five; thus, the causal statements would have the Supreme Self as their purport.

"Likewise at the end" means that the word "knower" (*vijñātṛ*), which occurs in the beginning and middle [of the passage], is supported by its cause and thus has that [Self] as its referent; this is the sense. "But surely" (*nanu*) means that even before the statement establishing the relationship with the beloved such as husband and wife, it is understood that the passage has the means for attaining immortality as its primary purport.
"For this very reason" means precisely because it has the teaching of the means for attaining immortality as its primary purport.

Regarding the phrase "of all": the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one, which is the fruit of the teaching of unity, [is possible] because the nature of the Self (ātman) is of a single form—namely, consciousness—in all beings from gods down to stationary objects, provided that [the Upanishad] has as its purport the presentation of the individual soul (jīva).
Thus, there is the teaching of the identity of the Self in the statement, "All this is what this Self is," since the forms of gods and so forth are not the nature of the Self.
And there is the negation of otherness through such passages as, "He has excluded everything from him," and so forth;
and [the passage], "For where there is duality, as it were..."

And thus, by the negation of manifoldness, it is stated that within the Self, which is of a single nature, the manifoldness resulting from the distinctions in the transformations of the primordial material causes (prakṛti) such as gods and so forth is false.

Furthermore, such passages as "Verily, this Rigveda and so forth are the breath of this great Being" are also appropriate, because the origin of the world has the Person as its cause by virtue of His being the presiding controller over primordial nature (prakṛti).

Thus, when it is determined that this statement has the Puruṣa as its primary subject, then, by virtue of having a single purpose with it, all the Vedāntas denote only the Puruṣa established by their own system; therefore, it is Nature (prakṛti) presided over by Him alone that is the material cause of the world, not the Lord (īśvara).

How is this possible? For there are many individual souls (*jīvas*), and they do not stand to one another in the relation of cause and effect; anticipating this objection, [the author] states that it is established because the mode [of manifestation] is identical. This constitutes the answer.

"...and the denial of otherness [of the Self] with respect to [entities] from the gods down to stationary objects. Since the forms of the gods and so forth are non-self-forms, their non-otherness [from the Self] has been stated. Therefore, the meaning is that what is called "the perception of otherness" regarding the Self is the perception of forms such as those of the gods as distinct from the isolated essential nature; thus, its status as a cause of misfortune is being declared. As for the phrase "for where": since non-self-forms such as godhood and the like are manifold, it is denied that godhood and so forth exist within the Self, which is of a single form. This is the meaning.

"Because of having the Puruṣa as its cause. This means that since the production of sound, which is a quality of space, arises from the Pradhāna presided over by the Jīva, its being the cause of the Ṛgveda and so forth is logically established.
This being the case, we reply: "On account of the syntactical connection. It is the Lord of All alone who is understood in this passage.
Why?
Because it is only in this way that the mutual connection of the constituent parts of the sentence becomes coherent.
When Yājñavalkya had stated, "But there is no hope for immortality through wealth," [Maitreyī replied],
"What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which your reverence knows."

Thus, because wealth and such things are not means to immortality, Maitreyī—disregarding them and seeking only the means for attaining immortality—was taught that this Self, which is to be seen as the means thereto, is indeed the Supreme Self;

for by such passages as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," and "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path," it is established that the knowledge of the Supreme Person is the sole means to immortality.

The true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the Self (*ātman*), which is the attainer and constitutes a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), is to be understood as being useful for the knowledge of the Supreme Person, which is the means (*sādhana*) to liberation (*apavarga*); it is not [to be understood] as a means in its own right. Therefore, in this context, the Supreme Self alone is taught as "that which is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) and so forth, by virtue of being the means to immortality. Likewise:
"Verily, this Ṛgveda is the breath of that great Being."

The causality of the entire universe, which is being stated by such passages, is not possible for any person other than the Supreme Person—whether that be one who is subject to karma, one who is liberated, or a mere person devoid of activity. Thus, [the doctrine] becomes "samañjasaḥ"—meaning it becomes natural or intrinsic. For others assert a forced (asvarasa) connection; the intended meaning is that the "naturalness" of the Śruti consists in its having a single sense with similar scriptural passages.

"Paramapuruṣa" (the Supreme Person): the meaning is that it is natural for the sentence to have a single unified sense with the preceding statement concerning the primary means [of liberation]. "It is not possible for anyone other than the Supreme Person": the meaning is that since a bound soul lacks omniscience and other such qualities, and a liberated soul is devoid of activity regarding the world, the state of being the cause of the entire universe is not possible for either. "Of a mere person"—that is, of a mere individual soul (*jīva*). By the particle *mātra*, its limited power is indicated. "Of the Immortal"—[referring to] the knowledge of reality as it truly is. *Note: The text contains variant readings noted in the footnotes: "yāthārthyavijñānam" for "yathārthavijñānam"; "bha, i, gha" refer to manuscript variants.*
It is precisely that—no [other].

By the passage beginning with "Verily, by the seeing of the Self, my dear," the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is stated; this is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self, who is the Self of all.

As for the claim that—because the selves (*ātman*) possess a single form—the knowledge of one self is said to be the knowledge of all selves—that is incorrect; for, due to the absence of knowledge regarding the insentient phenomenal world (*acetana-prapañca*), there would be an absence of all-encompassing knowledge. Furthermore, in order to substantiate the initial proposition (*pratijñā*), [the text states]: "This is Brahminhood, this is Kshatriyahood..."
Having begun thus, [the text] says, "All this is what this Self is.

By pointing to the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is established through perception and other means and consists of a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, with the word "this," and then teaching its identity with the statement "This is this Self," such an instruction of oneness (aikātmya) is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self. For the world, which is denoted by the word "this" and is a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, does not attain identity with a person—whether that person is conjoined with the unconscious, separated from it, or abiding in their own nature.

For this very reason, there is the censure of knowing everything as something distinct from the Self, expressed in the passage: "He who knows everything as other than the Self is abandoned by all that he knows.

This is what is intended. Regarding the phrase "by the knowledge of one": the meaning is that even the promise of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one—which results from [the fact of] being the cause—is a means of establishing the final conclusion (rāddhānta).

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of establishing the proposition," he states the impossibility of teaching a single self-nature (*aikātmya*). The word "this" (*etat*) in the commentary is used in place of the word "this" (*idam*) found in the scripture (*śruti*), in order to indicate that it belongs to his own sentence. Thus, "this is this Self" (*idam ayam ātmā*) is an instruction regarding the identity of the effect with its cause. As for the passage beginning with "not indeed" (*na hi*): for indeed, the possibility of the identity of nature between the effect and the cause [is what is being considered].

The meaning is that the Supreme Self (paramātman) has both subtle and gross bodies composed of consciousness and non-consciousness; for with Him alone, as the cause, can identity with the world—which is His effect—be possible. This does not apply, however, to the individual soul (jīva), whether bound or liberated, because the soul is neither the cause nor identical to the world.

For this very reason—that everything has the Supreme Self as its essence—there is the prohibition against "finding fault" (vyatireka-nindā), which means the prohibition against contemplating anything as not being of the nature of that [Self]. It does not mean a prohibition against perceiving [the world] as gods and so forth; for the reason for the prohibition against [perceiving] difference has already been stated. Likewise, in the first Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa:

The qualities such as greatness and so forth, heard in the scripture as "the great being, infinite, and boundless," are possible only in the Supreme Self; therefore, He alone is what is being expounded here.

As for what was stated—that because the husband, wife, son, wealth, cattle, and so forth are dear to the individual self (*jīvātman*), and because [the self] is presented at the beginning as that which is to be sought, this sentence refers only to that [individual self]—that is incorrect; for if the term "self" (*ātman*) in the phrase "but for the sake of the self" (*ātmanastu kāmāya*) were to denote the *jīvātman*, it would result in a lack of syntactic connection with the subsequent statement, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*). [This is so] because of the phrase "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen."

Thus, it is understood that [the Self] was taught for the purpose of being perceived as the Self, in the passage: "But for the sake of the desires of the Self. "For the sake of the desires of the Self" means for the fulfillment of the desires of the Self. "Desire" (kāma) is that which is desired; that is to say, for the attainment of what is dear to the Self.

Since husbands and others are dear for the sake of accomplishing one's own desired ends, it would be inconsistent to say that one should abandon what is dear to husbands and others and instead seek the nature of the Self as dissociated from them. On the contrary, if it were said that "husbands and others are not dear because they are subordinate to [the Self], but rather husbands and others are dear because they are subordinate to the Self," then those very persons, being subordinate to oneself, would simply become objects to be acquired.

If the phrase "But for the sake of the self, everything becomes dear" were not connected with what follows, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result. Even if such a syntactical split were admitted, no purpose for the preceding sentence would be observed.

Therefore, just as it is understood that the Self alone is to be sought after by renouncing all things dear, such as husband and others, so too must the meaning of the sentence be described. This is stated as follows:
"But there is no hope for immortality through wealth."

Thus, having established that wealth and the like are not the means for attaining immortality—which is eternal, faultless, and of the nature of unsurpassed bliss—it is taught as follows: "The fact that wealth, sons, husband, wife, and so forth are experienced as being momentarily dear, though mixed with surpassable suffering, is not caused by the inherent nature of the husband or others; rather, it is caused by the Supreme Self, whose very essence is unsurpassed bliss.
Therefore, that which, being itself unsurpassed bliss, brings about even a slight degree of dearness in others, that Supreme Self alone is to be seen."

"Pratyuta" means that not only is there an inconsistency with one's own intended meaning, but there is also an inconsistency with what is unintended. "Upādeyāḥ syuḥ" means that, prior to the abandonment of everything else, there would indeed be a contradiction in the self being the object of vision.

"By the subsequent"—that is, by the subsequent sentence beginning with "The Self, verily. "Splitting of the sentence" (vākyabheda) means a split in the great sentence (mahāvākya). According to the maxim, "When a single unified sense is possible, a split of the sentence is not desired," the meaning is that even though it is easy to achieve consistency through a single unified sense, a split of the sentence is untenable.
"Thus" means that, since the opponent's position is untenable in this way, it is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the [text] has another meaning.

"He himself brings about [bliss]"—the meaning established is that the bliss of Him upon whom the bliss of others depends is one of infinite, unsurpassed excellence. Just as, for example, when a person bestows knowledge or wealth upon others, his superior knowledge and superior wealth are established as a matter of course; so too is this the intended sense. This is clearly stated in other scriptural passages such as "That is the one bliss of Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1), "From which words turn back," and "This [Self] is indeed the essence" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).
By the phrase ending with "is taught," the purport of the scripture has been stated.
1. By way of being the remainder—da. 2. It would follow—ṭha. This is the meaning:
"Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear."

Indeed, husbands, wives, sons, wealth, and so forth, do not become dear by virtue of one's own volition—such as the thought, "May I be dear to him for my own sake"; rather, they exist for the sake of the Self—that is to say, for the fulfillment of the desired object consisting in the attainment of what is dear to the worshipper of the Supreme Self.

For the Supreme Self, when propitiated through ritual acts, brings about the state of "dearness" regarding various objects for those worshippers, according to the specific nature, measure, time, and place corresponding to each respective action;
for "He alone causes bliss."
Thus says the Śruti. But it is not that each respective object is pleasant or unpleasant by its own inherent nature. As it has been said:
"That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, later becomes a source of pain;
for that same thing becomes a cause of anger and also a cause of serenity."
"Therefore, nothing has suffering as its nature, nor does anything have happiness as its nature.
Thus [it is said].

Even though the passage "But for the sake of one's own self" (*ātmanastu kāmāya*) refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*), the statement "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*) concerns the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone. In this regard, the meaning is as follows:

since husbands and the like are not accepted as objects of affection because they are dependent on others for the attainment of their desired ends, but rather are accepted as objects of affection by the independent Self for the sake of attaining its own desired ends, therefore—

"Specifically determined" (*pratiniyata*) means: "restriction of essential nature" (*svarūpa-niyama*) refers to the restriction that, regarding garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, "this alone is the object of enjoyment for this [person], and nothing else. "Restriction of dimension" (*parimāṇa-niyama*) refers to the restriction of the dimension of enjoyability. For indeed, a garland or other object fit for human enjoyment does not possess the same degree of enjoyability as a garland or other object fit for divine enjoyment. "This very one... is the scriptural authority (*śruti*) regarding the attainment of what is dear to those who have taken refuge [in Him]. "That alone is for the sake of pleasure" (*prīti*).

If the dearness of any object were caused by its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), it would be dear to everyone at all times; however, that is not the case. The meaning is that the dearness or non-dearness of something toward someone depends upon the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) of another. Regarding the phrase "of the Self... [the meaning is]: by that very sovereignty through which one proceeds toward the vision of one's own Self, one proceeds toward the attainment of the Supreme Brahman, which consists of unsurpassed bliss and is naturally endowed with limitless, innate, and unsurpassed bliss. [Śrī Bhāṣya 1.4.6]

"Indeed, that Supreme Self alone—which is the self's own unconditional, faultless, and limitless beloved—is to be seen; not such objects as wife, children, wealth, and so forth, which are mixed with suffering, consist of little pleasure and much pain, are dependent on others, and possess various transitory natures."

In this context, however, since even the word denoting the individual soul (jīvātman) refers to the Supreme Self alone, according to the method previously stated in the passages "But for the sake of the Self" and "The Self, my dear, is to be seen," the two instances of the word "Self" have one and the same referent. || 19 ||

In order to demonstrate that even according to another opinion the word *jīva* can denote the Supreme Self, he says: "129. Āśmarathya [holds] that it is a sign for the fulfillment of the initial proposition. (1.4.20)

This is the logical mark (*liṅga*) because the thesis that "all cognitions [are one] through a single cognition" is established. As for the word denoting the individual soul (*jīvātman*), its deviation from the usual sense of the word "Self" (*ātman*) must be tolerated due to the excellence of the suitability of the meaning—namely, that supreme bliss alone is what is to be sought. This is like the deviation of the word "Brahman" found in the two sentences of the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, "By austerity Brahman is built up" and "Therefore this is Brahman. Thus is the sense. "[The two words refer to] the same object."

The intention is that there is no absence of the opposite of the word "ātman. As for the phrase "because of the designation of the individual soul (jīvātman)," this was stated with the view that words denoting the individual soul have as their ultimate referent the Supreme Self, according to the method set forth in the sūtra to be cited later. || 19 ||

The teacher Āśmarathya held the view that [the word "Self"] is a designation for the Supreme Self (paramātman). If this individual soul (jīva) were not the Supreme Self itself by virtue of being an effect of the Supreme Self, then, because it would be distinct from Him, the knowledge of this [individual soul] would not be accomplished through the knowledge of the Supreme Self. [As it is said:
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."
Thus, because of the determination of oneness prior to creation, [it is said]:
"Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks of the same nature fly forth by the thousands, even so, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable (akṣara), and into it they also merge."

Because of such passages as these, which record the origin of individual souls (*jīvas*) from Brahman and their subsequent dissolution into that very same [Brahman], the identity of the individual souls with Brahman is understood through their being effects of Brahman.
Therefore, the term ‘individual soul’ (*jīva*) denotes the ‘Supreme Self’ (*paramātman*). || 20 ||
130. Auḍulomi [holds that the soul departs] because it is about to depart from such a state. 1.4.21.

This is the position of Yādavaprakāśa, which has been introduced here by way of the [logical] reason; for in that system, both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—both in their causal and effected states—are held to be innate. || 20 ||
The statement following the word "jīva" refers specifically to one who is about to depart [from the body];
for this is the opinion of the sage Auḍulomi, based on the attainment of equality with Brahman.
1. Knowledge of the Supreme Self—i.
by means of the individual self (jīvātman)—da. the Supreme Self alone is—i, ga. • of the individual selves and so forth—da. • denoting the individual self—da.

As for what was stated— that Brahman is presented by means of the term "jīva" in order to establish the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" through the identity of the jīva with Brahman as its effect—
that is incorrect; for [the scripture says], "The wise one is neither born nor does he die."

Because of such [scriptural] passages as these, which declare that [Brahman] is eternal; because it is accepted that the world is created by the *jīvātman* for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its prior karma; and because otherwise, the creation of an unequal world would be inexplicable; therefore, liberation—which consists in the *jīva*, being an effect of Brahman, attaining the state of Brahman—is unavoidable, just as in the case of ether and other elements. Furthermore, the injunctions and performance of the means to that [liberation] would be rendered useless, and since liberation, like a jar or similar objects, would consist in the destruction resulting from the merging back into the cause, it would not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
The justification for the doctrine of the origination and dissolution of the *jīvātman* will be elaborated upon later.
"On account of the abiding [of the individual soul in Brahman], so says Kāśakṛtsna. (1.4.22)

As for what was stated—that because the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of Brahman when about to depart, it is designated by that [Brahman] term—that too is untenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis. Is this non-Brahman-nature of the individual self prior to its departure innate (*svābhāvika*), or adventitious (*aupādhika*)? Even in the latter case, is it ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real?
If it were innate, the state of being Brahman would be impossible; for since difference is inherent to one's own nature, as long as that nature exists, that difference cannot be removed.

Now, if it is argued that its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) also departs along with the difference, then, because it would have perished, it could not attain the state of Brahman; furthermore, defects such as it not being a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) would follow. If, on the other hand, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), then since it was already Brahman even prior [to liberation], it would be improper to state the distinction made in the Sūtra: "Because of its becoming such [Brahman] precisely at the time of departing" (*utkramiṣyata evambhāvāt*).

For on this view—since there is no other entity apart from Brahman, and since it is impossible for the partless Brahman to be "cut" by an adjunct (*upādhi*)—the distinction resides solely in the adjunct; therefore, even prior to departure, it is Brahman itself. Since the distinction based on an adjunct is not ultimately real, [one might ask: "Whose state of being Brahman is this during departure?"

In order to eliminate the position favored by the opponent from among the two possible alternatives, an alternative between being intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) and being adventitious (*aupādhika*) has been made. Furthermore, an alternative between being ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) and not ultimately real has been made; this is done to make it known that both positions stated by Śaṅkara and Bhāskara—which were indicated by the single sūtra "of one who is about to depart" (*utkramiṣyataḥ*)—are intended to be refuted by this [present] [sūtra].
Thus it must be said.
[If it is argued: "It is Brahman itself whose own nature is concealed by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*),"...

No; for it is impossible for that whose very nature is eternally liberated self-luminous knowledge (*svaprakāśajñāna*) to have its manifestation obscured by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). Obscuration, by definition, is the cessation of the manifestation of a thing while its essential nature remains present.

If one accepts that "manifestation itself is the essential nature of the thing," then there would be either an absence of obscuration or the destruction of the essential nature itself. Therefore, since its own nature is eternally manifest, there is no distinction between its state as Brahman and its departure; thus, the qualification "of one who is about to depart" (*utkramiṣyataḥ*) is indeed redundant.

By the phrase, "having risen up from this body," it is not stated that one who was previously not of such a nature attains the state of Brahman at that time; rather, it refers to the manifestation of a pre-established essential nature. For it will be stated later:
"The manifestation [of the self] occurs through its own [nature], because of the word [itself]."
By such [statements] as these.
Therefore, [it is said]:

"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman)"; "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is the inner controller (antaryāmin), the immortal Self"; and "He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know—this is the inner Self of all beings, the one divine God, Nārāyaṇa, free from evil."

...it is indeed useless. For the state of being Brahman belongs to the soul that is about to depart, whereas it does not belong to one who is not such; since there is no difference [between them], there is nothing to be excluded.

Manifestation (*āvirbhāvaḥ*)—like the making manifest of light that was previously existent but concealed by removing the impurity from a gem; it is the bringing forward of the eightfold qualities (*guṇāṣṭaka*) inherent in the very nature of the Self. [Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): "having risen from this body, one attains the supreme light"—Iśa Upaniṣad, Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā].
At that time—[as stated by] Da. Siddha—Tha. [says]:

Because [the Lord], as the Teacher who has entered within all people and is the Self of all, abides as the Self within the individual soul (jīvātman) which constitutes His own body, the teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintained that the word *jīva* refers to Brahman. Furthermore, it was already stated previously that the word *jīva* denotes the individual soul only insofar as it culminates in the Supreme Self, and not merely the individual soul alone.
In the passage: "Let me evolve name-and-form."

Thus, by establishing identity through the state of the self being the body, the Sūtrakāra has accepted the view of Kāśakṛtsna alone; for in this way, all the Śrutis—those concerning the Supreme Brahman's freedom from sin, omniscience, and so forth; those concerning the ignorant, grieving individual soul (jīva) and its liberation through the meditation on Brahman; those describing the creation and dissolution of the world; and those intent on teaching the identity of the world with Brahman—are properly accounted for.

This is the meaning of the passage here: when Maitreyī asked about the means to immortality, Yājñavalkya, having stated that meditation on the Supreme Self is the means to immortality through the words "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen," and so forth, concludes with "When the Self, indeed, my dear, is seen..."— because an interpretation according to any other doctrine would be untenable.

"Because of abiding" (*avasthiteḥ*): the meaning is that [the Lord] abides within those [bodies] by way of being unknowable to them, being their controller, and being free from defects. "And the word 'jīva'": the meaning is that the application of the principle of the generic form (*ākṛtinaya*) to words denoting bodies has been established. By the phrase "in this [sūtra]," the meaning of the sūtra has been explained.

Since this sūtra was not placed before the statements of the views of Āśmarathya and Auḍulomi, and since no other view is introduced thereafter, it is understood that the resolution according to the view of Kāśakṛtsna is the intention of the author of the sūtras.

The two terms "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and "omniscience" (*sarvajñatva*) are intended to demonstrate the possession of both sets of attributes. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to qualities such as freedom from old age (*vijaratva*) and omnipotence (*sarvaśaktitva*). By the phrase ending with "those that speak of liberation," the scriptural texts concerning difference (*bhedaśrutayaḥ*) are intended. The phrase "creation and dissolution of the world" is stated with the intention of [establishing] non-difference (*abheda*). "Properly" means in such a way that there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, nor any mutual internal contradiction. The meaning is that the reason for accepting this interpretation is its consistency with the primary sense of all the scriptures and its lack of conflict with them. "And another, O King, is that Supreme... [etc.]

Having thus generally described the characteristics of the object of meditation (*upāsya-lakṣaṇa*) by means of such passages, as well as the restraint of the "instruments" (*karaṇa*)— beginning with the mind— which serve as the equipment for meditation through analogies such as the drum,
[the text continues] with the passage beginning, "Just as from a fire fed with damp fuel... (*sa yathā 'rdrāidhāgneh*).

Having extensively taught— by means of such passages as "Just as the ocean is the one goal of all waters"— that the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of meditation, is the sole cause of the entire universe and the regulator of the entire collection of organs that serve as the root of activity toward all objects, [the text continues]: "Just as a mass of salt..."
Having stated, "A mass of consciousness alone, arising from these elements, perishes after them," and then saying,

"There is no consciousness after death," [the text] describes the absence of knowledge regarding forms such as gods and so forth within the self— having identified it with the aggregate of elements— due to the absence of contraction of its natural, unlimited knowledge at the stage of liberation; and then again,

By the passage beginning with "For where there is duality as it were," it is shown that the perception of "things" as manifold, due to their not having Brahman as their self, is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*). Having refuted the perception of difference for one who has discarded all ignorance and experiences the entire universe as having Brahman as its self—since there is no other entity apart from Brahman—the regulation of the instruments [of knowledge] is elaborated through the demonstration of specific details; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of encouragement": the meaning is that when it is understood that one's own true nature alone is the goal to be attained, then activity and so forth arise.

"Having established [the point] by stating an illustration": this refers to "the conformity with the transformation of the elements. The meaning is that when the elements perish, this [self] perishes. Regarding the word "perishes" (*vinaśyati*): "perishing" here means the absolute contraction of knowledge; for this does not contradict the immediately following statement, "Indeed, this self is indestructible" (*avināśī vā are ayam ātmā*). The word *pretya* refers to the end of the final body, as is recognized from the meaning of another scriptural passage: "not remembering his rebirth" (*nopajanaṃ smaran*).

The intention here is that its subject matter is liberation (*mokṣa*), because even in this context, immortality (*amṛtatva*) is stated [as the goal] in the words, "This much indeed, O Āre, is immortality. Regarding the term "natural" (*svābhāvika*): the fact that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of knowledge is stated in passages such as, "As a mass of salt... From this, its naturalness is established. By the word "immediately following" (*anantara*), since its consisting of knowledge is stated even externally, it is proven that it possesses knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*).

The intention is that its being unlimited is established by another scriptural passage: "For he, as a seer, sees all. [Regarding the phrase] "once again": delusion is of two kinds—the notion of the body in what is not the self, and the notion of independence due to not having Brahman as one's essence. Among these, by the statement "after departing there is no consciousness," the cessation of the delusion of identifying the body with the self—which persists during the state of bondage—is declared; now, the cessation of the notion of self-subsistence is being stated. "In which" refers to that particular state.

"Duality, as it were, comes to be"—that is, a separation from the Supreme Self, a separation existing by virtue of its own inherent nature. The word "as it were" (iva) indicates that such independence lacks scriptural authority. Regarding the phrase "by not having Brahman as its self": since the negation of manifoldness applies to manifoldness other than that which is prescribed [in scripture], the intention is that the manifoldness existing by its own nature is what must be negated. Regarding the phrase "by the absence of the appearance of Brahman...": for knowledge that lacks scriptural authority arises from a defect; however, in the absence of defects, one realizes the actual existence of reality, as in: "By what means would one know Him through whom one knows all this?"

And thus: "By which Supreme Self (paramātman), abiding as one's own self, the individual soul (jīvātman) has been infused with knowledge and thereby perceives—by what could one perceive That? By nothing at all.
Having established the difficulty of comprehending this Supreme Self, it is stated that [the individual soul] perceives this "all" [through Him].

By the passage beginning with "Not this, not this" (neti neti), it is declared that this Lord of All is by His very nature distinct from all other sentient and insentient entities; that He exists as the Self of all, having everything as His body; and that He is not touched by the defects residing in those sentient and insentient entities which constitute His own body.
Having thus taught, [the text] concludes: "O Maitreyī, you have received the instruction: 'By what means, my dear, could one know the Knower?'"

"O dear one, this much indeed is immortality"—having thus stated that the means to immortality is this very meditation (*upāsana*), and that the attainment of Brahman is what is designated as immortality, [the Teacher] declared: "How could one not know the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who is of a nature entirely distinct from all other things, who is the sole cause of the entire universe, and the knower of all? Thus he spoke.

Therefore, it is established that in this passage the Supreme Brahman alone is being propounded; thus, the Supreme Brahman is the cause of the world, and not the Puruṣa nor the Prakṛti presided over by him. || 22 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the syntactical connection of sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||

The meaning is that [the Self] cannot be established without being perceived. Regarding the phrase "distinct from its own other...": since a negation of a prescribed mode is impossible, and because the modes of consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*) are established by other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the two instances of the word *iti* refer back to those modes, while the two subsequent negations exclude the modes residing in consciousness as well as those in non-consciousness (as in the passage: "Not this, not this"). The phrase "the knower" (*vijñātāram*) demonstrates qualities such as omniscience, which pervade the causality mentioned at the beginning of the context.

The sense is that the word "vijñātṛ" (the knower) [is used]. The statement "vijñātāram" (the knower) is intended to conclude the previously mentioned means by way of excluding other means. The meaning is that the statement beginning with "etāvat" (only this much) is intended to conclude the goal to be attained.
Thus ends the section concerning the syntactical connection of the sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||
2. *sarva* [is] by means of which—*vā*. *rūpa*—*i*, *gha*, or *vā*. By being the body of all—*da*.

Being—*vā*. Fault—*vā*.
