Section 34: The Topic of the Primordial Nature (Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1.4.7.

Although the Vedāntas establish the omniscient Lord as the cause of the world on account of His association with qualities such as *īkṣaṇa* (seeing), nevertheless, it is perceived that "by the Vedāntas themselves, the *pradhāna* alone is established as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. For the Vedāntas do not convey the causality of the world for an omniscient, unchanging presiding Lord (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) without the *pradhāna*, which is the insentient, changing object of His governance (*adhiṣṭheya*).
For it is thus: they study this [Self] as unchanging, and Nature as changing while presided over by Him—[as stated in the scriptures]:

"Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless"; "This indeed is the Great Self, undecaying and immortal"; "The unborn, eternal, eightfold Nature, the producer of transformations"; and: "Presided over by Him, she (Nature) thinks, she expands, she produces again; and directed by Him alone, she brings forth the world for the sake of the Puruṣa."
"She is the white one, without beginning or end, the mother, the bringer-forth of beings.

Likewise, it is heard in scripture that "the Lord creates the entire universe by presiding over *prakṛti* as its material cause," provided there are no obstacles. Since, in the absence of such obstacles, the primary sense of the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) must be maintained, the Vedāntas establish that Brahman is also the material cause. Thus, in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the relationship between the result and the means is that Brahman alone is the material cause.

In the phrase "seeing and so forth" (*īkṣaṇādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to bliss (*ānanda*) and other qualities. The underlying sense is that these very [attributes] are intended by the Vedāntas as having Brahman as their sole cause, precisely as you yourself maintain. Regarding the words "for not": since the Lord is sentient, he is unchanging and acts as the presiding controller; whereas the Pradhāna is insentient, it undergoes transformation and is the object to be controlled. This fact of being established by the Vedāntas serves as the reason for the proposition stated. The passage beginning with "without parts" (*niṣkala*) concerns the Lord's state of being unchanging.

Regarding the phrase "the producer of transformations": this refers to the fact that *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is subject to transformation and is that which is presided over [by the Lord]. "The mother" (*janitrī*) means she who effects the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*). "The bringer of beings" (*bhūtabhāvinī*) means she who effects the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*). Thus, in the passage establishing *pradhāna*, the Lord's status as the presiding controller is shown by way of its qualification. In the passage establishing the Lord, he demonstrates his distinction from that *pradhāna*, which serves as the material cause, by virtue of being its presiding controller.
The meaning is that by the word "Maheśvara," it is intended to express the state of being the impeller of Māyā with respect to the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa) designated by the word "Māyin.
As it is said: "From Him, the Māyin creates this entire universe... one should know Māyā to be Prakṛti and Maheśvara to be the Māyin. Smṛti also states:
"Under my supervision, Nature (prakṛti) produces the world of the moving and the unmoving.

Thus, even though the fact that Pradhāna is the material cause is not explicitly heard [in this verse], the nature of Pradhāna and its status as the material cause of the world when presided over by the Lord are established solely through the necessity of otherwise accounting for Brahman's causality of the universe as taught in scripture.
This being the case, it is replied: "And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

That is to say, it is both the material cause (*prakṛti*)—meaning the substrate (*upādāna*)—and not merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); Brahman alone is the material cause as well. Why? Because...

Because there is no contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For in this very way, neither the proposition nor the illustrative example are contradicted.
First, the proposition:
"You have not truly asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3)
Thus, the knowledge of one thing is the object of the knowledge of all things.
And the illustration is:
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known," and "just as, my dear, by means of a single nugget of gold."
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter," this refers to the knowledge of the effect arising from the knowledge of the cause.

If Brahman were merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of the world, then the entire world would not be known through the knowledge of it; for a pot and the like are certainly not known through the knowledge of a potter and the like. Therefore, there would indeed be a contradiction between the initial proposition and the illustrative example.

If Brahman alone is the material cause—just as by the knowledge of a lump of clay, a piece of iron, or a magnet (the *nakhanikṛntana*), which serve as material causes, one comes to know their effects such as a jar, a water-pot, a bracelet, a crown, an axe, or a hatchet—so too, when Brahman, who is the material cause of the entire universe, is known, that entire universe, which is His effect, would be known. This is the illustration of the cause itself in its different states. The employment of many illustrations is for the purpose of making the intended meaning clear.
By the word "not," the impossibility [of the opposite] in the case of the contrary view has been stated.

"Of Brahman alone"—thus he states the reasoning for the point already explained. In this way, the word expressing the reason in the Sūtra has been interpreted. "The cause alone"—in this manner, the meaning of the passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) has been stated; for therein, the identity of effect and cause is established. By supporting the initial proposition through examples such as clay and its modifications—showing that the "arrived at" effect is not a different substance from its cause—it is determined that Brahman alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world.

As for the claim that "the distinction between the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) is perceived by scripture itself"—that is incorrect; for the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause is perceived [in the text]:
"Or rather, did you ask for that instruction (ādeśa), by which what is unheard becomes heard? That by which one instructs or commands is the "instruction" (ādeśa).

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (akṣara)... Here, the agent is intended in the sense of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). From the statement, "Ask him who instructed you—that instructor by whom what was unheard becomes heard," it is understood that there is an identity between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), since it is by that instructor, the presiding controller, through whom even the unheard becomes heard.

"Brahman alone. Now, an objection is raised: "If Brahman is the material cause only in its state denoted by the term 'unmanifest' (*avyakta*), then because it would lack the status of being the material cause of everything, there would be a contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñā*). Alternatively, if Brahman is the material cause even in states such as that of a jar, then since clay would lack the status of being the material cause, there would be a contradiction with the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To this we reply: the first horn of the dilemma does not apply, as it is refuted by our own non-acceptance [of that position]. As for the second, there is no contradiction, because Brahman—possessing as its body the substance existing in states such as clay—is indeed the material cause.

The causal relationship between the mere substance of clay, which serves as a qualification, is cited as an example because it is well-known in the world. However, the causal relationship of Brahman—whose very body consists of the substance in its various respective states—is the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika), since such a relationship is not well-known in the world; thus, there is no contradiction with the example in the formal proposition.
As for the phrase "yattu" (but as for that), it restates the establishment of the difference between the efficient cause and the material cause by the scripture itself:

because of the determination of oneness prior to creation in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," and because of the exclusion of any other presiding agent by the word "without a second."

Now, an objection may be raised: if this is so, how can the eternity of Prakṛti and its status as the material cause of the world—heard in such scriptural passages as "the mother of transformations" and "the cow [Prakṛti] is without beginning or end"—be logically established?

To this it is replied: even there, Brahman itself, in its causal state where name and form are undifferentiated, is designated by the word "Prakṛti"; for there exists no other entity apart from Brahman. Thus indeed say the Śrutis: "He who knows all else as different from the Self," and "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"
"Everything abandons him," and so forth;
"All this, indeed, is Brahman."
And because of the scriptural teaching: "All this has that as its self," which means that the entire world, in both its state as effect and its state as cause, has Brahman as its self.
This is what is being said:

"He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know"—this being so, meaning that since Brahman alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world; [the opponent objects]: "Regarding the beginning and end": it is improper for Prakṛti to have Brahman as its material cause, because she is heard in scripture to be eternal. Therefore, the intention [of the objection] is that Prakṛti alone is the material cause, and Brahman is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*).

By the word *prakṛti*—that is, by a word denoting primordial nature (*prakṛti*). "Due to the absence of *brahman*" means due to the absence of any other entity established as separate (*yutasiddha*). "By what could one see what?"—by what? By a means of perception that is not of the nature of *brahman* but is established in itself; what? An object established in itself; who? A conscious being. "Could see"—the meaning is that there exists neither a means for perceiving an object established in itself, nor an object of sight established in itself, nor a seer thereof.

In this context, the negation of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing is not what is to be established; for by a portion of its own statement, "But where everything has become the Self alone," and by other passages such as, "The seer sees everything," the experience of all things as being of the nature of Brahman is enjoined. The scripture has already stated that there is no other entity existing independently of itself. In the passage beginning with "All this indeed," the scripture provides the scriptural authority for the fact that everything has that [Brahman] as its self. Starting from there, it says: "He who moves within the Unmanifest, whose body is the Unmanifest, whom the Unmanifest does not know..."

"Who, moving within the Imperishable (akṣara), of whom the Imperishable is the body, whom the Imperishable does not know; who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, of whom the earth is the body, who controls the earth from within"—beginning thus, and so forth.

"And [it is said]: 'He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Thus, the Supreme Brahman is at all times the Self of all, having all conscious and unconscious things as its body; sometimes it has differentiated names and forms, and sometimes it has undifferentiated names and forms. When its names and forms are differentiated, it is spoken of as manifold and as the effect; and when its names and forms are undifferentiated, it is spoken of as the one, non-dual cause."

Thus, at all times, that causal state of the Supreme Brahman, whose body consists of both conscious and unconscious entities, in which name and form are undifferentiated, is "that which has a beginning and an end, such as the cow."

"It is designated by such [scriptural passages] as 'the ignorant producer of transformations' and 'the one unborn,'" thus from the scriptural texts concerning dissolution (*pralaya*), the origin and dissolution of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) are perceived. And likewise in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest, which consists of the three qualities, was produced [from Him];
O Brahmin, the unmanifest dissolves into the inactive Puruṣa."
This is not a fault; for Brahman, whose body is non-sentient matter, has as its effect the state consisting of the three guṇas, which is denoted by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta).
As it is said: "When there was darkness, neither day nor night existed."

Thus, because it is stated that even during the state of total dissolution (kṛtsnapralaya), the extremely subtle insentient reality (acidvastu) which has Brahman as its self persists, the extremely subtle insentient reality—which constitutes a mode (prakāra) of the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the world—is indeed eternal; and Brahman itself, having that as its mode, is designated in such passages as "Gaurī is without beginning or end."

For this very reason, it is heard in scripture that there is merely a state of becoming one with darkness, as in: "The Imperishable dissolves into darkness; darkness becomes one with the supreme deity"; it is not, however, a dissolution (*laya*). By the term "becoming one" (*ekībhāva*), what is designated is the abiding of Brahman—which is of the nature of subtle consciousness—in a state where name and form are undifferentiated.

This is not a fault. For even in the unmanifest state (*avyaktāvasthā*) of the signless entity, a subtle state is possible; that state is Brahman qualified by consciousness (*cidviśiṣṭa*), meaning it is the unmanifest cause (*avyaktakāraṇa*). The proof for this is the verse beginning with "When there was darkness" (*yadā tamaḥ*).

Therefore, even at that time, the meaning is precisely because of the existence of the insentience (*acittatva*) which is a mode of Brahman denoted by the word "darkness" (*tamaḥ*). The distinction between words is based on the distinction between their referents; and the distinction between referents occurs in accordance with all the Śruti texts—this is the intended sense. Regarding "becoming one" (*ekībhāva*): this becoming one occurs only when the state of being darkness is established, and from that state, there is the attainment of an even subtler condition.

Indeed, darkness that was previously divided does not later become one; rather, there is merely a difference in state (*avasthāvaiṣamya*). For division is indeed a difference in state. Therefore, division is the state of being slightly less subtle. Non-division (*avibhāga*), on the other hand, is the attainment of the highest degree of subtlety. Even in the absence of identity of the essential nature (*vastusvarūpa*) of the things, the use of the word "one" is observed based merely on their inclusion within that [state]; for example, the word "one" is used for wood before fire has emerged from friction. Thus, the meaning of the word "dissolution" (*laya*) is simply the attainment of another state, and not the destruction of the substance (*dravya*). This is the sense.

"Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; there was no sign of anything. That One was born from the power of darkness"—this also refers to this very same thing. And likewise, the statement of Manu:
"This world existed as darkness, unperceived and without distinguishing marks."
"Beyond reasoning and unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
"From this, the Master of Māyā creates this entire universe."
And so forth; this will be demonstrated immediately hereafter, as will the scriptural texts concerning the unchangeability of Brahman.

As for the argument that it is impossible for one and the same entity to be both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), and that an effect must be produced by a single causal factor because such a rule is observed in the world—therefore, like the statement "sprinkle with fire," the Vedāntic texts are incapable of establishing production from a single source alone—this is [refuted as follows]:

To this it is replied: everything is possible for the one Supreme Brahman alone, who is distinct from all else, omnipotent, and omniscient. For non-intelligent matter such as clay and the like lacks the capacity to act as a presiding agent due to the absence of knowledge; and for presiding agents such as potters, there is an absence of the power for diverse transformations, as well as a lack of volitional intent, which necessitates the observed regularity [of their actions]. Therefore, Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world. 23.

For this reason as well, both are Brahman alone:
"He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "It thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

Thus, because the Creator, Brahmā, teaches his own resolve to become manifold: for creation is taught as being preceded by the resolves, "May I alone become many in the form of diverse conscious and unconscious beings," and "May I be born forth. 1.4.24. And because both [the self and the world] are directly declared [in scripture]. 1.4.25.

This matter is not determined merely by means of propositions, illustrations, intentions, and instructions; rather, that Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause is directly declared in the sacred tradition.

The phrase "from this" (*itaśca*) means that this reason is connected with the proposition (*pratijñā*) found in the preceding sūtra. The literal meaning of the words of the sūtra has been stated up to the point "because of the teaching of volition" (*saṅkalpopadeśāt*). The term "variegated" (*vicitra*) is used to exclude the possibility that becoming many is like [the case of] Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. Since the creation of fire and the other elements was mentioned immediately prior in the passage "He created fire" (*tattejo'sṛjata*), the intended meaning is that "becoming many" refers to the state of being manifold in the form of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). Furthermore, because He Himself becomes many, He is the material cause (*upādāna*); for this becoming many is in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with His volition.

"I declare to you with my mind, O wise ones: Brahmā stood presiding over, sustaining the worlds. Herein, when it is asked from a worldly perspective, "What was the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Creator Brahmā? And what were his instruments (*upakaraṇa*)?", it is resolved that for Brahmā—who is distinct from everything else—the possession of all powers is not contradictory; thus, Brahmā alone is both the material cause and the instruments.
Therefore, both are Brahmā. || 25 ||
Because of self-origination. (1.4.26)

"He desired: 'May I become many; may I procreate. The intended meaning is: "What was that forest?—where was he previously situated? "What was that tree?—what was the material cause? "That upon which he stood, supporting the worlds"—the meaning is: "What were the instruments and other means by which the Lord, while supporting the worlds, presided over them? In the reply as well, "Brahman is the forest"—meaning the locus. "Brahman is that tree"—meaning the material cause. In the phrase "they carved out," the plurality is not intended to be significant.
Because of the scriptural statement, "As he fashioned them in the beginning," which declares that heaven, earth, and so forth have a single creator, a plurality of creators is impossible.

[Objection: But is this not contradicted by the statement that [Brahman] is "the source of both"? For there is the perception of identity between the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and the agent (*kartṛ*). [Reply: It is not so; for causal factors are included within two categories: the object to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya*) and the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). Indeed, the material cause, the locus, and the instruments fall under the category of the object to be presided over. For it is heard in scripture: "That which he presided over" and "Brahmā presided over, supporting the worlds. Therefore, it is logical that [Brahman] is the source of both. || 25 ||

Because of the teaching— that is, because it is made known by the very scripture stating, "It [Brahman] made itself by itself" (*tadātmānaṃ svayamakuruta*)— that the Self, which is none other than the Supreme Brahman, acts as the instrument for its own creation in the form of the universe, Brahman is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the created object; therefore,
Brahman is said to be both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*).

Thus, regarding Brahman under discussion as desiring to create, from the statement "He made Himself by Himself," both the objecthood and the agency of creation are perceived; since He Himself brought about His own manifoldness, it is perceived that He alone is both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). Since the Self, whose name and form were undifferentiated, is the agent, and that very same Self—whose name and form were undifferentiated—is the effect, there is no contradiction between agency and objecthood. By the words "Himself" and "made Himself," He is shown to be both the efficient cause and the material cause. (26)

"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"; "Brahman is bliss"; "It is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst"; "It is partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless."

Regarding this very Great Self, which by its very nature has the scent of all defects pertaining to sentient and insentient beings removed, and which consists solely of unsurpassed knowledge and bliss—belonging to the Supreme Brahman—how is the "becoming manifold" (bahutvakaraṇa) of the Self possible through the prior volition of becoming many, in the form of the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness, which is the locus of diverse and infinite human goals? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "mūn... (He entered).

"Of the self alone" means that for the self, its own status as agent toward itself is untenable; for that which is an effect is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas the agent is already established (*siddha*). Thus, there is a contradiction between being established and not being established for one and the same entity. "Undivided" means that there is no contradiction between establishment and non-establishment due to a difference in form (*ākāra-bheda*). "By itself" means the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause (*nimitta-upādāna-ekya*). || 26 ||

"Truth" (*satyam*). Since the subject sentence of the preceding sūtra is located within the *Ānandavallī*, and because the absence of defects and the possession of auspicious qualities—along with their lack of contradiction—are immediately perceived in the preceding and following passages of that section, the two sentences beginning with "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) are first cited. The word "truth" (*satya*) refers to the state of being free from modification (*vikāra*); other passages such as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*) serve to clarify this quality of being devoid of defects and so forth. 136. On account of transformation (*pariṇāmāt*), 1.4.27.

Because transformation is its inherent nature. The intended meaning here is that the nature of this transformation being taught with respect to the supreme Brahman is not "being subject to defects," but rather, on the contrary, it is precisely "bringing about unimpeded sovereignty. For it is in this very way that transformation is taught.

The Supreme Brahman is that which is solely devoted to auspiciousness as the antidote to everything that is to be abandoned without exception; which is distinct from all other things; which is omniscient, whose will is ever true, and who has attained all desires; who is infinite and unsurpassed bliss; and who constitutes the Self of the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient entities—which serve as the instruments for His own sport—by virtue of being their body.

When the phenomenal world, which is His own body, remains reduced to a single, extremely subtle insentient substance denoted by the term *tamas* through the successive causal chain beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, [He remains] even when that *tamas* is His body...

Regarding the phrase "because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*): in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the scriptural texts concerning the distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), as well as the impossibility of explaining the faultless scriptures otherwise, were presented as the reasons. In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, two types of scriptural presumptive testimony (*śrutyarthāpatti*) were shown to establish the final position, namely: "Because of the non-contradiction of the initial proposition and the illustrative example" (*pratijñādṛṣṭāntānuparodhāt*) and "And because of the teaching of [Brahman's] volition" (*abhidhyopadeśācca*). Furthermore, by means of the two sūtras beginning with "And directly from the mention of both" (*sākṣāccobhayāmnānāt*) and by the sūtra "For He is also declared to be the source" (*yoniśca hi gīyate*), the scriptural passages that establish the final conclusion have been demonstrated.

The meaning of the sūtra "from transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*) is that it is intended as a refutation of the scriptural citations and the presumptive arguments (*arthāpatti*) presented by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). Regarding the term "transformation": one might raise the objection that when "from transformation" is stated, it is perceived only as a cause for contradiction, and not as a cause for the removal of contradiction; anticipating this, [the author] states, "the intention is not...". The word "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to a specific kind of transformation.

In expressions such as "Bring the cow," the use of a general term is observed to intend a specific particular. In [Sūtra passages] such as "He is known from the word alone" (ŚB 1.3.24) and "Because of the mention of dharma" (ŚB 1.3.25), a general reference is seen in the Sūtra itself to intend a specific meaning. Just as in the phrase "from the word understood here," the meaning is "from the transformation understood here."

When that [Brahman] has attained oneness within itself through falling into an exceedingly subtle state that is not fit for separate designation, it is Brahman with such a body of darkness (*tamas*). Then, having formed the resolve, "May I become one whose body is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, with names and forms differentiated as before"—it transforms itself into the body of the universe through the process of superimposition (*adhyāsa*); this is the teaching of transformation (*pariṇāma*) found in all the Vedāntas.
Similarly, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the fact that the entire world is the body of Brahman and that Brahman is its "Self" is recorded in scripture (*āmnāyate*).

Beginning with: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," and so forth.

"Of whom water is the body," "of whom fire is the body," "of whom the intermediate space is the body," "of whom air is the body," "of whom heaven is the body," "of whom the sun is the body," "of whom the quarters are the body," "of whom the moon and stars are the body," "of whom space is the body"—it would be improper to mention these separately. However, it is not intended here that they are entirely incapable of being mentioned; for just as fire, which is included within burning, is not mentioned separately from the burning itself, yet is still designated by the word "fire" when distinguished from external fire.

The intention is as follows: just as there exists a disparity consisting of a specific degree of subtlety even while the nature of fire is not abandoned, so too, even when the nature of darkness (*tamas*) is not abandoned, there exists a disparity in the form of an excellence of subtlety between the differentiated darkness and the non-differentiated darkness.

This is stated by taking up the entire collection of scriptural passages beginning with "She whose body is water" (*yasyā āpaḥ śarīram*), in order to show that although the intermediate principles (*avāntaratattva*) are heard to be causes for each subsequent one, the causality belongs only to the Supreme Self who has those very principles as His body—thus [concluding] the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa*.
"Of whom darkness is the body," "of whom light is the body," "of whom all beings are the body."
"Of whom breath is the body," "of whom speech is the body," "of whom the eye is the body."
"Whose body is hearing," "whose body is mind," "whose body is skin," "whose body is discernment," "whose body is semen."
Thus ends the reading in the *Kāṇva* recension.

"whose self is the body. Furthermore, the status of the world, the Veda, and the sacrifice as the body of the Supreme Self is additional [in this version].

Thus it is said. Here, by the word ‘death’ (*mṛtyu*), the extremely subtle non-sentient substance denoted by the word ‘darkness’ (*tamas*) is designated; for in that very Upaniṣad, the sequence is recognized thus: “The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into darkness. Since it is the root of all souls’ ignorance and its concealment of knowledge, that very darkness is indeed what is designated by the term ‘death. Furthermore, in the Subāla Upaniṣad itself, it is stated that those elements which are of the nature of Brahman as His body dissolve into Brahman alone.

It is taught [in scripture]: "The earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air; air dissolves into ether; ether dissolves into the senses; the senses dissolve into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); the subtle elements dissolve into the *bhūtādi*; the *bhūtādi* dissolves into the Great Principle (*mahat*); the Great Principle dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (*akṣara*); the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness (*tamas*); and Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. Even in the state of attaining non-distinction, the conscious and unconscious reality remains in an extremely subtle state, accompanied by its karma and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), as will be explained later.

Since the word ‘mṛtyu’ (death) is used to denote both a particular deity and transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and since neither of these two is suitable for connection here, he says: "of all. Because it consists of the obscuration of knowledge, it is denoted by the word ‘tamas’ (darkness). The meaning is that because that very [obscuration] is the root of the misfortune consisting of the obscuration of knowledge, it is denoted by the word ‘mṛtyu’.

In the passage, "Space [is merged] in the sense-faculties, the sense-faculties in the subtle elements," the term "merger" (*laya*) is not employed because there is no actual state of merging. In that context, mere concomitance (*sāhitya*) is intended. There is no intention behind the plural number in the word "subtle elements" (*tanmātreṣu*); it is like the expression "Aditi [bound] the fetters" (*aditiḥ pāśān*). The meaning is "in the subtle element of sound. Regarding the phrase "attainment of non-distinction":

just as the plurality of conscious beings is established because an unequal creation would otherwise be impossible, so too the status of the conscious reality (*cidvastu*)—which conforms to the creation of bodies according to their respective karmas—is established by the force of the impossibility of a modification of its own essential nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*).
Thus it is said.

Thus, from that very one, non-dual, unsurpassed blissful, omniscient, and true-willed Brahman—who is the extremely subtle body consisting of both sentient and insentient entities and who has become one with the Supreme Self such that He cannot be designated as distinct from Himself—there is heard a transformation into the form of the world, preceded by the volition to become manifold by way of having a gross body consisting of sentient and insentient entities fit for the differentiation of name and form. This is stated in the passages:
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite";
"Different from this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss"; and "For He alone causes bliss."
"He desired: 'May I become many; may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he emitted all this, whatever exists here. Having emitted it, he entered into that very thing.

Having entered it, he became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and non-consciousness, and the real and the unreal—he became the Real."
Thus [it is said].

Here, by the word "austerity" (*tapas*), knowledge consisting of the contemplation of the structure of the world from a previous [cycle] is denoted; for there is the scriptural text: "His austerity consists of knowledge," and so forth. The meaning is that, having contemplated the configuration of the world created previously, he now created the world with that same configuration. For in this very way, Brahman creates a world of identical form in every cosmic cycle (*kalpa*).

The phrase "unfit for the designation of division" means that just as the state of having name and form undifferentiated—which, though not explicitly stated in the *Ānandavallī*, is understood through other scriptural passages such as those establishing unity—is accepted; so too, it must be admitted that the state of having the sentient and insentient as its body is intended here in the causal condition. Regarding the word "ālocya": the meaning is "contemplation of the world" due to propriety. The sense is that the word "tapas" is derived from the verbal root √tap in the sense of "contemplation" (*ālocana*).

"Having that same configuration" means with the intention of creating as before. "For in that very way" means that the demonstration of creation as it was before serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for that observation.

As it is said: "The Ordainer fashioned the sun and the moon as before; he fashioned heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and also the sky. And: "Just as the seasonal signs of various forms appear in their cycle according to the seasons..."
"Those very same things are seen in each successive age," according to the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

The meaning of this is as follows: The Supreme Self (Paramātman), whose nature is self-revealing knowledge and bliss, who is beyond all limitation, and who—due to His extreme subtlety—is "without conceptualization" (asaṅkalpa) yet consists of that [knowledge-bliss] because He has as His body the conscious and unconscious entities that serve as the instruments for His own sport; desiring to engage in diverse and infinite play, transformed Himself through a succession of His own embodied bodies consisting of the collective totality of Prakṛti and Puruṣa down to the gross elements, making Himself identical with them; and then, becoming identical with those [elements], assumed the form of the universe—consisting of a mixture of various conscious and unconscious beings from the gods down to stationary objects—which is denoted by the terms *sat* and *tyat*.

"It entered into that very thing; having entered it," it is said: "The Supreme Self alone, who existed as the Self in the causal state, remained as the Self even of the substance undergoing modification into the form of the effect, and thus became each of those things."

Thus, when the Supreme Self undergoes transformation into the form of the world as a composite of consciousness (cit) and matter (acit), all defects that constitute non-human goals (apuruṣārtha) reside solely within the conscious portion that serves as the body of the Supreme Self; likewise, all modifications reside within the insentient portion. Within the Supreme Self, there is the state of being the effect in those two respective conditions, yet He possesses the nature of the Self by virtue of being their controller. The Supreme Self, however, being the Self of those two which have become His own body, is not touched by the non-human goals or the modifications residing therein.

Consisting of undivided knowledge and bliss, He remains eternally of one single nature, yet abides through the sport of the transformation of the world. This is expressed by the text: "Both the real and the unreal became the Real. Although Brahman undergoes modification in the form of the manifold sentient and insentient universe, He remains truly real—meaning He remains of one single nature, free from even a trace of defect, consisting of undivided knowledge and bliss.

"All conscious and unconscious entities, whether in their subtle or gross states, are the instruments of the dissolution of the Supreme Brahman; and creation and the rest are His pastimes (līlā)," so it has been stated by the venerable Vāyāyaṇa, Parāśara, and others: "This entire world, from the unmanifest (avyakta) up to the specific (viśeṣa), which is joined with the process of transformation—let it be understood that all this is the perishable play of Hari. "Behold His activity, like that of a playing child," and "as a child [plays] with toys."

By such statements as these, and as he will further state—namely, "the [qualities] residing in the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) which constitute its modes are not the goals of man"—in order to distinguish them, there is a designation of difference between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, who are the "bearers of the body" (*śarīrabhṛt*) of Brahman; for even though they have become one with Brahman at that time by falling into an extremely subtle state that precludes such designation, they are designated as distinct, since this is consistent with passages such as "He made Himself His own Self" (*tadātmānaṃ svayamakuruta*). And thus says the *Mānava* [Smṛti]:
"Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures, he, having meditated, emitted water from his own body; into that [water] he deposited his seed.

For this very reason, the scriptural texts concerning Brahman's "faultlessness" and "changelessness" are justified. Therefore, Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world. (27)

By this collection of logical principles stated in the four quarters [of this chapter], all specific passages in all the Vedāntas that are intent upon propounding the cause of the world are explained as being intent upon propounding Brahman—the omniscient and omnipotent one who is distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious. The repetition of the word "explained" (*vyākhyātāḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. || 29 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the explanation of all [scriptural passages]. (8)

The inquiry is as follows: Do these specific statements of the proponents of causality (*kāraṇavādin*), which have not been explicitly cited, refer to the Brahman characterized as previously described—distinct from both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*)? Or do they not? To that end, the question is: Are those statements outside the scope of the aforementioned logical arguments (*nyāya*), or are they within its scope? Is it possible for them to be within its scope, or not? When it is not possible, then because they are not within its scope, there is an absence of reference to the Brahman characterized as previously described. When it is possible, then because they are within the scope of the aforementioned logical arguments, they do indeed refer to the Brahman characterized as previously described; such is the relationship between the means and the result.

The phrase "by this" (*etena*) refers to what was stated in the four quarters [of the *Brahma-sūtras*], in order to exclude the notion that it merely refers to the logic of the *prakṛtyadhikaraṇa*. "Specific passages" (*vākyaviśeṣāḥ*) means those not previously cited whose meaning was uncertain. For omniscience and omnipotence are indeed necessary for [Nārāyaṇa’s] status as both the efficient and material cause. Thus, it is established that Nārāyaṇa’s causality—through the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with others—is demonstrated by the four quarters. This is the repetition of the term.

Regarding the statement "those explained and those unexplained": if the words *vyākhyāta* (explained) and *avyākhyāta* (unexplained) were compounded into a single word (*aikapadya*), it would follow that all specific statements [of the sūtras] would not be said to have been explained. To avoid this, he states the purpose of the repetition (*abhyāsa*) in order to indicate that they are separate words rather than being compounded. || 29 ||
Having thoroughly examined the venerable commentaries composed by previous wise men, this concise *Ṭippaṇī* has been well-composed for the benefit of students. *Oṃ namaḥ paramarṣibhyaḥ*.
Thus ends the section concerning the authority of all commentaries (Section 8).
The Recitation for Final Peace (*Uttara-śānti-pāṭha*):

Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest to me. You two are the leaders of the Veda; do not abandon what I have heard. By means of this study, I shall speak throughout the days and nights; I shall speak the truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace! I join [the parts] together. May the Truth protect; may it protect the speaker.

May Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us. Homage to you, Vāyu! You alone are the manifest Brahman. To you alone, the manifest Brahman, have I spoken. I have spoken the *ṛta*; I have spoken the truth. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. It has protected me; it has protected the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
Oṃ. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor enmity toward one another. Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace!
Oṃ. That is fullness, this is fullness; from fullness, fullness arises. When fullness is taken from fullness, fullness alone remains. Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.

Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and likewise strength and all my senses, swell with vigor. May I never deny Brahman; may Brahman never deny me. Let there be no denial, let there be no denial for me. May those virtues that reside in the self-delighting ones who are devoted to the Upaniṣads be in me; may they be in me. Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!

Oṃ. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones. With steady limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods. May Indra, of far-reaching fame, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheels are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.

Oṃ! Salutation to Brahman! May there be retention for me; may there be no forgetting. May I be a retainer. What has been heard by my ears, let that not depart from me—neither here nor in the hereafter—for such-and-such a person. Oṃ! Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!

Oṃ. May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman. Thus ends the Supplements (anubandhāḥ) composed by the venerable Rāmānuja.

2) The Essence of Reality (Tattvasāra), composed by the venerable teacher Vātsyavarada.

In the *Chāndogya*, some say that in the passage "they asked about the instruction (upadeśam) which is most excellently taught (ut-tama-ādeśam)," the prefix *āṅ* reveals the sense of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) as belonging to the existent (*sat*), whereas the suffix *ghañ* does not denote the agent. Here, the *ghañ* is not used in the sense of the agent, but is counted among the suffixes for the object; thus, the existent (*sat*) is the agent in the act of teaching (*śāsti*), not the object.

"It may be so; it may be so" (syāt syāt) [is used] in the instruction regarding karma; thus this very thing is to be taught by means of the word "instruction" (ādeśa). Some—the Advaitins—in the *Chāndogya*, that is, in connection with the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, in the passage beginning "Or did you ask for that instruction? (*uta tam ādeśam aprākṣyaḥ*), [the word] preceded by the prefix *āṅ*—that is, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*—ends in the suffix *ghañ*.

This is a word-by-word commentary on the *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṃgraha*, the *Tattvasāra*, and the *Adhikaraṇasārāvalī*, composed from the beginning by the editors of these works, N.S. Rāmabhadrācārya.

The word *ādeśa* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* and the root *diś* (meaning "to point out," i.e., the verbal root *diś*). It reveals—that is, it propounds—the instruction (*upadeśa*) concerning the Existent (*sat*), which is Brahman as denoted by the word *sat*; that is, it makes known what was previously unknown. However, it does not reveal—that is, it certainly does not communicate—the governance (*praśāsti*) of the Existent, meaning the regulation presided over by the entity that is the Existent. (If one asks why? Because the suffix *ghañ* does not denote the agent; the suffix *ghañ* is not established by grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) as conveying a meaning in the form of an agent.

(But) only in the case of [the root] *karman*, which signifies the meaning of "action" (*karma-rūpa-artha-bodhane*), [it is used] according to the grammatical rule established by Pāṇini: *agaṇi*—"and in the sense of a factor other than the agent, when it is a name" (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*). Here—in this context—the reality denoted by the word *sat* would be the agent (*kartṛ*) in the acceptance of the meaning of the act of teaching (*śās-tau*); that is, it would be precisely the agentive factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*) with respect to the action denoted by the verbal root *śās*, and not the object (*karman*), meaning it would not be the objective factor (*karma-kāraka*) at all (that is to say, it would not be a factor distinct from the agent). That—

For that reason, this—being "existent" (sat)—in the context of "instruction" (*upadeśa*), where the root *diś* has the sense of instructing, would be the object; it would indeed be the object. Therefore, by the word "instruction" (*ādeśa*), they say and describe it thus: this, which is signified by the term "existent," is declared as the very object of instruction—the subject matter intended by the Śruti. || 16 ||

To this we reply: [The word] *praśāsti* denotes the act of commanding; it does not denote instruction, for that is already well-known. Nor is there here any occasion for an unintended meaning. It is appropriate through the use of a common term; even though the suffix *ghañ* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), here the intended meaning (*vaivakṣikatva*) is expressed by the grammatical rule regarding the factors of action (*kāraka*): indeed, there may be an intention to express the agent (*kartṛ*) by means of the instrument (*karaṇatayā*). (17)

Regarding this objection that has been raised, we reply: we describe the resolution in this way. In this sentence, the word "ādeśa" used with the prefix *āṅ* in the sense of direction (*diś*)—as he instructs or speaks—it conveys through its power only the meaning of commanding, namely *niyamana* (restraint). It does not, however, convey *upadeśa* (instruction), which is the making known of what was previously unknown. (If one asks why? That verbal root *diś*, preceded by *āṅ*, is extremely well-known in the sense of teaching or instruction (*praśāsana*).

The domain of common usage belongs to others—that is, to the meaning in the form of instruction just mentioned; for it is certainly not well-known here, in the sense of "ruling" (*praśāsana*), that there would be an occasion for a required meaning—the introduction of the meaning in the form of a command suitable for being the instrumental cause—[an introduction] which is appropriate and consistent by virtue of being joined with a unique expression, namely, the statement of a quality exclusive to the Supreme Self.

In this context—either in the section prescribing the *ghañ* suffix, or regarding the word "instruction" (*upadeśa*) itself—a certain *ghañ* suffix has been taught even for the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), because of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*; as should be understood from the fact that *ghañ* is applied here in the sense of the instrument). Now, the fact that grammatical factors (*kāraka*s), such as the object and so forth, are determined by intention—that is, they are dependent upon the speaker's intent—is indeed expressed by words; for the grammarians have certainly accepted that "the *kāraka*s arise from the speaker's intent. (Therefore...)

Even though Brahman is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sense of being the causal factor of agency (*kartṛ-kāraka*) in the act of commanding, there may be an intention to regard it as the instrument (*karaṇa*); that is, its status as the instrumental causal factor (*karaṇa-kārakatva*) could indeed be the intended meaning, and this is entirely appropriate. || 17 ||

3) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, composed by the venerable Vedāntācārya: Thus, when the Supreme Self— characterized as the cause of the universe, established by the scriptures, and the fit object of unconditional, supreme love— is presented as being "uncreated" (*akṛta*), it might be argued that such a nature would not belong to Him, just as it does not belong to *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, who are unfit for inference and other means of knowledge.
And since those two are untouched by suffering, the subsequent exposition proceeds in due order. || 54 ||

Thus, by means of this introductory section (*upodghātapeṭikā*) consisting of four topics: [the Brahman] which is "uncreated" according to the established view; which is the object of the valid knowledge produced by the scripture as its "established essential nature"; which is to be understood through the definition of being the cause of the universe—that is, having the form of being the cause of the world; which is to be established by the scripture and whose true nature is to be determined by nothing other than the scripture; and which is worthy of unconditional supreme love—as that which is uncontradicted and infinite...

In the one possessed of extraordinary bliss, in the Supreme Self—the highest of all, the Self of all, the Supreme Person—who has become the object of inquiry (prasakta) by virtue of possessing the attributes necessary for being an object of investigation; then, in the second section, in the fifth and sixth chapters respectively, suchness—that is, the causality of the universe and so forth established in the first section—would belong, as appropriate, to both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, namely to the *pradhāna* accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.

It is logical that there be no contradiction regarding those two principles denoted by the term *puruṣa*; yet, those two—the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*—are incapable of being [known] through inference and so forth, meaning they are beyond the scope of such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and they are untouched by suffering, meaning they are incapable of connection with suffering. [The opponent argues: "They cannot be thus; rather, they must be within the scope of inference and so forth, and they are indeed touched by suffering. Such is the statement of the opponents' prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). [The author] clears away this by refuting it after having examined it. || 54 ||

That observation [of becoming many] is secondary due to its association [with the primary sense]; it is not at all a primary perception of becoming many. Here, through examples and other means, an inference is fashioned which appears as such; thus, it is logical that birth [proceeds from the Unmanifest].

Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the word "Sat" (Being) denotes the root-prakṛti while excluding its modifications, because other [entities] are excluded by the Śruti and because there are signs and so forth that refute what you intend.

Regarding "sati"—in the entity signified by the word "sat" (Being), the perception of becoming many—that is, the knowledge in the form of a volition (*saṅkalpa*) directed toward becoming many, such as "May I become many"—is certainly not primary; it cannot be non-figurative, but is indeed only secondary (*gauṇa*).

Because of the association with secondary seeing (*gauṇekṣā*)—since [the term "seeing"] is recited together with secondary seeing, which consists of the tendency toward creation, as found in fire, water, and so forth, in passages such as "That fire saw" (*tatteja aikṣata*); and because here, in the context of the Knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*), there is the appearance of an inference through examples and other means—such as the example beginning with "Just as, my dear, by a single lump of clay"—it appears that inference is the subject at hand. Therefore, the birth of the gross [world] must proceed from such an insentient source, namely the Pradhāna, which is established through inference.

The arising of the insentient world is logical—it becomes established. By that aforementioned reason, the word "Being"—this word "sat" mentioned at the outset in the phrase "Being alone [existed]"—is itself devoid of modification, being non-substantial in its own transformations.

"Root-nature" (*mūlaprakṛti*)—precisely that which is denoted by the term "root-nature"—one should utter—that is, one should propound—and not the conscious [Self]; thus, such a reflection is not tenable. This is because there is the intention to refute the meaning accepted by you through the direct Upaniṣadic word containing the term "Self," namely, "This is its Self" (*aitadātmyam*), as well as through the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and other evidence that contradict what you maintain.

Because of the cessation of other [factors]—such as the manifesting causes (prakṛti) and their indicative signs (liṅga)—due to the indicators such as "seeing" (īkṣaṇa), there is an obstruction to their manifestation. || 55 ||
The proposition "when one is known, all is known" is stated for the sake of establishing non-duality;

and the triad of clay, its effects, and so forth, are mentioned here as its various illustrative examples. Therefore, the claim that "the inference of the Unmanifest [Prakṛti] has been stated" is a vain longing, because no reason has been given, and because similarity and other such reasons have already been refuted above, while here only a mere possibility is asserted.

"In one place"—in a single object; for when it is known—that is, when it has been fully understood—"everything is known"—the entire world becomes known. This proposition (*pratijñā*)—of such a form, consisting of the statement of the object desired to be proven and serving as a member of the inference—is heard in the *Upaniṣad*. And that [proposition] serves to establish unity; it is the motivator for the realization of the non-difference between cause and effect. Here—in the task of establishing the meaning of the proposition—it [is the motivator].

Regarding the non-difference between cause and effect (which is what is sought to be established), there are three types of illustrative examples—distinct instances cited and explained as specific illustrations: clay and its effects such as a jar or a bowl; a piece of iron and its iron product; and a nail-cutter and its product, which is black iron. By means of this statement of the proposition and the illustrative examples, the "unmanifest inference" (avyaktānumāna) of the Sāṅkhya is [established].

The objection that "only inference has been stated regarding the Pradhāna" is essentially what has already been addressed; it is a vain longing—a mere curiosity that is fruitless—because no reason has been stated. This is because there is an absence of a logical statement (*hetuvākya*), which is the primary member of an inference; furthermore, as for the reason consisting of "similarity" (*sārūpya*)—namely, the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the common form of the world-process and the Pradhāna due to their nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—that has already been refuted later on in the section concerning the Sāṅkhya.
In this context—within this section—because it is stated as a possibility, merely dispelling the doubt of impossibility, there is no tautology. || 56 ||

Because of the teaching of identity with You through terms such as "Ādeśa," "Ātman," and "Svaśabda," which offer no other refuge; because of the entry of the non-conscious aggregate—along with its ego and its sense of "I"—into its own self as the individual soul (jīva); and because of the statement that "by the knowledge of One, all is known," which expresses identity with all, the Knower of the Universe, whose form is the universe, becomes manifold even through the various branches of knowledge and so forth. || 57 ||

By these words—namely "instruction" (*ādeśa*), "Self" (*ātman*), and "own" (*sva*)—which are not dependent on anything else (meaning, which cannot be established by any other means of proof) and are heard in such scriptural passages as "that instruction," "He is the Self," and "he has gone to his own."

By means of words [acting as indicators], because of the instruction of their identity in the phrase "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*)—which serves as the indicator through the teaching of non-difference between the referent of the word *tvam* and the referent of the word *tat*—by means of itself, that is, by its own nature as the individual soul (*jīva*), together with the ego-sense (*sāhaṅkaraṇam*), meaning preceded by the notion of its own agency, there occurs an entry into—that is, an internal penetration into—the non-"I," meaning the collection of insentient things distinct from the referent of "I"; thus, by a single cognition, all [is known].

By the word "known" (vidita)—that is, by the statement in the form of a proposition, "When this is known, all this becomes known," and by the scriptural utterance expressing the identity with all, "All this has that as its self"—which establishes the universal selfhood of Brahman; and from other branches of knowledge within the same Veda, such as the Taittirīya branch, as well as from other meditations such as the Dahara-vidyā, and likewise from the Smṛtis and Purāṇas which serve as indicators—He who was about to become many, thinking, "May I be many."

The one who possesses agency preceded by volition, the knower of all—omniscient—and whose form is the universe—having the entire world as its body—is the Supreme Self alone, denoted by the word "Being"; it is not the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) favored by the Sāṅkhyas. || 57 ||
4) *Adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha* composed by Śrī Mahācārya:

Thus, by means of the four sūtras, the establishment of the subject matter to be examined—consisting of the demonstration that the Vedānta texts possess authority regarding Brahman—and the establishment of its auxiliary elements have been accomplished; now, the examination of the specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is undertaken.

In the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, having raised the objection that— in the passage "In the beginning, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*)— the insentient [matter] denoted by the word "this" has as its cause that which is denoted by the word "Being," and since a cause must necessarily share the same nature as its effect, the cause denoted by the word "Being" is none other than the insentient *pradhāna*— it is stated that the one denoted by the word "Being" is the Supreme Self, because of the scriptural mention of "seeing" (*īkṣati*) and because the Supreme Lord, whose body consists of both consciousness and unconsciousness, can possess all the characteristics [attributed to the cause].

5) The *Nayasaṅgatimālikā*, composed by the illustrious Śrīnivāsācāryas of Lakṣmīpura—a science that is the very essence of Vedānta—declares that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the cause [of the world]. Thus, the refutation of this objection shall now take place in the section concerning the "seeing" (*īkṣati*) in the Sūtra. (31)
Thus, many types of conjunctions have been described according to their various divisions; among them, the primary one has been summarized here for the sake of pacifying the student's distraction.
Thus ends the section concerning "Iksati" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.5–11).
The Section Concerning that Which Consists of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa) || 1.1.6 ||

1) In the *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha*, [the author] refuted the view that the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes a modification (*vikāra*), fearing that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) might thus be suspected of being "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). Instead, he established that it denotes abundance (*prācurya*), because [the status of being a modification] is impossible [in this case] and because [such an interpretation] would lead to the abandonment of [the meaning of] "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*). || 13 ||

Regarding the suffix *mayaṭ*: in the word *ānandamaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies a modification (*vikāra*), being prescribed by the rule "the modification thereof" (*tasya vikāraḥ*). For this reason—from such a cause—one might suspect that the *ānandamaya*—that which is denoted by the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) read in the *Ānandavallī*—is the *kṣetrajña* (the embodied soul), having raised the objection that it is merely the individual self (*jīvātman*). However, because of impossibility—that is, because the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) is contradicted in the case of the individual self—and because of the abandonment of the meaning of modification for the *mayaṭ* in the very word *prāṇamaya* (due to its occurrence in the *prāṇamaya* section), [one concludes] "on account of abundance" (*prācurya*). Thus, the *mayaṭ* contained within the word *ānandamaya* [denotes abundance].

By the rule "mayat [is used] in the sense of 'made of that' when referring to the subject at hand," [the suffix] is taught as denoting only the sense of abundance; thus Bādarāyaṇa refuted—and cast aside—the doubt that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is of the nature of the individual soul (jīva). || 13 ||

There is also the hearing of the suffix *mayaṭ*, which denotes a meaning that is a modification (*vikāra*); for these reasons, the "tail"—that which is read as "Brahman is the tail, the support"—must indeed be Brahman. Being unknown to the world, partless, changeless, and inherently pure, it is fit to be denoted by the word "Brahman. However, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman; the object expressed by the term *ānandamaya* cannot be Brahman.

And that [sheath], namely the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), like the *annamaya* (consisting of food)—just as the object denoted by the word *annamaya*—is described and established by the Śruti as being merely an external casing, serving as a means for descending into the supreme Brahman. || 18 ||

The arguments for [the Self] being the tail have been refuted because: it is the primary subject expressed in the masculine gender; it is the principal topic under discussion; it is designated by words not shared with anything else; the verses do not mention a "tail"; it possesses its own inherent nature (*svarasa*); there is no other internal principle; because of its state as a constituent part indicated by the genitive case and so forth; because of its representation as being limitless; because of its conformity; because of its synonymy; and because of its expression as having no nature other than itself. (Verse 19)

The word "he" (*saḥ*) in the sentence "He desired" (*so'kāmayata*)—which is masculine in gender, primary, and refers to the subject under discussion—is [the basis for the conclusion]. Furthermore, there is the description (*rūpaṇa*) by means of limbs such as the head, wings, and tail, which are not different from the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) itself; and likewise, the verses beginning with the one concerning the Self consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with those concerning the Self consisting of bliss do not state that these are the tail.

They certainly do not say "no tail" (which would be a non-statement)! For us—who maintain that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) alone is Brahman—this is the natural meaning, expressing a literal sense without figurative interpretation. Furthermore, the Sūtra—the Sūtra concerning the section on the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamayādhikaraṇa-sūtra*)—also supports this; likewise, there is no absence of the phrase "another inner self" (*anyo'ntara ātmā*) in the section on the one consisting of bliss, as there was in each of the preceding sections. These points establish that the one consisting of bliss is indeed the Supreme Self.

And [the arguments] beginning with the genitive case: in the phrase "of that" (*tasyaiṣaḥ*), the word "of that" (*tasya*) is in the genitive; there is no mention of the *ānandamaya* in the verse; Brahman’s partlessness; the hearing of the "embodied self" (*śārīra-ātman*); the statement that the *ānandamaya* is to be purified; and that the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of modification—such is the form [of the objection]. As for the reason regarding the "tail": it is the point established by the proponents of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) through the establishment of the tail itself as Brahman; however, the meaning [of our position] is due to the state of being a part—that is, because the relationship of part and whole is understood—and because [Brahman] is known without limit.

Because the suffix *mayaṭ* conveys abundance (*prācurya*) by virtue of [Brahman] having the nature of unsurpassed bliss; because it is a figurative representation (*rūpaṇa*), for even though [Brahman] is partless, parts such as a head and a tail are accepted as mere figurative representations for the sake of intellectual ease; because of its conformity (*ānurūpya*), since purification consisting of the induction of serenity—which conforms to that [bliss]—is admitted with respect to the Supreme Self; because of synonymy (*paryāyatva*), since the words "Brahman" and "consisting of bliss" bring about the same meaning; and because it expresses a non-different essence—for this very reason, [it excludes] any other essence...
Because it is impossible for it to have the form of a statement that makes known [the probandum], it is rejected—that is, it is reduced to the status of a fallacy (a *hetvābhāsa*). || 19 ||
3) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

If the primary inquiry (*mukhyekṣā*) is desired, let it be so; however, that [inquiry] applies to the nature of the individual soul (*jīvatattva*), for in the *Sadvidyā* [section], the identity of that [Self] which exists above with the three words [of "That" and "Thou"] has been stated. To pacify the doubt arising from such an inference, the Creator of the universe, who is the inner Self even of the individual soul and possesses unsurpassed great bliss, is now established here. (58)

If "īkṣā"—the act of seeing described in the passage "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), which is primary (not figurative), unique to a conscious being, and of the nature of volition—is intended as the desired meaning, then let that distinct act of seeing be admitted as existing in the principle of the individual soul (*jīvatattva*)—that is, in the living being denoted by the word *puruṣa*—which is indeed fit for such a connection with that kind of seeing.

For, in the *Sadvidyā*—by means of the three words contained within the *Sadvidyā*, namely the three terms "That," "Thou," and "Art"—the identity with that *Sat* (Being) which was introduced as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), that is, the non-difference of the referent of the term "Thou" from the Being who is the referent of the term "Sat," is stated nine times in succession; thus, by this method, through *ūha*—relying on the reasoning consisting of the contemplation of what is appropriate—[it is established].

In order to pacify the opponent who is intent on denying that Brahman—which transcends both the conscious and the unconscious—is the cause of the world, and to establish the Lord as the author of the universe by accepting Him without agitation; then—in this subsequent section, namely the *Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa*—the one previously characterized as the cause of the world is introduced: He who possesses unsurpassed great bliss, being a vast ocean of natural supreme bliss; the creator of the universe, the maker of the world; and [He who is] even for the individual soul... merely.

Even for this conscious being, there is a connection with volition; the Inner Self—the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who, residing within, is the sustainer, the controller, and the sovereign—is established—that is, determined through the prior exposition of logical reasoning. || 58 ||
It is incorrect to argue that because the suffix *mayaṭ* was seen previously in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*), it must likewise apply here at the end;

for its absence is observed in the middle cases. Furthermore, the suffix here denotes abundance (*prācurya*), as any other meaning is precluded. This abundance of bliss refers to the supreme happiness under discussion, since it has attained its limit through the minimal presence of suffering.
There is no dependence on the minimization of suffering, because the Teacher—who destroys the misfortunes of others—is the very opposite of such [limited] states.

Because it was observed—that is, known—that in the first instance, in the word *annarasamaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* was taught as signifying a modification (*vikāra*), this serves as a reason for the suspicion that even in the final instance, in the word *ānandamaya* heard at the end, it should likewise be so—that is, let it signify a modification; however, this is improper, as it is not uncontradicted. For in the middle—in the words *prāṇamaya* and so on—a break in the sense of *mayaṭ* signifying modification is observed.

Because of this observation, here—in the word *ānandamaya*—the suffix (*mayaṭ-pratyaya*) expresses "abundance" (*pracura*), because any other meaning is precluded, as no meaning other than abundance is applicable to that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*). It denotes, that is, makes known, only an object possessing the abundance of its own primary referent. Furthermore, the abundance of bliss—that is, the state of possessing abundant bliss—is independent of the scarcity of suffering; it does not depend upon a deficiency of suffering co-located with itself in relation to its own self as a limiting correlate.

Because they have attained a limit due to the inferiority of the happiness of others under discussion—namely, those beings from humans up to Prajāpati who are distinct from the Supreme Brahman, having obtained their own limit through the deficiency of happiness relative to Him—and because they are destroyers of the misfortunes of others—that is, the eradicators of the sins rooted in the suffering of others—and because they are the rulers, the controllers of all, of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), there is a contradiction with that [state of being], namely, the sublation of the possession of even slight suffering. || 59 ||
"It is His very Self"—thus it is stated in order to declare that He alone is not of the nature of anything else;

and the mention of the "embodied one" (śārīra) with respect to Him refers to His being the Self of all bodies, functioning without limitation. His state of being "to be purified" is in accordance with various specific purposes; thus, for the Lord, it consists merely in His being propitiated.
When this [Self] is attained as the goal, the "transmigration" (upasaṅkrānti) of the higher knowledge takes the form of attainment within the ocean of bliss.

In order to state—that is, to establish—this very [supreme] Self's uniqueness (anitarātmatvam), which is its freedom from any other controller, [the scripture] declares: "This indeed is His Self" (in the section concerning the *ānandamaya*, it says: "This indeed is His embodied Self"). This was spoken—that is, recorded—in the Śruti.

In that Supreme Self—which is understood through scripture even as being bodiless—the description of Him as "the embodied self" (*śārīra ātmā*) is a characterization of His connection with a body; yet, because He is the "Self of all" as established by scripture through His state of having the entire universe as His body, this application is non-restricted—that is, it is primary and not figurative. "The state of being purified" (*śodhyatva*) means the state of being an object of purification. "In accordance with those respective meanings" means it is inherent to the very nature of the entity.

However, it is not of a single uniform kind everywhere; for that reason, the cause of purification pertaining to the All-pervasive One—the Supreme Brahman who consists of bliss, who is the controller of all, and the purifier of all—is merely the state of being propitiated. This consists solely in bringing about His graciousness by removing His intention to punish, and not in the removal of impurity as occurs in the case of the conscious and the unconscious.

In the ocean of bliss—the unsurpassed great ocean of joy—which is the Supreme Self (paramātman) established by scripture as the goal to be attained by the liberated; for the knower of the Supreme (paravidaḥ), that is, the devotee of the Supreme Self, there is "approaching" (upasaṅkrānti)—the approaching mentioned in the scripture, "He approaches the Self consisting of bliss"—which consists precisely in the experience of the nature of the Supreme Self, a state not previously experienced, and which takes the form of attainment. Thus, everything is perfectly consistent. || 60 ||

If it is argued that in this bodiless and partless [Brahman] there can be no assumption of a head, wings, tail, and so forth, and therefore the statement "the tail is the support" refers here to the Supreme Brahman appearing as such—[we reply: if the assumption of "tail-ness" is accepted, why would the other [limbs] not be admitted? For the statement regarding the Self being the support of Brahman must be understood as intended to proclaim its lack of dependence on any other substratum.

In this Supreme Brahman—which is established by scripture as being bodiless through such texts as "the bodiless," and which is understood from scripture as being partless through such texts as "without parts" (meaning devoid of limbs)—there can be no construction of a head, wings, tail, and so forth; that is, the conceptualization of limbs such as the head, flanks, and tail is simply not possible, for it is not at all consistent.

Therefore—for that very reason—in this context of the *ānandamaya*, it is stated that "the tail is the support" (*pucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*). If you argue that the entity actually mentioned in the scripture as "Brahman is the tail, the support" appears to those who contemplate the meaning of the scripture to be the Supreme Brahman itself, denoted by the term "Supreme Brahman"—if such a doubt is raised, it is certainly not logical. For the postulation of being a "tail"—that is, the conceptualization of something having the form of a tail even in an entity that is partless—is untenable unless it is accepted [as a figurative device], even if it lacks logical justification.

If, on the other hand, the "other"—that is, the head, wings, and so forth beyond the tail—is to be postulated, on what basis or for what reason (*kaṃ hetum avalambya*) could it be so conceived? It would not be accepted—that is, it would not be admitted—as there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Regarding Brahman, who is designated by the term *ānandamaya* as the Supreme Self, the statement concerning its being "established in itself" (*ātmapratiṣṭha*)—the declaration that it is its own support—is solely for the purpose of proclaiming that it has no other substratum, and for the sake of strengthening the fact that it is established in its own majesty (*sve mahimni*). || 61 ||

On account of having a body—namely, because of the evidence of possessing a body as inferred from the mention of specific parts such as "golden-bearded, golden-haired, unto the very tips of his nails" and so forth—the Person established by scripture as residing within the solar orb in the passage "He who is within the sun," is a certain conscious being alone, namely the individual self (the *jīva*), distinguished by superior merit and excellence.

However, [the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa] dispelled—meaning he removed—the doubt, that is, such a challenging thought, by means of attributes belonging to the Supreme Self, such as being the Lord of the worlds, which consist of being the Lord of desires, freedom from sin, and so forth; these are attributes of the Supreme Self, excluded from anything other than the Supreme Self, and are read within the context of this section. || 14 ||

"Kam" means water; by the etymological derivation "that which drinks water," it refers to the stalk of a lotus (*kamala-nāla*). "Bhavati kapiḥ" means it ought to be denoted by the word "monkey" (*kapi*). Regarding that lotus-stalk understood by the word "monkey," whatever object has its natural seat (*āsa*)—where *āsa* denotes a particular mode of sitting—that object situated on the stalk is what the wise, such as Brahmanandin and others who know the meaning of the Vedas, call "kapyāsa," denoted by the term "kapyāsa."
