They intend this: in the manner described, that which is signified by the word "kapyāsa"—the lotus (*saroja*), meaning the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) which is radiant, endowed with an excellence of beauty, and sublime, being exceedingly vast—is declared to be the illustrative example for the eyes of the Lord, the Blessed Nārāyaṇa; it is made known by the Śruti text: "Just as the lotus is the *kapyāsa* upon his [face], so are his two eyes. || 21 ||
"Kamudaka" here means "thirst," whether it be its seat or its origin;

thus the poets have declared it "kapyāsa" (monkey-arse) because of the emergence of water from that deep [well]. The lotus is cool, sweet, and glorious, appearing like the glance of the eye of Śrī-Dāmodara;
the letter *api* (the syllable 'a' in 'kapyāsa') has its form lost, as if concealed by the following vowel. 22.
*Kam*—the meaning denoted by the syllable *ka* contained within the word *kapyāsa*; *udakam*—water itself; *iha*—in the water.

"Āsana" means that which has its location (*sthiti*); that is, for whatever kind of object it is possible [to exist]. Or else (*yadi vā*), "here" (*iha*) means in water; "pyāsa" refers to the meaning of the word "pyāsa" contained within the compound "kapyāsa"; or "udbhava" means that which has the sense of arising or origin. Thus, for whatever kind of object it is possible—that entity in the form of a lotus (*ambhoja*) which either resides in water or is produced in water—is called "kapyāsa" by the poets (*kavibhiḥ*), those seers (*ṛṣibhiḥ*) who possess beautiful vision, as in: "The eyes are like the *kapyāsa* lotus."

Thus it has been stated—that which is explained by the word *kapyāsa* as found in the Śruti—[the lotus] is "cool and sweet" due to its arising and abiding in deep water; that is, it is full of extreme coolness capable of warding off all heat and of extraordinary loveliness capable of captivating all the senses. It is "glorious," meaning endowed with supreme splendor. The "lotus"—that is, a flower most tender and delicate—becomes the object of the gaze of the eyes of Damodara, [as performed] by Śrī Yaśodā.

This may serve as a comparison for the eyes of the Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is captivated by the bond of parental affection (*vātsalya*). Furthermore, the prefix *api* contained within the word *apyāsa* has its vowel *a* elided; indeed, it is simply a case where the vowel *a* is not heard. This is like the word *apihita* and others; just as in words such as *apihita*, the form is established through the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule "Bhāguri accepts the elision [of the vowel] after *vaṣṭi*" (*vaṣṭi bhāgurirallopam*), so it is here. || 22 ||

Regarding the word *pyāsa* within the compound *kapyāsa*: just as the solar disc is the referent of the term *pyāsa*, and just as the lotus of the heart is the locus for the worship of Hari, so too are the two eyes of the meditator; however, the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) itself is not present there. The statement "his two eyes" is figurative (*gauṇa*). Since both terms [of the compound] are thus made syntactically independent, even if one disregards the necessity of supplying [the word "lotus"], the mention of that [lotus] occurs above [in the compound] because it resides in a word that has a common substratum (*samānādhikṛta*). || 23 ||

*Kapyāsam*—the solar disc (*bhānubimba*), which is the *sūryamaṇḍala* and serves as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for that which is denoted by the word ‘monkey’ (*kapi*, i.e., the Sun); and likewise, the heart-lotus (*hṛtsaroja*), the lotus of the heart of the embodied soul; just as it is established in the scriptures that the place of worship for Hari (*haribhajanapada*) is the site for the meditation upon the Blessed Lord, in that very same way, the pair of eyes of the worshipper—the two eyes connected to the consciousness of the devotee—is also the place of worship for Hari, the site for the meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (Thus [it is said] of Him...)

"The meaning of the Śruti passage, 'Just as a lotus is golden-hued, so are his eyes,' is not [correctly explained] in that way; indeed, such an interpretation is utterly improper because, in that context—the sheath of the heart—the word *puṇḍarīka* is secondary (*gauṇa*), being based on a similarity to a lotus and thus non-primary, derived from a commonality of qualities. This applies to both words situated in the Śruti: 'his' (*tasya*) and 'eyes' (*akṣiṇī*)."

Along with the disregard—that is, the defect consisting of disregard—for the existing mutual connection between the two words whose meanings are related as part and whole, and for their independence in conveying meaning—that is, their capacity to convey meaning without depending on other words—there is also the defect consisting of the *adhyāhāra* (supplying of ellipsis), namely the supplying of the unspoken words "the place of worship" (*upāsanasthānam*) and "of the worshipper" (*upāsakasya*), because one imagines a mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between the two words elsewhere [than where they actually occur].

There is also the fault of abandoning that natural application—namely, the state of having different bases for their respective occurrences while sharing a single core referent—which belongs to the pair of words "kapyāsa" and "puṇḍarīka," which denote the qualifier and the qualified respectively, possess a common substratum, and terminate in the same case-ending. (Likewise,) "afterwards"—that is, subsequent to the sentence concerning the "monkey's anus"—means that it occurs only when the subsequent "Eye-Knowledge" has already taken place, and not prior to it.

In the Antarāditya-vidyā, the mention of the eyes of the worshipper by the words "thus [are] the two eyes" as the locus for the worship of the Blessed One is a defect; this is because of tautology—these are the defects. || 23 ||

Someone says: "The 'hip of a monkey'—how can this be intended as a simile for the eyes of the Blessed One when another possible interpretation exists? Here, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words is established; why should it be abandoned?
If that word [‘kapyāsa’] qualifies the lotus, then it is similar to it; however, in that case, the word would be used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). (24)

Regarding the "monkey" (*markaṭa*)—that is, the ape—the term *kapyāsa* refers to its hindquarters, the posterior part. Someone speaks [thus], being one who does not consider the hidden metaphorical comparison found in the scriptures, poetry, and so forth, as understood by the word *kapyāsa* occurring in the sacred texts; he explains it [in a way that] says whatever comes to mind, rather than explaining the meaning that is entirely appropriate.

"In another way"—meaning in another manner or by another means—"only when existing"—that is, while it is indeed present—"of the Blessed One, the all-surpassing Śrī Pūrṇa Nārāyaṇa," "of the eyes"—of the two eyes—"this"—the object consisting of the hips, which pertains to the lower region—is "renowned as something to be abandoned"; that is, it has attained the status of a "simile"—an object of comparison. How can this be accepted? Since it is a lowly object of comparison, how is it possible to admit it?

In this sentence, regarding the two words *kapyāsa* and *puṇḍarīka*, why is their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—which is obtained through the sharing of the same case-ending, which is naturally established and uncontradicted, and which consists in denoting a single object qualified by multiple qualifiers—abandoned? For what reason is it disregarded? If that word—the word *kapyāsa*—qualifies the lotus—that is, the object in the form of a *puṇḍarīka*—as being characterized by a similarity determined by the back of a monkey...

If you say it does [indicate it], then in your position—that is, in your view—regarding an object possessing a resemblance to that (tatsadṛśi), the word "that" (tacchabdaḥ)—namely, the word *kapyāsa* which denotes that [resemblance]—would necessarily follow as being figurative (gauṇaḥ), that is, functioning in a non-primary sense. || 24 ||

Someone said that the word *kapyāsa* means "half-blown," yet this [meaning] is connected to the lotus used as a metaphor for the eyes of the Blessed One. Nevertheless, that [meaning] does not exist in that sense, because the word was never derived from its constituent parts, either individually or in combination. (25)

Someone else, intent on providing an elaborate description of the term *kapyāsa*, explains it as "slightly blossomed"—that is, having attained a slight expansion—and thus describes the meaning of the word *kapyāsa*. However, this approach is distinct from the previous one; this method of describing the meaning is superior, provided that it remains consistent with the analogy of the lotus as the eye of the Blessed One—even though the lotus, being the object of comparison for the Blessed One’s eyes, possesses the very fitness for such a connection.

Even that—that description of the meaning—is not correct; indeed, it is not at all proper. Why? Because that word—the word *kapyāsa*—is not found in any [lexicon], whether worldly or Vedic, which is accepted by the learned for the purpose of explaining the etymology of words and their meanings, in that sense of "slightly blossomed," whether by deriving it from its parts (*avayavaśas*), through a derivative (*yaugika*) analysis, or as a whole (*saṃhatyā*) through a collective derivation.

Or, [by conventional usage], it was not "vyudapadyata," meaning it did not at all attain its etymological derivation. || 25 || When six meanings have been proposed, three—the proponents of the *kapyāsa* [comparison]—are clever; they are accepted by the venerable Rāmānuja based on the root *gambhīrāmbhas*. Those others who are excluded from that acceptance should be rejected by those who know the truth.
Thus has this division been declared by me in these six verses. (26)

Regarding "samīriteṣu" — among the six meanings of the word *kapyāsa* that have been clearly explained; specifically, among the six types of meanings of the term *kapyāsa*, there are three kinds of meanings stated in the three verses beginning with "The sun is the monkey (*kapi*)," "The monkey is not capable," and "Water is *ka*"; these [three] were accepted by the venerable Rāmānuja, as commenced in the *Śrīmati Vedārthasaṅgraha* with the passage beginning "arisen from deep waters" (*gambhīrāmbhassamudbhūtē*).

Having been accepted, they are clever, suitable for the stated simile, and provide nourishment. As for "the others"—those in addition to what was mentioned—there are three types of meanings presented in the three verses beginning with "The monkey's anus," "Someone prattles," and "Slightly blossomed."

"Excluded from their acceptance"—set aside by the commentators because they were not accepted by them; "to be abandoned"—(for this very reason) to be avoided, by me, Vātsyavaradārya, who knows the intention of the venerable Āmānuja. This division—this act of demonstration consisting of a discrimination between those points accepted by them and those not accepted—has been thus declared, revealed in this manner, by means of these six previously mentioned verses numbering six. || 26 ||

3) *Adhikaraṇamālā*: By the power of the accumulation of abundant and infinite merit, there arises—according to the logic of Śakra and others—a continuous stream (*pravāha*) of lords who possess the aforementioned abundance and bear bodies composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). Among them, he whose majesty consists in a divine form not produced by karma, who is the ruler of all men, and who is heard of as possessing eternal glory within the body of Viṣṇu—he alone is the one referred to by the words "He who [is that]. (62)

Of the majority—meaning those who have attained extreme excellence; of the infinite—meaning those whose number is impossible to count; by the power of the accumulation of merits—meaning through a specific capacity resulting from an abundance of particular virtuous deeds; of those in whom the aforementioned plenitude has been awakened—possessing the majesty of creatorship and so forth, which is capable of producing its fruit; of those who bear bodies composed of the three qualities (guṇas)—meaning those who possess distinct bodies made of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; [of] the lords—meaning specifically those distinguished persons who are fit for the sovereignty over the entire universe.

The "stream" (*pravāha*) refers to a continuous succession of a single kind. According to the principle of Śakra and others—that is, following the logic established in the Purāṇas and other texts regarding the continuity of a specific individual possessing equal sovereignty as the lord of the three worlds in every *manvantara*, even though each such individual is distinct—it would indeed be established that [the stream continues]; however, there is no insistence that the Lord must be one and the same at all times.

That is not so—the aforementioned suspicion is not logical. [The Supreme Person] possesses a majestic form produced by non-karmic manifestation, is independent of karma, and possesses an auspicious body composed of primordial light; He is endowed with specific powers of manifestation and sovereignty, is the ruler of all persons, possesses natural lordship over all sentient beings, and is eternally possessed of glory, being the refuge of a splendor that never departs throughout the three periods of time.

Because He is heard of as being present within the solar orb—the *braghna-bimba*—as understood from the scriptural text, "He who is within the sun" (*ya eṣo'ntarāditye*), He is referred to as "He who" (*sa yaḥ*). This same one is also established in the *Taittirīya* [Upaniṣad] by the passage, "He who is within the sun" (*sa ya eṣo'ntarāditye*). Therefore, this one—the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who is the ruler of all, as heard in the text "He who is within"—is indeed one alone, remaining undivided across all places, all times, and all states; [it is not a succession of various lords]. || 62 ||

The *Antarāditya-vidyā* declares that [the Lord] has indeed risen above all impurities (*kalmaṣa*). Therefore, one might argue: "Let there be a connection with merit (*puṇya-yoga*) for the All-pervading One (*vibhu*), who grants permission for the remainder. This is not so. For it is taught that He is not subject to another's command, possesses His own independent results, and does not become increased by the good; thus, even through the application of the term *lakṣmī*, there is no "well-done" (*sukṛta*), as indicated by the word *pāpman*. (63)
Regarding the term *vibhau*:

the Upaniṣad, consisting of such scriptural passages as "This golden person who is within the sun" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.6.6), declares that [the Supreme Self] has indeed risen above all impurities; thus, O friend, it says that [the Supreme Self] is untouched by any sin. This is established by the statement: "He alone has risen above all evils. (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.6.7).

Therefore—since only the connection with evil is prohibited, while the remainder is permitted, according to the maxim accepted by the experts in the Tantras that "when there is a specific prohibition, the remainder is permitted"—here, in this Vidyā, let there indeed be a connection with merit for the All-pervading One, the Supreme Self; (and thus, the individual soul itself, possessing a connection with merit, would be the subject taught in the Antaryāmin-Āditya Vidyā).

Not so—this position is not tenable; for it is declared in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other scriptures that He (the Lord of All) is "not subject to another's command" (*ananyaśāsya*), meaning He is beyond the jurisdiction of the commands of others, and "possessing fruits dependent on Himself" (*svavaśaparaphala*), meaning He possesses the control over the desirable and undesirable fruits belonging to others.

Likewise, by means of "good" (sādhu)—that is, meritorious (puṇya) action—it is traditionally taught that "this" (eṣaḥ), namely the Supreme Self, "would not become more" (na bhūyān syāt), meaning He would not undergo increase; this is also stated in such scriptural passages as, "He does not increase through action. Furthermore, even in the case of "merit" (puṇye)—in action denoted by the word *sukṛta*—the term "sin" (pāpman)—the word signifying sin—applies by way of secondary indication (lakṣmayogāt), because of its association with the characteristic of sin, which consists in having undesirable results. Thus, the word for sin indeed functions as a denoter even with respect to an object consisting of merit.

And this meaning is established by the scriptural passage beginning with "neither good nor evil": "Neither merit nor demerit; all evils turn back from there. This is proven by the Vedic statement which, while referring to both merit (*sukṛta*) and demerit (*duṣkṛta*), employs the word "evils" (*pāpmānaḥ*). There exists a certain well-known, pure *sattva*, a faultless substance distinct from the unmanifest (*avyakta*). That form of the Lord shines in heaven, as does the remainder—the portion of Śeṣa known as the "Soundless" (*anādaḥ*). That [substance] is eternally served by the *sūris*; it is the Supreme Deity who never abandons His own essential nature.

Without ever abandoning its own nature, it transforms its own form—which consists of pure *sattva*, is eternal (*sanātana*), and perpetual (*sadātana*)—into various specific manifestations for the sake of the cessation of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-śānti*) for conscious beings (*puṃsām*) wandering since beginningless time. It does so through prior arrays (*vyūha-pūrvaiḥ*), that is, through divisions consisting of the *vyūha*, *vibhava*, *arcā*, and *hārdā* forms, which are eternally served by the wise (*sūri-sevya*) and are supreme (*paratara*) beyond all else.

He causes [the body] to transform into various forms. (64) If it is argued that [the body] is composed of the seven constituents (*dhātu*), possesses the three impurities (*mala*), arises from demerit (*agha*), is a source of suffering, and is subject to destruction because it has parts and is therefore non-divine (*adeva*), then that is incorrect, because it is sublated by the authoritative means of knowledge (*māna*). Sublation (*bādha*) would never occur regarding that which is known solely through the scripture (*śāstra-ekavedya*); otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As for what he displays among those who act according to their own will, even that is for the purpose of causing a delusion among the Asuras. (65)

(The divine form of the Blessed One: It is composed of the seven constituents (*dhātu*)—namely, as stated, "the constituents are blood, bile, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen"—it is bound by the three impurities (*trimala*), and its very nature is established through the power of karma consisting of merit and demerit (*aghabhava*).

If it is argued that [the body] is a producer of suffering for embodied beings because it is a body—whereby "body-ness" (*dehatva*) is a probans (*jñāpaka-dharma*) inseparable from such a probandum—and that it is subject to destruction and characterized by disintegration because it possesses parts, etc., where "having parts," "visibility," and so forth are probans inseparable from destruction; if this is said, it is incorrect. For this would be a proof that "body-ness," "having parts," and so forth entail being a transformation of the seven constituents (*dhātu*) and being perishable.

It is vitiated by fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). This is because there is sublation (*bādhāt*)—that is, contradiction—by means of valid cognition such as scripture (*āgama*) and history (*itihāsa*), which establishes the form of the Blessed One through the measurement of the subject (*dharmimāna*); for it is certain that the subject possesses the absence of the property intended to be proven. Alternatively, in the case of something "knowable solely through scripture"—where a determination is made by scripture alone—there can be no sublation regarding any object whatsoever; that is, there can be no valid cognition of non-existence produced by another scripture or a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Such a sublation simply does not exist.

Otherwise—that is, if one were to admit that even by means of a fallacious semblance of a valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) there could be a sublation of an object established by the preeminent scripture—there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because it would follow that even such things as the existence of the Self (*ātman*) taught in the Vedas could be sublated by perception and other means of knowledge.

In His incarnations by His own will—those manifestations of power (*vibhava-avatāra*) such as Rāma and others, which depend solely upon His own resolve—whatever suffering and so forth He displays, such as that born from separation from beloved ones, through His own actions or words, He shows it to the world for the purpose of destroying the Asuras; that is, for the destruction of those like Kaṃsa who possess an Asura nature.
(For indeed, when they perceive Him in His divine forms with the notion that He is a mere human, their destruction becomes easy. [65]

Having raised the objection that because "He is one" indicates the oneness of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and the one residing within the solar orb, the *ānandamaya* must be the individual soul (*jīva*) itself—the final conclusion is established as follows:

since in the very *Antarāditya-vidyā*, qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which are impossible for individual souls, are heard [of the one within the orb]; and since even the Supreme Self possesses a natural, eternal form endowed with hands, feet, and so forth, the one residing within the solar orb is the Supreme Self, and thus the *ānandamaya* is also the Supreme Self, non-different from Him.

5) By the scriptural statement "He who is this," which follows as a supplement to the preceding section, the status of merit and the individual soul as the cause [of the world] is negated within the internal method. (34)
Thus ends the section concerning the intermediate state (antaradhikaraṇa). ||7||
The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa) || 1.1.8 ||
In the section concerning the vital breath (*prāṇādhikaraṇa*), [the author] summarized the collection of principles from the *Śārīraka*:

"Is that very same [cause] the source of the worlds by the specific name 'Space' (*ākāśa*)? Or rather, is it the 'Vital Breath' (*prāṇa*)? He refuted this [latter view] by means of signs such as the dissolution of the elements. (15)

Regarding the term "ākāśa"—by means of this specific word, which serves as an indicator through its particular name found in the scripture, "All these... indeed from space alone," and which has the nature of space (*ākāśatva*) as its unique defining property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), that very thing which is the source of the worlds—the cause of the entire universe at its beginning—must indeed be it; it must undoubtedly be space itself.

Nor is it anything else; or rather—alternatively—the *prāṇa*, as stated in the scripture, "They enter into *prāṇa* alone," might indeed be the source of the worlds—that is, the cause of the entire universe. This kind of doubt was set aside by the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, through the indicative marks (*liṅga*) consisting of the support for the dissolution of all beings and so forth, which were mentioned in that very context by the phrase "they enter into" (*abhisaṃviśanti*). Thus, he refuted this [objection]. || 15 ||
2) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

Although, by means of the threefold knowledge (*vidyā-traya*), the embodied beings—whether moving or stationary, sentient or insentient—may possess a status superior even to the unmanifest source (*avyakta*) and the multitude of individual souls (*jīva-varga*) as they are all effects of the Universal Cause; nevertheless, in this chapter, [the author] extols His attributes through a series of topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), while sequentially restraining those who are soft-natured and those established in cruelty, according to the distinction between their respective means of emergence.

In this manner—by the aforementioned method, through the triad of Vidyās consisting of the Sadvidyā, the Ānandamayavidyā, and the Antarādityavidyā, which have been investigated by means of three Adhikaraṇas—[the nature] of the Lord, the Supreme Brahman, who is the cause of all (possessing every kind of causality as both efficient and material cause) and whose body consists of the aggregate of sentient and insentient beings (both moving and stationary), [is established] from the Unmanifest.

In comparison with the *pradhāna* denoted by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and also in comparison with the class of individual souls (*jīva*)—namely, the threefold group of conscious beings consisting of the bound, the liberated, and the eternal—the state of being "exceedingly greater" constitutes a distinction in the form of loftiness; and while this may indeed be established as a matter of fact, [it remains so].

Nevertheless—despite the existence of that [previous] attainment—here, in this *Śārīraka-śāstra*, or regarding Brahman thus established, there are those who have raised objections (*pratyavasthāna*) by way of different approaches (*dvārabheda*), due to the distinctness of the subject matter that serves as the basis for the opponents' challenges. These objections were raised sequentially, following the contemplation of scriptural passages according to their clarity—whether indistinct, distinct, or resembling a shadow. They are "gentle in their commencement but cruel in their conclusion," appearing at first like those who accept the formal arrangement of means and objects of knowledge (*pramāṇa-prameya-vyavasthā*) merely to demonstrate their skill in debate.

Having approached with gentleness, yet intending to bring about a conclusion in cruelty regarding the nature of reality at the end, the Lord Bādarāyaṇa—in this remaining first chapter—desiring to restrain the opponent who persists in such a manner, clearly elucidates, by way of specific distinction, the qualities belonging to the Supreme Self through the collection of the remaining combined topics (*adhikaraṇas*). || 66 ||

That certain single Cause, measured in the head of the Vedas by words such as "Sat" and "Brahman," is conceived as having specific attributes through notions of volition and habitual practice that are inconsistent with it; then, by casting aside those attributes through names residing in the Cause that are apt to give rise to the suspicion of being the elemental ether and so forth, [the scripture] enjoys [its true nature] by declaring the impossibility of the collection of Vedic texts applying to anything other than its feet (the individual soul). || 67 ||

By words headed by "Brahman"—that is, by words such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*) which denote the cause of the universe; in the crest of the Śruti—the Upaniṣads such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*) and "Verily, in the beginning, this was Brahman alone" (*brahma vā idamekamevāgra āsīt*)—a certain thing, unascertained in its specific form, one—a single cause that serves as both the efficient and material cause of the entire world—has been measured, i.e., brought within the scope of valid cognition.

By those things "not conforming to that"—meaning distinguished from other sentient and insentient entities—and by those consisting of the practice of resolve (saṅkalpa), specifically by the particular non-material, divine, and auspicious forms practiced through the culmination of the unsurpassed state of resolve regarding the creation of the universe; "that particularity" refers to the specific sentient being called the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is distinct from the general categories of primordial matter (pradhāna) and individual souls (jīva), as well as from meritorious souls; and "contemplated" means determined after having been investigated in the preceding topical sections (adhikaraṇas).

In the remaining portion of the [second] quarter—that is, in the remainder of the quarter beginning from the *Ākāśādhikaraṇa*—by means of names such as "ether," "vital breath," "light," and "Indra," which are conventional designations arising from the potential for doubt regarding the elemental ether and so forth, and which produce a doubt characterized by the modes of being the well-known elemental ether, being the elemental vital air, being the light of the sun and other luminaries, and being Indra, the lord of the three worlds—all of which are heard in the scriptural passages (*kāraṇasthaiḥ*) that establish the cause of the universe—it is [that Brahman].

Having set aside—that is, having refuted from the perspective of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)—the mark (liṅga) unique to the Supreme Self (paramātman) considered in the three preceding sections, [the author states: "The specific conscious entity" (bhā. tat)—that is, precisely that mark unique to the Supreme Self—by means of stating the impossibility of the collection of scriptural passages (śruti-samudaya), [he] demonstrates through the exposition of the impossibility of a mere material nature (rūpyātmaka) unaccompanied by yoga being an agent of action; [thus he says: "He enjoys"—that is, He protects. ||67||
The words "space" (ākāśa) and "vital breath" (prāṇa) must be interpreted by setting aside their conventional meanings, as they have no other possible application here;

however, let the word "light" (jyotis) convey the Puruṣa through its conventional sense as one distinguished by divine splendor. Subsequently, well-known terms such as "Indra" and others are restricted to denote that [Puruṣa] as qualified by those [attributes].
Thus, this section consists of two pairs [of terms], following the sequence of the functions of words. //68//

The two words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and "breath" (*prāṇa*), which have no other possible referents and whose ultimate nature has been fully expounded, are devoid of any alternative interpretation because they occur within sentences containing common characteristics. In the scriptural passages, "From ether, [beings] arise" and "They enter into breath alone," the words "ether" and "breath" must be interpreted by setting aside their conventional meanings—that is, by abandoning the collective power established in common usage—and by relying solely on the etymological power of their constituent parts (as in "that which shines everywhere" for *ākāśa*). Thus, they are to be understood as denoting the Supreme Self.

As for the word "light" (*jyotis*)—the word "light" found in the passage, "Now, that light which is beyond this heaven"—it clearly conveys, through its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), that is, by the power of the whole word itself, the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), the Supreme Being (*paramapuruṣa*), who is distinguished by supreme divine splendor and characterized by a form composed of non-material light.

Thereafter, the word "Indra" and so forth—which occurs in the scriptural passage under consideration immediately following that [preceding section], and which possesses the fitness to denote the well-known Indra and others—is "restricted" by its application to the Supreme Self as qualified by those [individuals], meaning it has attained a restrictive rule through functioning as a denoter of the Supreme Self insofar as He is the substratum (prakārin) of specific individual souls (jīvas) such as Indra. Thus, according to the aforementioned method, by the sequence of the word's function—namely, its purely etymological (yaugika) function and its conventional (rūḍhi) function resting solely upon the qualifying attributes—it [denotes the Supreme Self].

Following the inclination toward the understanding of the meaning, this "box" (peṭikā)—consisting of four sections beginning with the section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa)—possesses two pairs; that is, it would consist of two intermediate boxes, each comprising a pair of sections: the pair consisting of the sections on Space and Vital Breath (Prāṇa), and likewise the pair consisting of the sections on Light (Jyotis) and Indra-Vital Breath. || 68 ||

"Here, in the *Sāman* [text], Ākāśa is seen as the source and place of dissolution of all things without exception; moreover, in the *Taittirīya*, it is designated by its own name as not produced by anything else, since its own origin is stated from itself. Do not say so. For this is merely a restatement of what is already established; furthermore, qualities such as being the supreme goal to be attained do not belong to it. Since the Self is heard in scripture as the "knower" (*vipaścit*) who is its agent, the production of the Self from itself is refuted.

In this context—in the first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, regarding the Sāman—the word "Ākāśa," which exists as a conventional term denoting its own specific meaning, is known through the sequence: "From [Brahman]... all beings arise; they merge back into Ākāśa. Thus, it is established as the source and place of dissolution for the entire multitude of created beings. Furthermore, in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad as well, it is specifically pointed out in the Śruti as "Ākāśa" alone, perceived as the foundational substratum.

Even in the passage found in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, the ether (*ākāśa*) is described as being of the nature of ether through the statement that its own manifestation arises from its very self—since the Vedic text states, "From the Self, the ether was produced"—it is indicated as not produced by anything else, being understood through the reading of the scripture as unproduced by another; thus, [the opponent argues] it is the worldly ether itself that is the [material cause] of the world.

[Regarding the objection that this is] "the cause of origination and dissolution"—this being the position reached—it is not so; such a suspicion is not at all logical. For this reason: this scriptural passage from the Chāndogya, "All these indeed," is a restatement of what is already established—a reiteration of a matter previously known. And that which was previously known as the cause is precisely the referent of the word *sat* (Being), as understood from the statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1).

And in that [context], the word "ākāśa" has no mere conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*); on the contrary, it refers to what was just mentioned—namely, the quality of being the supreme goal (*parāyaṇatva*), being greater than all else, and so forth. These qualities are not possible in the worldly ether (*laukikākāśa*) which would be denoted by the word through mere convention alone. Furthermore, the "Self" (*ātman*) is the entity whose nature is the Self; "the All-seeing One" (*vipaścit*) is one who possesses consciousness that perceives various things, and He is heard in scripture as the creator of even the ether, as the maker of the "Self."

Because it is established by the Vedic scripture stating, "Space was produced," the production of that [space]—namely, the origination of space—from its own self—that is, from its own essential nature—is refuted, sublated, and rendered impossible. || 69 ||
3) Summary of the Topic (*adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*):

In the section concerning ether (*ākāśādhikaraṇa*), there arises the following doubt: since the text states, "Indeed, all these beings arise from ether alone," and because the word "ether" is used [as the source], ether itself must be the cause. Anticipating this objection, [the Sūtra] states that because it is impossible for ether to be the cause of the entire manifold (*prapañca*)—comprising both sentient and insentient entities—as denoted by the word "all" in the phrase "all beings," [ether is not the cause].

Based on the etymological derivation "that which shines everywhere" (*samantāt kāśate*), it is established as the final conclusion that the term "ether" (*ākāśa*) refers to the Supreme Self; thus, the Supreme Self is the denotation of the word "ether."

M 4) A specific indicative mark (liṅga) that is consistent with the method [of interpretation] is considered stronger than a general scriptural statement (śruti). Here, in the method regarding ether (ākāśa), the opposite is the case; therefore, this is presented as a counter-example. ||35|| Thus ends the section on Ether (Ākāśādhikaraṇa). || 8 ||

The Section on Prāṇa (Prāṇādhikaraṇam) || 1.1.9 || 1) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*: It is well known here that the body and its various directions are dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, its status as the cause [of the body] as stated in the Śruti is firmly established by its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) and must not be set aside like [the case of] space (*vyoma*).

Therefore, that [objection] does not apply to the Prāṇa, because its greatness in wood and so forth is a restatement as before, and because its universal life-giving function is seen in the Blessed Lord, just as the mention of "space" [is seen to refer to the Supreme]. ||70||

For this reason: here, in this world, it is known—that is, universally established—that the body and so forth (the body, senses, etc., which are perceived) are dependent on *prāṇa*, meaning their activity is governed by *prāṇa*. By that stated reason, the fact of its being the cause—as taught in the Śruti, namely the Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage, "All these beings indeed enter into *prāṇa* alone and emerge from *prāṇa* alone"—is established; that is, by its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*), *prāṇa* alone is the cause of the origin and so forth of the entire universe.

On account of the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) inherent in the word "prāṇa"—which is conducive to understanding the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—and because it must be determined with firmness, that is, without doubt, like the sky (*vyoma*), its status as the cause of all things is not to be sublated, nor is it to be rejected; thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), that aforementioned objection is not tenable.

In the case of objects such as wood and so forth, which are included within the world and are being produced, the greatness of the Prāṇa—that is, the greatness belonging to the Mukhya-prāṇa consisting in its capacity for independent activity—is destroyed; and because there is a restatement (anuvāda) just as before—just as in the case of the previously mentioned Ākāśa—the status of this [passage] as a restatement is established by the observation of the word "ha vai. This is just like the use of the word "Ākāśa" for the Blessed One in the passage, "That which is this Ākāśa," where the term Ākāśa is applied to the Blessed One. In the Blessed One...

Because the term "prāṇa" is used for the Blessed Lord—as in "the breath of breath" (prāṇasya prāṇaḥ) and so forth—and because the very ground for the application of the word "prāṇa," namely the act of breathing that consists in being the animator of all living beings, is seen to exist in the Blessed Lord through such passages as "Who indeed could breathe, who could live? (ko hyevānyāt kaḥ prāṇyāt), the meaning of the word "prāṇa" taught in the Chāndogya Śruti is the Blessed Lord alone; it is not the well-known primary vital air (mukhya prāṇa). || 70 ||

2) Summary of the meaning of the section: In the section concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is well known that the vital breath is the basis for the existence of the entire collection of living beings, as their subsistence depends upon the vital breath.

Because, in its own statement—namely, in the sentence establishing the light, "This indeed is that light which is within this person"—characteristics of the Supreme (paraliṅgadharmāḥ), which are the exclusive attributes indicative of being the Supreme Self, are not at all heard; therefore, as for the light understood from the sentence, that is merely the light well-known in the world, the third among the elements mentioned in the sequence "earth, water, fire"—that is, simply the material light consisting of the element of fire (thus, the prima facie view).

This—that the light understood from the scriptural passage possesses the state of being the third of the elements—is not to be doubted; for it is impossible for doubt to arise because all the elements, which consist of the class of sentient beings, are well-known in the world as its [the light's] "feet," yet they do not deserve to be considered its "feet" in the sense of limbs. On the contrary, the established conclusion is that they deserve to be the "feet" of the Supreme Person alone. || 16 ||

2) The *Tattvasāra* states that the *Gāyatrī*, known as the crest-jewel of the Sāma-Veda, is meditated upon as the Supreme Light (*parajyotis*). It is established as fourfold through its six aspects—namely, the elements (*bhūta*), the earth (*kṣiti*), the body (*tanu*), and the heart (*hṛdaya*)—along with the corresponding modes of chanting (*gāna*) and protection (*trāṇa*), etc., due to the distinctions in the explicit expressions found in the scriptures. Thus, the mention of speech (*vāk*) and breath (*prāṇa*) is for the sake of the Supreme; this is dependent upon the scriptural conclusion regarding the essential nature (*svarasa*). ||27||

In the *Sāmaśrutiśiras*—that is, in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, which belongs to the *Tāṇḍya* branch of the Sāmaveda—the fourfold nature [of Brahman] is established through four objects: the elements (*bhūta*), the earth (*kṣiti*), the body (*tanu*), and the heart (*hṛdaya*), which correspond respectively to the group of conscious enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-cetanavarga*), the earth (*pṛthivī*), the body (*śarīra*), and the heart (*hṛdaya*). This constitutes the possession of four feet (*catuṣpādatva*). By means of these specific modes related to that fourfold nature—namely, those consisting of the functions of singing (*gāna*) and protecting (*trāṇa*) [the elements]—[Brahman is characterized by] being the singer of the elements and the protector of the elements.

By way of being the agent (*kartṛtva*), being the support of the elements (*bhūtapratiṣṭhātva*), not transcending the elements (*bhūtānativartana*), being the support of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhātva*), and not transcending the vital breaths (*prāṇānativartana*), the Supreme Light (*paraṃjyotiḥ*)—which, like the sixfold method, is like the light that illuminates all lights as described in the Śruti, "The Supreme Light beyond heaven"—is the Supreme Brahman; it is called by the name *Gāyatrī* because it possesses the status of being denoted by the word *Gāyatrī* through its similarity to the [metrical] Gāyatrī; and it is studied (*adhyāyi*) as the expression of speech and life-breath, according to the statement, "Speech indeed is Gāyatrī."

The glorification [of speech] and likewise the glorification of the vital breaths—on the grounds that "in this [speech], these vital breaths are established"—are for the sake of another; they serve as means to achieve further purposes consisting of the attainment of the status of being the agent of singing and protection, as well as the state of being the foundation of the vital breaths. This is known precisely from the difference in the modes of expression found in the Śruti: from the distinct manner of speaking regarding the fourfold group beginning with the elements, and from the distinct manner of speaking regarding speech and the vital breaths, which depends upon the possession of that fourfold group beginning with the elements.

The contemplation of Brahman as being the Gāyatrī—based on its similarity to the Gāyatrī through its four-footed nature and its sixfold nature dependent on its being the agent of singing and so forth—is grounded in the scriptural conclusion that is natural in sense; namely, that scripture which, possessing a naturalness consisting in conveying a non-figurative meaning, summarizes both the four-footedness and the sixfold nature in the form: "This very [Gāyatrī] is four-footed and sixfold. This [contemplation] has that [scripture] as its basis. || 27 ||
3) *Adhikaraṇasārāvaliḥ*:

No indicative mark (*liṅga*) contradicts the statement; rather, there exists a mark consistent with the well-known reality, and the word is heard as having no other referent. Thus, [the Supreme Self] is not to be known through the statements regarding the "Supreme Light" (*jyotiḥ*) and so forth. To one who objects that even in the absence of a statement on the origin of the universe, that indicative mark is understood here, [the author] refutes him by means of two topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) and the reasoning that it is characterized by the appropriate categories of sentient and insentient beings. (71)

The statement—that the Vedic word "light" (*jyotis*) and so forth, which by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) conveys things well-known in the world such as fire, does not contradict (*na vyāhanti*), i.e., does not sublate (*na bādhate*), any mark (*liṅga*)—that is, any particular uncommon property residing in a specific object distinct from that [fire], consisting in the capacity understood from the co-occurring words; rather, on the contrary, it is renowned as being favorable to that [fire], compatible with the connection to the reality of fire and so forth as established in the world; whereas the mark [itself] consists in the identity with the gastric light (*kaukṣeyajyotis*) and so forth.

There is, however, an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*): it indeed exists; it is "not restricted to anything else"—meaning it is devoid of the status of denoting the Supreme Self alone in an exclusive sense—and the word itself, consisting of "light" and so forth, is indeed a word that is clearly recited in the Śruti. (Therefore,) the object to be known through the mention of light and so forth—the referent expressed by words such as "light"—cannot be the Supreme Self.

"Even though the origin of the universe is not explicitly mentioned here—in this sentence composed of words such as 'light' (*jyotis*), etc.—and even though there is no word in this passage that directly teaches the creation of the world and so forth, its *liṅga* (inferential mark)—the indicator consisting of unsurpassed luminosity, which is invariably concomitant with being the cause of the universe—is known from the scriptural fragment: 'Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven. Thus [the opponent] objects, based on such reasoning regarding this scripture."

Regarding the opponent who has set out to refute the supremacy of the Supreme Self by being intent on establishing worldly objects of enjoyment—[the author] now proceeds with two subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇas*) which are presented immediately thereafter; by means of the reasoning concerning the distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) between the groups of conscious and unconscious entities appropriate to those [sections], he establishes that it is only in the Supreme Self that there exists a unique (*asādhāraṇya*) connection with a distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*), a particularity (*viśeṣa*), an excellence (*atiśaya*), or a difference (*vailakṣaṇya*), compared to the well-known conscious beings such as Indra and the like, and the unconscious beings such as fire and the like.
By means of reasoning established in scripture, which consists of that very yoga, he "blocks"—that is, he refutes it. || 71 ||
It has been stated here that the gastric light is one with that supreme light, and its being the material cause of the universe is known from other Vidyās;

therefore, let fire be the cause. This is not correct; for there is no sublation of the recognition of the Supreme Person as declared by the words of the *Puruṣasūkta*, and the mention of the *Gāyatrī* is made on account of similarity, while its feet are described as consisting of the elements and so forth.

In this context—the Śruti passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—it is stated that there is identity—that is, non-difference—between the supreme light (parajyotiḥ), which is described as "the light beyond heaven" and denoted by the term *parajyotis*, and the gastric light (kaukṣeyajyotiḥ), namely the digestive fire residing within the belly; this is established by the statement: "This indeed is that light which is within this person. Now, regarding that supreme light which is non-different from the gastric light, its status as the material cause of the universe—that is, its being the cause of the world—is as follows:

Furthermore, it is well known from specific Upaniṣadic passages that expound the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and other such teachings; therefore, on account of the aforementioned scriptural statements (*śruti*) and indicative marks (*liṅga*), as well as common worldly renown, let fire—the well-known *agni*—be the cause; indeed, let it be accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe. What is the harm? (Thus, when the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] has been reached: Not so. Acceptance in the manner described is not withstands critical inquiry, for the Supreme Person (*parapuruṣa*) spoken of in the verses of the Puruṣasūkta says: "All beings are but one quarter of Him."

The recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*)—exactly as established by the statement within the *Puruṣasūkta*, "His three feet are immortality in heaven"—which arises from the statement located in this very context of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, namely, "One foot of His are all beings; His three feet are immortality in heaven," is such that it cannot be sublated (*abādhāt*), because it is impossible to refute it. Since this recognition establishes the status of the Supreme Person, that which is to be propounded here is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

It is not the worldly fire. As for the mention of the *Gāyatrī*: the word "Gāyatrī" being applied to the Supreme Light, which is the subject of the context, is based on its similarity to the Gāyatrī mantra—namely, by virtue of possessing a fourfold division consisting of the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart (as the four feet), and by possessing the six characteristics of singing, protection, being the support of all beings, and non-transgression [of those limits]. Thus, it is based on its resemblance to the Gāyatrī.

Of Brahman, which is denoted by the word ‘Gāyatrī,’ the quarters beginning with ‘beings’ (bhūta) are likewise [parts]; the class of enjoyers, consisting of individual souls (jīvātman), is denoted by the word ‘all beings,’ and their merit...

The earth-form, which has its acquisition dependent upon sinful karma, is the locus of enjoyment; the body, which is a form of the abode of enjoyment like a creation dependent on such karma; and the heart, which is the substratum for the soul's existence within such a body—these four, being constituent parts as qualifiers of the qualified Brahman, have indeed been declared and clearly established in this context. || 72 ||

In the first pair of topics (*adhikaraṇa*), [the Sūtra] "The rising [is Brahman], because of the light" establishes that the cause is pervasive through its mark (*liṅga*). How could the Bhāṣya's statement—"another mark has been prescribed in its own words"—be possible? It is thus: while there exists here a mark such as the universe and so forth, the mark desired by the opponent does not exist.

Observing this, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) proceeds with his argument; thus, there is no room for doubt regarding that contradiction. In the pair of sections concerning "Light" (*jyotis*) and so forth—in the two sections known as "Light," "Indra," and "Prāṇa"—there is an "arising," meaning the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which is a limb of the inquiry. Having introduced it by means of a "mark" (*liṅga*) pervaded by the cause—that is, by a characteristic indicative property necessarily connected to being the cause of the world—it is stated clearly in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). Subsequently, in "his own words"—that is, in his own statement—it is "prescribed," meaning it is made known, as a "mark."

The commentary states: "That which makes [something] known must have an unerring nature as its characteristic; it is not recited in the Śruti. This commentary intends to convey this meaning. [Question: How could it be so? Or how is it to be construed so as to have an uncontradicted meaning? [Answer: It is to be construed in the manner that will be explained hereafter.

For instance, the "mark of being the universe" (*viśvādiliṅga*)—namely, the mark that implies the causality of the universe, characterized by being the illuminator of all things as understood from such scriptural passages as "in the back of everything"—although it exists here in its own very context, nevertheless constitutes a "mark desired by others" (*parābhīṣṭaliṅga*). This is a mark accepted as residing in the Supreme Person alone, which establishes the nature of the Supreme Person as possessing both marks.

But [the opponent] does not perceive that it is indeed impossible within his own statement; thus conjecturing—imagining and reflecting—the proponent who raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) as a limb of inquiry, proceeds in such a manner: he formulates the *pūrvapakṣa* from a reason (*liṅga*) pervaded by the probandum (*kāraṇa*), while simultaneously demonstrating the absence of such a unique reason (*asādhāraṇaliṅga*) in his own statement. Therefore, there is a contradiction—a mutual inconsistency between the words of the commentary itself—and this is not to be suspected—that is, it should certainly not be imagined. || 73 ||
4) Summary of the meaning of the section:

In the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa*, having raised the objection that—in the passage, "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven"—because of the hearing of the word "light" (*jyotis*) and because there is no contradictory indicative mark within its own context, the well-known light itself must be the cause; [the author] refutes this.

Although there is no contradictory mark within its own sentence, because a contradictory mark in the form of "having feet consisting of all beings" is heard in the opening sentence, it is established as the final conclusion that the one denoted by the word "light" is the Supreme Self.

5) [The *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* states: "Because no specific marks of Brahman are observed here in the words spoken by the text itself, the 'Light' (*jyotis*) is what is under consideration; therefore, this is a connection by way of a counter-example. Thus ends the section on the Light (*jyotiradhikaraṇa*). 10.
The Section Concerning Indra and Prāṇa (Indraprāṇādhikaraṇa) [Sūtra 1.1.11]

1) *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasamūha*: But in the case of Indra, since his status as the individual soul (*jīva*) has been determined, he would indeed be the cause [of the world] because of the word "his own worship" (*svopāsti*). This is not so; for according to the perspective of the scripture, such an instruction is given [to him], and immortality is his "attribute" (*dharma*). (17)

In the case of one whose status as the individual soul (*jīva*) has been determined—meaning one whose nature as a *jīva* is established by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, *Purāṇa*, and *Āgama* accepted as authoritative—in the case of Indra, however, that is the well-known Indra himself, because of the word "his own worship" (*svopāsti*), since such a word enjoining the meditation on his own [nature] is heard in the Upaniṣad; he—the well-known Indra alone—would indeed be the cause, for he must surely be the reality known through the Vedāntas as the cause of all. This kind of doubt is not correct; it is certainly not sound.

For this reason: his—that is, Indra’s—teaching in that manner is a teaching [of him] as an object of worship; and by following the method seen in the scriptures (*śāstra*) among Vāmadeva and others in the *Atharvaśikha* and other texts, such as "I became Manu and Sūrya," and because the merit (*dharma*) to be accomplished through this meditation, as well as immortality—which is liberation itself—is attained. || 17 ||
With his first foot, he proclaimed himself as the omniscient one, consisting of bliss, possessing form, radiant, the cause of life, the well-situated Self, and the source of the universe.

The Omniscient One—He who is the substratum of uncontracted knowledge regarding all objects necessary for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; consisting of Bliss—abounding in bliss that is cultivated as culminating in a state beyond compare; possessing Form—having a divine body not dependent on karma; Radiant—self-luminous, independent of others, and the cause of the illumination of all things; the Cause of Life—the cause of the life of the entire world; and the Excellent Abode—the non-material, divine realm.

Bādarāyaṇa elucidated—clarified through the lens of the Upaniṣads—with the first quarter [of the first chapter] of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā], the Self whose nature consists of brilliantly shining light, who is the inner essence of other deities such as Agni and Indra, and the Supreme Self who is the source of the world and for whom the possibility of being the cause of the world has been refuted. || 18 ||
2) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

The *Prātardana* section teaches that Indra is the object of meditation as the most beneficial means; yet, even though he is endowed with the well-known marks of Prāṇa and Indra, one might argue that he is therefore the Creator of the Universe. This is not so, for Brahman is indeed to be meditated upon in three ways—enveloped by manifold sentient and insentient forms and by its own nature—and the introductory context concerning Prāṇa and Indra is shattered by the more powerful contradiction of the Great Mahāvākyas. (74)

That—well-known in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad—is the Prātardana-vidyā, a series of scriptural passages intended to instruct the Kṣatriya named Pratardana in a specific form of meditation, which begins with the words "Pratardana, indeed... It concerns Indra himself—that particular deity renowned in the Purāṇas by such terms as "King of the Gods" and "Lord of Śacī"—even though he is endowed with the well-known characteristics of the vital breath (prāṇa) and Indra; yet [the opponent argues] that in common worldly usage, there is the vital breath that sustains the body...

The king of gods is Indra; his identifying marks include being the regulator of life-span, having three heads, and the slaying of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ. Although he is thus established by the Śruti, [the text] speaks through the sequence of Indra’s own words, "Worship me," declaring that among those things denoted by the word ‘hita’ (beneficial)—namely ritual actions and the like which serve as means of worship—the worship of him is the most beneficial (*hitatama*) because it bestows the supreme human goal, *niḥśreyasa* (liberation). Thus, he is the one to be adored.

It explains: "That"—therefore, "this one"—the well-known Indra himself—is the creator of all, accepted by the Śruti as the cause of the universe—if this is the objection, such a doubt is not tenable. For, Brahman—the Supreme Brahman to be worshipped for the sake of the highest good—is [manifested] in three ways: as having various kinds of conscious and unconscious coverings—that is, having diverse forms of sentient and insentient bodies—and likewise as His own self, directly and by way of His essential nature. Thus, it is threefold.

That which is to be worshipped—that which is to be propitiated through worship—the introductory reference to Prāṇa as well as the introductory reference to Indra, though characterized by the unique attributes of Prāṇa as known in the world and likewise by the possession of the unique attributes of Indra, have their power indeed frustrated when they come into conflict with the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), which is far more powerful than the introductory references. This Great Sentence consists of the entire context from beginning to end; and when there is a contradiction with it, [the weaker passages] are rendered powerless.

That Liṅga which is said to abide solely in the Cause (Kāraṇa) within the Lord of Light (Jyotiṣīndra), is indeed established as being primarily fixed in Prakhyāti; therefore, its emergence from the mouth [of that Lord] is impossible. If it is argued that there is no looseness in the context because the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of that [Liṅga] has not been attained, [we reply: this is true;
however, this doubt arises here by anticipating the preceding statement according to the method of the discourse regarding Viṣṇu’s birth. || 75 ||

Regarding "in the case of *jyotis*"—that is, in the *jyotis* which is the subject matter set forth in the relevant scriptural passage, and in the case of *indra*—that is, in the *indra* who is known from the relevant scriptural passage concerning *indra* and *prāṇa*—"it is considered to abide as the sole cause" means by virtue of being pervaded by the status of being the cause of the world. That "mark"—which is intended as an indicator and described as having the nature of a unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇadharma*)—is that which has been stated and described by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

That [word], namely that very mark (liṅga), is established as residing in one [entity] alone—namely, it refers exclusively to the Supreme Person whose status as the cause is established by other scriptural texts; this was determined previously in the section concerning the ether (ākāśādhikaraṇa).

Therefore, since this was already deliberated upon and resolved in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is impossible for a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the world’s causality in relation to Indra and others—who are well-known through signs (*liṅga*) pervaded by causality—to arise by way of that [preceding] discussion. Upon its examination—that is, in the investigation of the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the world’s causality and the specific sign, and in the determination thereof—since [the matter] was not previously established (*aprāpte*), there is no slackening of the present topic; for the *Śārīraka-śāstra* is intended to provide a definitive conclusion regarding the single cause of the entire universe.

If it is argued that the doubt regarding the refutation of the proof of the Supreme Brahman as the cause is swallowed by the impossibility [of such a proof], and if this suspicion arises that, due to such agitation, the pair of *adhikaraṇas* (sections of inquiry) would not proceed—this is true: the suspicion regarding the non-proceeding of the *adhikaraṇas* is indeed real in one respect; yet it is not so in every respect. (If one asks, "Which is the specific aspect?"—it is the aspect derived from the methodological principle of the statement of Viṣṇu’s birth found in the Purāṇas concerning the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.)

Regarding the statements that describe births—the method of interpreting them being such that "the birth of the Blessed One in the form of avatāras like Upendra and others is not common to mortals nor dependent on karma"—having followed that method, even with respect to the objects mentioned here as objects of worship, such as Indra and others, one should reflect upon the meaning of the Śruti by first considering the *purovāda* (the introductory narrative) recorded therein—namely, the speech in the form of legends and so forth—and then performing an *utprekṣā* (interpretive visualization), leading [those passages] toward the status of Upendra and the other [divine forms]. This is preceded by a doubt.

Regarding the "arising of the position" (*pakṣotthānam*): the fact that Upendra and others are the objects of worship need not be determined here, as it has already been settled elsewhere; rather, the point to be determined is that the Supreme Self alone, having Indra and others as its body, is the object of worship—and by so doing, the section achieves its purpose. || 75 ||

The words *jyotis* (light), *prāṇa* (breath), and *indra*, as well as the attributes of being the cause and all-pervading, rightly refer to the Supreme; their application to these [terms] occurs merely by way of conventional designation, though they possess many obstacles [to such an interpretation]. Here, the one whose nature is the fire within the belly is described for the sake of attaining its fruit through meditation; yet even those signs belonging to the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) and others lead to liberation through the worship of the Supreme Being who is beneficial. 76.

The interpretation that the terms *jyotis* (light), *prāṇa* (breath), and *indra*—as heard in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, as well as the terms *indra* and *prāṇa* in the *Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad*—refer to the Supreme Being alone, because they are taught in the scriptures as possessing attributes that are invariably characteristic of the Cause, such as unsurpassed radiance and being the object of the highest meditation; and because this is the correct way to resolve the matter, as it is acceptable to both disputants. **Note on Diacritics:** * *tvatyukti* (your statement) * *ītibhramata* (due to the delusion of [interpreting] the style) * *bha* (the letter 'bha') * *tyadhyādirītibhramata* (due to the delusion of [interpreting] the style beginning with 'tyadhi', etc. * *ā* (the letter 'ā') * *jyotiḥ* (light) * *prāṇendraśabdāḥ* (the words *prāṇa* and *indra*) * *chāndogyaśrutaḥ* (heard in the *Chāndogya*) * *jyotiśśabdaḥ* (the word *jyotis*) * *kauṣītakyāṃ śrutau* (in the *Kauṣītaki* scripture) * *indra-prāṇaśabdau* (the two words *indra* and *prāṇa*) * *kāraṇavyāptadharmāt* (because of the attributes pervading the Cause) * *kāraṇaikāntaniratiśaya* (exclusively and unsurpassedly belonging to the Cause) * *dīpti-hitatamopāstikarmatvādeḥ* (of the nature of being radiance, the most beneficial, the object of meditation, etc. * *dharmasya* (of the attribute) * *śrutau paṭhanāt* (because of its recitation in the scripture) * *jñāpakāt* (because of the indicator) * *parataraviṣayāḥ* (having the Supreme as their object) * *paramātmamātrapratipādakāḥ* (establishing the Supreme Self alone) * *ityetat* (this) * *evaṃ nirvahaṇam* (such a resolution) * *sādhu* (correct) * *ubhayavādisammatatvāt* (because it is agreed upon by both disputants) * *samīcīnameva* (indeed appropriate)

Of these—the aforementioned words such as "light" (*jyotis*) and so forth—though their application (*vṛtti*) toward what is merely well-known, namely the celebrated light, the celebrated Indra, and the celebrated vital breath (*prāṇa*), is indeed characterized by manifold contradictions; therefore, for the reason stated, the one whose nature is the fire within the belly—the gastric fire—is none other than the Supreme Self. Thus, through meditation—that is, through worship characterized by identifying the gastric fire with the body—for the sake of that fruit...

For the sake of attaining the perfection of the fruit—namely, beauty, fame, and attainment—as understood from the concluding passage, that which was stated here as "This indeed is that light which is within this person" possesses the characteristics of the vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) and so forth. These are its unique, supreme natures: the well-known characteristic of sustaining life residing in the vital breath, and the well-known characteristic of being three-headed and having his head struck off residing in Indra. Through the meditation on the Supreme [Brahman] as conditioned by these, [one meditates on Him] as characterized by having the vital breath as His body (*mukhya-prāṇa-śarīrakatva-viśiṣṭasya*). (Likewise...)

And it is precisely for the purpose of making known that liberation—meaning the attainment of liberation—is possible through the means consisting of the meditation upon the Supreme Self as characterized by having the well-known body of Indra. || 76 ||

Whatever object is an effect—that is, something produced—and is firmly established by etymological derivation (*rūḍhi*), may, in certain instances, refer to Brahman when it is indicated by words whose conventional meanings have been set aside, according to the principle of Indra (*aindrī-naya*). This occurs through the force of understanding that the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of Brahman cannot be otherwise accounted for; thus, there may be an intention to speak of the Lord as qualified by those marks, as in the case of the mention of "light" (*jyotis*), "Indra," and so forth, or when the word "I" (*aham*) and the like are uttered. As for the phrase "whatever object": an entity such as ether (*ākāśa*), fire (*agni*), and so on, which is an effect—meaning something produced—and is "firmly established"—that is, determined without doubt.

When [the Supreme Self] has been indicated by such terms as "thou" (*tvam*) and so forth, then—by the force of apprehending that its specific marks cannot be otherwise accounted for—that is, by relying on the force consisting of the certainty that the unique marks (such as being an effect, being subject to karma, and so on) cannot be explained otherwise, there would indeed be an intention—that is, the state of being the intended object of the *śruti* and other means of knowledge—with respect to the Supreme Self as qualified by those respective meanings established by the conventional usage of the words, namely the meanings of Jyotiṣ, Indra, and so forth. || 77 ||
The Lord, who is the cause of all by His own will, whose joy is infinite and boundless due to the abundance of auspicious qualities,

whose divine form arises from pure karma, whose nature is beginningless like the unconditioned ether, who is the life-breath of the universe that is differentiated by the distinction between those with breath and those without, who possesses divine luster, and who is the inner self within Indra and the other gods, has been established by means of the seven logical grounds.

And by means of seven topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*)—namely, those concerning the "Beholder" (*īkṣati*), the "Consisting of Bliss" (*ānandamaya*), the "Space within" (*antar-ākāśa*), "Breath" (*prāṇa*), "Light" (*jyotis*), and those titled "Indra" and "Prāṇa"—which constitute the seven in number belonging to the first chapter (*pāda*) of the *Śārīraka-śāstra* (in their respective order): [He is] the cause of all by His own will—the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe dependent upon His mere volition; [He is] auspicious...

Harṣa is the great ocean of immeasurable bliss, characterized by infinite, unsurpassed, and unlimited excellence consisting of the auspicious qualities and sovereign glory of the entire universe; he whose nature is pure action, whose divine and auspicious form is independent of karma and composed solely of existence, whose essence is uncontracted natural luminosity, who is the life-force that animates all sentient and insentient beings, whose divine radiance consists of non-material light, and who is the self of the vital breaths, Indra, and the rest.
The Supreme Person, the Lord of all, the Controller and Master, having entered within from the very Indra whose nature is the vital breath (prāṇa), has been established—fully demonstrated. || 78 ||
...3) Summary of the meaning of the section:

In the section concerning Indra and Prāṇa (*indraprāṇādhikaraṇa*), regarding the passage "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa... where [Indra] is designated by the word "Indra" as the object of the most beneficial meditation in the statement "Meditate on me...", and because the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son is seen at the very beginning, one might raise the doubt that the one described as the object of the most beneficial meditation is none other than the well-known Indra. Having raised this doubt:

Because the marks (liṅga) of the Supreme Self are seen in many passages, and because the opening statement (upakrama) is weaker than the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), it was established as the final conclusion that the one referred to by the word "Indra"—who is described as the object of meditation for the sake of the highest benefit—is indeed the Supreme Self having Indra as its body. 4) Regarding the connection of the method (*naya-saṅgati*): From the previously mentioned *Upakramaparākrama*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises; however, in the section concerning Indra and Prāṇa (*indraprāṇādhikaraṇa*), the connection is one of exception (*āpavādika*). Thus, in the first section (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*lakṣaṇa*), they have thus come together.
The three boxes and also the eleven topics; [the eleventh is] the topic of Indra and Prāṇa. || 39 || || Indraprāṇādhikaraṇam || 11 ||
The first quarter of the first chapter is completed.

The Second Pāda of the First Adhyāya: 1) This collection of the essential principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā] is as follows: In this scripture, Brahman alone—the very cause of the worlds, whose body is directly composed of consciousness (cit) and non-consciousness (acit)—is the subject. With the aim of clarifying this meaning, [the author] composed the remaining three pādas. (19)

In this treatise—the Śārīraka—Brahman alone, the Supreme Brahman, whose body consists of the conscious and the unconscious (cidaciccharīra), being itself directly (sākṣāt) and without mediation, is the source (nidāna) of all worlds; desiring to clarify this very point, Bādarāyaṇa then composed the remaining three chapters—the second, third, and fourth—consisting of the three subsequent sections. || 19 ||
Therein, by the second [reason], the body was shown to be the entire expansion of the conscious and unconscious;
by the third, its identity with that [Self]; and by the fourth, the refutation of the opposite view. || 20 ||

In that regard—within the three feet beginning with the second: by the second [foot], first of all, it is deliberated and determined that the entire manifold of the conscious and the unconscious (*cidācit-prapañca*) exists as a body for Him—that is, as something whose subordinate status (*śeṣatva*), state of being supported (*dhāryatva*), and state of being governed (*niyāmyatva*) are defined by the Supreme Brahman. By the third [foot], there is the investigation into His nature as the Self (*tadātmabhāva*), namely, the investigation into His sovereignty over the entire world consisting of the conscious and the unconscious. By the fourth [foot]...
By this [verse], its opposite has been refuted, and the contradiction regarding the sentient, insentient, and embodied [jīva] being the cause of the Supreme Self has also been eliminated. || 20 ||
12. The Section on Being Renowned Everywhere (Sarvatra-prasiddhi-adhikaraṇa). 1–2–1.
Because it is caused by its own karma, because of its application [to various bodies], because of its smallness, and because of its having a small abode—
having raised all these doubts, [the self] is established as the living being (jīva) through its well-known nature, its qualities, and traditional scripture.

On account of the charge of being the cause [of the world] through one's own karma—that is, because of the implication that the individual soul is the cause of the world’s creation by virtue of being bound to its own auspicious and inauspicious actions; on account of its smallness, as indicated by the scriptural statement, "It is subtler than a grain of rice"; and on account of its having a small abode, as indicated by the suitability for dwelling in a small place mentioned in the text, "The Self within the heart"—having raised all these doubts regarding the individual soul (jīva), which is conscious and subject to karma, the scripture [states], "All this indeed... [to resolve them].

Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the Self] is denotable by the word "all," [the author] refutes it on the grounds that it is impossible for the causal nature—which is the object of the well-known usage indicated by the word "indeed" (*khalu*) in the phrase "All this, indeed"—to apply [to the individual soul]. Furthermore, because of its qualities—namely, the scriptural mention of qualities uncommon to others such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*); because of the indicative evidence of the *Smṛti*, "And I am in the heart of all"; and because even in the case of the Supreme, the state of having the small abode called the heart is possible—the [author] has rejected the individual soul (*jīva*) and dismissed the claim that the soul is the referent of the word "all" occurring in the scripture. || 21 ||
2) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

Herein, Brahman is primarily established in the first section (*pāda*) through the methods of excluding non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and excluding connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), which are rooted in the [first] quarter and the [subsequent] three quarters [of the *Śrībhāṣya*], beginning with the soft [topics] and culminating in the firm ones. Then, the [remaining] three quarters are set forth for the sake of pacifying all objections; they were composed to uproot every dispute, preceded by the removal of occasional objections. || 1 ||

Here, in the first [section]—in the first chapter of the *Śārīraka*, consisting of three quarters (*pādas*)—[the topics] are established by means of portions comprising one quarter and portions comprising three quarters; they are accomplished with gentle beginnings and difficult conclusions—meaning with little effort at the outset and with increasingly greater exertion thereafter; and they generally follow the method of excluding both non-connection and improper connection—(respectively) primarily through the exclusion of the impossibility of Brahman being the cause of the world, and likewise [through the exclusion of] the possibility of anything other than Brahman being the cause of the world.

And by means of chapters (adhikaraṇas) abounding in the exclusion of other [entities] as Brahman, Brahman is to be established—the Supreme Brahman, distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious, which is to be demonstrated as that which is known through the Vedāntas.

Therefore—for the reason stated above—the first quarter (pāda) here—that is, the first section belonging to the first chapter—is set forth for the purpose of pacifying the entire objection; it is composed to quell the objection that arises regarding the subject matter of all Vedānta texts concerning the failure to establish a Brahman that is distinct from all sentient and non-sentient beings. As for the remaining three quarters here—that is, the other three sections of the first chapter—they deal with specific [objections].

It has been composed and written for the purpose of total eradication—that is, for the purpose of refuting, in due order, the objections raised against all Vedānta statements that have proceeded one after another, following the initial objection regarding the non-establishment of Brahman as the subject matter of certain specific Vedānta passages. || 1 ||

In the *Bhāṣya* on the introduction of the lamp (*Dīpāvatāra*), the deliberation upon sentences possessing indistinct, distinct, or more clearly manifest marks of consciousness (*cid-liṅga*) has been undertaken by means of various methods within the first three chapters (*tripādī*).
