However, some maintain that the first chapter (*pāda*) concerns subjects endowed with extremely indistinct marks; in this regard, there is a fixed gradation determined by the respective strengths of the views held by the ancient [authorities] and those of the third chapter.

In the *Tripādī*—that is, in the three sections beginning with the second of the first chapter—by means of the "multitude of methods" (*nayagaṇaiḥ*), i.e., the collections of topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*), there has been undertaken (*sampravṛttā*) a determination preceded by inquiry into the Vedānta passages that do not immediately produce the comprehension of attributes common to both sentient and insentient beings (*aspaṣṭa-cintā*), which are such as to cause the cognition of those attributes, as well as those Vedānta passages that do immediately cause the cognition of such attributes; this is stated in the *Bhāṣya*, the work of Śrī Bhāṣya, and also in the *Dīpāvatāra*.

In the same way, it has been clearly demonstrated in the *Avataraṇikā* (Introduction) to the *Vedāntadīpa*. However, certain other commentators on the *Bhāṣya* maintain—that is, they propound—that the first quarter (*pāda*), the first section, concerns subjects characterized by extremely clear marks (*liṅga`), consisting of an inquiry into passages where the marks of the conscious (*cit*) and unconscious (*acit*) are not very distinct. Such is this gradation—this distinction—among those various Vedāntic passages.

It should be understood that [the conclusion] is established by means of the *śruti* and other authorities which grasp the application (*viniyoga*), which are determined by fixed intrinsic powers, which possess a well-ordered gradation of their own respective strengths, and which are considered the third part of the ritual action—established in the third chapter of the *Karmakāṇḍa*. In the first [section], the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was constructed by means of principles whose forms were not yet established according to one's own intellect; in the second, the counter-objection (*pratyavasthā*) was made by means of those [principles] which are established, common, yet constrained by specific conditions. Then, in the subsequent [section], there are the formulations of the opponent’s views characterized by clear and unique features. Thus.
The thirty-one principles (*nyāya*) here should be sought out as they are distributed according to each chapter and its divisions. || 3 ||

In the preceding section (the first *pāda*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arose from various disputants who, through their own intellectual fabrications, presented reasons characterized by forms imagined by their respective intellects—reasons that were unestablished in nature (*asiddharūpa*), specifically suffering from the fallacy of being unestablished in essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*) due to not residing in the subject (*pakṣāvṛttitva*). This was a point to be resolved through the methods of logic (*nyāya*).

In the second [quarter], in the immediately following foot (*anantarapāda*), the method of raising the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣotthānaprakāra*) consists of opposing [the position] by means of reasons (*hetu*) that possess two characteristics—namely, subsisting in the subject (*pakṣavṛttitva*) and subsisting in what is other than the subject (*pakṣetara-vṛttitva*)—which are common even to those who have attained success (*siddha*), and which are constrained by a limiting condition (*upādhi*), meaning they possess a concomitance with the probandum (*sādhya*) dependent upon that condition; or rather, [opposing it] by showing them to be non-deviant from the probandum only insofar as they are qualified by a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*). In the subsequent third quarter, [the opposition is shown] clearly through the state of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatva*), which is more manifestly recognized.

The establishment of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) occurs through reasons that demonstrate the non-commonality (*asādhāraṇatā*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). Now, in the fourth quarter (*pāda*), the counter-position is established through reasons that resemble the restatement of the opponent's intended meaning, following the formulations of their doctrines. By means of these aforementioned methods, here—in this first chapter—there is a division according to each quarter (*pāda*), accompanied by a division of meaning consistent with the division of the quarters; or rather, it is accompanied by various non-restricted differentiating characteristics, consisting of thirty-one principles of logic (*nyāya*).

The number of topics (*adhikaraṇas*) is thirty-one; they are to be sought—that is, they must be investigated with skill. || 3 || In the second quarter, the group of sentences is considered while explaining that "the body is the universe"; in the third, one intent on declaring "He is the Self, the support of the universe" must reflect upon it;

and in the fourth, the delusion arising from the recitations of the Sāṅkhya and other schools must be dispelled—thus some have declared this three-quarter [section], which is likewise a means for the mental composure of the listener. || 4 ||

Some—certain other commentators who reflect upon the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra—in the second quarter (pāda) within the first chapter, specifically in the second quarter of the first chapter, consider—that is, investigate and determine—the group of statements which teaches that "the entire universe is the body" (*viśvaṃ samantaṃ jagad vapuḥ*), meaning that the multitude of Vedāntic passages declare that the world is the body of the Supreme Brahman.

In every third quarter [of each verse], that Self—the Supreme Self who has the universe as His body—is to be reasoned out, that is, investigated and determined by means of a collection of statements intended to convey such a meaning; namely, a group of Vedānta passages whose sole purpose is to establish that He is the support of the universe and possesses the quality of being the support of the universe, which serves to demonstrate His having the universe as His body.

"In the fourth, the fourth quarter, the delusion regarding Sāṅkhya and other systems—namely, the delusion that the Vedāntas merely restate the very objects established by the positions of the Sāṅkhya, Pātañjala, and others—is to be uprooted; it must be eliminated so as not to sprout again. In this manner, they spoke of the "three-quarters"—the three quarters possessing distinct meanings for each quarter. This aforementioned method also serves to clarify the division of the subject matter for the intellect of the listener.
For those curious about hearing [the teachings], meditative concentration (samādhi) becomes a method that quells the thirst of longing. || 4 ||

The Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, which is intent upon the practice of meditation on Him whose vital breath (prāṇa) is the body—that very [Brahman] which is the most beneficial—produces the notion of "livingness" (jīvatva) regarding that [Self] who is the progenitor of the world. And because of the logic of the preceding [section], self-restraint (damana) is appropriate here; thus, since the commencement [of the topic] follows what was stated at the outset, the Mahāvākya unifies them. || 5 ||

Of whom—of that Supreme Self whose body is the universe; whose "breath" (prāṇa) is the entity called breath, which is the cause of the vitalization of the world, and which possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to command, and being subordinate, serving as the object of meditation for one's highest welfare—that Supreme Self is sought through the meditation on Him who is the most beneficial to oneself. Indeed, He has been introduced in the preceding section, in the *Indraprāṇādhikaraṇa*; [meditate] upon that Reality, who is the progenitor of the world and is established by the Śruti as the cause of the universe.

Regarding the subject, there is the suspicion of being a living soul—the delusion that "an object characterized by such qualities must necessarily be a living soul. The series of scriptural texts (*śruti-tati*) consisting of statements such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" from the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā in the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad produces [the opposite certainty]. That is to say, it exists [to dispel that doubt].

Regarding "from the standpoint of the Great Sentence" (*mahāvākyataḥ*): by virtue of the conformity of the multitude of many sentences—which possess a single intended meaning throughout the entire section from beginning to end—to the subduing of the initial context, which is to say, the alteration of the intended meaning of the sentence situated at the commencement; "it is logical" (*yuktam*) means it is sanctioned by reasoning (*nyāyasammatam*), thus following the previous reasoning—the reasoning stated in the *Indraprāṇādhikaraṇa*—when there is an "arising here," that is, when the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds in this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), [we have] the "Great Sentence" (*mahāvākya*), which contains within it many sentences sharing a single intended meaning.

The section concerning "rootless and tipless" [trees] is "consistent with what was stated at the outset"—that is, it is not non-conclusive, as it does not contradict the purport of the statement situated at the beginning. [The author] unifies them; [here the Sūtrakāra] demonstrates the principle of "uniformity of voice" (*aikakaṇṭhya*) alone. || 5 ||
Having first introduced the distinction here [in this section], for what reason was the introductory statement (*adhikāra*) spoken?

It is appropriate that the subsequent restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the unity of the injunctions is solely for the purpose of enjoining a quality (*guṇavidhi*). True; having granted this, even if a dispute were to arise in some Upanishad or elsewhere, this reflection would serve as an illustrative example. However, it should be understood that the establishment of the meaning follows the deliberation of other systems of thought.

In this context—within the scriptural passages belonging to the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā—having "resorted to" (anvāruhya) a distinction—that is, either a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) between the words *brahman* and *manomaya*, or a difference in meaning (*artha-bheda*) between *brahman* and the individual soul (*jīva*), even though such a distinction is not actually accepted as if it were accepted—the author asks: for what purpose, for what aim, was the "treatment of the subject" (*adhikāra*) presented in the first arrangement (*prathama-yojanā*) in the Śrībhāṣya? [This is done] regarding the unity of the injunctions stated in "He should perform the ritual resolve" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*) and "He should meditate in a state of tranquility" (*śānta upāsīta*).

Regarding the view that the meditation on the seasons (*ṛtu*) and the meditation [on the Self] belong to a single unified knowledge (*vidyā*), another [objection] is raised: "The injunctive portion, 'He should form a resolve (*ṛtuṃ kurvīta*),' is intended solely for the purpose of enjoining a quality; that is, it is rightly understood as being merely for the sake of making known that the quality of tranquility residing in the worshipper is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the meditation within this specific knowledge. (When this objection has been set forth: "True—some portion of what has been stated must indeed be accepted."

In a certain part of an Upaniṣad (*kvacid upaniṣadi*), having accepted the existence of Brahman (*brahmānumatya*), and in another part of that same Upaniṣad (*kvāpi*), when a dispute (*vivāde*) or a contradictory argument (*viruddhe vāde*) is to be suspected, this reflection (*eṣā cintā*)—composed from the perspective of another school (*paramataracitā*)—should be understood as an illustration (*udāhṛtiḥ*) or an example (*dṛṣṭāntarūpā*) intended for a different system of thought (*matāntare*). Thus, the accomplishment of the purpose of the section (*arthasiddhiḥ*), which is the fulfillment of the objective of the discussion (*adhikaraṇaprayojanasampattiḥ*), is to be known.

If it be argued that "omnipresence" is applicable only to the individual soul (*jīva*)—who possesses birth through its own actions, for whom the word "Brahman" is used by others [figuratively], who occupies a small space, has limited knowledge, and experiences both pleasure and its opposite—it is not so. For the status of being "born from Him" and so forth has not been stated [of the *jīva*]; because various distinctions of qualities are observed; and because omnipresence and other attributes are natural [to Brahman].
Thus, the atomicity [of the soul] must be understood here as caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), intended for the sake of meditation upon the Supreme.

In the individual soul (*jīva*), whose birth is dependent upon its own karma consisting of merit and demerit, "allness" is possible—the state of being the self of all as declared by the Śruti, "All this, indeed, is [Brahman]"; this is logically consistent. Likewise, the word "Brahman"—the term "Brahman" used in the expression "This is Brahman"—is also applicable, without contradiction, even to the individual soul which is distinct from the Supreme Brahman.

If it be argued: "The object [of the word *jīva*] is one that resides in a small location—namely, the place of the heart which is called 'small'; it is of small measure, having an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*); it is the experiencer of pleasure and its opposite—the experience of happiness and suffering; and it is the *jīva* alone, the individual self, and not the Supreme Self"—if such a doubt is raised, it is not appropriate. Why? Because of the attributes such as "being born from That" (*tajjatva*), which are well-known from the scripture, "From which indeed these [beings are born]" (*yato vā imāni*), namely: being born from Brahman, merging into Brahman, and having existence dependent on Brahman; for these are not left unmentioned by the phrase "*tajjalān*" ("born from That, merged in That, and breathing in That").

Because of the restatement [of the same entity], because various distinct qualities are observed—since scriptural texts establish specific, mutually distinct, and non-common attributes of Brahman such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth—and because of the natural fitness of the term "allness" (sarvatva), that is, its nature as the self of all; and also because of the appropriateness of residing in a single conscious being rather than in many conscious beings, here "atomicity" refers to a subtle dimension as stated in the phrase "smaller than a grain of rice," and this is in reference to the "greater," that is, the unsurpassedly vast Supreme Self.

"For the sake of worship"—that is, for the ease of meditation—it would be "conditioned by an adjunct" (upadhikṛta), meaning it would be based solely on the limitation of the location consisting of the heart; it would not be produced by its own nature. || 7 ||

Regarding the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman," one might raise the objection that since the instruction here concerns the identity of everything from the four-faced Brahmā down to stationary objects with Brahman, and since such identity with the four-faced one and so forth is possible even for individual souls (jīvas), the term "Brahman" must refer to the jīva itself.
Anticipating this doubt:

The established conclusion is that the Supreme Self is the one indicated by the word "Brahman," because the origin and other states of the world are taught as being well-known causes in the phrase "tajjalān" (from that, they are born, etc.), and because it is well-established that these states belong to the Supreme Self, who has all things as His body, making His identity with everything logically consistent.
4) Nayasaṅgatimālikā:
Now, in this second chapter, through the division into triads and dyads, there are the two sections on worship (*upāsti*) concerning abiding in small stations and great stations. (40)
The mark of Brahman contained within the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) is declared to be powerful;
by such a mark, doubt is dispelled in every system of thought. (41)
Thus concludes the section on "Establishment Everywhere" (Sarvatraprasiddhyadhikaraṇa). ||1||
The Topic of Discussion || 1-2-2 ||
1) "The collection of arguments in the *Śārīraka-nyāya-kalāpa-saṅgraha* [asserts]:

'But the self is the individual soul (*jīva*), not another independent entity; for that very soul is the experiencer of the fruits of its own karma. This too is incorrect; for that [self] is the substratum of the consumption [of results] through the infusion of death into all things moving and stationary. (22)

The meaning established by the scripture through the phrase "of whom Brahman is" (*yasya brahma ca*) is the Self (*ātman*); however, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed only the individual soul, and cannot be the Supreme, the Paramātman, because [the individual soul] is dependent, whereas He is independent. For this reason—that very one, the individual self alone, must be the enjoyer of the fruits of action—the experiencer of the results of actions consisting of merit and demerit acquired by itself—such a doubt as this is also incorrect; for that which is stated in the scripture is true.

"Eating" (adana) refers to the devouring of the world—consisting of both the moving and the stationary—preceded by the sprinkling of death; "drinking" (apiti), however, is simply the withdrawal of the entire universe performed by the Supreme Self. || 22 ||
2) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

"The one who eats the rice and so forth is indeed the Supporter"—this [eater] might be understood from the Kaṭha Śruti as being the individual soul (*jīva*), yet it cannot be so, because of the statement regarding its dissolution [into that Being], which implies the swallowing of all moving and unmoving things drenched by death. Furthermore, the exclusion of the individual soul is known from the context; however, the mention of two enjoyers may be due to their fixed roles as the beloved and the impeller, according to the maxim of the parasol-bearer and the king, or otherwise. (8)

Of "odanādeḥ" (of rice and so forth), that is, of edible substances such as food; "attā" means the eater. "Bhavabhṛt khalu" means indeed the living being (*jīva*) who is wandering by the power of karma within the wheel of *prakṛti*. For this reason, even though the eater is recited in the Kaṭha Śruti in the passage, "He whose [food] Brahman and Kṣatra are..."—that eater must be the living being itself (this is the prima facie view). It cannot be so—the eater mentioned in the scripture cannot be the living being (this is the final answer).

By the statement that [Death] devours all things—both stationary and moving—along with the sprinkling of the essence of death itself, which serves as an indicator; for the dissolution of that [world] is taught in the Śruti through the very act of devouring, which consists of the dissolution of the universe, and because such [devouring] is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, the exclusion of the *jīva* is clearly indicated by the description of attributes unique to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and this is well-established by the context of the Supreme Self, as seen in passages such as "the great, all-pervading one" and "this Self [is not... and so forth.

Regarding the two—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*puruṣottama*)—the designation of both as "enjoyers" (*bhoktṛ*) is due to the description of their agency in enjoyment, characterized by "drinking," as stated in the verse "drinking the *ṛta*. This is intended solely to denote the respective enjoyership of the individual soul and the Supreme Self, corresponding to their specific natures, by way of their fixed roles as the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*) and the prompting agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Alternatively, it may be according to the logic of "those with umbrellas" (*chatrin-nyāya*), based merely on being included within a group formed by those possessing umbrellas.

Just as in the usage of the term "parasol-bearer," that designation may also apply to the Supreme Self when it is included within a collective group consisting of the agent, the fruit, and the enjoyer.

By distinguishing that the "knower" (jña) is the *sattva* which does not eat while eating the sweet [food], the statement "the *sattva* is the intellect (*buddhi*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*)" is indeed false here; for "of the two who do not drink, one is the living being (*jīva*)," [and] "the other is the *asat*. Do not say so; this scriptural mention of "being" (*sat*) is appropriate for the living being who experiences the fruits of karma even while not eating.
Furthermore, the introduction of the question regarding that [living being] has another intention, and this has also been explained by those who consider the preceding and following contexts.

"Because of the analysis—'sattvam' means the entity called *sattva*; 'svādu atti' means it eats [enjoys] with prior relishing; 'jñaḥ' means the object that serves as the substratum of knowledge; 'anaśnan' means being devoid of the state of being an enjoyer"—since it is explained in this manner by distinguishing [the terms] in the Paiṅgi Śruti, the *sattva* studied in the Paiṅgi [text], namely the entity denoted by the word *sattva* recited in the Paiṅgi Śruti, must be either the intellect (*buddhi*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that is, it can be the entity in the form of the intellect or the entity known as the vital breath.

For this very reason, here—in this section of the Kaṭhavallī, concerning the two who "drink the *ṛta*" as stated in the scripture (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*)—one of those two is the individual soul (*jīva*), which is one of the meanings of the term *sattvajña* (according to the prima facie view). [To this we reply: It is not so; the aforementioned method is not appropriate. For this scriptural passage on "being" (*sat-ca-śruti*), which has been shown to consist of a metaphorical identification (*sampad-ātmikā*), is observed to be applicable to a living being (*jantu*) and to convey the sense of a sentient creature.

The *karmabhuk*—the individual soul (*jīva*) established by the Śruti and other authorities as the enjoyer of the fruits of action—is not [to be understood] as one who does not eat; that is, it cannot be one who lacks the state of being an enjoyer. For that reason (*tat*), the sequence of questions—the manner of questioning by Naciketas—possesses a distinct intention (*anyāśaya*).

This distinct purpose of the question is also declared (*abhāṣi*) through the means of determining the purport (*tātparyanirṇāyaka*), such as the beginning and conclusion (*upakramopasaṃhāra*) and so forth, in the *Śrībhāṣya*. ||9||
3) Summary of the Topic:

Regarding the section on the locus (*adhikaraṇa*): In the passage beginning with, "He for whom both the Brahmin and the Kshatriya are food," since it is heard that there is the state of being an enjoyer caused by [past] actions, one might suspect that the "Eater" (*attā*) is merely the individual soul (*jīva*). Having raised this doubt:

Since death is established as the "sprinkling" (the accompaniment) for the food consisting of the moving and the unmoving, and since that [act of consumption] takes the form of the withdrawal of the universe—which is unique to the Supreme Self—it has been stated: "The Eater is the Supreme Self."
4) *Nayasaṅgatimālikā*:

If there is no state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), then that [entity] is simply the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) who is the individual soul (*jīva*). Because of the doubt that he might be the "eater" (*attā*), this is the connection [of the topic] as a counter-example. ||42|| Thus ends the section (Adhikaraṇa) 2.
The intermediate section. 1-2-3.
1) "This [self] is within the eye" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.2)—is this well-known [self] the individual soul (*jīva*), or the reflection, or even the deity?
This too is incorrect, because of the mention of immortality, the hearing of bliss, and because of the impossibility of [the self being] unstable. //23//

As for "that which is within the eye"—the object understood as residing within the orb of the eye in the Chāndogya Śruti passage, "That which is this in the eye," by means of the indicator consisting of the co-occurrence of the word "this" (*ya eṣaḥ*) which denotes well-knownness—this might be the individual soul (*jīva*), the presiding agent of the body subject to karma; or else it might be the reflection (*bimba*)—or rather, the reflected image (*pratibimba*) perceived within the eye;
or even, it might be a deity (*daiva*), a specific divine being.

The suspicion that [the person in the eye] might be the individual soul (*jīvātman*), a reflection, or a particular deity—raised by the statement "also here"—would be unfounded; it would not be correct. This is because of the mention of immortality in the word "immortal" (*amṛta*)—since the person in the eye is declared immortal in the phrase "the immortal, the fearless"—because of the hearing of bliss in the words "bliss, space" (*kaṃ kham*), which declare his nature to be unconditioned bliss, and because of the impossibility of stability, since reflections cannot reside continuously within the eyeball. ||23||

This which is being heard—namely, the meaning established by the Chāndogya Śruti, "This person who is seen in the eye"—is understood from the indicative power of the context, such as the use of the word *yat* (which), which expresses well-knownness; it refers either to the individual soul (*jīva*), the presiding agent of the body, or else, it refers to the deity of the eyes, the Sun (*arka*).

If it is argued that the presiding deity of the eye is the Sun, or else, according to another view, that there is a visible image—that is, something seen within the eyeball or a reflection of another person who is looking—such a suspicion is not at all sound.

Because of the study of such scriptural passages as, "This is Brahman; this indeed is the immortal, this is the fearless, Ka, Kha," and because the qualities of being Brahman, immortality, fearlessness, as well as the nature of bliss and the nature of space are recited in the Śruti regarding the Person in the Eye; and by virtue of the unique marks of the Supreme Person—namely, the qualities beginning with *saṃyadvāmatva* (the convergence of blessings); and by the strong mark consisting of His fixed residence in the eye due to the power of the rule of location; and also because of the mention of the path beginning with light (*arcis*).

Furthermore, because of the teaching of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), which leads only to the one established in Brahman through the experience of the Person within the eye, it is the Supreme Person alone—the goal to be attained by the liberated—who is the Person to be meditated upon as residing within the eye; it is not the individual soul (*jīva*) nor the images of the sun. (10) In the independent *Śrutis*, there is no doctrine that only that which bestows a fruit is to be known, since knowledge is purposeful even through the force of an injunction, as in the case of the "beholding of the auspicious" (*kalyāṇālokanādi*).
Therefore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is appropriate that the person within the eye is a representative image.
This same principle should be applied, as far as possible, to the preceding and succeeding sections as well. || 11 ||

In the case of the *śrutis*—the Vedic words—which are "adorned with sovereignty" (*svātantryottaṃsitāsu*), meaning they are embellished by sovereignty in the form of being the cause of engagement and withdrawal independently of logic, worldly convention, and so forth; and because meditation (*upāsana*), which depends solely on injunction (*vidhi-mātra-adhīna*) and is governed by scriptural mandate (*vidhi-balataḥ*), possesses purposefulness—that is, it is fruitful—therefore, the doctrine that only that which is capable of bestowing fruit is the object of knowledge (*vedya*) follows: for only a reality (*vastu*) that is capable of granting a result can be the object of knowledge. Just as the sight of an auspicious mirror or similar acts are like the sight of a beautiful woman, they bring about auspiciousness. Thus, because meditation is fruitful, only that which is capable of yielding a result is the object of knowledge.

There is no such rule that [the object of meditation] must be the one to be worshipped. Therefore—for the reason stated above—the person situated within the eye, who is prescribed as the object of worship by residing within the eye, is appropriately understood, according to the method of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), to be a representative person, namely, a person consisting of a reflection; this alone is logical. This is the principle—that is, the principle set forth which gives rise to the prima facie argument.

(An activity consisting in setting aside the deliberation on whether a matter stated by scripture is logical or illogical) should, as far as possible, be applied even to the preceding and succeeding sections—that is, to the prior and subsequent topical discussions—taking into account the specific subject matter and other factors of each respective place; although not explicitly stated, it must be considered as that which gives rise to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). In the previous principle (*nyāya*), the knowledge of the fires (*agnividyā*) was introduced at the outset, whereas here it appears in the middle;
therefore, just like that, the inclusion of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) does not occur [here], and thus the knowledge of the eye (*akṣividyā*) must be something different from that.

Not so; for there is no interruption by the constituent parts (aṅgas), nor is its status as a subsidiary (aṅgatā) limited, since it has many bases. Furthermore, the fruit described here is consistent with the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), and previously, the meditation on [the self] as Brahman was not [intended]. ||12||

But previously—in the previous rule (*pūrvanyāya*), namely in the subject passage of this section from the *Kaṭhavallī*, concerning the knowledge of Agni—the knowledge of Agni, beginning with the question "The self is the Agni that leads to heaven" and ending with "People shall proclaim this very Agni to you," was presented earlier; that is, it stood prior to the knowledge of Brahman. But here—in the subject passage of the *Antarā* section from the *Chāndogya*, however—it is presented in the middle; that is, it stands in the midst of the knowledge of Brahman.

Therefore—for the reason stated—just as in the case of the subject-matter passages of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (*tadvat*), here—in the subject-matter passages of this section concerning the "Inner" (*antara*)—there is no continuous succession of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā'nugati*); that is, the knowledge of Brahman does not persist without interruption. The "Eye-knowledge" (*akṣividyā*), spoken of as "this person who is seen in the eye," is distinct from the other knowledge of Brahman spoken of as "Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman. (Thus it is.)

[To this] objection, [the author] replies: "Maitra"—such a description is not correct. "By the subsidiaries" (aṅgaiḥ) means by those ritual elements prescribed as subsidiaries in the Veda; "interruption" (vicchittiḥ) means the non-continuation of the nature of the principal rite (aṅgin). For it is indeed well-established in the earlier system (Pūrva-tantra) that [interruption] does not occur—that is, it does not arise.

And the subsidiary status (*aṅgatā*)—that is, the quality of being an auxiliary (*upakārakatā*)—of this *agnividyā* belonging to the *Chāndogya*, is established by various means (*bahudhā mitā*) through numerous types of evidence; and the fruit mentioned here—which is heard at the conclusion of the instruction on the *agnividyā* and consists of longevity, fame, and so forth—is indeed conducive to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā'nuguṇam*), meaning it is productive of the knowledge of Brahman and not contrary to it.

And prior to the teacher’s instruction—that is, before the instruction concerning fire as the agent—there is no "viewing as Brahman"; that is, it does not take the form of an injunction to view non-Brahman, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as Brahman, because it has not been so perceived. || 12 ||
3) Summary of the meaning of the section:

In the intermediate section, regarding the passage beginning with "This person who is seen in the eye," since that which resides in the eye is designated as something well-known, and since that well-known status is applicable to a reflection, the individual soul (*jīva*), the sun, and so forth—on the grounds of perception, reasoning, and scripture—one might suspect that "the person in the eye is one of those. However, because qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (*saṃyadvāmatva*) are possible only in the Supreme Self, and because its residence in the eye is well-established in passages such as "He who dwells in the eye," it is stated: "The person in the eye is the Supreme Self."

4) In the section on "Extreme Difficulty to Perceive" (*durdarśatā*), Sudarśana may be seen with the eyes; then, through the connection of counter-examples (*pratyudāhṛti*), there arises the commencement of the "Intermediate Section" (*antarādhikaraṇa*). ||43|| Thus ends the Intermediate Section (3).
15) The Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa) ||1.2.4||
1) *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha*:

"Because of the word 'seer' (*draṣṭṛ*) here, and because of the negation of another seer in the supplementary passage; because it says 'it speaks to the Knower of the Field who controls from within'; this [Self] does not wake, because of the word 'immortality'. (24)

In this context, within the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) related to the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*—specifically in the sentence "The unseen seer" (*adṛṣṭo draṣṭā*) and so forth, which constitutes a subordinate member of the principal statement—from the word "seer" (*draṣṭā*), which indicates the agency of seeing dependent on the eyes and thus serves as an indicator of the individual soul (*jīva*); and from the negation of another seer—that is, the negation of any other agent of seeing found in that very same passage through the phrase "There is no other seer than He" (*nānyo'to'sti draṣṭā*).

Regarding the phrase "controlling from within" (*antaryamayantaṃ*): [the opponent] suggests that the meaning is one whose nature is to govern by entering into everything, namely the *kṣetrajña*, and asserts that this refers specifically to the form of the individual soul (*jīva*)—this is the doubt raised by the scripture in the form of the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*. However, this does not hold; it is not established, because of the word "immortality" (*amṛtatva*). This is due to the scriptural expression "the inner controller who is immortal" (*antaryāmyamṛtaḥ*), which indicates the immortality unique to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in reference to that entity whose nature is to govern by entering within. And that substance called darkness (*tamas*) is dense, thin, black, and moving.

We accept [the authority of scripture] because no sublation has been observed anywhere by anyone; therefore, a cause must be postulated. Thus, verbal cognition also prevails, for it is said that "the eye reveals even in the absence of light" (as seen in the *Darśanavāda*).

We perceive darkness as a substance possessing both density and interstices, and as being both blue in form and a substratum of motion; we directly perceive this entity, well-known to all people as "darkness," as a substance.

By no person whatsoever, in any place whatsoever, or at any time whatsoever, has any sublation—namely, a cognition that negates action in the form "darkness lacks blueness" or "darkness is immobile"—ever been observed; nor is it established by experience. (Likewise,) no defect in the cause is experienced that would lead one to infer the erroneous nature of the prior cognition.

Therefore, since there is an absence of subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) and causal defects (*kāraṇadoṣa*), and [darkness] being established as a substance by virtue of possessing qualities and actions, the cause—the entity that serves as the cause for the production of darkness and for the perceptual arising of darkness—must be postulated; it is inferable (*anumeya*). Furthermore, verbal cognition (*śābdī pramitiḥ*)—knowledge consisting of valid apprehension produced by scripture—is victorious; that is, it remains unassailable by opposing arguments.

For—since the eye, the sense organ called "eye," which is devoid of light (*nirāloka*) and not assisted by light, manifests—that is, illuminates—the object consisting of darkness; and this is established by virtue of perception (*darśana*), because in the absence of light, one directly perceives the absence of color-form (*rūpābhāva*) and the absence of luminosity (*tejo'bhāva*). ||28||

3) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*: If it is argued that the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the individual soul (jīva), because [the scripture] speaks of the activity of the intellect (dhīvṛtti) being dependent on various instruments and because of the statement "there is no other seer" (na-anyaḥ draṣṭā), [we reply: no, for this excludes another controller. For the nature of being a seer and so forth consists essentially in the form of the intellect as structured by its respective objects; indeed, these attributes belong primarily to the Lord (īśa). Furthermore, the Kaṇva and Mādhyandina recensions both declare that His very Self is the body (tasya ca ātmā śarīram). //13//

That Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)—described in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* as abiding within the eye and other organs, governing each respectively—is none other than the individual soul (*jīva*), the living self (*jīvātman*). This is because there is a restatement of the various mental modifications dependent on the manifold instruments [of perception], such as "the seer, the hearer," which reiterates the state of possessing functions consisting of knowledge dependent on the various senses like the eyes; and because of the statement in the complementary passage, "There is no other seer," which asserts that there is no seer other than this one.

If it is argued that [the Lord is distinct from the individual soul] because there is a statement denying anything other than the individual soul for one who perceives things as dependent on causes—this suspicion is not at all correct, because of the exclusion of any other controller. This is known from the Śruti, "There is none other than Him," which makes it known that "there is no other controller of the Supreme Person who exists as the controller over everything, including the earth and so forth. Furthermore, [the Lord is known] through the possession of knowledge whose form consists of those respective objects—the knowledge having as its object the form, the substratum of that form, the word, and the substratum of that word.

That which consists of possessing knowledge and so forth is one thing; however, as for "being a seer" and so forth—namely, the qualities of being a seer, a hearer, and so on mentioned in such passages as "the seer, the hearer"—these belong primarily and in a non-figurative sense only to the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman, who is the controller of all. These attributes, consisting of the governance of the entire universe and so forth, reside in the Paramātman alone.

The uncommon attributes (*asādhāraṇa-dharmāḥ*) recited in the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina [recensions] have been studied with clear meaning by the followers of the Kāṇva branch through the sequence beginning with "He who dwells in consciousness" (*yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan*), and by the followers of the Mādhyandina branch through the sequence beginning with "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*). And for that Supreme Self spoken of as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) in such a manner, the "self" (*ātman*) is the class of conscious beings, and the "body" (*śarīra*) possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate. ||13||

Because they occur in the same location, the two terms *ātman* and *vijñāna* recited in these two branches have a single meaning; this is unshakable. Therefore, to say that even that [single meaning] refers merely to the intellect (*buddhi*) is pointless. For, following their established usage in common worldly parlance and the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), these two terms are focused exclusively on consciousness (*cetana*).

There is no contradiction whatsoever in this matter, and through such [arguments] as "that is He," there is a state of perfect harmony (*sāmarasya*). Here—in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* contained within the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, as recited in both branches, namely the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions—the two words "Self" (*ātman*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)—namely, the word "Self" in the passage "He who dwells in the Self" and the word "consciousness" in the passage "He who dwells in consciousness"—both [refer to the same thing] because of their identical location [in the hierarchy of sheaths], following the skin and preceding the semen (i.e., existing between the skin and the semen). (Note: The variants in the footnotes indicate that in one version it is said to be "after the skin" (*tvacaḥ anantaram*), while in another it is "before the semen" (*retasaḥ pūrvam ca vidyamānatārūpasya*);
furthermore, the phrase *paṭhitigatā* refers to the textual reading.)

Because the locus is one, the two terms have a single meaning—that is, they denote an identical referent—and thus this is unshakable; this must be accepted without contradiction. Even so, to say that [the scripture] "speaks of the intellect alone" means that it "makes known the internal organ alone"; for this is indeed a description of an unestablished object and is therefore meaningless, since both these terms—"self" (ātman) and "consciousness" (vijñāna)—follow from what is well-known in the world and in the Vedic tradition.

By their continuous application in a single form toward the conscious individual self (*jīvātman*), these two words—"Self" (*ātman*) and "Knowledge" (*vijñāna*)—are primarily expressive of oneness. In this case, where the two words have an identical referent, there is no sublation by any powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as *Śruti* or *Smṛti*; that is, there is no obstruction.

In the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the breath" (*sata*), [the text states] "That is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal" (*sa ta ātmā antaryāmyamṛtaḥ*); and in the passage "This is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal" (*eṣa ta ātmā antaryāmyamṛtaḥ*), there is a state of harmony with the sentences containing the distinct designation "those are your Selves" (*te ātmā*), and their unity of purport is established. ||14||
4) Summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*):

In the *Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa*, having raised the objection that the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*) mentioned in passages such as "He who dwells in the earth" must be the individual soul (*jīva*) endowed with a particular yoga, because the passage "the seer, the hearer" indicates that his knowledge is dependent on instruments, [the Sūtra] states: "The Inner Ruler is the Supreme Self. This is because by this very same passage the governing of all things—which is an attribute of the Supreme Self—is designated, and because terms such as "seer" and so forth refer to the direct perception of form and other objects, which is applicable to the Supreme Self.

5) The *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* establishes that the person situated within the eye is indeed Brahman; thereafter follows the section on the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), which provides the introductory connection (*upodghātasaṅgati*) thereto. ||44||
Thus ends the section concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa). || 4 ||
The Section Concerning the One Possessing Qualities such as Invisibility (Adṛśyatvādiguṇaka Adhikaraṇa) 1.2.5.
1) The *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha* [states]: By negating grossness and visibility, the *pradhāna*—which possesses the qualities of subtlety and invisibility—is [established].
[However,] it would be incorrect to claim that the *kṣetrajña* alone is the *akṣara*, because [the *akṣara*] is superior to that [the *kṣetrajña*] according to the scriptural proposition. ||25||

By the [words] "sthūlatva... and so on—through the exclusion of "grossness" by the term "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣmam*) and the exclusion of "visibility" by the term "unseeable" (*adeśyam*)—the entity denoted by the word "subtle" in the scripture, namely "extremely subtle," is indeed the Pradhāna, the unmanifest root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) characterized by the quality of invisibility; whereas the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*), denoted by the word *akṣara* in that same passage, is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) alone, that is, the individual soul (*jīva*)—if one were to accept this, it would be incorrect, indeed improper, because of the [initial] promise (*pratijñayā*).

By the declarative statement, "Now, the other [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained," the Imperishable to be understood is indicated; or rather, by the declaration of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one, it is shown to be "higher than the high"—that is, because it is superior to the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*), and because it is even more exalted than the Person who is the aggregate of individual souls (*kṣetrajña-samaṣṭi-puruṣa*). Therefore, the Imperishable Source of Beings is indeed the Supreme Brahman alone. ||25||
2) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:
The negation of "visibility" and other attributes applies to the *akṣara* (the Imperishable) that possesses transformation, because of its proximity [to the context];

that *akṣara* mentioned in the fifth [chapter] may be that very one, but let it not be the twenty-fifth principle. Rather, the *akṣara* first mentioned is pure Brahman, because of the perception of omniscience and other such qualities.
But that which was mentioned later—the individual soul and so forth—is [not the primary subject], because it is spoken of as a limit (avadhi) for the sake of distinction from that [Brahman]. //15//

The negation of visibility and so forth—meaning the communication of the absence of visibility, graspability, and the like, by means of passages within the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* such as "indescribable and ungraspable"—occurs with respect to the *akṣara* (the Imperishable) which possesses modification, that is, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) which is fit for the states denoted by the term "modification. This is what is stated [by the following reasoning]: through proximity—that is, through the connection consisting of the recollection of earth and other elements which are the substrata of the visibility to be negated.

The word ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyukta*)—namely, the word "akṣara" in the phrase "akṣarāt parataḥ"—is expressed by the term "akṣarāt" in the ablative; that [term] must necessarily refer to *pradhāna* alone. As for the meaning that is "higher than" (the limit of) that—that which takes such an *akṣara* as its limiting point—it may well be the thirty-fifth principle, namely the individual soul (*jīva*) as described in Sāṅkhya, and not the Supreme Brahman. [Such a doubt] should not arise—it is impossible.

On account of the vision of omniscience and other attributes—since the scripture beginning with "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" establishes that qualities such as omniscience, which belong exclusively to the Supreme Self, reside in the Imperishable (akṣara) that is the source of beings—the first-mentioned "Imperishable," which is understood from the outset by the word *akṣara*, is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself, pure in its essential nature and devoid of modification both in its intrinsic being and its character.

But what was stated secondly—namely, that which is denoted by the word ‘akṣara’ (the Imperishable) mentioned in the phrase ‘higher than the akṣara’—whether it be the individual soul (jīva) or primordial matter (pradhāna), [is not the subject here]. This is because, by taking that as a limit through distinction—that is, based on the distinction consisting in its being the limit for excellence in the form of ‘being higher’—the Supreme Brahman, who is the substratum of that excellence relative to that limit, is spoken of as ‘higher than the high’ (*parataḥ paraḥ*). Thus, it is the Supreme Brahman who is referred to by that statement. || 15 ||
3) Summary of the meaning of the section:

In the section concerning that which has qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatvādiguṇaka*), regarding the statement, "Now, the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable (*akṣara*) is attained," there arises the following doubt: since the invisibility and other qualities negated by the phrase "invisible" (*adreśya*) and so forth suggest a subtle non-conscious matter (*acid-upasthāpaka*) of the same genus as the earth and other elements, the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is the Pradhāna (Primordial Matter); and the one who is "higher than the Imperishable" is the individual soul (*jīva*). Having raised this doubt:

Because he is the proponent of the attributes of the Supreme Self, such as omniscience and the like, He is the Imperishable (akṣara), the Supreme Self. He is superior even to that individual self (jīva) which is the inner self (pratyagātman) distinct from the Unmanifest (avyakta); therefore, He is the Supreme Self. For this very reason, it is established by the conclusion [of the scriptures] that "He is higher than the high Imperishable."

4) *Nayasaṅgatimālikā*: In the section concerning "the invisibility" (*adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*), because the status of being a seer and so forth was not mentioned, there arises the doubt as to whether it is *prakṛti* or the *puruṣa*; hence, this counter-example is provided. (45)
Thus ends the section concerning the one whose qualities are invisibility and so forth. ||5||
By this verse, it is established— through the sense of the context— that the world has that [Brahman] as its body,
by means of grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and by means other than that.

By this second quarter (pāda), that is to say, by the second line, in this manner—that is, from the sense already stated—the fact that the universe (*jagat*) has the Supreme Self as its body (*taccharīratā*), meaning its being the body of the Supreme Self, has been established and demonstrated through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—by the use of a single case ending in the expression "All is Brahman" (*sarvaṃ brahma*)—and through non-coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇya*) by other expressions such as "That is my Self" (*sa ātmā*). ||28||

2) [Objection: The Vaiśvānara-self, whose head and other limbs are fashioned from heaven, sun, air, ether, water, and earth, is the object of meditation as something unstable and manifold in its objects, because of the similarity of words, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth. [Reply: Not so; because of the scriptural study [of the word] "Brahman," and because of the connection with the body of the world (*bhuvana-tanutva*), the word "fire" (*agni*) refers to the Supreme Consciousness due to its preeminence, or because it is a subordinate part of the ritual action; likewise, the cognition of the Gārhapatya and other fires [is subordinate]. (Verse 16)

By way of arrangement: having first performed the mental construction (*kalpanā*) of the specific locations consisting of the head, eyes, breath, middle body, bladder, and feet—which correspond respectively to the heavenly world (*suvarloka*), sun, wind, ether, water, and earth; [the Vaiśvānara Self] is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*). That Vaiśvānara Self, known as Vaiśvānara, who is taught in the *Chāndogya* as the object of worship in such passages as, "But he who worships this Vaiśvānara, [measured] even by a span..."—that very one is the stable possessor of many objects.

—[This is] a ground for doubt with many difficult-to-avert alternatives, because of the similarity of the word, the inferential mark (*liṅga*), and so forth; that is to say, because the word *vaiśvānara* is common to four possible referents—the digestive fire and the others—and because their respective characteristic marks (*liṅga*) are present: the state of being the support for the offering of breaths in the digestive fire; the nature of light in the elemental fire; the status of being a deity; and the quality of burning away sins in the Supreme Self, which is all-pervading. Such being the objection raised, [the author replies]: "Not so"—this kind of doubt is not appropriate.

Because of the study [of the passage] beginning with "Brahman"—specifically because the word "Brahman" is used in the statement, "Who is the Self? What is Brahman?"—and because, in the absence of any sublation, the word "Brahman" refers exclusively to the Supreme Self; and likewise because of its being the body of the universe, as stated in the passage beginning with, "The head itself is the radiant one."

As for the word "Agni": the application of the word "Agni" to Vaiśvānara in the passage "This is that Agni Vaiśvānara" occurs either by way of etymological derivation (*yoga*), based on the analysis of its parts as "he leads" (*nayati*); or by way of distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*), specifically the distinction consisting in the relationship between the body and the embodied; or [it refers] to one's own body—that is, in the body of the meditator—the cognition of the Supreme Self (*paradhīḥ*) which consists in the conceptualization of the limbs of the Supreme Self, as stated in passages such as "The head itself is the radiant one" (*mūrdhaiva sutejāḥ*); and likewise, the cognition of the *gārhapatya* and other fires within one's own body, as in "The chest itself... (*ura eva*).

Furthermore, the mental conception consisting of the imaginative attribution (*kalpanā*) of the Gārhapatya fire and so forth to the heart and other parts—as taught in passages such as "The altar is the heart, the Gārhapatya is the heart"—is a subsidiary part of the ritual action (*kriyāṅga*), meaning it is an auxiliary to the ritual acts such as the oblation to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) which constitute a limb of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

[Objection: "The wise do not attain the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by perceiving one thing in another; therefore, this Vaiśvānara is not the Supreme [Brahman], because the result is merely food, success, and so forth. [Reply: This is not so. For in this context, Brahman itself is indeed constituted through the association with the perception of another, since there is no sublation of the word "Brahman" and so forth.
The destruction of all evil has been declared; the fruit is also the Supreme Brahman, and food is all-pervading.

By means of a cognition consisting in the contemplation of one thing as another—that is, by regarding one entity as being a different entity—in some instance, namely in the contemplation of such a view, the attainment of the supreme good—the realization of liberation—does not occur for the wise; that is, it cannot possibly be accepted by those knowers who are devoted to the instruction of such contemplative views.

Therefore—since the meditation on the visible (the physical body) does not accomplish the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), this Vaiśvānara taught as the object of meditation in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā cannot be the Vaiśvānara-Self; that is, he cannot be the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*). For this reason, the result—the purpose obtainable through the meditation on the Vaiśvānara-Self—is also known from the scriptural statement of results such as the attainment of food to be merely the acquisition of food and so forth.

When the doubt arises that there is no liberation, [the author] says: "Not so"—such a doubt is not correct; for, in this context, Brahman alone—the Supreme Brahman itself—is taught as the object of meditation, constituted by the application of other perspectives, namely, its own nature as the subject of views such as having heaven as its head and so forth.

It is not something else, because there is no sublation of the words "Brahman" and so forth; for since the words "Brahman" and "Self," introduced in the questions "What is Brahman? and "Who is the Self?", are connected without sublation, it is impossible to abandon their meaning. Thus, the destruction of all evils—the total eradication of all sins—is stated [in the text]: "All evils are burnt away," which is spoken as the fruit of meditation.

Moreover, the fruit—namely food—is also pervaded; that which is designated by the word "food" as the purpose of the meditation is likewise all-pervading and connected everywhere. And it is the Supreme Brahman, as stated in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "I am food, I am food. || 17 ||

Among these three [Upanishads], for those who worship here, that which is within the limited space of the heart-cave and the eyes is said to be the object of meditation; then, in the [remaining] three, the object of meditation is described as having a vast dimension due to its nature as the inner ruler of the universe and so forth.

Furthermore, in the six [Upanishads], the terms *brahman* and *ātman*, as well as the word *puruṣa*, refer to the range of the field (*kṣetra*), the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
When the universal cause has ceased, they bow by means of the application of names, due to the restriction of the context. || 18 ||

In this context, regarding the first three sections (*adhikaraṇas*), for those who worship for the sake of liberation, the Supreme Self is described as being within the limited cavity of the heart and within the eyes; that is, by virtue of abiding within the small-sized cavity of the heart and within the eyes, He is said to be contemplated through such scriptural statements as "within the heart," "hidden in the cave," and "this one within the eye," and is thus taught as the object of worship. Now, in the subsequent three sections, however, taking His state as the inner controller of the universe—namely, His state as the inner controller of the entire world—as the reason, [He is established as the object of worship].

"Of vast magnitude"—by virtue of possessing a great dimension contrary to that [limited one]; "to be meditated upon"—stated as the object of worship. "In the six"—in the six topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) belonging to this chapter; "the words *Brahman*, *Ātman*, and also the word *Puruṣa*"—these terms, namely *Brahman*, *Ātman*, and *Puruṣa*; "distinct from the field and its knower"—different from the world consisting of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*); "the cause of the universe"—therefore, the Supreme Self who is both the efficient and material cause of that [world]; "due to the restriction of the context."

Due to the restriction resulting from their dependence on the context of the Supreme Self, they "bow"—that is, by way of a function consisting of conventional usage (rūḍhi), they become designations (saṃjñā). || 18 ||

Because it is produced from that [Brahman], the entire world was previously declared to be of the nature of Brahman; and the status of being the inner controller of all, as well as the state of having all things as its body, was proclaimed for the Lord. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras here refuted, by means of logical arguments, the entire web of trivial and intoxicated utterances wandering in vain through various kinds of fallacies such as the denial of non-duality.

On account of being produced from that, and so forth—that is, by taking as reasons the fact of being born from that, the fact of merging into that, and the fact of depending on that for its vital functions—in the previous section [the *Sarvatra-prasiddhy-adhikaraṇa*], the entire world—the whole universe—was declared to be Brahman, determined as having identity with Brahman; and the nature of the Supreme Self, the cause of the entire world, consists in His being the inner controller of all, His being the self of all (the state of being the inner controller of everything), and His being the body of all (the state of having the entire universe as His body).

This has been set forth from the beginning in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* and established; therefore—for that reason—the entire (*nikhilam*) net of the "Unity of the Universe" (*viśvaikya-jālam*)—that mass of words appearing like the drunken ravings of the ignorant, which has entered into a succession of delusions caused by contemplating meanings contrary to various types of Śruti such as "The universe and Brahman are one," "Brahman alone is real," and "The universe is sublated"—the Sūtra-author, Bādarāyaṇa, has refuted (*nirāsa*) here by means of the *nayaiḥ*, that is, the topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*) belonging to this [fourth] chapter. || 19 ||

In the second chapter [of the first book], the venerable Śrīnivāsa—the crown jewel of the multitude of scriptural texts—has been proclaimed as the subject of the primary definition: He who exists through His entire being by virtue of His independent existence, maintenance, and activity of all things; who has swallowed everything yet remains eternal and imperishable; whose body is the entirety of all forms, though He assumes bodies such as fire for His own purposes; and who is the object of the cognition of Vaiśvānara, whose limbs are the worlds beginning with the celestial realm (Svarloka).

Regarding the first characteristic—in the second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter (adhyāya), in the second section (caraṇa): "svādhīnā... [means] by virtue of being independent; that is, because He possesses the power to determine the time of attaining His own nature in relation to the entire universe and its continued existence and activity. "Existing as a state" (bhāvena tiṣṭhan) means abiding in identity with the entire universe. "Having swallowed the remainder" (grastaśeṣaḥ) means having devoured all moving and non-moving beings without exception. "Having an eternal station in the eyes" (akṣinityasthitiḥ) means abiding permanently within the orb of the eyes of embodied beings.

Akhilatanuḥ—one whose body is everything; kalpitāgnyādigātraḥ—characterized by qualities such as having the sky as his head, which are attributed to him for the sake of meditation according to the passage "Agni is his head"; bhūtaḥ—the Real; śrutinikaraśiraḥśekharaḥ—the crest-jewel upon the heads of the entire collection of Śruti texts; śrīnivāsaḥ—the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who bears that name; proktaḥ—thoroughly determined after careful investigation (by Bādarāyaṇa). || 20 ||
3) Summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*):

In the *Vaiśvānara* section, regarding the passage beginning with "This very Self, indeed, as Vaiśvānara," since the word "Vaiśvānara" is observed to be used without distinction for the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), the elemental [fire], the third deity, and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there arises the doubt that no definitive conclusion can be reached as to whether it refers to the Supreme Self.
Having raised this doubt:

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the term "Vaiśvānara," though common to many, can be determined to refer to the "Supreme Self" because it is qualified by marks of the Supreme Self, such as being questioned by those seeking liberation.

4) The *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* [states]: "First, the presentation of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) was established by means of its having heaven as its head and so forth. By way of that [presentation], the Vaiśvānara-vidyā is now considered by way of refutation. Thus, the characteristic of the two sections (*peṭikā*), which is skillful in its application to the subject matter, is well-connected in the second quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter. Thus ends the section on Vaiśvānara (Vaiśvānarādhikaraṇa). 6.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.

—0— This is appropriate, clearly because of the word "Self" (*ātman*); specifically because of the direct scriptural statement, "Know Him alone as the one Self" (*tamevaikaṃ jānathātmānam*), which teaches the state of being the Self free from limiting adjuncts; and because of the designation [of Brahman] as that which is to be approached by the liberated (*muktopasṛpya*). Furthermore, it is because the status of being the supreme goal for the liberated is primarily established [in this context] by the passage, "Then the wise one, having cast off both merit and sin... attains equality. (Therefore, the Supreme Self alone is the abode of heaven and earth; not the individual soul. || 29 ||

—Clearly, 2) here indeed a statement established in Brahman, endowed with clear marks such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, is being proven; why then is there no mention of an *adhikāra* (topic-heading) in the middle of these three? [The answer is: because that is stated in connection with each respective context. Furthermore, in this [section], the refutation of the semi-materialists (*ardhalokāyatika*) is useful for the subject matter at hand.

In the seven subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning other subjects as well, that Supreme Self—the ground of the intended meaning, the ultimate limit of what is to be established, the support of all, the cause of the existence of the entire world other than Himself, the abode of His own majesty, and established in His own majesty—is described—that is, propounded—in this section, beginning with the *Akṣarādhikaraṇa* and others, for the sake of establishing Him: namely, for the purpose of perfecting His status as the support of all while being Himself without any other support.

The "primacy of the teaching" (*śāsanādyam*)—consisting of [qualities] such as being the ruler of all—is "interwoven" (*mithaḥsyūtam*), meaning it is closely connected through the mutual fulfillment of their respective purposes; this is what must be "contemplated" (*ālocanīyam*), that is, reflected upon. This has been established in the sixth section (*pramitādhikaraṇa*) of this very chapter. Furthermore, "lordship over all," which is lordship over both the past and the future, is to be "protected" (*rakṣyam*) by the final reasoning—the method of "being something else" (*arthāntaratva*) and so forth—in the concluding section. || 2 ||

It has already been established in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* that the Supreme Brahman is described as being distinct through its various attributes; why then does this [text] grind what is already ground, needlessly repeating it? True, the suspicion of a difference in the method of exposition arises because of the vivid attributes of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*); however, by making this distinction known, the [notion of duality] is uprooted so that it may never arise again through these words.

Even earlier—in the preceding section on "Invisibility" (*adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*)—it was established and determined after deliberation that the Supreme Brahman, the supreme reality to be investigated, is [the subject] by virtue of its specific attributes such as omniscience which are unique to It, and because of the mention of difference—that is, the statement of supremacy consisting of the distinction from the individual soul—as taught in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* (the *Muṇḍaka Śruti*). Thus, even though it was not the immediate occasion (*akāṇḍe*), this [point], which is present in the mind, [is now addressed].
Why [does he do this]? For what reason does he "grind what has already been ground," as it were—re-examining with this verse-foot that which has already been crushed? Such is the doubt.

This being so—the portion concerning the fact that [the subject] has already been investigated is accepted; however, there is no "grinding what is already ground. By means of the characteristics of the *kṣetrajña* (the embodied soul)—namely, those attributes unique to the individual soul such as being the locus of the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth—which are clearly perceived and thus bring about the suspicion of a difference in method or the arising of doubt regarding a different context, [the author] establishes recognition by means of the characteristics unique to the Supreme Self, such as being the bridge to immortality (*amṛta-setu*), and declares: "This is indeed the Supreme Self previously introduced."

Having stabilized the conviction that "there is no other," [that ignorance] is uprooted—that is, eradicated—by means of the instruments of knowledge beginning with scripture (*śruti*), preceded by verbal testimony, so that it may never arise again. || 3 || If it be argued that He in whom the mind is woven together with the other groups of organs, who is born in manifold ways, who is the support of the channels (*nāḍī*), and who moves within, is the instrument (*karaṇī*) and the enjoyer of karma; we say no. Because He is established as distinct [from the individual soul] due to His being the Self who is the support of the universe, because He bestows immortality, because He is said to be the object of delight for the liberated, because of the unity of the previously mentioned method, and because of His manifestation even while remaining without food. || 4 ||

Together with the other groups of instruments—the remaining vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as well as the clusters of organs of action and knowledge—the mind (*manas*, i.e., the consciousness) is woven into that [Reality]—that entity in which it is inherent; that which arises as manifold; that object which becomes the locus of birth through many forms such as the gods and others; that which is the support of the channels (*nāḍī*), that object which serves as the substratum for the entire collection of channels; and that which...

If it is argued that the one who moves within—the very entity that possesses movement within the body—is such an entity as the "agent" (karaṇī), the "experiencer of action" (karmabhoktā), the possessor of the collection of organs, and indeed the experiencer of the fruits of merit and demerit (namely, the *jīva* itself)—such a doubt is not correct; it does not hold.

Because He is the self-nature that supports the universe—having the nature of being the substratum of the entire world characterized by heaven and earth; because He bestows immortality—being the giver of liberation, which is denoted by the word "immortality"; because He is said to be the object of attainment for the liberated—according to the scriptural teaching that He is reached by liberated souls who have attained supreme similarity [with Him]; because of the unity of the method previously described—the non-difference in the context stated in the preceding verse; and because of His unceasing radiance even while conjoined with non-eating and shining—that is, being accompanied by the absence of enjoyment of the fruits of karma—from these, His distinctness from others is established.
Because there is the cognition of a specific person distinct from the individual soul (jīva), he who is described as "in whom heaven [rests]" is indeed the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 4 ||

If it is argued that there is no room for this [individual soul] within that which is all-pervading, then what of it? His birth is said to be by his own will; he becomes the navel of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra), and as the Supreme, he abides in the form of the heart. Furthermore, even the movement of one who is internally pervading and immovable exists in the world through auspicious bodies;
or else, as taught in the Saubāla Upaniṣad, this "movement" may be merely a figurative designation (adhiṣṭhānamātra).

In this [Paramātman], who is all-pervasive—according to the stated manner of "pervading all that is within and without"—if even the sense organs and so forth, which are contained within everything, are *ota* (woven or eternally connected), then what is lost here by that mere connection with the senses? Furthermore, the birth of this Paramātman—His assumption of a body dependent upon His own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*)—has been declared and established in the statement, "being born in many ways."

In the form of the heart—that is, in the form of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) designated as "Heart"—abiding, meaning situated within the region of the body called the heart, that Supreme One—the Paramātman who is the subject of the Vedāntas—is indeed the navel, meaning He is fit to be the support, of the network of channels (nāḍīcakrasya), the multitude of vessels. Even though the Paramātman is immovably pervasive—meaning He possesses a connection with all things even without movement—His internal movement within the world (loke)—that is, within the universe—is also for the purpose of bestowing grace upon His worshippers.

There is indeed the movement within the heart known as *sañcāra*, as well as action; likewise, there is also movement by means of auspicious bodies designated as "auspicious abodes"—non-material, divine forms—which is possible in the form of existence, manifestation, and so forth, as sanctioned by the scriptures. Or else, according to the sequence stated in the *Subāla Upaniṣad*: "He who moves within the earth," this movement is also described as "he moves within," as stated in the passage "this very one moves within."
It would be a mere presiding presence—there would be only a state of abiding in the form of being the inner controller (antaryāmin). || 5 ||

Because of the scriptural statement, "This is the bridge to immortality," which declares that being the means to immortality is a characteristic unique to the Supreme Self, and because the connection of the channels with the heart is logically possible in the case of the Supreme Self, it is established as the final conclusion that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self.
And 4) Nayasaṅgatimālikā:

Now, by means of two, four, three, and one arguments respectively, there is a set of four boxes in the third section. (48) The connection between heaven, earth, and so forth was previously established at the end of the [first] section; [here], the determination of the existence of the earth and so forth in the individual soul is made by way of refutation. (49)
Thus ends the section on the root *bhū* and others. || 1 ||
— 0 The Section on the Grounds [of Knowledge] ||1-3-2||

1) Having begun with the summary of the collection of principles concerning the embodied soul (*śārīraka-nyāyakalāpa-saṅgraha*), the instruction has been completed regarding the individual self (*jīva*) as the vital breath.
Therefore, one should not suspect that [the Self] is the "Fullness" (*bhūman*); rather, it is superior to that because of the teaching on Truth (*satya*). || 30 ||

Beginning with "Name and so forth"—starting from "Meditate upon Name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.4)—the instruction was given by Sanatkumāra to Nārada in the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya; that instruction was concluded with reference to the individual self (jīva) denoted by the word "Prāṇa," being brought to a close with the words, "For Prāṇa alone becomes all these. Therefore, for that reason, he—the one concluded at the end of the instruction—is indeed the individual self known as Prāṇa.

One should not suspect that the meaning of the word "Bhūman" (the Infinite), which was stated as the object of inquiry in the passage, "But the Bhūman indeed must be sought to be known," refers to something other than this; such a doubt must not be entertained. This is because it is taught as being superior to that—superior even to Prāṇa—and because the very category of "Satya" (Truth) is taught as the object of meditation. || 30 ||

The Supreme Brahman, denoted by the word "Satya," is superior to the lower self called Prāṇa—that which is expressed by the term "Prāṇa"—being more exalted than the individual soul (jīva). It is taught as the object of inquiry in the statement, "But Satya alone is what one should desire to understand. Furthermore, by the force of the word "but" (*tu*) in the sentence, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly through Satya," it follows that the person who possesses the quality of speaking surpassingly regarding the object known as Satya is superior to the person who knows Prāṇa.

It is taught that "the best" is superior to that [preceding one]. For, as for the statement "he who speaks the truth"—namely, the sentence found within the context of the Agnihotra, intended to praise the Agnihotra, which says, "But he indeed is an Agnihotrin who speaks the truth"—this cannot, by virtue of understanding the Agnihotrin under discussion (that is, from the Agnihotrin understood through the sentence read in the context), lead to or indicate another Agnihotrin (a different Agnihotrin). It is not capable of doing so.

It becomes capable; because of the absence of that capability, the word "but" (*tu*)—the breaking or abandonment of the natural force (*svarasatā*) of the word "but"—is tolerated only as a last resort (*agatyā*). However, in the present context, the abandonment of the natural force of the word "but" is indeed detrimental. Thus, one who speaks the truth (*satyātivādī*) is indeed superior to one who speaks of life-breaths (*prāṇātivādī*). || 29 ||
3) *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

To Nārada, whose grief did not cease despite his longing for self-knowledge, Sanatkumāra addressed these words: "That living being (*jīva*) who is incapable of violence [is the Self]. If it be argued that this [Self] is indeed this very [living being], which is a multitude of minor adversaries yet possesses infinite bliss—no, [it is not].

For here, that which is expressed by the word "Truth" (*satya*) is taken up as the object of meditation in a superior sense than the one called "vital breath" (*prāṇa*). [This occurs] because of the desire for self-knowledge—that is, from the wish to know the Self—on the part of Nārada, the sage named Nārada, who was not free from sorrow—that is, whose grief had not ceased. The speech of Sanatkumāra—that is, the collection of statements contained within the "Knowledge of the Fullness" (*bhūmavidyā*), consisting of the instruction given by Sanatkumāra—was directed toward him; it proceeded until it came to rest upon the vital breath—that is, it reached its conclusion when the subject matter in the form of the vital breath had been taught.

If it is argued that this very thing—the object denoted by "prāṇa"—is fit to be harmed (*hiṃsanāhaḥ*), meaning it is worthy of being killed; that it is the living soul (*jīvaḥ*), which is conscious and endowed with vital breath; that the meaning of the word "bhūman" (the Infinite) is also the antithesis of the meaning of the word "alpa" (the small) mentioned in proximity to it; and that it is possessed of limitless bliss, being of the nature of undivided bliss—then such a doubt is not tenable. Why? Because in this context, that which is expressed by the word "satya" (Truth)—

"That which is designated by the word 'Truth' (satya) must indeed be sought to be known. This object of worship—that is, the thing to be meditated upon—is presented as superior, more extensive, and more excellent than the one called "Prāṇa"—the living self denoted by the term "Prāṇa. || 6 ||
