It might be argued that because names and so forth are taught up to "peace" (śānta) as objects of knowledge, and because more is stated through questions and answers, the instruction regarding the Self under discussion may find its limit in the vital breath (prāṇa), since the discourse rests there. This is not so. For here, the vital breath is said to have been born from the Supreme Self, just like name and the rest; it is not the case that it was born from itself.
This is because the natural syntactical division of the words does not allow for such an interpretation. 7.

Regarding the fourteen objects—beginning with "Meditate on Name" and ending with "Meditate on Hope"—which are prescribed as objects of knowledge starting from "Meditate on Name" up to "Meditate on Hope," [the conclusion is reached] through the questions in the form "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than Name? and so forth, and through the answers in the form "Speech, indeed, is greater than Name," and so forth; thus, by the statement of the "greater" (adhikokti)—that is, the teaching of progressively superior entities—the culmination in Prāṇa is established by viewing the rest to find their final repose in Prāṇa.

Because it is seen in the Śruti, the instruction concerning the Self under discussion—the instruction related to the Self that has been introduced—should have that as its limit; it should end precisely there. (When such a doubt arises: It is not so; such a doubt is not appropriate, because here—in this context of instruction regarding the object to be known—the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being like the objects beginning with Name (*nāman*), has also arisen from the Supreme Self.

It was stated: "From the Self, the vital breath [arises]"; thus, its very origination has been established. Here, regarding that statement of origination from the Self found within the scriptural passage—the phrase "from the Self" (*ātmataḥ*)—it might be thought that it means "from itself," implying an appearance caused by itself. However, such a reflection is indeed improper, because it would result in the subversion of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), which by its very nature expresses a relationship between producer and produced characterized by a natural distinction, and because it would entail the impossibility of the case ending conveying its own inherent meaning. || 7 ||
If it be argued that the one who perceives the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the "exceeding speaker" (*ativādī*), and because he is impelled by repeating after that [breath], his speech is truth;

therefore, the vital breath alone is the meaning of "I" for all and the progenitor of all beings—this is not so. For this person is called "the exceeding speaker" due to speaking beyond what was previously stated, and thus he is distinct from that [breath].
Indeed, there is no other *agnihotrī* [here], for the application of the term "dharma" (or "excellence") occurs here only within the abode of one’s own greatness.

The "perceiver of breath" (*prāṇadraṣṭṛ*) is a person whose nature is the direct realization of the object in the form of *prāṇa*, which is the final stage in the succession of objects of meditation beginning with name and so forth. The "one who speaks beyond" (*ativādī*) is described as one who possesses the quality of speaking beyond (*ativāditva*) by virtue of declaring his own object of meditation, *prāṇa*, to be the most excellent. "Speaking the truth" (*satyavāda*) refers to the matter consisting of speech regarding the true reality; it was enjoined as an auxiliary element by the sentence, "But he indeed speaks beyond who speaks beyond by means of the Truth. This was prompted [by the injunction] "eṣa tu vā ativadati, yaḥ satyenāti vadati" (But he indeed speaks beyond, who speaks beyond by means of the Truth).

Therefore—since it is certain that the statement "But he indeed speaks surpassingly" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.4) prescribes truthful speech as an ancillary part of the meditation on Prāṇa—the referent of all instances of the word "I" used by everyone, or rather, the one spoken of later in the passage "I alone am all this," is none other than Prāṇa, the progenitor of all beings, who possesses the status of being the creator of the entire universe through his own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and is the very object denoted by the term "Prāṇa."

If it is argued that [the one who speaks the truth] is merely the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—such a suspicion is by no means tenable; for, by the sentence "But he indeed speaks more" (*eṣa tu vā ativadati*), which contains the word "but" (*tu*), there is an explicit statement of difference (*bheda*) between this person who performs the "speaking beyond" (*ativāda*) based on the Truth, and the previous one—the speaker regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Just as there is another performer of the *agnihotra* who is distinct from a previous performer of the *agnihotra*, so too there is no other person here who is distinct from the speaker regarding the vital breath, such as this speaker regarding the Truth. There is no such thing as a separate agent.

It is not the case that [the quality of speaking the truth] is mentioned as part of the context; rather, it is appropriate to state that speaking the truth is an auxiliary (aṅga) enjoined by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the previously mentioned Agnihotra. "Abiding in its own majesty" means established in its own greatness. For here—in the Supreme Self alone—the compatibility of all attributes mentioned in the context, such as natural immortality and so forth, is possible through their connection without contradiction. || 8 ||

In the beginning is Name, and Speech is above it; following that is Mind, then the Citta which is named Saṅkalpa, and beyond that is Dhyāna. Furthermore, there is Bala, and previously [there was] Vijñāna. Then come Food, Water, Fire, and Space; after that comes Manmatha, as well as Āśā, Prāṇa, Satya, and Parātman. Thus, the "entirety" (sakala) is understood to be regulated within the Bhūma-vākya.

In the section concerning the knowledge of the Earth (*bhūmavidyā*), within the context of the discourse related to that knowledge, first—at the very beginning—is the object consisting of Name, which is stated as the thing to be known; and after that, following Name, is Speech—the reality in the form of speech; and after that, following Speech, is Mind—the object of knowledge in the form of mind; and then, following Mind, is the object called Volition (*saṅkalpa*); and after Volition, there is the entity called Thought (*citta*), as well as Meditation (*dhyāna*), which likewise follows from that.

—Even after the meditations (*dhyāna*), there would be the power preceded by consciousness (*vijñāna*); that is, consciousness and power (*bala*) are to be known, as well as food and water—the object in the form of food and the object in the form of water immediately following that (and likewise) fire and space—fire and ether; then—immediately after that—there would be *manmatha* (the god of love)—*smara*, which has the meaning of "remembering" (*smaraṇa*) and is taught as a synonym for *manmatha*.

Likewise, *āśā*—the very meaning consisting of the directions—is taught as that which is to be known (*vedyatvena*). After that, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), designated as the individual soul (*jīva*), is taught; and then (*tataśca*) the one who governs all through restraint (*sakalaniyamayitā*), the inner controller of all, the Supreme Self (*parātmā*)—designated by the term "Supreme Self"—the True One (*satya*), whose nature is truth, is understood and made known as the object to be realized. || 9 ||

4) Summary of the meaning of the section: In the section concerning the "Fullness" (*bhūma*), there arises this doubt: Since the instruction on the Self (*ātman*) introduced in the passage, "The knower of the Self overcomes grief," culminates in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and because the context remains uninterrupted by the series of questions and answers beginning with, "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than the vital breath?"—therefore, that which is indicated by the word "vital breath" is indeed the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), and that which is indicated by the word "Fullness" in the sentence, "where one sees nothing else," is also that same Self. Having raised this doubt:

"Knowledge itself would be the power"—Ṇā. 4; "The controller"—Ā.; "It would be memory"—Ā.; "Life-breath, and then truth, the Self"—Ā. Because of the designation as superior to even the inner self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word "prāṇa" in the passage, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of the Truth," it is established in the Siddhānta that the "Truth" denoted by the word "satya" is the Bhūman, which is the Supreme Self (paramātman). — *Nayasaṅgatimālikā*

By the very fact that the subject matter has been stated as a single unit, and by the reasoning of the established conclusion, the objection raised in the *bhūman* section—that [the self] is the individual soul (*jīva*)—has been refuted. Thus ends the *bhūman* section (2).
The Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) || 1.3.3 ||
The Compendium of the Logical Principles of the Śārīraka:

"Is the unmanifest (avyākṛta) indeed consciousness, or rather the Imperishable (akṣara), the substratum of space? [If it is argued] that it is the substratum of the effect because it is the locus of the non-conscious, that too is incorrect, because its support [of the world] is due to its presiding over it. (31)

The "abode of the sky"—that which is spoken of as the substratum with respect to space—is the "Imperishable" (akṣara), the reality denoted by the term "akṣara-pada. It is either the "Undifferentiated" (avyākṛta)—meaning either the subtle elements of the material world or the Pradhāna—or else it must be the "Conscious One," that is, the individual self (jīvātman) alone. [The opponent argues: This is not correct, because it is the abode of effects; for the Pradhāna is the substratum of modifications, while the individual self is the substratum of non-conscious things. [The reply: Even such a doubt is not sound, because of its being the support and the controller.

Because in this context, the holding (dhāraṇa) and the supreme peace (praśānti) of the Pradhāna—which are unique to the Supreme Self—are heard [in scripture], and because it is impossible for this Imperishable (akṣara) to be either the Pradhāna or the individual soul (jīva). || 31 ||
The *Adhikaraṇasārāvali* states:

Because it carries forth its own modification known as space, the Pradhāna is called the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*). If it were said that even this [Pradhāna] possesses the nature of space, then it would follow that it is the support of the entire universe and the locus of that [space]. This is not so; for it is characterized by being a seer and other attributes exclusive to it, and its sustenance is dependent on the Command (of the Lord).
Furthermore, the exclusion of any other seer here implies the negation of any seer equal to Him. || 10 ||

"Renowned" (*prakhyātā*)—because it serves as the substratum for its own modifications, such as space (*ākāśa*), which are well-known in the world; "called the Imperishable" (*akṣarākhyam*)—that which is denoted by the word "Imperishable" in the passage, "This, O Gārgī, is indeed that Imperishable"; "Pradhāna"—it must necessarily be the Root-Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), even though there is a mention of its being "space" (*ākāśatā*)—if the designation by the word "space" is accepted; then, "supporting the entire universe"—the sustainer of the whole aggregate of sentient beings—and "to be known through the field" (*kṣetritavyam*) refers to the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*).

[The opponent argues: "It must be the individual soul (*jīva*) itself; it ought to be that which is denoted by the word 'syllable' (*akṣara*) here" (this being the prima facie view). [The author replies: This is not so. It is not proper for either the primary matter (*pradhāna*) or the individual soul to be understood by the word 'syllable';

rather, it is the Supreme Self alone. This is determined by the attributes beginning with "being a seer" (*draṣṭṛtva*), which are not restricted to anything else—such as being associated with "imperishability" (*akṣaratva*) and other qualities impossible in anything other than the Supreme Self—and by the scriptural hearing that He is sustained by His unimpeded will through a sustenance dependent upon His command.

Furthermore, here in the statement, "There is no seer other than this," the exclusion (*vyudasanam*) of another seer—that is, the communication of the non-existence of any other agent of seeing—is precisely the cognition of the absence of any other seer who might be similar to Him by virtue of being the support of the universe, the controller, and so forth; it is not, however, the communication of the non-existence of the seer in general. || 10 ||

The summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the Imperishable (*akṣara*): In the section on the Imperishable, concerning the passage beginning with "This indeed is that Imperishable, O Gārgī," since the word "Imperishable" is seen to be used for both the Pradhāna and the individual soul (*jīva*), a doubt arises that the one denoted by the word "Imperishable" must be one of those two. Having raised this doubt, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Imperishable is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is indicated as the support even of the Pradhāna—which is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) and is the substratum of all modifications existing in the three periods of time.

This garland of the consistency of reasoning regarding the *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa*—namely, that they are established in their own majesty—is stated by way of negation (apavāda) as "it exists"; thus arises the system of the Imperishable (*akṣara-naya*). || 51 || Thus ends the Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). || 3 ||
Section on the Object of Beholding (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa) || 1.3.5 || Summary of the Śārīraka Nyāya:
That world of Brahmā which is taught as being superior to the earth and the intermediate space is the world of the Creator (Vidhātṛ).

"In that regard," [it is said: "The world of the Creator (vidhātṛloka) would be non-existent if it were to be meditated upon as the three-measured *praṇava* by means of designations such as 'immortal' (*amṛta*) and so forth. "From the earth"—in relation to the world of humans; "from the intermediate space"—in relation to the intermediate world—[the world] is taught as superior, being described in the Śruti as the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) to be attained by one who meditates on the three-measured *praṇava*. That which is the referent of the term "world of Brahman" found in the Śruti is indeed the world of the four-faced Brahmā, who is the aggregate of individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*).

In this regard, the doubt that "Dhātṛ is none other than Hiraṇyagarbha residing in Satyaloka, who is to be meditated upon through the three-measured Praṇava and worshipped by means of the Oṃkāra consisting of the three measures"—such a doubt would be unfounded; it would be set aside by the indicative marks such as the names Amṛtā, Abhayā, and so forth. || 32 ||

This one person who has become Lakṣmī herself is indeed the Kṣetrajña (the Knower of the Field) here, who meditates and perceives; he is the Lord of the Egg, superior to the other Supreme Being and distinct from the individual souls. If this were not so, there would be an inconsistency regarding the section on the enjoyment of earthly and other realms;
yet that is incorrect, because in him the mention of the supreme qualities such as peace and immortality would be impossible. 11.

In this context, regarding such statements in the *Praśnopaniṣad* as "one should meditate upon the lower person" (*aparaṃ puruṣamabhidhyāyīta*) and "he beholds the person dwelling in the city, higher than the high" (*parātparaṃ puriśayaṃ puruṣamīkṣate*), it is well known that the object of meditation—the person denoted by the word *puruṣa* found in the scripture—and the object of vision, which serve as the respective targets (*lakṣmībhūta*) for the meditation understood from the root *dhyai* and the vision understood from the root *īkṣ*, are indeed one and the same; they are non-different.

(Since that which is to be meditated upon is precisely that which is to be seen: This very object, which is the focus of meditation and vision—the Lord of the Egg (aṇḍādhipaḥ), meaning the master of the cosmic egg; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajñaḥ), meaning the individual soul (jīva) known by the name Brahmā; he, the sovereign of the cosmic egg—is superior to others (itaraparāt), meaning more excellent than other insentient things, and superior to his own other souls (svānyajīvāt), meaning more excellent than the class of sentient beings other than himself; thus he is indeed "higher than the high" (parātpara eva). Otherwise—if this were not accepted—then...

The contradiction regarding the sequence of worlds of enjoyment—consisting of the earth, the intermediate space, and the world of Brahmā—as presented in the section on the experience of [planets] such as Mars, becomes unavoidable; to think in this manner is improper and inconsistent. This is because, in that case, the four-faced Lord of the Egg (Brahmā) is described by terms such as "peaceful" (*śānta*) and so forth, and since qualities like peace and immortality are well-known to belong to the Supreme Self, such a description would contradict [the status of the four-faced one]. || 11 ||

Now, one might argue that the abode of the Lotus-Dweller (Brahmā), namely the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), should be [the destination] due to its proximity to the earth and the intermediate space, which correspond to the fruits enumerated for the three measures (*mātrā*) of the syllable *Oṃ*. But this is not so; for it has been stated that "this [world] is attained by one freed from sin," following the attainment of the Sun.

"The separation [from the world] must be endured by those in the middle worlds"—this is the complete path of resolution. Here—in the section concerning the meditation on the *praṇava* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*) from the *Praśnopaniṣad*, through the proximity of the syllable *Oṃ*—the three measures (*mātrātritaya*) that constitute the object of meditation belonging to the *praṇava* "Oṃ" are [to be understood]; and by the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the two worlds known as Earth and Atmosphere, which have entered into the stages of the fruit [of that meditation], the World of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) is indicated.

When the objection is raised that the meaning denoted by the term "Brahma-world" (*brahmaloka*) in the scriptural passage, "He is led up to the Brahma-world by the Sāman chants," must be the abode of the four-faced [Brahmā] as well-known in the Purāṇas—that is, let it be simply the world that serves as his residence, and not the station of the Supreme Self (Paramātman)—it is replied: "Not so; such an objection is not appropriate, because this—"

The world of Brahman has been described; by a person who, according to the stated manner—"Thus indeed he is completely freed from evil"—has abandoned all connection with sin, there occurs the attainment of the sun, preceded by his merging into the radiance: "He has merged into the radiant sun."

In the manner stated [in *Praśnopaniṣad* 5.5], it is said that [the goal] is "to be attained" (*labhya*)—meaning it is to be reached—after first reaching the Sun; this is established in that very Śruti. Regarding the phrase "by the middle worlds"—meaning by the worlds situated above the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and below the world of Brahmā—the term "obstruction" (*vyavadhi*) signifies a separation that must be "endured" or "tolerated. Since such an obstruction cannot exist for the abode of the Supreme Self when mentioned alongside the intermediate space, therefore... [of that].

How is there proof? This is the manner of resolving the objection: [the position] is the same for both those who maintain that the abode of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the goal to be attained and those who maintain that the world of the four-faced Brahmā (*caturmukhaloka*) is the goal to be attained; for even in the case of the world of the four-faced Brahmā, there is no difference in its lack of separation from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). || 12 || (3) Summary of the Meaning of the Section.

In the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*), regarding the passage beginning with, "But he who meditates upon that supreme Person by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures," and concluding with, "he sees the Person dwelling in the city, higher than the high," there arises the following doubt: Is the Person designated as the object of the act of seeing the four-faced Brahmā?

For, after describing the attainment of the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*) for one who meditates on the two-measure [syllable], the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*)—which is stated to be the goal for one who meditates on the three-measure [syllable]—is the world of the four-faced Brahmā, since it is situated beyond the intermediate world.
Anticipating this objection:

It has been stated that [the object of sight] is the Supreme Self, because it is designated as the Supreme Self in the passage beginning with "that which is peaceful, undecaying, and immortal," and because the highest heaven can also be understood as being beyond the intermediate space (antarikṣa).

Since the previously mentioned "seeing of the unseen" is not connected here, this constitutes a counter-example in the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*). Thus ends the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (Section 4).
The Section Concerning the Small One (Daharādhikaraṇa) || 1.3.5 ||

**The Compendium of the Collection of Principles on the Śārīraka:** "But the 'small' [space] must be the ether, or else it is the conscious [Self], because of its conventional usage and because of its association with qualities.

This is not correct; for there is no reality in the ether, and desires are not established by nature in the individual soul (jīva). (33) "But the 'small'"—in the scriptural text, "In this [city] there is a small space within," the object denoted by the word "small" (dahara) must be the ether (kha)—that is, the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa)—because of its conventional usage, as the word "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known in that very sense.

[The opponent argues: "It might be either the conscious [Self]—that is, the individual soul (jīva)—due to its connection with qualities, because of the existence of a relationship with qualities such as being free from sin which are to be sought after; or it might be this [body], for this is not tenable, this is not logical, because (hi) in the sky—the well-known ether—there is no reality, that is, the reality spoken of in the passage, 'This is the true city of Brahman,' does not exist at all."

In the living being—the conscious self—even the objects of desire, namely the qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth, though established by nature—that is, unconditioned—do not exist at all. || 33 ||

Furthermore, there is a fourfold lack of intrinsic cogency in the opponent's view: first, the discordance between the word and the indicative mark (*liṅga*); second, the connection [of the term] "in that" with the lotus of the heart, which is not proximate and lacks expectancy; third, the interruption of the injunction for the experience of desire as it is actually required; and fourth, these two [points] in our own position.
When there is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) of the word *yat*, that which occurs there as a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*)— || 30 ||

In the view of others—that is, in the view of the Advaitins—there is a fourfold lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya-catuṣṭaya*) in describing the meaning of the passage from the *Dahara-vidyā*: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, the small space within it; that which is inside that, one should seek, that indeed is what one should desire to understand. In this description of the meaning, there exists a fourfold defect arising from attributing an unnatural sense to the words.

(If it is asked, "What is that?": It is the defect consisting of a reversal of gender (*liṅgaviparyāsa*), caused by the masculine term *antarākāśaḥ* previously mentioned being grasped by the neuter relative pronoun *yat* occurring in the phrase "that which is within it" (*tasmin yad antaḥ*). This occurs when one describes the meaning according to that [masculine] method, disregarding the word *tasmin*, and is accompanied by the futility of justifying the locative-ending pronoun *tat* found in the aforementioned phrase, as well as by the intervention of the referent of the word *ākāśa*.

In the lotus-shaped object known as the heart, which was previously specified as "the small lotus" (*daharaṃ puṇḍarīkam*) and which exists within [the body] such that an intervention [of other things] would be encountered; there is a connection (*anvaya*) by way of being referred to by the word "in that" (*tasmin*). Likewise, there is likewise a rejection of the injunction for the experience of desired objects, which entails the abandonment—even though it is necessary—of the injunction for meditating upon the qualities related to the Supreme Self, such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which are denoted by the word "desires" (*kāma*).

(Thus. However, in our own position—that of the Viśiṣṭādvaitins—there are two points of lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*). This refers to the portion concerning the acceptance of the singular ending in the word "yat" according to the teaching [of the *Bhāṣya*]; that is what is meant by "saḥ" (that). || 30 ||

In the Taittirīya Śruti, the space within the lotus of the heart is declared to be the "small" (dahara); that which is likewise sung by the Chandogas as the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is one and the same. That [ether] is the primordial element (bhūtādya), because of its well-known greatness; thus, it cannot be refuted by various opposing arguments.
Furthermore, the Vedic tradition regarding the Lord is powerful, being supported by characteristic marks and descriptions. (13)

In the *Taittirīya* scripture, specifically in the *Taittirīya Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, regarding the "small lotus" (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*)—that particular location within the body known as the heart, which resembles a lotus—it is stated that there is a "small space" (*daharaṃ gaganam*). This refers to the subtle entity denoted by the term "space," as expressed in the passage: "Therein is a small, stainless space; even there is a small space. It is referred to by the two words "small" (*daharaḥ*) and "space" (*ākāśaḥ*). Furthermore, concerning its location within the heart-lotus and its specific nature:

The *vastu* (the reality) is sung by the *Chandogas*—those who study the Sāma Veda—in the passage: "Now, that which is within this small space here. Both of these [passages] are indeed one and the same, without any difference.

That entity indicated by the two words "gagana" and "ākāśa"—on account of its established greatness (*prasiddher mahimataḥ*), that is, due to the preeminence of its renown—is not merely the first among the five elements, namely the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) of common experience; thus, such a doubt is inappropriate. For by numerous specific marks and characteristics (*liṅgavarṇaiḥ*), that is, by many uncommon groups of reasons such as being the Self free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhikātmatva*) and being devoid of sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), the Supreme Self is established, as in [the scriptural passage]: "This Self is free from sin... (*eṣa ātmāpahatapāpmā*).

The prevalence of the use of the word "ether" (ākāśa) for the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Self, as stated in such passages, is "sanāthā"—meaning supported—and is "śrautī," obtained from the Śruti; this indeed would be powerful—that is, it becomes an obstacle to the cognition that the word "ether" refers to the elemental ether. || 13 ||

And since this [inner space] is indeed just like that external space, the words *ātman* and *brahman*—which denote the unafflicted Truth (*satya*)—cannot in any way be construed with the physical ether. Furthermore, that which was reckoned as the support of desires by the term "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is eternal;
for the statement "this is its Self" is a reference to that very [eternal entity], and thus its qualities are the inconceivable objects of desire.

And the external space—the elemental space well-known in the world—possessing whatever qualities such as vastness it may have; this [small space] within the heart is also like that, possessing such vastness and other attributes. This statement regarding the relationship between the object of comparison and the comparison is "unstrained"—that is, it follows naturally—in the case of the Supreme Self, which is distinct from the external space. Furthermore, in the case of the mere ether (*nabhas*), the words "existent," "Self," and "Brahman" apply.
—Having stated, "This is the true city of Brahman; this is the Self," [it is asked] how these words—"true," "Self," and "Brahman"—[are used], even in their primary sense...

Or, in a secondary sense, they do not attain—that is, they do not obtain—the appropriate connection (anvaya). And that very object which, by being the substratum of desirable qualities (*kāma*), was reckoned as such in the Śruti—"In this, all desires are contained"—is eternal, meaning it is devoid of modification both in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its inherent character (*svabhāva*). Here, by the term "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) occurring in this sentence, that very [Self] was reckoned—that is, described. For indeed, of that alone...

Indeed, this subsequent statement—beginning with "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless" and so forth—is a restatement (*anuvāda*) or reference (*parāmarśa*) to the small ether (*daharākāśa*) itself as the locus of the desired qualities, by declaring "This is the Self. Therefore, since the small ether is the Supreme Self, its qualities—from being free from evil up to having true resolves—which are inseparable from it, are the "desirable objects of thought" (*cintyakāmāḥ*); they are to be meditated upon just like the Supreme Self, they are objects of longing, and they are also desired as things that ought to manifest within oneself. || 14 ||

By the statement that it is the support of all, let the space within the heart (*hṛdayavyoma*) be understood as that [Brahman]; likewise, the word "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) found in the *Chāndogya*—as in the section concerning the Nīpāda chief—is [Brahman]. Āpastamba spoke of the city of Vaibhājanapura as Brahman, which has become the self of all;
for all living beings would belong to that [city], and that city indeed exists because it is the abode of all. (15)

That which has been studied—the entity designated by the term "ākāśa" as recited in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* within the *Vājasaneyi* branch—is accepted [as the subject], because it is described as the secret abode of the Lord of All through the statement that He is the support of all: "This *ākāśa* which is within the heart... therein He lies... the Lord of all. Whether it be the "space of the heart"—that is, the well-known *ākāśa* in the form of a subtle cavity called the "heart"—is what is being affirmed.

The term "Brahmaloka" and so forth found in the *Chāndogya*—that is, the words "Brahmaloka," "Brahmapura," and others recited in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*—are the locus for the application of the principle of the "Niṣāda-sthapati" (the maxim concerning the Niṣāda chief), which maintains that a *karmadhāraya* compound is more appropriate [in this context]. Furthermore, Āpastamba—the sage of that name—also [teaches] Brahman as the Self of all, namely Brahman whose body is the entire universe consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious.

The city of Vaibhājana—because living beings are capable of abiding separately according to their respective karmas—it is the city denoted by the term ‘Vaibhājana. Thus he said: "That indeed is the city of Vaibhājana," and he formulated this in the Sūtra. Of that Supreme Self, the ‘citizens’ (pūḥ)—those who are fit to abide in fullness—are the living beings; all creatures would be [the citizens].

That too—although it is the city for all with respect to Brahman, that supreme Brahman also would indeed be a city because it is the abode of all (sarvavāsāt), meaning it serves as the substratum for all; for it is certainly well-ordered, adorned, and fit to be a dwelling! || 15 ||

The individual soul (*jīva*) is the Self (*ātman*) because it is observed to be connected with a multitude of qualities, because of the perception of its reflection [in the intellect], and because of the logical necessity of its smallness; yet this is not so when considering qualities such as "truthful resolve" (*satya-saṃkalpatā*) which are free from limiting adjuncts (*anupadhika*). Furthermore, its status as the sole substratum of the universe and other such attributes would indeed be adventitious (*aupādhikī*) in the higher sense;
however, in the passage concerning Prajāpati, those qualities are described in reference to the liberated soul from the perspective of the supreme state.

In that case—since it is untenable for elemental space to be the "small space" (daharākāśa), and because of the presence of a multitude of qualities—the fact that qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are uncontradicted and observed to be referred to therein—and because the apprehension of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is seen in the scripture in the statement, "He said: 'This is the Self'"—therefore, this Self, described by the words "this is the Self, free from sin," etc., must be the individual soul, the Self in the form of a living being.

[The opponent argues: "Because of its smallness and because of logical reasoning—since the quality of smallness and so forth must be understood as applying to the individual soul (jīva), and since this is indicated by the use of the word ‘small’ (dahara)—this [objection] is invalid. Such a doubt is incorrect. Why? Because of the collection of qualities such as having true resolves (satya-saṅkalpatā) which are unconditioned and eternal, beginning with unimpeded will; and also because of being the support of the universe, that is, because of being the primary substratum for the entire world, as stated in the Śruti: "Within this [space], heaven and earth are contained. Therefore...

Indeed, this very Self has been described as "the supreme Self, free from evil," and so forth. However, with respect to the supreme Self—which is all-pervading—its limited dimension must be merely adventitious (*aupādhikī*), based solely on its limitation by the heart; it is not inherent. This is evident in the dialogue between Prajāpati and Indra, which demonstrates Prajāpati’s instruction regarding the nature of the Self to Indra: "That Self which is free from evil... and so on.

In the statement consisting of the Śruti text, "Thus indeed Prajāpati said," the description of those qualities—namely, the mention of attributes such as being free from sin and so forth—refers to the individual soul (jīva) when it is liberated and has attained the supreme light, existing in a state of supreme similarity with the Supreme Self through its highest realization. || 16 ||
The statement "He bestows the final release" is intended here as a declaration of grace;

however, in the Prajāpati passage, the repetition of the phrase is for the purpose of extracting the ultimate meaning. Thus, through expectancy and other criteria, those two pairs of sentences—each consisting of both [the Prajāpati and the Udgītha passages]—are mutually connected.

It is appropriate that there is no mutual contradiction and so forth here; for that state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) is indeed what is taught in the Sūtra. The "Space within the Heart" (*daharākāśa*): The Supreme Self, designated by the term "Space within the Heart" in the Upaniṣad, is the bestower of liberation—the giver of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) to those who meditate upon Him. To declare this—to establish this meaning—here in the passage concerning the "Knowledge of the Small" (*daharavidyā*), there is the mention of "perfect serenity" (*samprasāda*), namely the use of the word *samprasāda* in the sentence: "This perfect serenity [emerges] from this body."

In the statement of Prajāpati to Indra, and in the statement of Brahmā to him beginning with "He is that Supreme Person," the successive enumeration is for the purpose of extracting the ultimate goal—the clear and distinct communication of the system of the supreme Self as the object to be attained; therefore, by reason of what has been stated, [it proceeds] through expectancy and the other criteria.

When there exists a pair of sentences—namely, the *dahara* section and the *Prajāpati* section—which relate to both [the supreme self and the individual self] through their mutual presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*āsatti*), and which are thus "connected" (*anvita*) by way of being harmonized without contradiction; then, in these two aforementioned sentences, there can be no such thing as mutual sublation, such as the assumption that the meaning to be understood in the *Prajāpati* section is sublated by the *dahara* meditation section, or conversely, [that the latter is sublated by the former].

Nor is it reasonable to assume that the meaning understood from the passage concerning the Dahara-vidyā is sublated; for that would not be consistent. Indeed, their "sāmarasya"—the demonstration that those two passages convey an uncontradicted and non-figurative meaning—is correctly established by the Sūtra (the Śārīraka-sūtra). || 17 ||

The summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the "small" (*dahara*): In the passage, "In this [city], there is a small inner space," one might raise the objection that because the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is commonly known to refer to elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), and because there would otherwise be no other object to be sought, the "small space" is indeed elemental space.
Having raised this doubt:

Because the subsequent passage establishes qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) in connection with the small ether (*daharākāśa*), and because it is precisely these qualities that are to be sought after, it is concluded that the small ether is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The connection of the method has been determined previously regarding the Person Residing in the City through the power of the scriptural texts concerning the Puruṣa. Now, by way of a counter-example, the commencement of the section on the "Small" (Dahara) arises. Thus ends the Section on the Small (Daharādhikaraṇa), the fifth.
The Section on the Measured (Pramitādhikaraṇa) || 1.4.6 ||

In the statement, "The lord of the vital breaths moves about, having gathered the collection of the principles of the Śārīraka," the claim that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed measured by the size of a thumb based on common usage is certainly incorrect; for in this very sentence, the word "Īśāna" (the Lord) is heard. (34)

In the passage, "The lord of the vital breaths wanders according to his own karmas, thumb-sized and resembling the sun," because the individual self (jīvātman) alone is well-known by tradition to be measured by the size of a thumb—the meaning established by the word "thumb-sized" (*aṅguṣṭhamātra*) in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, namely "the person is thumb-sized"—it would also be incorrect to claim that this must necessarily be the individual self alone.

Such a suspicion is likewise entirely without foundation; for in this very sentence from the Kaṭhavallī—the sentence containing the term "thumb-sized" (aṅguṣṭhamātra)—the word "Lord" (īśāna) is heard: "The person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self, the Lord of what has been and what is to be. Thus, the word "Lord," which makes known His sovereignty over the world, is explicitly mentioned in scripture. || 34 ||

The *Adhikaraṇasārāvali* states: It has been mentioned in some places that the Lord of Life (Prāṇeśa) is the size of a thumb as he wanders about according to his own karmas; elsewhere it is seen that Yama cuts out even a person the size of a thumb. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the Upanishad speaks of the individual soul (jīva) as being measured by that [thumb-sized] standard, because the Lordship and other attributes [of the passage] do not derive their authority from the limitation of the heart, for that [heart] is merely a measure. (18)

In some [scriptures]—in specific Vedic texts—the Lord of Life (prāṇeśa), that is, the individual soul (jīva) designated by the term "Lord of Prāṇa," who wanders everywhere by assuming various bodies through his own actions as means—namely, his good and evil deeds—is described as being "the size of a thumb" (aṅguṣṭhamātra), meaning measured by the dimension of a thumb; and in other [works]—in certain specific treatises such as the Itihāsas—it is stated that the Person (puruṣa) is "thumb-sized," meaning limited to the measure of a thumb.

It has indeed been observed that the object denoted by the word *puruṣa*—namely, Yama, the son of Vivasvat—drew him out (*niṣkarṣa*) from the body; thus, this is seen through the form of a Smṛti statement. Therefore, for this reason, the Kaṭha Upaniṣad—in the form of the passage, "The *puruṣa* the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self"—speaks of the *jīva*, that is, it refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*), as an object measured by the size of a thumb, which is established by that very authority. [To claim otherwise] is incorrect.

For this [claim] is indeed devoid of reason; that measure—the size of a thumb—is determined by the very statement [of the scripture], because the lordship and other qualities residing in the sentence are understood from that statement itself through the mark (liṅga) of being the Lord of the Universe and so forth. It is concluded that [this limitation] arises solely from the confinement to the region of the heart within the human body, and not from its own inherent nature. || 18 ||

For the heart, which is the abode of all living beings, is not merely the size of a thumb; rather, the mention of its being of that measure occurs in certain instances as a reference to human qualification within the context of the Supreme All-pervading One. The specific details of that [qualification] are considered in three sections (adhikaraṇas) contained within two pairs of sūtras. However, the procedure (itikartavyatā) intended to be rejected here is not to be established by those third [sections]. (19)

"Of the size of a thumb"—delimited by the shape of a thumb; "the heart"—the place known as the heart, for it does not indeed belong to all living beings—that is, it is not related to every single creature—for that reason, in the case of the "all-pervading," the supreme, transcendent Brahman, the mention of its being measured by a thumb in the Śruti is merely figurative; [it applies] only to the heart of a man qualified for meditation in certain instances.

"Not everywhere"—by stating this, when the occasion for discussing the qualification of human beings arises—that is, when the context of declaring that "only humans have the qualification for meditation" has been reached—the statement regarding the authority [of scripture] within the two pairs of sūtras—namely, the pair of sūtras beginning with "From the word itself" (*śabdādeva*) and "But because of the heart, [it refers to] humans, since they alone have the qualification" (*hṛdyapekṣayā tu manuṣyādhikāratvāt*), as well as [the sūtra] "Because of trembling" (*kampanāt*)—is the expression of its being the means of knowledge.
1. *tanmānatoktiḥ* — Ā. 2. *tātave* — Ā.

By means of the three sections consisting of the *devatādhikaraṇa*, the *madhvadhikaraṇa*, and the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*—which constitute the core of the two sūtras beginning with "jyotirdarśanāt"—the specific principle, namely the specific qualification (*adhikāraviśeṣa*), is investigated, deliberated upon, and determined. By means of the sections belonging to the third chapter, that which is to be established through investigation—the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding meditation—is determined as its constituent parts.

The subject matter (*adhikriyā*)—that which is denoted by the term "topic" (*adhikārapada*)—is not intended to be disregarded nor is it what one wishes to make known (*na bubodhayiṣitā*; with the causative sense internalized), in these three topics undertaken for the purpose of determining the specific qualification (*adhikāra-viśeṣa*) for meditation (*upāsanā*). A summary of the meaning of the topics:

In the *Pramitādhikaraṇa*, having raised the doubt that the individual soul (*jīva*) is measured by the thumb—based on the hearing of the phrase "thumb-sized person" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣaḥ*) and the hearing of the individual soul's thumb-size in passages such as "thumb-sized, with a form like the sun" (*aṅguṣṭhamātro ravitulyarūpaḥ*)—[the author proceeds].

Because of the scriptural statement, "The Lord of what has been and what is to be," and because the measurement by a thumb is possible for the Supreme Self when conditioned by the heart, it is said that the Supreme Self is the size of a thumb.
"May the *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* [proceed].

However, regarding the section on the measured (the individual soul), it is objected that Brahman must be of small measure; but this is countered by the statement that the individual soul (*jīva*) would be [Brahman] because of the specific scriptural testimony concerning Him. Thus ends the section on the Measured (*pramitādhikaraṇa*). 6.
The Section Concerning the Deities (Devatādhikaraṇa) || 2.3.7 ||
The collection of arguments regarding the embodied nature [of the gods]:

"In the accomplishment of a formless [deity] as if it were embodied, the gods are not entitled to be worshipped"—this too is incorrect; for since they possess imagined names and forms, they are capable like human beings. (35) "In the accomplishment of a form" means that which is fit to be performed by those possessing bodies; "in worship" refers to sacrifices, meditations, and so forth, which are the means for propitiating the gods.

When an action has been performed, those who are "without bodies" (avigrahāḥ)—meaning bodiless—and "gods" (devāḥ)—meaning conscious beings who have attained the state of gods and so forth—would not be "authorized" (adhikṛtāḥ), that is, they would certainly not be eligible for [the fruits of] action; even such a doubt is "unfounded" (asat)—it is not correct.

They too—those sentient beings who have attained the state of gods, like humans who have obtained the mortal state—are merely possessors of names and forms (nāma-rūpa) produced by the volition of the Lord; therefore, for that very reason, even they—the gods—possess authority consisting of both desire and capability. ||35||

The essence of reality is that the worship of the Blessed One is possible even for the gods who possess sharp bodies and are subject to the heat of worldly existence. Now, even a hundred words of explanatory praise (arthavāda) are authoritative here, like the words of mantras, provided they are free from defects and not of human origin.

For those endowed with bodies, senses, and so forth possessed of an excellence of beauty, yet afflicted by the heat of worldly existence—those possessing a most intense physical form who perceive *bhava* (existence) as the experience of the Supreme Self—even for conscious beings dwelling in the celestial realms (*diviṣad*), when compared to humans, meditation (*dhyāna*) consisting of the contemplation of the Blessed One (*bhagavaccintana*) is possible; indeed, it is entirely appropriate for them to regard such meditation as a means of alleviating their suffering.

The hundreds—that is, the countless—forms of the Vedic sentences known as *arthavāda* (explanatory passages), which are subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*) because they serve to provide the meanings required for the performance of rituals and so forth; and likewise the Vedic sentences known as *mantra* (invocatory formulas), which remind one of the objects inherent in the ritual performance, such as the materials and deities; all these, in this context, like injunctive sentences such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," are not of human origin (*apuṃprabhava*), that is, they are *apauruṣeya* (not authored by a person), and for that very reason, they are free from defect (*apadoṣa*).

There exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is the instrument for knowledge corresponding to reality, and which is far removed from the possibility of defects such as error and deception. || 31 ||

In this context, the primary purpose of praise is to generate a desire for one's own goal among those to be instructed, by instilling respect for the qualities that are to be expressed. Otherwise, it would not succeed, just as in the case of injunctions; for how can there be praise through the mention of a non-existent quality, even for those who know the truth? (32)

In this context—referring to the *arthavādas* and other such passages intended as supplements to injunctions—the first type, namely the *arthavāda* Vedic statement consisting primarily of praise, exists for the sake of its own accomplishment; that is, for the purpose of producing that specific desire characterized by the state of being something to be performed (*anuṣṭheyatva*) regarding the objects of the injunction, such as sacrifices, which are the subject matter of the injunction. It functions as if it possessed a primary intention toward the qualities (*guṇas*) expressed within itself, just like one who possesses regard for the qualities to be described.

Otherwise—if there were no primary intentionality (*mukhyatātparya*) regarding the qualities to be understood from the words of the *arthavādas*—then, just as in the case of injunctions (*vidhis*), even in the *arthavādas* which are engaged in the description of qualities, that intent toward describing those qualities would not be established; it would simply not be accomplished.

How, or in what manner, can there be praise—meaning the recognition of actual excellence in that which is worthy of worship or veneration—by those who know the reality of things (tattvavidām), that is, by the discerning who possess thorough knowledge of the true nature of reality, based on a quality (*guṇa*) that is non-existent in fact (*asatā vastutaḥ*) and merely described through words (*kathitena vāṅmātrataḥ*)? || 32 ||
Now, the sages indeed assist the ritual procedure through the means of instructing those who are to be disciplined; for they generate in him the cognition of the form of the deity and so forth.
How then can that deity, whose body is absent, be capable of assisting him by entering into his cognition? (33)

Now—immediately after the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the *mantras* assist the injunction (*vidhi*)—the prescriptive scripture—by means of their function of making known the things to be enjoined; that is, by way of reminding one of the substances and deities connected with the sacrifices and other rites to be performed. Since they do so by producing an excellence required [for the ritual], those *mantras*, generating the cognition of the gods' bodies and so forth—that is, producing the knowledge that even the gods possess bodies and the like—assist this injunction.

Indeed, they are certainly capable—able—to endow [the deity] with the intended excellence! For how, or by what means, could the deities—the individual entities such as Agni, Indra, and others who are the objects of sacrifice—ascend to the intellect—that is, become established in the mind—if they were devoid of form, lacking a physical body? || 33 ||

Furthermore, you have clearly mastered the grammatical analyses of the deities within the concluding sections of the Vedic meters, as well as the enumerations of the manifestations of gods, humans, animals, and stationary beings; and you have understood their movements and the methods of their worship. (34)

Now, in the later portion of the Vedic collections—specifically in the Upaniṣadic section, within those scriptural passages that describe the creation of the fourfold world consisting of gods, humans, and so forth—the corporeal forms (vigrahas)—that is, the bodies and so on—of the deities such as Agni, Indra, and others, are most clearly and without doubt [established].

Likewise, having studied—that is, having recited—the methods of worship, you should discern—meaning determine through reflection—the "course," which is the manner in which the eligibility of the deities is established within the sections that expound upon the worship of the Lord. ||34||
Through hundreds of scriptural citations, through histories such as the *Devatā-vigraha*, and through the *Dharma-śāstras* and *Purāṇas*,
it has been clearly stated that one possesses the qualification for the worship of the Infinite.
Therefore, this class of immortals is capable and seeks that fruit. ||35||

By means of hundreds of *nigamas*—the various roots of the Vedic word; by *itihāsas*—literary compositions such as the *Mahābhārata* and others that set forth past events; by *dharmaśāstras*—the *smṛti* texts taught by Manu and other expounders; and by *purāṇas*—those which set forth the creation, dissolution, and other such topics.

Even though the physical forms and so forth of Indra, Agni, and others—who are the intended objects of worship—are described with extreme clarity through the primary mode of expression (*vācyavṛtti*) in texts known as the *Purāṇas*, nevertheless, because they possess such physical forms and so on, this class of immortals is endowed with bodies, sense organs, and the like, as is well-known from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Itihāsa*.

The *agni-indra-devatā-stoma* is [the subject]; one who desires its fruit—that is, one who longs for liberation, which is the fruit of the meditation on Brahman under discussion—and who is capable—meaning endowed with tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities necessary for meditation—is qualified. Thus, regarding the practice of meditation upon the Infinite—the Supreme Self which is free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as space and time—the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of this host of gods, who possess both desire and capability, is established by scripture and by their very nature; such fitness is undeniable. (35)

In this very context, we indeed perceive that configuration (*saṃsthāna*) follows after the form (*ākṛti*) in its entirety; and we likewise state that it applies to other [universals] as well, even where they are not visible, such as in the case of other classes (*jāti*). In the various cognitions preceded by "cowness" and so forth, there is a common [element], namely the class;
such is the expression "class, class," and my own position follows this very path. (36)

In this very section—the section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*)—consider the "form" (*ākṛti*), that is, the genus denoted by the word "form," as being distinct from the configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which is known as the arrangement of various parts; for it is because that [genus] is that configuration.

The thing denoted by the word is indeed the very object; first of all, it is "concomitant"—we perceive it as such, we know it, or we believe it, and we speak of it—we express it exactly as such—and furthermore, nothing else whatsoever beyond the configuration has been seen by anyone as being concomitant in that way. Even in the alternative case—that is, even in the theory of universals distinct from configuration—in the case of many universals, such as those headed by "cowness" and "horseness," [the concomitance is not observed].

The common cognition "genus, genus" is a pervasive apprehension of the form "genus, genus"; this applies equally to verbal expression and to practical usage. This is indeed so on my own path—even under the view that a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) alone constitutes a genus—it remains entirely consistent; for [according to that view] a configuration is precisely that which possesses those respective unique forms, and it is that very thing which is the genus. ||36||

Let that universal (*jāti*) be accepted which is one, pervasive through many individuals, complete in each individual, distinct from their specific configurations (*saṃsthāna*), and without beginning or end. Otherwise, how could our recurring cognition and verbal expression "cow, cow" occur? And how could there be an understanding of the application of words such as "cow" to innumerable individuals? (37)

It is pervasive across many individuals—subsisting in numerous substrates; it is complete in every individual—its nature being undiminished (unbroken) in each and every instance; it is a single entity devoid of internal differentiation dependent upon individual differences; it is without beginning or end—free from origination and destruction; and it is distinct from configuration—differentiated from the specific arrangement of parts.

Furthermore, whatever may be denoted by a general term, let that be accepted as the universal (*jāti*); let it be admitted that this alone is what is expressed by the word "universal. If, however, it is not so admitted—if it is not accepted in that way—then how could the recurring cognition and verbal expression "this is a cow" (the conceptualization and linguistic usage of "cow") be possible, or how could they be justified, with respect to the cow perceived as following through all individual cows? For us, among the innumerable individuals—individuals that are impossible to count—[how could these be explained otherwise?]

How is the acquisition of linguistic proficiency regarding words such as ‘cow’ (*gauḥ*) and others established? Or in what manner is even the grasping of the connection between a word and its referent accomplished? (37) To this we reply: We perceive some other entity, namely that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, called ‘cowness’ (*gotva*), which is the object of recurrent linguistic usage; for such a thing was indeed observed. What was said in the theory of universals (*jātivāda*) regarding another entity that is common to ‘cowness,’ ‘horseness,’ ‘assness,’ and so on—an entity that persists through many individuals and serves as the basis for the application of words such as ‘universal’ and the like? (38)

In this regard—this being the prima facie position reached—we reply: we state the following counter-argument. Is there some entity called "cowness" (*gotva*), denoted by the word "cow," which is distinct from the dewlap and other features found in cows and so forth, which is the object of inclusive cognition and linguistic usage—that is, the scope of a uniform cognition and the application of such a word across many individuals—and which is something that can be apprehended through a means of valid knowledge? Even upon diligent investigation, what do we perceive? What do we know? We perceive nothing at all;
for that [entity] is simply the possession of the dewlap and so forth.

Indeed, such a thing—which produces the cognition and linguistic usage [of "universal"]—has been observed; that is, it is seen. Even in the theory of universals (*jātivāda*), which accepts a distinct general property (*sāmānya*), within the various universals such as "cowness," "horseness," and "assness"—that is, among the numerous universals denoted by the term "universal"—there exists another single entity, distinct from their respective configurations (*saṃsthāna*), which serves as the basis for the application of words such as "universal" and so forth; that is, it is some one thing that accounts for the employment of terms like "universal."
What was said regarding the object (*vastu*), or has it been established? The meaning is: it has not been established at all. || 38 ||

Since the occurrence of linguistic usage cannot be explained otherwise by the non-perception of anything else, and since it is impossible for [the universal] to be postulated as something independent, the word "genus" (jāti) and so forth—which relies on the force of the conventions established by both parties—is appropriate; for such a word, being capable of producing an understanding through its own internal connection with the mutually supportive notions of speech, manifests that very form which is the object of the other's convention. (39)

Because there is no perception of any other object—namely, an entity distinct from configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that is fit to be denoted by the word "universal"—and because it is not apprehended in individual instances such as cows and the like; and because the functioning of all worldly transactions is established in an entirely different manner, through a different means; and because even the possibility of postulation is absent—that is, because there is an absence of being an object of postulation based on the impossibility of explaining things otherwise even for that which is unperceived—one who relies upon the configuration acknowledged in the consensus of both parties [the proponent and the opponent]...

Precisely because it has as its object a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that is accepted without dispute by both parties, every word—whether a genus-word (*jāti*), quality-word (*guṇa*), action-word (*kriyā*), or arbitrary word (*yadṛcchā*), thus divided into four types—is "connected" (*yukta*), that is, associated, with its own denotatum among those various objects belonging to the same class which are to be understood through those respective words; for indeed (*hi*), that configuration (*saṃsthā*) exists as being mutually very similar, that is, possessing extreme mutual resemblance.

(For this very reason,) it is precisely capable of being the basis for the linguistic usage and conceptualization of a pervasive cognition—that is, for the sake of regulating such a cognition, such a conventional usage, and the apprehension of such a power. Of whatever nature that [cognition] is, it is of that very nature; of whatever nature that configuration—which consists of a specific arrangement of parts—is, it is that very thing which manifests the "form" (*ākṛti*)—the universal nature of the genus (*jāti*) denoted by the term *ākṛti* as accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas and other proponents of the theory of a distinct genus, according to the principle: "The genus is apprehended through the form."
It manifests [the universal] according to the stated principle: "The universal is manifested by the configuration that follows [it]. || 39 ||
Indeed, the non-existence of non-existence is certainly existence according to the view of others; tell me then, is the non-existence of a jar and such things not likewise existence?
For the destruction of a jar is indeed the state of being shards, while another [form of] non-existence is the state of being a lump; what other [non-existence] is seen here at all? (40)

In the view of others, namely the Naiyāyikas and so forth, a positive entity (*bhāva*)—an object such as a jar that serves as the basis for the linguistic usage "it exists"—is indeed the absence of an absence; for being of the nature of the absence of the absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the jar, it is indeed made the object of the cognition "the absence of the jar does not exist."

(Since the absence of a second absence is of the same nature as the counter-positive of the first absence), in this manner—according to the method stated—the absence of a jar and so forth, when conceptualized as "the jar is not," consists of the difference from the jar; does even that absence not become an absence—is it not fit to be denoted by the word "absence"? It certainly is; tell me—reflect and speak.

The destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of a jar—defined as the absence denoted by the term "destruction" which has the jar as its counter-positive and is characterized by the mental representation, "A jar was here previously, but today it is not"—is indeed the state of being shards; for it is established as having the nature of a property residing in the shards that constitute the parts of the jar.

As for the other absence of the jar—namely, the absence designated by the term "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva), which has the jar as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) and is expressed as "the jar will exist here, but today it does not exist"—the state of being a lump (piṇḍatva), which is the clay that serves as the material cause (upādāna) of the jar, is indeed an absence called "lump-ness" that is positive in nature (bhāvarūpa). Is there anything else here—in this sphere of the cognition and linguistic usage of absence—that is not at all established as an absence, or something that could be expressed by words such as "not" (nañ)? The meaning is: in no way is there any such thing. ||40||

The wise here understand non-existence as merely a relational absence (saṃsargābhāva), while regarding existence itself as non-existence—just as the portion of ground other than the spot where a jar stands is considered the non-existence of that jar. As for that region such as the courtyard of a house which, at a particular time, is conjoined with the absence of a jar and is recognized by others as its locus: what additional entity is perceived there? None whatsoever. ||42||

Not perceiving non-existence (*abhāva*)— thinking that everything is indeed existence (*bhāva*) alone— and determining through inquiry that it is of the nature of existence, the wise— the learned of subtle intellect— understand "non-connection" (*saṃsargābhāva*), which is one among the types of non-existence, as being precisely the negation of the connection between a jar and a house and so forth in such cases as "there is no jar in the house," according to the method to be described hereafter.

In that context, the meaning denoted by the term "absence" (*abhāva*) is the bare ground, as opposed to the jar—for instance, in relation to the ground which serves as the locus for the jar. However, the distinction from other parts of the earth is merely another specific region of the ground. According to others who maintain that absence is a distinct category (*pṛthaktvavādibhiḥ*), that which constitutes the substratum of the absence of the jar is a specific location—such as a courtyard belonging to a house—which is connected to a particular time consisting of preceding and succeeding moments. This is what has been determined by them.

As the locus (*ādhāra*) for the category of the absence of a jar, that specific location has been determined. For us, who maintain that absence is of a positive nature (*bhāvātmaka-abhāvavādin*), such a particular place serves as the site designated by the term "absence. It is the perception—the observation—of some additional object (*adhika-artha*) which is fit for conventional usage (*vyavahārārha*).
In comparison with this, where could there exist a state of non-existence that is distinct from it? || 41 ||

Having created [the world] as "truth" and "thatness," You enter into both the conscious and the unconscious; therefore You have been called the "All-pervading One who encircles the universe with Your skin," and indeed the entire universe is Your body. By means of various scriptures that expand the heart through the practice of non-duality, those who imagine a cause for the delusion of non-duality—while [in fact] there is only duality and non-duality [coexisting]—have been refuted. (42)

O Blessed One—O Lord endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers beginning with knowledge! You, having created—that is, having brought forth—the sentient and the insentient (the totality of conscious and unconscious beings), namely "Sat" (Being), which is immutable in its essential nature, and "Tyat" (That), which is subject to modification in both essence and nature, have entered into them; you have effected an internal penetration within them.

And because you have thus effected an entry into both the sentient and the insentient, you are called the "Viśva" (the All); you are established as the universe itself in such passages as, "All this is indeed the Puruṣa."

The entire world—consisting of both the sentient and the insentient—is indeed Your body, for the following reasons: because it originates from You (tvajatvāt), meaning it has You, who are denoted by the term *brahman*, as its non-different instrumental and material cause; because it dissolves into You (tvallayanatvāt), meaning it merges into You who are denoted by the term *brahman*; and because its very life is dependent upon being denoted by the term *brahman*. Thus, it is well-known in the Śruti, Smṛti, and other scriptures that everything is Your body; You are addressed as "Thou" (*tvam*), and You are established in such passages as "All this, verily, is Brahman."

(a) *Abhedavyavahṛtihṛdayam*—by those who expound at length (*vistṛṇānaiḥ*), that is, by describing in detail through various scriptures consisting of Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and so forth, which are intent upon establishing the entry of the Supreme Self into the world, as well as [the world's] origination, sustenance, and dissolution from the Supreme Self, and its being the body of the Supreme Self—the intention of the Śruti, which serves as the cause for the conventional usage of non-difference between the world and Brahman.

Those who, relying on [certain texts as] indicators, postulate difference and non-difference as the cause— thinking by their own intellect, without following the Śruti and other authorities, that "the very difference and non-difference existing mutually between Brahman and the world are themselves the causes for the empirical usage of the non-difference of the world and Brahman"— namely Bhāskara, the followers of Yādava, and the Śāṅkaras, who postulate the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman and the error (bhrama) of Brahman regarding the world as the causes for the empirical usage of non-difference— they have been refuted and rejected. || 41 ||

Now follows the incidental discussion on the *aruṇā* (the red cow): after the determination of these specific meanings—which arose as secondary consequences (*prasaṅktānuprasakta*) from the investigation in the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*)—it follows that the discussion of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* as stated in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, which possesses a connection known as "incidental" (*prasaṅga*), must likewise be examined. This is the meaning.

In the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the Guru [Kumārila] has established that the connection with redness (*āruṇya*) is not expressed directly by the word "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*), but is rather brought about through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*). This is because the expression "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*) denotes a mere quality, while the substance is indicated by the word itself.
Words ending in case-inflections, when mutually connected, do not constitute a sentence. || 43 ||

In the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* system, this has been raised and thus determined after deliberation: in the sentence "He purchases Soma with a one-year-old [cow], tawny-eyed and red" (*aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā ekahāyanyā*), which is intended to teach the means for the purchase of Soma, the "one-year-old" (*ekahāyanī*) mentioned there does not indeed attain—nor does it reach—the connection with redness (*āruṇya-anvaya*), that is, the relation to the quality of the color red, as a primary denotation (*ābhidhānika*)—that is, through direct verbal expression; rather, it is attained through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*), established solely by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*).

Because—*yat*—for which reason, the word "aruṇayā" (with the red one), which is situated in the sentence like the word for a substance (*dravya*) in a statement indicating a substance, is a verbal expression (*gīḥ*) consisting of the word *aruṇa* ending in the third case; it denotes (*brūte*) "mere quality"—that is, redness (*āruṇya*) consisting solely of a qualifier even without a substance. [This is because] words ending in case-inflections that express grammatical relations (*kāraka*), such as the accusative or instrumental, are seen to end in the second or other case endings that convey relations such as being the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the word "aruṇayā"...
Words such as "one-year-old cow" and so forth cannot be mutually—i.e., with respect to one another—coherent; that is, they are not at all capable of possessing a connected meaning. || 43 ||

By the Guru—the Prābhākara Mīmāṃsaka—in the section concerning the *aruṇā* (the passage on the red cow): "That path of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* which was traversed by the venerable sage Rāmānuja is appropriate here, while the other is inappropriate; this becomes clear in an assembly of the learned. (44)

By the venerable sage Rāmānuja—by those excellent ascetics known as Rāmānujācārya—the method pertaining to the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the red cow)—namely, the procedure regarding the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—was thoroughly analyzed and demonstrated; this alone is appropriate, being faultless and useful for determining the purposeful meaning. Any other method, distinct from this one and presented by the Prābhākaras and others, is inappropriate, being defective.

"In the assembly of the learned"—in a gathering of those whose sole skill lies in the contemplation of the true meaning of reality—it becomes clear, that is, it becomes manifest, that [the teaching] is not capable of determining the purposeful meaning [of the scriptures]. (The sense is: this matter is not easily determined by the dull-witted who merely grasp what has already been grasped. || 44 ||

Even when a substance has been grasped, its specific distinction transforms according to its nature through the removal of dissimilar case-endings; indeed, this is the view of the Ākṛti-naya. However, the case-ending expresses the identity of meaning between two words alike;
that threefold ending would indicate the application of number and the cognition of the kāraka.

Even when a substance is explicitly mentioned—as in "He buys Soma with a red, one-year-old cow"—where the substance in the form of a cow qualified by the state of being one-year-old is directly stated, [the quality] is nonetheless connected through the principle of the *ākṛti* section (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇanyāya*). This is because there is no indication of a non-identical case-ending (as in "the whiteness of the cloth"), due to the removal of dissimilar case-endings; rather, the qualification—the possession of the quality of redness—is established by the base word "red" (*aruṇā*), which functions as the base for the third-case ending.

It indeed culminates—it indeed reaches its conclusion! Regarding the two words "aruṇayā" and "ekahāyanyā," the fact that the heard case-ending is identical—that is, it is the same single case-ending consisting of the instrumental (tṛtīyā)—expresses, indeed, the non-difference of the substratum (*dharmi*) between the qualities of redness (*āruṇya*) and one-year-old-ness (*ekahāyanatva*); it establishes this very point. It possesses three forms: [namely] being a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhaktitva*),...

Possessing the three formal characteristics consisting of having the same case-ending and being singular in number—that third-case ending—would indeed be capable of producing a cognition of the *kāraka* (instrumental factor), namely a cognition whose object is the status of being a means to the purchase, by way of its form as a case-ending prescribed for the instrumental sense according to the rule "and for the instrument and the locus," just as it [produces] a connection with the number one through its form as a singular number, as if it were conveying the connection with number itself. || 45 ||
This auspicious first chapter of the *Tattvasāra* by the venerable Śrī Vātsyavaradārya has been provided with a commentary by Rāmabhadra from the beginning.

—(That which belongs to her) would have a nature designated by words, characterized by forms perceived in the world; it could not, however, be of a different nature or unknowable. Therefore, because of its nature as sound, or because of its form as worldly fire and so forth, the worship of that deity—namely, the meditation on Brahman consisting of contemplation prescribed by the Vedāntas for the sake of liberation—is simply not possible. Such a description is useless, being far removed from the intended meaning of the Śruti.

(For: "The rejection of what is heard" means the non-acceptance of the satisfaction of the deity—which is established by scripture through such statements as "he pleases this [deity]"; and the non-acceptance of qualities residing in the deity, such as being the swiftest, which are mentioned in passages like "the deity is the swiftest"; as well as the postulation of what is not heard, namely that which is not stated in scripture: that the deity consists of sound (*śabdātmakatva*), that the deity possesses a worldly form (*laukikākṛtimattva*), and that the *apūrva* alone—produced by the ritual act—is the bestower of the fruit.

"Nor from a deity," and so forth; [if one were to claim] that there is contemplation of that non-existent object by means of one's own intellect, then two faults would ensue. Furthermore, let the Supreme Person, the creator of the universe and the maker of all worlds, not be an object of inference—let this conclusion that He is not accessible through scriptural inference remain unshaken.

For this [Lord]—the Supreme Self who is the cause of the universe—is established by those devoted to Him—that is, by those for whom the primary purpose is the exposition of the Lord—as being "uncontradicted," meaning free from any other subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is established through the scriptures (*śāstra*), such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1), and "In the beginning, this was Brahman alone" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1); and this has already been firmly established in the section concerning the scriptures being the source [of knowledge regarding Brahman] (*Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*).
Today, even by the Lord Himself—the omnipotent Supreme Self—it cannot be denied; it unfolds in a nature that is entirely incapable of being denied. ||20||

If the deities, who possess appropriate bodies by virtue of their own power, were to become objects of petition for those suffering from affliction, then even they would be entitled to the category of worship by others. Proclaiming everything found in the Mantras, Arthavādas, and so forth to be false because it lacks sublation (*bādhadoṣa*), these people here forget the intrinsic validity (*mānatā*) that has been declared [for them]. 21.
