"Of those possessing suitable bodies"—meaning those endowed with the perfection of a physical form fit for the practice of worship; "of the deities"—meaning of sentient beings who enjoy the state of divinity; "capacity"—the fitness, by virtue of birth, action, and intellect, for the undertaking of a means, for the completion of the means once begun, and for the attainment of the fruit therefrom; "desire"—the longing for the means that liberates from suffering—of those "subject to affliction," precisely because they partake in the threefold suffering; "shall be attained"—that it shall indeed come to pass.

Even for those deities, there exists the qualification for the class of higher worship—that is, they indeed possess the status of practitioners in all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) which serve as means to liberation. This is clearly understood and well-known from the mantras employed as constituent parts of ritual acts in the *mantra* and *arthavāda* sections, from the *arthavādas* intended to praise the ritual acts, from the *brāhmaṇa* portions that enjoin rituals, and likewise in the *Upaniṣads*.

"Nikhilam" means everything, including the forms, qualities, and glories of each respective deity. "In the absence of sublation or defects" means even when there is no contradiction by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and no defect in the cause of that valid cognition. Yet, those who proclaim it to be "mithyā"—meaning non-existent or unreal—namely the atheistic Mīmāṃsakas, who boldly and boastfully prattle on in this regard concerning the entire collection of the Vedas, [deny] its self-evident authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇyam*), which was declared by the Vedas themselves.

Their authority is independent of other means of valid cognition; they speak without even remembering [the source], yet they do not say anything that contradicts what they themselves have previously stated, nor anything that contradicts the subject matter. || 21 ||

The function in the context of praise (stuti) is twofold: that which proceeds by way of one's own qualities and that which proceeds by way of another's qualities. Of these, the former is intended for the sake of a specific purpose (*artha*). In the latter case as well, the primary attribute (*mukhya-dharma*) or a portion thereof must be determined by one of keen intellect. Furthermore, regarding that [function] which has the sense of "pleasing" (*ruci*), there is no pleasing through the telling of falsehoods; for what praise could there be for a reality already known to one who is not deluded? Thus it was stated by the Sage to exclude [the possibility of] figurative usage (*gauṇatā*) and the like. // 22 //

Devas are capable of assuming various bodies—possessing the power to take on multiple forms simultaneously; for in the *śrutis* (the Vedas), there exist accounts (*vṛttāntas*) that establish the greatness inherent in such deities. How then could they be incapable of being present simultaneously? Or how could they fail to be present when many rituals are being performed at once? Because of their continuity—the fact that the stream of deities is beginningless—there is no lack of constant connection.

It is as follows: even in the description of my own deity as having an impermanent form and so forth, no fault arises for the Vedas in the form of a connection with impermanent objects, because the eternity of the Vedas is established—since their eternity, characterized by the fact that their sequence has never been inverted, is proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the mention of authors at the beginning of the *kāṇḍas*—such as the *Kāṭhaka*, *Vaiśvāmitra*, *Sūkta*, and other specific portions of the Veda—the claim that sages named Kaṭha and others are the creators is restricted to their role as teachers; it refers to those very individuals who [taught] at the beginning of the Kalpa.

[The Lord's role] depends on His being the proclaimer of those respective portions [of the Vedas], and not on His being their independent creator; for even though the phonemes are produced one by one during the creation of letters, the Lord—the Sovereign of All, the Blessed Nārāyaṇa—would "teach" the Vedas—that is, the collections of words characterized by specific sequences—which were established in the sequence of the previous Kalpa, without deviating from that very sequence established in the prior Kalpa, providing instruction to Brahmā even in a subsequent Kalpa. Thus, there is no contradiction with the eternity of the Vedas. || 23 ||

If, on the grounds that they are the Lord’s own compositions, you maintain that there is no violation of the fixed order of the Vedas due to differences between *kalpas*, then the same would apply to the portions consisting of mantras; however, this is certainly not appropriate, because [mantras] are equal to *vrīhi* grains, *soma*, and so forth.
Thus, whether the sequence of injunctions (*vidhi*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is fixed or optional, such being the case, [the same principle applies].
May this school of Akṣapāda reach the pinnacle of the assembly of opposing doctrines for us. || 24 ||

Regarding the distinction between kalpas—when another kalpa has commenced, there would be a violation of the fixed order—the breach of the sequence—of the Vedas, that is, the Śrutis; this must occur through the intellect of Īśa—that is, by the volition of the Lord—if it is accepted—that is, if it is admitted. Then, it would likewise apply to the portions of the mantras—the parts constituting the Veda denoted by the words of the mantras—that there would be an acceptance of a breach of the fixed order.

Therefore—the non-acceptance of the refutation of the fixed sequential order in the case of mantras—is indeed not proper; it is certainly not consistent. (Why? Because of the similarity to rice, *soma*, and so forth—just as there is the efficacy of producing a sacrifice in the case of substances such as the grain called *vrīhi* and the creeper called *soma*, which serve as the material bases for the *gīya* and *havis* offerings, so too it is for the mantras that present the deities and substances integrated into the performance, since they are equal in their capacity to establish the rule of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to the sacrifice.

In this manner—just as there is a fixed sequence among mantras, so too is the order of injunctions (*vidhi*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) unavoidable: namely, in injunctive sentences that convey the essential nature of a sacrifice, as well as in explanatory passages that provide praise for the sacrifice. Thus, by the stated reason, if a reversal of sequence were admitted either universally with respect to the entire Veda as such, or even partially, then the fixed sequence found within the mantra portion—which constitutes a part of the Veda—would likewise be undermined.

Once this has been accepted, let this position of Akṣapāda—which is far removed from the consensus of the Vedāntins, which has gained widespread currency as the system of Gautama, and which, in accordance with the intention of us Vedāntins, may indeed enter the ranks of the assembly of rival doctrines, that is, the realm of non-Vedic tenets—what loss is there? || 24 ||

Even the hosts of gods, though existing in the present, are not perceived due to subtlety, similarity, association with a companion, the removal of a concealer, mental preoccupation, extreme proximity, extreme distance, being overwhelmed by something more powerful, non-manifestation, or impairment of the sense organs; for they likewise possess the power of invisibility (*antardhi*).
The various well-known types of supernatural powers (siddhi) also arise from birth, austerity, yoga, mantras, and medicinal herbs. || 25 ||

Even present objects—though situated not far away—may remain unperceived due to: (1) subtlety (*saukṣmya*), such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like, because of their minute dimension; (2) similarity (*tulyābhighāra*), such as oil poured into oil, because of contact with an object that is extremely similar; (3) being overpowered by a concurrent cause (*sahakāryapagama*), such as an object in darkness, because of the absence of auxiliary causes like light; (4) being concealed (*chādaka*), such as an object hidden behind a cloth or the like, because of an intervening cover; and (5) due to the inattention (*ānyaparya*) of the perceiving person.

Because the mind is distracted by other objects; because of extreme proximity—as in the case of dust and the like situated on the eyeball—due to being too near; because of extreme distance—as in the case of the configuration of stars and so forth situated in the vault of the sky—due to being too far away; because of being overpowered by something stronger—as in the case of a lamp and the like at midday—because its perception is obstructed by another object that has been grasped by a more powerful sense; and because of non-manifestation—as in the case of the rays of the eye—due to the absence of that manifestness which is necessary for direct perception.

Due to these causes—namely, from the impairment of the sense organs (such as eye diseases) and from the deficiency of the faculties—they are indeed not seen, for they are not grasped by the eye. Just so, in various instances, even those things which are perceptible by the senses are not grasped. Likewise, due to the power of invisibility (*antardhi-śakti*)—that is, because of possessing a power capable of concealing one's own true nature—even the hosts of gods (*suragaṇa*), the multitudes of deities worthy of dwelling everywhere, are not seen; they are not perceived by the eye. [The word] *janana*...

Whether by birth from herbs, or through the power of austerity, or through the power of yoga, or through the power of recited mantras, or by the potency of medicinal plants—even the various *siddhis*, the specific accomplishments conducive to invisibility (*antardhāna*) and so forth—are indeed well-known, being famous in the world, in the scriptures, and elsewhere. (Therefore, it is entirely logical that even though deities exist, they may not be perceived. || 25 ||
Summary of the Topic (*Adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*):

In the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, an objection was raised that gods and others, being free from suffering and bodiless, lack both desire and capacity; therefore, they have no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached that they do indeed possess qualification, because their possession of bodies is established through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in the sections on creation and meditation, and because desire and capacity are possible due to their being overwhelmed by the three-fold suffering.

The *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* establishes that worship has human beings as its primary qualification based on authoritative testimony; it refutes the view that gods have such qualification and is thus opposed to the *Devatānaya*. 55.
Thus ends the section concerning the deities (Devatādhikaraṇa). 7.

For the lay devotee (*upāsaka*) who possesses volition, there is the state of being one to be propitiated—the quality of being pleased through worship—and likewise, his own station, which is the very place experienced by himself, is the fruit—the goal to be attained through worship. Here, when the thought arises that "there is no eligibility for such a specific form of worship because of [the devotee's] lack of agency," it should not be so; a conclusion reached by this method is not appropriate.

Those desiring liberation—those seeking release—worship Him in two ways: as the inner self of all, who has entered within and governs all things, sentient and insentient; and as the one who bears His own body, having Himself as His own physical form. Thus, in these two modes, they perform worship.

(Therefore,) at the beginning of a *kalpa* or a *manvantara*—that is, at specific times such as the commencement of another *kalpa* or *manvantara*—even his own station (*svapada*), namely the very fruit consisting in the attainment of the status of a Vasu, having become the fruit resulting from the worship performed by the Vasus and others, returns—that is, it is indeed obtained once again—due to a specific desire (*kāmāt*) such as: "May I myself become a Vasu even in the immediately following *kalpa*. || 26 ||
The summary of the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the Madhu-vidyā:

In the *Madhv-adhikaraṇa*, having raised the objection that because things such as the Vasus cannot be objects of meditation with respect to [entities] such as honey, the Vasus and others have no qualification for the various forms of knowledge like the Madhu-vidyā, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached that they do possess such qualification.

This is because it is Brahman alone, having the Vasus and others as its body, that is the object of meditation, and because it is possible for them to attain the status of Vasus and so forth in another kalpa.

Although the possibility of [the application of] *sāmarthya* and so forth may exist in the general category of *upāsti*, the occurrence of the *madhu-vidyā* and other such rules serves as a counter-example. (56)
Thus ends the section concerning honey (Madhu-adhikaraṇa). 8.

"Having realized the Supreme Person—the Supreme Puruṣa—through reflection and having made Him the object of their intellect, let them worship Him; indeed, let them propitiate Him through the yoga of devotion. Such an assumption is neither true nor correct, because of the prohibition of everything from hearing (śravaṇa) up to meditative contemplation (nididhyāsana), as these are forbidden for those outside the three castes (atraivarṇika). || 37 ||

By those [means]—namely, by hearing the *Mahābhārata* and other such works—one ought not to be "enriched," meaning one should not become possessed of a clear understanding of their meaning. Murabhid—the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself—stated with reference to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu: "Therefore, these fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) are not to be touched by Śūdras—that is, by those other than the three higher castes; they are not at all fit to be connected with through study and so forth. Thus, even the fourteen branches of learning are not to be touched by Śūdras and others.

He spoke thus with the verse beginning, "O Yudhiṣṭhira! Therefore—due to the reason that they have not accomplished the initial knowledge of the Vedas and their meaning—the qualification for meditation (upāsādhikāra), which is the fitness for engaging in meditation for the sake of liberation, cannot exist for those of impaired intellects who possess deficiencies regarding the knowledge enjoined by the Śruti and other scriptures; it is certainly not established for them. || 28 ||

The singing [of the Lord] by Śūdras and others, as well as their exclusive devotion through their own appropriate duties—such as Dharmavyādha, Tulādhāra, and Vidura—are established as being due to the practice of previous births. By addressing Janaśruti as "O Śūdra," the speaker reveals his inner sorrow.

For his status as a Kṣatriya is indeed clearly known from signs such as the instructions of the *kṣattṛ* (the charioteer). Even for those of the fourth and other castes—those belonging to the *śūdra* class and so forth—the worship of the Supreme (*parabhajana*), which is the service of the Supreme Self, is to be performed solely through their own appropriate duties (*svārhadharma*), namely by acts such as remembering the Lord’s name, bowing to Him, and offering flowers and the like; that is, it is to be accomplished through knowledge, which is synonymous with *upāsanā* (devotional meditation).

With this intention, it was sung by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the *Bhagavad Gītā* in passages such as, "O Pārtha, by taking refuge in Me alone... (18.66). Furthermore, Dharmavyādha, Tulādhṛk, and Vidura—these well-known figures from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts who knew the true meaning of the Vedas—were indeed possessed of knowledge attained through the practice of meditation performed in previous lives when they were qualified for the Vedas; it was not by means of [knowledge] belonging to their current birth.

The speaker, Raikva—who was engaged in giving instruction based on dependence upon others—addressed the Kṣatriya named Jānaśruti with the word "Śūdra," calling out to him as "Śūdra," thereby manifesting—that is, making clear—the sorrow of this disciple, Jānaśruti, which arose from his failure to obtain the knowledge of Brahman.

For indeed, his—Jānaśruti’s—status as a Kṣatriya, that is, his birth into the Kṣatriya caste, is clearly and unmistakably known through the indicative marks such as the command to a Kṣattṛ and others mentioned in close connection with him, namely, the sending of a Sūta for the purpose of searching for Raikva. It is certainly well-established! || 29 ||

"But a Śūdra cannot be entitled to knowledge merely because he possesses the capacity and the desire for it"— it is for the purpose of refuting such a doubt that the *apaśūdra-naya* (the principle concerning those other than Śūdras) arises. (57)
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa).

It assumes the designations of gods, humans, and so forth, as well as the corresponding forms; subsequently, when the state of Brahman—the condition of being Brahman occurring after liberation—is attained, it "abandons," meaning it relinquishes both the designations and the forms.

Therefore, [the claim] that "the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the referent of the word 'ether' (*ākāśa*) here" is improper—such a doubt is unjustified. For this very one previously mentioned as "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) in the preceding sentence is indeed the object to be attained; for the act of attaining (*abhisambhavana*), expressed by the verb "I shall attain," has as its objective precisely that which is for the purpose of becoming Brahman (*brahmatva*). Furthermore, it is taken up again by the statement "Ether, verily... (*ākāśo ha vai*); [here] *brahmatva* refers to the natural state of being Brahman residing in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Dharma (that which is expressed by the term "Brahmaloka") is not intended to consist of adventitious attributes or states; rather, it is indeed intrinsic. For even in the Vedic texts—within the scriptural passages—it is simultaneous, occurring at the same time, as both knowledge and ignorance, and so forth.

— "Omniscience and sovereignty reside in Brahman, while ignorance and lack of sovereignty reside in the individual soul (jīva). Thus, the attributes of the jīva and Brahman are distinct; even though described separately according to their unique characteristics, they remain differentiated. (Therefore, this sentence refers exclusively to the Supreme Self. || 30 ||
Summary of the Meaning of the Section.

In the section concerning designations such as "being something else" (arthāntaratva), the following doubt was raised: in the passage beginning with "Ākāśa, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form," the word "Ākāśa" refers to the liberated soul, because in the subsequent passage, "like a horse its hairs," the liberated soul is the subject under discussion. Having raised this objection, the established conclusion (siddhānta) was reached as follows: because the quality of being the bringer-forth of name and form is heard in scripture to be characteristic of the Supreme Self alone, and because the Supreme Self is also the immediate subject of discussion in the phrase "I shall attain the world of Brahman," the Ākāśa is the Supreme Self.

Thus, through a continuous sequence of related topics, this *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* has treated the four sections; therein, the *Arthāntaranyāsa* refuted the objection raised regarding the term "burning."
Thus ends the section concerning designations such as "being a different entity" (arthāntaratva), etc. [Section 10].

The state of being unafflicted (*akliṣṭabhāva*) consists in not being a locus for the afflictions produced by the connection between the body and its constituent channels, and in having the nature of bliss (*sukharūpatā*), which is the nature of supreme, unconditional bliss (*nirupadhi-mahānanda*). The state of being a ruler (*praśāsitṛtva*) consists in being the controller of the entire universe. The state of being worthy of refuge (*śrayaṇīyatā*) consists in being the object of meditation upon the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) with its three measures (*trimātra*). The state of having superior qualities (*guṇottaratva*)—[as stated because even one's own qualities are to be meditated upon as being like oneself]—consists in being the locus of auspicious qualities that are themselves objects of meditation. The state of being beyond reproach (*ajugupsatā*) consists in having the size of a thumb, which is dependent upon the resolve to bestow grace upon those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

The majesty residing in the Supreme Self—consisting of His being beyond the need for a presiding deity, His being free from the necessity of a supervisor, His capacity to sustain the names and forms created by Himself among both sentient and insentient beings, and His role as their ultimate guide—is thus set forth and correctly elucidated in this third quarter (pāda).
The nature of the self of both Pradhāna and Jīva, in their individual and collective aspects, has been described in sequence;
furthermore, in the third [chapter], its status as the teaching is also stated.

Regarding the individual and collective forms of both *pradhāna* and *jīva*—namely, the individual non-sentient (*acid-vyaṣṭi*) and the collective non-sentient (*acid-samaṣṭi*), as well as the individual sentient (*cid-vyaṣṭi*) and the collective sentient (*cit-samaṣṭi*)—their "selfhood" (*ātmatā*), which consists in the Supreme Self’s pervasion of these and His governance over them, has been stated respectively in the first and second sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, in the third section—that is, in the third *adhikaraṇa*—His "sovereignty" (*śāsanatā*), that is, His nature as the Ruler (*śāsitṛtva*), is also stated and established in addition to the aforementioned selfhood. ||40||

But by means of the fourth and fifth [sūtras], its status as the Self is established both in its essential nature and through its attributes for the purpose of being the object of meditation; such is the purpose of [establishing] its status as the Self. (42)

By means of the fourth and fifth sections—that is, by the fourth and fifth topics—both in terms of its essential nature and its attributes: both as the pure nature of Brahman and likewise through the mediation of its auspicious qualities—for the purpose of being worshipped, that is, for the sake of establishing it as the object of meditation—the state of being the Self (ātmatva), meaning the Supreme Self’s existence as the inner pervader everywhere, is thus established as the purpose of ātmatva; in this way, the fruit residing in the Supreme Self as the Self is defined. ||41||

"Even here, because of being the Lord (Īśa) in each respective relationship, He does not feel aversion"—according to this principle, it was stated by the Sixth [Lord] for the sake of establishing the nature of the Self. 42.

"In connection with each of those"—that is, in relation to the world consisting of sentient and insentient beings that have assumed various forms such as gods and so forth, which are connected to the Supreme Self—even though it is "to be rejected," meaning loathsome—because of His lordship, because the Supreme Self is the Lord of all, He does not feel loathing; the Supreme Self does not incur any sense of disgust. This is the point to be established. For the sake of establishing the nature of the Self—that is, to obtain the logical justification for the "Self" as described in relation to the Supreme Self—it has been explained, made clear, by means of the sixth principle—the sixth section (adhikaraṇa). ||42||

In the middle [section], as an incidental discussion, the eligibility for the Vidyā-mantra of the Śūdras and the absence thereof regarding the two specific types of Devadevas was established; furthermore, from the seventh [chapter] onwards, their status as lords (Īśitṛtva) has been confirmed by virtue of their capacity as knowers (Nirvoddhṛtva). || 43 ||

By way of a relevant digression from the sixth section—that is, by way of a connection in the form of a contextual extension—it has been established that both gods and specific classes of gods possess the qualification for knowledge (*vidyādhikāra*), in the sense that their eligibility for engaging in knowledge (*vidyāpravṛttiyogyatā*) is appropriately demonstrated as being based on factors such as desire and capability. Furthermore, it has been established that for *śūdras*—those other than the three higher castes—there is an absence of such qualification.

From the seventh—that is, from the seventh section—by taking the capacity to sustain name and form (*nāmarūpanirvāhakatva*) as the reason, the Lordship (*īśitṛtva*) of the Supreme Self, meaning His status as the controller of all, has been established and rendered free from doubt. || 43 ||
Thus, by these three quarters, Brahman has been established as the cause;
by the fourth [quarter], it is further demonstrated that causality belongs to Him alone. (44)

In the manner thus described, by means of the first, second, and third quarters (pādas), it has been established that Brahman is the cause—that is, it has been argued that Brahman is the cause of the universe. From the fourth—the *turīya* quarter—it is demonstrated—that is, properly established through reasoning—that this causality, namely the aforementioned status of being the cause of the universe, belongs to that alone; i.e., to Brahman alone, and not to anything else. || 44 ||
The *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*:

The Soul of the Universe, infinite in magnitude, the ordainer and sustainer, whose very nature is the object of enjoyment for the liberated; who, as the ruler of all, dwells within the heart in a minute state yet is the support of His own vast self; He is the one to be worshipped by the gods beginning with Vasu, and is to be served by them as their own Self.

The Lord, the sole creator of names and forms, who is unfit for worship by Śūdras and others, has been understood here as the Soul of the Universe—the support of the world consisting of the earth, the intermediate space, and the celestial realm; one whose abundance is infinite, whose nature consists of limitless sovereignty and bliss; the ordainer and sustainer, acting as the substratum of all effects through His governance; and whose very essence is the object of enjoyment for those liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra, according to the teaching: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1) || 32 ||

In the manner thus stated, [the Self] has the sole nature of being an object of enjoyment; it is the "all" within the small substratum—meaning the entire phenomenal world exists within its own small substratum, which is designated by the word *dahara* (the small) for the purpose of meditation; it is the controller of all through its state of being limited by the heart—meaning that, by resorting to the state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the size of a thumb, which is measured by the small location called the heart, it is the agent who governs the entire universe; and it is the object of worship for gods and others—[namely] gods, asuras, rakshasas, gandharvas, kinnaras...

He is worthy of worship even by those born of divine origins such as the Rādīs; He is to be served as His own self by the gods headed by the Vasus—meaning that even by specific deities who have attained the status of the Vasus and others, He is the object of worship as their very body. Yet, He is unfit for worship by Śūdras and others—by people other than the three twice-born classes who are not authorized for Vedic study—and He cannot be worshipped according to the method prescribed in the Śrutis by those [others]. He is the sole creator of names and forms.

The Lord, the Supreme Person, the Sovereign of all, who is the primary bestower of names and forms to the created universe consisting of consciousness and matter—He has been understood here, in this third quarter, made the object of knowledge as is appropriate. || 32 ||
This *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* consists of four pentads and ten topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*); thus, the third quarter of the first chapter is well-integrated. (59)
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.

The "body" (śarīra) itself—that which is called the body—is the very object to be controlled, namely the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is denoted by the word "Unmanifest" as recited in the Śruti. The "Person" (puruṣa)—the referent of the term *puruṣa* established by the Śruti as being higher than all else—is this Supreme Person (*paraḥ pūruṣaḥ*). He is none other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is celebrated in all the Vedāntas as being higher than the highest; he is not the twenty-fifth principle, the individual soul (*jīva*), as asserted by the Sāṅkhya. || 45 ||

In the fourth quarter (pāda), the collection of statements already determined as referring to the Supreme (Brahman) is further elucidated through those words which follow the shadow of various clear marks (liṅgas) such as the individual soul (jīva). Therein, by means of six and two principles (nyāyas), he pacifies the doubts arising from Sāṅkhya and Yoga. Some have stated that this eighth section, containing the aforementioned conclusion, is called the "Ghāghaṭṭa. || 1 ||

The clear indicators of the individual soul (*jīva*): a collection of scriptural passages that explicitly set forth unique attributes of the *jīva* and so forth, which—after being determined through inquiry to have the Supreme Self as their intended meaning—are resolved as referring to the Supreme Being.
However, in the fourth chapter (*pāda*), [those passages] that follow the shadow of various [systems], such as Sāṅkhya and others—

In the third quarter (pāda), [the meaning] is established with certainty. However, in the fourth quarter, the author of the Sūtras elucidates—meaning he makes manifest through reasoning—that speech appearing to have a meaning similar to the statements found in the Tantras is actually a Vedānta statement; that is to say, it has the intention of propounding the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa).

Therein—within the collection of topics contained in the fourth quarter (pāda)—by means of the first six topics known as *ānumānika*, *camasa-saṅkhyopasaṅgraha*, *kāraṇatva*, *jagadvācitva*, and *vākyānvaya*, [the author] dispels the doubt arising from Sāṃkhya—the delusion instilled by the study of the Sāṃkhya system—and by means of the two subsequent topics known as *prakṛti* and *sarvavyākhyāna*, [he dispels] the doubt arising from Yoga.

And he pacifies—that is, removes—the delusive cognition produced by the practice of Yoga philosophy; having cast that aside, he establishes the person in a mind that is studying Vedānta. In this manner—by this method—the two *ghaṭṭau* (sections) become properly joined (*jāghaṭṭaḥ*). Some—certain other teachers, however—[place] the eighth, which is the final [section] of all the commentaries...

The *karaṇa* (the means of proof) is the stated conclusion (*nigamana*); it is that which culminates in the summary of all the logical principles (*nyāya*) established in the *Samanvaya-adhyāya*. Thus they spoke—that is, they demonstrated. || 1 ||

By two [verses], the Pradhāna of the Kapila doctrine is to be rejected; then by one [verse], the number mentioned by others; and by the fourth [verse], the limit of the theory of the Unmanifest (avyākṛta) is established through the function of the door. Furthermore, the pure and impure Jīvas are to be excluded immediately thereafter from the pair of substrata; the remainder of this eighth quarter of the chapter consists of the refutation of the Īśvara taught in other systems.
In this— having begun to explain— the group of eight topics (adhikaraṇas) contained within the eight quarters of the fourth chapter,
by means of the first two topics, which concern inference and the name "camasa," the doctrine of Kapila— Kapila's...

The "Pradhāna" intended by the great seer [Kapila]—that is, the Pradhāna which is synonymous with *mūlaprakṛti* and *avara*, and which is non-Brahman in nature—is to be logically determined as not being the referent of the word *avyakta* occurring in the Śruti, and likewise as not being denotable by the word *ajā*.

Now, as for the first [view]: following that, from the single section named "Inclusion of Number" (*saṅkhyopasaṅgraha*), the enumeration of principles (tattvas) maintained by the followers of Kapila—which rests at exactly twenty-five and is stated elsewhere—must be rejected through reasoning by means of the fourth section concerning causality. Furthermore, even the term "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) occurring in the Śruti must be understood through its secondary function (*dvāravṛtti*) as a designation for Brahman in its aspect as *prakṛti*, by the all-pervading Lord.

The Supreme Person, who possesses all-pervasive extension, is established as the "limit"—meaning He is established as the ultimate terminus of the power of words—and this is confirmed through reasoning. Following that, in the pair of subsequent chapters—namely those titled "The World as the Referent" (*jagadvācitva*) and "Syntactic Connection" (*vākyānvaya*)—the two types of conscious beings, both pure and impure, namely the one liberated from the bondage of karma and the one possessing the bondage of karma, must be excluded from the suspicion that they are the Supreme Reality (as appropriate to each case).

These two are to be set aside. As for the remainder—the remaining section concerning the exposition of all [other systems]—it is composed for the purpose of refuting the Lord (Īśvara) as described in other philosophical systems (*tantrāntara*), and for determining that the nature of the Lord established in Patañjali’s *Yoga-darśana* is not in conformity with the Vedas (*śruti*). || 2 ||

It is incorrect to say that the *Vallī* [of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad], having analyzed the manifest (the intellect and so forth) as inferior, insentient, and then [describing] the Puruṣa as the ultimate goal, sets forth the system taught in the supreme [text] of the Kaṭhas; for it describes the primary sequence of the various objects to be mastered as proclaimed in numerous passages therein.
Viṣṇu is described here as the peaceful self, the supreme Puruṣa, and he is made known through recognition.

The *Vallī* of the Kaṭhas—referring to that specific portion designated by the word "Vallī" which is to be studied by those of the Yajurveda school known as the Kaṭhas—beginning with the senses (the term *akṣa* being a synonym for the organs), and extending up to the Unmanifest (the term *avyakta* being a synonym for *pradhāna*), [describes] the category of insentient reality (*jaḍa*, i.e., that which is other than consciousness); then, following that, having distinguished—that is, having analyzed and shown—the Puruṣa, the reality denoted by the term "Puruṣa," who is the ultimate limit of all principles.

The suspicion that [the author] "speaks"—that is, describes—the system (prakriyā), namely the method of enumerating the principles (tattvasaṅkhyānapaddhati) studied in the Sāṅkhya doctrine (sāṅkhyamatābhyasta), as something "recited by the supreme one" (paramatapaṭhitām), is untenable.

There is no contradiction, because the various preceding and succeeding statements found in the *Kaṭhavallī*—the numerous utterances therein—demonstrate precisely the sequential relationship (*pūrvāparībhāva*) among the various primary subjects to be mastered. Here, in the statement from the *Kaṭhavallī*, the "Supreme Person" (*paraḥ puruṣaḥ*)—the meaning expressed by the phrase "the Supreme Person"—is Viṣṇu, who is called by that name because He is Himself peaceful (*śānta*) and because He is the means for the peace of all selves (*ātman*).

It is the Blessed One alone; not merely a conscious being, but he is also recognized—by means of scripture, he is made the object of recognition through the realization "this is that very one. || 3 ||

For objects are not the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the senses, nor is the mind intended to be their cause; nor does the intellect (*buddhi*) produce this [mind], nor is the Great One (*mahat*) born from the Great One known as the intellect. Greatness is appropriate for the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and "selfhood" (*ātmatā*) would not exist in the Great One. By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the term "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers here to the body; thus, the system of Kapila is not recognized here. || 4 ||

Objects (*arthāḥ*) are sound and the rest, which are the spheres of the senses; and the senses (*indriyāṇām*) are the auditory organs and so forth, which grasp sound and the rest. It is certainly not accepted [in our view] that *prakṛti* (according to the Sāṅkhya doctrine) is their cause. Furthermore, the mind (*manaḥ*)—the internal organ—is not desired as the cause of these senses and objects; it is not at all intended to be their causal source.

And that object denoted by the word "intellect" (*buddhi*)—this entity in the form of the mind—does not produce, nor does it generate, anything; nor indeed does the object known as the "Great One" (*mahat*), which is synonymous with "intellect" (*buddhi*), arise—that is, it is certainly not produced! It is logical for the enjoyer to possess greatness: for the individual soul (*jīva*), who appropriates insentient principles for its own enjoyment, to have greatness in relation to them; this is consistent with worldly observation.

Furthermore, there can be no selfhood in the Great Principle (*mahat*), for even in the insentient *mahat-tattva*, being denotable by the term "Self" is not at all appropriate. By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*): among those [entities] mentioned in the mantra "He made the Self the rider of the chariot," all others have been specified in the subsequent mantra "Higher than the senses are the objects"; therefore, because it remains as the only one left over, the mention of the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*)—in the phrase "Higher than the Great is the Unmanifest"—refers to the body, which has been metaphorically described as a chariot in the passage "But the body is indeed the chariot."

In the human practitioner, for the sake of accomplishment, [the Self] exists as the awakener within the body itself, which is to be brought under complete control. Therefore, for this reason stated above, in this mantra—"The objects are indeed higher than the senses"—it is not the case that Kapila [is being referred to]; rather, the recognition—namely, the recollection of the process of creation and so forth as taught by him through the thought "these very things are those presented in the *Kapila-tantra*"—is by no means appropriate. || 4 ||
In the fourth quarter of the first chapter of the *Nayasangati-mālikā*, he composed the "Eightfold Logic" (*nītyaṣṭaka*).

Therein, by means of six principles (*naya*), he refuted the Sāṅkhyas, and by two, the followers of Yoga. The distinction from the liberated state mentioned previously at the end of the [third] quarter is not tenable; for the objection regarding the opponent's [view] is indeed addressed in the section concerning inference (*ānumānika*). Thus ends the section on the inferential (*ānumānikādhikaraṇa*).
The Section on the Chamasas (Camasādhikaraṇam) || 1.4.2 || A Compendium of the Essential Principles of the Śārīraka:

In the statement "the Unborn" (*ajā*), that which is called *pradhāna* in the [Sāṅkhya] system is spoken of because of its independence and its role as the cause of the creation of the entire world. However, this is certainly not the case here; for in this context, only the act of creating is mentioned, "due to the absence of any specific distinction," whereas the Śruti indeed speaks of specific distinctions. || 46 ||

Regarding this statement, "the unborn" (*ajā*)—in the sentence found in both the *Taittirīya* and *Śvetāśvatara* [Upaniṣads], which have slightly different word orders—"the unborn" (*ajā*), as expressed by that term, refers to the *pradhāna* mentioned in the Tantras; that is, the entity in the form of the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), synonymous with *pradhāna* as taught in the Sāṅkhya system, because of its independence—that is, by relying on its own sovereignty, it effects the creation of the entire world—the production of the whole universe, [and] manifold offspring...

Because of such an instruction as "producing many offspring" and "creating," this formulation of doubt is by no means appropriate. For in this very statement that has been uttered, what is being expressed—what is being propounded—is merely the act of creating (*sṛjati*), which is simply the performance of creation.

But there is no independence [of the individual soul], because there is no such distinction—since there is no mention in the Śruti of any portion that would indicate autonomy and so forth. Therefore, the Śruti—in the mantra immediately following this one, namely the Vedic voice of the Upaniṣads such as "The waters are seated in purity" and "Two birds..."—speaks of the distinction: that everything, both sentient and insentient, is dependent upon the Supreme Self and is a manifestation of the Supreme Self; indeed, it makes this very point clear. || 46 ||

In a certain specific Upaniṣadic passage—the statement "the one unborn [female], red, white, and black"—it is indicated that the "unborn" (ajā), denoted by the word *ajā*, possesses the quality of being the progenitor of all (*nikhilajanakatā*), that is, the creatorship of everything; for this is shown by the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* (in the forms *janayantīm* and *sṛjamānām*), which—when accompanied by words conveying dependence on another—indicate that her agency consists in independence (*svātantryeṇa*), meaning she is not subject to any other. Thus: "producing many offspring" (*bahrīṃ prajāṃ janayantīm*) and likewise "creating many offspring" (*bahvīḥ prajāḥ sṛjamānām*).

He is awakened! The unborn one is bound—the eternal individual soul (jīva) subject to karma; he lies there, upon the object denoted by the word "unborn" (ajāpada), which is to be awakened, and remains fast asleep (with intense affection, like a calf with its mother).

If there is such a doubt as follows: "There is another, unborn (*aja*), eternal *jīva* distinct from that [Prakṛti]; he abandons—leaves behind, casts away—this very Prakṛti, who is designated by the word 'unborn' (*ajā'), who has had her enjoyments experienced (meaning she possesses portions of objects of enjoyment tasted by him), and whom he himself had resorted to with affection"—since it is described thus, this [entity] denoted by the word 'unborn' is indeed the Root-Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) propounded in the Tantras of Sāṅkhya; there is no doubt about this. [The response: If such a suspicion is raised;

This is not improper, because the mere statement of "not being born" (ajātvamātra) establishes only the absence of origination without contradicting dependence on another; for the lack of independence is well-known—since among insentient entities, the absence of self-initiated activity independent of others is observed in the world, there is no need to state it separately. Furthermore, even the use of the root *sṛj* (in the term *asṛjat*) implies being impelled by another—that is, the status of an instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛtva*) consisting of agency dependent on another, or the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*).

That which is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should not be obstructed—that is, it cannot be sublated at all. (Therefore, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), whose essence is Brahman, is itself the cause of creation, possessing activity dependent upon the volition of Brahman. || 5 ||

The summary of the meaning of the *adhikaraṇa* in the *Camasādhikaraṇa*: Having raised the objection that in the passage beginning with "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*) and including "creating offspring" (*prajāḥ sṛjamānām*), since independence in creation and so forth is perceived, the word "unborn" (*ajā*) denotes *prakṛti*, which is not of the nature of Brahman; [the following is established].

It has been stated that those [entities] which do not have Brahman as their essence are not the subject here, because there is no specific reason for their inclusion; rather, since the statement from another Vedic branch, "smaller than the small," reveals that the Unborn (Ajā) has Brahman as its essence, it is the primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of Brahman, that is denoted by the word "Unborn."
The Section on the Comprehension of Numbers (Saṅkhyopasaṅgrahādhikaraṇa) || 1.4.3 ||
In the *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha*,

regarding the statement "in which the five peoples, the five [elements], and the sky," because the enumeration of numbers is clearly grasped therein, this counting according to the *tantra* (system) does not indeed prevail; for it exists as the support of Brahman, due to its preeminent manifestation, and by virtue of being a designation (*saṃjñātva*).
And because there are seven when the five sense organs, beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa), are added, they are called the "Seven Sages" (saptarṣayaḥ). ||47||

In the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad—"In which the five groups of five and the ether are established"—the number is clearly indicated by the inclusion of the term "five times five," which unambiguously conveys the number twenty-five, consisting of five multiplied by five; thus, the calculation according to the system [of the text] shows that the Śruti of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka follows precisely the method of enumerating the principles (tattvas) as accepted by the followers of Kapila.

It is not otherwise—such is the doubt; for [the aggregate] does not breathe, nor indeed does it possess its own self-nature. This is because the pentad of organs beginning with breath—the pentad of organs starting with the sense of touch, which is nourished by the air characterized as "breath"—exists with Brahman as its support. This is shown by the description of its being well-established by relying on Brahman, which is denoted by the word "that" (*yat*) in the phrase "in which it is established," and by the manifestation of its excellence in the phrase "the light of lights."

Furthermore, because it is of the nature of light—the ultimate limit of the excellence of the internal light that manifests through the perfection of the preceding mantras—and also because of its status as a technical name (*saṃjñātva*), namely, because the term "pañcajana" functions as a designator for the five sense organs either through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or through etymological-figurative usage (*yogarūḍhi*).

One should not raise the objection: "When it ought to be said 'pañcajanāḥ,' why is it 'pañca pañca'? Just as in the case of the expression 'saptarṣayaḥ' (the seven seers), where the word 'sapta' appears again even though it was already present in the compound 'saptarṣayaḥ'—this repetition being for the purpose of making known the number seven with respect to the objects designated by the name 'saptarṣayaḥ'—so too, the word 'pañca' is used here for the purpose of making known the number five with respect to the sense organs designated by the name 'pañcajanaḥ'. ||47||

In the mantra beginning with "yasmin pañca" — namely, in this mantra "yasmin pañca pañcajanā ākāśaśca pratiṣṭhitaḥ" — the number twenty-five, consisting of twenty plus five (pañca-yuktā viṃśatiḥ), which is reckoned by others and accepted by the Sāṅkhyas, pertaining to the twenty-five principles beginning with *prakṛti*, is stated (*proktā*) without doubt in this [Vedic] passage.

But as for what was stated regarding the locative case: [if it is objected that] "that which is denoted by the word *yasmim* ending in the locative case" refers to an object understood through scripture (*śruti*) that is "not dependent on anything else"—meaning it is not accepted as being subordinate to the Supreme Self as the Upaniṣads maintain—and that this "multitude of persons" (*puruṣagaṇaḥ*) is simply the collection of individual souls (*jīva*) designated as *puruṣa* by the Sāṃkhyas; (to this doubt) we reply: "Not so"—such a doubt must indeed be refuted, because [the term refers to] "of the ether"—that is, to the one called ether, which is included within the twenty-five principles established by the Sāṃkhyas.

Because the reality (*tattva*) is mentioned separately by its own name, the word "space" (*ākāśa*), it is stated as being distinct from the number twenty-five; and likewise, because of the non-sublation of the locative case-power (*saptamī-śakti*)—even while adhering to the non-sublation of the power of the locative case residing in the word "in which," which conveys the state of being the substratum of all—in this context, the present sentence, that which is known as the "substratum of all" (*sarvāśraya*), renowned in other Vedic texts (*śruti*) as the support of everything, [is established] through its nature as Brahman and so forth.

Distinguished by attributes such as being Brahman without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), the Twenty-sixth is indeed the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who transcends the Twenty-fifth; He is restated—by the word *yat* (which has the character of a restatement referring to what was previously known)—and is made known by the Śruti as the Sustainer. || 6 ||

This compound here in the Veda is based on a designation (*saṃjñopādhi*); according to the rule of the "Seven Sages" (*saptarṣi*), this group of five known as the organs of cognition—beginning with breath (*prāṇa*) and ending with the mind (*manas*)—is fixed by the context. This [set] is understood from another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*) by the word "light" (*jyotis*). Any deficiency in the number should be supplied: the word "speech" (*vāk*) denotes the sense of smell, the word "taste" (*rasanā*) denotes the tongue, and the word "breath" (*prāṇa*) signifies the skin.

In this context, regarding the Vedic statement cited here—"In whom the five *pañcajanāḥ* [dwell]"—this compound consisting of the word "pañcajana" is a technical name (*saṃjñopādhi*), functioning as a specific designation based on its conventional usage, similar to the expression "the seven *saptarṣayaḥ* are seven. By virtue of its collective power (*samudāyaśakti*), it conveys a specific meaning according to the rule: "Directional words and numerals form compounds when they constitute a technical name" (*diksaṅkhye saṃjñāyām*).

But it is not a collective dvandva compound meaning "an aggregate of five persons. That [term] "five persons" (pañcajanāḥ) is to be understood here as "five," restricted by the context—clearly established in this context as neither fewer nor more than five—consisting of breath and so forth ending with the mind (*manas*), namely: breath, eye, ear, food, and mind; that is, the pentad known as the organs of cognition (*dhīndriya*), a group of things characterized by the number five.

This pentad of the organs of knowledge has been described by the word "light" (*jyotis*)—specifically by the term "of lights" (*jyotiṣām*), which denotes the light that serves as the ultimate limit for the excellence of the supreme light, as known from another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*), namely the Kāṇva recension. As for the objection regarding the omission [of the word "food"]—namely, that the reading "the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the mind of those who know the mind" lacks the word "food"—it is to be understood that what is not stated here may be taken from elsewhere, according to the principle: "What is not mentioned [in one place] is to be supplied from another."

By logical necessity, the term *anna*—the word "food" occurring in the phrase "the food of food"—should be understood by supplying the required additional parts; it expresses both the sense of smell and the sense of taste—that is, the pair of organs known as the nose and the tongue—simultaneously, conveying them through a single function. As for the word *prāṇa*, which was stated in the phrase "the life-breath of the life-breath," it signifies the skin; because it is nourished by the air characterized as *prāṇa*, the word *prāṇa* serves to indicate the tactile organ. || 7 ||

The summary of the meaning of the section concerning the inclusion of the number (*saṃkhyopasaṅgrahādhikaraṇa*) is as follows: Regarding the statement, "In whom the five groups of five (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*)," one might raise the objection that because the term *pañcajana* is qualified by the word "five," twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are understood; thus, this sentence must be a presentation of the principles established in the Tantras. Having raised this doubt, it is stated that since the "five groups" (*pañcajana*), who are understood to have Brahman as their substratum through the phrase "in whom... they are established" (*yasmin... pratiṣṭhitāḥ*), are distinct from the principles established in the Tantras, this sentence does not present the principles established in the Tantras.

Because there is no connection with the method [of enumeration] and because of the absence of another statement, and because it would contradict the enumeration of the principles (*tattva*), this is a counter-example arising from doubt regarding the view that accepts the number [of categories]. Thus ends the section on the "Inclusion of Number" (3).

Furthermore, the objection that—because of the various statements of causal words (i.e., sentences denoting causes), which consist of diverse word-sequences intended to convey a cause, and because of such expressions as "Brahman" being applied to some things—it is impossible to reach a definitive conclusion regarding any single object, namely that "this alone is the cause and not another"—such a doubt is certainly not tenable. It cannot possibly be correct.

For this reason—from whatever cause—in all cases, even in causal statements composed of various terms such as "existent" and "non-existent," it is determined that the Supreme alone is the subject to be followed and connected as the qualificand; for He is drawn upward by indicators such as *liṅga*, *prakaraṇa*, and *guṇa*—namely, by attributes pervaded by supremacy through the context (*prakaraṇa*) related to the Supreme Self, and likewise by those qualities known from other scriptural passages (*śruti*) as residing in the Supreme Self alone. || 48 ||

In the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*: If it be argued that the scriptural declarations regarding the material cause of the universe—namely, the descriptions of it as "being" (*sat*), "non-being" (*asat*), and the "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*)—apply to the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) mentioned by the opponent [of Vedānta], and therefore all other [terms] should be interpreted as referring to that [Pradhāna] here, we say: No. For where terms such as "being" and so forth are seen, and where the context makes them known [to refer to Brahman], there the mark of omniscience and the rest is present; and since the desire "May I be" is not perceived [in the Pradhāna], the word "Self" (*ātman*) and others, which are firmly established here, remain uncontradicted. (Verse 8)

Existing in various Śrutis, expressing the material cause of the universe—that is, conveying the meaning that [Brahman] is the causal substance of the world—and containing statements regarding the existent, the non-existent, and the unmanifest—namely, the statement of the "existent" in "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed existent," the statement of the "non-existent" in "This was indeed non-existent," and the statement of the "unmanifest" in "That became differentiated; it was unmanifest"—all these fit the Unmanifest, for they truly cohere with the Pradhāna as taught by others, the Sāṅkhyas; therefore, because it is thus determined.

If it is argued that "all else"—meaning everything other than what was stated, such as all speech regarding the Self and so forth—is to be applied here to the primary subject alone by resorting to a figurative sense (*gauṇa-vṛtti*)—such a suspicion is not correct. For in whatever scriptural passage (*śrutivākya*) non-existence and so forth are observed—where non-existence, existence, or the unmanifested state (*avyākṛtatva*) of the cause of the world is understood—in such a context, that which is known from the context (*prakaraṇavidita*), namely omniscience and the rest [is the intended meaning].

The word ‘all-knowing’ (*vipaścit*), understood from the term ‘all-knowingness’ and so forth, which has a common substratum with non-consciousness; the mark consisting of volition, which is unique to conscious beings and recited in the Śruti as ‘May I be many’; and that which is indicated by words such as ‘non-existent’ (*asat*)—which makes known the Supreme Self—being stable because it cannot be construed otherwise and thus not established otherwise: for these reasons, in this sentence which conveys the meaning of the cause of the world, the word ‘Self’ (*ātman*) and so forth [refers to the Supreme Self].
The word [Brahman], whose nature consists of Ātman, Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, and so forth, is to be applied by its primary, uncontradicted sense alone. || 8 ||

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" refers merely to the state of dissolution; it does not mean that "nothing at all" existed, because [the scripture] subsequently negates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the like. The state of everything being unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) is due to the absence of differentiation; its essence is the aggregate of those various substances in such a state. Thus, it is here designated by expressions such as "existent," "non-existent," and "unmanifest. (9)

Regarding the statement "In the beginning, this was..."—by the scriptural passage "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*), it is merely described that [the world] was in a state of dissolution—that is, it had simply attained a specific condition known as *pralaya* (dissolution); it is not said that [anything] did not exist at all.

Furthermore, even the passage from the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*—namely, "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; it was rootless and without support"—is intended to convey dissolution (*vilaya*), meaning its purport concerns the state of the world during the period of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). This is because it negates both the "voidness" (*śūnyatā*) and so forth accepted by the Buddhists (the doctrine of universal void), as well as the "annihilation without residue" (*niranvayavināśa*) accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, thereby demonstrating through the scriptural texts on dissolution that those views are untenable. Moreover, it establishes the "unmanifested state" (*avyākṛtatva*) of everything—that is, the state of being denoted by the term "unmanifested" (*avyākṛta*).

Because of the absence of differentiation—that is, due to the non-existence of the division of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) prior to creation—for that reason, "here"—in the various causal statements found in the Śruti—"that which is denoted by the expressions 'Being,' 'Non-being,' 'the Undifferentiated,' and so forth," namely the object to be conveyed by such words, is the Supreme Self alone, existing in such a state, who is the controller of the specific conscious and unconscious substances situated in those conditions characterized by the non-differentiation of subtle and gross name-and-form. || 9 ||

Section 1.4.5: The Topic of the World Being the Object of Speech (*jagadvācitvādhikaraṇam*). *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpa-saṃgraha*: One might object that the person referred to here as "the agent" and "whose action [it is]" is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), because he possesses agency, because he possesses objects of action, and because his state as an enjoyer is perceived through his innate and inherent qualities. Such a doubt should not even be raised; for in this context, the word "action" (*karman*) denotes the world.
The mention of "living being" (jīva) here for the purpose of [showing] the vision [of Brahman] is because Brahman is the substratum of deep sleep. || 49 ||

The "Person" (puruṣa) who is the agent—referred to in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad as one to be known, in the words, "O Bālāka, that person who is the maker of these persons, or he whose work this is, is to be known"—is here the transmigrating individual soul (jīva) alone; specifically, it is the twenty-fifth principle (pañcaviṃśaka) adopted by the Sāṅkhya system, and not the twenty-sixth principle taught in the Upaniṣads.

Because of agency—since agency produced by contact with *prakṛti* is possible only in the individual soul (*jīva*); because of the possession of karma—since merit and demerit, consisting of good and evil actions, reside in the individual soul alone; because of the perception of the state of being an enjoyer through innate, inherent qualities—since the experience of being an enjoyer of pleasure, pain, and so forth is established by the universal experience of all as residing in the individual soul alone, it is most appropriately consistent that the creatorship of the world for the sake of one's own enjoyment belongs to that very soul.

Thus, one should not entertain such a doubt—it is not appropriate to raise an objection in the manner stated; for in this statement—the previously mentioned Kauṣītaki passage—the object denoted by the word *karman*—the reality conveyed by the term *karman* through its etymological derivation as "that which is done" (*kriyate iti karma*)—is none other than the universe (*jagat*), the entire world being created.

But the karma consisting of merit and demerit pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*) is not [the subject here]; rather, in this context, the mention of both "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) and "individual soul" (*jīva*)—as in "Now, in this very vital breath he becomes one-fold" for the vital breath, and "In this way this conscious self enjoys through these its own selves" for the individual soul—is for the purpose of observation—that is, for the sake of completing the meditation under discussion (for the purpose of familiarizing oneself with the essential natures of the object of meditation and the meditator by distinguishing them from one another)—because [the vital breath] is the locus of deep sleep.
The object that serves as the locus for the individual soul (jīva) upon reaching the state of deep sleep is the Supreme Brahman itself, known as Brahma or Prājña. || 49 ||
In the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, it is stated: "He who is to be known as the one whose work this is"—from such a statement, there is the perception that [the Self] is subject to karma;

thus, the claim that He alone is the agent of men through the transformation of His own creation is refuted by the introduction [of the argument]. For Ajātaśatru, who was instructing Bālāki—who did not know the inner reality—[the following would apply here]:...
Therefore, the statement regarding the knowledge of that [state] is purposeless in this world; thus, the word "akarma" (non-action) is used here in its primary sense. || 10 ||

From the statement of Yājñavalkya—namely, from the words of Ajātaśatru found in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad, "He whose this is the karma, he indeed is to be known"—there is the perception that [the self] is subject to karma; for it is only an entity dependent upon karma, consisting of merit and demerit, [that is meant].

From this understanding—that very one, namely the individual soul (jīvātman) itself—by means of its own performed transformation, that is, by way of the maturation of its own karma known as merit and demerit, would be the creator of men who have attained the fourfold states beginning with the gods, or the creator of conscious beings such as the Sun and others mentioned as objects of worship—such a doubt is refuted by the introduction; it is blocked by the opening of the context.

For instance, Bālāki, whose true nature was unknown—namely, that there is another reality, the creator of these [dreams], which was not known by the Brāhmaṇa Gārgya named Bālāki—the statement regarding that knowledge by Ajātaśatru, the Kṣatriya of that name, who teaches and makes it known as something new, would be purposeless—that is, it would become fruitless—if his activity here in this context were merely a description of objects already understood by Bālāki as things to be known. Here, the word "karma" (action/task) [is used].

The word "action" (*karman*) found in the sentence "or for whom this is action," is used in its primary sense—possessing the full grounds for its application—by virtue of being something already performed (*kṛtatayā*), that is, by reason of its having been accomplished; it refers to the world, meaning the object in the form of the phenomenal universe (*prapañca*), and is not used in a secondary sense. || 10 ||

Thus, when the subject matter is determined to concern that which is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), the mention there of the "individual soul" and the "principal vital breath" (*mukhya-prāṇa*) does not cause any damage here; for even the one who possesses the vital breath (*prāṇabhāj*) is the substratum, according to the manner stated in the *Vājivākya*.
For the sake of making Brahman known, the exposition of that which is other than it is indeed the universal establishment (sthāpanā). 11.

Following this stated method, when the subject matter—which is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), that is, characterized by a nature different from the jīva—is determined without doubt by the means of proof called *prakaraṇa* (context) which decides the meaning, then, within that very context determining what is distinct from the jīva, there exists the mention of the individual soul and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—namely, the reference to the chief vital breath as "the great one clad in white" (*bṛhan pāṇḍaravāsaḥ*) and the reference to the individual soul as "he rose up from that very place. By that [mention]...

By the mention of *prāṇa* and *jīva*, there is no contradiction here; nor does it entail the subversion of the fact that the subject matter refers to the Supreme Self, who is distinct from both *prāṇa* and *jīva*. For, in this way—by way of being the modes (*prakāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—meditation (*upāsā*, i.e., *upāsana*) proceeds with the Supreme Self as its object, characterized by those two attributes known as the *jīva* and the chief *prāṇa*.

According to the method stated in the *Vājivākya*, by way of the similarity of meaning found in the dialogue between Bālāki and Jātaśatru in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, or by the logic set forth in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*—namely, that even for the *prāṇa* (the vital breath) and the *prāṇabhāj* (the one who possesses breath), that is, the *mukhyaprāṇa* (the chief vital breath), as well as for the *jīva* (individual soul) which is the substratum of the *mukhyaprāṇa*, there is a description of "others than that"—the mention of the *jīva* and the *mukhyaprāṇa* who are distinct from Brahman—in the form of their being the locus (*adhikaraṇatayā*), characterized by the state of being a support, for the sake of making Brahman known (*brahmajñapti*), that is, for the purpose of accomplishing the meditation on Brahman.
Thus, the establishment is as follows: indeed, this very method of describing the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is universal; it is preeminent because it remains uncontradicted. ||11||
Summary of the Topic:

In the section concerning the world being the diversity [of names and forms], there is an objection: in the passage beginning with "O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons," because of the hearing of the connection in the words "he whose work this is," that which is stated as the object to be known is not Brahman, but rather the individual soul (jīva). Having raised this doubt:

Based on the etymological derivation from the root *kṛ* (to do), since the word "karman" (action) denotes the universe, it has been stated that the Supreme Self alone, who is the cause of the universe, is presented here as the object to be known.

The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is connected by way of method (*naya*): first, through the connection with the introductory section (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; then, by means of the indicative marks of the individual soul (*jīvaliṅga*); and finally, as an exception (*apavāda*), there is the method concerning that which denotes the world (*jagadvācinaya*). || 65 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the diversity of the world (*jagadvicitratvādhikaraṇa*).

This is the scriptural demonstration of the living self (*jīva*) as a mark of the embodied form (*rūpa*); for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) abides within the body—which is the locus of production and destruction—as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the living self, by virtue of His presence in the manner stated [in scripture]: "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*). || 50 ||

The Śruti reiterates that the husband and others are dear to the Self for the sake of fulfilling its desires; therefore, the notion that the Self is the enjoyer of the fruits arising from merit and demerit contradicts the introductory context and other [evidences]. Indeed, this reveals the Lord’s dearness to the individual according to His will as the bestower of those respective enjoyments. Furthermore, this [Self] must be seen as the object of liberation; thus, it is made known here through a multitude of scriptural texts. (12)

For this reason, the Śruti—the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti—reiterates, that is, makes known as already established in the world, the fact that for the sake of fulfilling one's own desires (kāmasiddhi)—namely, for the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility (iṣṭāpūrta)—the husband and others possess a state of being dear to their wives and other relatives, or rather, that they are objects of affection or service for those relatives.

For that very reason, the doubt that "this Self—described as one who serves what is dear—is the individual soul (jīva), the experiencer of the fruits produced by merit and demerit, being the agent who tastes the results brought about by actions consisting of merit and demerit, and not the Supreme Self," is contrary to the introduction and other indicators; it contradicts the opening statement and so forth.

For this reason: the dearness of those [objects] such as husband, wife, and son—consisting in their being served by the self according to one's own will—is due to the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa), the All-pervading Lord (Vibhu), who bestows various enjoyments through His specific volition (svasaṅkalpaviśeṣa) with respect to those very things acting as instrumental causes for sentient beings; that is to say, it arises solely from His specific resolve (viśiṣṭena saṅkalpena).

This very one—the Supreme Self alone—who makes various things dear through His own particular volition, is to be seen for the sake of liberation—that is, with the attainment of immortality as the goal—as established by the entire corpus of Vedānta through the multitude of Śruti texts; He is recognized here—in this statement, "The Self, indeed, O Maitreyī, is to be seen"—as being identified thus: "He is that very same one. || 12 ||

For by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the word *ātman* reveals the Supreme Brahman; or else, [it does so] "by way of compounding" (*asamāsāt*). Furthermore, there are these positions: "The word *jīva* expresses its own primary meaning, yet it denotes the Supreme through the function of a door. Āśmarathya [teaches] identity due to the oneness of the individual manifestation (*vyakti-ekya*); Auḍulomi [teaches] non-duality in the state free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupadhika-daśā*); and Kāśakṛtsna [teaches] that the word *jīva* refers to the Supreme because of its abiding therein (*tat-sthatvāt*). Thus, he spoke of the word *jīva* as having the Supreme as its object. (13) Regarding the word *ātman*: in the sentence "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," it is the Supreme Brahman [that is meant] precisely by the power of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*) through etymology—namely, "It pervades (*āpnoti*), therefore it is the Self (*ātman*)."

This word "ātman" reveals—that is, makes manifest—the reality that is the nature of Brahman, which transcends both consciousness and unconsciousness. Or else, alternatively, by virtue of its conventional power (*rūḍhi*) as a compound term, this aforementioned word "ātman" possesses a meaning, being denotative of the Supreme Self who is the indweller of all bodies.

Or else—alternatively—the word *jīva* here, although inherently capable of denoting the commonality of "that which is other than insentient," is primarily employed for the individual soul (*jīvātman*) on the basis of its function of sustaining the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The word *ātman*, however, by way of a secondary function (*dvāravṛtti*)—taking as its medium the conscious principle whose nature is to sustain the wind called *prāṇa* within the body—denotes both: it expresses the *jīva* as a qualifier and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as the qualified. Such are the positions; thus, in this manner...

Three interpretations are observed. Āśmarathya—the great seer of that name—spoke, having made his own intention clear, by relying on the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva), which is an effect of the Supreme Self, from the nature of the Self (ātman), just as a jar, though an effect of a lump of clay, is non-different from the nature of clay; thus, he declared that the word "Self" (ātman)—which is known for its inherent capacity to denote a living being—is used here with reference to the Supreme (para) as its denotable object.

And Auḍulomi—namely, the teacher named Auḍulomi—referred to the Supreme Being by the word "jīva" (individual soul), relying on the non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman established in the state where the connection with the body conditioned by ignorance has ceased, due to the non-duality of the state free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupadhika*).

Kāśakṛtsna—the teacher of that name who contemplates the reality of Brahman—however, on account of its abiding therein—that is, by relying on the Supreme Self’s abiding within that individual soul as its ruler, its master, and its sustainer, according to the manner stated in the passage "He who dwells in the self"—used the word *jīva* (individual soul) to refer to the Supreme Being. The various readings found here should be interpreted as appropriate. 13.

It is incorrect to say that this embodied soul would attain the state of Brahman upon the removal of the limiting adjuncts of difference; for its perception of difference is eternal, as indicated by the terms "equality" (*sāmya*) and "common nature" (*sādharmya*) even while remaining within transmigratory existence. Furthermore, the sequence of clay and its products is refuted by hundreds of scriptural passages.
Therefore, because the individual soul resides within Him, Kāśakṛtsna maintained that the term "individual soul" (*jīva*) refers to the Lord; this is the established doctrine of Vyāsa.

When the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of difference have ceased—that is, when defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*), which cause the distinction between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), have been removed—then this "bearer of existence" (*bhavabhṛt*), the living being who is the substrate of the currently perceived embodied state, would attain the state of Brahman (*brahmatām iyāt*). Such a view of the teacher Auḍulomi is unreasonable and contradicts logic; for it takes as its object a living being who has transcended existence, having passed beyond *saṃsāra*, based on the words "equality" (*sāmya*) and "similarity" (*sādharmya*) found in such passages as: "The stainless one attains the highest equality" (*nirañjanaḥ paramaṃ sāmyamupaiti*), and "My... [and so forth].

By employing the terms *sāmya* (similarity) and *sādharmya* (homogeneity) in the phrase "they have attained homogeneity," [the author] indicates that their difference is eternal; for one observes in the Śrutis and Smṛtis descriptions of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman as existing at all times. Furthermore, the sequence of cause and effect, such as the example of a lump of clay and the jar or bowl produced from it, is refuted by hundreds of scriptural passages, such as: "The perishable is the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the self. And so forth.

This [view] is contradicted by numerous scriptural passages (*śruti*) that demonstrate the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For various reasons, the teacher named Kāśakṛtsna—relying on the fact that the Supreme Self abides within the individual soul as its instrumental cause—justified the use of terms denoting the individual soul for the Lord (*īśvara*) in this context; that this point constitutes the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Vyāsa, the author of the Sūtras, and his own intended meaning, is what is established here. || 14 ||
The summary of the meaning of the section:

In the *Vākyānvaya* section, regarding the passage beginning with "Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self (*ātman*) that the husband is dear," one might raise the objection that the Self mentioned as the object to be seen in the statement "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" is the *puruṣa* established by the Sāṃkhya system (*tantra*), because it is that very [Self] which is taught at the beginning, middle, and end [of the Upaniṣads]. Anticipating this doubt:

Because of the statement, "But there is no hope for immortality," and because the consistency of the connection of those passages—which teach that [the Self] is the cause of being an object of meditation and the means for attaining immortality—is established only if they refer to the Supreme Self, it is concluded that the one described as "that which is to be seen" is the Supreme Self. || 6 ||

The connection [of this section] with the *Nayasaṅgati* is due to the impossibility here of the principle known as *anyathopapatti* (establishment otherwise); or rather, in the context of the interpretation of statements (*vākyanīti*), there may be a connection by way of a counter-example arising from doubt. (66)
Thus ends the section on the syntactical connection of sentences (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||

To say—that is, to assert—that the Supreme (paraḥ), meaning the Supreme Self (paramātmā), cannot be the material cause (upādāna)—that is, cannot be the material cause—is not possible for us; this is our thesis (sādhya). Why? Because of the proposition (pratijñā), [which implies] the inseparable connection with being the material cause.
