Because the cognition of the cause is stated in the form of a definitive conclusion regarding the cognition of the effect in the Śruti passage, "Indeed, when that is known, all this becomes known," and because both [causality] are stated by the Śruti itself—which is the supreme authority—directly (without employing methods such as indirect implication) in the verses beginning with, "What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth?"—it follows that the Supreme Self alone is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
And because the twofold nature of causality has also been explicitly established [by the author]. || 51 ||

In this world, the potter and others are distinct from the lump of clay and so forth; likewise, the Primordial Cause (Ādikartā) is not the material cause (*upādāna*), because He is devoid of modifications (*vikāra*). It is not the case that He is a modification merely because of the example of clay and the like, for such a modification would not apply to the Supreme. This is because it has been demonstrated that His activity occurs through the medium of the body, just as the spider acts through its web, which is both its source and its modification. ||15||

In the case of the collection of causes and effects perceived in this world, such as a pot and the like, the agent—namely the potter and others who constitute the instrumental cause—is indeed observed to be distinct and separate from the material cause, such as the lump of clay. In that very same manner, by analogy with that, the Primordial Creator—the entity that serves as the causal source of the universe—is likewise devoid of modifications (*vikāra*), [as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad]: "Partless... (*niṣkalam*).

Because it is established by such scriptural texts as "the stainless" (*nirañjana*), and because of the reason that it is devoid of all modification (*vikāra*), the objection—that Brahman cannot possibly be a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) characterized by modification denoted by the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*)—is entirely untenable.

[The term "this" (*asau*) refers to the following: merely as a door—meaning, with respect to causality, only in that aspect which is accepted as the door [to the effect]; because of the acceptance of modification (*vikāra*)—which is denoted by the word "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) and is the cause of being the material cause (*upādānatva*)—(since the designation belonging to the door is not lost when applied to the one who possesses the door, as in the expression "the boy has become a youth"); and merely from the example of clay and so forth—meaning, merely from the demonstration in the Śruti of the modified object as an illustrative example, in passages such as "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay... This...

The status of being the material cause (upādānatā) established by scripture belongs to the Supreme Self’s own nature—that nature which is denoted by terms such as "truth" and "knowledge," and which is changeless; nor would there be any modification, for it would not become a substratum of transformation.

Like the transformation of a spider and so forth—just as spiders, designated by the term *ūrṇanābhi*, undergo a modification known as their own essence; because activity through the medium of the body—the Supreme Self’s status as the material cause of the universe within itself—is established by making its own conscious-and-unconscious body the instrument; and because this has been clarified in such scriptural passages as, "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web]," and so on. ||15||

The Lord, through His own knowledge and other powers, becomes the source of what is produced by Himself and brings about conjunction with that which is distinct from Himself; for when conjunction resides in corporeal entities, Primordial Matter (prakṛti) may also be the instrumental cause due to its activity. In this regard, the desire to become many—"May I be many"—is established by the logic of Saubhari;
and here, there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference, because of the connection with a qualified unity.

One's own cognition and so forth—even according to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas and others—have the self as their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) because they are inherent in the self; thus, cognition, desire to act, effort, and the like are produced by the self. (This is because the verbal suffix *lakāra* is used in the sense of the agent in expressions such as "he knows," "he desires," and "he acts. Furthermore, because the self is the agent, these states also have the self as their efficient cause (*nimitta*).

The Lord—the Sovereign of all—creates His own conjunction—that specific relation termed the conjunction of Himself with that which is other than Himself—and He also brings it forth (for, being the agent with respect to the conjunction inherent in Himself, He is also the efficient cause of that conjunction).

When conjunction—known as the quality of *saṃyoga*—is produced as inhering in two corporeal substances (i.e., as inherent in two material entities such as atoms), that pair of corporeal substances, although being the *prakṛti*—that is, the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), which is synonymous with the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*)—would indeed be the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), by means of the action residing within itself which generates the conjunction; for this is certainly the case! This applies to that which was initially, prior to creation, single, devoid of various names and forms, and non-dual.

The becoming manifold of the conscious Brahman—expressed as "May I be many"—is the attainment of the capacity for various names and forms preceded by the volition "May I be many," a principle established by the logic of Saubhari. This is well-attested by the manner in which the single sage named Saubhari assumed various bodies through his own volition; for there is no mutual contradiction between the material cause in its prior state and the effect in its subsequent state.

And here—in this established doctrine that Brahman is the material cause—there is no contradiction because of the possibility of a qualified identity; for there is no sublation of non-difference with respect to the substrate (dharmin) which is qualified by two states. Thus, there would be no conflict between the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference: those establishing the distinction between the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) and "The one God rules over the perishable and the imperishable self" (*kṣarātmānāv īśate deva ekaḥ*); and those establishing non-difference, such as "There is not any diversity here" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*) and "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

The state of expressing mutually contradictory meanings would indeed be established [in that triad], because the mutual difference produced by their own essential natures (*svarūpa*) and the non-difference produced by the qualification of being sentient and insentient (*cetanācetana-vaiśiṣṭya*), which is established through inference, are both accepted in common worldly and Vedic usage. || 16 ||
For when the effect is one, the proposition is established, and a corresponding collection of examples is cited;

here, the Śruti declares that the Creator had the intention "May I be," and speaks of his becoming trees and so forth. Furthermore, it says, "He made himself by himself"; thus, his being the source of all beings has been stated.
Therefore, the Lord must be both the agent and the material cause, the inner self of all principles. (17)
The proposition (*pratijñā*) takes the form: "Indeed, in that [Brahman]... all this becomes"; it is the proposition that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all.
For this is only possible when the non-difference of the cause from its effect is established through the identity of their effects.

Accordingly, a collection of examples (*dṛṣṭāntavarga*) consisting of clay and its products—which are favorable to the realization of non-difference—has been cited and presented, having been extracted from what is already well-known in the world.

In this context—where the inquiry into the difference and non-difference of cause and effect has been introduced—the Vedic statement "May I be many, may I procreate" expresses, that is, clearly establishes, the meditative reflection (*abhidhyā*) of the Creator, the Lord who is the author of the world; this meditative reflection consists of a volition directed toward the effect and serves as the causal condition for its production.

Likewise, [the scripture] speaks of its state as a forest (*vana*) and its state as a tree (*vṛkṣa*), stating: "Brahman was the forest, Brahman was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth. Thus, the Śruti itself designates "forest-ness" (*vanatva*) as indicative of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) and "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) as indicative of being the instrumental cause (*upakaraṇatva*). (Therefore, the threefold causality consisting of efficient causality (*nimittatva*), material causality (*upādānatva*), and instrumental causality (*upakaraṇatva*) is understood to reside in Brahman.)

[The text explains that] the Supreme Self (paramātman) alone, by means of His own will (svasaṅkalpa), brought forth [the universe] from Himself—that is, from His own essential nature (svarūpa)—independently of anything else. Specifically, He acted as the material cause (upādāna) through the mode of being distinguished by subtle consciousness and unconsciousness; He acted as the instrumental cause (upakaraṇa) through the mode of being distinguished by time, unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa), and so forth; and He acted as the efficient cause (nimitta) through the mode of being distinguished by volition (saṅkalpa). Thus, the Śruti declares: "He made Himself from Himself" (*tadātmānaṃ svayamakuruta*). This means He brought about [the world] characterized by various, diverse, infinite, and wonderful forms.

Regarding its being the source of all beings: it has been stated that this very Supreme Brahman is the material cause of all beings, as established by the Vedic scripture, "The wise perceive that which is the source of all beings. Therefore, from the collection of evidences shown, the Lord—the self-luminous Supreme Self, the inner self of all principles—is the controller of all principles by virtue of being their inner ruler (*antaryāmin*).

Therefore, the agent, by virtue of possessing knowledge, desire, and effort that conform to the effect, is indeed the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); likewise, primordial matter (*prakṛti*)—being characterized by both the conscious and the unconscious through its transformative nature—is also the material cause (*upādāna*). This is certainly possible; there is no reason for disagreement here. || 17 ||
We know that there is no such thing as a "material cause" (upādāna) distinct from a "formal cause" (nimitta);

for it is illogical to claim that what is established as a formal cause does not partake of the nature of a material cause. Since both [causal roles] are integrated through the distinction of intended forms, and since this is established in accordance with worldly usage and the Vedas, the attempt to introduce a definition based on one's own whim is merely a deceptive maneuver, like the vain concern over the cooking of food.

Any material cause whatsoever—whatever entity is endowed with the nature of being a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)—cannot possibly be a formal cause (*nimitta*); that is, it cannot be characterized as a formal cause. Or rather, whatever entity is established as a formal cause—that is, determined to be a formal cause—that does not partake in the state of being a material cause; such an entity never attains the status of a material cause.

Because we understand that "other" thing—which serves as the instrumental cause—to be a cause distinct from both the inherent and non-inherent causes; this [view] is incorrect. Such an observation is far removed from reason, because it fails to consider the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two types of causality—namely, the nature of being an instrumental cause and the nature of being a material cause—arising from the mutual distinction between the specific properties (*dharmaviśeṣa*) that necessitate instrumentality and materiality, which are themselves different due to their distinct forms.

When the conformity with both the world and the Vedas is established—that is, when the worldly and Vedic conventions of cause and effect are well-harmonized—then this "independent fabrication" (svacchandakusṛti), which disregards the means of valid knowledge and follows only one's own whims, is the pursuit of an evil path characterized by the creation of [false] instrumental and material causes; it is merely the ripening of the deliberations of the immature whose wisdom is unripened, and not the ripening of the reflections of learned people. || 18 ||
Having stated that there is the dissolution of those intermediate [evolutes], and then declared that [the remainder] is mere oneness in darkness (*tamas*),

and having explained through Vedic and Vedantic statements the beginninglessness and other attributes of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; and since the statement regarding dissolution— that "these two dissolve into the Supreme"— follows the analogy of iron and water,
therefore this creation of the universe, consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth, is perfectly logical.

Having described the dissolution (*laya*)—which consists in the attainment of the causal state preceded by the abandonment of the state of being an effect—of the other principles (*tattvāntarāṇām*), namely the principles such as earth and the rest that are distinct from *tamas*, by means of the passage in the *Subālopaniṣad* beginning with "Earth dissolves into water" and ending with "The Imperishable dissolves into *tamas*"; then, subsequently, [one attains] mere oneness (*ekatāmātram*)—a synonym for becoming one—with You, who are of the nature of *tamas*, a conjunction with the Supreme Self that is incapable of separation.

It is merely a distinction, and not the dissolution previously described. This has been stated by the scriptural passage: "Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. Furthermore, the beginninglessness and the absence of origin and destruction of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—that is, the fundamental principles of primordial matter and the individual soul—are established by Vedic statements such as "the one unborn female" (*ajāmekām*) and "the two unborn, the Knower and the Unknower" (*jñājñau dvāvajau*), as well as by the words of those who know the Vedas, such as Vyāsa and others, in passages like "Know that both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are indeed beginningless."

And by the statement, which has been explained in such a way that it is free from doubt, it means that both of them—Prakṛti and Puruṣa—merge, that is, attain dissolution, into the Supreme Self (Paramātman). As for the word "dissolution" (laya), it refers to: "That Prakṛti which I have described, whose nature consists of the manifest and the unmanifest..."

As for the statement of Parāśara, "And both these—the Puruṣa and [Prakṛti]—merge into the Supreme Self," it should be understood according to the analogy of iron and water: just as when water is poured onto an object made of iron, such as a weapon heated by fire, the water is not perceived externally and remains inseparable from the iron itself, so too does that statement teach the inseparable union of Prakṛti and Puruṣa with the Supreme Self.

But it does not teach that the state of being the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and the *puruṣa* (spirit) must first be abandoned before the state of being the Supreme Brahman is attained. For that reason stated, this creation of the universe—the emergence of the world established by Śruti and Smṛti—is "proper," meaning its establishment is uncontradicted, [proceeding] from the Supreme Brahman who is the source of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth, and who has the conscious and unconscious as His body, and time as His body. || 19 ||

In the *Nayasaṅgatimālikā*, it was previously stated that everything possesses a dual causality; having properly raised an objection to this in the section concerning *prakṛti*, its definitive resolution is now provided.
Thus concludes the section concerning the primordial nature (prakṛti). 7.

Śrīpati: If Nārāyaṇa, who is served by the Vaiṣṇavas as the Lord of Śrī (Śriyaḥ patiḥ), is indeed the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśa)—meaning, if he is called Īśvara, the Controller of the entire world—then how can this Nārāyaṇa, who is denoted by the title "Lord of All" (Sarveśvara), have authority for protection alone? Among the acts of creation, preservation, and dissolution, how could he be the master of preservation alone? For he must indeed be the master of everything.

This being the case, even though you have traveled far by establishing the distinctness of Nārāyaṇa from Brahmā and Śiva—undergoing an effort comparable to traveling a great distance—you will still be pained by the comparison with Brahmā and Śiva; for even Viṣṇu, who is included among the three forms (trimūrti), experiences specific instances of suffering whenever he is impelled toward actions that fall within his own jurisdiction.

Because the equality between Brahmā and Rudra was unavoidable, it was like "dawn at the toll-house": for a merchant carrying a load of merchandise who had set out to travel by another route, avoiding the path associated with the toll-station, it happened that at the very moment of dawn he reached that same toll-station due to losing his way.

Because of the fruitlessness of such effort—let it not be so; do not entertain such a doubt. For in our Puruṣa—in the glorious Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Reality propounded in the *Puruṣasūkta* and is esteemed by us; in Him who is of infinite and vast prowess, possessing great power in the form of being all-surpassing and all-expanding; in Him who is the Creator of Brahmā—the progenitor even of Viriñci and Śiva—this [fact] that Viriñci and Śiva have been ordained as His incarnations occurs, just as in His forms as the Fish and others.

In the incarnations of the Blessed One as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, there is a dramatic performance (*nāṭya*) that imitates His own majesty—namely, the very activity of the world-drama consisting of His own divine play (*līlā*), which takes the form of emulating Brahmā and Rudra who are included within His own manifestation; it is not an activity dependent on the subordination to another, as is the case with Vidhi (Brahmā) and Śiva. ||21||

The summary of the meaning of this section [is as follows]: In the section concerning the interpretation of all [scriptural passages]—having raised the doubt that in those specific passages not cited in the preceding section where only the status of being the cause of the world is heard, but not the attributes exclusive to the Supreme Person such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth, there is no contradiction even if one accepts the entity as it is understood [therefore], and thus they do not refer to the Supreme Self—[the author proceeds].

Even though no other attributes exclusive to the Supreme Brahman are heard [in those passages], since it has been established by previous topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) that being the cause of the world—like the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth—is unique to the Supreme Person, it is concluded as the final position (*siddhānta*) that the very fact of being the cause of the world proves that these passages refer to a specific deity denoted by the term "Supreme Brahman," who is the cause of all things in every way and distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious; thus, it is He alone who is taught even in those sentences.
The connection of the methods (*nayasaṅgati*) and the resolution (*nirvāha*) everywhere according to the manner already stated should be inferred by oneself;

thus, all the principles previously mentioned are extended here [by implication]. (68) In this way, the group of eight topics (*adhikaraṇī*), joined with two sections (*peṭikā*), has arrived as the textual composition in the fourth quarter of the first chapter. (69)
Thus ends the section concerning the explanation of all [scriptural passages]. || 8 ||

Because of the recognition of the process [of creation], because of the description of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because of the inclusion of the number [of principles], as well as due to mutual contradictions; because of the description of the connection with *karman*, because of the hearing of terms such as *pati* (Lord), and because of the perception of difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) in the world—there is no certainty at all that Brahman alone is the cause and nothing else. (Verses 52–53)
Thus, that which was stated in the Tantras has been refuted by this. ||54||

[and so on].

Because of the statement, "Whose this action is," which establishes a connection with the merit and demerit (puṇya-pāpa) residing in the individual soul (jīva); and because of the mention of a "lord" (pati) and so forth—likewise, since the scripture teaches that the husband, wife, and others are unique to the individual soul who is subject to karma; and because the difference between the material cause (upādāna) and the efficient cause (nimitta)—namely, their distinctness—is observed in the world when they are defined by a single effect, as seen in the case of the clay substance which is the material cause of a jar and the potter who is its efficient cause.

And because [the potter] is clearly perceived, it is understood that Brahman alone is the cause and nothing else; thus, this claim of the Vedāntins—that the Supreme Brahman alone is the cause of the universe in both ways—is not a certainty that can be established as uncontradicted. This is what was stated by the Tantrikas: "The statement seen among the proponents of the Sāṅkhya system, which is of such a kind, is refuted by this fourth quarter. All of that [is refuted] by this fourth quarter.

"By three [sections], there would be the refutation of Pradhāna; by the fourth, the resolution of mutual contradictions; and by the fifth and sixth, the soul that has attained liberation and the soul that is bound are distinguished. (55) "By three"—namely, by the three sections known as *Ānumānika*, *Camasa*, and *Saṅkhyopasaṅgraha*—"there would be the refutation of Pradhāna": this means that the notion that the *pradhāna* favored by the Sāṅkhya school is indeed what is taught by the Śruti is removed.

From the fourth [adhikaraṇa], namely the section concerning the cause (*kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa*), there is the "dissolution of mutual contradiction"—the liberation from the delusion that the scriptural passages regarding the cause of the world possess mutually distinct intended meanings. From the fifth and sixth [adhikaraṇas], namely the sections concerning the connection of the passages on the world's being Brahman (*jagadvācitva*)—

The soul that has attained liberation and the soul that remains bound—the individual self that has reached freedom from the bonds of *saṃsāra* and that which is fettered within the bondage of *saṃsāra*—have been clearly demonstrated to be excluded; that is, they do not constitute the intended meaning of the scriptural statements concerning the cause. By this collection of aphorisms, [the author] has refuted the atheistic Sāṃkhya.

And desiring the identity of the cause and the Lord, he shook off the remainder—the Sāṃkhya system without a Lord (nirīśvara)—that is, the Sāṃkhya of Kapila which does not accept a Lord, by means of this series of sūtras beginning with the *Ānumānika-sūtra* and ending with the *Avasthiteḥ-sūtra*, making it clear that its subject matter is not intended by the Śruti.

From the remainder—that is, from the collection of sūtras beginning with the *prakṛti-sūtra* and ending with "By this, all [other systems] are explained"—the author of the sūtras, desiring the identity of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), and wishing to establish the non-difference between the Lord who is the efficient cause, the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, and the ruler of all, refuted that [system] which includes the Lord—the Sāṃkhya of Patañjali, which accepts a Lord—Bādarāyaṇa makes it known that it grasps meanings not intended by the Śruti. || 56 ||

Thus, by all the statements of those who propound the cause of the world, speaking with one voice, it is established that Brahman alone—the omniscient and possessed of infinite power—is the source of these worlds. (57)

Thus, by the aforementioned method, through all—the entirety of—those statements of those who propound the cause of the world, that is, through all the sentences contained within the Vedānta that establish the reality which constitutes the cause of the world; being of one voice—that is, possessing a non-contradictory, single purport—it is *Brahman* alone that is [the cause], which is omniscient—possessing knowledge regarding the entire universe in its gross and subtle forms consisting of all sentient and insentient things—and possessed of infinite power—possessing unobstructed capacity regarding all sentient and insentient things in their gross and subtle forms.

"The Supreme Brahman alone is the source of these worlds"—this has been stated, meaning that He is the primordial cause even of all these innumerable worlds; this has been established by sufficient reasons. || 57 ||

That Supreme Brahman, having a subtle body composed of consciousness and the unconscious, attains the state of being the cause; furthermore, having a gross body composed of consciousness and the unconscious, it attains the state of being the effect.

That Supreme Brahman—Brahman understood through the Śruti as the cause of the entire universe—becomes the cause, that is, attains the status of being the cause for the creation of the objects to be created, while being invested with a subtle body consisting of sentient and non-sentient entities in their specific state denoted by the term "subtle. Furthermore, that very same Brahman becomes the effect, that is, attains the status of being the effect, while being invested with a gross body consisting of sentient and non-sentient entities in their specific state denoted by the term "gross."

It attains the nature of the object being created. || 58 || This *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, a compendium of the collection of logical arguments composed by the noble Seneśvara, [is established] because of the mention of the process described in Sāṃkhya; because of the creation favored by that [system]; because of the arrangement of its enumeration; because of the unity of the manifested as declared therein; because of the statement regarding its own defects; because of the connection with the faults of its results; because of the distinction between the agent and primordial matter (*prakṛti*); and because of the scriptural testimony of multiple causes such as Brahmā, Śiva, and others.

That which was cast down and described in three verses protected [the world] by revealing the heart of the Vedas. Sāṃkhya... [is so called] because it establishes the acceptance of principles such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) favored by the Sāṃkhyas, as found in the *Kaṭha-śruti* and other texts.

Because of that demonstration: since the process of creation accepted by the Sāṃkhyas—namely, the theory of creation having as its cause the *pradhāna* which is non-Brahman and non-Self—is understood through such scriptural passages as the *ajā-śruti* (the "Unborn" scripture), and because the enumeration of those principles is established; since the method of counting the categories of reality (*tattva*) favored by the Sāṃkhyas is determined and stated by such scriptural passages as "In whom [rest] the five," and so on; and because of the identity with the *avyākṛta* (the Undeveloped) proclaimed therein—due to the non-difference between the category of the *avyākṛta* accepted in the scripture "This was then undeveloped" and the *pradhāna* spoken of by the Sāṃkhyas.

Because of the mention of his own evil deeds—in the Vedic text "He whose karma is this," it is stated that the karma consisting of merit and demerit residing in the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the term *durita*, pertains to the object to be known; because of the connection with the defects of its fruits—the mention of association with undesirable human goals such as wife, son, and so forth, which consist of the fruits of one's own performed actions; because of the difference between the agent and primordial matter (*prakṛti*)—since there is a rule of mutual distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); [and] Druhiṇa...

And because of scripture—since the scriptures establish the causality of many factors other than Nārāyaṇa as the cause of the world—this has been "cast aside," that is, refuted by these reasons for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of this [fourth] section. The meaning established by the three preceding sections—the first, second, and third sections of the first chapter—is "preserved" by the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa; that is, he accepted it as not to be rejected and explained it, because the intention of the scripture was made clear through the [proper] interpretation of the scripture. ||22||

Since the reality of Brahman— the indweller of all moving and unmoving beings, both conscious and unconscious— is established as the object of inquiry by the Vedas and other authorities themselves, this natural course of the words of the causal scriptures is well-expressed. Those followers of the *Musalī* school, who describe here in many ways various forms of sublation and obstruction regarding the internal and external,
should be expelled from the presence of the *Niṣad* Upaniṣads for the sake of establishing their immovable stability.

When the reality of Brahman has been established as the object of inquiry—that is, when it has been posited as that which must be investigated and determined by those afflicted by the three-fold suffering for the sake of attaining immortality—and when its perfectly established nature is understood as being embodied by all moving and non-moving beings, both sentient and insentient (the term *brahman* being applied to this supreme reality through its connection with unsurpassed greatness), then the natural course of the scriptural passages concerning the cause—which teach the reality that constitutes the cause of the universe—is as follows: [previously...]

The unafflicted engagement has been demonstrated by the scriptures alone—that is, by the very texts consisting of Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth, which establish the ultimate reality. In this regard, concerning the meaning established in the first chapter, there is no sublation (*bādha*)—that is, no cognition of impossibility produced by other means of knowledge—nor any obstruction (*rodha*), which is the absence of a definitive determination of the stated meaning due to the cognition of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣitatva*). Furthermore, there is no external or internal [contradiction], that is, nothing detrimental from the systems of others, [and thus] it stands as a valid means of knowledge.

Describing in many ways—that is, through the expansion of their own voluminous texts—the manner in which [the opponent's position] is inconsistent with the scriptures they themselves accept; being "Musalyas"—meaning those who do not rely on a sharp, subtle intellect for determining the true meaning, but instead proceed to determine the meaning of the scriptures and so forth solely through the impressions of their own prior prejudices; being of dull and coarse intellect; and being, in the subsequent chapter, those who [misinterpret] the Nipada Upanishads by means of a false door.

In order to establish the immovability—that is, the firmness—in those portions of the Śruti that set forth Dvārakā-Brahman, by way of demonstrating their own meaning without contradiction, those who determine meanings associated with defects are expelled; they are made to feel remorse by being informed: "It is you who have determined faulty meanings. || 23 ||

Because this Supreme Brahman is the inner self (*antarātman*) of the universe filled with all beings, and because He has all beings as His body (*śarīraka*), the heavenly world—which is denoted by the word "fire" (*agni*)—is the head of this Virāj-form. Both the sun and the moon occupy the place of the eyes. All directions, beginning with the east, occupy the place of the ears. All Vedic utterances, consisting of vocal expressions, constitute His speech. The ever-moving wind occupies the place of the life-force (*prāṇa*) that sustains the body.
One should know and meditate upon the entire world as being situated within the mass of flesh called the heart; the whole earth is its place corresponding to the feet.
7. "The Person the size of a thumb, smokeless like a light, is the Lord of the past and the future; He alone is today, and He is tomorrow. This indeed is That. (Praśna Upaniṣad).

One should know [the Self] by means of the instruments of valid knowledge (*pramāṇas*) along with their explanations (pṛ.saṃ.), having distinguished it as being distinct from oneself and endowed with attributes such as possessing a body, through the wholesome knowledge produced by practices such as meditation (*upāsanā*), which serves as the means— just as one might distinguish and recognize the *iṣīkā* reed situated within the *muñja* grass while looking at that specific grass. One should know Him as independent of anything other than Himself, self-luminous, the source of the illumination of all things dependent upon Him, and possessed of unconditioned immortality (*amṛtatva*).

9. "The Person the size of a thumb dwells in the center of the self; he is the ruler of what has been and what is to be, and one does not shrink away from him. This indeed is that. "The Person the size of a thumb... dwells":

He is the Ruler of All (*sarveśvara*), the controller of all things existing within the three periods of time—past, future, and present. For the sake of bestowing grace upon the worshiper, He abides in the central region called the heart, which is connected to the body of the worshiper, assuming a dimension the size of a thumb.

Since he remains established by relying on such a state through his own volition alone, for that very reason, he never experiences a sense of loathing directed toward objects—even those connected to him—whether conscious or unconscious, which do not constitute human goals.

"I am free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst; my desires are true. *Prasthāna-bheda with Commentary: A Compendium of the Sources of Knowledge* **Introduction** The purpose of this work is to provide a concise summary of the various systems of Indian philosophy (*darśana*), illustrating how each system establishes its own foundational principles (*pramāṇa*) and arrives at its respective conclusions regarding the nature of reality. **The Six Systems of Orthodox Philosophy (Āstika)** 1. **Nyāya**: This system establishes four means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*): perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*). It asserts that the ultimate goal is liberation (*mokṣa*) through the knowledge of the sixteen categories (*tattva*), beginning with proof (*pramāṇa*) and ending with the absence of pain (*apavarga*). 2. **Vaiśeṣika**: This school accepts three means of valid knowledge: perception, inference, and verbal testimony. It posits six fundamental categories (*padārtha*): substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*). Its primary aim is the attainment of liberation through the discernment of these categories. 3. **Sāṃkhya**: This system recognizes only two means of valid knowledge: perception and inference. It propounds twenty-five principles (*tattva*), including the primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the eleven organs (*indriya*), and the individual self (*puruṣa*). Liberation is achieved through the discriminative knowledge of the difference between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. 4. **Yoga**: Building upon Sāṃkhya, Yoga accepts the same two means of valid knowledge. It emphasizes the practical methods for achieving liberation, such as the eight limbs of yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*), including ethical restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). 5. **Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā**: This school accepts only one means of valid knowledge: verbal testimony, specifically the Vedic injunctions. It maintains that the Vedas are eternal and not authored by any person. Its primary focus is the performance of ritual actions (*karma-kāṇḍa*) as prescribed in the scriptures. 6. **Uttara-Mīmāṃsā (Vedānta)**: Also relying solely on verbal testimony, this system interprets the Upanishads (*jñāna-kāṇḍa*). It is divided into several sub-schools, such as Advaita (Non-dualism), Viśiṣṭādvaita (Qualified Non-dualism), and Dvaita (Dualism), each offering a distinct perspective on the relationship between the individual self (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*Brahman*). **The Three Systems of Heterodox Philosophy (Nāstika)** 7. **Cārvāka**: This school rejects all means of valid knowledge beyond direct perception. It asserts that consciousness arises from the combination of material elements and denies the existence of an afterlife or a soul. Its goal is the pursuit of worldly pleasure (*bhoga*) within the limits of reason. 8. **Jaina**: This system accepts two means of valid knowledge: perception and inference. It posits seven categories (*tattva*), including the soul (*jīva*), non-soul (*ajīva*), influx of karma (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), stoppage of influx (*saṃvara*), shedding of karma (*nirjarā*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). Liberation is attained through the practice of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and ascetic discipline. 9. **Bauddha**: This school accepts four means of valid knowledge: perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony. It is further divided into two main branches: Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika (which accept external objects) and Yogācāra and Mādhyamika (which deny external objects). The ultimate goal is the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha*) through the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path. **Conclusion** This compendium provides a systematic overview of the diverse philosophical traditions of India, highlighting their respective methodologies and soteriological goals. By understanding the foundations of these systems, one gains insight into the intellectual landscape of classical Indian thought. *Note: This text is based on the standard classification of Indian philosophy found in the Prasthāna-bheda.*

Regarding what was stated by the mantra fragment "the cup with its mouth downward": the head, consisting of the region above the throat, is indeed that which is described; it is called a "cup" (*camasa*) because it is the instrument for consuming [food] in the form of the mouth. It is "mouth-downward" (*arvāgbila*) because of the opening in the form of the mouth located below; it is "upward-bottomed" (*ūrdhvabudhna*) because of its shape as a base (*budhna*) consisting of the thick, upper part.
For in the world, a well-known cup (camasa) has its opening upwards and its base horizontal; but this portion above the throat, possessing the aforementioned qualities, is a distinct kind of cup.
[The authoritative texts with their commentaries.]
Praśna Saṃhitā, Prapāṭhaka 5, Section 108: "This is the tail, the foundation."

Of this person consisting of food (*annamaya-puruṣa*), which possesses limbs such as the head, these two feet visible below the navel are called "tail" because they serve as a support, being the cause of stability.

109. That which was stated as "this is Brahman, this is Kṣatra... this is the Self"—that very Brahman is the form of everything, including the Kṣatra, the worlds, the gods, and so forth; it is that which is denoted by the word "all."

110. "'All this is what this Self is'"—that which was called "this Self" is Brahman; that very same [Brahman] has all bodies as its substrate and is denoted by the word "all. 111. "'It created all this, whatever there is. Having created it, it entered into it. Having entered it, it became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat).'"

II. "This... what more? 112. "'Indra, lord of Śacī; oppressed by Bala; the unshakable bull; victorious in battles' (?). Indra is the husband of the goddess named Śacī, the sovereign of the gods. Although he suffered affliction from the asura named Bala, he nevertheless remained steadfast and impossible to dislodge from his position; for he was one whom others could not overcome on the fields of battle, or who thoroughly overcomes others.
113. ‘O Indra, come!
O Lord of Bay Horses, come! O Sovereign of the Gods, endowed with supreme majesty, accompanied by the excellent horse named Uccaiḥśravas—come to our sacrifice to accept your portion of the oblation.
114. ‘The senses... [from] their objects. 115. ‘For the objects are superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects.’
The intellect (buddhi) is superior to the mind (manas), and the Great Self (mahān ātmā) is superior to the intellect.

"Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal. (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.28)

III: "Higher than the senses..."

The body, which serves as the chariot for the rider known as the Self; the senses, which serve as the means of guidance for the seeker of liberation in the task of withdrawing from sense objects—those senses which have been described as requiring mastery; in comparison to these, the objects such as sound and so forth within their range must be brought under even greater control, being established by remaining out of one's immediate presence. Even more than those, the mind, which performs the function of grasping objects, must be brought under supreme control.

In relation to that, the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of determinative resolve (*adhyavasāya*), must be brought under control by means of the elimination of false resolve. Furthermore, the conscious being (*cetana*) must be made to possess right volition (*saṃkalpa*), for it is more subject to control than even that [intellect], since determinative resolve follows volition. Therefore, the body—even more so than the self—must be brought under control such that its engagement in and withdrawal from activities within the scope of prescribed and prohibited acts occurs according to rule; otherwise, the fault of unrestrained license (*ucchṛṅkhalatā*) would ensue.

In relation to that [individual soul], the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*)—who is to be brought under control with even greater excellence, who is denoted by the term "unconditioned person" (*nirupādhikapuruṣa*), and who possesses the resolve to bring about the completion of His own worship by the devotee—is the one to be accomplished; for all activities and cessations of action are dependent upon His will. Once the Supreme Person has been brought under control through taking refuge in Him, nothing else whatsoever remains in the world that must be further subdued. He alone is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), the final and ultimate goal.
(Praśna Upaniṣad 1.16: "These three deities..."; 1.17: "The Lord of what has been and what is to be.")
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with their commentaries [are contained] in the *Prasannapadā*.
"I shall lead you."

120. "O Jābāla Satyakāma! I shall initiate you; I shall bring about for you the state of being consecrated by the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), which is necessary for the study of the Vedas and other such pursuits.
121. "Both heaven and earth are contained within him; both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and the stars are all contained within him."

Within this Supreme Self, denoted by the term "small ether" (daharākāśa), heaven, earth, fire, wind, the sun, lightning, and the stars—all these exist perfectly contained within its interior, as if they were not known by anyone at all.
122. "The chest itself is the altar; the hairs are the sacrificial grass; the heart is the Gārhapatya fire."

Of this very Self known as Vaiśvānara, who is the locus for the offering of the vital breaths (prāṇa), the region of the chest belonging to the body of the worshipper is the sacrificial altar (vedi). All the hairs on the body of the worshipper are the sacrificial grass (barhis). The digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) delimited by the heart-lotus occupies the place of the Gārhapatya fire. As it is said in the Praśna Upaniṣad: "The knowers of Brahman, those who have maintained the five sacred fires, and those who have thrice performed the Nāciketa rite, speak of two drinking the fruit of their good deeds in the world of merit—having entered the cave of the heart, in the highest supreme state—as Shadow and Light. (Praśna Saṃhitā 4.7)
The authoritative means of knowledge with their commentaries,
*Pra.saṃ.* 125: "This is the true city of Brahman."

This supreme Brahman, known as the subtle ether (daharākāśa), exists like a city because it possesses the objects of enjoyment, the places of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the class of enjoyers; it is the Truth, immutable, or rather, it possesses truthfulness characterized by its role as the regulator of both the conscious and the unconscious. 126. "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman."
164,250 II This is the immortal (amṛta) 238.

That person who is seen by yogis abiding within the eye is indeed the controller of all; this very one possesses immortality, which consists in being the unsurpassed object of enjoyment and is unmixed with suffering, and it is Brahman, possessing unsurpassed greatness.

127. "O Satyakāma! This *oṃkāra*—the *praṇava*—is indeed both the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*) Brahman. Therefore, the wise man follows one or the other by this very path. O Satyakāma! That which is the *oṃkāra*, the *praṇava*, is non-different from the Brahman consisting of both the higher and the lower, because it is the designator (*vācaka*) of both [and because of the figurative identification of the designator with the designated]. For that very reason, the practitioner, relying solely upon the path whose nature is *oṃkāra*, meditates upon Brahman in either its higher or lower form.

128. "Having departed from here after death, I shall attain that"—the conscious one who has perfected his meditation should remain free from doubt, thinking: "Having ascended out of this body produced by *prārabdha*-karma, I shall certainly attain the Supreme Self, distinguished by a specific non-material realm. 129. "Higher than this mass of living beings, higher than the high."
"From this Self [proceed] the vital breaths ... from the gods [proceed] the worlds" (II). "'From this ... they issue forth in different directions.'"

131. "O Gārgī! By the command of this Imperishable (akṣara), men praise one who gives; the gods depend upon the sacrificer, and the ancestors depend [upon him]. O Gārgī! It is by the command in the form of the ruling authority of that Supreme Brahman—which is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all conscious beings and is denoted by the word 'Imperishable' because it is devoid of decay—that those who perform actions such as giving are praised. The gods and the ancestors are likewise dependent [upon the fruits of such actions].

The authoritative scriptures (*pramāṇas*), along with their commentaries, praise those devoted to giving— such conscious beings whose inner hearts have been drawn by that very action— openly, saying, "This person has performed such an act that is pleasing to the Blessed One. Similarly, the gods rejoice in those conscious beings who, in accordance with the Vedas and other scriptures which constitute the command of the Blessed One, perform sacrifices and the like, as their own minds are drawn by those sacrifices and deeds they have performed.

When a person performs ancestral rites (*paitṛka-karma*) in accordance with the command of the Blessed One, as if uttering the *svadhā* invocation, the ancestors—whose hearts are drawn by that *svadhā* and other offerings—render him possessed of good fame with great satisfaction.

132. "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart; under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart; under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, moments, hours, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years stand held apart. "Under its... they stand. (264, 316)
III "Of this... O Gārgī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8) [which is] nowhere unopposed.

The divine form that exists, transcending old age and death, and endowed with numerous auspicious qualities such as dispassion and sovereignty—that is the abode in the supreme heaven.
134. ‘The creator of these persons. 135. ‘By this very sacrifice, the Kāpeyas caused Caitraratha to sacrifice.
By the aforementioned sacrifice, the Kāpeyas—Brāhmaṇas born of the Kapila lineage—acting as priests, caused the Kṣatriya named Caitraratha to perform the sacrifice.

136. "In this very way, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know: 'We shall merge into Being. Just as the juices of trees such as the *vakula* and *kuṭaja*—which are designated by the term *makaranda*—when brought to a state of uniformity as honey by bees, do not discern and know, "I am the juice of this particular tree," in the same way, all creatures [behave].

(Consisting of volition) at the time of deep sleep, within the Self of the Wise (prājña-ātman) denoted by the word "Being," they do not perceive any specific distinction—such as "I am his son," "I have this name," "I have merged into Being," or "I shall merge into Being"—regarding that dissolution designated by the term "mergence" (sampatti), which is not inconsistent with their subsequent re-emergence.
137. "In this very way, this serene being (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form."

Just as air and other elements, having approached their own causal substance and abandoned their state of being effects, become distinguished by a form resembling that of the cause; even so, the individual soul (jīva), having reached the Supreme Brahman characterized by a specific location via a particular path (the path beginning with light, etc.), abandons its transmigratory state and manifests its own true nature—which is similar to the functioning of the Supreme Self—and thus becomes one for whom the previously concealed qualities such as freedom from sin have ceased to be hidden.

138. "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true. The Supreme Self, denoted by the term "the small ether" (*daharākāśa*), is untouched by good or evil deeds; it is devoid of old age and death, free from the connection with grief and its cause—karma—and far removed from hunger and thirst. It is distinguished as the Imperishable and the Supreme Ether, and its resolve is unimpeded. (Praśna Upaniṣad).

139. "This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman..."
They call this "the gathering of all that is lovely," for indeed, all lovely things gather toward it.
And he is also "the leader of the lovely," for he leads all lovely things.

This very one is indeed the "Light-bringer" (*bhāmanī*), for he shines in all worlds. Satyakāma Jābāla, addressing Upakośala—who possessed an intense mental disposition for receiving instruction—instructed him: "O Upakośala! That Person who is directly realized by yogins as residing within the locus of the eyes, he is this very one, acting as the Controller, denoted by the term 'Self' (*ātman*). This very reality possesses immortality, which consists in being the unsurpassed object of enjoyment; it possesses fearlessness, which consists in being unmixed with suffering; and it possesses Brahminhood, which consists in unsurpassed greatness."

The wise call this Person "Saṃyadvāma" (the one in whom all desirable things are gathered). Because all things worthy of prayer are contained within him alone, he is the sole locus of all auspicious qualities. Since he bestows beautiful intelligence upon those who take refuge in him, he is called "Vāmanī" (the bestower of beauty). Since he possesses a radiant form that pervades all the aforementioned worlds, he is therefore called "Bhāmanī" (the possessor of light). 140.
"It is He alone who causes him to perform good deeds whom He leads upward from these worlds; it is He alone who causes him to perform evil deeds whom He leads downward.

That conscious being whom [the Lord] intends to elevate from the mortal worlds—such as this one—which are fit for the experience of the fruits of mere karma, and lead him to the world of the Blessed One, Him this Supreme Self alone causes to perform good deeds, which serve as the means for that end. But as for that conscious being [whom He intends to lead] even from these attained mortal worlds...
If He desires to lead [the individual] to the lower worlds that conceal the bliss of the Self, He impels him to perform those actions that obstruct spiritual practice.
141 1 "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."

142. "But he indeed is an *agnihotrī* who speaks the truth.

He who performs truthful speech—which is a primary subsidiary (*pradhānāṅga*) of the *agnihotra*—is alone worthy to be called an *agnihotrī* by virtue of performing the *agnihotra* with all its subsidiaries. But he who does not do so would not be an *agnihotrī* at all; for that which is performed contrary to the injunction is equivalent to what was not done. 143. "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly through the truth. "But he indeed speaks surpassingly... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16.1] 230, 231, 233. II. "But he indeed speaks surpassingly... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16.1]

One who speaks of that which is characterized by the Supreme Brahman—the object of meditation—which is changeless due to its constant, uniform nature, and is therefore denoted by the term "Satya" (the Real); such a person, speaking of his own object of meditation as being the most excellent of all, is truly an *ativādī* (one who speaks beyond), and no other. 144. "'This is the world of Brahman, O Emperor,' so he said. Yājñavalkya spoke thus to Janaka: "O Lord of the Mandala! That Self which was described as the object to be seen in the words, 'One should see the Self in the Self alone'—that very Self is this world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), for Brahman itself is the world."
145. "This is my Self within the heart; this is Brahman. (228, 230, 133, 147)

This [Self] in the heart (II' epa ... hṛdaye), characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*), is subtler than rice and other grains, and greater than the earth and other elements; it possesses all actions, all desires, and so forth, and because all its desires have been attained, it is the Self of all.

147. ‘This is my Self within the heart, greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds.
It possesses all works, all desires, all odors, and all tastes; it pervades all this, and is speechless and indifferent.’

This Supreme Self, who has become the Supreme Brahman and is present within my heart, possesses a greatness that surpasses all objects perceived by us—from the earth, which is the greatest of all things seen by us; greater than that, the intermediate space (antarikṣa); greater than that, the heavenly world (dyuloka); and greater than all these worlds combined, He is the creator of the entire universe, supremely pure, endowed with every kind of object of enjoyment and the means of enjoyment, and non-material in nature.

He is enriched with all kinds of fragrances, tastes, and so forth, which are common, eternal, faultless, unsurpassed, and constitute His own objects of enjoyment; He has taken possession of all auspicious qualities and, having attained every desire, sits maintaining the supreme silence of indifference toward all these things already obtained.

148. "This is the Lord of the worlds, this is the Ruler of all"—endowed with the sovereignty previously described, this Supreme Self alone is the Master of all worlds, the one who relishes the aesthetic delight of the play consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and the Controller of all sentient and insentient beings.
149. "This is your path":

when liberation, which has been indicated as the fruit of the meditation (*upāsana*) performed according to the method prescribed in the Vedāntas, is sought to be attained, the very rites seen by the seers (*ṛṣis*)—those to be accomplished through the Gārhapatya and other fires—which are devoid of desire for rewards and are performed as auxiliary limbs of knowledge (*jñāna*), constitute your auspicious path free from obstacles.
150. "This is your holy, well-made world of Brahman."

"O you who are devoted to sacrifice! Come, for this world belonging to the Four-faced One (Brahmā), which has been acquired through the meritorious deeds performed by you, now belongs to you alone. Thus they call out to those who have offered oblations into the Agnihotra and other rites—which are subsidiary to the meditations prescribed as means to liberation—and who have performed those rituals according to rule and at the proper time, addressing the sacrificer, the performer of the actions.
(Praśna Saṃhitā)

151) state: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form."
"He is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa. (20, 84, 120) 229, 392, 152.

This Supreme Self, dwelling within the hearts of all moving and unmoving beings, is their controller; untouched by good or evil deeds, shining in His divine abode, He is the non-dual One denoted by the term Nārāyaṇa—the Supreme Self.
(153) "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of all beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer, so that these worlds may not be confounded."

(Devoid of excellence produced by good or evil actions according to the manner described) — this one is the Supreme Self, possessing the sovereignty over the entire world consisting of both the sentient and the insentient; He alone is the sovereign (śeṣin) of all living beings; He alone is the protector of all creatures through His unconditioned compassion; He alone, having established the inviolable boundaries of conduct, is the guardian of the distinct and regulated affairs of all the worlds like a dam (setu); and by that very fact, He is the sustainer of the entire world.
154. ‘This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
it is seen by those who perceive the subtle, through a subtle intellect. (Praśna Upaniṣad)
The Giver of Bliss (Ānandayitā), having bestowed the Pramāṇas along with their commentaries upon living beings according to the Prajñāsamuccaya, makes them joyful as is appropriate for each.

There is no other whatsoever. "This, my dear! is both our knowledge of the sciences and our knowledge of the Self. "O Somaśarman! O Upakośala! [He said: "Prāṇa is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman"; "Earth, fire, food, and the sun"; "Water, the quarters, the stars, and the moon"; "Prāṇa and space."

Know that this knowledge which was taught to you as "Heaven" and "Lightning" is the knowledge pertaining to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); likewise, it is the knowledge pertaining to us, who consist of the forms of the fires—the Gārhapatya, Anvāhāryapacana, and Āhavanīya. (Thus understand. 157. "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self. "All this has that as its self.

42, 56, 120, 404 This is the truth: the entire world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, as established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is pervaded by this Brahman, which serves as both its material cause (*upādāna*) and its inner ruler (*antaryāmin*). That Supreme Self is the controller of all. (Therefore, O Śvetaketu! you are of the nature of that very Brahman. 158. "The mind is woven across with all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)," Praśna Upaniṣad...

Praśna Saṃhitā: Janaka’s question is, "What is the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with their explanations? Yājñavalkya’s reply is: "That person (*puruṣa*), who is the individual soul (*jīva*), whose characteristic is consciousness (*vijñāna*), who resides within the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—which is designated by the term 'breath' (*prāṇa*)—and whose essential nature is light (*prakāśa*)—which is designated by the term 'light' (*jyotis*)—is indeed the Self (*ātman*)."
"Which is that deity?

"It is *prāṇa* (breath)," he said. "For indeed, all these beings enter into *prāṇa* alone and emerge from *prāṇa* alone. This is the deity connected with the *prastāva*. Had you chanted the *prastāva* without knowing it, your head would have fallen off."
"Having superimposed [this] upon the two *prastāva* sections, which deity have you meditated upon as the object of worship?"—this is the question posed by the *Prastotṛ* to Uṣasti.

This is the answer to Uṣasti: "Having superposed [the meditation] upon the Prastāva section, the deity to be meditated upon is the one whose nature is 'Prāṇa' (the Life-force). [He is called] Prāṇa because he causes all things to breathe. Since all beings, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, which are perceived, go to dissolution in the very entity called Prāṇa, and from Prāṇa they emerge, therefore that deity whose form is Prāṇa—as established in the Vedānta—is indeed that, being the locus of the dissolution and origination of all beings."
"And if you had performed the *prastāva* without knowing that deity who is the nature of breath, then your head would surely have fallen off; there is no doubt about this."
165. "O Śākalya, why do you speak of this person as if he were Raikva with the cart?

Ah, Haṃsa! This king named Jānaśruti is indeed praised by you as being 'of great splendor. On account of what greatness do you praise him? Is this king endowed with such great majesty as Raikva, who sat beneath a cart and was a knower of Brahman? Not at all. Therefore, this praise of yours is fruitless. 166. "The agent, the Lord, the Person, whose source is Brahman..."

Gārgī asks Yājñavalkya: "What is that entity which serves as the support, by being woven like warp and woof, for all objects delimited by the three periods of time—past, future, and present—that is called unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa)?
168. "To whom will you give me? (kasmai māṃ dāsyasi) [referring to the questioner].

"O you who are intent on giving away all your possessions! My father, the gifts you have given thus far are fruitless because of the gift of old cows; for they are unfit for use. But I might somehow be useful for some task or other, as there might be some work to be accomplished by me for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) due to my youth. Therefore, tell me—whom among the officiating priests will you strive to give me to? Thus spoke Naciketas.

169. To whose sacrifice do the gods come, and to whose do they not? Among many sacrificers, he who first secures the deities sacrifices to them on the following day. Since there is a plurality of sacrificers performing sacrifices such as the New and Full Moon rites, a doubt arises as to which kind of sacrificer’s sacrifice the deities, who partake of the oblations, might attend; for in the absence of a determining factor, uncertainty would prevail. Therefore, one should perform the rite called *anvādhāna* on the preceding day itself, in order to secure the deities for the sacrifice to be performed on the following day.

And in that regard, one should form the intention (saṅkalpa): "I shall sacrifice to these deities with this particular substance—be it fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, a sacrificial cake, or another such material. Then, when the following day has arrived, one should perform the sacrifice to those deities. Thus, because the deities have already been formally grasped on the previous day, no room for doubt regarding them arises.

170. What is the cause? What is the nature of that reality which is extolled in the Śrutis and other scriptures as being denoted by the term *brahman* due to its being the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe?
171. "What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth? O wise ones, ask this with your mind: upon what did he stand while supporting the worlds?"
Pṛ.saṃ.
Pramāṇas with commentaries.

Who are those of a reflective nature and discerning? Indeed, in this world, a man desiring to build a house cuts down a certain tree in the forest and constructs his house with its timber (wood).

By that analogy, consider this as well: from what kind of tree born in the forest did the Creator of the world fashion the celestial realm? What might that forest have been, serving as the locus for such trees? And what might that tree have been—the material cause of wood existing within such a forest—by which the abode of the world was constructed? Furthermore, what kind of entity, endowed with such great majesty, could it be that, acting as the agent, sustained all worlds within itself and exercised control over them? Go to a teacher, inquire about this matter to be considered, and learn!
172. "But action itself must be thoroughly investigated.

Action—which is synonymous with exertion and effort, consisting of the restraint of the mind through the contemplation of what is to be discarded among other things to be heard—must be accomplished because it is the cause of the steadfastness characterized by the resolve, "Brahman alone is to be heard.
173. "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"

"What entity exists that is our inner controller (*antaryāmin*), which has become our very self (*ātmabhūta*) and possesses unsurpassed greatness? This must be determined"—thus the learned priests (such as Prācīnaśāla and others) came together and deliberated in one place.
"Who indeed could breathe, who could inhale, if this bliss (*ānanda*) were not present in this space (*ākāśa*)? For it is he alone who brings about bliss.
Having gone [to him], they [realized this].
