"O Bālāki, at what time did this person experience sleep? In what place did he obtain sleep? And from what place did he emerge and arise? (Thus Ajātaśatru questioned Bālāki.)

176. ‘The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara. The one God rules over both the perishable and the individual self (ātman). Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through becoming His true essence, there occurs at the end the cessation of all cosmic illusion (māyā). Prakṛti, denoted by the term *pradhāna*, is called the “perishable” (*kṣara*). And the individual soul (*jīva*), who takes away that which has become an object of enjoyment for his own sake, is called the “imperishable” (*akṣara*) because he is free from the nature of death.

These two, denoted by the terms *kṣara* (the perishable) and *akṣara* (the imperishable), are the sentient and the insentient; the Lord, who is devoid of any equal or superior, governs them. Through the repeated contemplation (*saṃśīlana*) of that Lord—the object of support—by means of yoga, which consists of the practice of contemplating the object of meditation even when one has emerged from formal practice, and through the manifestation of reality (*tattva*) resulting from that practice which serves as a means, consisting of reflection in a form identical to direct perception, there occurs at the end of the body a complete cessation of the connection with the entire *prakṛti*, which is denoted by the term *māyā*, such that it never arises again.
177. "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this.

Because it possesses the four-footed nature found in a specific form of the Gāyatrī, and because it is similar to the Gāyatrī, the Supreme Brahman itself is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī"; it is the self of all manifest beings, both moving and non-moving. 178. "The Cow is without beginning or end, belonging to the All-pervading Lord."
the means of valid cognition with their commentaries, Prajñāsamuccaya.

181. "Four fifteen-night [sacrifices] (d)... they go to godhood. There are four specific sacrifices to be accomplished over a period of fifteen days. And the sacrificers, the qualified persons, attain the state of being the self—the state of being the controller—of that particular body denoted by the term "god.
182. "From the moon to lightning; there a person who is non-human..."
By them he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman. Those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool.

(The conscious knowers of Brahman: Those who travel by way of the light and other stages reach from the moon a superphysical person (*puruṣa*) named Lightning. That person named Lightning is designated as "non-human" (*amānava*). That non-human being leads these knowers of Brahman—who have perfected the means—to Brahman. And this path, beginning with the light, is called the "path of the gods" because it is led by divine superphysical beings; and it is called the "path of Brahman" because it leads to Brahman.

By this path beginning with light (*arcis*) and leading to Brahman, those who depart do not return again to *saṃsāra*—that cycle of birth, death, and so forth, which is most terrible because it is difficult to cross and abounds in afflictions, and which brings about the acquisition of human and other bodies. "From Him, the Illusionist (*māyin*), creates all this—the Vedas, sacrifices, rituals, vows, the past, the future, and whatever the Vedas declare; and in Him another is confined by illusion. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.9) All the Vedas known as the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva...

The meters, as well as the five great sacrifices beginning with the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the ritual rites (*kratavaḥ*) such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the vows (*vrata*) such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, and whatever else is declared in the Vedas—whether pertaining to the past, present, or future—all these are brought forth by the Lord (*īśvara*), the presiding controller of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) known as *māyā*, from this very instrument denoted by the word *māyā*.

Through the object in the form of *māyā* which rests upon the Lord, the individual soul (*jīva*)—whose innate nature is concealed—transmigrates, being distinct from the Supreme Self who is the presiding controller of *māyā*.
(Prasthānasaṃgraha)
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries [are found] at Pra.saṃ.
186. "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than heaven, greater than these..."
"Greater than the worlds... greater than the intermediate space.

(187) "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord; the unborn worlds are joined with the objects of experience for the enjoyer. But the infinite Self, whose form is the universe, is indeed the non-agent. When one perceives these three as this Brahman..."

The Lord is possessed of uncontracted knowledge, and the individual soul (*jīva*) is possessed of contracted knowledge; both of these are indeed devoid of origin. Likewise, there is another single *prakṛti* which is endowed with the purpose of providing experience for the experiencing soul; that too is likewise devoid of origin. (Even though all three entities share the commonality of being devoid of origin, their distinct differences remain clearly manifest.)

Since the Supreme Self (paramātman) is present within every body, being unlimited and the source of infinite auspicious qualities, He is devoid of agency associated with the desire for fruits; for this very reason, He is not bound by primordial nature (prakṛti) for the sake of His own enjoyment. Thus, he who determines the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord as distinct from one another through the knowledge consisting of meditation, becomes endowed with the qualities of Brahman, such as uncontracted knowledge and so forth. "One should restrain the intellect within the Great Self.
Page numbers for the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* with commentaries.
Page numbers.
Having realized this, he has abandoned the joy caused by the acquisition of objects and the sorrow caused by their non-acquisition.
190. "The gods worship him as the light of lights, as life, and as immortality."

That which, by virtue of its luminosity, is the bestower of light upon all things known to the world and the scriptures—such as the sun, the moon, lightning, and so forth—and which is the primary cause of the vital breath (prāṇa) consisting of inhalation and exhalation for all living beings; which is unlimited by time because it is free from birth, old age, and death, characterized by mortality; that Supreme Brahman, who is the Self of all, is worshipped by the gods who dwell above human beings.
191. ‘He threw it with a staff. 192. ‘The gods indeed worship this very Self; therefore all worlds and all desires are attained by them.’

All the remaining gods perform worship upon this very Self—this individual soul (jīvātman) endowed with the eight qualities beginning with freedom from evil, which was taught by Prajāpati to Indra, and which Indra himself received and taught to the gods after learning it from Brahmā; and they likewise worship the Supreme Self, the Highest Person who is to be attained. They do not, however, worship that [Self] as it was first grasped by Virocana.

Therefore, for the gods who worship such a Self, there arises the experience of Brahman, characterized by the attainment of all worlds and all desires; however, for asuras like you, there is no room for such an experience of Brahman. 193. 1. "Some call him the twenty-sixth, while others, the knowers of the Atharvaśiras, call the Puruṣa devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) the twenty-seventh. 2. "Him... while others."

That Supreme Self who is remembered through the mantras prescribed in the Atharva Veda—that Supreme Person, whose existence is not dependent on the three *guṇas* and is therefore denoted by the term "Nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities), and who is to be known by means of a pure intellect (*buddhi*) denoted by the word "Saṅkhyā"—some call this the twenty-sixth *tattva*. Others, however, count the *tattva* of Time (*kāla*) separately.
(40. .pra. saṃ.)

The proponents of the *Prasaṅgaparigha* (Pra.saṃ.vādinaḥ) declare the twenty-seventh principle to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with its commentary; they understand this matter through those scriptural portions (*śrutibhāga*) that constitute the head of the *Atharvaveda*.
194. "He initiated him": the teacher performed the sacrament called *upanayana* for that young brahmin who had come for the purpose of acquiring knowledge.
"Whatever they become here—whether a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar... or a gnat, or a mosquito—they become that very thing."

Those living beings who have become unified with [Brahman] during the specific state known as deep sleep (suṣupti), upon arising from that deep sleep and reaching the waking state, [recall] prior to the deep sleep [beings such as] tigers, lions, wolves, boars... gadflies, mosquitoes, and so forth. 195.

Whatever kind of body they possessed, they maintain the same kind of ego-identification with that very body; permeated by their former latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they arise exactly as they were. 196.
"Those who have drunk that [nectar]."
135 197. "That fire thought.

By its own volition alone, the Supreme Brahman attained another state in the form of a body of light; [it thought]: "I myself, having created the world consisting of the gross and the subtle, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—comprising the pure and the impure, the auspicious and the inauspicious, the moving and the unmoving, and the sentient and the insentient—and having entered into every object by pervading all things as their underlying substrate, remain as that alone."

Having entered [into the world], while remaining in its changeless state as that which is eternally of one form in the nature of consciousness, yet simultaneously being that which possesses the nature of consciousness as the locus of modification consisting in the abandonment of its prior state, Brahman itself became the possessor of the names and forms of both the conscious and the unconscious.

And that very [Brahman], though it assumes the names and forms of the sentient and the insentient—designated as "real" and "unreal"—and though it becomes the insentient world through its possession of genus, quality, and action (which is denoted by words expressing genus, quality, and so forth), and the collection of sentient beings which is devoid of genus, quality, and so forth; the collection of sentient beings which is the substratum of the insentient class, and the insentient class which is dependent upon it; and likewise, though it possesses both an un-inert nature and an inert nature, Brahman remains indeed its own self-nature, characterized by immutability and non-abandonment.
202. "That is to be sought.
203. "Regarding this, there is also this verse:"
Regarding that very same matter established by the preceding portion of the Brāhmaṇa, this verse consisting of a mantra also remains awake, providing support for the stated meaning:

"Then it made itself its own self. When Brahman existed as one whose name and form were undivided, it itself, having accepted its own essential nature as the material cause (*upādāna*), performed the work consisting of bringing about the manifestation of its own name and form.

205. "He cast that oblation into the very Self, into the fire Vaiśvānara within the heart. He performed the casting of the offering as an oblation precisely into the fire whose nature is the Self, which is designated by the term Vaiśvānara and resides in the location of the heart. 206. "This is the truth: as from a well-kindled [fire]... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10, 4.18).

The Brahman previously described, characterized by qualities such as omniscience, is the Truth—eternal and devoid of the six kinds of phenomenal change. Just as sparks arise from fire residing within a heated iron ball, all objects in the form of effects are born from the Supreme Self. [Thus end] the means of valid cognition with their commentaries.

Praśna Saṃhitā 207: This very thing has been stated in the Ṛgveda with reference to Brahman, known as Gāyatrī, which consists of four feet and is endowed with sixfold aspects; having referred to that which possesses unlimited greatness by means of the verse to be cited later, namely "So great is His majesty," it is thus described.
208. "It entered into that very [Being]; having entered into that," 209.

"Regarding this, there is this verse: 'The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Taking up as the subject matter for exposition this triad—the nature of Brahman as established in this statement, the knowledge thereof, and its fruit—the Vedic utterance consisting of the words of the mantra beginning with "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" has proceeded.
210. "In the beginning, it thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.3.6; 4.1.2; 8.1.281)
II. "Then he thought... may I be many, may I procreate" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3). The authoritative texts with their commentaries [are as follows].

Having meditated upon that Supreme Brahman as the object of worship, the sage named Vāmadeva—while in a state of meditation—realized his own identity with everyone, including Manu and others, as well as the Sun and others, thinking, "My very self is the self of Manu and the rest, and my very self is the self of the Sun and the rest," and even, "I am the self of the wise seer named Kakṣīvat. (213) Both the gods and the asuras perceived this. They said: "...Indra indeed set out among the gods, and Virocana among the asuras."
"Agreeing with one another, they both approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands.

Having heard and understood Prajāpati’s discourse—concluding with the words, "The Self which is free from evil... having found it, one knows it"—both the gods and the asuras did so by way of tradition (*aitihya*). Having understood it, they spoke of it within their respective circles. From among the assembly of the gods, Indra alone set out on a journey toward Prajāpati, his teacher; and Virocana, the leader of the asuras, did likewise.
Both of them, each revealing his own inner disposition to the other, took fuel as their offering and went into the presence of Prajāpati.
"That is Brahman, that is the Immortal" (214);
"That which one should place within the peaceful Self" (215).
216. "One should restrain that [breath] in the self of knowledge. 217. "The Vasus live upon that which is the first nectar.

Among the five nectars previously mentioned, such as the red one and so forth, that which is the first nectar called "the red"—the form perceived as red at the time of seeing the sun—that is enjoyed by the Vasus, headed by Agni, in the manner to be described hereafter.

218. "Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes, and the spokes are fixed upon the nave, even so these elements (*bhūtamātrā*) are fixed upon the elements of discernment (*prajñāmātrā*), and the elements of discernment are fixed upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This very vital breath is the self of discernment—blissful, undecaying, and immortal.

Just as the rim of a chariot wheel (the circular wooden part of the chariot wheel) is connected by the relationship of support and supported to the pieces of wood denoted by the word "spoke," which are connected to the nave (axle) of the chariot. *Praśna Upaniṣad*.

Just as the spokes (arāḥ) together with their descriptions in the *Praśnopaniṣad* are connected by the relationship of support and supported to the axle (akṣa)— which is denoted by the term "hub" (*nābhi*) and situated in the center of the chariot wheel— so too everything comprised by the term "elements" (*bhūtamātrā*), having entered into the state of the grasped and the grasper, is entrusted to those conscious beings denoted by the term "intellect-elements" (*prajñāmātrā*)— connected by the relationship of support and supported.

And all those volitions, denoted by the term "mere intellect" (*prajñāmātra*), are connected through the relationship of substratum and superstratum with the Supreme Self, which is denoted by the term "Prāṇa. This Supreme Self, the substratum of everything, denoted by the word Prāṇa, is the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*), the locus of unconditioned omniscience, bliss, agelessness, and immortality. 219.

"Just as a chief enjoys [the wealth] with his own [subordinates], or as his subordinates enjoy the chief, even so this conscious Self enjoys with these selves, and even so these selves enjoy him. (Praśna Upaniṣad)

Just as experts know the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with their explanations, so too all living beings—though reaching daily during deep sleep the Supreme Self, who is like a hidden treasure, who is the ultimate object of desire for conscious beings, who is denoted by the word "Brahman," and who is the space within the heart—do not recognize or attain Him. Although they go into His presence, they do not perceive it due to ignorance regarding their own departure to that place; for they have been led to a different state of being by the karma called *avidyā*, which is designated by the term "untruth."

221. "Just as a tuft of *iṣīkā* grass thrown into a fire is consumed, even so are all his evils consumed. 222. "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice; whatever first oblation he may offer, let him offer it with the words, 'Svāhā to Prāṇa! For a man established in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā who is seated for the purpose of eating, the food that arrives first is itself the means for the sacrifice consisting of the Prāṇāgnihotra.
If that eater should offer the first oblation with that food, then he should offer that oblation with the mantra: "To Prāṇa, Svāhā" (200, 211).

223. "This very syllable, O Gārgī, is unseen but the seer; unheard but the hearer; unthought but the thinker; unknown but the knower. There is no other seer than this, there is no other hearer than this, there is no other thinker than this, there is no other knower than this. In this very syllable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven, warp and woof."

O Gārgī! That which was previously introduced as the Supreme Brahman denoted by the term *akṣara* (the Imperishable) is this very thing: while remaining unperceived by conscious beings other than yogis, it is the direct perceiver of form and other qualities. Likewise, while remaining outside the scope of verbal knowledge dependent upon the ears of non-yogis, it is itself capable of hearing all objects; while remaining outside the scope of reflection, observation, and so forth dependent upon the minds of non-yogis, it is itself capable of reflecting upon and observing all objects.

Being beyond the scope of meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*) for those of immature intellect and false practitioners, it is itself capable of all such reflection. There is no other seer, no other hearer, no other thinker, and no other knower like this in the world. O Gārgī, within this very Brahman called the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which has been described thus far, the previously mentioned space (*ākāśa*) is woven as warp and woof, its own nature being entirely dependent upon it. (The authoritative texts with their commentaries are cited in *Praśna-saṃgraha*.)
Pra. Saṃ.:

"The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. The "supreme abode" (*paramaṃ padam*) refers either to the station of Mahāviṣṇu—which is non-material (*aprākṛta*), the substratum of immortality, and all-pervading—or to His most excellent essential nature (*svarūpa*). Those conscious beings designated by the term "wise" (*sūri*), possessing knowledge whose expansion is unimpeded due to the removal of all veils, perceive that [abode] directly and without interruption.

"The subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) dissolve into the source of the elements (bhūtādi); the source of the elements dissolves into the Great One (mahat); the Great One dissolves into the Unmanifest (avyakta); the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (akṣara); the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness (tamas); and Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. "It was differentiated by name and form"—Brahman alone, whose body is the undifferentiated, having been distinguished by its possession of name and form, was made manifest on all sides by itself. "Those who practice austerity and faith while fasting... (2.2.5).

Those renunciants who constantly cultivate faith—characterized by an intense devotion toward the perception and other forms of engagement with Brahman, which is denoted by the word ‘tapas’—attain the supreme ether (paraṃ vyoma), which is the abode of the Imperishable Person.
"By austerity, Brahman is built up; from that, food is produced."
From food come vital breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality in ritual actions.

The Supreme Brahman, by its own volition in the form "May I become many," itself attains a state of orientation toward creation. From such a Supreme Brahman arises the unmanifest (avyākṛta), characterized as an aggregate of sentient and insentient entities in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

And from that unmanifested state denoted by the word "food"—which consists of a collective aggregate of consciousness and unconsciousness—there arise all these: the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the class of enjoyers, the worlds such as heaven which serve as the ground for enjoyment, and the karma conducive to liberation within the web of karma.

229. "Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; there was no sign of distinction... from that [darkness], by its greatness, the One was born. Prior to creation, there existed a reality denoted by the word "darkness" (*tamas*), in which name and form were undifferentiated. And that which had this [darkness] as its body was Brahman alone. Because it had as its body the darkness in which name and form were undifferentiated, it was "One"—the various scriptural authorities with their commentaries [establish this].
*Praśna-saṃhitā*.

Brahman, abiding as the primordial cause (*pra-saṃ-tva*), having become differentiated in name and form due to the darkness (*tamas*) that serves as its gateway and instrumental cause, and having taken recourse to the state of "Greatness" (*mahattva*), manifested itself in the form of the manifold and variegated universe. 230. "Speak of that Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*)."
"Tell me of that Inner Controller who controls this world, the other world, and all beings from within.

(231) "Him, the supreme Great Lord among lords, Him, the supreme Deity among deities"—the most excellent among those possessing lordship, such as Brahmā and others, and therefore the Lord distinguished by greatness; the most excellent object of worship among those worthy of adoration, such as Agni, Indra, and others (we realize the Supreme Self through supreme knowledge).
232. "The Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting."

In order to attain the state of being fit for meditation upon the Supreme Self—who is characterized by qualities such as omniscience and omnipotence and is useful as the object of knowledge and the goal to be attained—one may employ the study of specific Vedic branches received from the mouth of a teacher according to prescribed rules, ritual action in the form of sacrifices involving material offerings and the propitiation of deities, charity in the form of bestowing wealth earned by righteous means upon worthy recipients, austerity in the form of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other penances performed without desire for rewards, and fasting.
The members of the three higher castes intensely desire this. "One who knows it thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journeying forth" (Praśna Upaniṣad).
These are the authoritative texts along with their commentaries.
235. "Thinking of that Self thus, the wise one becomes the immortal Brahman, the Immortal.
236. "Only by knowing that very [Self] does one go beyond death."

Only by knowing the Supreme Person, who shines forth above and beyond the sphere of primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (traiguṇya), and whose form is composed of light, does a conscious worshiper transcend saṃsāra.
237. "By the very path of the syllable Om, the wise one follows that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme."

The person who worships the *praṇava* goes by means of the *oṃkāra* itself as the instrument of travel to that world which the wise (*sūrayaḥ*)—who, according to the teaching "the wise always behold that highest step of Viṣṇu," have attained transcendental vision—behold. Having gone there, he attains Brahman, which is free from the six waves, devoid of old age and death, fearless from any quarter, and supreme as the cause of all.
[See Praśna Upaniṣad 2.8: "Of these two, one eats the sweet *pippala* fruit, while the other looks on without eating. 238. 148.
239. "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
(225, 228, 232) 240. "From him was born one named Caitraratha, a lord of the Kṣatriyas. (thīnām ekaḥ)
Pṛ.saṃ.: The means of valid cognition with their commentaries;
Pra.saṃ.: [The same].
"From that very Self, indeed, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth.
From space, air [arises]."
61, 70, 92, 364 II "From that, indeed... [the fire] was produced" III "From that, indeed... space [arose]"
IV. "From that... from the Self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).

Because it possesses the nature of truth, knowledge, and infinity as described in the Vedic mantra "Truth, Knowledge," the ether (*ākāśa*) was produced from the Supreme Self, who is the Supreme Brahman. From that ether, which constitutes the body of the Supreme Self, the wind (*vāyu*) was produced. And from the wind, which is of the nature of the Supreme Self, fire (*agni*) was produced. And from the fire, which is of the nature of the Blessed Lord, the waters (*āpaḥ*) arose. And from those waters, which are of the nature of the Blessed Lord, the earth (*pṛthivī*) was born.

244. "Therefore, from this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5). This means that distinct from the individual self denoted by the term "consisting of consciousness" which was previously introduced, there is an even more internal self denoted by the term "consisting of bliss," namely the Supreme Self.
Pramāṇas with commentaries, Pūrva-saṃskāra.
II. "Of him... for a long time":

For that person who is established in the contemplation of his own Self as being of the nature of Brahman and who has perfected his practice, the delay in attaining Brahman is only so long as he is not liberated from the body commenced by *prārabdha* karma. Immediately upon liberation, however, he shall become one with Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sadrūpa*).
249. "Of him, as... 250. "Of him, the *karka* [Sāman]..."
"He who knows thus [knows] the deity.
251. "Verily, this Rigveda is the breath of this great Being."

This collection of Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, has manifested effortlessly— like a mere breath— from the Supreme Self, who is the previously mentioned cause and material source of the universe and who is denoted by the terms "Great Being" (mahadbhūta) and "Word" (śabda).
252. 1. "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the urine is *sutejas*" (Pr. Sū. Pr.).
[The following are] the authoritative texts along with their commentaries.
Pṛ.saṃ.
255: "This indeed is its head.
For the person called the body, which consists of the essence of food and is perceived in a gross form, the head is simply the head as seen through direct perception.
256. "This very one is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā) of that [previous one]; he who is the self of the former. "This very one is his ... self."

That which is the self (ātman) of the entire collection of categories beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) and ending with the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), that alone is the self of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya); there is no other. The meaning is that while everything else has another as its inner self, the one consisting of bliss has no other self.
257. "Then those waters thought" (9.11): the bodiless Supreme Self (paramātman) formed a resolve in the manner that will be described.
258. Regarding those [who desired to know the Vaiśvānara-Self], Uddālaka said: "Sirs, this Aśvapati, the King of Kekaya, is currently studying this very Self known as Vaiśvānara; let us go to him.

Addressing the men led by Aupamanyava who were desirous of knowing the Vaiśvānara-Self, Uddālaka spoke: "O noble ones! This Aśvapati, the King of Kekaya, is now worshipping the very Self we desire, known as Vaiśvānara. By good fortune, let us go to him for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara-Self. 259. "So great is His majesty..."

That which was previously stated—that [Brahman] is endowed with four feet known as the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart, and is endowed with sixfold attributes consisting of the functions of singing, protection, being the foundation of the elements, and not being transgressed by the elements; and the functions of being the foundation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and not being transgressed by the vital breaths—all that is the majesty of Brahman known as Gāyatrī.
260. "Of these, I shall make each one threefold."

"Among those deities consisting of fire, water, and food, I shall make the deity that is fire and the deity that is food possess a mutual conjunction characterized by the capacity necessary for creation. [Prapāṭhaka Saṃhitā with Commentary] (Pr. Saṃ. [The authoritative texts (pramāṇas) along with their commentaries.]

By means of that third body which had been placed upon the earth by Viṣṇu, Indra, being positioned behind Viṣṇu, became capable of uprooting and seizing that thunderbolt. 262. "Those who had attained the yoga of meditation beheld the divine power of the Self, established through its own qualities."

The sages, perfected through the worship denoted by the term *dhyāna-yoga*—the means for the direct realization of the Supreme Brahman—perceived Prakṛti, who is denoted by the term *śakti*, as she functions as the instrument of the Lord Nārāyaṇa (who is their own Self), and who is endowed with her own qualities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
263. "Whatever is between those two... 264. "They proceed to the light (*arcis*); from the light to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight..."

Those knowers of Brahman who have reached the culmination of the science of the eyes attain, in every way, the deity presiding over the light (*arcis*). Having attained that, they reach the deity presiding over the day (*ahan*); from that, they reach the deity presiding over the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
265. "These five others become ten."

There are five related to the deities (*daivata*), namely fire, sun, moon, water, and wind—of which four are "swallowing" (*apiyant*) and one, wind, is "being swallowed" (*apīyamāna*). There are five related to the body designated as the self (*ātmapadavācya-dehasambandhin*), namely speech, sight, hearing, mind, and breath—of which four are "swallowing" and one, breath, is "being swallowed. Thus, totaling five, when those called *adhidevata* and those called *adhyātma* are combined, they attain the number ten. Consequently, these should be understood to possess the number ten, just like the dice known as *kṛta*.
266. "In all worlds, there is no freedom of movement for them."

In this world, or within the body, for those sentient beings who depart from this world without having performed the meditation upon the Supreme Self—denoted by the term "the small ether" (*daharākāśa*)—and its related auspicious qualities, there is no unrestricted movement at will through all the worlds suitable for the experience of consciousness. Their state is one of dependence alone, because they remain subject to the power of their past actions (*karma*).
267. "Those two lived there as celibate students (*brahmacarya*) for thirty-two years; Prajāpati then said to them: VER.
Pṛ.saṃ.: The means of valid cognition with commentaries. Pra.saṃ.: [Abbreviation for *Pramāṇasaṃgraha*].

Indra and Virocana, departing from the assembly of the gods and the assembly of the asuras respectively, set out toward Prajāpati. Both of them remained in the presence of Prajāpati for more than thirty years, devoted to the duties of a student—observing the rules of *brahmacarya*, intent upon their meditation, and dedicated to service to the teacher.
268. "The two of them approached a sleeping man...
[and] he struck him with a staff."
II. "The two of them... went [to him]" (371, 378).

Ajātaśatru, occupying the position of a teacher (*ācāryasthāna*), and Bālāki, occupying the position of an inquirer (*jijñāsusthāna*), both approached a certain man in the royal palace; that is, they came into his presence.... Even when called, that man remained lying there in silence, so Ajātaśatru struck him with a staff. 269. "One who has kindled the *Nāciketa* fire three times, having attained union through the three, and performing the three duties, transcends birth and death."

One who has studied the three sections beginning with "This indeed is he who purifies" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.16.1), who performs sacrifices, study, and charity—or who is a practitioner performing *pākayajñas*, *haviryajñas*, and *somayajñas*—attains a connection through the practice of the three fires, which have become the means [of attainment], together with the meditation on the Supreme Self; thus, one transcends the worldly defects known as birth, disease, old age, calamity, and death.
270. "Three quarters of him are the immortal in heaven. 271. "I slew Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son."
"I gave the Arunmukhas, who were ascetics, over to the hyenas. "I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ.

(Indra said to Pratardana: "O Pratardana! Indeed, I destroyed the three-headed one named Viśvarūpa, the son of the divine artisan Tvaṣṭṛ. Furthermore, I delivered certain deceivers—those who are far removed from the knowledge of the Vedas and Vedāntas and merely wear the outward signs of ascetics—to the wild dogs known as *sālāvṛkas* for them to devour."
272. "Choose for yourself a boon from me, whatever you consider to be most beneficial for a human being. [Here follow the authoritative texts with their commentaries.]
Page [Number]:

O Indra! Having perceived that which is most beneficial for the conscious being who has attained human birth—namely, that which accomplishes the supreme human goal—you alone should bestow that upon me. 273. ‘A girdle made of darbha grass’ refers to a specific type of cord; that girdle should be fashioned from the material of a particular kind of grass called darbha.
274. "In this small space within, there is an ether; that which is within it is what must be sought.
"The small... ether," 266, 380.

III. "I am small in this [body]," said Aupamanyava in the presence of Kekaya: "O Blessed One, O King! I am one who meditates upon the Vaiśvānara Self whose body is the heavenly world (dyuloka), you who are endowed with greatness produced by knowledge. Thus spoke Aupamanyava to Kekaya.
276. "For the divine, formless Puruṣa is both external and internal, unborn; he is indeed without breath, without mind, pure, and higher than the highest beyond the Imperishable.

That Puruṣa who exists, established in the station known as the Supreme Sky (*paramavyoman*) designated by the term "Heaven" (*dyu*), who is devoid of material form due to his all-pervasive nature and lack of constituent parts—he is the self-nature of all things, both external and internal. Due to his lack of sense organs, he is free from any connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) or the mind (*manas*), which are the impellers of those organs.

He is "pure" (*śubhra*) because he is devoid of origination, being stainless, the locus of auspiciousness, or the bestower of auspiciousness. He is "higher than that" (*tasmāt paraḥ*), meaning higher than the Pradhāna—which is designated as the "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) and expressed by the term "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*)—and even higher than the *samaṣṭi-puruṣa* (Hiraṇyagarbha), who is the cause of that [Pradhāna].
277. "'The sages call it the difficult path' (*durga pathas-tatkavayo vadanti*).
For the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*) is indeed difficult to attain—difficult to reach; only those who know the truth understand and speak of its path to those desiring to know.
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Praśna Upaniṣad)

The two authorities, along with their commentaries, are mutually equal in qualities such as being free from sin; they are inseparable companions and resemble each other as members of the same class. Both are conscious entities who, like two birds, dwell together by relying upon one and the same body—which, like a tree, is incapable of being cut down. Between them, one is the *jīva*, which experiences and enjoys the fruits of karma that are subject to fruition. The other, however, is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is devoid of the experience of karmic fruits and remains awake with an inherently uncontracted radiance.
281. The "treatises on Dharma" (dharmaśāstrāṇi) are indeed the secondary sciences (aparā vidyā), such as the Ṛgveda and others; the treatises on Dharma are also included therein.
282. "Having shaken off the body."

283. ‘The performance of meditation... by the sacrificers. 284. ‘It is meditated upon, it is occupied by him; it is expanded and impelled again; and presided over by that very same [principle], the world brings forth the goals of human existence.’
"She is fair, without beginning or end, the mother, the source of all beings.
"The world is meditated upon... "She is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech."
And the Supreme Self is not perceived by visual cognition; likewise, it is not perceived by cognition produced by speech—that is, by verbal cognition.
[The following are] the means of valid knowledge with their explanations.

Prasaṅga: There exists no protector or controller whatsoever of the Supreme Self—who is devoid of body, senses, and the like; who is peerless and unsurpassed; who is natural; and who possesses qualities such as all-surpassing knowledge, power, strength, and sovereignty; rather, He alone is the protector of all and the controller of all.

Not even a single indicative mark of this [Being] is perceived in anything; He alone is beyond the reach of speech and mind, the cause of all causes, and the Lord even of the individual soul (jīva), who is itself the master of the senses. There is no other creator for this creator of all, nor any other overlord for this overlord of all. 289. "No effect or instrument of His is found; neither anyone equal to Him nor anyone superior to Him is seen. His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent."

For this Blessed One, the Lord of all worlds, there exists no body, sense organs, or the like subject to karma—as is the case with Brahmā and others. No one else can possibly be conceived as equal to or superior to this Blessed One, the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, His sovereignty, consisting of infinite and immeasurable, wondrous powers such as knowledge, strength, and majesty—which transcend all else and depend solely upon His own nature—is heard of in the Śruti and other authoritative sources:
"The Seer sees neither death nor disease, nor even suffering.
The Seer sees everything; He attains everything in every way."

The wise one who perceives Brahman as described does not perceive death, diseases such as fever, or anything adverse in this world that is a manifestation of the Lord’s glory. Being the witness of all, he obtains at all times whatever objects he intends merely by his will, and he becomes manifest with the eightfold qualities beginning with freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*).
"After departing, there is no consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13); "Obeisance to the seers, the makers of mantras" (Ṛgveda 10.97.1).
By means of power derived from asceticism, divine favor, and so forth, preceded by the vision of the mantras, an internal salutation is performed to the sages who are their proclaimers.
293. "I have no thief"— the authoritative means [of knowledge] with their commentaries, Prajñāsamuccaya.
Praśna Saṃhitā 294: "Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear.

"In this world, between a husband and wife, it is indeed the case that the husband is dear to the wife! And that dearness perceived in the husband is not produced by the power of the husband's own volition, but rather solely by the power of the Supreme Self’s volition. 295. "Verily, it is not for the sake of all things that everything becomes dear... Verily, the Self, Maitreyī, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. When the Self, verily, is seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, then all this is known."

Whatever object—such as a house, garden, field, or the like—may be dear to any person whatsoever in this world, that thing cannot truly be dear to that individual except by means of the will (*saṅkalpa*) of the Supreme Self; rather, it is solely through the will of the Supreme Self. Therefore, since the dearness of husband, wife, wealth, and so forth depends upon His will, for the sake of propitiating that Supreme Self, that very Supreme Self must be brought to direct realization through hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*).
O Maitreyī: when the Supreme Self is realized through hearing, reflection, and so forth, the entire world—which is its effect and subject to its governance—becomes known.
As it is said: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker.

The attainment of the human goal does not come through the mere knowledge of the name; rather, through the act of utterance produced by the organ of speech presided over by the mind, one should know the pervader of names—that is, the Supreme Self alone, whose body is the individual soul (the speaker).
"Indeed, for him the sun neither rises nor sets; it is always day for him who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman thus."

For one who practices this knowledge of Brahman in the form of the Madhu-vidyā, the sun neither rises nor sets for that knower of Brahman. He has no need whatsoever for the rising or the light of the sun. For that knower of Brahman, it is always as if day; "it is always day" means that it is indeed a single, ever-risen day, or rather, that it is perpetually day. The meaning is that he possesses a continuous, direct realization of all objects. [Prapāṭhaka 1, Section 2: The authoritative texts with commentary]

Pūrva Saṃhitā 298: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant. But for one who is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1) 26, 82, 268.

For a person who is joined with a body produced by karma consisting of merit and demerit, the avoidance of the pleasure and pain corresponding to that [body] is simply not possible. Pleasure and pain, which are occasioned by connection with such a body, do not attach themselves to a person who is indeed devoid of connection with a body produced by karma.
"There is no seer other than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).

The individual soul (*jīva*), whose cognition depends on the instruments of perception, is distinct from the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*) who possesses unconditioned seeing; being itself unseen by others, it does not possess knowledge of form and other objects.
"There is no other seer than He. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23)

There is nothing other than the Supreme Self that is similar to it, which, while being unseen by others, serves as the locus for the quality of being a seer without limiting adjuncts. 301. "The name is Brahman":
one should perform meditation upon the name—that is, upon the word that denotes—by viewing it as Brahman.

302. "The bringer-forth of name-and-form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2). 303. "I shall manifest name-and-form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2). 304. "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only whomsoever this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3).
These are the scriptural authorities (pramāṇas) along with their commentaries.
Pūrva Saṃhitā 305: "In his family, there shall be no one who does not know Brahman"—
referring to one for whom the form of Brahman has become manifest through meditation (*upāsana*) that is identical in aspect to the vision attained in the form of joy.
In the lineage of the wise and conscious one, a person who does not worship Brahman is never born.
306. "The Stainless" (Nirañjana). 307. "And that which was declared... became Truth. (Niruktaṃ ca ... satyam abhavat).
308. ‘Nirguṇa’:
although He is the creator of the entire phenomenal world, the Supreme Self alone is devoid of being subject to the three qualities (guṇas).
309. ‘Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless.’

The Supreme Brahman is partless because its purposes have been fulfilled; it is inactive, being devoid of the six waves such as hunger and thirst; it is free from defects such as aversion toward that which is dependent upon it; and its nature is non-attachment.
310. "But the final goal itself must be sought to be known."

In order to bring about a faith characterized by urgency, which serves as the means for hearing Brahman, one must also necessarily accomplish a steadfast resolve (*niṣṭhā*)—which itself is a means to that faith—consisting of the determination: "Brahman alone is to be heard, and nothing else. 311. "A Brāhmaṇa ought not to speak thus; my dear, fetch the fuel."

(This is the reply spoken by Gautama to Satyakāma Jābāla: "O Soma-seller! O young man! Having received the factual account regarding your birth, lineage, and so forth from your mother, you have spoken words that are true; such speech endowed with sincerity as this, no one outside the three [upper] castes—such as those of the fourth caste and others—is capable of uttering. When it comes to matters that ought to be told, they invariably mix in something crooked or untrue."

But you, being such as you are, speak with straightforwardness; this is to be commended. I wish to perform the *upanayana* sacrament for you; therefore, bring a fuel-stick suitable for that purpose. 312.

"In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here—rootless and without support. From it these creatures are born. The divine, singular God Nārāyaṇa is the eye and that which is to be seen; Nārāyaṇa is the ear and that which is to be heard. [The authoritative texts with their commentaries.]

Before the creation of the manifested world, in this sphere of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), that which was the original cause—distinct from any effectual entity dependent on another for its origin or persistence, and distinct from any eternal substance dependent on another for its existence—did not exist in any form whatsoever; from that [cause], these creatures are born, and the entire universe consisting of both sentient and insentient beings comes into being. It resides in the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*).

The Supreme Self alone, whose nature consists of light and who is denoted by the term Nārāyaṇa, became the cause of all beings being created. The sense organ called the eye, which is the means for perceiving form, as well as form itself which is its object; likewise, the sense organ called the ear, which is the means for perceiving sound, and sound which is its domain—all such things obtain their own existence only when presided over by Nārāyaṇa. 313. "The five peoples" (pañcajanāḥ).
314. "The five [groups of] five peoples" (pañca pañcajanāḥ).

315. "The Lord of the universe, the Self-Sovereign" (patiṃ viśvasyā'tmeśvaram): The entire universe exists depending upon the Supreme Brahman named Nārāyaṇa, who is the controller of the whole world consisting of sentient and insentient beings, who protects all with parental affection like a mother and father, who is devoid of any other individual who rules Him, and whose sovereignty over all is self-dependent. 316. "The Supreme Person" (paraṃ puruṣam).

(As previously introduced: He who meditates upon—the Supreme Person, the Paramātman—with the Praṇava "Om" consisting of three morae—that worshipper, having become perfected within the solar orb, becomes free from all sins.

317. "Having attained the supreme light, he emerges in his own form" (this refers to the individual soul known as *saṃprasāda*). Having reached the Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by a specific location, by means of the specific path beginning with light (*arcis*), it manifests in a form equal to that of the Supreme Self—characterized by freedom from sin and other qualities—preceded by the abandonment of its transmigratory state.
318. "Its supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are innate.
319. "Having examined the worlds..."

He who is a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) and has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) and the *Śiras* sections— that person [is qualified]. [The following are] the authoritative texts of the Śrauta-sūtras together with their commentaries.

Having examined, in accordance with reason, that the deities to be propitiated are subject to decay because they possess a perishable nature, or that the objects of enjoyment are likewise perishable, one should attain detachment [with the realization]: "The eternal Supreme Person is not attained by means of impermanent, goal-oriented ritual action.
320. "The *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood."
The sacrificial vessel called the *juhū*, which is the means for performing oblations in a sacrifice, must be made from the *palāśa* tree, which is denoted by the word ‘*parṇa*’.
321. “He sees without eyes; he hears without ears.”

The Supreme Self (paramātman) is the direct perceiver of form and its possessor even without depending upon the sense organ of sight; it is likewise capable of apprehending sound even without depending upon the sense organ of hearing.
322. "One foot of His is all beings; His three feet, the immortal, are in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).

The three feet of Brahman, presented here in the form of the Gāyatrī, manifest in a specific non-material realm denoted by the word "heaven" (dyu), which exists beyond both the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi).

323. ‘The killer of a father, the killer of a mother’ … [since] the father, mother, and all others are indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); when one reviles those who possess that breath, such as fathers and mothers, [one is reviling the breath itself].
Even when some slight reproach was uttered against him, people said, "You are a patricide; you are a matricide. [Prasannarāghava, with commentary].
The *pṛ.saṃ.* states:

Just as the *annamaya* [self] possesses a head, wings, a tail, and so forth, the *prāṇamaya* is likewise fivefold. The earth, which serves as the support for the ether that constitutes its essence, is called the "tail," just as a tail provides stability for living beings that possess one.

329. "Earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air; air dissolves into space; space dissolves into the senses; the senses dissolve into the subtle elements (tanmātras); the subtle elements dissolve into the principle of ego (bhūtādi); the principle of ego dissolves into the Great Principle (mahat); the Great Principle dissolves into the Unmanifest (avyakta); the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (akṣara); the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness (tamas); and Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. [It is said: "Earth dissolves into water."

The earth, having abandoned its state as earth and its state as the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) which serves as its precursor, becomes the state of water and merges with the waters previously existing in the oceans and so forth. Having attained continuous contact, it is said to have reached oneness. Likewise, the waters, having abandoned their state as water and their state as the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), become the state of fire and, becoming conjoined with the fire previously existing there, attain oneness with it.

Fire, having abandoned its state as fire and its state as the subtle element of form, becomes the state of air and merges into the previously existing air—it attains oneness with it. Air, having abandoned its state as air and its state as the subtle element of touch, reaches the state of ether and goes to oneness—dissolution—into the previously existing ether. Ether, having abandoned its state as ether and remaining in the state of the subtle element of sound, becomes conjoined with the sense organs.

First, the sense organs are merged with space; subsequently, they become merged in the subtle elements of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). The portions of the subtle elements of sound go to dissolution in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); and the ego dissolves into the principle called the Great One (*mahat*). The Great Principle dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), characterized by the equilibrium of the *guṇas*; and that principle called the Unmanifest dissolves into the principle denoted by the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*), which contains the collective totality of consciousness and is characterized by the unmanifest equilibrium of the *guṇas*.

And that Imperishable (akṣara) dissolves, respectively, into the extremely subtle state called Pradhāna, which is differentiated darkness (vibhakta-tamas), and into the Reality characterized by its orientation toward attaining the states beginning with the Imperishable. That differentiated darkness merges into the undifferentiated darkness (avibhakta-tamas)—the darkness designated by the term "Imperishable" and devoid of any orientation toward attaining the states beginning with the Imperishable—and attains oneness within the Supreme Self, whose body is such darkness. Furthermore, it becomes so closely fused that even the relationship of body and embodied cannot be predicated. [The proofs with their commentaries follow.]
Praśna Saṃhitā, Praśna Saṃhitā 3.30: "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through both battle and manly prowess."

The son of the Kṣatriya named Divodāsa, a Kṣatriya named Pratardana, being endowed with strength that serves as a means for battle and with innate heroism, was summoned by Indra and attained the realm called Svarga, which is most beloved as the place of enjoyment for Indra, the king of the gods.

331. "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra. Regarding the two terms *pradhāna* and *kṣetrajña*: He is the sovereign of both Nature (*prakṛti*) and Spirit (*puruṣa*), that is, the master of the insentient principle and the sentient principle. He is the substratum of the six qualities consisting of knowledge, vigor, strength, sovereignty, heroism, and splendor; or rather, He is the Supreme Self who transcends the three *guṇas*. He is the determining cause of the state of bondage in *saṃsāra*, which consists in remaining in a condition where the non-Self is identified with the Self, as well as the cause of its persistence and its cessation. 346.

"O Prastotṛ, that deity which is connected with the Prastāva"—O officiating priest named Prastotṛ, that deity who exists as the object of meditation, having been superimposed upon the Sāma-chant portion called the Prastāva; (she must certainly be known).
"Mounted by the conscious Self, he goes forth, letting go."

This individual self, the living soul (*jīva*), which corresponds to the position of the chariot, having entered into a specific relationship with the omniscient Supreme Self who corresponds to the charioteer, departs after casting off the body. As it is said:
"Embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātman*), he knows nothing external, nor anything internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21).
Sammitiya-pramāṇas with commentary.

Pūrva Saṃhitā 3.37: "Consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) refers to the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is distinct from and inner to that consisting of food (*annamaya*), due to the predominance of the function of breathing.
It is denoted by the term "consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya).

338. "'The breath of breath' (prāṇasya prāṇaḥ)": the Supreme Self is the cause of the activity called breathing for the vital breath, and its own breathing is independent of the vital breath; like the body, it possesses an existence that does not depend on the wind known as the vital breath.
339. "Those who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of the mind.
(II) "The breath of breath" (III) "Of breath."

Those who know that substance which imparts to the tactile organ—nourished by the air denoted by the term *prāṇa*—the capacity to perceive touch and its substratum; which imparts to the visual organ the capacity to perceive form and its substratum; which imparts to the auditory organ the capacity to perceive sound; which imparts to the gustatory organ the capacity to perceive taste; and which imparts to the mental organ the capacity for reflection—they [know] that which stands above all, which is prior to all, and supreme.
(They should determine Brahman): "The lord of the vital breaths wanders about according to his own karmas. (340)
He who is the size of a thumb, whose form is like the sun, and who is endowed with volition and egoism—
[these are] the measures [of the self] along with their explanations.

Praśna Saṃhitā 3.42: "He understood that breath is Brahman" (the cause of the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of all living beings). Bhṛgu realized that breath alone is endowed with the defining characteristics of Brahman.

343. "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātman); meditate upon me as life (āyuḥ) and immortality (amṛta)," said Indra. "O Pratardana! I am the one whose body is Prāṇa, having the living being (jīva) as my body, which is designated by the term 'conscious self. Meditate upon me, who have the living being and Prāṇa as my body, as 'life' and as 'immortality. 344. "Prāṇa indeed is the father; Prāṇa indeed is the mother. Truly, even the referents denoted by such terms as 'father' and 'mother' are the living being itself!

345. "For these eighteen forms of sacrifice are indeed fleeting and unstable; they are said to be inferior acts among which ritual action prevails. Those fools who rejoice in this [path] enter again and again into old age and death. Persons whose primary focus is on rituals such as sacrifices—which lack even a slight inclination toward the propitiation of the Supreme Person—become truly incapable of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, like a worn-out boat.

Regarding those rites being performed by them, it is stated that there are eighteen participants—consisting of sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the wife, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—and because of the presence of an intention for fruit, the karma is characterized as bondage and is thus considered inferior.

Those who rejoice, thinking that even such karma—which is a means for achieving results in this world and the next and is synonymous with bondage—is a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), have fallen into delusion. Having begun their experience of pleasure through karma, they subsequently enter again and again into the very wheel of old age and death similar to what was previously experienced; they do not become liberated from bondage.
346. "Bahudāyī" (the grandson of a Kṣatriya named Putra, a Kṣatriya named Jānaśruti) was exceedingly devoted to giving to beggars; he gave more than what was requested.

347. "Being born in many ways" (348. "One who cooks much"): [Pautrāyaṇa, a Kṣatriya named Jānaśruti,] was one who caused food to be cooked in great abundance for the purpose of serving guests and visitors in his house.
349. "May I become many" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.6; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3; Praśna Upaniṣad 6.2). 350. "Creating many offspring of similar form" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.5.1).
II. "Creating many offspring" (351); "The Great Self is higher than the intellect" (115) [to be seen at 333, 339, 342];
"Both the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya."

353. "'O student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), we do not worship this [Prajāpati] as you have described him. O student of sacred knowledge! We do not worship Prajāpati, whose nature you have described, as the *saṃvarga* (the absorber); rather, we perform the meditation upon the Supreme Self alone as the *saṃvarga*."
"Having known and realized the adorable God, born of Brahman, one attains this ultimate peace.

Because he is born from Brahman and because he is a knower, the individual soul (jīvātman)—that is, oneself as the worshiper—is designated by the term "born of Brahman" (*brahmaja-jña*). Having understood through the scriptures that this soul is of the nature of Brahman, which is the object of worship, and subsequently having directly realized one's own self as being of the nature of Brahman through meditation, one attains the peace consisting in the crossing over of saṃsāra—denoted by the words birth, old age, and death—as set forth in the first half of this mantra, namely, the state of freedom from rebirth. 355. "Brahman is your speech."
"O Ajātaśatru! O King of Kāśī! I shall teach you Brahman," said Gārgya Bālāki. "Brahman is the tail, the support. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.1; 8.4.1)

Here, it appears that the word "tail" (*puccha*) intends to refer to the spinal column (*brahmadaṇḍa*), which is the root of even the tail; for it is understood from Ayurveda, Yoga-śāstra, and other sources that all the parts constituting the root of the body's functions are connected to that very spinal column. Therefore, the word "tail" refers to a support (*ādhāra*). Because Brahman, as the foundational support, is the cause of the supreme stability, it possesses the nature of being the "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*).
The meaning is that in the Supreme Self, which abounds in bliss, it serves as the unsurpassed foundation of bliss in its form as Brahman.
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries.
Summary.
357. "Brahman was the forest, Brahman was that tree from which they fashioned heaven and earth. O wise ones, I declare this to you with my mind: Brahman stood supporting all the worlds."

The Teacher provides the answer to the three questions posed by the wise ones: Since He brings forth heaven and earth from that forest-born tree, Brahman alone is like that forest and like that tree; because of His omnipotence, whatever materials are required for whatever is to be produced, all of them exist within that very Brahman. That same Brahman sustains all worlds within Himself and governs them Himself.
O wise ones! I am the Teacher.
Having reflected in my mind, I speak to you various answers; determine the meaning. 358. "May I attain the world of Brahman" (26, 27, 28, 35):
one who meditates upon Brahman, the locus of unsurpassed greatness, attains none other than that very Brahman which is his own object of meditation and is the most excellent of all.
360. "From fear [arises] fire... the fifth...
II "From fear the fire burns."

361. "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. By "from fear... it blows," it is meant that the god Vāyu blows, remaining vigilant in his own function out of extreme dread of transgressing the command of this Supreme Self. The sun, too, being afraid, remains intent upon its entire work of rising. Likewise, Agni, Indra, and Death also move with haste and rapidity for the sake of accomplishing their respective duties.
362. "But the Plenum (Bhūman) alone is to be sought to be known."

The Supreme Self alone is to be known as the substratum of the excellence of qualities and the vastness of form, because He is extremely favorable to conscious beings; the meaning is that one should know the nature of the Supreme Self as consisting of abundant bliss. 363. "O, O Bhallākṣa! Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out equally with the sky. Do not touch it, lest it burn you! (Praśna Upaniṣad).
The authoritative texts with their commentaries (*Pramāṇasavivaraṇa*).

O friend, O you who possess a vision capable of discerning subtle meanings like the weapon called *bhallā*! (In essence: O dull-eyed one! The splendor of King Jānaśruti—the son of Putra—is spread everywhere, resembling the light of the sun which illuminates heaven. Do not become attached to that splendor; let that splendor not consume you. (Thus spoke one swan, addressing another: "Travel with caution.")

364. "O Maghavan! This mortal body is indeed seized by death; it is the substratum for this immortal Self. O Maghavan! This body alone is subject to death. Not only is it subject to death, but it is also pervaded by death (overcome, characterized by constant perishability). Such is this body: the locus of experience for the Self whose nature is immortality, defined by the absence of a body produced by karma. It has been assumed by the individual soul (*jīva*), who is subject to karma, for the sake of experience. 365. "But the intellect (*mati*) itself is what must be sought to be known."
Meditation (*manana*) itself, which serves as the means for the worship of Brahman (*brahmopāsana*), is what must be accomplished.
366. "Having reflected, the wise man abandons joy and sorrow" (*Praśna Upaniṣad* 2.7; see also *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.8). 367. "He understood that the mind is Brahman. (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.4)

It was stated at the outset that the characteristic of Brahman is such that, by knowing the mind to be endowed with it, Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, attained knowledge through austerity that "the mind is Brahman. (368) "The mind... is Brahman."

Because it is greater than speech and the other organs, the mind (*manas*) is indeed Brahman. (Therefore, one should perform meditation upon the organ of the mind as "Brahman," by means of the understanding that it is Brahman.
369. "Consisting of mind" (*manomaya*):

between the food-sheath (*annamaya*) and the vital-breath-sheath (*prāṇamaya*), the mind-sheath alone is the Self. The mind is "consisting of mind" because it abounds in mental modifications (*vṛtti*); among the functions of the internal organ known as mind, intellect, ego, and thought, the function of the mind is predominant.

370. "I am composed of mind, have vital breath for my body, consist of light, possess true resolve, have space as my self, perform all actions, encompass all desires, possess all odors, possess all tastes; I pervade all this, and am without speech or regard. (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.10)
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries.
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries.
Page 375: I. "Beyond the Great... the supreme goal";
II. "Beyond the Great... the Supreme Person."
376. "A great terror, a raised thunderbolt.

377. "The Great Being, infinite and boundless"—like salt dissolved in water, the Supreme Brahman, which transcends all sentient and insentient beings in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), its inherent character (*svabhāva*), and its qualities (*guṇa*); it is indivisible and the Self of all.

378. ‘The Mahat dissolves into the Unmanifest; the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable. (405) 379. ‘Having realized the Great, all-pervading Self, the wise man does not grieve. Having directly perceived the Supreme Self—the inner ruler of all sentient and insentient beings, possessing a wondrous majesty that transcends everything—the wise person established in wisdom becomes one whose worldly suffering has ceased.

"Worship me—(who have the individual soul as my life-breath and body)—as being present there within the range of the external eye in the form of Indra, with the understanding that I am 'life' and 'immortality.
381. 'Know me alone.'"

Worship me—the very body of Indra, which is the nature of the Supreme Self—by contemplating me incessantly, having first renounced all else. "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti (Nature), and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) to be the wielder of Māyā; by his limbs, this entire world is pervaded. "Māyā to be... the Great Lord."

One should understand that it is *prakṛti* itself, presided over by Īśvara and producing a manifold creation of objects, which is designated by the term *māyā*. However, one should know its presiding controller to be my Lord (*maddeśvara*). Since the entire non-conscious universe is pervaded by individual souls (*jīvas*) who are non-different from Him and constitute His very parts, [the world is unreal]. As stated: "Death is the condiment for whom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.11), and "Do not indeed speak to me falsely" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.1).
"O Bālāki! By speaking with untruthful words, you have indeed caused me to engage in a conversation that consists of nothing but non-Brahman discourse," said Ajātaśatru.
Page [number]: The means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) with their commentaries, [in] Prakarṣasaṃkhyā.
385. "Whatever desire he desires arises for him by his mere volition; endowed with that, he is magnified.

Whatever kind of desired fruit he longs for, all of that is accomplished for this liberated self through his specific knowledge consisting of volition alone. And by means of that, this liberated self becomes prosperous and is praised.

386. "He whom the earth does not know"—he who meditates upon that supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*), he becomes united with the heat of the sun. Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he indeed freed from evil. He is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman; from this mass of living beings, he beholds the Puruṣa dwelling within the city (the body), who is beyond it.

He who is a worshiper of the Supreme Person, having previously engaged in meditation for the sake of inferior fruits by means of the syllable "Om"—composed of the three phonemes *a*, *u*, and *m*, consisting of three morae (*mātrā*)—meditates uninterruptedly upon the Supreme Self with direct orientation; that meditator, becoming united with the Sun which consists of a sphere of light, is liberated from the accumulation of sins acquired through various births and rebirths, like a snake casting off its worn-out old skin.

By means of the mantras situated in the third station, which are denoted by the word *sāman*, one reaches the world of Brahman; there, one realizes the Supreme Self, the innermost self of all, who is beyond this cycle of worldly existence and even beyond the four-faced Brahmā. "Who, moving within the earth, has the earth as his body; who, moving within the waters, has the waters as his body.
"Who [moves] within the earth... the earth does not know him."

That Supreme Self who dwells within earth and water, to whom earth and water stand as the supported, the subordinate, and the subservient, and whom earth is unable to know even though He resides within her very self—he is the divine, singular God, Nārāyaṇa.

"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know; whose body is the earth; who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3)
Page number. Sequential number. The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with commentary. Sequential number.
II "He who... governs from within the earth.
III "He who dwells within the earth":

that Supreme Self who dwells within the earth, for whom the earth exists as a substratum, as something subject to His will, and as subordinate to Him; and whom the earth is not able to know, even though He resides within her very self.
He who, having entered within the earth, exercises control over its activity and cessation,
and who possesses unconditioned immortality— he is the Supreme Self alone, your very Self.

390. "He who, dwelling in the self (ātman), is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller (antaryāmin), the immortal. [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22; Maitrī Upaniṣad 6.11; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.12; Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11] "He who... controls" (III). "He who, dwelling in the self" (I).

Of whatever nature the Self is—which, although existing within every individual soul (*jīvātman*), remains unknown to it, and which, while having that very soul as its body, enters into it and governs its worldly activity consisting of engagement and withdrawal—that alone is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), characterized by unconditioned immortality, who is your Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). 391.

"That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand; he who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all his desires."

That individual self (jīvātman) which is free from the attachment to sins consisting of good and evil deeds, devoid of old age and death, unconnected with sorrow and the karma that causes it, far removed from hunger and thirst, possessing unobstructed will and unimpeded resolve, and whose essential nature is distinct from the body—that is what must be sought after and likewise meditated upon.

But he who, being conscious, makes that Supreme Self the object of his cognition through knowledge born of the scriptures from the mouth of a Guru, and meditates upon it incessantly—he, being liberated, transcends subjection to karma and becomes one who attains all desires in all worlds according to his own will, which is in accordance with the will of the Lord.
(Praśna Upaniṣad 5.7): "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun, and who controls the sun from within."
The authoritative texts with their commentaries [state]:

That Supreme Self who dwells within the radiant energy called the sun, yet is distinct from the sun; that Supreme Self whom the sun is not even able to know, even while remaining within Himself; and toward whom the sun stands as the supported, the subordinate, and the subservient; He who, while abiding within the sun, causes it to engage in its established functions—He alone is your Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*).

"He who controls this world and the other world, and all beings, from within"—that Supreme Self who, having entered within, causes this world denoted by the word "this" (which is perceptible by the senses) and that world denoted by the word "yonder" (which is imperceptible by the senses), as well as all beings consisting of the moving and the unmoving, to engage in their respective activities; (He alone is your immortal Inner Controller).
"He who is the creator of these... and whose work this is."

He who is the creator of those persons, such as Āditya and others, whom you have taught to be Brahman—of whom these Ādityas and others are objects of creation, and for whom the entire universe consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, brought near by means of perception and other valid cognitions, is the effect—he alone is the one to be known and worshipped. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1) "This person who consists of consciousness—where was he then, and from whence did he come? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1–2).

He who arises at the very moment of awakening, having cast off the nature of the consciousness of all sense objects—he is this Puruṣa. [The teacher] asked: "Where was this one situated during the state of deep sleep prior to being roused by the pressing of the hands?
From where has he emerged at this time? 396. 1. "This person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self," he said; "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
