"This person who is seen within the sun, golden-hued, with a golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to his very nails—his eyes are like a lotus blooming at dawn. His name is 'Ut' (Risen), for he has risen above all evils. Indeed, whoever knows this rises above all evils.
The *Ṛg* and the *Sāman* are his two joints... thus far with respect to the divine."

That Person who is directly perceived by yogis devoted to meditation—residing within the locus that consists of the solar orb, possessing a form that is beneficial and beautiful during the state of meditation, and radiant; he whose beard and hair are beautiful, whose entire body from the nails to the crest of the head is of beautiful form, whose eyes are as stainless and sharp as the petals of a white lotus blossomed by the rays of a pure stalk arisen from deep water, and for whom the word "Ut" serves as his name—he [is this].

He is named "Ut" because he is devoid of any connection with all kinds of karma, whether meritorious or sinful, which are denoted by the word "pāpa" (evil). One who possesses knowledge dependent upon meditation perceives that Person by means of such a characteristic as being named "Ut. Both the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*, which are studied by the Vaidikas, are indeed in the form of hymns to the qualities of this Great Person. 398. "O venerable ones, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice."
"O Uddālaka and the others, great Vedic scholars, Brāhmaṇas of immense majesty! I shall perform a sacrifice in a very short time," said Aśvapati, the King of Kekaya.
"Whatever is seen or even heard in this world... [399] "...whatever exists here... [397].

"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without. Whatever exists in this perceptible world—whether in close proximity to the senses or at a distance, and thus whatever is seen or heard—all of that Nārāyaṇa abides in, having entered into its internal and external parts without distinction, specifically by way of attributes such as being the controller. "Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have, all that is contained within him; within him all desires are contained. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1)

Whatever collection of objects of enjoyment belongs to a lay follower (upāsaka) in this world, and whatever exists here only within the range of his imagination but does not exist in reality— all those objects of enjoyment are contained within this small space (daharākāśa), which is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
[The following are] the authoritative texts (pramāṇas) along with their commentaries.
Pṛ.saṃ. [states]:

"It is perfectly established. And within that Supreme Self, which is of the nature of the small ether (*daharākāśa*), all auspicious qualities—desirable by individual souls (*jīvas*) because they are to be experienced as the ultimate object of enjoyment—are present in their full perfection.
401. "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self of knowledge (*jñāna*)."

"One should restrain knowledge within the Great Self; one should restrain that within the Peaceful Self" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.13). A wise person, having set out for the vision of the Supreme Self and being habituated to the journey along the path of the Self, should—having taken hold of speech—subdue and establish all the organs of action and knowledge that have attained outward expansion within the mind. Having brought the organs of action and knowledge under his own control, he should place the mind, which is the faculty of determination residing in the Self, in an unshakable state within the Self.

One should bring under control and establish such an intellect—consisting of determination and characterized by the desire that is the cause for the activity of the intellect and other faculties—within the Self (*ātman*). And one should bring under control and establish that agent, the individual soul (*jīva*), within the peaceful Supreme Brahman, which is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all.

"From whence indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they depart—that is Brahman; seek to know that. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) "From whence indeed... they are born... that is Brahman. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) "From whence indeed... they are born... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1)
IV "From whence, indeed, these [beings]... 87,92 2, 126"

All beings, established by valid means of knowledge, derive their essential nature from that very Reality which serves as both their efficient and material cause; they depend upon that Reality—which exists as their own self—for all their activities and cessations; and they attain the causal state from the state of effect. That very Reality into which they enter as the substratum of dissolution is the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of all beings, and is the entity denoted by the term *Brahman*.
(Therefore, worship That alone through hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration.)
403. "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained [it].
(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1) The authoritative texts (*pramāṇa*) along with their commentaries.

Page [saṃ...]: Those engaged in describing the full extent of the experienced bliss of Brahman—speech, which consists of the subtle elements and the mind as its organ—having failed to reach the ultimate limit characterized by the measure of that very bliss intended for description, withdraw their activity from it and resort to silence; the worshipper who knows such immeasurable bliss as being immeasurable does not become afraid of anything whatsoever.

404. "That which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, and fearless. 405. "That which the seers, the wise ones who possess transcendent vision, perceive—that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu," as it is well known; they behold that most exalted state. (The wise man attains that state by way of the path of the syllable *Oṃ*). 406. "That which is unseen... [the steadfast one perceives it]."
II. "That which is invisible and ungraspable" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1);
"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

But when, for this individual soul (*jīva*), every object whatsoever appears as non-distinctly established from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and as having a single nature, then in that state, by what cause could anything of a distinct nature be perceived? Or by what means could one directly perceive any distinct object, or who—being a distinct agent and independent—could know it? That is altogether impossible. 408. "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūman*). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (*alpa*). (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1)

That entity which, when being experienced, nothing other than itself is seen, heard, or even cognized, is the Infinite (bhūman). That in which, while it is being seen, something else is seen; while it is being heard, something else is heard; and while it is being cognized, something else is cognized—that is characterized as the opposite of the Infinite, meaning it is the finite (alpa). [The means of valid knowledge with their commentaries are in the *Prasthāna-saṃgraha*.]
Pṛ.saṃ.
409: "For where there is, as it were, duality"—that is, in that state in which there is the manifestation of things as existing independently and separate from the Supreme Self.
(Then, there would be an existence separate from the Supreme Self; it would bring an object established as separate from the Supreme Self within the range of vision.
410. "Whatever else one sees, that is limited.

When a person, while experiencing one object, is able to see another (or is able to hear or cognize another), that object which provides the opportunity for the experience of other objects at the time of its own experience should be understood as small.

411. "Where this person consisting of consciousness was when he slept—having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness—he lies in that space which is within the heart."

In the waking state, the individual soul (*jīva*), denoted by the term "the person consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya-puruṣa*), experiences various objects through the primary instrument of the mind and the auxiliary instruments of the eyes and so forth; it is thus filled with various forms of identification (*abhimāna*). In deep sleep (*suṣupti*), however, with all instruments from the mind downwards ceased, and with all identifications as a god and so forth departed, it goes to rest in the form of non-differentiation within the Supreme Self, which is of the nature of the space within the heart.
(Praśna Upaniṣad 3.5): "According to what one's resolve (*kratu*) is in this world, so does one become after departing from here."
The authoritative texts with their commentaries, 1.
Saṃhitā 414: "Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he indeed freed from evil."

"By means of the Sāman chants, one is led to the world of Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5) "Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of similar form emerge, so too, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also merge. Just as numerous sparks of identical nature arise from a heated iron ball, or from a fire well-blazing within a house or other dwelling, even so, from Brahman—which possesses a subtle body of consciousness and matter—there arise the manifold categories of effects consisting of gross forms of consciousness and matter, and into that very source they dissolve.

416. "Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter"—O dear one! when one particular object made of iron is known, by making that very knowledge the cause [of understanding all else], just as all other iron objects become known, so it is here.
417. "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known... Just as, my dear, by means of a single [lump of clay]..."

420. "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread], as herbs arise upon the earth, and as hair and body-hair grow from a living man, so does this universe arise here from the Imperishable.
"As a spider... and reabsorbs..."

Just as a specific type of insect called a spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), from within its own interior, emits threads outward by its own will without depending on anything else and draws them back inside; and just as infinite plants arise in the field that is the earth without the nature of the earth itself being destroyed; and while the embodied person is still alive, insentient things such as nails, hair, and body hair are produced from him.

Likewise, from the Supreme Brahman—the ineffable, the transcendental, independent of any other cause, and changeless—the entire universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings and distinct from one another, comes into existence.
421. "Whatever he prays for with this oblation, may he attain it; may he prosper in it; may the gods grant him that.

Whatever fruit the sacrificer expects from this performed sacrifice—may he enjoy that fruit; may he experience it; and may that fruit increase. And may the gods accomplish that desired object for him.

422. "When there was neither day nor night, when that which is called existent and non-existent, the manifest and the unmanifest, and the distinction between day and night had ceased, and only darkness alone (the mere Māyā of the Blessed Lord) remained— at that time, the Supreme Self alone existed. 423. "When the seer beholds the one who is of golden hue, the Maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman—then the knower, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality."

At the time when the conscious one who perceives Brahman directly realizes Vāsudeva— who is designated by the term ‘Puruṣa’, who is the controller of the world, the primordial cause of the universe through both His nature as the material cause and His volition, and who possesses a resplendent, divine, and auspicious form— then that wise man has his merit and demerit cast away.
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries.
Summary.

Having brought about the removal of its natural limitations, it attains supreme equality with Brahman through the perfection of the innate qualities of Brahman, such as being free from sin and so forth.

424. "When one truly discerns, then one speaks the truth. That is to say, when the conscious one becomes possessed of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—which is designated by the term "Truth" and attained through meditation—he immediately thereafter becomes characterized by speaking the truth and so forth. He comes to possess a natural disposition to proclaim the supreme excellence of that which he himself meditates upon. 425. "When a person is asleep and does not see any dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this Prāṇa alone. From this Self, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) proceed in their respective directions; from the vital breaths, the gods (*devāḥ*); and from the gods, the worlds (*lokāḥ*)."
II "When one is asleep... [he] becomes... from that very self... they emerge.
16, 17 III "When... [he] becomes..."
IV. "When one has fallen asleep... he goes together with it. 426.
"Whatever there is in this entire world, having issued forth, vibrates through *prāṇa*. A great terror, a raised thunderbolt—it is this that they know; those who know this become immortal."
"Out of fear of Him the fire burns; out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra, Vāyu, and Death as the fifth run on.

The entire universe—consisting of all moving and stationary beings related to the three periods of time—exists as something supported within the Supreme Self designated by the word "Prāṇa. Although it was created from that very Prāṇa, it trembles with fear born of that Supreme Person, as if from one who has raised a thunderbolt.

Those who, through meditation, directly perceive this Supreme Brahman—the cause of the trembling of the entire world and the protector of the world’s boundaries—attain immortality by being liberated from the bondage of *prakṛti*. Even the five—Fire, Sun, Indra, Wind, and Death—who are terrifying to the world, proceed incessantly in their respective functions out of fear of this Prāṇa, the Supreme Self.
427. "That which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace..."

Śrī Saṃvat.

"428. That which is above the sky, Gārgī, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—that is woven, warp and woof, in space alone. "That which is above... [below] the earth."

"O Gārgī! Whatever collection of things exists above the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), whatever collection of things exists below the earthly world (*pṛthivīloka*), whatever collection of things exists in the interval between these two worlds of heaven and earth, as well as these very worlds of heaven and earth themselves, and whatever they designate as delimited by the three periods of time—all that exists in a state of inseparable connection within that which is called space (*ākāśa*), which transcends all else, just as a cloth exists upon its long and crosswise extended threads."
Yājñavalkya stated that [Brahman] is invariably connected by way of being the substratum, being governed, and so forth:
"If this bliss did not exist in the ether," and "This bliss which is in the ether."
If this Supreme Self, whose essence is undivided bliss, were not to exist, who would attain worldly or liberative happiness? No one at all.
430. "The wise behold that which is the source of all beings."
Page numbers for the authoritative texts with their commentaries.

That which is called the eye is situated in the sense organ; [it is] that immortal Self, the Inner Controller, characterized by being contained within it, being perceivable by it, and having it as its body.
— 436. "But he who worships this very Vaiśvānara Self, the measure of a span and all-pervading, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all Selves. — "But he who worships...
ATT 209.
"But he who... this celestial mansion":

Furthermore, the seeker of liberation who meditates upon—constantly contemplates—this Self which is designated by the term Vaiśvānara; which, for the sake of the practitioner's ease, possesses a manifested form delimited by the measure of the regions from heaven down to earth, yet is actually free from all measurement (unlimited) due to its pervasiveness everywhere; and who experiences the food that is of the nature of Brahman, abiding in all worlds, all beings, and the self of all.

437. "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, as well as the mind together with all the vital breaths—know him alone as the Self; cast off other words. He is the bridge to immortality."

Make that very Self—the one denoted by the word *akṣara*, in whom the three worlds consisting of earth, the intermediate space, and heaven, as well as the mind, vital breath, and all else useful for conscious life are perfectly and inseparably united—the object of your knowledge, as the pervasive reality that governs everything other than itself. Completely cast away all speech that has as its object anything other than that Self.
This Self, which is expressible by means of syllables and words, is like a bridge that leads to the attainment of the shore called Immortality, which stands beyond the ocean of saṃsāra.
"In Him the five groups of five and the ether are established; knowing the Self thus, the wise man becomes the immortal Brahman. (438)
In that immortal light, wherein the five senses designated as the "five peoples" (*pañcajana*),
as well as the five elements beginning with space, have attained a firm foundation— such is the immortal [light]. (Praśna Saṃhitā).

Having reached the firm conviction, as explained in the authoritative texts (pramāṇas), that "the nature of light is the Supreme Brahman," even a human being other than the gods previously mentioned becomes immortal— that is, he transcends saṃsāra and becomes one whose immortality has been manifested.
439. "He whose body is the eye— that is, for whom the sense organ named 'eye' is the substrate, the subordinate, and the dependent [is that very Inner Controller, the Immortal Supreme Self]."

440. "He whose body is the moon and the stars"—that is, for whom the moon and the constellations are the substratum, the governed, and the subordinate (that Supreme Self is the Inner Controller, the Immortal).
441. "He whose mind is the body."

That entity for which the internal organ called *citta* is the substratum (*ādheya*), that which is to be governed (*vidheya*), and that which is subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*)—that is the Supreme Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
[Cf. BhG 3.15]: "Whose austerity consists of knowledge. [BhG 4.18;

"He whose body is darkness—that reality whose nature is darkness, which is the locus of being supported, being commanded, and being subordinate—is the Supreme Self, the immortal one existing as the inner controller (antaryāmī).
444. He whose body is light..."

Of that entity which has light as its nature, and which possesses the qualities of being the substratum, the object of injunction, and the subordinate element— that entity, whose form is the Supreme Self, is the locus of inner rulership and immortality.

445. "He whose skin is the body"—that is, for which Puruṣa the skin is the instrument (indriya), possessing the qualities of being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate—he is the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), the Immortal Supreme Self (paramātman). 446. "He whose directions are the body."

The object in the form of the quarters, which, with respect to a particular person, possesses the nature of being that which is to be contained (*ādheyatva*), that which is to be governed (*vidheyatva*), and that which is subordinate (*śeṣatva*)—the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) who is immortal, he is the Supreme Self.
[Praśna Upaniṣad 4.11]: "He whose body is heaven... etc.
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) along with their commentaries are on page [number].

The object in the form of the world is that person toward whom there exists the state of being a locus (*ādheyatva*), the state of being governed (*vidheyatva*), and the state of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*).
The Immortal is the Inner Controller, the Supreme Self. "He whose body is the earth; whose body is the waters; whose body is fire."

"Of whom wind is the body; of whom space is the body; of whom the Imperishable is the body; of whom death is the body—He is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa.
"Of whom... is the body."

That Person with respect to whom the objects consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the imperishable, and death possess the qualities of being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate— He is this Lord, the controller of all beings, from whom all evil has been dispelled, who shines in the station of the supreme ether,
and who is devoid of any second equal or superior.
Nārāyaṇa:

449. "He whose body is breath, for whom the object [of experience] is of the nature of breath, and toward whom [the body] possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate—that Puruṣa is immortal."
The Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

He is the Person for whom the object consisting of intellect (buddhi)—of which it is said that "intellect is His body"—is that which possesses the nature of being supported, being directed, and being subordinate. That Person is [the Supreme Self].
Nārāyaṇa is the inner controller and the immortal.
"He for whom both the Brahminhood and the Kshatriyahood are the rice, and for whom death is the condiment—who truly knows where He is?"

This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, characterized by the two castes known as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, is made into a libation for Death—that is, it is to be withdrawn at the time of dissolution so that it may be deposited within that Person in the form of a seed. Who, then, is capable of knowing the specific nature of that Supreme Self, the withdrawer of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, which is distinguished by such a light and is unique among all things other than itself? No one at all.
This is the meaning. (Being a condiment—*upasecanatva*:
while being eaten by oneself, it acts as an auxiliary to the eating of another, as in the case of a side-dish or *upadaṃśa*.
*Pra.saṃ.* (Prasthānasaṅgraha)
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries [are found] at Pra.saṃ.
452: "He whose mind is the body..."

The mind—synonymous with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is the instrument for the experience of internal pleasure, pain, and so forth. That person toward whom [the mind] possesses the qualities of being supported, being subordinate, and being a subordinate element is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), the Immortal Nārāyaṇa.
[As stated in the scriptures: "He whose body is death, who moves within death, whom death does not know—he is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa.
(II) "Whose... body... (I)

Death, which is a synonym for darkness, is that which must be supported and controlled by the Person; the Person stands within the interior of death. Nevertheless, that Person whom death is not able to know at all—this Person who dwells within the category of death as its inner controller, the internal ruler of all beings, free from all defects, residing in the imperishable supreme ether, whose nature is self-luminous, devoid of any equal or superior, is the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa. (454) "He whose body is semen..."

That Person who is the seed of the entire universe, whose nature consists of being the locus, the object of control, and the subordinate (śeṣatva) of that substance denoted by the word *retaḥ*—which is the seed of all volitions and the source of all existence—and who exists as the one to be presided over [by him], he is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), the Immortal Nārāyaṇa;
and he is also that which has become the subordinate.
And he who...

455. He whose speech— meaning the organ named *vāk*, which is the cause for the utterance of sound— is characterized by being supported by, subject to the will of, and subservient to Him (that Supreme Person, the Inner Controller, Nārāyaṇa).

456. "He whose body is air— that object which is of the nature of air, presided over by Him through the states of being supported, being commanded, and being subordinate (that Person is the Inner Controller, Nārāyaṇa)."

457. He whose body is consciousness (*vijñāna*), whose nature is knowledge (*jñāna*), whose very essence is cognition (*jñānasvarūpa*), and who is synonymous with sentience (*cetanā*)—the Self (*ātman*) toward whom [everything else] possesses the state of being supported, the state of being governed, and the state of being subordinate (that Person is the Inner Controller, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa). *Praśna-saṃhitā*.

459. "He whose ear is His body—that is, the sense organ named 'ear' which serves as the instrument for perceiving sound—is that toward whom [the ear] possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate; [that Person is the Inner Controller, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa].
450. "He whose body consists of all beings..."
That Person who is the Inner Controller, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, with respect to whom all beings possess the qualities of being supported, being subject to command, and being subordinate;
[as it is said: "He whose body is space. 61.412.

The object whose nature is space, which is presided over by [the Puruṣa] through the states of being the substratum, the object of injunction, and the subordinate element—that [Puruṣa] is the Inner Controller, Nārāyaṇa.
(He) "whose body is the Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.4;
Mahābhārata 61.414).
463. "He whose body is fire" (412):
that person who, with respect to an object in the form of fire, possesses the status of being supported by it, being subject to its control, or being subordinate to it.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa is the inner controller:
"He whose self is the body," and "He whose body is the sun."
That person who stands in relation to the object that has the form of the sun as its substratum, its locus of predication, and its subordinate element—
that person is the Inner Controller, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa.

466. "He whose body is the intermediate space—that is, the entity denoted by the word 'intermediate space'—toward whom [the intermediate space] possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to control, and being subordinate; that Person is the Inner Controller, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa."

467. "He whose body is water, and for whom water possesses the state of being supported, the state of being subject, and the state of being subordinate— that person is the Inner Controller" (Praśna Upaniṣad).
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with their commentaries, page 468. "He whose unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the body... he whose imperishable (*akṣara*) is the body."
"He whose body is death... he is the inner self of all beings" (I);
"He whose body is the unmanifest... he whose body is the imperishable" (III);
"He whose body is the unmanifest. (II)

Nārāyaṇa is the controller of that entity denoted by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta), toward whom it possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to command, and being subordinate; he is the controller of that entity denoted by the word "imperishable" (akṣara), toward whom it possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to command, and being subordinate; he is the controller of that entity denoted by the word "death" (mṛtyu), toward whom it possesses the qualities of being supported, being subject to command, and being subordinate; and he is the controller of that entity denoted by the word "all beings" (sarvabhūta).

469. "He whose body is egoism" (ahaṅkāra): that person (the Inner Controller, the Lord Nārāyaṇa) with respect to whom the entity denoted by the word "egoism" possesses the qualities of being contained within, being subject to control, and being subordinate.
470. "By whose truth he speaks... 471. "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from him this Brahman, name, form, and food are born.
"He who is all-knowing... [whose] austerity..."
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving. (III) 186, 320;

The subject introduced as the source of all beings (*bhūtayoni*) is that which possesses, without limitation, knowledge regarding all things and all their modes; from that Brahman—which is oriented toward creation by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) and requires nothing other than its own resolve as an instrument for creation—there proceeds the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) Brahman, and through that, the world enveloped in name and form, consisting of both the objects of enjoyment and the enjoyers, designated by the term "food" (*anna*).
[Here follow] the authoritative texts (*pramāṇas*) along with their commentaries.
Pṛ.saṃ.
473: "He who, dwelling in all worlds...
The Supreme Self (paramātman) who, having entered within all things—whether their nature is specified or unspecified—is their controller, sustainer, and sovereign; He is the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī).

474. "He who [is] in all the Vedas": that Supreme Self (paramātman) who exists having entered within the specific deities presiding over all the Vedas, being their sustainer, controller, and sovereign—He is the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī), the Supreme Self.

475. "May we be able to attain the Nāciketa fire-altar, which is the bridge for those performing sacrifices, the imperishable Supreme Brahman, and the fearless further shore for those desiring to cross over.
[This means: it serves as a support like a bridge for those who perform rituals such as sacrifices ordained by the Vedas, and it bestows the fruits of all ritual actions.

That which is called the supreme Brahman, immutable, and that which is the fearless, firm shore for those desiring to cross the ocean of saṃsāra—that very reality attainable through the fire denoted by the term *nāciketa*—is what we are capable of meditating upon. Therefore, the sense is that one should not fear because of the thought that Brahman is difficult to meditate upon.

476. "That Aditi, consisting of the deities, who comes into being with Prāṇa; who, having entered the cave, abides there, and who was born together with the elements"—[this refers to] that which, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma, exists in the form of the individual soul (jīva) denoted by the term *Aditi*, joined with Prāṇa, subject to enjoyment through the senses, residing within the hollow of the heart-lotus, accompanied by the elements such as earth and the rest, and is born in various ways as the self of gods and others (that form, which is of this nature, is identical with Brahman).

477. Regarding the phrase "as long as the vital breath (prāṇa) dwells in this body, so long is life," the reading found in the Upaniṣads is "yāvaddhi asmin. In this visible body composed of the five elements (pañcabhautika), for as long as the vital breath remains, for that duration alone does life, characterized by inhalation and so forth, exist. 478. "As much wealth as I shall give to each individual priest, so much shall I give to your honors; please remain, sirs."
Pramāṇas with commentaries, page numbers... [etc.]

O you who are worthy of worship! In this sacrifice, I have resolved to give a certain amount of wealth to each officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)—such as the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and others—for the performance of the rite; I am now desirous of giving that same amount of wealth to you, my venerable guests. May you, my venerable ones, take up residence here in my abode. 479.
"'As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart.

The object indicated by the word "space" (ākāśa), which resides in the center of the lotus of the heart, is vast like the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) and is that which is to be designated by the word "this" (idam).
480. "By what the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known.
"By what the unheard becomes heard."
"By what [means] the unheard becomes heard" (8.481).
"If by that [knowledge] I were not to become immortal, what would I do with it? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows here."

With whatever wealth I have obtained from you, I am not able to become immortal—liberated from all bonds; what indeed could I do with that external wealth? I am unable to attain any supreme fruit. Since you, O venerable one, know that which brings about immortality, please teach that very thing to me as well.

482. "By what means could one know that by which one knows all this? [This means: This individual soul (*jīva*), being graced by that serene Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is capable of becoming omniscient; by what cause, then, could one be able to know that Supreme Self? (The meaning is that without the grace of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self is difficult to comprehend.
483. "Regarding this person who has died, there is this doubt: some say 'He exists,' and others say 'He does not exist.
"Instructed by you in this knowledge, this is the third of the boons. (Praśna Upaniṣad 1.340) "Regarding this which [happens] when one has died... (Praśna Upaniṣad).

When a human being— having attained the qualification for liberation through meditations prescribed by the Vedas and other means, and having achieved release from all bonds— still harbors this doubt (in the form of uncertainty) regarding that Self, consisting of the conflicting views of "it exists" or "it does not exist," as presented in this verse; for the purpose of removing (distantiating) that doubt, you, O Mṛtyu, the omniscient one, have clearly imparted instruction after having discerned the true nature of such a Self.
May I know [this]. This very attainment of knowledge from you is my third boon granted by you.

"He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know; he who moves within Death (mṛtyu), whose body is Death, whom Death does not know—he is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa. (90, 394)
II. "He who is the Imperishable... Nārāyaṇa":

He who is the Supreme Self, dwelling within the insentient entity called the Imperishable (akṣara)—the womb of the world—and likewise dwelling within the insentient form of death (mṛtyu), which is the aggregate of all that is non-conscious; he of whom the Imperishable and Darkness possess the qualities of being supported, being subject to command, and being subordinate; and whom the Imperishable and Darkness do not even know as existing within themselves—he is this very one who, having entered into the interior of all beings, is the Controller, free from all defects, and whose abode is the supreme, imperishable heaven (paramavyoman).
He is self-luminous, without equal or superior, and is denoted by the term Nārāyaṇa.
485. "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed delivered the Vedas to him"—these are the authoritative texts along with their commentaries.

486. *Pūrva-saṃhitā-prathama-saṃhitā*: "He who moves within death, whose body is death, whom death does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, the sinless, divine, unique God, Nārāyaṇa. 487. "He who alone presides over every womb."

The Supreme Self, being Himself one alone, renders even those diverse objects—such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the great principle (*mahat*), and so forth—which constitute the source of the universe, subject to His own governance in order to perfect their status as sources; (having realized such a Supreme Self through the knowledge called meditation, one attains supreme peace).

"O Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities without knowing this Imperishable—one who does so for many thousands of years, that act of theirs comes to an end. O Gārgī, whoever departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable; but he who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, O Gārgī, he is a true Brāhmaṇa."

Indeed, that person who, without realizing the Supreme Brahman called the Imperishable—the ruler of all which you have taught—performs in this world asceticism, sacrifices, and other rites for an exceedingly long life lasting up to a thousand years, and carries out actions achievable through great expenditure of wealth and effort, and likewise attains another world or another body, even the karma performed by that person does not yield eternal fruit.
He too is indeed to be pitied, because even though he has obtained such a body and an excellent lifespan, he remains one who has failed to attain the supreme goal of human life.

On the other hand, that person who, through devotion and other means, realizes this Imperishable Ruler, attains knowledge of Brahman, and casts off the acquired body— he is truly a *brāhmaṇa* in every respect.
He is not to be mourned; for he has accomplished the supreme goal of human life, having rendered both his body and his lifespan fruitful.

489. "He who, dwelling within consciousness—that which is the very nature of knowledge and characterized by the quality of knowledge—resides within the individual self (jīvātman), He alone is your immortal Inner Controller."
490. "O child, he who is the maker of these persons, or whose work this is—he indeed is to be known. (Praśna Upaniṣad). The authoritative texts with their commentaries.
PU. Saṃ.
II: "He who indeed... that action";
III: "He who indeed, O Bālāki."

O fools! You must understand that the very entity who is the creator of those persons such as Āditya and others whom you have taught to be Brahman—persons like Āditya and the rest being His effects—and likewise the entire world, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, which is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions, is also His effect; that alone is the reality which is the cause of the persons such as Āditya and of the world composed of the conscious and the unconscious, and not the things that are effects.

"He who moves within the Unmanifest, whose body is the Unmanifest, whom the Unmanifest does not know; he who moves within the Imperishable, whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know"—thus it is said.

That Supreme Self who, dwelling within the unmanifest entity denoted by the word "unmanifest," and dwelling within the insentient entity called the "imperishable" (akṣara) which contains consciousness as its core—He whose support, subordination, and subservience belong to both the unmanifest and the imperishable, and whom even the unmanifest and the imperishable do not know while they abide within Him—he is this Nārāyaṇa, designated by that term, who has entered within all things as their ruler.

This—the Person in the Sun, who is established in the form perceived by the eye through the medium of its rays—is the benefactor of the person in the eye (for in the absence of connection with the solar rays, the person in the eye, who is the Supreme Self, lacks the capacity to perform its own function). 493.

The venerable [author] [describes] this Prakṛti, which produces the sixteenfold transformation consisting of the eleven faculties and the five elements; which consists of the eightfold primary nature known as Prakṛti, Mahat, Ahaṅkāra, and the five Tanmātras; which is itself insentient; and which is remote from both origination and destruction—[this Prakṛti] is enjoyed by those of small wisdom who, though sentient, perceive it with the notion that it is an object of enjoyment.

And this primordial nature (prakṛti) is made an object by the Supreme Self through His knowledge consisting of volition (saṅkalpa). Being presided over by that very Supreme Self, it is brought to a gross state denoted by the term "expansion" (vistāra). Set in motion by that same volition and presided over by that same presiding Lord, she brings forth the world—which consists of the enjoyer, the objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment—as required for the sake of experience.

And this is Prakṛti; she is designated by the term "cow" (go) because she yields the essence of the Lord’s playful sport (līlā-rasa). Being devoid of beginning or end, she is eternal. She is the agent of both collective (samaṣṭi) and individual (vyaṣṭi) creation, and she exists endowed with the colors known as red, white, and black through the medium of fire, water, and earth.

And this [Prakṛti], by virtue of undergoing transformations in accordance with various respective karmas, is impartial. Individual selves (*puruṣa*), however, having failed to distinguish this Prakṛti from their own selves and thus remaining ignorant, are called "children" due to their dull intellect; consequently, being under the sway of karma, they experience [Prakṛti] with the notion that it is an object of enjoyment. The one Supreme Self (*paramātman*), on the other hand, being independent of karma, experiences her for the sake of divine play (*līlā*), while her nature, existence, and activity remain dependent upon His own volition.
And this Lord, having brought this very Prakṛti under His own control, enjoys it through the operations of His will and creation for the sake of the delight of His own divine play (*līlā*).

This Prakṛti is the common yielder of fruits for all bound individual souls (*jīvas*); like a mother providing milk for her calf, she becomes the means of experience when transformed by the selves—who are dependent on their own karma—into forms corresponding to the fruits of each respective action.

[Praśna Upaniṣad 1.8] This means that from the Supreme Person alone, who possesses a form composed of the brilliance of the color of lightning, all things consisting of gross, subtle, and other forms were produced.

"Or rather, he, seeing these desires with that divine eye— the mind— rejoices in those which are in the world of Brahman."

This very Self, distinct from the body and all the senses, the Person whose body and senses have been shaken off by the performance of the *vidhūnana* rite, shines forth as one possessed of bliss, experiencing through the eye known as *dharmabhūtajñāna*—which is included within His own essential nature (*svābhāvika*) and denoted by the term "mind"—all those qualities beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve that reside in the small space (*daharākāśa*) called the world of Brahman, as previously described.

"He who, seeing thus, thinking thus, and knowing thus, finds delight in the Self, sports with the Self, has the Self as his companion, and finds bliss in the Self—he becomes a self-ruler; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. But those who know otherwise than this are ruled by others; their worlds are perishable, and they have no freedom of movement in any world. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2)

This conscious lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) directed toward the previously mentioned Self that is the Plenum (*bhūman*), has directly realized the Self known as the Plenum; he becomes a partaker of every kind of bliss, which is rooted in various objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment, because within that bliss all other forms of bliss are included.

He becomes independent of karma; with his knowledge unobstructed by karma, he is liberated. Having experienced the worlds of transformation—which are the manifestations of Brahman—he is satisfied according to his desire. But those who worship in a manner other than that which has been described become servants to the injunctions and prohibitions. Likewise, they possess worlds that are subject to decay. Furthermore, they do not have the power of unimpeded movement within the various other worlds of transformation that constitute the manifestations of the Blessed Lord.

"He who sees thus, thinks thus, and knows thus, becomes an *ativādī*. In the preceding sentence, the individual soul (*jīva*), designated by the word "prāṇa,"—while making his own self the object of reflection in the manner previously described, and while being a worshiper who realizes [it] through that same mode—becomes one who proclaims the preeminence of the object of his worship. *Ativāditva* (the state of being an *ativādī*) consists in possessing the character of proclaiming the supremacy of one's own deity of worship, which confers brilliance upon rival disputants equal to Bṛhaspati;
and this ultimately culminates in the excellence of the deity being worshipped.
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries. The Prasaṅga. The Prasaṅga.
588. "This very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*).
This body has been created through the sequence beginning with "From the Self, space was produced," and is thus a transformation of the essence of food.
589. "That indeed is the great, unborn Self, undecaying and immortal."

This Supreme Self previously introduced is free from birth, old age, and death; (He is not subject to saṃsāra). 590. "That indeed is this great, unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth. This Supreme Self previously introduced is far removed from birth and, by implication, from old age, death, and so forth; He is the provider of food necessary for sustaining the body, and the source of the wealth required for procuring clothing and other necessities related to life.
And furthermore: 591. "He is to be known as such.
592. "In all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves, he eats food."

593. "Immediately upon rising, Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa spoke to the *kṣattṛ*": having somehow passed the night, King Jānaśruti, while still leaving his bed, addressed the *kṣattṛ*—a member of a specific mixed caste (*pratiloma*) born of a *kṣatriya* father and a *vaiśya* mother—and said this.
594. "'The Puruṣa has a thousand heads.'"

The Supreme Self is the support of innumerable heads, the knower of all, full everywhere, or ancient; or He is so called because He lies within the city known as the body (*puri*). 595. "He said: 'I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (*prajñātmā*); meditate upon me as life and immortality. These are the authoritative texts along with their commentaries.

"O Gārgī, it is devoid of shadow and the like; this very [reality] called the Imperishable (the Supreme Brahman), the knowers of Brahman describe everywhere and on all sides in just this way," thus Yājñavalkya spoke to Gārgī.
597. "But bliss indeed is what one must desire to understand": regarding Brahman, which is to be heard, that which is absolutely favorable [to the self] must be known.

598. "'The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as before; and heaven and earth..."* [The remainder of the verse follows: "...the intermediate space, and the years, and the waters. *Rig Veda X.190.3*
"Then he fashioned the stars and the sky; Sūryā... he ordained"—[referring to] the four-faced one (the ruler of the world that has attained existence) for the purpose of ordaining day and night.
Just as in a previous kalpa, so too in this kalpa, the Sun and the Moon created the earth, the intermediate space, the heavenly world, and the world of light.
"This very [Vedic knowledge] is four-footed."

This very aforementioned *bhūta-pṛthivī* (the elemental earth), possessing four feet known as the body, the heart, and so forth, is denoted by the term "Gāyatrī" because its attributes are similar to the attributes residing in [the verse] Gāyatrī; it is thus of the nature of Brahman.
600. "This is the inquiry into bliss (*ānanda-mīmāṃsā*)," meaning that this following investigation concerning bliss is about to be undertaken.

601. "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he emitted all this, whatever exists here. Having emitted it, he entered into that very thing. Having entered it, he became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and non-consciousness, truth and falsehood; [it was] truth that became [all]. I. "He... "...may I procreate. III. "He... "...may I procreate. IV. "He desired. 84, 408, 75, 98, 100, 409.

The Supreme Self, consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), formed the resolve for creation regarding both the conscious and unconscious realms—both individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*)—thinking: "May I become manifold in the form of gods, humans, and so forth; for that purpose, may I be born in the form of ether and the rest. That Supreme Self performed *tapas* in the form of contemplation upon what was to be created.
And *tapas* consists of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) along with their explanations (see page numbers).

Having performed the primary creation (*pratisarga*), He created the entire universe consisting of both sentient and insentient beings. Having produced the world—comprising the gross and the subtle, the moving and the non-moving, and taking the form of the conscious and the unconscious—He entered into it everywhere as its underlying continuity. And having thus entered, He Himself became Brahman in the form of the unchanging consciousness and in the form of the changing insentience.

And that very Brahman—though itself becoming the ultimate substratum for all those names and forms belonging to the non-conscious (acetana) category, which are devoid of genus, qualities, and so forth, and are denoted by the words "non-intelligent," "unborn," "insentient," "false," and which belong to the conscious (cetana) category, which do possess genus, qualities, and so forth, and are denoted by the words "intelligent," "dependent," "sentient," and "real"—remained truly real (*satyam eva abhavat*) because it did not abandon its own innate nature, which consists in being changeless (*nirvikāratva*).
"He reaches the end of the path; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

603. "He, O gentle one, shatters the knot of ignorance right here in this world"—O gentle one! the conscious being who possesses the direct realization of the nature of Brahman, known as the Imperishable Person (akṣara-puruṣa) mentioned previously, casts off ignorance which is as difficult to untie as a knot.
604. "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman."
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries. Introduction. Introduction.

By what single object, when made the subject of reflection (*manana*), would everything not made the subject of reflection also come to be within the range of reflection; and by what single object, when made the subject of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), would everything not made the subject of meditative contemplation also come to be within the range of meditative contemplation? Have you learned, through inquiry in the presence of the Guru, that supreme object which is the ruler of all and is denoted by the word "Instruction" (*ādeśa*)? Only when that object is known does this state of being stunned become appropriate as being caused by fullness.

607. "Learn from me, my dear, the end of sleep. When a person here is said to be 'sleeping,' then, my dear, he has become united with Being; he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ). Therefore they say of him 'he sleeps' (svapiti), for he has gone to his own."

"Come, my dear Śvetaketu! I have begun to speak to you concerning deep sleep; understand that matter clearly from my words. Indeed, when a certain person enters that particular state called sleep, then—at the time of sleep—that person attains a dissolution in the form of absorption into that which is designated by the term 'Being' (sat)."

The Supreme Self (paramātman), whose body is His own self (svaśarīraka)—meaning He is free from the impurity of egoistic identification dependent upon the names, forms, and so forth of gods and other beings—one becomes absorbed into that very Self. For this reason alone, people say of a person in deep sleep, "He sleeps" (*svapiti*); because, having attained the Supreme Self denoted by the word *sva* (own/self) due to being of the nature of His own body, he has become dissolved therein. "In His own greatness" (*sve mahimni*):
the Supreme Self is designated by the term *bhūman*, which signifies vast bliss; He is supported solely by His own self, and unlike other objects, He does not have a support other than Himself.

609. "Alas! Entering these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me unfold names and forms"—this was the resolve of the Supreme Deity denoted by the word "Sat" [meaning]: "Having entered the three elements—fire, water, and earth—which are presided over by their respective presiding deities, through a living self consisting of myself, may I become the manifester of names and forms. 610. "The channels called *hitā*... at that time he exists within them."

When one has fallen asleep and does not see any dream whatsoever, he becomes one with this vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone; then speech enters into him together with all names... the mind enters into him together with all thoughts. (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.11)
The authoritative texts with their commentaries [state]:

"O venerable Saṃyadvāma, when he awakens—just as from a blazing fire sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self the vital breaths (prāṇas) disperse to their respective stations; from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds."

Because they bring about one's own welfare, certain channels connected to the heart are designated by the term "hita. During the time of sleep, the individual soul (jīva) takes its resort within those exceedingly subtle channels.

And when this individual soul (jīva), having left the waking state and entered within, becomes asleep and ceases from the perception of dreams, then, following the dream state, this jīva becomes unified with the Supreme Self whose body is vital breath (prāṇaśarīra); it remains situated free from the impurities characterized by the egoistic identification with the body produced by states such as waking.

Immediately thereafter, this individual self (jīvātman), as it dissolves into the Supreme Self (paramātman), departs together with the organ of speech and its functions, namely the utterance of names; the organ of sight departs together with its function, which consists in the cognition of forms; the organ of hearing departs together with its function, which consists in the cognition of sounds; and the mind also departs together with its functions, such as meditation and the like.

And when this individual soul (*jīva*) attains the state of waking, then from this Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who serves as the substratum of dissolution, the individual souls designated by the term "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) set out for their respective stations like sparks from a fire. In the same way, from the individual soul, the sense organs proceed, and from the sense organs, their respective cognitions become directed toward their own functions, just as before. 611. "The heart is the *gārhapatya* fire, the mind is the *anvāhāryapacana*, and the mouth is the *āhavanīya*."

For one who worships Vaiśvānara, the digestive fire delimited by the heart-lotus is the Gārhapatya fire; the digestive fire delimited by the mind and the senses is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; and the digestive fire delimited by the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1) "Those who know him, fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind, they become immortal. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1)

(Tai. Nā. U. 1-11): This Supreme Self cannot be grasped by the eyes and other senses; it is to be grasped by the mind alone, accompanied by devotion and fortitude. Those who realize such a Supreme Self through meditation become liberated from all bonds (and become blissful). [The authoritative texts with their commentaries].

Pūrva Saṃhitā 6.13: "Now, for one who listens to his Veda, there shall be the filling of the ears with molten lead and lac; for reciting it, the cutting off of the tongue; and for retaining it in memory, the destruction of the body."

For this Śūdra who is intent on hearing the mass of syllables known as the Veda being recited by Brāhmaṇas and others, the penance for hearing it is the filling of the ear-cavities with lead and lac. If the Veda is uttered, the penance is indeed the cutting off of the organ of the tongue, which is the instrument of utterance. If, having heard it, he should retain it in his heart, then the penance for that is the splitting of the body. 614. "That which possesses qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman], because of the mention of its attributes."

The entity that possesses the attributes such as invisibility mentioned in the passage beginning with "indescribable" (adreśyam) is none other than the Supreme Brahman; for attributes exclusive to the Supreme Brahman, such as omniscience and so forth, are stated to reside in that very entity in passages such as, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving. [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.5.3.10] "For this divine speech, consisting of the Veda, was emitted by the Self-existent in the beginning—without beginning or end—from which all emanations proceed."

By the Creator, who is designated by the term "Svayambhū" (the Self-existent), at the time of the commencement of creation, this divine speech (*daivī vāk*)—which consists of the Vedas and is devoid of origin and destruction—was merely manifested; it was not produced anew. From this very speech, which is composed of the Vedas, all these various creations have come into being. 616. *Anukṛtes tasya ca* (And because of the imitation of that). 617. *Api smaryate* (It is also recorded in Smṛti). 618. *Arthaikatve dravyaguṇayor aikakarmyān niyamaḥ syāt* (When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction [of application] due to the unity of function between the substance and its quality).
Page numbers for the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* with commentaries. Page numbers.

619. "Ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt" [Taittirīya Ānandavallī]: The referent denoted by the term *ānandamaya* occurring in the Taittirīya Ānandavallī is indeed the Supreme Brahman; (it is not [the individual soul]).
The other is the individual soul (*jīva*), because it possesses the fitness for experiencing unsurpassed bliss through repeated practice.
620. "This was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without defining marks, beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep."

II. "This was then enveloped in darkness" (II.9). This visible world, prior to its creation and at the time of dissolution, existed merged in a subtle form, having attained the state of *prakṛti*. Even *prakṛti* existed as the Self of Brahman—unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), that is, not yet having undergone the differentiation of name and form. Therefore, it remained imperceptible, inferable, impossible even to conceive through logic, and unknowable even through verbal testimony; it existed as if asleep, incapable of producing its own effects. [Pāṇini Sūtra: *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*].

The *kṛtya* suffixes and the suffix *lyuṭ* occur diversely (*bahulam*) in various senses. Wherever they are prescribed, they occur even elsewhere. Although the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), they also occur with other *kārakas*. For example: *snānīyaṃ cūrṇam* (powder for bathing) and *dānīyo brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brāhmaṇa worthy of a gift). The suffix *lyuṭ* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the abstract action (*bhāva*); it also occurs elsewhere, as in: *upasecanam* (sprinkling), *avasrāvaṇam* (draining), *rājabhojanāḥ śālayaḥ* (rice fit for the king's meal), *rājācchādanāni vāsāṃsi* (clothes for the king's covering), *praskandanam* (leaping forward), and *prapatanam* (falling down).

Due to the inclusion of the term "mostly" (*bahula*), other *kṛt* suffixes as well deviate from their primary denotation as it applies. For example: *pādābhyāṃ hiyate* — *pādahārakaḥ*; *gale copyate* — *gale copakaḥ* (Kāśikāvṛtti). 622. "The fourth caste is of a single birth and does not deserve sacramental rites. (Source unknown)

The Śūdra is distinct from the three higher castes (traivarṇika) in that he possesses only a single birth, consisting merely in his emergence from his mother’s womb; he is not established by Śruti or Smṛti as having a second birth like the members of the three higher castes. Therefore, he is not entitled to the sacraments (saṃskāra) pertaining to the three higher castes. [Brahma-sūtra 4.4.17: "Except for the activity of governing the world. For the liberated one, whose every veil has been removed, sovereignty consists in the unimpeded experience of Brahman—[this applies to] all...

[This is] excluding the determination of the distinctions in the nature, state, and activity of the sentient and the insentient. (Why? Because all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), along with their commentaries, [establish this].

First: The governance of the world is indeed taught in the context of the Supreme Brahman alone, through passages such as "From which indeed these [beings arise]," and so forth; it is not, however, taught in the context of the individual soul (jīva). Likewise, in all these instances concerning the governance of the entire world, read within their respective contexts, the proximity of the liberated soul (mukta) is also not observed.
624. "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]."

That very supreme Brahman is the object of inquiry, from which proceed the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this manifest universe—which is filled with various and diverse enjoyers and objects of enjoyment—as well as liberation in the form of absolute dissolution.
625. "Because of the mention of the feet of light" (Jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt).
626. "The suffix mayaṭ is used in the sense of being made of that" (Tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ).

The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case that is semantically capable and denotes something presented in abundance. (Example: *annamayam*—food is the subject; "the sacrifice consists of food" means food is the primary constituent in it).
627. "Then the Grandfather [Brahmā] was in the egg."

628. "The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning 'originating' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth"; this effect, namely the world, is non-different from that supreme cause, the Supreme Brahman.

The absence of difference [between cause and effect] is established by means of authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*) consisting of scriptural statements (*śrutivākya*) such as "the modification is a mere verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāraḥ*), which contain the word *ārambhaṇa*. 629. Regarding the rule "In the case of names, [words for] directions and numbers [are compounded] with a word ending in a case-suffix that is in grammatical apposition":

words denoting directions and numbers are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix that stands in apposition; this results in a *tatpuruṣa* compound when the context concerns a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: "Pūrveṣu Kāmaśamī" (The Kāmaśamī in the east) and "Apareṣu Kāmaśamī" (The Kāmaśamī in the west). For numbers: "Pañcāmrāḥ" (The five mango trees) and "Saptarṣayaḥ" (The seven sages). Why "in the case of a name"? [Counter-examples: "Uttarā vṛkṣāḥ" (The northern trees) and "Pañca brāhmaṇāḥ" (Five Brahmins).
630. "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word.
Pramāṇas with Explanations.
Page 631:

"If it be argued that [the inequality of creation] cannot be so because of the non-distinction [of souls from Brahman] prior to creation, we say no; for [the cycle] is beginningless, and this is both logical and observed. This objection—that since scripture declares the non-distinction of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman at the time prior to creation, the specific karma belonging to each soul which serves as the cause for the unequal creation could not have existed at that time—is not tenable.

Even though the individual souls (*jīva*) and their respective karmas—which serve as the causes of inequality—exist prior to creation, the scriptural statement regarding non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) is appropriate because it refers merely to the absence of the distinction between name and form (*nāma-rūpa*). Furthermore, since the individual selves and their karmas are not characterized by having a first beginning, the beginninglessness (*anāditva*) of the souls is clearly understood from such scriptural passages as, "The wise one is neither born nor does he die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18). 632. "One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow for him. Regarding the phrase "not... the Dharma," the authoritative texts along with their commentaries [are cited] in the *Prasthāna-saṃgraha*.
Praśna-saṃhitā:

"There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the sacraments. There is no sin for a Śūdra arising from the non-performance of the *saṃdhyā-vandana* and other rites, because he is ineligible for sacraments such as the initiation (*upanayana*). 636. "Because it must be perceived thus. 637. "Always [the suffix *ṇini* is used] after words such as *vṛddha* and *śara*."

The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) classified as "vṛddha" (where the first vowel among the vowels of the stem is *vṛddhi*) and after those belonging to the *śara*-group, provided they do not refer to food or clothing. First, examples from the "vṛddha" stems: *āmramayam* (made of mango). (From the *śara*-group: *śaramayaṃ barhiḥ*—sacrificial grass made of reeds). 638.
"But [the suffix is applied] after a word denoting the material, because that is what is heard [in the source]."

The agency residing in the individual soul (jīvātman) is dependent solely upon the Supreme Self, the supreme Brahman who acts as the controller; it is not dependent on the soul alone, because of the scriptural understanding that the Supreme alone is the ruler of all, as stated in the passage: "He has entered within, the ruler of people.
639. *Pṛthv-ādibhya imanij vā*.

The suffix *imanij* optionally occurs after nominal stems such as *pṛthu* and others in the sense of "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*). The mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence of other suffixes such as *aṇ*. The state of being broad is *prathimā* (also *pārthava*, *pṛthutva*, *pṛthutā*). 640. "There is elision of the final vowel of *bahu*, and *bahu* becomes *bhū*."

In the case of the word *bahu*, there is the elision of the superlative suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *iman*, and *īyasun*. Furthermore, in place of that *bahu*, the substitute *abhū* occurs. Examples: *bhūyān* (comparative), *bhūmā* (superlative). 641. "Because of the designation of difference. 642. "Because of the indicative mark of equality in mere enjoyment."

For the liberated individual soul (jīvātman), equality with Brahman exists only in the enjoyment consisting of the experience of Brahman; this is stated by the Śruti: "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman. From this indicative evidence as well, it is determined that the "supreme equality" mentioned in the statement "the stainless one attains supreme equality" excludes the world-activity and so forth, and does not apply in every respect. 635.
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries,
as compiled by Pūjyapāda Saṅghadāsagaṇi.
The means of valid cognition with their commentaries. (Pra.saṃ. The means of valid cognition with their commentaries. (Pra.saṃ.)

The complete sūtra is: *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ*. In the domain of Vedic (*chandasi*), in place of the case endings (*supām*), these substitutes occur: *su*, *luk* (elision), *pūrvasavarṇa* (the preceding homogeneous vowel), *āt*, *śe*, *yā*, *ḍā*, *ḍyā*, *yāc*, *āl*. For example: *anṛkṣarā ṛjavaḥ santu panthānaḥ*. Although the plural form *panthānaḥ* would have been expected, [by this rule] there is the singular substitute *su*, resulting in *panthāḥ*. Similarly: *ādre carman* for *carmāṇi*.

In the year 650 [after the Flood], desiring to emit various kinds of progeny, he, having meditated, first created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed. That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun.
Within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.

"He, the eternal Supreme Self, having meditated and formed the resolve necessary for the creation of the world, desiring to create subjects of manifold, diverse, and infinite kinds from His own body, first created the element of water; and therein He cast His seed. The seed of the Supreme Self cast into the waters became a golden egg, radiant like the sun. And within that golden egg, Brahmā, the grandfather of all worlds, was born of his own accord."
651. "And because of the designation of places and so forth.
652. "For this divine speech, consisting of the Vedas, was emitted by the Self-existent One at the beginning; it is without beginning or end, from which all manifestations proceed."

At the time of the commencement of creation, by the Supreme Self—whose existence is not dependent on anything else—that very Vedic speech which is perceivable through hearing alone, untouched by birth or destruction, consisting primarily of words whose sole nature is the knowledge of supersensuous realities, and which is impersonal (apauruṣeyī), was manifested externally from His own inner being in the form of a breath. Relying solely upon that [Vedic speech], all worldly creations have proceeded.

653. "The unmanifest dissolves into the inactive Puruṣa-Brahman. The entity called the unmanifest, through the resolve of the desire to withdraw [the world], becomes completely dissolved into the Brahman-Puruṣa who is devoid of action; it enters a state where name and form are undifferentiated. (Or, "O Brahman" may be taken as a vocative. 654. "From the unmanifest down to the specific elements, it is endowed with the power of transformation."

"Understand that all this is the play of Hari and is perishable. Whatever exists, beginning from the *mahat-tattva* down to the *viśeṣas*, which serves as the locus for the modifications of being such as growth and decay—all this has been created by the Lord's sport; let it be determined that it is denoted by the term "perishable" (*kṣara*). 655. "That which arises from scripture... [is] declared. 656. "I shall describe the first creation":
I shall speak of the primordial creation. 657. "Behold His activity like that of a playing child": Listen to the sport of the Supreme Self, which resembles the play of a sporting infant.

658. "For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the Blessed One—which consists of manifestation preceded by the assumption of forms such as those of gods—is not born from the cause of karma, unlike that of the individual soul (jīva). Rather, for the Blessed One, who transcends the reach of speech and mind, it is essentially an incarnation and so forth, pervading various objects, places, and times, possessing an unimpeded nature, and having solely the welfare of the world as its purpose. 659. "O great sage, both knowledge and action have been declared to be the means for attaining Him."

"Knowledge is likewise said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discrimination. O Great Sage! Among these, the first type of knowledge is twofold: indirect (parokṣa) knowledge produced by hearing the scriptures, and another form of knowledge consisting of meditation aided by the sevenfold means beginning with discrimination. (Praśnasaṃgraha)

660: "There, from the navel of the sleeping Lord, a lotus was born."
O fortunate one! Upon that lotus sat one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

Born from Brahmā, he was addressed by him: "O great sage, create progeny! O one endowed with great fortune! A certain lotus arose at the navel of the Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, who was sleeping upon the Ocean of Milk in yogic slumber (yoganidrā). Upon that lotus situated at the navel, Brahmā—the four-faced one—was born, possessing complete knowledge of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches (*vedāṅgas*) spontaneously. That Brahmā was told by the Blessed One: "O you of great contemplative nature, perform the creation of beings. That very thing which had been for his pleasure now turns again into sorrow.
"Since that very same thing arises for both anger and favor, therefore nothing has the nature of suffering, nor does anything have the nature of happiness.

Since a single object, in accordance with differences of time, place, individual, and so forth, becomes the producer of both pleasure and pain, and the cause of both anger and favor; therefore, it is impossible to define any single object as being either essentially happy or essentially painful.
662. "Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest has arisen as consisting of the three qualities (guṇas)."

From the indeterminate—that entity consisting of darkness (tamas) which is incapable of the differentiation of name and form—there arose a differentiated darkness that serves as the substratum for the three qualities characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. 663. "O Brahmins, know him whose head they call the sky, whose navel is space, and whose eyes are the moon and sun; know his ears to be the quarters and his feet the earth—he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings."

Know that the Supreme Self, the creator of the entire world consisting of the moving and the unmoving, who is of the nature of Virāṭ and whose essential form is indivisible, is he whom the wise declare to have the heavenly realm as his head, space as his navel, the moon and sun as his eyes, the eastern, western, and other directions as his ears, and the earth as his feet.

"The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an assemblage of the elements. Even when this Supreme Self, who possesses the aforementioned majesty, assumes an incarnation in the world, His body during that period of incarnation is not constituted of the parts of the aggregate of the five elements, such as earth and the rest. [Prapanchasārasaṃgraha, with commentary]. **Explanatory Notes on the Authorities:** 1. **The Body is Not Elemental**: The *Prapanchasārasaṃgraha* establishes that the physical form assumed by the Supreme Lord during an incarnation is not a mere collection of the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*). This is because the Lord, being the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is inherently beyond material nature (*prakṛti*). His manifestation is a display of His divine power (*vaibhava*) and is not subject to the laws of elemental composition. 2. **Divine Nature of Incarnations**: While He appears in human or animal forms for the sake of the world, these forms are essentially spiritual. They are sustained by His own divine energy (*māyā-śakti*) rather than being bound by the causal chain of karma or the accumulation of matter. Thus, the "body" of an avatar is a temporary vessel for His infinite attributes, not a biological organism formed from the union of semen and ovum or the subsequent development of the five elements. 3. **Scriptural Support**: Various Purāṇic and Tantric texts describe the incarnations (*avatāras*) as manifestations of the Lord’s limbs or powers. For instance, in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, it is stated that the Lord manifests through His portions (*aṃśa*) or portions of portions (*aṃśāṃśa*) to uphold dharma. These descriptions emphasize that the incarnate forms are integral to His divine essence and not products of the material world. 4. **Distinction from Ordinary Bodies**: An ordinary human body is a result of past actions (*karma*) and is subject to decay and death. In contrast, the body of an incarnation is a deliberate manifestation of the Lord’s will, intended for specific cosmic purposes, and is therefore distinct in its origin and nature from the bodies of mortal beings. In summary, the authorities cited affirm that the Supreme Self’s incarnate body, despite appearing to be made of flesh and bone, is fundamentally non-material and is a direct expression of His supreme majesty. It is a specialized mode of existence that transcends the limitations of the five-elemental compound.

"In the beginning, he [Brahmā] fashioned from the words of the Veda alone the names and forms of all beings, as well as the expansion of their activities, including those of the gods and others. (Praśastapādabhāṣya 665)

O Lord, for all four classes of embodied beings—known as gods, humans, animals, and stationary objects—their names, such as the designations of their species (god, human, deer, tree, etc.), their forms, such as being unblinking, bipedal, quadrupedal, or possessing branches, and the expansion of their duties, such as the performance of sacrifices with oblations and portions, are [all derived from Him].
Nārāyaṇa, whose very nature is self-luminous, is thus superior to all and is the supreme cause. From that very Nārāyaṇa, even the four-faced Creator was born.
667. "The primordial nature (prakṛti) which I have described, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, and the person (puruṣa)—these two dissolve into the Supreme Self."
"And the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, is the substratum of all.

O Maitreya! That Prakṛti, consisting of gross and subtle forms and denoted by the word "Tamas," which was previously explained by me (Parāśara), as well as that Consciousness (Cetana) which consists of both the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi)—both these, namely Prakṛti and Puruṣa, remain in a state of non-distinction within the Supreme Brahman at the time of dissolution. And that Supreme Self, who has become the Supreme Brahman, is the substratum and the controller of all. 668. "As a child with his toys..."

Just as a man in the state of childhood plays with toys and, while playing, experiences nothing but joy, so too the Supreme Self engages in the activities of creating, maintaining, and dissolving the universe, yet remains one who finds delight in divine play.
669. ‘Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons are seen again and again in their recurring cycle, so too do all things appear at the beginning of each Yuga.

Just as the leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth found on trees and other plants serve as indicators of the seasons—such as spring and the rest—which are parts of the year, and how these very same types of signs reappear whenever the seasons revolve within another year; so it is with all beings at the start of the ages.
