"Salutation to Him who is the Self of the worlds, whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is the sky, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the sun, and whose ears are the quarters."

Salutations to that Supreme Self, whose form is the Virāj, whose mouth is fire, whose head is the heavenly world, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the sun, and whose ears are the quarters—possessed of such inconceivable majesty and having all the worlds as His body. "By rain, the seed was gladdened. By the falling of rain, the seed—which is the cause for the production of grain—became characterized by a specific state preceding its sprouting.

673. "Manifest is Viṣṇu, as well as the unmanifest, the Person (*puruṣa*), and Time itself."

The unmanifest (avyakta) is that which is denoted by the term *pradhāna*; the manifest (vyakta) is that which is denoted by terms such as *mahat* and so forth, ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*); the individual soul (*jīva*) is that which is expressed by the term *puruṣa*; and likewise, time (*kāla*), which is the cause of the differentiation of all things—all these have their essential nature, existence, and activity dependent upon the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), and they constitute His body. Thus, it is not untenable for the Supreme Self, whose body these are, to be the cause [of the world].

"One should cause the four castes to hear [these teachings], having placed the Brāhmaṇa at the forefront. 676. "O King, that other great form of Hari, in which all these powers are established, possesses a nature both universal and diverse.

O King, that form of the Blessed One in which all the aforementioned powers—known as ignorance (*avidyā*) and consisting of bound and liberated karma—are well-established by means of their respective presiding deities; that body of the Lord, whose configuration is distinct from the world, is a different substance established by such Vedic texts as "of solar hue" (*ādityavarṇam*). 677. "Because the Infinite One is omnipresent, He alone abides as I. From Me everything arises, I am everything, and everything exists within Me, the Eternal.

Because the Supreme Self, Mahā-Viṣṇu, is undivided by space, time, or substance, and because He exists pervading all things, and because He abides as the very Self of all—on account of this, I am indeed identical with Him. Since everything is born from, subsists in, and dissolves into that Supreme Self who is my own Self, the entire universe is indeed the Supreme Self, who is my own Self.

"Everything that has become my own self is indeed sustained by the eternal Supreme Self; of this I have no doubt. 678. O Goddess Lakṣmī! Having first created the element of water designated as "Nāra," I abide within that element of water. It is precisely by abiding within the water-element called "Nāra" that my name "Nārāyaṇa" was established. Furthermore, in every kalpa, I repeatedly sleep upon that water called "Nāra. While I am thus resting in sleep, a single lotus arises from my navel.

While I was reclining, resting upon my navel-lotus, the four-faced Brahmā was born from that navel-lotus of mine; and I ordained his role as the creator of progeny. [Prasannapadā] citations with commentary.

Vāsudeva, whose nature is to govern the entire universe consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, stands within the heart-region of all beings—the locus where arises the knowledge that is the root of all engagement and withdrawal—having mounted the machine called *prakṛti*, which He Himself has fashioned in the form of the body and senses. By means of His own *māyā* composed of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest, He causes all beings to proceed in accordance with those qualities. Know Him alone to be the Protector.
685. "Understand that all beings have this as their womb;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe."

O Arjuna! Understand that all my beings—consisting of a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, existing in high and low states, and originating from my two natures (prakṛtis) as previously described—are mine. Therefore, understand that I alone am the source of the entire universe, I alone am its dissolution, and I alone am the substratum.
"In the matter of being the effect, the cause, and the agent, nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause."

"The Puruṣa is said to be the cause for the experiencing of pleasure and pain. [This refers to] the body; likewise, Prakṛti, presided over by the Puruṣa, is the cause for the mind and the organs of knowledge and action in performing their respective functions. All activities that serve as the means of experience depend upon Prakṛti, which has transformed into the form of the field (*kṣetra*) and is presided over by the Puruṣa. The Puruṣa is merely the presider. When conjoined with Prakṛti, the Puruṣa becomes the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain.
"The perishable consists of all beings; the immutable is called the Akṣara (the Imperishable)."
All things from Brahmā down to a blade of grass are conjoined with the insentient (acit) by virtue of their perishable nature; these are designated by the term "jīva" (living being).

"This ego (ahaṅkāra)—thus is my nature divided eightfold. The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), which is the cause of the production of this world with its manifold, diverse, and infinite modes, is divided into eight forms: earth together with the subtle element of smell; water together with the subtle element of taste; fire together with the subtle element of form; air together with the subtle element of touch; ether together with the subtle element of sound; the mind accompanied by the five organs of cognition and the five organs of action; and the principle of the Great One (mahattattva), also known by the synonym intellect (buddhi), which is the principle of ego (ahaṅkāratattva).
And this is my other nature (prakṛti). 693. "There is nothing else whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya;
all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems upon a thread.

O Dhanañjaya! Just as I am the highest because I am the cause of all and the sovereign of all, so too am I alone the highest by virtue of possessing qualities such as knowledge and power. There is nothing whatsoever that is higher than Me.

In Me— who am such a cause of all, the remainder of all, endowed with the most excellent qualities, and who abide as the sustainer and the body for everyone like a thread— every effect exists as My own body, abiding in the state of being sustained, governed, and subordinate like a collection of gems. (Gītā 9.10) "Under Me as the supervisor, nature produces the moving and the unmoving."

"By this cause, O Kaunteya, the world indeed revolves. [694] "Impelled by Me... it moves," O Kaunteya! By Me—who possess true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*), who am capable of direct perception of all things, and who occupy the position of the navel (the center) of everything to be created—this My own *prakṛti* creates the world of moving and non-moving beings in accordance with the karma of the *kṣetrajña*. Indeed, by the cause consisting of My glance in accordance with the karma of the *kṣetrajña*, this world exists as something subject to constant change.
[695] "He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as the Supreme Person..."

Indeed, that lay follower (*upāsaka*) who knows me—the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*)—as being distinct from the Person consisting of all beings denoted by the word "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), and from the immutable Person denoted by the word "the Immutable" (*akṣara*), on account of my possession of qualities such as imperishability, pervasiveness, and sustaining power; (he knows everything that is to be known as the means for attaining me). *Prasthāna-saṃgraha*: Explanatory authorities with commentaries.
"O mighty-armed one, the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, born of primordial nature (prakṛti), bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body."

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three *guṇas*, which are specific modifications inherent to the very nature of *prakṛti* (definable solely through their effects, such as illumination and so forth). These bind this imperishable embodied soul—who is connected to bodies such as those of gods and humans, produced by the series beginning with the *mahat* and ending with the gross elements—to the body; though the soul is inherently free from connection with the *guṇas*, it is bound by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of its existence within the body.
697. "O son of Kuntī, all beings go to my own *prakṛti* at the end of a cycle (*kalpa*). At the beginning of the next cycle, I send them forth again."

O Kaunteya! At the conclusion of the final day of Brahmā, all beings—consisting of both the stationary and the moving—attain my Prakṛti, which is designated by the word "Tamas" (darkness), which is devoid of the differentiation of name and form, and which constitutes my own body; they do so solely through my will, as they are incapable of maintaining a separate existence. Then, at the commencement of the next Kalpa, I alone bring forth all those beings again by my own will.
(698) "And I am seated in the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss."

In the locus called the heart, which is the site for the arising of knowledge—the root of all activity and cessation for every class of living beings—I am established as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). Therefore, from me alone comes the memory of all beings, which consists of knowledge born solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previously experienced objects; likewise, the certain knowledge of things produced by the senses, logical marks, scripture, or yoga; and even the process of reasoning (*ūhana*), which consists of the withdrawal of [false] knowledge or is of the nature of deliberation, arises from me alone and is entirely dependent upon me.

In specific meditations such as the Madhu-vidyā, there certainly exists the possibility of eligibility for worship even for those who have attained the status of the Vasus and other gods; for in all meditations, whether in every case or in a different body, it is Brahman alone that is to be directly realized through meditation, and since that meditation remains uncontradicted even in their case. 144,332.

700. Regarding the phrase "that which is within it" (*tasmin yadantaḥ*) in the passage on the *dahara-vidyā*: by the portion stating, "That which is within it is what must be sought; that indeed is what one must desire to understand," there is a clear indication that the very auspicious qualities of the Lord, which are the objects of desire, are what must be sought. 701. "Indeed, a Śūdra is a cemetery; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."

That which is called "the Śūdra, the fourth caste," is a moving cremation ground—an absolute locus of manifold impurity. For that reason, the act known as the study of the Vedas is forbidden in a location situated near such an impure Śūdra. 702. "The co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of words with different grounds for application (pravṛttinimitta) in a single referent [is defined as]...

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in two words having a single referent despite having different meanings due to their qualifiers; that is, the two grounds for the application of the two words reside in a single substratum.
703. "But the Plenum indeed"—the Plenum is Brahman; for it is taught as being superior to the Self through the succession beginning with Name.

The meaning of the word "bhūman" (the Infinite), as stated in the sentence "But the bhūman alone is to be sought after," is the Supreme Brahman, which is unsurpassed and infinite in its essential nature and attributes. Having taught that everything from name up to speech, mind, volition, thought, meditation, understanding, strength, food, water, fire, ether, memory, hope, and finally vital breath, each is superior to the one preceding it, and having described how one who possesses knowledge of the reality of what has been taught attains the status of an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond), [the text] explains that the "ativāda" of the Supreme Self, known as Truth, is in fact the ultimate *ativāda*.

Having stated that consciousness (*vijñāna*), intellect (*mati*), faith (*śraddhā*), steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), action (*kṛti*), and bliss (*sukha*) are to be known for their utility toward that [Brahman], [the text] then states that the Infinite (*bhūman*) is to be known precisely as consisting of bliss; and it provides the proofs, along with their explanations, for the Infinite—which is of the nature of no small bliss—as it is being experienced. (Praśastapādabhāṣya)
Prasam:

[This is so] because, immediately after the individual self (jīvātman) denoted by the word *prāṇa*, there is taught a state of being of the nature of unlimited bliss (*aparicchinnānanda-rūpatā*), which provides no opportunity for the perception or hearing of anything other than itself.
704. "Māyā is wisdom (*vayuna*)," that is, knowledge (*jñāna*).

These are synonymous terms for *māyā*, *vayuna*, and *jñāna*. Therefore, in the context of creation, the word *māyā* denotes the unimpeded volition (*saṅkalpa*) of the Blessed Lord, which is instrumental in the production of diverse objects.
705. "Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), are both nature and modification;
the group of sixteen is only modification; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither nature nor modification."

There are twenty-five principles (*tattva*), beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with *puruṣa*. Among these, the primordial *prakṛti* is called "root-nature" (*mūlaprakṛti*) because it is the root of all things to be created. For this very reason, it is not the effect of anything else. Following that are seven principles—the Great One (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which are transformations (*vikṛti*) because they consist of the modifications of root-nature.

Because they are the causes with respect to the sixteenfold group beginning with the mind (*manas*), they are called "primordial natures" (*prakṛti*); thus they are described as "both primordial natures and transformations" (*prakṛti-vikṛtayaḥ*). These sixteen principles consist of: the mind (*manas*), the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin—the names of the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*); likewise, those known as the organs of action (*karmendriya*)—speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ; and the five gross elements (*bhūta*) beginning with earth. Altogether these constitute the sixteen principles; because they are of the nature of transformations of the Great One (*mahat*) and the others, they are exclusively of the form of modifications (*vikāra*). However, the individual soul (*jīva*), denoted by the term *puruṣa*, is neither a primordial nature nor a modification, because it is neither a cause nor an effect.
706. Regarding the rule *śucerdaśca*: from the root *śuc*, meaning "to grieve" (*śuca śoke*), the suffix *rak* is applied, and the letter *d* becomes the substitute for the final letter.

707. "My dear, at that time he becomes united with Being (*satā somya tadā sampanno bhavati*). From this union and non-union, it is understood that [the self] is completely embraced by the conscious Self (*prājñenātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ*); thus he says.

The proofs for the Supreme Brahman as the cause of the universe, along with their explanations, [are established] by the two indicators—namely, "attainment of Being" (*satsampatti*) and "non-attainment distinct from Being"—as understood from Upaniṣadic statements such as, "At the time of deep sleep, the individual soul (*jīva*) attains union with the reality denoted by the word 'Being'. (This is because attainment occurs in the cause alone, as established by both reasoning and scripture. **Proof 1: Attainment of Being (*Satsampatti*)** *Śruti*: "O Maitreyī, when a person is thus asleep—he becomes one with this *sat* (Being), my dear; he has gone to his own (*svapiti*). (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15) *Yukti*: Furthermore, during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the cessation of all mental modifications is observed. This cessation cannot occur unless the mind merges into its own material cause. Since the mind is composed of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), its cause must be the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*). And since that Great Principle is non-different from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the Unmanifest is the cause of the mind. Moreover, the Unmanifest is non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as stated in the *Gītā*: "Know Me to be the source of the unmanifest. Therefore, the merging of the mind into the Supreme Self is established. **Proof 2: Non-Attainment Distinct from Being (*Sadbhinnāsampatti*)** *Śruti*: "But when there is something else, as it were, then one sees the other, one smells the other, one tastes the other, one speaks to the other, one hears the other, one thinks of the other, and one touches the other. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31) *Yukti*: Furthermore, during the waking and dreaming states, the perception of objects is observed. This perception cannot occur unless the mind is in contact with those objects. However, since the mind is not omnipresent, it cannot reach all objects simultaneously. Therefore, the mind must be atomic (*aṇu*). Now, if the mind were eternal, it could not have originated from its material cause. Consequently, the mind must be non-eternal. And since the mind is non-eternal, its material cause must be the Unmanifest. Thus, the merging of the mind into the Unmanifest is established. Since these two proofs establish that the mind merges into the Unmanifest, and since the Unmanifest is non-different from the Supreme Self, it is proven that the Supreme Self is the cause of the universe. Furthermore, the fact that the mind merges into the Unmanifest is confirmed by the following scriptural passage: "When a person departs from here, he passes into the breath (*prāṇa*); the breath into fire; the fire into the supreme deity (*devatā*). (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6). Here, "breath" refers to the Unmanifest, and "fire" refers to the Great Principle. Therefore, the Supreme Self is the cause of the universe. This is also supported by the following statement: "All this, verily, is Brahman. From Him it arises, into Him it is dissolved, and in Him it breathes. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1). Thus, the Supreme Brahman is the cause of the universe. This is the conclusion.

"Soundless" (aśabdam) refers to that in which sound alone is not the means of valid cognition; "inferential" (ānumānikam) refers to the Pradhāna. "I" (aham) refers to the Supreme Self whose body is the inner self (pratyagātman).

Mutual exclusion (*anyonyavyavaccheda*) is mutual differentiation (*parasparavyāvṛtti*). Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is conjunction (*saṃsarga*), [referring to] properties of a positive nature (*bhāvātmakadharma*) such as blackness, youthfulness, and so forth.

*Apavarga* is the cessation of suffering that does not reside in the same locus as the causes of further suffering.

Having entered into these aggregates—beginning with the gods and extending down to himself—in the form of their essential nature (rātmatayā), He manifested name and form (*nāma-rūpa*). He thus established that such an aggregate alone constitutes reality and is the referent of words. Precisely because of this manifestation of name and form, it is understood that "all expressive words denote the Supreme Self as qualified by the non-sentient and the individual soul."
And thus, with respect to everything conscious and unconscious, Brahman exists as the Self; the entire world, including all that is conscious, becomes its body.

For this very reason, words denoting forms (*ākṛti*) such as "cow," "downward," or "human"—which terminate in the individual body (*piṇḍa*) as their specific instance (*prakārin*), since that body is also a form [of the conscious being] by virtue of being the body of a sentient entity, and since the sentient being whose body is that aggregate is also a form of the Supreme Self—terminate in the Supreme Self alone. Thus, the Supreme Self alone is the denoted object (*vācya*) of all words; therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting the Supreme Self is indeed primary (*mukhya*).

And this being so, because the individual soul (jīva) is related to the Supreme Self (paramātman) as its body, the attributes belonging to the individual soul do not touch the Supreme Self. Just as the attributes such as childhood, youth, and old age residing in one's own body do not touch the soul itself.

Therefore, in the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), the word "That" denotes the Supreme Self who is the cause of the universe, and the word "thou" denotes that very same [Self] having the embodied individual soul as its body. (59, 60%)
Therefore, it is understood that this other one who causes bliss— the *ānandamaya*— is the Supreme Self (paramātman), distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) which is the object of bliss.

36. Because of the attainment of that which is denoted by the word ‘rasa’—which consists of bliss—the one denoted by the word ‘jīva’ becomes blissful. When it is stated that "one becomes blissful through the attainment of something," what sane person would say that "he who becomes blissful through the attainment of something is that very thing itself"? 37. Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Brahman, which is denoted by the word ‘pradhāna’, is a distinct entity from the object denoted by the word ‘jīva’.

Of that very Supreme Brahman—who is distinct from everything else due to His being of the singular nature of infinite knowledge and bliss, which are opposed to all that is to be discarded—there exist natural, infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities. Just like those qualities, His divine form is also natural; it is a treasure-house of an infinite multitude of qualities such as matchless, uniform, inconceivable, divine, wonderful, and unsurpassed brilliance, beauty, fragrance, tenderness, loveliness, and youth.

It exists. It is He who, out of favor toward His devotees (*upāsaka*), assumes various forms according to their respective modes of practice; He is the ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous conduct, affection, and magnanimity; He from whom every trace of that which is to be abandoned has been removed; He who is free from all evil; the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the Supreme Brahman, the Highest Person (*puruṣottama*), Nārāyaṇa.

45: Indeed, the Supreme Brahman exists in both the causal and the effected states; as the body of the subtle and gross sentient and insentient entities, it is at all times the Self of all.

46. (The Supreme Self) consists of mind (*manomaya*) and is to be grasped by the single, purified mind. Indeed, it is grasped by a mind rendered pure through the worship of the Supreme Self, which is supported by the seven means such as discrimination and liberation. By this, its nature as distinct from everything else is expressed; for it is solely intent upon auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all that is to be abandoned.

Because that which is impure is grasped only by those with impure minds. 47. Being the locus of attributes (*ādheyatva*), being subject to control (*vidheyatva*), and being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) are the grounds for the application of the term "body" (*śarīra*).

48. For it is not merely residing within a body that is the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain; rather, it is being under the sway of karma in the form of merit and demerit. This, however, is not possible in the case of the Supreme Self, who is free from all taint (*apahatapāpman*).
49. Therefore, such agency consisting of the power to withdraw the world belongs to the Supreme Self alone.

50. However, those who are proficient in the Upaniṣads (trayyantaniṣṇātāḥ) declare that liberation is precisely the experience of the Supreme Self—which is the sole cause of the entire universe, which is the inner self of all, and which exists as the body (śarīra) of the individual soul (jīva)—that soul being a mode (prakāra) of the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is agreeable and consists of limited knowledge, and whose true nature is concealed by beginningless karma in the form of ignorance (avidyā); [liberation is] preceded by the destruction of that ignorance.

51. Indeed, having opened their eyes and looked up, they determine the station and movement of the individual self (*jīvātman*) within the body. 161 52. For all of these, immortality and other such qualities, being devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), are simply not possible. Therefore, the Person in the Eye (*akṣipuruṣa*) is [the Supreme Self].
(Kra. Saṃ. Pū. Saṃ.)
Therefore, since such a form characterized by having heaven as its head and so forth belongs to the Supreme Person alone, Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Person.

58. For indeed, the state of being the *puruṣa* (the Person) belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) when it is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). 59. For a dam (*setu*) in relation to rivers and the like is that which provides support for the bank. 60. And the word "Self" (*ātman*), when devoid of limiting adjuncts, [denotes the same].
It is used in its primary sense with reference to the Supreme Brahman. "He attains" (āpnoti) means pervasion by virtue of being the controller of everything other than Himself;
for it is indeed He who is possible [to be called] the Self (ātman).

61. Indeed, they are liberated from the bonds of *saṃsāra*; they have shaken off merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*) and are stainless (*nirañjana*). They are also completely freed from name and form (*nāma-rūpa*). For it is precisely the state of possessing name and form—which results from the contact of consciousness with merit and demerit—that constitutes *saṃsāra*. Therefore, that Person (*puruṣa*), who is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, and who is indicated as the goal to be attained by those who have shaken off merit and demerit, who are stainless, and who have reached supreme equality with the highest Brahman through being devoid of contact with *prakṛti*, is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself. (219, 220)

62. It is established that one [being] partakes of the fruit of action, while another, though not partaking of the fruit of action at all, exists within the body merely by virtue of its luminosity. In this context, it is the omniscient one—who does not partake of the fruit of action, who is luminous, who is the bridge of immortality (*amṛtasetu*), and who is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—who must be the locus of heaven, earth, and the rest; certainly not the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which partakes of the fruit of action and is subject to sorrow. Therefore, it is proven that the supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the abode of heaven, earth, and the rest.

63. For example—milk being drunk by one afflicted with bile produces little pleasure and even the opposite effect according to the degree of that bile; yet that same milk becomes solely for the sake of pleasure for one not afflicted by bile. Just as for a prince, the father’s act of punishment, when perceived as being unjust, fails to produce affection, but becomes most beloved when perceived as just; so too is it with Brahman, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss.

The world, when considered as consisting of that [Brahman] and as an instrument for His divine play (*līlopakaraṇa*), surely leads to unsurpassed joy for one who is a mine of countless, infinitely superior, and auspicious qualities.
Therefore, experiencing Brahman—which is characterized by sovereignty over the world and consists of infinite, unsurpassed bliss—one sees nothing else whatsoever; nor does one perceive suffering.

Therefore, because of the teaching that "the Infinite" (bhūman) is Brahman— denoted by the word "Satya"— which is a different entity from the inner self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word "Prāṇa," the Infinite is the Supreme Brahman.
(Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad).

Page 65: "For even the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the referent of 'I', has the Supreme Self as its Self"—this is stated in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* and other texts. Therefore, since the inner referent culminates in the Supreme Self, the word 'I' (*ahaṃ*) also culminates in the Supreme Self; thus, this instruction on the "seizing of the I" (*ahaṅgrahopadeśa*) is for the purpose of meditating upon the Supreme Self by way of having the inner self as its body.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the knowledge that the Supreme Self has the inner self as its body, one should perform meditation through the method of "I-grasping" (ahaṅgraha). It is thus established that that which, through ignorance of it, leads to the attainment of saṃsāra, and through knowledge of which, the attainment of immortality occurs—that is indeed the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman.

68. "Supremely peaceful, undecaying, fearless, and immortal"—for this is indeed the nature of the Supreme Self alone. 69. For he whose embodied state is caused by karma is called a "wealth of individual souls" (*jīvadhana*). 70. Even though the sun possesses excessive speed, the expression "the sun moves like an arrow" is intended solely to negate any slowness of its motion.

Just as those who do not know the location of a buried treasure of gold do not find it, even though they are constantly walking over it; in the same way, although people go day after day right over the small ether (*daharākāśa*)—which exists as the inner self (*antarātman*) and is the supreme human goal—they do not find it because they do not know it.
To exist at all times within everything is indeed the majesty of the Supreme Brahman, which sustains the world.

73. The well-known designation [of Brahman] as being endowed with qualities such as "freedom from evil" (apahatapāpmatva) is stronger than the common usage of the term for the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa). 74. For it is through the mention of qualities that there is praise; indeed, if those qualities were non-existent, the very nature of praise would be lost.

Furthermore, no enthusiasm is generated by describing a quality that does not exist; therefore, the *arthavādas*, while promoting the action, do so only by making known the actual existence of those qualities. First, the state of being a seeker (*arthitva*) arises from the torment of unbearable sufferings such as those of a spiritual nature (*ādhyātmika*), and from the knowledge that the Supreme Brahman is free from even the scent of all defects, possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, and is the object of unsurpassed enjoyment.

Capability also exists by virtue of possessing a more refined body, sense organs, and so forth. And the possession of a body, sense organs, and so forth is heard of in all the Upaniṣads within the sections on creation, as well as in the sections on meditation, concerning Brahmā and the others.
Therefore, since gods and others also possess both desire and capability, it is established that they have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.

K.S.P., p. 77: This alone constitutes the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) and eternity (*nityatva*) of the Veda; namely, that it is uttered in that very same specific sequence by means of remembering that same sequence through the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the sequence of utterances of each preceding [generation]. For us, however, there is this distinction: [the Veda] manifests itself spontaneously, without depending on mental impressions at all.
This is the same even regarding the Lord of all. Puruṣottama reflects upon this:

since the knowledge acquired through the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), as established by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), is the very means for the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*), a Śūdra lacks the capacity for such meditation on Brahman. As for Vidura and others, however, they possessed knowledge because they did not lose the knowledge acquired in previous lives; and due to the force of their *prārabdha* karma, they were born in such [low] births. Thus, they remained steadfast in Brahman. (301, 302)
By the word "śūdra," it is indicated that he possesses the very capacity for the instruction of knowledge; it does not refer to his status as a member of the fourth caste.
Otherwise, the Upaniṣad would be rendered impotent and its purpose frustrated.
Therefore—
Therefore, this Ākāśa, which brings forth name and form from the inner self (pratyagātman) that itself possesses no name or form, is a distinct entity—the Supreme Brahman itself. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pp.
Kra. Saṃ.

89: Indeed, this world, which is denoted by the word "this" and is a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness, does not attain identity with the Puruṣa—either with him as conjoined with the unconscious or with him in his essential nature!
90: For it is only that which is dear that ought to be sought.

91. The fact that wealth, sons, husbands, wives, and so forth, are experienced as being occasionally dear while mixed with excessive suffering, is not caused by the essential nature of the husband or others; rather, it is caused by the Supreme Self, whose very nature is unsurpassed bliss. Therefore, it is taught that "He who, being unsurpassed bliss itself, causes even other things to become objects of even a slight degree of dearness, He alone—the Supreme Self—is to be seen."

92. Indeed, the Supreme Self, when propitiated by ritual acts (*karma*), brings about for the worshippers—according to those respective acts—the specific nature, dimension, and the state of being dear to each object, determined by its particular place, time, and form.

93. The teacher Kāśakṛtsna held the view that because the Supreme Self abides as the very self within the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is its own body, the word "living being" (*jīva*) refers to Brahman. Furthermore, the word "jīva" denotes the living being only insofar as it culminates in the Supreme Self; it does not denote the individual soul alone.

Thus, when identity is established through the relationship of the self with the body, all the Śruti texts—which describe the Supreme Brahman as being free from sin, omniscient, and so forth; which speak of liberation for the ignorant, grieving individual soul (jīva) through the meditation on Brahman; and which are intent on teaching the identity of the world with Brahman—become properly explained. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras has accepted precisely the view of Kāśakṛtsna.

95. All is rendered possible only by the one Supreme Brahman, who is distinct from all, omnipotent, omniscient, and unique. This is because non-conscious substances such as clay lack consciousness and are therefore incapable of acting as a presiding agent; furthermore, conscious agents such as potters lack the power for such diverse transformations and possess intentions that are not infallible. Such is the observed rule. Therefore, Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the universe.

The Self, when name and form are undifferentiated, is the agent; that same Self, when name and form are differentiated, is the effect. Thus, there is no contradiction between agency and objecthood. "By itself, the Self made itself thus"—it is both the efficient cause and the material cause.
The intention here is that the transformation taught in this context does not inherently entail any defect in the Supreme Brahman; on the contrary, it brings about absolute sovereignty.

98. [He is] the one who is the antidote to everything that is to be abandoned without exception, whose nature is an uninterrupted stream of auspiciousness, and who possesses as His body all conscious and unconscious entities by virtue of being their own essence.
That Supreme Brahman, which has become his very self, [manifests] through the causal succession of the subtle elements, ego, and so forth, within the phenomenal world that constitutes His own body.
*Kramasamuccaya-prakaraṇa-saṃgraha*.

When the extremely subtle non-sentient reality denoted by the word "tamas" remains as the sole residue, and when that *tamas*—having reached a state of extreme subtlety such that it cannot even be designated separately as its own body—attains oneness with Himself, Brahman, possessing such *tamas* as His body, forms the resolve: "May I become the body of the manifold world consisting of a mixture of sentient and non-sentient beings, with names and forms differentiated as before. Then, through the process of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), He transforms Himself into the body of the universe. This is the teaching of transformation (*pariṇāma*) found in all the Vedāntas.

99. Since it is the root of all suffering consisting in the obscuration of knowledge for all selves, that very thing is designated by the terms ‘darkness’ (*tamas*) and ‘death’ (*mṛtyu*). 100. Even in the state of non-differentiation, the conscious and unconscious reality remains in an extremely subtle state, accompanied by karma and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). 101. It is said: “In the causal state, the Supreme Self alone, abiding as the self of the substance that undergoes modification into the form of the effect, having remained as the self of that very substance, became this or that.”

102. Thus, in the transformation of the Supreme Self into the form of the world as a composite of consciousness (cit) and non-consciousness (acit), all defects that constitute the lack of human purpose (apuruṣārtha) reside in the conscious portion (cidaṃśa) which constitutes the body of the Supreme Self; likewise, all modifications reside in the non-conscious portion (acidaṃśa). The state of being an effect belongs to the Supreme Self insofar as He is the self who governs those two portions in their respective states. However, the Supreme Self, being the self through His governance of those two which constitute His own body, is not touched by the defects or modifications residing therein.

Consisting of unlimited knowledge and bliss, He remains eternally of one form, yet abides through the nature of the world’s transformation. All sentient and insentient entities, whether in their subtle or gross states, are the instruments for the divine play (*līlā*) of the Supreme Brahman; and creation and so forth constitute this play—thus it has been stated by the venerable Dvaipāyana, Parāśara, and others. These texts are cited as authoritative sources in the *Śrībhāṣya*.
